The afferent limb of the oculocardiac reflex is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1) with the efferent limb being the vagus nerve (CN X). Stretch receptors are activated in the ocular and periorbital tissues, with the nerve impulses being carried in the short and long ciliary nerves. The signals are transmitted to the ciliary ganglion, then to CN V1, followed by the Gasserian ganglion, and then terminate in the trigeminal nucleus. Internuclear communication occurs between the trigeminal nucleus and visceral motor nucleus of the vagus nerve. The signal is then transmitted to the sinoatrial node via the vagus nerve, resulting in negative chronotropy. The oculocardiac reflex is due to direct pressure on the eye or traction on the extraocular muscles, leading to a > 20% reduction in the heart rate. The reflex is often seen in ophthalmologic procedures such as strabismus surgery but can also be observed during ophthalmologic nerve blocks and manipulation of the eye and surrounding soft tissues. The incidence of the oculocardiac reflex tends to decrease with age, so children are at the highest risk. The negative chronotropy of the reflex can lead to sinus bradycardia and asystole. The definitive treatment of these complications from the oculocardiac reflex is the immediate removal of pressure or halting manipulation of the orbit and surrounding tissues. Oculocardiac reflex The afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex is mediated by CN II (optic nerve), with the efferent limb mediated by CN III (oculomotor nerve).
Answer C: The afferent limb of the gag reflex is mediated by CN IX (glossopharyngeal), with the efferent limb mediated by CN X (vagus nerve). The afferent limb of the oculocardiac reflex is the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve with the efferent limb being the vagus nerve. The Hering-Breuer reflex is a pulmonary reflex that prevents overinflation of the lung. As the lung expands, stretch receptors fire in the smooth muscles of the bronchi and bronchioles in response to stretching. The firing receptors send signals via the vagus nerve to the ventrolateral nucleus of the solitary tract, resulting in the inhibition of inspiratory neurons. As a result, inspiration is inhibited, and expiration occurs. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Oculocardiac Reflex (B)" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Diaphoresis is mediated by sympathetic stimulation via release of acetylcholine and stimulation of muscarinic receptors and is the only symptom that may be seen in a patient who is hypoglycemic and on beta blockers. The normal response to hypoglycemia is an increase in sympathetic discharge, cortisol release, and glucagon release with symptoms of diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, altered mental status, and possibly even seizures. The sympathetic nervous system is composed of preganglionic neurons located in the lateral horn of the spinal cord from T1-L2. The preganglionic axons are short and synapse quickly in the sympathetic or prevertebral ganglia and the signal transmitted to the postganglionic neuron is through the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and nicotinic receptors. The postganglionic neuron then projects axons to effector organs and releases norepinephrine with stimulation of alpha or beta receptors. The exception is with sweat glands and the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, both of which are stimulated by acetylcholine via muscarinic (sweat glands) and nicotinic (chromaffin cells) receptors. The adrenal medulla is essentially a modified postganglionic sympathetic neuron. This patient is taking the nonselective beta blocker propanolol which will block both beta-1 mediated tachycardia and hypertension along with beta-2 mediated relaxation of the ciliary muscle of the lens which improves distance, not near vision. The parasympathetic nervous system originates from the brainstem and sacral spinal cord and uses acetylcholine at all synapses. Acetylcholine binds to nicotinic receptors at the autonomic ganglia and muscarinic receptors at the effector site. Answers B & C: This will be blocked by propranolol.  Sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic nervous system and utilize acetylcholine with muscarinic receptors, therefore beta blockade will not prevent sweating with hypoglycemia which may be the only symptom seen in this setting. Hypercarbia leads to a right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve subsequent to acidosis from increased hydrogen ion concentration. This right shift of the curve portrays increased unloading of oxygen to tissues during increased CO2 and consequently decreased pH – this is also known as the Bohr Effect. Figure: Oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. The percent of saturated hemoglobin is plotted against the oxygen tension. Alkalosis shifts the dissociation curve to the left and decreases oxygen unloading to the tissues.
Answer B: Carboxyhemoglobin strongly increases the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen, thus shifting the dissociation curve to the left and decreasing oxygen unloading to the tissues.
Answer C: Decreased 2, 3-DPG concentration shifts the dissociation curve to the left and decreases oxygen unloading to the tissues. 2, 3-DPG may decrease significantly during hypoxemia. It also decreases in the blood cell products during storage. Hypercarbia, acidosis, hyperthermia, and high 2,3-DPG levels, all shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right and increase oxygen unloading to tissues. Red cell 2, 3-DPG in stored blood diminishes in storage and is effectively zero after 1-2 weeks (rate of decline depends on types of preservative used). After transfusion, red cell 2, 3-DPG returns to 50% after 7 hours and to normal level after 48 hours. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Epinephrine is not metabolized in the lungs or while in the pulmonary circulation (B). The lungs and components of the pulmonary circulation play a significant role in the metabolism of multiple hormones, many of which have vasoactive properties. The following table provides an overview and several important examples are discussed in more detail below. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is found in great quantities on pulmonary endothelium. The enzyme cleaves almost 70% of the angiotensin I that passes through the pulmonary circulation into angiotensin II. Bradykinin (A) is also cleaved by ACE, but this results in the former’s inactivation. Pulmonary endothelium selectively takes up norepinephrine (C) and serotonin (D) from the pulmonary circulation and degrades the hormones intracellularly. Up to 30% of norepinephrine and >95% of serotonin is removed from the blood with a single pass through the pulmonary circulation. Intracellular monoamine oxidase (MAO) breaks down both hormones while catechol-omethyltransferase also degrades norepinephrine. Dopamine, epinephrine (B), and histamine are not metabolized or removed from the pulmonary circulation since the pulmonary endothelium lacks an active transport mechanism for these hormones. The metabolism and degradation of vasoactive hormones within the lungs plays an important role in the pathogenesis of carcinoid syndrome. The classic “carcinoid triad” consists of flushing, diarrhea, and right-sided cardiac involvement. It is caused by tumor release of vasoactive amines (e.g. serotonin, norepinephrine, histamine, and dopamine), polypeptides (e.g. bradykinin, somatostatin, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and glucagon), and prostaglandins. The cardiac involvement is generally limited to only the right side of the heart since, as discussed above, most of the vasoactive hormones are metabolized while in the pulmonary circulation before returning to the left side of the heart.  The lungs and components of the pulmonary circulation play a significant role in the metabolism of multiple hormones, many of which are vasoactive. Review the table above. The parasympathetic system is the dominant nervous system involved in bronchial airway innervation. When it is activated, the parasympathetic nervous system is involved in bronchial smooth muscle constriction leading to bronchoconstriction. Bronchoconstriction is secondary to the acute narrowing of the large airways secondary to the tightening of the smooth muscle, often combining with inflammation to further narrowing of the airway. Bronchoconstriction can produce symptoms of chest tightness, cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, and fatigue. The prototypical bronchospastic disease is asthma, and, although the exact reason for hyperresponsiveness is not known, the pathophysiology is understood. Other diseases associated with bronchospasm include emphysema, allergen-induced bronchoconstriction, and exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (sometimes collectively referred to as subsets of asthma). During bronchoconstriction, airway smooth muscle constriction leads to a decreased airway caliber, causing increased resistance to flow. This is partially due to parasympathetic nervous system activation. The parasympathetic system is the dominant neuronal pathway in the control of airway smooth muscle tone. The postganglionic parasympathetic fibers release acetylcholine, which binds to the muscarinic receptors on the smooth muscle layer surrounding the bronchi. This causes a series of intracellular changes, resulting in muscle constriction. When the muscle contracts, the diameter of the airway decreases, leading to increased resistance. Coinciding with this smooth muscle contraction is increased inflammation and excessive mucous production. Both of these cause further narrowing of the airway. There are several other mechanisms by which bronchoconstriction can occur, including a decreased release of neuromodulators (such as vasoactive intestinal polypeptide and nitric oxide). Mast cells secrete many chemicals, such as histamine, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes. All of these substances are capable of inducing bronchoconstriction, mucus secretion, and mucosal edema. It is thought that mast cells are involved in the pathophysiology of asthma, so mast cell stabilization would not be a factor in causing bronchoconstriction. In fact, it would be the reverse; mast cell stabilization would help decrease the risk of bronchoconstriction.
Answer C: The sympathetic nervous system acts to counter smooth muscle constriction that occurs with bronchospasm. There is negligible sympathetic innervation of the airway smooth muscle, so this counterbalance often is not helpful. Many of the neurohormones released from the sympathetic nervous system will help with bronchodilators. One example is epinephrine, which is a potent bronchial smooth muscle dilator. The parasympathetic nervous system contributes a great deal to bronchoconstriction. The etiology of bronchoconstriction is only partially known, and research is ongoing. Redistribution of heat from the core to the periphery is the largest contributor to the initial reduction in core temperature during general anesthesia. This does not result in loss of body heat content or mean body temperature, but instead shifts flow of heat to the periphery. The major thermoregulatory defenses in humans include sweating, arteriovenous shunt vasoconstriction, and shivering. General anesthetics substantially reduce the body’s thresholds for vasoconstriction and shivering. Anesthetized patients are thus poikilothermic over a broader range of core temperatures. Instead of core temperature regulation to within tenths of a degree, the body’s inter-threshold range increases by 10-20 fold during general anesthesia. Redistribution of heat to the peripheral tissues via vasodilation is responsible for the first 0.5-1.5 degrees Celsius drop in core body temperature. Prevention or reduction of this can be accomplished by pre-warming the patient’s extremities, especially the lower extremities, for at least 30 minutes prior to the induction of general anesthesia. This will decrease the temperature gradient between the body's core and the periphery, therefore decreasing the redistribution of heat. The two mechanisms of undesired heat loss in the operating room are: 1. Impaired thermoregulation secondary to anesthesia. 2. Low ambient temperature of the operating theater. The four types of heat loss that occur from a patient to the relatively cold operating environment are: 1. Radiation 2. Evaporation 3. Conduction 4. Convection The main mechanism of heat loss is radiation, accounting for approximately 67%. Radiative heat losses occur anytime an object is above absolute zero. The magnitude of the radiation is proportional to the fourth power of the temperature difference between the two sources. This heat loss typically follows redistributive heat loss in a linear fashion depending on ambient temperature, size of the operation, and efficacy of warming devices. Evaporation accounts for approximately 17% of heat loss. Patients under general anesthesia typically do not sweat, which is the main way that heat is lost due to evaporation. Together, conduction and convection account for approximately 16% of heat loss from a patient to the cold operating environment. Conduction refers to the transfer of heat from direct contact with objects. It is less important in the operating room because the patient is usually lying on foam or rubber which is well insulated. Convection can play an important role since air turnover constantly removes heat as the patient’s body exists in an equilibrium of heat transfer between itself and the surrounding air. However, this does not account for the initial reduction in core temperature. Conduction contributes little to heat loss in the operating room and refers to heat loss through direct contact with objects.
Answer B: Radiative heat loss to surroundings is the main mechanism for heat loss following an initial decrease in core temperature due to redistribution. Redistribution of heat from the core to the periphery is the largest contributor to the initial reduction in core temperature during general anesthesia. Prevention or reduction of this can be accomplished by pre-warming the patient’s extremities prior to the induction of general anesthesia. Radiation is the main mechanism for patient heat loss in the operating room following this initial redistribution of heat.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The amount of gas remaining in the lungs at the end of a normal, tidal volume exhalation is the functional residual capacity (FRC). The FRC is comprised of the expiratory reserve volume (ERV) and the residual volume (RV). Functional residual capacity is the primary determinant of oxygen reserve in humans when apnea occurs. As humans age, the lung parenchyma loses its elasticity and becomes more compliant, resulting in an age-related increase in FRC. Factors that decrease FRC include obesity, pregnancy, pulmonary edema, pulmonary fibrosis, pleural effusions, and kyphoscoliosis. Individual lung volumes are noted in blue and lung capacities (the sum of 2 or more individual lung volumes) are noted in red. Expiratory reserve volume* (ERV*) indicates the volume that is forcefully exhaled from the lungs when pulmonary conditions promote early airway closure and atelectasis. (Volumes: RV = residual volume, ERV = expiratory reserve volume, TV = tidal volume, IRV = inspiratory reserve volume, ERV* = expiratory reserve volume with atelectasis, CV = closing volume; Capacities: VC = vital capacity, IC = inspiratory capacity, TLC = total lung capacity, FRC = functional residual capacity, CC = closing capacity). The ERV is the largest volume of gas that can be forcibly exhaled after the end of a normal tidal exhalation. It is measured by subtracting the RV from the FRC.
Answer C: Residual volume is the gas remaining in the lungs after maximal exhalation. Functional residual capacity is the volume of gas remaining in the lungs at passive end expiration. Furthermore, FRC is the primary determinant of oxygen reserve in humans when apnea occurs.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The Haldane effect explains the increased ability of hemoglobin to carry carbon dioxide (CO2) from the tissues to the lungs for exhalation. Deoxygenated hemoglobin has 3.5 times more capacity for CO2 compared with oxygenated hemoglobin. Therefore, in the presence of low oxygen (O2) concentrations, hemoglobin binds more strongly to CO2, and, in areas of high O2 concentration, hemoglobin binds less strongly to CO2. Deoxygenated hemoglobin is a strong base that binds to hydrogen ions. In the tissue, O2 is released, and CO2 enters the erythrocyte. The CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid by way of carbonic anhydrase and then ionizes to form hydrogen ions and bicarbonate. The hydrogen ion binds to the histidine residue on hemoglobin, while the bicarbonate (HCO3-) diffuses outside the erythrocyte. To maintain electric neutrality, chloride replaces the HCO3- (chloride shift). After it is in the lungs, hemoglobin is exposed to high concentrations of O2, causing it to have less affinity for the hydrogen ion, which is then released. The hydrogen ion then binds with bicarbonate to form CO2 and water. The CO2 is then exhaled and eliminated. The increased delivery of O2 at the tissue level can be partly explained by the Bohr effect. According to the Bohr effect, an increase in the CO2 and hydrogen ion concentrations will cause hemoglobin to have a decreased affinity for O2. This is seen as a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. As a result, hemoglobin will release O2 to the tissues that are metabolically active and are producing CO2. It is the complementary action to the Haldane effect. Whereas the Haldane effect provides an explanation for increased binding of CO2 for delivery to the lungs, the Bohr effect provides an explanation for decreased binding of O2 for delivery to the tissues. When hydrogen ions are in abundance, the hemoglobin has less affinity for O2 (Bohr effect and occurs in tissue), and, when oxygen is in abundance, the CO2 has less affinity for hemoglobin (Haldane effect and occurs in lungs).
Answer C: Helium helps deliver O2 to asthmatic patients in relation to the Reynolds number and the increase in laminar vs turbulent flow. When a patient has an asthma attack, obstruction to airflow results in turbulence and restricted flow to the lungs. Laminar flow is more efficient, and the Reynolds number helps predict whether airflow will be turbulent or laminar. The Reynolds number is determined by inertial forces (velocity, density, and length) divided by viscous forces. Flow is more likely to be turbulent and ineffectual when the Reynolds number is greater. Helium is less dense than nitrogen, and, by combining helium with oxygen, the density of the gas decreases. As the Reynolds number decreases, the airflow is more likely to be laminar, thus improving ventilation in the lungs. The Bohr and Haldane effects are complementary principles that help explain the efficient delivery of O2 to the tissue and of CO2 to the lungs. According to the Bohr effect, in areas of high CO2, the hemoglobin has less affinity for O2, which is more readily released for consumption by the tissues. According to the Haldane effect, deoxygenated hemoglobin has a higher affinity for CO2. After the deoxygenated hemoglobin reaches the lungs, the high O2 concentration decreases this affinity, and the CO2 is released.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. After one month of severe calorie malnutrition, the brain will obtain nearly two-thirds of its energy from ketone metabolism with the remainder from glucose. During periods of fasting, exercise, or very low carbohydrate diets, the brain will begin to use ketone bodies (acetone, acetoacetic acid, and β-hydroxybutyric acid) as an alternative source of energy. After 3 days of low blood glucose, ketone body metabolism supplies approximately one-third of the brain’s energy. After 1-1.5 months, they supply two-thirds of the brain’s energy. Glucose continues to account for the remainder. The increased use of ketones decreases the body’s demand for glucose which allows for decreased catabolism of muscle for conversion of amino acids to glucose. Under normal circumstances, the brain uses glucose as its sole energy source.
Answer B: Unlike other organs, glucose transport into brain neurons is independent of insulin concentration. Although insulin receptors exist on neurons in the brain, the presence or absence of insulin binding these receptors does not affect neuronal glucose uptake. Instead, glucose transport is driven primarily by extracellular glucose concentration. This becomes clinically important since excess or inadequate blood glucose (approximately > 200 mg/dL and < 70 mg/dL, respectively) is associated with potential neurologic injury, particularly in the setting of preexisting neuronal injury (e.g. surgery, intracranial hemorrhage, or trauma).
Answer C: Although ketone bodies are created from incomplete oxidation of fatty acids in the liver, the brain does not metabolize fatty acids directly for energy. Under normal circumstances, the brain exclusively utilizes glucose for energy. During periods of fasting, exercise, or starvation, the brain also uses ketone bodies for energy. When the presynaptic terminal is depolarized by an action potential, calcium channels open, resulting in an influx of calcium that triggers acetylcholine release. Potassium channels then open which allow for an efflux of potassium which rapidly restores the membrane potential. Meanwhile, the released acetylcholine travels across the cleft to bind to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane which results in depolarization of the endplate. This depolarization opens sodium channels which generate an action potential in the muscle. Figure: The action potential travels along the presynaptic neuron to the presynaptic terminal, which leads to intracellular calcium influx. The influx of calcium causes acetylcholine vesicles to adhere to the presynaptic terminal membrane. After the acetylcholine molecule is released across the synaptic cleft, it binds to the central ion channel, which causes a net inward flux of sodium, which then allows for muscle contraction to occur. Potassium ions restore the membrane potential of the presynaptic terminal and are less closely associated with generation of the postsynaptic membrane end plate potential that triggers an action potential than sodium.
Answer C: Calcium ions trigger acetylcholine release and are less closely associated with generation of the postsynaptic membrane end plate potential that triggers an action potential than sodium. The opening of sodium channels on the postsynaptic terminal triggers an action potential. The voltage gated sodium channel can be in one of three states: open (excited), inactivated (desensitized), or closed (resting). American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Renin is released from the kidneys in response to a decrease in blood pressure. It cleaves the peptide angiotensinogen to create angiotensin I (C). Renin is created and stored by the cells in the afferent arterioles of the kidney. Renin secretion can be caused by 3 different mechanisms: a decrease in serum NaCl concentration sensed by the kidneys, a decrease in blood pressure sensed by kidney baroreceptors, or activation of renal B1 receptors by norepinephrine. Decreases in blood pressure, such as that displayed by the patient above, would cause a release of renin into the serum by at least one of these mechanisms. Renin then acts by cleaving the peptide angiotensinogen to create angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is then converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE). Angiotensin II (Ang II) has several effects, which combine to increase systemic perfusion in patients. The most immediate response to Ang II is an increase in blood pressure caused by an increase in systemic vascular resistance. Ang II activates the angiotensin1 (AT1) receptors on vascular smooth muscle cells, causing constriction of the arterioles. Ang II also augments the sympathetic nervous system by inhibiting norepinephrine reuptake into nerve terminals. It also stimulates the release of catecholamines from the adrenal medulla. In addition, Ang II causes a centrally mediated increased thirst and enhances the release of vasopressin. These effects are almost immediate, but are not long-lasting. Ang II also has longer lasting effects in the body. In addition to its effects on blood pressure, it stimulates remodeling of the cardiovascular system, causing hypertrophy of cardiac cells and increased collagen deposition. It also has profound effects on the kidney, causing a decrease in the urinary excretion of both sodium and water. Lastly, Ang II stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and release aldosterone. Aldosterone also acts on the kidneys to decrease the urinary excretion of sodium and water. This ultimately leads to an increase in blood volume and therefore blood pressure. Angiotensin II leads to the increased release of aldosterone. Angiotensin II also increases blood pressure by direct vasoconstriction.
Answer B: Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin converting enzyme.
Answer D: Both angiotensin II and aldosterone act on the kidneys to decrease the urinary excretion of sodium and water. A decrease in blood pressure stimulates the release of renin into the serum from the renal tubules. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II by ACE. Angiotensin II causes an increase in blood pressure by direct vasoconstriction, enhancing the sympathetic nervous system, and causing an increase of aldosterone.  Brunton, LL. et. al. Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 12th edition, Chapter 26 American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Hypovolemia: Renin-angiotensin Response"

The target sites for sympathetic cardiac innervation include α1, β1, and β2 adrenergic receptors. The sympathetic cardiac innervation originates from T1-T4. The nerve fibers travel through bilateral stellate ganglions prior to ending as cardiac nerves. The right stellate ganglion tends to exert more effect on heart rate. The left stellate ganglion has a stronger effect on mean arterial pressure and contractility. All three adrenergic receptors are involved with sympathetic cardiac innervation: α1: Positive inotropy β1: Positive chronotropy, dromotropy (conductivity of a nerve), lusitropy (myocardial relaxation), and inotropy β2: Positive chronotropy > inotropy Answers B & C: The sympathetic cardiac innervation originates from T1-T4 and is associated with α1, β1, and β2 adrenergic receptors.  The sympathetic cardiac innervation originates from T1-T4 and is associated with α1, β1, and β2 adrenergic receptors. A left stellate ganglion block can be performed to reduce the risk of arrhythmias associated with long QT syndrome. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 328, 336, 339. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Adrenergic Receptors: Cardiac”

The prothrombin time is an excellent marker for hepatic synthetic function in almost every patient population. Cirrhosis occurs secondary to chronic liver injury; it leads to portal hypertension and a multitude of other problems. The progression and degree to which cirrhosis impacts the body depends on the cause and other comorbid conditions. Once decompensation occurs, the mortality is approximately 85% over five years. The liver is integral to body homeostasis. It is involved in metabolism and detoxification. The liver also acts as a major synthetic organ. Liver dysfunction is often measured based on a variety of biochemial studies that can help determine the degree of hepatocellular injury. Albumin is a major protein that is synthesized in the liver (there are numerous other proteins also synthesized in the liver). Approximately 10 grams of albumin is synthesized and secreted daily by the liver. When the liver has been chronically damaged, albumin may be low due to decreased synthesis. However, it may also be decreased in chronic malnutrition and it is also altered by the transvascular escape or clearance thus alterations can be due to other factors. When interpreting low albumin levels, the clinician must take into account the overall status of the patient. The synthesis of coagulation factors is also an important function of the liver. The liver produces coagulation factors I, II, V, VII, IX, X, and XI. The prothrombin time (PT) measures the conversion of prothrombin to thrombin, which requires factors II, V, VII, and X. Almost all of these factors require vitamin K (II, VII, IX, and X are vitamin K dependent). As with albumin, malnutrition can cause vitamin K deficiency and alter the liver's ability to synthesize those factors. Because of these flaws in albumin and PT, other tests have been trialed to help determine the liver's synthetic capabilities. Cirrhosis is associated with several complications. Variceal bleeding, ascites, spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, and encephalopathy are all risks. Any kind of bacterial infection can lead to decompensation and exacerbate hepatic dysfunction. Portopulmonary hypertension is a dreaded complication that results in pulmonary artery pressures greater than 40 mmHg with a significant increase in morbidity and mortality. Alanine transaminase (ALT) is an excellent marker of hepatocellular injury.
Answer C: Gammaglutamyl transferase (GGT) is found in hepatocytes and is a sensitive marker for hepatobiliary disease however, it is also seen in many other types of disease (pancreatic disease, renal failure, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease). The liver is extremely important in synthesizing several important proteins. Biochemical testing to determine the liver's synthetic capability is important for the evaluation of patients however, no perfect test has been found. Albumin and prothrombin time are used currently. There have been many studies attempting to classify cirrhosis and predict outcomes; Child-Pugh-Turcotte classification and the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) are the two most commonly used. Child-Pugh-Turcotte uses total bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time (PT)/international normalized ratio (INR), and the presence of ascites or hepatic encephalopathy. MELD uses serum bilirubin, creatinine, international normalized ratio (INR) for prothrombin time, and sodium. MELD is a more accurate predictor of short-term mortality. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cirrhosis: Hepatic Synthetic Fxn (B)" Durand, F. Assessment of the prognosis of cirrhosis: Child-Pugh versus MELD. Journal of Hepatology. 2005(42): 100-107. Limdi, J. Evaluation of abnormal liver function tests. BMJ. 2003(9): 307-312.

Myocardial oxygen supply has several determinants. It is associated with oxygen content and blood flow. It is unaffected by left ventricular systolic pressure. First, the oxygen content is determined to evaluate oxygen availability or supply: CaO2 = (Hgb * 1.34 * SaO2) + (0.003 * PaO2) Where: CaO2 = arterial oxygen content (mL/dL), Hgb = hemoglobin (g/dL), SaO2 = oxygen saturation, PaO2 = arterial partial pressure of oxygen (mm Hg). Oxygen dissolved in arterial blood (0.003 x PaO2) raises the total value by only a small amount. If PaO2 is increased, there is little change in CaO2 and it is therefore considered of little significance by most when determining oxygen content. Optimizing Hgb amount is one way to ensure maximal oxygen content. Secondly, myocardial blood supply is determined by coronary blood flow (CBF), which has its own set of modifying components: 1) Heart rate: Left ventricular blood supply from the coronary arteries occurs primarily during diastole. A slower heart rate means more time is spent in diastole which allows more time for CBF to the left ventricle. 2) Coronary perfusion pressure: Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is represented as the difference between the aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP). CPP = AoDP - LVEDP 3) Coronary vascular resistance (CVR): Increased CVR such as from vasospasm or atherosclerosis worsens myocardial oxygen supply. Providing vasodilation with medications such as nitroglycerin improves CBF. Coronary blood flow is therefore represented by the following equation: CBF = CPP / CVR, or, CBF = (AoDP – LVEDP) / CVR. Myocardial oxygen extraction also plays a role in supply, but this value is usually at its maximum value and changes very little under times of stress. Left ventricular systolic pressure (LVSP) is more often associated with changing the myocardial oxygen demand (not supply) by changing afterload. An elevated LVSP will increase wall stress and require more myocardial oxygen. Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is represented as the difference between the aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) and the left ventricular end diastolic pressure (LVEDP).
Answer B: Increased coronary vascular resistance such as from vasospasm or atherosclerosis worsens myocardial oxygen supply. Providing vasodilation with medications such as nitroglycerin improves CBF.
Answer C: Left ventricular blood supply from the coronary arteries occurs primarily during diastole. A slower heart rate means more time is spent in diastole which allows more time for CBF to the left ventricle.
Answer D: Optimizing Hgb amount is one way to ensure maximal oxygen content. Myocardial oxygen supply is affected by AoDP, LVEDP, heart rate, Hgb, and CVR. Left ventricular systolic pressure affects myocardial oxygen demand.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Myocardial Oxygen Supply and Demand" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 1074-1075.

Oxygen diffusion is increased during exercise because of the recruitment of non-perfused capillary beds. Diffusion of a gas is a process by which the gas molecules move from an area of high partial pressure to an area of lower partial pressure. The movement of oxygen from the alveoli to the pulmonary capillary blood (and from the blood to the tissues) is passive. As oxygen moves from alveoli to the hemoglobin molecule, it must pass through: 1) the alveolar membrane (containing surfactant), 2) the capillary endothelium, 3) the plasma, 4) the red blood cell (RBC) membrane, and 5) the RBC intracellular fluid. Diffusion capacity of oxygen can be affected by changes to any of the factors mentioned above. The thickness of the alveolarcapillary membrane may affect the ability of oxygen to diffuse properly. During exercise, the total lung volume is increased, resulting in thinner, more distended alveoli. This increases the surface area of the lung allowing for greater oxygen diffusion. The tidal volume increases (up to 60%) with activity by encroaching into the inspiratory reserve volume. Therefore, during exercise, the inspiratory reserve is decreased. During exercise, increased pulmonary blood flow increases oxygen diffusion. The recruitment of capillary beds that were nonperfused at rest increases not only blood flow, but also the capillary cross-sectional area. Capillaries are recruited as groups, not individually. Areas with low capillary density are recruited first. This also improves the ventilation/perfusion ratio. RBC capillary transit time is the amount of time a single red blood cell spends in the capillary, where it is exposed to the alveolar gases. In other words, it is the amount of time a RBC has to pick up oxygen. At rest, the capillary transit time is approximately 0.8 seconds. Cardiac output is one of the factors that can change the capillary transit time. During exercise, the cardiac output increases causing a decrease in capillary transit time. There is no consensus on the impact of decreased transit time on oxygen diffusion during exercise. However, the minimum needed time for oxygen to diffuse into a RBC is 0.25 seconds. Capillary transit time decreases due to an increased cardiac output during exercise.
Answer B: Inspiratory reserve is decreased during exercise. Exercise increases oxygen diffusion by increasing lung surface area (thinner, more distended alveoli) and by increasing blood flow (capillary recruitment).  Lumb, Andrew. A large myocardial infarction would likely cause a decrease in cardiac output. With a lower cardiac output, the body has more time and needs to extract more oxygen from the blood, leaving the patient with less oxygen in the blood returning to the heart, and a lower SvO2. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is the percentage of oxygen bound to hemoglobin in the blood returning to the right side of the heart. A true SvO2 is drawn from a pulmonary artery catheter and includes all of the venous blood returning from the SVC, IVC, and coronary sinus. A normal SvO2 is approximately 75%, which is essentially the amount of oxygen “left over” after the body has extracted what it needs. It is useful to help us recognize when the body is extracting more oxygen than normal, either due to increased demand or decreased supply. SvO2 is calculated via the Fick equation. The Fick equation states: SvO2 = SaO2 – [VO2 ÷ (CO x Hgb x 1.36)] SvO2 = mixed venous oxygen saturation SaO2 = arterial oxygen saturation VO2 = total body oxygen consumption CO = cardiac output Hgb = hemoglobin concentration Based on the Fick equation, SvO2 is DECREASED in the following settings: - Increased oxygen consumption (e.g. hyperthermia, shivering, or pain) - Decreased cardiac output (e.g. myocardial infarction or hypovolemia) - Decreased hemoglobin concentration - Decreased arterial oxygen saturation Mixed venous oxygen saturation levels are INCREASED in the following settings: - Increasing the hemoglobin concentration via blood transfusions - Increased SaO2 - Decreased VO2 (e.g. cyanide toxicity, sepsis, carbon monoxide poisoning, methemoglobinemia, hypothermia) - Increased CO (e.g. sepsis) A left to right intracardiac shunt, in addition to increasing cardiac output, also shifts oxygenated blood from the left side of the heart to mix with deoxygenated blood on the right side, thereby falsely elevating the SvO2. Note that SvO2 is a measurement of global oxygen delivery. High SvO2 measurements may represent the inability of tissue to extract oxygen such as in the setting of methemoglobinemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, or cyanide poisoning. Sepsis usually causes a decrease in SvO2, but can also cause an increase due to high flow state and/or poor oxygen utilization. An elevated SvO2 may also be due to hyperdynamic circulation and overall increased oxygen delivery. In addition, measurements of SvO2 can be used as an implied gross measurement of cardiac output if SaO2, VO2, and Hgb remain constant. In a patient with a large myocardial infarction, you can assume they have a decreased cardiac output and therefore would have a decreased SvO2. A left to right intracardiac shunt would increase the SvO2 both by causing an increase in cardiac output and by leading to a mixing of oxygenated blood from the left side with deoxygenated blood on the right side. Note that systemic output may decrease (compared to pulmonary output) but overall cardiac output increases slightly. The major contributor, however, is the mixing of oxygenated blood.
Answer B: Cyanide toxicity, carbon monoxide poisoning, and methemoglobinemia would increase SvO2 as less oxygen would be transferred to tissues.
Answer C: Increasing the arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) would increase the SvO2 (SaO2 is part of the formula for SvO2: SvO2 = SaO2 – [VO2 ÷ (CO x Hgb x 1.36)]) Mixed venous oxygen saturation is directly related to Hgb, SaO2, and CO. It is inversely related to VO2.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Hypercarbia causes a rightward shift of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, thereby decreasing hemoglobin (Hb) affinity for oxygen and increasing oxygen unloading to tissues. The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve describes the arterial oxyhemoglobin saturation in relation to the PaO2. The shape of the curve is sigmoidal with the steep portion of the curve allowing for a predictable correlation between SaO2 and PaO2. Various conditions exist where Hb will bind oxygen tightly at lower PaO2 values (increased affinity) and also where Hb will unload oxygen at higher PaO2 values (decreased affinity). Oxyhemoglobin affinity for oxygen Increased Affinity (oxygen binding, leftward shift) Decreased Affinity (oxygen unloading, rightward shift) Hypothermia Hyperthermia Alkalosis Acidosis Hypocarbia Hypercarbia Decreased 2,3-BPG Increased 2,3-BPG Fetal Hb Adult Hb abbreviations: 2,3-BPG, 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate; Hb, hemoglobin Answers A & B: Conditions that lead to a leftward shift (increased Hb affinity for oxygen) include hypothermia, alkalosis, hypocarbia, decreased 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), and also fetal Hb (relative to adult Hb). Conditions that lead to a rightward shift (decreased Hb affinity for oxygen) include hyperthermia, acidosis, hypercarbia, increased 2,3-BPG, and adult Hb (relative to fetal Hb)  Several physiologic factors determine hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen. Factors that decrease hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen and therefore increase oxygen unloading to tissues include hyperthermia, acidosis, hypercarbia, and increased 2,3-BPG. A mnemonic to help remember what shifts the curve to the right is: "CADET, face Right!" for CO2, Acid, 2,3-DPG, Exercise, and Temperature. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Hypercarbia: O2 release to tissues” Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 700-701.

Laparoscopic insufflation causes a decrease in diaphragmatic excursion simply by increasing intra-abdominal pressure. If the ventilator settings are not changed, the tidal volume will decrease leading to CO2 retention and hypoxemia. Most patients require an increase of 30% in minute ventilation to counter the increase in CO2 from insufflation. Physiologic changes that take place during insufflation include: - Decreased lung compliance and increased inspiratory pressure, due to an increase in intra-abdominal pressure and Trendelenburg position. - Increased ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch, due to atelectasis and decreased functional residual capacity (FRC). - Elevated CO2, due to CO2 insufflation and decreased lung perfusion and ventilation. Most patients require an increase of 30% in minute ventilation to counter the increase in CO2 from insufflation. A modest increase in inspiratory pressures is needed to counter the reduced lung compliance and FRC associated with pneumoperitoneum. Hypercarbia needs to be significant before oxygenation is affected to this degree.
Answer C: Compression of the inferior vena cava (rather than the superior vena cava) would cause a decrease in preload and resultant hypotension, but would not cause hypoxemia. Laparoscopic insufflation causes a decrease in tidal volumes when using pressure-control ventilation. Hypoxemia can be due to atelectasis and decreased diaphragmatic excursion. During laparoscopic procedures, it is best to use either volume-control or pressure-control volumeguaranteed modes of ventilation. Pressure control alone can assist with achieving appropriate tidal volumes, but at the risk of over-ventilation with position changes and desufflation. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Laparoscopy: Hypoxemia (B)” Complications in Anesthesia. 2nd Ed. pp 831 - 835.

Less soluble anesthetics have a faster rate of rise of the ratio of the fractional concentration of alveolar to inspired anesthetic (FA/FI) because less anesthetic is required to saturate the blood. This results in an increased speed of induction. Anesthetic uptake can be tracked over time by assessing the ratio of the FA to FI. The more quickly the FA rises, the more quickly will be the induction of the anesthetic because the alveolar fraction is proportional to the partial pressure of the anesthetic in the central nervous system (CNS; PA = Pblood = PCNS, where PA, alveolar partial pressure; Pblood, blood partial pressure; PCNS, CNS partial pressure). Several factors affect the FA/FI ratio: • Blood:gas solubility • Cardiac output • Minute ventilation • Alveolar partial pressure - mixed venous partial pressure (PA - Pv) gradient As the solubility of the anesthetic increases in the blood, the uptake is faster in the blood, but the partial pressure in the blood is lower. The blood then requires more time to saturate with the anesthetic, taking longer to equilibrate with the alveoli and the CNS. Increasing cardiac output will enhance the uptake of the anesthetic if ventilation is fixed, decreasing the FA and slowing the rise of the FA/FI ratio. The increase in cardiac output and the slow rise of the FA/FI ratio affect soluble anesthetics more than they affect insoluble anesthetics. Finally, an increasing PA - Pv gradient will result in a slow rise in the FA/FI ratio because the anesthetic has a higher solubility in the blood, which takes longer to equilibrate with the CNS. Anesthetic uptake is inversely proportional (not directly proportional, which is the opposite) to blood:gas solubility. Low blood:gas solubility would result in a faster rise of the FA/FI ratio because the partial pressure of the gas would be higher and would take less time to equilibrate with the alveoli and the CNS.
Answer B: A low, not high, cardiac output would result in a faster rate of rise of FA/FI ratio because the anesthetic concentration would be able to build up faster as the blood spends more time exchanging gas with the alveoli.
Answer C: An increasing PA - Pv gradient will result in a slower rate of rise in the FA/FI ratio because the anesthetic has a higher solubility in the blood, which will take longer to equilibrate with the CNS. Factors affecting the fractional concentration of alveolar anesthetic/fractional concentration of inspired anesthetic (FA/FI) ratio include blood:gas solubility, cardiac output, minute ventilation, and alveolar partial pressure - mixed venous partial pressure gradient. Less soluble anesthetics have a faster rate of rise of FA/FI because less anesthetic is required to saturate the blood.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Anesthetic blood:gas solubility" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Inhaled anesthetics. 8th ed. E-book. Pages 463-467. Gropper M, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. Inhaled anesthetic uptake, distribution, metabolism, and toxicity. 9th ed. E-book. Pages 514-520.

Functional residual capacity (FRC) is defined as the volume of air left in the lungs at the end of breathing during tidal volume breathing. Functional residual capacity is an important lung capacity. Functional residual capacity is the most important determinant of the effectiveness of preoxygenation. Functional residual capacity decreases in many different physiologic states, including obesity, supine positioning, pregnancy, and while under general anesthesia. FRC = residual volume + expiratory reserve volume Or FRC = total lung capacity − inspiratory capacity The expiratory reserve volume is the amount of air that can be actively exhaled at the end of a tidal volume breath.
Answer C: Residual volume is the amount of air left in the lungs after maximal exhalation. Functional residual capacity is the volume of gas left in the lungs at the end of a tidal volume breath. Functional residual capacity is essential to the effectiveness of preoxygenation.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "FRC: Definition" Gropper MA, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. 9th edition. Ch. 13: Respiratory Physiology and Pathophysiology

Insulin deficiency can recover, at least partially, in patients with improved glycemic control. Diabetes mellitus is a pathophysiologic process that has both genetic and environmental influences. It is diagnosed on the basis of raised plasma glucose levels and can be controlled by lifestyle modifications, oral agents, or exogenous insulin. There are two types: type 1 involves the destruction of the pancreatic beta-cells leading to inadequate or complete lack of insulin secretion, and type 2 involves insulin resistance, usually with an insulin deficiency. Insulin deficiency occurs secondary to a reduction in beta-cell mass. This can occur with autoimmune destruction, as in type 1 diabetes, or in type 2 diabetes when the pancreas can no longer keep up with the demands. The insulin secretory deficit is progressively worse with more severe hyperglycemia and can recover partially with improved glycemic control. Insulin deficiency is necessary for the diagnosis of diabetes; however, it is not always sufficient to cause the disease. Insulin deficiency occurs secondary to pancreatic beta cell dysfunction, not alpha cell. The beta cells are responsible for insulin secretion and the alpha cells are responsible for glucagon secretion.
Answer C: Insulin deficiency and insulin resistance often occur together in type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Answer D: Type 1 diabetes mellitus is primarily an autoimmune disease. Type 2 diabetes was previously thought to only caused by weight gain and lack of adequate exercise, but is now is thought to have a multifactorial etiology with environmental and genetic influences. Insulin deficiency occurs secondary to a loss of beta-cell mass in the pancreas. A lack of insulin results in hyperglycemia and the symptoms associated with diabetes mellitus. Surgical stimulus and heightened states of arousal (e.g. fear or anxiety) cause hyperventilation. This typically causes a leftward shift and increased slope of the carbon dioxide ventilatory response curve (VRC). A VRC illustrates how changes in a patient’s arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) will alter minute ventilation. The VRC is typically linear between PaCO2 values of 20-80 mmHg, such that increasing PaCO2 levels correspond to resultant increases in minute ventilation. Various factors can shift the PaCO2 baseline of a minute ventilation response. This baseline is illustrated as the PaCO2 at which a VRC intersects a ventilation curve (grey dotted line in these figures). The slope of the VRC represents the sensitivity of the ventilatory centers to elevated PaCO2. See the figure below for more details. MAC: minimum alveolar concentration. Volatile anesthetics at ≤1 MAC cause a rightward, parallel shift of the VRC. Volatile anesthetics >1 MAC reduce sensitivity to elevated PaCO2, cause a rightward shift, and reduce the slope of the VRC.
Answer C: Opioid, barbiturate, and other sedative-hypnotic medication administration shift the VRC to the right and depress the slope, in a dose-dependent manner. The result is a reduced minute ventilation and higher baseline PaCO2 therefore reducing minute ventilation.
Answer D: A change in end-tidal oxygen concentration from 20% to 60% will generally have no significant effect on a patient’s VRC. If the change represents correction of arterial hypoxemia, however, the curve may shift to the right with a decrease in the slope. Factors that cause a leftward shift and an increased slope of a carbon dioxide ventilatory response curve include arterial hypoxemia, metabolic acidemia, surgical stimuli, and certain central nervous system pathologies. Factors that cause a rightward shift and a reduced slope of the curve include opioids, barbiturates, and sedative-hypnotic drugs. Volatile anesthetics ≤1 MAC cause a rightward, parallel shift of the VRC.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Co2-Vent Response Curve: Left Shift" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 271-273.

Septic shock is typically associated with a normal or increased mixed venous oxygen saturation caused by impaired tissue oxygen utilization in the setting of high cardiac output. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is measured by sampling blood from the proximal pulmonary artery. It reflects the average oxygen saturation of the blood returning from the body to the right heart and can be monitored perioperatively to evaluate the balance between global oxygen delivery and consumption. Normal values of SvO2 range between 65 and 80%. Values lower than 50% are associated with tissue hypoxia, anaerobic metabolism, and lactate production. SvO2 = SaO2 – VO2 / (1.34 * Hb * CO) (SvO2: mixed venous oxygen saturation in fraction, SaO2: arterial oxygen saturation in fraction, VO2: oxygen consumption [mL/ min], Hb: hemoglobin [g/dL], CO: cardiac output [L/min]. 1.34 mL of oxygen is carried by each gram of hemoglobin) The formula above explains the variables associated with SvO2. Decreases in arterial oxygen saturation, hemoglobin concentration, or cardiac output will result in a reduction in SvO2. Conversely, increases in these variables will result in a higher SvO2, which can be accomplished during the perioperative period by improving oxygenation, transfusion, optimizing fluid status and the use of inotropic agents. Also, factors that lower oxygen consumption, such as hypothermia, sedation, anesthesia, analgesia, and respiratory support will increase SvO2, while conditions such as hyperthermia, stress, shivering, pain, agitation, and thyrotoxicosis will decrease SvO2 due to increased tissue oxygen consumption. In a normal circumstance, the body compensates for decreased oxygen delivery by increasing the tissue oxygen extraction. However, this can be compromised in the setting of septic shock. Septic shock is associated with both decreased oxygen delivery and impaired oxygen extraction. Therefore, although tissue oxygenation is often severely reduced, SvO2 remains normal or even increased. An elevated level of lactate is often present, indicating unmatched oxygen demand and tissue hypoxia. Cyanide toxicity is another example of impaired peripheral oxygen utilization where SvO2 is elevated despite evolving tissue hypoxia and lactate production. It is important to keep in mind that SvO2 does not effectively reflect regional blood flow and tissue oxygen delivery. Inadequate regional blood supply, as with limb or intestinal ischemia, can coexist with a normal or high SvO2. Additionally, the presence of a wedged pulmonary artery catheter tip, mitral regurgitation, or left-to-right shunts can increase SvO2 and may lead to inaccurate interpretation of patients’ hemodynamics. An intrapulmonary shunt is a condition where a significant proportion of lung unit has a ventilation-to-perfusion ratio of zero, causing an increased amount of venous admixture and systemic oxygen desaturation. SvO2 is reduced due to decreased SaO2.
Answer B: Heart failure is associated with decreased SvO2 secondary to decreased cardiac output, which results in decreased global oxygen delivery.
Answer C: Hyperthermia increases global oxygen demand, therefore, leads to a decrease in SvO2. Mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is an indicator of global oxygen supply and demand balance. A low SvO2 indicates increased tissue oxygen extraction due to decreased oxygen supply relative to the demand. Septic shock and cyanide toxicity are conditions associated with normal or increased mixed venous oxygen saturation secondary to impaired tissue oxygen utilization. Central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2) measured by sampling blood through a central venous catheter located in the superior or inferior vena cava is often higher than SvO2. This is because of the venous blood with significantly low oxygen saturation entering from the coronary sinus and mixing in the right atrium. Botulinum toxin may be distributed from the gastrointestinal tract or lungs to cholinergic nerve endings where it blocks the release of acetylcholine at muscarinic and nicotinic receptors. It does this by inhibiting the intracellular fusion of acetylcholinecontaining vesicles to the nerve-terminal membrane for release into the synaptic cleft. This leads to flaccid paralysis that progresses until the respiratory muscles cease to contract. After ingestion, symptoms of blurred vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, swallowing difficulty, dry mouth, constipation, muscle weakness, and shortness of breath, may occur within 18-36 hours. Normal release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction is mediated a complex called SNARE which includes synaptobrevin, SNAP-25, and syntaxin. These allow the acetylcholine containing vesicle to fuse to cell membrane prior to release. Botulinum toxin enters the cell and cleaves SNARE proteins, which prevents fusion of the acetylcholine vesicle, and hence its release. Sarin is a neurotoxin that potently inhibits acetylcholinesterase, causing continual transmission of nerve impulses and inability to control respiratory muscles. This is not the mechanism for botulinum toxin.
Answer C: Non-depolarizing muscle relaxants such as rocuronium are competitive acetylcholine receptor inhibitors, effectively preventing the contraction of respiratory muscles. This is not the mechanism for botulinum toxin. Botulinum toxin can cause symptoms of muscle paralysis by preventing the release of acetylcholine-containing vesicles from the axon terminal into the synaptic cleft. Botulinum toxin acts inside the axon terminal at the neuromuscular junction. Tetanus toxin travels via retrograde axonal transport to the central nervous system where it acts. The closing of the mitral valve corresponds with the electrical R wave of the QRS complex. The cardiac cycle is depicted in Figure 1 below with respect to the left heart. This tracing may be derived during a left heart catheterization. It is divided into electrical events according to the electrocardiogram and corresponding mechanical events. These events include the opening and closing of the mitral and aortic valves in conjunction with pressure changes within the left atrium, left ventricle, and the aorta. A similar tracing may be illustrated with lower pressures from the right-heart involving the right atrium, right ventricle, and the main pulmonary artery. Figure 1. The cardiac cycle as depicted from the left side of the heart. The R wave signifies the beginning of left-ventricular systole, where the mitral valve closes and left ventricle (LV) isovolumetric contraction begins. The pressure in the LV builds until it exceeds the aortic pressure. The aortic valve then opens (immediately after QRS), isovolumetric contraction ends, and the LV ejects stroke volume into the aorta. Once the LV pressure falls below the aortic pressure, the aortic valve closes (end of T wave repolarization) and LV isovolumetric relaxation begins. The LV pressure continues to fall until it equals the left atrial pressure, and the mitral valve opens. MV = mitral valve, LVP = left ventricle pressure, LAP = left atrial pressure, a = left atrial contraction, c = closed MV bulges into left atrium at start of LV systole, v = left atrial filling, AoP = aortic pressure, AoV = aortic valve, P-QRST = ECG wave complex, IC = isovolumetric contraction, IR = isovolumetric relaxation. Answers A & C: Once the LVP falls below the AoP, the AoV closes, LV isovolumetric relaxation begins, and ventricular diastole ensues. This corresponds with the end of T wave repolarization on ECG. The LVP continues to fall until it equals the LAP, the MV opens, and isovolumetric relaxation ends. The LV begins to fill and the cycle continues. The R wave signifies the beginning of LV systole, where the MV closes and LV isovolumetric contraction begins, and LVP begins to exceed LAP. The pressure in the LV builds until it exceeds AoP, the AoV then opens, isovolumetric contraction ends, and the LV ejects stroke volume into the aorta. This occurs directly after the QRS complex on ECG. The closing of the mitral valve corresponds with the electrical R wave of the QRS complex.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cardiac Cycle: ECG" Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 724. Kaplan, Essentials of Cardiac Anesthesia, 1st edition, pp. 23-25.

Cytochrome p450 is a heme protein that utilizes molecular oxygen to oxidize organic compounds. Cytochrome p450 is not a single enzyme, but rather consists of a group of closely related proteins that are embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum. The structure of cytochrome p450 consists of iron (Fe), which serves as a binding site for oxygen molecules. Metabolism by cytochrome p450 has been extensively studied, and is involved in the oxidation of thousands of diverse drugs and chemicals. One atom of molecular oxygen is used to oxidize the drug, while the other atom is combined with hydrogen atoms from NADPH to form water. The liver is the principal site for drug metabolism. For many drugs, metabolism occurs in two phases. Phase I involves modifying the drug through oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis. These reactions typically inactivate the drug. Phase II involves conjugation, where a molecule (glucuronic acid, sulfate) is added to the drug to make it more easily excreted from the kidneys and liver. Cytochrome p450 is the most important enzyme system in phase I and catalyzes the oxidation of many drugs. Conjugation is part of phase II metabolism, where molecules are added to the drug to make it more readily excreted. Cytochrome p450 is involved with phase I oxidation.
Answer B: Hydrolysis is part of phase I, but is not mediated by p450 group.
Answer D: Reduction is part of phase I metabolism. However, cytochrome p450 catalyzes oxidation in phase I. Cytochrome p450 is involved in phase I metabolism by oxidizing many drugs. Chronic barbiturate use increases cytochrome p450 activity. As a result, the metabolism of drugs by p450 is increased (as seen with benzodiazepines). Gibson G and Skett P. Functional residual capacity (FRC) goes up with increased height and advanced age. FRC will go down with increased weight, decreased height, and in females compared with males. A decrease in FRC can also be seen in lung disease such as idiopathic fibrosis, pneumoconiosis, and different forms of granulomatosis and vasculitis. Following a lung resection a reduction in FRC will be seen; occasionally the remaining lung will expand to fill in some of the space left. FRC increases with age because of loss of elastic lung tissue, which lessens the contractile force of the lung and moves the balancing point between the outward force of the chest wall and the inward force of the lung to higher lung volume. In patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), FRC increases faster over the years than in normal subjects because of an effect of chronic air trapping and more severe loss of elastic tissue (in particular in emphysema). Functional residual capacity is the amount of air that is left in the lungs after a normal expiration. It is approximately 30 mL/kg in an average adult. FRC is dependent on age, sex, height and weight. The volume is determined by the balance of the inward forces of the lungs against the outward force of the chest wall. The inward forces are referred to as the “elastic recoil” and consist of the lung tissue and the contractile forces of the airway smooth muscle and surface tension of the alveoli. The outward force is exerted by the ribs, joints and muscles. If the alveoli completely collapsed after exhalation, the amount of force that would be required to reopen them would be tremendous thus a residual amount of air must remain. For newborns, the PaO2 in the first few days after birth rapidly increases. The PaO2 initially is low due to a decrease in FRC and fluid-filled alveoli. The FRC in neonates increases over the first few days of life until day 4, at which point it reaches adult levels. Answers B & C: FRC will go down with increased weight, decreased height, and in females compared with males.  Functional residual capacity increases with age due to loss of elastic lung tissue which acts as an inward force pulling the lungs closed. An increase will also be seen with increased height secondary to the larger lungs compared to short counterparts. Other causes of low FRC are PANGOS: Pregnancy, Ascites, Neonatal, General anesthesia, Obesity, Supine position. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Increased FRC: Causes (B)" Miller’s Anesthesia. 7th Edition. Respiratory Physiology. Pages 363.

Calcium ion movement does not play a role in neuronal action potential termination. Action potentials are brief, localized depolarizations on cell membranes used to transmit an electrical signal across a distance. Neurons generally have a resting membrane potential of -60 to -70 mV. A localized membrane depolarization that surpasses a certain threshold is able to then generate and propagate an action potential. This initial depolarization causes voltage-gated sodium channels to open from their closed state, allowing rapid influx of sodium ions which further depolarize the membrane to activate more local and downstream sodium channels in a positive feedback mechanism. At its peak, an action potential generates a cell membrane voltage of nearly +40 mV. Termination of the action potential occurs primarily via two mechanisms. First, the voltage-gated sodium channels terminate their positive feedback by self-inactivation within milliseconds of opening. Inactivated sodium channels do not allow further sodium ion influx despite a still depolarized membrane. Second, both voltage-gated and voltage-independent potassium channels open in response to depolarization and allow potassium efflux out the cell. Combined, these effects result in neuron membrane repolarization back towards the resting potential. During this time, the sodium channels transition from an inactivated state (unable to potentiate an action potential) to a closed state (ready to open upon threshold stimulation). However, the potassium channels are slower to close than the sodium channels and overshoot the repolarization, causing a brief period of hyperpolarization. The cell membrane returns to its resting potential due to numerous other ion channels/pumps, namely the sodium-potassium-ATPase. This is the combined effect of steps one and two for action potential termination.
Answer B: This is the first step in action potential termination.
Answer D: This is the second step in action potential termination. A neuron action potential is terminated by membrane repolarization caused by the inactivation and then closing of voltage-dependent sodium channels and the opening of potassium channels that promote potassium efflux. Local anesthetics block nerve impulse transmission by reversibly binding to the intracellular portion of the voltage-gated sodium channels and thereby preventing sodium ion influx. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Nerve AP termination mechanism" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 218-220, 532-534.

Both aerobic and anaerobic glycolysis start with the same initial reactions that convert glucose to pyruvate. Most human cells utilize two primary mechanisms for the generation of ATP: anaerobic glycolysis (anaerobic metabolism) in the absence of adequate oxygen and aerobic glycolysis (aerobic metabolism) in the presence of adequate oxygen. Both types of metabolism begin the same: conversion of one molecule of glucose into two molecules of pyruvate within the cytoplasm. This process consumes two ATP but produces 4 ATP (net +2 ATP). At this point, the two processes diverge. In anaerobic metabolism, the two pyruvate molecules are converted into lactate in order to regenerate NAD+ consumed in the initial stages of glycolysis. This process occurs without any additional ATP formation and is thus not efficient at the cellular level. Aerobic metabolism utilizes three additional major processes in order to increase the ATP yield per molecule of glucose. First, pyruvate enters the mitochondrion where it undergoes conversion to acetyl CoA via the Link reaction. Second, the acetyl CoA then enters the citric acid cycle (Krebs cycle) where multiple key substrates are generated (GTP, FADH2, and NADH) and carbon dioxide is released as a waste product. Finally, the FADH2 and NADH molecules undergo oxidative phosphorylation within the mitochondrial inner membrane. Within this process, the FADH2 and NADH donate high-energy electrons that proceed down an electron transport chain, reduce oxygen gas to water, and ultimately generate approximately 30 ATP (per molecule of glucose). The figure below summarizes anaerobic and aerobic metabolism. Note that the number of ATP generated during oxidative phosphorylation during aerobic glycolysis (34 in the figure below) is actually variable and may be between 30-36. Anaerobic metabolism produces approximately 30 fewer ATP than aerobic metabolism per molecule of glucose.
Answer B: Anaerobic and aerobic metabolism both use glucose as the initial substrate.
Answer C: Carbon dioxide and water are the end products of aerobic metabolism. Lactate is the primary end product of anaerobic metabolism (hence lactate production when oxygen does not get to tissues).
Answer D: The majority of ATP generated during aerobic metabolism is produced in the mitochondrion (i.e. the powerhouse of the cell). Only two molecules of ATP are generated in the cytoplasm. Aerobic metabolism produces approximately 16 times the ATP of anaerobic metabolism. The additional ATP is produced within the mitochondrion via the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation. Both anaerobic and aerobic metabolism start with glucose, but anaerobic metabolism generates lactate while aerobic metabolism produces carbon dioxide and water. In anaerobic glycolysis, the free energy of oxidation (NADH to NAD+) is wasted as heat, whereas in aerobic glycolysis 2.5-3 ATP are produced per NADH. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Aerobic Versus Anaerobic Glycolysis" Alberts, Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition, pp. 91-103. Image: Anaerobic vs. Aerobic pathways. SparkNotes (Open Source). 2016.

An increase in left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) results in greater compression of subendocardial blood vessels, impedes coronary blood flow (CBF), and lowers coronary perfusion pressure (CPP). Coronary perfusion pressure of the left ventricle is defined as aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) minus LVEDP: CPPLV = AoDP – LVEDP A myocardial pressure-volume loop (see below) may be utilized to illustrate key parameters of the cardiac cycle. Diastolic filling occurs as the left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV) increases towards the left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV). The difference in these volumes ultimately translates into the ventricular stroke volume (SV). The corresponding pressure of the LVEDV is the LVEDP. The LV pressure increases from the LVEDP towards the AoDP during systole. The aortic valve opens once the LV pressure exceeds AoDP and the ejection period commences. Blood is ejected into the aorta until the LV pressure equilibrates with the aortic systolic pressure (AoSP). The aortic valve then closes and the mitral valve opens. Coronary perfusion then occurs during diastole and ventricular relaxation. Normal myocardial pressure-volume loop. LVESV = left ventricular end-systolic volume, LVEDV = left ventricular end-diastolic volume, LVESP = left ventricular end-systolic pressure, LVEDP = left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, CPP = coronary perfusion pressure, AoDP = aortic diastolic pressure, AoSP = aortic systolic pressure, SV = stroke volume. Lower values of LVEDP improve cardiac perfusion by reducing the resistance to blood flow through the coronary arteries and branches. A simultaneous reduction in myocardial oxygen demand occurs due to a reduction in ventricular volume and wall tension. Preload reduction decreases ventricular stretch (wall tension) which lowers LVEDP, and therefore increases CPP.
Answer B: Pulmonary artery occlusion pressure (PAOP) may be used as a proxy for LVEDP. A decrease in PAOP is generally regarded as a decrease in LVEDP, which leads to an increase in CPP.
Answer C: An increase in AoDP increases CPP. CPPLV = AoDP - LVEDP. Hemodynamic variables that increase LVEDP will decrease CPP. Autoregulation of CBF is compromised with coronary stenosis. Autoregulation fails first in the subendocardium, resulting in subendocardial ischemia and ST segment depression.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Coronary Perfusion Pressure" Source: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 1074-1075. Guyton, Medical Physiology, 7th edition, pp. 110-112. Kaplan, Cardiac Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 445.

Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist with peripheral cholinergic agonism that can be used to decrease the gastric volume in patients with impaired gastric emptying. Metoclopramide decreases gastric volume by its prokinetic effect, increases lower esophageal sphincter tone, but has no effect on gastric pH. It is contraindicated in patients with pheochromocytoma. It should also be used with caution in patients with Parkinson disease due to the risk of causing rigidity and exacerbation of extrapyramidal symptoms. Metoclopramide is also used perioperatively as an antiemetic, though it has weak antiemetic action. Ranitidine will increase, not decrease the gastric pH. It has no effect on gastric volume.
Answer C: Sodium citrate is a weak base and reacts with hydrochloric acid in the stomach to increase, not decrease, the gastric pH.
Answer D: Sucralfate does not affect the gastric volume and only has a local effect on gastric pH. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that increases lower esophageal sphincter tone, enhances gastric emptying in patients who have slowed gastric emptying, and decreases gastric fluid volume. Unfortunately, its antiemetic properties are weak. Current guidelines recommend using a higher dose (25-50 mg) of metoclopramide when used as an antiemetic as this medication has weak antiemetic properties. Additionally, the "Society for Ambulatory Anesthesia Guidelines for the management of Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting do not recommend metoclopramide as an antiemetic for a patient who has received prophylactic ondansetron intraoperatively." American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Metoclopramide: Pharm Effects (B)" Gan TJ, et al. Consensus guidelines for the management of postoperative nausea and vomiting. Insulin levels are decreased during the stress response. The metabolic effects of the stress response act to mobilize glucose stores available and increased insulin would not contribute to this. Following any kind of trauma, the body reacts in an organized pattern through hormonal and metabolic changes. This is often termed the stress response and the effects are seen in every organ system. This response developed in order to survive, however in modern-day it can be detrimental, especially in the perioperative period. Numerous studies have been devoted to finding a way to diminish this response and it appears the degree of stress response activation is proportional to the degree of injury (i.e. larger surgeries result in higher degree of activation). When the body is under stress, the endocrine system ramps up secretion of a variety of hormones. The hypothalamic-pituitary axis and the sympathetic nervous system are activated by afferent nerve input from the area of trauma or injury. Activation of the sympathetic nervous system will cause an increased secretion of catecholamines from the adrenal medulla (norepinephrine is the primary neurotransmitter). Activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis will result in increased secretion of certain hormones from the pituitary which will act on the target organs. In review, the hormones released from the pituitary gland include adrenocorticotrophic hormone (corticotropin, ACTH), arginine vasopressin (AVP), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), as well as thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), growth hormone (GH), prolactin, and oxytocin. In response to stress, GH, ACTH, prolactin, and AVP all have an increased secretion while TSH, LH, and FSH are unchanged (although some studies report an increased secretion of TSH). The increased pituitary secretion will cause an increase in the target organ secretion: cortisol and aldosterone in the adrenal cortex, glucagon in the pancreas. Cortisol promotes glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, protein catabolism, lipolysis, and ketone body production. Protein catabolism is stimulated during stress predominantly from the skeletal muscle but also through some visceral muscle protein breakdown. Fat metabolism occurs mainly through lipolysis (conversion of triglycerides to glycerol and fatty acids). In addition, glucagon also promotes hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. In the perioperative period, insulin levels vary depending on multiple factors. In the operative period, the pancreas releases less insulin and a certain degree of peripheral insulin resistance is observed. Insulin is a key hormone that is usually secreted in response to hyperglycemia, promoting glucose utilization in the cells. During the stress of surgery, the islet cells of the pancreas, where insulin is made, are inhibited secondary to catecholamines. The metabolic results of this endocrine response include mobilization of energy stores along with alterations in salt and water metabolism. Blood glucose concentrations increase during stress and the degree of glucose elevation is related to the intensity of the surgery. Postoperatively, insulin concentrations escalate because of the increases in plasma glucose that occurred during the operative period and the epinephrine-induced beta-adrenergic stimulation. Several hormones alter salt and water metabolism in order to preserve adequate body fluid volumes. Arginine vasopressin promotes water retention and its secretion is increased for several days following surgery. Anesthesia likely has profound effects on the stress response associated with surgery. Opioids suppress the hypothalamic and pituitary hormone secretion. Regional anesthesia is thought to decrease the stress response but findings have been conflicting. Lipolysis is increased during the stress response due to increased catecholamine secretion. Triglycerides are metabolized to fatty acids and glycerol which is a gluconeogenic substrate.
Answer B: Insulin resistance occurs later in the stress response. It is thought that it occurs secondary to a defect in the insulin receptor-intracellular signaling pathway.
Answer C: Glycogenolysis, which is the breakdown of glycogen to glucose, is increased during the stress response due to epinephrine secretion. Glycogenolysis occurs in the liver and muscle tissues and helps to increase glucose stores available for cellular use. During the stress response, a metabolic cascade of events occurs in an attempt to provide the body with needed energy. This puts the body in a relative catabolic state. In modern medicine, these often are a detriment to the patient. In the surgical period, decreasing the degree of the stress response can help influence postoperative outcome. The anterior pituitary secretes all hormones except antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) and oxytocin. Anterior --> Thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotrophic hormone (corticotropin, ACTH), follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), luteinizing hormone (LH), thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH), growth hormone (GH), and prolactin. Posterior --> antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) and oxytocin. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Stress Response: Metabolic Effect (B)" Millers Anesthesia. 8th edition.
