The primary goal of denitrogenation (preoxygenation) is to displace the nitrogen in the functional residual capacity (FRC) with oxygen to provide an oxygen reserve for the apneic period. Removal of nitrogen from the FRC increases the content of oxygen available for apneic oxygenation after induction of anesthesia. With room air-breathing, 95% of the FRC is filled with nitrogen which provides little reserve of oxygen during apnea. Denitrogenation is most successfully employed by breathing 90% to 100% O2 with a tight-fitting oxygen mask at 10 to 12 L per minute of flow at normal tidal volumes. Time to desaturation to SpO2 of <90% in healthy nonobese patients can be greater than eight minutes vs only one to two minutes without denitrogenation. In patients with obesity, respiratory gas exchange impairment, elevated oxygen consumption (eg, neonates), or restricted lung volumes, this is even more important because the time to desaturation in these individuals is limited, even with adequate denitrogenation. Results of one study provided evidence that the time to desaturation in patients with obesity who had adequate denitrogenation was only 2.7 minutes versus six minutes in nonobese patients. Dissolved arterial oxygen content does not contribute substantially to apneic oxygen reserves due to the poor solubility of oxygen in the blood.
Answer C: The inspiratory reserve volume is the volume above the tidal volume inspiration with maximal inhalation effort. This volume does not contribute to oxygen reserves during apneic periods. Denitrogenation (preoxygenation) of the functional residual capacity allows a greater apneic oxygenation time during the induction of anesthesia.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Denitrogenation Primary Goal (B)" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Airway Management. Page 768. 7th editon.

Vasopressin is also known as antidiuretic hormone (ADH) and arginine vasopressin (AVP). An increase in plasma osmolality will lead to secretion of the hormone. Arginine vasopressin (AVP) is an endogenous peptide made in the hypothalamic supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei that is stored in the posterior lobe of the pituitary. There are certain conditions that either stimulate its release or inhibit its release. Two of the most important factors responsible for secretion of AVP are hyperosmolality and reduced effective circulating volume. Other factors that stimulate its release include: angiotensin II, stress, pain, nausea, hypoglycemia, pregnancy, and certain drugs like nicotine. Factors that inhibit its release are hypoosmolality, increased effective circulating volume, cortisol, and drugs such as caffeine. AVP stimulates water resorption by increasing intracellular levels of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and activating protein kinase A. It also stimulates vasoconstriction by activating G protein and phospholipase C, which releases calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. There are two classes of AVP receptors: V1 receptors present in vascular smooth muscle and V2 receptors present in the distal and collecting tubules of the kidney. AVP is metabolized by the kidneys and liver after its release into the plasma. Its half-life is 15-20 minutes. Caffeine would inhibit the release of AVP.
Answer B: ADH (AVP) hypersecretion occurs in cortisol deficiency. Cortisol deficiency results in increased hypothalamic secretion of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), an ADH secretagogue. Cortisol feeds back negatively on CRH and ACTH, an inhibitory effect that is removed with adrenal insufficiency. Both cortisol and antidiuretic hormone are released in response to surgical stress, but it should be noted that cortisol appears to directly suppress ADH secretion.
Answer C: Increasing effective circulating volume would inhibit the release of AVP. AVP is the main physiologic factor in water resorption. It is released from the pituitary in response to hyperosmolality, reduced effective circulating volume, angiotensin II, stress, pain, nausea, hypoglycemia, pregnancy, and certain drugs. Angiotensin I (AI) is cleaved and converted to Angiotensin II (AII) in the pulmonary circulation by the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Renin is produced in the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney and secreted into the circulation in response to reduced renal perfusion pressure. Renin (a protease) cleaves circulating angiotensinogen (globulin made in the liver) into angiotensin I. Angiotensin I travels into the pulmonary circulation, where ACE cleaves AI into AII. Angiotensin II has multiple physiologic effector sites including the zona glomerulosa of the adrenal glands, where the secretion of aldosterone is promoted. Angiotensin II serves to increase vascular and sympathetic tone and raise the intravascular volume. Angiotensin I is cleaved and converted to Angiotensin II in the pulmonary circulation by the angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE).
Answer C: Epinephrine is also not affected by pulmonary circulation. Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by intravascular ACE in the pulmonary circulation. Carbon dioxide (CO2)is transported in the blood as dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and carbamino compounds. Carbon dioxide is 10 times more soluble in blood than in oxygen: 0.031 mmol/L/mmHg vs 0.003 mmol/L/mmHg, respectively. Despite this, most CO2 is transported as bicarbonate. This occurs because red blood cells and vascular endothelium contain carbonic anhydrase, an enzyme used to convert CO2 to bicarbonate. The enzyme also catalyzes the reverse reaction. In both cases, the transient intermediate carbonic acid is created. Bicarbonate production: H2O + CO2 ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3−. Carbamino compounds also transport CO2 in the blood. Carbamino compounds are produced from a reaction with proteins. The small amount of CO2 transported in this manner mostly interacts with hemoglobin proteins and, to a lesser extent, plasma proteins. Carbamino compound production: R-NH2 + CO2 → R-NH-CO2- + H+. Methyl carbamate is not related to CO2 transport.
Answer C: The full reaction proceeds so quickly that blood never contains appreciable quantities of carbonic acid. Carbon dioxide is transported in the blood as dissolved CO2, bicarbonate, and carbamino compounds.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Carbon Dioxide: Blood Transport" Marino PL. Norepinephrine is more selective for β1 receptors than β2 and accordingly, does not cause significant bronchial smooth muscle relaxation. Bronchial smooth muscle relaxes in response to β2 adrenergic stimulation leading to bronchial dilation.
Answer B: Norepinephrine and epinephrine are the two endogenous catecholamines responsible for sympathetic stimulation but are differentially selective for the β-adrenergic receptors. Epinephrine acts at both β1 and β2 and causes significant bronchial smooth relaxation and bronchodilation.
Answer C: Bronchial smooth muscle contracts in response to muscarinic (M3) stimulation causing bronchial constriction. Stimulation of β2 adrenergic receptors causes bronchodilation while M3 receptor stimulation causes bronchoconstriction. Epinephrine causes significant bronchodilation. Norepinephrine does not cause significant bronchial smooth muscle relaxation as it is more β1-selective.  Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 327. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Diastasis is a slow filling which occurs during ventricular diastole. It is the second of three phases of ventricular filling. The cardiac cycle, discussed mainly from the standpoint of the ventricles, consists of diastole and systole. Ventricular diastole involves filling of the ventricles and can be broken down into isovolumetric relaxation followed by filling. Isovolumetric relaxation starts with the closure of the aortic valve and ends with the opening of the mitral valve signaling the onset of filling. The filling phase is further broken down into early rapid filling, diastasis (also called slow filling), and then atrial systole. Early rapid filling is caused by negative intracavitary pressure in the ventricle created by fast myocardial relaxation. This is referred to as diastolic suction. Ventricular systole follows atrial systole starting with isovolumetric contraction marked by the closure of the mitral valve. Once intraventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, the aortic valve opens, and the ejection phase of systole begins. As blood is ejected and pressure falls, the aortic valve will close marking the start of diastole with isovolumetric relaxation. Diastole and systole are coordinated by the cardiac conduction system. The sinoatrial (SA) node, located in the posterior wall of the right atrium near the superior vena cava, is the pacemaker for a healthy heart. When it fires, electrical signals travel through the atria causing the atria to depolarize and enter atrial systole. The electrical signal travels to the atrioventricular (AV) node where it experiences a pause before moving onto the conduction system in the ventricles. From the AV node, the signal is conducted through the Bundle of His, to the right and left bundle branches, and then through the Purkinje fibers. Overlap occurs between atrial systole and ventricular diastole with the atria entering systole and contributing to ventricular filling while the ventricles are still in diastole. A delay in the conduction system at the AV node allows the ventricles time to fill from the atria before entering systole themselves. As the electrical current moves from the AV node into the ventricles, the ventricles will start to contract entering systole. Wiggers diagram, illustrating cardiac cycle. Isovolumetric contraction occurs during ventricular systole. It starts with the closure of the mitral valve and continues as pressure builds enough to cause the opening of the aortic valve, signaling the end of isovolumetric contraction and the start of ejection.
Answer C: The Purkinje fibers are part of the ventricular conduction system. When an action potential reaches the Purkinje fibers, the ventricles start to contract signaling the start of ventricular systole. The cardiac cycle, discussed mainly from the standpoint of the ventricles, consists of diastole and systole. Ventricular diastole starts with isovolumetric relaxation following by rapid filling, diastasis (slow filling), and atrial systole. Ventricular systole starts with isovolumetric contraction followed by ejection of the blood from the ventricles. Most serious cases of carbon dioxide embolism reported in the literature occurred at the beginning of the procedure due to misplacement of the Veress needle (pneumoperitoneum needle) directly into a vein or parenchymal organ. Carbon dioxide embolism can manifest similar to an air embolus, causing obstruction to RV ejection, right and left cardiac failure, paradoxical embolism, arrhythmia, pulmonary hypertension, systemic hypotension, and cardiovascular collapse. Review of the literature varies as to the lethal volume of CO2, but it is likely between 600 mL to 1750 mL in an adult. A gas bubble composed of 100% CO2 will not enlarge in a patient inhaling 50% or even 75% N2O because CO2 is more soluble than N2O. CO2 will, therefore, move out or be absorbed or buffered more quickly than N2O will move in. This is not to deny that N2O should not be discontinued if CO2 embolism is suspected, but hemodynamic improvement will not typically be seen in the immediate period. Several reports have shown an increase in ETCO2 with hemodynamically unstable carbon dioxide embolism. One particular report showed a continuously recorded ETCO2 concentration that increased abruptly from 3.8 to 4.2% in carbon dioxide embolism patients who were diagnosed on the basis of a sudden abrupt onset of systolic and diastolic murmurs during laparoscopy. Another report showed a temporal association of cardiovascular collapse with an abrupt increase in ETCO2. Most reports, however, described significant decreases in ETCO2 with clinical episodes of carbon dioxide embolism. Answers A & B: Carbon dioxide embolism may increase or decrease PETCO2. Other effects include elevated pulmonary arterial pressure, elevated central venous pressure, hypoxemia, and increased PCO2. Hyperventilation (especially with 100% O2) increases carbon dioxide excretion and decreases the volume of the embolus. Discontinuation of N2O does not improve hemodynamic stability with 100% CO2 embolus. However, it should be discontinued to provide 100% oxygen during cardiopulmonary compromise. Decreased ETCO2 is more commonly seen, but increased ETCO2 may occur in CO2 embolus even in cardiovascular collapse.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Laparoscopy: CO2 Embolus" Park, et al. Lusitropy is defined as the rate of active myocardial relaxation. Positive (increased) lusitropy may be represented by a downward and rightward shift in the end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (EDPVR) curve of a pressure-volume loop, which is best illustrated by the curve corresponding to point A. In this state, increased myocardial compliance is demonstrated by an increased left ventricular end-diastolic blood volume for a given end-diastolic pressure. Pressure-volume (PV) loops may be used to illustrate the operating conditions of the heart by plotting the pressures within a ventricular chamber as a function of the volume within the ventricle throughout the cardiac cycle. The PV loop changes its shape and position in response to certain physiologic parameters, such as afterload, preload, inotropy, and lusitropy. A state of positive (or increased) lusitropy is observed when a more compliant ventricle with a greater rate of relaxation tolerates a higher end-diastolic volume at a lower end-diastolic pressure. This relationship is illustrated on the PV loop via a downward and rightward shift of the slope at the end of diastole (end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship or EDPVR). By contrast, an increase in preload would be indicated by rightward movement of the PV loop along the same EDPVR slope, as greater blood volume is subject to slightly higher pressures given the same degree of lusitropy. Meanwhile, an upward shift of the entire EDPVR curve would indicate decreased compliance or negative lusitropy. The end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) is represented by the upper left curve and is linear under physiologic conditions. The slope of the ESPVR serves as an index of myocardial contractility (inotropy). Accordingly, a decrease in inotropy would be represented as a downward and rightward shift of the ESPVR. This is not to be confused with an increase in afterload, which would be associated with greater end-systolic pressures and a higher end-systolic volume, causing the PV loop to translate upward and to the right along the same ESPVR curve. As an example, congestive heart failure with pure left ventricular systolic dysfunction would be seen as a downward shift in the ESPVR, signifying decreased contractility or negative inotropy. To maintain stroke volume, sympathetic activation and fluid retention would cause an increase in left ventricular volume, and end-diastolic pressures might increase as a result (producing a rightward translation of the PV loop along EDPVR slope). An individual can also exhibit decreased left ventricular contractility and decreased compliance simultaneously, which would substantially reduce stroke volume. For instance, such conditions may arise in the event of an acute myocardial infarction involving a large portion of the left ventricular wall, which would place the patient at risk of cardiogenic shock. Point B illustrates negative lusitropy compared to the baseline value. The end-diastolic pressure is therefore higher for a given end-diastolic volume. This state might be observed in a patient with significant diastolic dysfunction (e.g., profound concentric left ventricular hypertrophy).
Answer C: Point C illustrates negative inotropy compared to the baseline value. The end-systolic pressure is therefore lower for a given end-systolic volume. This state might be observed in a patient with significant systolic dysfunction (e.g., dilated cardiomyopathy due to left ventricular scarring).
Answer D: Point D illustrates positive inotropy compared to the baseline value. The end-systolic pressure is therefore higher for a given end-systolic volume. This state might be observed in a patient administered an inotropic drug such as dobutamine or milrinone. Pressure-volume loops can be used to illustrate changes in cardiac work due to changes in ventricular pressure as a function of ventricular volume. Positive lusitropy is depicted by a rightward and downward shift of the end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship curve, which illustrates a more compliant ventricle that can accommodate larger volumes at decreased pressures. In an average adult, a normal EDV (end-diastolic volume) and ESV (end-systolic volume) might be approximately 120 and 40-50 mL, respectively. Stroke volume (EDV-ESV) is therefore ~70-80 mL or ~60-67% in a normally functioning heart. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Lusitropy: PV Loop” Barash's Clinical Anesthesia. 8th ed. A right-shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve results in hemoglobin’s decreased affinity for oxygen, resulting in increased oxygen delivery to tissues, as occurs with hyperthermia, hypercarbia, and acidemia. A left-shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve results in hemoglobin’s increased affinity for oxygen, resulting in decreased oxygen delivery to tissues, as occurs in the presence of fetal hemoglobin, methemoglobinemia, carbon monoxide poisoning, or hypophosphatemia (a substrate for the production of 2,3-DPG). Oxygen delivery to the tissues can be calculated with the equation: DO2 = CO * CaO2 CO = cardiac output CaO2 = arterial oxygen content Where CaO2 = [1.34 * Hgb * SaO2] + [PaO2 * 0.003] Hgb = hemoglobin concentration SaO2 = arterial oxygen saturation PaO2 - arterial partial pressure of oxygen Oxygen delivery is also affected by factors that affect the P50, the partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated (the normal P50 is 27 mm Hg). This value is a marker of hemoglobin’s affinity for oxygen and is used to evaluate changes in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, which reflects the amount of oxygen delivery to tissues. CO binds to hemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin, which increases oxygen affinity of the remaining heme sites. This results in a left-shifted oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, with reduced oxygen delivery.
Answer B: Hypophosphatemia commonly occurs secondary to sepsis, malnutrition, refeeding syndrome, acute liver injury, and diabetic ketoacidosis (due to increased urinary phosphate excretion). Inorganic phosphate is a substrate for 2,3-DPG production, and if hypophosphatemia is not corrected, the decreased 2,3-DPG results in an increased affinity of oxygen for hemoglobin, a left-shifted oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, and reduced oxygen delivery. Oxygen delivery is dependent on cardiac output and arterial oxygen content, but is also affected by factors influencing the P50, the partial pressure of oxygen at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated. A left-shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin desaturation curve results in increased oxygen affinity and decreased oxygen delivery, whereas a right-shift results in decreased oxygen affinity and increased oxygen delivery to tissues. The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Cyanide primarily causes toxicity by impairing cellular aerobic respiration. The cyanide ion (CN-) binds to the ferric ion (Fe3+) in mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, inhibiting the final stage of the electron transport chain. Depletion of cellular ATP and the lactic acid produced by anaerobic metabolism can lead to profound acidosis. Symptoms of cyanide toxicity include altered mental status, weakness, headaches, loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure, and cardiac arrest. Blood cyanide levels will be elevated, although therapy should not be delayed for the laboratory result. The patients blood sample may appear "cherry red" due to normal circulating levels of oxygen with impaired utilization. Circulating oxygen is not impaired and cyanosis is a late finding.
Answer B: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. Therefore, PaO2 will increase.
Answer C: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. SvO2 will be increased. The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Anion gap is calculated by subtracting serum chloride and bicarbonate (anions) from serum sodium and potassium (cations). Anion gap = ([Na+] +[K+]) – ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]). In clinical practice, potassium is usually excluded. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 910, 1077. Miller Anesthesia, 8th edition, p. 2501. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cyanide Toxicity: Dx"

Alpha-2 stimulation will inhibit lipolysis. The stress response occurs when the body is placed under surgical or traumatic strain. The stress response is categorized by loss of fat and lean body mass. The response is termed an ‘obligate’ catabolic state which results in proteolysis, gluconeogenesis, lipolysis, hypermetabolism, and insulin resistance. This state is not reduced by exogenous nutrition as would occur in a fasting state. The body's response to surgery and trauma depends on the magnitude of injury, surgical time, and degree of postoperative pain. Lipid metabolism is altered during stress. Lipolysis is the hydrolysis of triglycerides into glyceride and free fatty acids which are then used as an energy source. In general, lipolysis is increased by beta-2 and beta-3 adrenergic stimulation but is inhibited by alpha-2 stimulation. Women are more sensitive to the lipolytic actions of catecholamines when compared to men. Lipolysis is increased by certain catecholamines - beta-2 adrenergic stimulation will increase lipolysis.
Answer C: Increased catecholamines, cortisol, and glucagon secretion all promote lipolysis.
Answer D: Women are more sensitive to the lipolytic actions of catecholamines. During the stress response, lipolysis increases in response to catecholamine stimulation. Lipolysis is the hydrolysis of triglycerides into glyceride and free fatty acids.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Stress Response: Lipolysis (B)" Miller Anesthesia. 8th edition. Nutrition and Metabolomics. Page 3134-3135. Burton, D. Endocrine and metabolic response to surgery. Critical Care & Pain. 2005(4): 144-147.

The hepatic arterial buffer response (HABR) is responsible for maintaining constant hepatic blood flow. Through the action of the HABR, changes in portal venous flow induce reciprocal changes in hepatic arterial flow. With an intact HABR, as portal venous blood flow decreases, the hepatic artery vasodilates resulting in increased hepatic arterial flow. The opposite occurs when portal venous blood flow increases. Changes in hepatic artery blood flow do not induce reciprocal changes in the portal venous system. The key player in the HABR is adenosine. Adenosine is produced in the space of Mall surrounding the local hepatic vasculature and diffuses into the portal vein. As portal venous blood flow decreases, the decreased flow allows the accumulation of adenosine in the hepatic vasculature. This increased concentration of adenosine causes vasodilation of the hepatic artery and increased hepatic arterial blood flow. As portal venous flow increases, the increased flow washes the adenosine out of the hepatic vascular system resulting in vasoconstriction of the hepatic artery. This is known as the “adenosine wash-out hypothesis.” The maximum effect of the HABR can double the hepatic arterial blood flow. The response can be abolished by endotoxemia and splanchnic hypoperfusion. The liver gets 20-25% of the cardiac output via the portal vein and the hepatic artery. The portal vein is responsible for 75% of the blood flow while the hepatic artery is responsible for 25% of the blood flow. However, both vascular structures each deliver 50% of the oxygen supply to the liver. Hypercapnia can modulate the blood flow within the hepatic vasculature; however, this does not describe the hepatic arterial buffer response.
Answer B: Decreases in oxygen tension of the portal venous system can result in increased hepatic arterial blood flow. Arterial hypoxemia can modulate liver blood flow. However, these are not qualities of the hepatic arterial buffer response.
Answer C: Nitric oxide has no role in the hepatic arterial buffer response. However, nitric oxide does play a role in regulating the resistance of the liver sinusoids. Cirrhosis can cause a disruption of the liver sinusoids and a resultant decrease in the activity of endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS). This results in decreased nitric oxide and may contribute to the development of portal hypertension. On the other hand, nitric oxide production is increased in the mesenteric vasculature during portal hypertension causing splanchnic hyperemia. With a functioning hepatic arterial buffer response, hepatic arterial tone is modulated by portal venous flow, via adenosine, in order to maintain hepatic perfusion. Glucagon causes dose-dependent hepatic arterial vasodilation. Angiotensin II causes vasoconstriction of hepatic arterial and portal venous systems. Vasopressin increases splanchnic vasoconstriction while decreasing resistance to portal venous flow. Wagener, Liver Anesthesiology and Critical Care Medicine. Carotid body chemoreceptors are primarily responsive to reductions in arterial partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2). The carotid bodies are located at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries bilaterally and contain afferent glossopharyngeal nerve branches that become stimulated in response to reductions in PaO2. Once the PaO2 falls below 60-65 mm Hg, neural activity increases to augment minute ventilation. Once the PaO2 increases to above 65 mm Hg, the neural input to the central respiratory centers ceases. Ventilation then falls again until the decrease in PaO2 surpasses this threshold again. Answers A & B: The carotid bodies are not stimulated by changes in arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) or arterial oxygen content (CaO2). Alterations in arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) do not stimulate the carotid body receptors sufficiently to produce changes in minute ventilation.
Answer E: The carotid body chemoreceptors do show some response to reductions in pH, however, the response is minor. The carotid body chemoreceptors are located at the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries bilaterally. The chemoreceptors are stimulated to increase minute ventilation in response to decreases in PaO2 below 60-65 mm Hg.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Carotid body: hypoxic drive" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 240.

Synthetic liver function is best assessed via the INR or PT which most closely correlates with factor VIIa levels. INR is the best lab value to assess hepatic synthetic function as it correlates with factor VIIa levels, which only have a half-life of 4 hours and thus will reflect acute or chronic declines in hepatic synthetic function reliably. This is obviously confounded in situations where the INR will be elevated for other reasons such as warfarin therapy, vitamin K deficiency, dilutional coagulopathy, or other coagulopathies. The other test used to assess hepatic synthetic function is albumin. Albumin is synthesized by the liver however it has a half-life of approximately 3 weeks (therefore not particularly useful for acute evaluation) and its value can be normal in cirrhosis or be decreased for a multitude of reasons such as poor nutrition, albumin catabolism, volume overload, and protein losing nephropathy. INR is superior to albumin in the assessment of hepatic synthetic function.
Answer C: Direct, or conjugated bilirubin, increases when there is a disruption with bile removal such as choledocolithiasis and would in fact reveal that the liver has the ability to convert unconjugated to conjugated bilirubin. It is not useful in the evaluation of hepatic synthetic function.
Answer D: Transaminase levels better reflect liver injury and can be normal or low in severe cirrhosis where most of the liver parenchyma is destroyed. It is not a very useful test to evaluate liver synthetic function. Synthetic liver function is best assessed via the PT/INR, which most closely correlates with factor VIIa levels.  Miller's Anesthesia. Hepatic Physiology and Pathophysiology in 8th edition. Pages 520-544. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Hepatic Synthetic Function: Labs (B)"

Tissue hypoxia from carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning can occur due to a left shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. This occurs as a result of hemoglobin’s (Hb) increased affinity for CO as compared with oxygen. This leftward shift therefore increases oxygen binding to the Hb molecule. Carbon monoxide poisoning is commonly associated with burn victims due to smoke exposure during a fire. Carbon monoxide has an affinity for Hb that is 200-300 times stronger than oxygen. Hemoglobin preferentially binds to CO (carboxyhemoglobin, or COHb) leaving less Hb available for oxygen to bind. In addition, oxygen that binds with Hb tends not to dissociate from Hb, resulting in a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. CO disrupts mitochondrial function, which leads to less adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production as a result of uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production. Combined, these factors result in tissue hypoxia and a metabolic acidosis (with an anion gap). Clinically, CO poisoning is difficult to discover without an adequate history because oxygen saturation is usually normal. Standard pulse oximetry is unable to distinguish between COHb and oxyhemoglobin as they both absorb light at similar frequencies. The diagnosis of carbon monoxide poisoning is made by co-oximetry, when elevated levels of COHb (> 15%) are found on arterial or venous blood gas analysis. Treatment includes high FiO2 which helps displace CO. Hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for patients with COHb > 30% and/or severe symptomatology (e.g., obtundation, delirium, bradyarrhythmia, etc.). CO disrupts mitochondrial function, leading to less ATP production due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation.
Answer C: The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production. Carbon monoxide poisoning causes tissue hypoxia and acidosis by decreased coupling of oxidative phosphorylation, a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, decreased ATP production, and increased lactate production. Inhalational induction is delayed in the setting of a right-to-left intracardiac shunt. The rate of inhalational anesthetic induction is determined by minute ventilation, functional residual capacity, blood/gas solubility, cardiac output, cerebral blood flow, and the presence of intracardiac shunts. A right-to-left intracardiac shunt delays inhalational induction since the volatile anesthetic-rich blood returning to the left heart is diluted by volatile anesthetic-poor systemic venous blood from the right heart. In addition, the uptake of inhaled anesthetics is prolonged with a right-to-left shunt due to a decrease in pulmonary blood flow. The chart below shows a summary of the various shunts and how anesthetic agents are affected. The rate of inhalational induction is virtually unchanged in the setting of left-to-right intracardiac shunting.
Answer C: The rate of intravenous induction in the setting of left-to-right shunt is decreased minimally, or not changed at all, due to increased recirculation of drugs into the pulmonary circulation.
Answer D: Intravenous induction is accelerated in the setting of right-to-left intracardiac shunting due to a partial bypass of the pulmonary circulation. Reflex bronchoconstriction is due to parasympathetic stimulation that occurs through the vagus nerve. Reflex bronchoconstriction is a result of the activation of parasympathetic nerves derived from the vagus (CN X) nerve. Sensory afferent nerves in the airway are activated, which send signals to the nucleus of the solitary tract. Efferent signals are sent via parasympathetic nerves, which release acetylcholine, activating both M2 and M3 (muscarinic) receptors on the smooth muscle in the bronchi and bronchioles. Activation of M3 receptors leads to smooth muscle contraction and bronchoconstriction. To prevent excessive bronchoconstriction, prejunctional inhibitory M2 receptors are also activated, which limits the degree of acetylcholine release. Reflex bronchoconstriction can occur with stimuli such as methacholine, cold air, histamine, allergens, and exercise. Stimulation of β-adrenergic receptors causes bronchodilation.
Answer B: There are two types of non-adrenergic non-cholinergic (NANC) neurons in the lungs (inhibitory and excitatory). Inhibitory NANC neurons cause bronchodilation through the effects of peptides such as vasoactive intestinal peptide and nitric oxide. Excitatory NANC neurons are responsible for bronchoconstriction and are activated by neuropeptides such as substance P and neurokinin A. These neuropeptides also stimulate the parasympathetic nervous system in the lungs.
Answer C: Stimulation of muscarinic, not nicotinic, receptors leads to bronchoconstriction. Reflex bronchoconstriction is a result of the activation of parasympathetic nerves derived from the vagus (CN X) nerve.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. This patient has hypoxemic and hypercapnic respiratory insufficiency related to opioids, benzodiazepines, and volatile anesthetic administration with a decrease in glossopharyngeal afferent nerve activity due to impairment of the carotid body chemoreceptors. Unlike CO2 chemoreception, which is mostly central with a smaller peripheral component, PaO2 sensing is purely peripheral, mainly occurring in the carotid bodies, which are paired structures located at the point of carotid bifurcation. PaO2 chemoreceptors can provide a very strong stimulus to the central pattern generator (i.e. pontomedullary network) via the glossopharyngeal nerves and nucleus tractus solitarii. However, since such strong stimulation is only triggered by hypoxic conditions with PaO2 ~55 mmHg, it is not commonly seen under physiological conditions (one example would be at high altitude where climbers with no supplemental oxygen will hyperventilate in spite of respiratory alkalosis). In addition, more recent studies found that the carotid bodies are not silent under normoxic conditions, rather they provide tonic stimulation to the central pattern generator. Because the carotid bodies are very sensitive to inhibition by volatile anesthetics, even at subanesthetic concentrations down to 0.1 MAC, and because the central pattern generator contributes to maintenance of upper airway patency (for example by stimulating the genioglossus muscle), it is likely that volatile-induced inhibition of the carotid bodies can contribute to postoperative airway obstruction in patients at risk such as those with obstructive sleep apnea. The critical closing pressure of the upper airway (Pcrit) is the pressure proximal to the velopharynx at which complete airway collapse occurs with no inspiratory flow during spontaneous breathing. For example if a patient is requiring 5 cm H2O CPAP to prevent complete collapse of the upper airway, then his/her Pcrit at this time is 5 cm H2O. Pcrit is negative in awake individuals, becomes less negative during sleep and often becomes positive during anesthesia
Answer C: Bilateral carotid endarterectomy would result in a similar phenomenon, however, this patient has no history of medical issues, and there is no mention of prior neck surgery or scarring, and thus it would be less likely than medication induced impairment of hypoxic ventilatory drive.
Answer D: The vagus nerve provides innervation to the aortic body which does have a very minimal contribution to control of hypoxic ventilatory drive but not to the extent that the carotid body does and its activity is likely decreased not increased. The carotid body chemoreceptors increase ventilation when PaO2 (not PAO2, CaO2, or SaO2) decreases through afferent impulses via the glossopharyngeal nerve to CNS ventilation centers. Their function is impaired by opioids, benzodiazepines, volatile anesthetics (as low as 0.1 MAC), and bilateral carotid endarterectomy. Do not confuse carotid bodies and carotid sinuses. Both are located at the carotid bifurcation, and impulses from both are transmitted via a branch of the glossopharyngeal (Hering’s nerve) but carotid bodies are chemoreceptors while carotid sinuses are baroreceptors. Peak pressure is used to calculate dynamic respiratory system compliance (C). The static compliance of the respiratory system indicates the “stiffness” of the respiratory system, which includes the lungs and chest wall. It is determined at the end of inspiration when there is no airflow, hence “static.” This can be accomplished, for example, during an inspiratory pause in a mechanically ventilated patient. Since compliance is the change in volume divided by the change in pressure of a system (C = ΔV/ΔP), the following formula is used to calculate static respiratory system compliance: CS = VT ÷ (PPL – PEEP) Where: CS is static compliance, VT is tidal volume, and PPL is plateau pressure. Dynamic respiratory system compliance, which is also a reflection of respiratory system resistance, can be measured at any point during inspiration when there is airflow. Commonly, dynamic compliance is measured using peak pressure during inspiration, the value of which simply replaces plateau pressure in the above formula.  Static respiratory system compliance is calculated using the following formula: CS = VT ÷ (PPL – PEEP). Elastance is the inverse of compliance: E = ΔP/ΔV. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 236-237. Hess DR, Bigatello LM. The chest wall in acute lung injury/acute respiratory distress syndrome. Curr Opin Crit Care. 2008 Feb; 14(1): 94-102. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Pulmonary compliance: Calculation"

The anterior cerebral artery supplies blood to the medial surface of the parietal lobe, which includes part of the primary motor cortex. The part of the cortex which is located medially, is that which gives motor function to the lower limb (B). The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) is a branch off of the internal carotid artery. It supplies blood to the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, the anterior 4/5 of the corpus collosum, the anterior portions of the basal ganglia and internal capsule, and the olfactory bulb and tract. ACA infarcts are rare, representing only 2% of ischemic strokes. The functional areas supplied by the ACA are: - Prefrontal cortex: functions in motivation, planning, and organizing of complex behavior - Supplemental motor area (dominant cortex): functions with Broca’s area for speech - Motor cortex (lower limb) - Sensory cortex (lower limb) ACA strokes on the left can lead to behavioral abnormalities as well as aphasia. Sensory and motor deficits are also commonly seen, but they are more often seen in the lower limb due to the anatomical division of the motor and sensory cortex, where the area of the cortex supplying the lower limb is medial (see picture of motor homunculus below). Right sided ACA strokes, on the other hand, can lead to left leg weakness and sensory deficits, behavioral abnormalities, and left hemineglect. A urine-to-plasma osmolar ratio (UOSM: POSM) >1.5 indicates prerenal oliguria (generally secondary to hypovolemia). In this patient, the urine osmolality would need to be >441 mOsm/kg (294 mOsm/kg x 1.5) (E). The UOSM: POSM is used to assess the tubular response of the kidneys to dehydration or hypovolemia. In this setting of prerenal oliguria, this formula evaluates the kidneys’ ability to retain Na+ and water and produce highly concentrated urine by increasing urine osmolality above 450 mOsm/kg. By comparison, normal plasma osmolality is 280-300 mOsm/kg. The UOSM: POSM indicates the kidneys' ability to concentrate urine. Tubular damage and acute renal failure, therefore, may be represented by a decreased ratio. The UOSM: POSM can also decrease with the administration of diuretics. As an aside, isosthenuria is a UOSM: POSM equal to 1. Answers A & B & C & D: In this patient, the urine osmolality would need to be >441 mOsm/kg (294 mOsm/kg x 1.5).  A UOSM: POSM ratio >1.5 is indicative of prerenal oliguria secondary to dehydration or hypovolemia. The UOSM: POSM evaluates the ability of the kidneys to concentrate urine and increase urine osmolality above normal plasma osmolality in the setting of prerenal oliguria. The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve (ODC) describes the relationship between arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) and the partial pressure of arterial oxygen (PaO2). The sigmoid curve that results from the cooperative binding of oxygen. This means that, when one molecule of oxygen binds to the hemoglobin, the affinity of the hemoglobin for the next oxygen molecule increases. Each hemoglobin can bind up to four oxygen molecules. The ODC can signify changes in hemoglobin affinity for oxygen by shifting either to the left or to the right. A leftward shift is associated with increased hemoglobin affinity, while a rightward shift is associated with decreased hemoglobin affinity. One way to measure the shift of the curve is by referring to the P50 value, which is the oxygen tension (PaO2) when SaO2 is 50%. A normal P50 value is 27 mmHg. A leftward shift will result in a lower P50 value, and a rightward shift will result in an increase in P50 value. Abbreviations: DPG, diphosphoglycerate; Hb, hemoglobin; PO2, partial pressure of oxygen; Temp, temperature. When the affinity of hemoglobin is low (rightward shift), more oxygen molecules can be unloaded from the hemoglobin into the tissues. In normal physiology, the ODC is shifted to the left at the level of the lungs where oxygen molecules must be picked up by the hemoglobin. As the oxygenated blood approaches the level of the tissues, the ODC shifts to the right, allowing these molecules of oxygen to unload. The affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen is affected by many factors. Temperature, hydrogen ion concentration, partial pressure of CO2 (PaCO2), and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) cause the ODC to shift either left or right. • Left shift (P50 < 27): seen with a decrease in temperature, PaCO2, 2,3-DPG, and hydrogen ion concentration (high pH) • Right shift (P50 > 27): seen with an increase in temperature, PaCO2, 2,3-DPG, and hydrogen ion concentration (low pH) Abbreviations: CAD, coronary artery disease; DPG, diphosphoglycerate; H+, hydrogen ion; PaCO2, partial pressure of arterial oxygen; PRBC, packed red blood cell. Other factors, such as drugs, diseases, and electrolytes, can change the affinity of the hemoglobin by affecting the concentration of 2,3-DPG: • Thyroxine has been shown to stimulate the production of 2,3-DPG, causing a rightward shift of the ODC. • Hyperphosphatemia stimulates 2,3-DPG production (rightward shift), while hypophosphatemia decreases 2,3-DPG (leftward shift). • 2,3-Diphosphoglycerate is also increased (rightward shift) in anemia, high-altitude hypoxia, heart failure, liver cirrhosis, and sleep apnea syndrome. • Propranolol causes a rightward shift of the ODC in patients with coronary artery disease, without affecting 2,3-DPG. • Stored packed red blood cells have decreased 2,3-DPG, resulting in a leftward shift. A decrease in hydrogen ion concentration (high pH) causes a leftward shift of the ODC.
Answer C: Myxedema coma, a complication of hypothyroidism, presents with low thyroxine and hypothermia. This results in a leftward shift of the ODC.
Answer D: Transfusion of packed red blood cells causes the ODC to shift to the left due to decreased levels of 2,3-DPG. A leftward shift of oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is caused by a decrease in temperature, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2), hydrogen ion concentration, and 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG). A rightward shift is caused by an increase in temperature, PaCO2, hydrogen ion concentration, and 2,3-DPG. Remember the mnemonic "CADET Face Right". Increase in CO2, Acid, 2,3-Diphosphoglycerate, Exercise, and Temperature result in Right shift. Cadets prefer to unload their guns (oxygen). American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Decreasing the tidal volume to 6 mL/kg (lung-protective strategy) could decrease the risk of renal injury related to positive pressure in the patient in this question by decreasing cytokine release. Multiple reports of studies have linked renal and lung injury together through multiple mechanisms. The ARDSnet trial provided evidence that lung-protective ventilation decreases the incidence of hemodynamic, coagulopathic, and renal complications with a lung-protective strategy. Unfortunately, renal effects secondary to mechanical ventilation are not as simplistic as alterations in cytokine release. Strategies employed to target specific renal consequences from positive pressure ventilation have not been proven effective. Renal effects from mechanical ventilation involve 3 broad categories: hemodynamic, neurohormonal, and biochemical. Induction of positive pressure ventilation affects hemodynamics by decreasing preload and increasing right ventricular afterload (both of which decrease cardiac output and renal blood flow) while promoting increased venous pressure, all of which have deleterious effects on the kidneys. Positive pressure ventilation also results in an increase in sympathetic nervous system output, which secondarily results in an increase in renin release through beta-1 receptor stimulation with resultant release of angiotensin-2 and aldosterone. This results in vasoconstriction with salt and water retention, which can decrease urine output. There is also an increase in the release of antidiuretic hormone (also seen with surgical stress), which increases free water reabsorption and decreases urine output; however, this is a minor component. Finally, there is a decrease in atrial natriuretic peptide, which decreases natriuresis and vasodilation. Biochemically, positive pressure ventilation induces cytokine release, which can cause endothelial activation, increase vascular permeability, and result in apoptosis of renal epithelial cells. The pattern of ventilation can have alterations in the amount of cytokine release and resultant renal injury as previously discussed regarding the ARDSnet trial. There is also evidence that positive pressure ventilation increases the release of nitric oxide and enhances nitric oxide synthase activity. The breakdown products of nitric oxide cause oxidative damage and increased vascular permeability and can result in cellular apoptosis. Sympathetic output is increased with positive pressure ventilation; however, this leads to decreased urine output.
Answer B: Antidiuretic hormone secretion would be decreased compared to a patient on positive pressure ventilation. Positive pressure ventilation exerts deleterious effects on renal function via alterations in hemodynamics, neurohormonal secretion, and biochemical mediator release.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Mechanical Ventilation: Renal Effects" Koyner JL, et al. Mechanical Ventilation and Lung-Kidney Interaction. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2008 Mar;3(2):562-570.

The liver is responsible for the synthesis and release of angiotensinogen. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) is one of the primary regulators of volume and blood pressure. Angiotensinogen circulates in the plasma until cleaved by renin to form angiotensin I. Renin is released by the juxtaglomerular apparatus in response to β1 activation, decreased renal perfusion pressure (glomerulus), or decreased NaCl concentration at the macula densa (distal convoluted tubule). Angiotensin I is cleaved to form the active angiotensin II by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the lungs. There are a multitude of biological compounds produced by the liver; many are shown in the table below. Notably, factor 3 (tissue factor), factor 4 (calcium), von Willebrand factor (endothelium), tPA, and platelets (megakaryocytes) are not primarily synthesized by the liver. Glucose (gluconeogenesis) Gamma-glutamyltransferase (GGT) Antithrombin III Plasminogen Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is released from the heart in response to myocardial stretch receptors in the right and left ventricles similarly to atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) released from the atria. Both ANP and BNP cause vasodilation, natriuresis/diuresis, and inhibition of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system in response to volume overload states (CHF, cirrhosis, renal failure, right heart failure). BNP causes inhibition of the sodium-potassium ATPase in the collecting ducts to promote sodium excretion.
Answer C: Platelets are synthesized and released by megakaryocytes, which are produced in the bone marrow. Of note, thrombopoietin (TPO) is produced by the liver and stimulates bone marrow release of megakaryocytes. Thrombocytopenia is a common finding in cirrhosis given a deficiency of TPO and hypersplenism.
Answer D: VWF is synthesized from the Weibel-Palade bodies and subendothelium. Desmopressin (or DDAVP) is sometimes used to facilitate the release of vWF in coagulopathic patients or in patients with von Willebrand disease via activation of the V2 receptor. Angiotensinogen is synthesized in the liver. The majority of clotting factors are synthesized and released from the liver with notable exceptions of factors 3, 4, and von Willebrand factor. Platelets are synthesized by megakaryocytes in the plasma. Factor VIII is synthesized in the liver as well as endothelial cells. Thus, it remains at normal (or high) levels when other factors are deficient in liver disease. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline 2014. Compliance is the change in volume divided by the change in pressure of a system (C = ΔV/ΔP) which is the inverse of elastance (E = ΔP/ΔV). The compliance (or elastance) of the respiratory system is dependent on the compliance (or elastance) of the lungs and the chest wall. Elastance of the respiratory system is simply the sum of its two components, but since compliance is the inverse of elastance: 1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW Where C is compliance, RS is respiratory system, L is lungs, and CW is chest wall. Therefore, using the above values, the CCW can be calculated: 1/CCW = 1/CRS – 1/CL 1/CCW = 1/100 – 1/200 = 2/200 – 1/200 1/CCW = 1/200 CCW = 200 Although it is unlikely to be encountered for testing purposes, CCW is directly calculated using the formula below: CCW = VT ÷ (PPL – PATM) Where VT is tidal volume, PPL is pleural pressure, and PATM is atmospheric pressure. However, under most circumstances PATM = 0 (except in the setting of negative pressure such as from an "iron lung" ventilator), so the calculation can be simplified: CCW = VT ÷ PPL Answers A & C & D: 1/CCW = 1/CRS – 1/CL = 1/200  The following formula summarizes the relationship of respiratory system compliance and its two components: 1/CRS = 1/CL + 1/CCW. Chest wall compliance is relatively high in neonates due to a pliable rib cage. However, this increases work of breathing since the rib cage provides less mechanical support, which in turn leads to significant retractions and earlier functional airway closure. Epinephrine is a potent vasoconstrictor and would be expected to decrease renal blood flow without increasing the glomerular filtration rate (GFR). While renal blood flow is autoregulated under normal physiologic conditions, it is also greatly impacted by other factors. The sympathetic nervous system provides constant baseline vascular tone, and, as sympathetic output (including the release of epinephrine) increases, renal afferent tone increases as well, which reduces blood flow to the kidney. Renal blood flow is also regulated by the renin-angiotensin system. Renin, a molecule released by the renal system in times of low blood flow, converts angiotensinogen in the bloodstream to angiotensin I. In the pulmonary system, this is further converted to angiotensin II, which is a potent vasoconstrictor. However, angiotensin II preferentially constricts the efferent renal vasculature, thereby relatively increasing GFR but also decreasing the renal blood flow. At very high levels of activation, angiotensin II loses its preferential effects on the efferent vasculature and reduces renal blood flow by strongly constricting the afferent and efferent vasculature. Angiotensin II also promotes the release of aldosterone, which increases sodium and water resorption, leading to higher blood pressure in general. Finally, various other local and hormonal factors also influence renal blood flow, including the vasodilators nitric oxide, prostaglandins, and atrial natriuretic peptide. Although angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor, the efferent arterioles will preferentially be affected, thereby increasing the GFR while slightly reducing the renal blood flow. Additionally, the increase in systemic blood pressure caused by angiotensin II will also help to maintain renal perfusion. At supraphysiologic levels, angiotensin II will constrict both afferent and efferent vasculature, thereby reducing renal blood flow.
Answer B: Atrial natriuretic peptide is released from the atria in response to high filling pressures. Atrial natriuretic peptide is a vasodilator of the afferent arterioles and a vasoconstrictor of the efferent arterioles and will, therefore, increase blood flow to the kidneys when it is released in response to stretching of the atria. The sympathetic nervous system provides baseline vascular tone in the kidney and, when it is activated, causes vasoconstriction that can decrease renal blood flow. Inhaled anesthetics cause transient, reversible depression in renal function. Glomerular filtration rate, renal blood flow, urine output, and urinary excretion of sodium are decreased. Excessive and rapid administration of normal saline can lead to a nonanion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with decreased plasma bicarbonate (HCO3−), increased plasma chloride (Cl−), and a decreased plasma strong ion difference (SID). Normal (0.9%) saline solution contains 154 mEq each of Na+ and Cl−. It has a strong ion difference of 0 because both sodium and chloride are strong ions. Normal human plasma has a SID of 40 to 44 mEq/L. Therefore, rapid administration of normal saline will cause a decrease in SID (by decreasing from 40 to 44 mEq/L closer to 0), leading to acidemia. The concept of SID proposes that plasma pH is determined by three independent factors: PCO2, SID, and total plasma concentration of nonvolatile buffers (Atot). The latter (Atot) represents the total plasma concentration of nonvolatile buffers (eg, albumin, globulins, and inorganic phosphate). Strong ion difference represents the difference between the charge of plasma strong cations (sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium) and anions (chloride and other strong anions [A−] such as lactate, sulfate, ketoacids, and nonesterified fatty acids). SID = ( [Na+] + [K+] + [Ca2+] + [Mg2+] ) - ( [Cl−] + [A−] ) ≈ 40 to 44 mEq/L. The increase in Cl−is compensated for by a decrease in HCO3−. The anion gap, therefore, typically remains in a normal range. Anion Gap = ([Na+] + [K+]) - ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]). Therapy for saline-induced hyperchloremic acidosis consists of intravenous administration of a crystalloid solution with a high SID, such as sodium bicarbonate or tromethamine ("Tham" solution). The SID will decrease, not increase, and the anion gap will be largely unchanged.
Answer C: The SID will decrease, not increase, due to the strong ion difference of normal saline being 0 mEq/L and the normal strong ion difference of the plasma being 40 mEq/L. A large volume infusion of normal saline will bring the normal 40 mEq/L closer to 0 mEq/L. Large volumes and rapid administration of normal saline can produce a nonanion gap hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Associated laboratory values include decreased plasma HCO3−, increased plasma Cl−, decreased strong ion difference, and a normal anion gap.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Anesth Analg. 2003;96:919-22.

Fetal hemoglobin shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, which decreases oxygen unloading allowing fetal hemoglobin to hold onto oxygen more tightly. This improves oxygen delivery to the fetus from the placenta. Causes of right shift include increases in factors such as pCO2, acidity or [H+] (so a decreased pH), 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), exercise, and temperature. Leftward shifts are due to decreases in these factors as well as increases in carbon monoxide, methemoglobinemia, and HbF (fetal hemoglobin). Oxygen is primarily transported in the blood via hemoglobin in red blood cells. It is also dissolved to a much lesser degree. The oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve describes the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen (pO2) and the % oxygen saturation of hemoglobin (SaO2). The graphical relationship between these 2 variables can best be described as sigmoidal shaped due to cooperative binding which refers to the phenomenon of oxygen binding further increasing the affinity for additional oxygen molecules to bind to the hemoglobin. The P50 refers to the oxygen tension at which the hemoglobin is 50% saturated. Under normal circumstances, P50 in adults is 26.7 mmHg. Several factors can alter the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen which results in a left or right shift on the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. Decreased affinity is represented by a rightward shift and is characterized by increased oxygen displacement from hemoglobin to be released to other tissues. The P50 is also increased with a rightward shift. Causes of right shift include increases in pCO2, acidity or [H+] (so a decreased pH), 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), exercise, and temperature. 2,3-DPG is formed in red blood cells and is part of an adaptive mechanism in which its production is increased in the presence of anemia or hypoxia. The rightward shift associated with increased 2,3-DPG levels allows more oxygen to be released at peripheral tissues. An increase in CO2 resulting in a rightward shift is known as the Bohr effect. Hemoglobin's increased affinity for oxygen is represented by a leftward shift and is associated with a lower P50. Leftward shifts can be caused by opposite changes compared to rightward shifts including decreases in pCO2, acidity or [H+], 2,3-DPG, and temperature. Low levels of 2,3-DPG can be seen in states such as sepsis and hypophosphatemia. Additionally, since hemoglobin binds to carbon monoxide around 240 times more readily compared to oxygen, the presence of carbon monoxide results in a leftward shift. Methemoglobinemia also shifts the curve to the left. Lastly, fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is structurally different from normal hemoglobin and the dissociation curve for HbF is relatively leftward shifted. Fetal arterial oxygen partial pressures are low and the left shift increases oxygen uptake at the placenta. HbF persists in a newborn until about 2-4 months of age and is usually completely replaced by adult hemoglobin at 6 months. Increased 2,3-DPG concentration causes a shift to the right.
Answer C: Alkalosis causes a shift to the left. This decreases the dissociation of oxygen from hemoglobin (holds on to oxygen). Acidosis would shift the curve to the right. Hyperthermia, acidosis, high pCO2, and high levels of 2,3-DPG cause a shift to the right. Fetal hemoglobin shifts the curve to the left.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of inhaled anesthetics is increased by use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI). Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia. Other factors include increasing age (especially > 40), hypoxia, hypothermia, induced hypotension, anemia, and certain drugs including α-2 agonists, lithium, large doses of cholinesterase inhibitors, lidocaine, opioids, barbiturates, and calcium channel blockers. By contrast, there are fewer factors that increase MAC. These include hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g., as caused by MAOIs, acute amphetamine use, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa). In general, those factors that decrease central nervous system (CNS) metabolic activity, neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and down-regulate CNS responses to chronically elevated neurotransmitter levels decrease MAC. Those factors that increase CNS metabolic activity and neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and up-regulate CNS responses to chronically depressed neurotransmitter levels increase MAC. Answers A & B & D & E: Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia.  Hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g. MAOIs, amphetamine, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa use) increase MAC requirements for anesthetic agents.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "MAC / Factors That Increase, Decrease" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 424-425.

Increasing hemoglobin increases arterial oxygen content, which will lead to increased oxygen delivery, assuming no concurrent changes in cardiac output. Oxygen delivery (DO2) is determined by the equation: DO2 = CO x CaO2, where CO is cardiac output and CaO2 is arterial oxygen content. Therefore, an increase in either CO or CaO2 will increase oxygen delivery. Each component of this equation can be further broken down to illustrate various physiologic effects on oxygen delivery. CaO2 = [(SaO2)(Hb x 1.34)] + (0.0031 x PaO2) Where: SaO2 is arterial oxygen saturation, Hb is hemoglobin, PaO2 is partial pressure of arterial oxygen. Assuming all other variables remain stable, this equation illustrates that when SaO2, Hb (A), or PaO2 increase, CaO2 and, therefore DO2 increase. Note, however, that increases in PaO2 usually produce a negligible increase in CaO2. Any decrease in CO will result in a decrease in oxygen delivery. Cardiac output can be described by several different equations. At its simplest: CO = HR x SV, where HR is heart rate and SV is stroke volume. This shows that increases in HR or SV can increase DO2, again assuming all other variables remain constant. Stroke volume, in turn, is determined by cardiac preload, afterload, and contractility. Increasing cardiac preload or cardiac contractility or decreasing cardiac afterload will increase CO (if the heart rate remains stable) and therefore DO2. Alternately, CO can be represented by: CO = BP / SVR, where BP is systemic blood pressure and SVR is systemic vascular resistance. Accordingly, as SVR increases, CO decreases if there is not a compensatory increase in blood pressure. Increasing SVR alone will decrease the CO (by increasing the afterload) and reduce DO2.
Answer C: Decreasing cardiac contractility will decreased CO and reduce DO2. Oxygen delivery is determined by CO and CaO2. Increases in HR, SV, and BP increase cardiac output and therefore DO2. Cardiac output and DO2 are inversely proportional to SVR. Increases in SaO2, Hb, and PaO2 increase CaO2 and therefore DO2.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "O2 transport: Quantitative aspects" Source: Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 212-213, 251.

When cardiopulmonary function is normal (absence of shunting), PCNS = Pblood = Palveoli. The goal of delivering inhaled anesthetics is to produce the anesthetic state by establishing a specific concentration of anesthetic molecules in the central nervous system (CNS). This is done by establishing the specific partial pressure of the agent in the lungs, which ultimately equilibrates with the brain and the spinal cord. For inhaled anesthetics at equilibrium, CNS partial pressure (PCNS) equals blood partial pressure (Pblood), which in turn equals alveolar partial pressure (Palveoli). This equilibration is primarily the result of three factors. Inhaled anesthetics are gasses that are rapidly transferred bidirectionally via the lungs to and from the bloodstream and subsequently to and from CNS tissues as partial pressures equilibrate. Plasma and tissues have a low capacity to absorb the inhaled anesthetics relative to the amount one can deliver to the lungs, allowing one to quickly establish or abolish anesthetizing concentrations of anesthetic in the bloodstream and ultimately the CNS. Metabolism, excretion, and redistribution of the inhaled anesthetics are minimal relative to the rate at which they are delivered or removed from the lungs; this permits easy maintenance of blood and CNS concentrations. Answers A & B: The relationships between PCNS, Pblood, and Palveoli are not additive and are not associated with a gradient at equilibrium.  As long as normal cardiopulmonary function exists (i.e. no intrapulmonary, intracardiac, or cardiopulmonary shunting), PCNS = Pblood = Palveoli of inhaled anesthetics at equilibrium.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Anesth partial pressures at equilibrium" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 415.

Argatroban is a direct oral thrombin (factor IIa) inhibitor. Direct thrombin inhibitors function by selectively inhibiting factor IIa. The only orally administered direct thrombin inhibitor is dabigatran. Argatroban, bivalirudin, and desirudin are intravenously administered direct thrombin inhibitors. These anticoagulants are easy to manage, and, because regular monitoring is not required, patient compliance is improved. An antidote for dabigatran is the monoclonal antibody idarucizumab. Abbreviations: UFH, unfractionated heparin; LMWH, low molecular-weight heparin. Apixaban is a selective, direct oral factor Xa inhibitor. Similarly to dabigatran, regular monitoring is not required.
Answer C: Dalteparin is an LMWH. It results in the indirect inhibition of factor Xa.
Answer D: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist that inhibits hepatic vitamin K epoxide reductase. As a result, there is a decrease in hepatic synthesis of the reduced, active form of vitamin K. Ultimately, this leads to a decrease in the γ-carboxylation and synthesis of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and proteins C and S. Dabigatran is a direct oral thrombin (factor IIa) inhibitor that does not require regular monitoring, which results in improved overall patient compliance. There are two forms of heparin, unfractionated heparin and low molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), both of which bind antithrombin III (ATIII), causing a conformational change resulting in anticoagulation. Unfractionated heparin results in enhanced ATIII degradation of thrombin and factor Xa, whereas LMWH causes much more specific ATIII inhibition of factor Xa. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Miller's Anesthesia. Ch. 50: Patient Blood Management and Coagulation: Antithrombotics, Thrombolytics, and Procoagulant Drugs. 9th edition.

The proportion of alveolar (FA) anesthetic concentration to inspired (FI) anesthetic concentration (FA/FI) will rise faster with agents with a lower blood to gas partition coefficient (insoluble agents). The blood:gas partition coefficient is a distribution ratio describing how a volatile anesthetic (and nitrous oxide) distributes itself between the liquid (blood) phase and the gaseous phase (in the alveoli) when the partial pressures are identical in both phases. If the blood:gas partition coefficient is > 1, then more drug is dissolved within the blood (higher solubility, such as isoflurane or halothane). If the blood:gas partition coefficient is < 1, more drug exists in the gaseous state than dissolved in blood (lower solubility, such as desflurane or nitrous oxide). These relationships hold as long as the partial pressures are EQUAL in both phases. The rate of induction of volatile anesthetics is determined by the rate at which equilibrium is established between three compartments: the alveoli, the blood, and the brain. Agents with higher blood:gas partition coefficients (soluble agents) will readily dissolve in alveolar venous blood. This will reduce the rate of rise of FA/FI (since FA does not increase as quickly) and therefore slow the rate of induction. Achieving equilibrium between the three compartments will therefore take longer. Every volatile anesthetic regardless of solubility has an initial rapid rise in alveolar concentration due to lack of uptake by the blood. Solubility and rate of uptake begin to affect FA/FI once the anesthetic gas begins to pass into the alveolar venous blood. Highly soluble agents have a slower rate of rise of FA/FI when compared to insoluble agents delivered with the same minute ventilation and cardiac output.
Answer C: Increasing minute ventilation will allow for rapid replacement of highly absorbed, soluble agents and increase the rate of rise of FA/FI. By contrast, inhaled anesthetics with very low blood and tissue solubility have an extremely rapid rise in FA/FI with induction. This suggests that there is very little room to improve uptake by increasing ventilation. A reduction in cardiac output will increase the proportion of blood saturated by the anesthetic gas and slow the rate of uptake by the alveolar venous blood. This will also result in a faster rate of induction and rise of FA/FI. During an inhalational induction, the FA/FI ratio of insoluble agents (e.g. desflurane, nitrous oxide) rises more quickly than that of soluble agents because insoluble agents are not readily taken up and dissolved into alveolar venous blood. Moderate changes in cardiac output and minute ventilation do not significantly alter the rate of rise of FA/FI of insoluble agents. The rate of induction for soluble agents with higher blood:gas partition coefficients (e.g. isoflurane, halothane) can be increased significantly with higher minute ventilation and a reduction in cardiac output. Inhaled anesthetics depress spontaneous ventilation. Minute ventilation will decrease (increased respiratory rate but decreased tidal volume) with increased inspired concentration and so will the rate of rise of FA/FI. This adds a margin of safety in preventing an overdose during spontaneous breathing induction. Controlled ventilation does not offer this margin of safety. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 415, 417-420. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Volatile Anesthetics: Ventilation Effects"

Aspirin inhibits platelet aggregation by blocking thromboxane synthesis. Aspirin inhibits the enzyme cyclooxygenase (COX). COX mediates the biotransformation of arachidonic acid into three eicosanoid compounds: prostaglandin, prostacyclin, and thromboxane. Platelet aggregation in response to epinephrine and ADP is only partially inhibited by aspirin. Thromboxane is responsible for platelet aggregation. The prevention of its formation by aspirin prevents platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet. Thromboxane is also a potent vasoconstrictor, and its inhibition may promote coronary perfusion. Prostacyclins are potent vasodilators that are also involved in platelet activation, though not aggregation. With lowdose aspirin therapy, prostacyclin production is selectively spared, decreasing clot formation and vasoconstriction seen with thromboxane production while still allowing vasodilation from prostacyclin.
Answer B: Prostaglandins are involved in mediating smooth muscle tone. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX, thereby preventing the synthesis of Thromboxane-A2.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Aspirin: platelet effect" Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Pages 399

Benzodiazepines do have some effects on the respiratory system, contrary to what some sources suggest. Benzodiazepines cause a decrease in tidal volume, which causes a decrease in minute ventilation. The respiratory rate is often preserved, but with higher doses of medication apnea may occur. The depression in minute ventilation seen after midazolam occurs rapidly (less than 5 minutes) and lasts for about 1 hour. Benzodiazepines are synergistic with opioids to depress minute ventilation. Benzodiazepines are anxiolytic, sedating, and amnestic; all properties that may be advantageous prior to surgery. Commonly used benzodiazepines include midazolam, lorazepam, and diazepam. Benzodiazepines act on the GABAa receptor and lorazepam has the highest affinity for the GABAa receptor of those listed. Midazolam has the fastest onset of action and shortest duration of action for those listed. Benzodiazepines reduce cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate. Additionally, benzodiazepines increase the seizure threshold and are often used to terminate seizures. Benzodiazepines have only moderate effects on the cardiovascular system, in a dose dependent manner. Midazolam causes the greatest decrease in mean arterial pressure of the benzodiazepines listed, but those effects are less pronounced than propofol or thiopental. Heart rate and cardiac output are unaffected by benzodiazepines. Benzodiazepines do not cause impairment of the gag reflex. Opioid medications depress upper and lower airway reflexes as well as suppress cough with antitussive properties. Opioids are often used to prevent ventilator dyssynchrony and increase tolerance of endotracheal intubation. Benzodiazepines suppress the baroreceptor reflexes.
Answer C: Benzodiazepines do have effects on the respiratory system, especially at higher doses. Benzodiazepines decrease minute ventilation and decrease the sensitivity to CO2. Benzodiazepines also are synergistic with opioids causing much more respiratory depression than either agent individually. Midazolam and all benzodiazepines cause a dose dependent decrease in minute ventilation. The decreased minute ventilation is mainly a result of decreased tidal volume. Benzodiazepines decrease the respiratory sensitivity to CO2 and act synergistically with opioids.  Miller, Ronald D. Miller’s Anesthesia. 7th edition. 2010. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Benzodiazepines: Respiratory Effects"

Efficacy is the maximum effect of a drug. It does not depend on dose. Potency is the relative dose required to achieve a given effect and is related to receptor affinity. Efficacy is the maximum effect of a drug. For example, morphine has a higher efficacy than buprenorphine because morphine is a full agonist while buprenorphine is a partial agonist at the mu-opioid receptor. Potency is the dose required to produce a given effect. The smaller the dose needed for a given effect, the higher the potency. For example, the potency of isoflurane is higher than desflurane because isoflurane has a lower MAC. Curve X represents the dose-effect curve of drug X. Curve Y represents the dose-effect curve of a full agonist of drug X, called drug Y. Curve Z represents the dose-effect curve of a partial agonist of drug X, called drug Z. Although the efficacy (maximum effect) of drug Y may reach that of drug X, the efficacy of drug Z will not reach that of drug X due to its partial agonism. The potency of a partial agonist may be higher than the potency of a full agonist depending on the doses of each. The potency of a partial agonist (curve Z) might be greater than a full agonist (curve Y) if a high dose of partial agonist is used. Relative dose to achieve a desired effect describes potency.
Answer B: Potency is not related to maximal effect. This describes efficacy.
Answer D: The efficacy (maximum effect) of a full agonist (curve Y) is always greater than the efficacy of a partial agonist.
Answer E: A partial agonist will have a flatter (NOT steeper) dose-effect curve. Efficacy is the maximum effect of a drug. It does not depend on dose. Potency is the relative dose required to achieve a given effect and is related to receptor affinity. The potency of a partial agonist may be higher than that of a full agonist. The efficacy of a partial agonist cannot be higher than that of a full agonist.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Efficacy / Potency: Definitions" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Page 170. Stoelting, Basics of Anesthesia, 5th edition, pp. pp. 45-46.

The amnesia provided by midazolam is anterograde in nature, meaning that the formation of new memories is inhibited after administration of the drug. Midazolam is a fast-acting benzodiazepine that is used for perioperative anxiolysis and sedation. It has the added benefit of providing dose-dependent amnesia, making it a useful preoperative adjunct. All benzodiazepine medications provide sedation, anxiolysis, and amnesia, although the dose required varies depending on the particular drug. Receptor subtype or occupancy determines the clinical profile of these medications. While increasing receptor occupancy may increase the number of patients who experience complete anterograde amnesia, midazolam at doses of 2 to 3 mg reduces recall during induction when it is used with propofol. Prevention of pre–induction recall requires administration of larger doses of at least 5 mg in adults. Midazolam causes anterograde amnesia.
Answer C: Midazolam primarily causes anterograde, not retrograde, amnesia. Retrograde amnesia is when memories created before drug administration are lost. Some reports contain low-quality evidence for retrograde amnesia with midazolam, especially in the period immediately prior (approximately one minute) to administration, but this is not the primary cause of amnesia by midazolam. Midazolam causes anterograde but not retrograde amnesia, even at large doses. Typical anxiolysis doses (eg, 2 mg IV in an adult) do not guarantee amnesia.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword.
