The correct precurarization dosage for any nondepolarizing agent prior to succinylcholine administration is 10% of the ED95 dose. For rocuronium, this would be 0.03 mg/kg. Succinylcholine is a medication that has been used in anesthesia practice since the 1950s. It has a rapid onset and short duration, making it an ideal muscle relaxant for rapid intubating conditions. It is a depolarizing muscle relaxant that works by activating acetylcholine receptors causing depolarization prior to muscle paralysis. One of the foremost reasons it is used is in patients with ‘full stomachs’, where the endotracheal tube must be placed into the trachea rapidly in an attempt to prevent pulmonary aspiration. Muscle fasciculations occur after administration of succinylcholine in 80%-90% of patients, which can result in an increase in the intraabdominal pressure. Normally the difference between intragastric pressure (typical mean value of 10 cmH2O) and lower esophageal sphincter pressure (normal value 36 cmH2O) prevents reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus. When succinylcholine is given, the increase in intragastric pressure due to fasciculations can reach levels as high as 40 cmH2O, which may lead to aspiration of gastric contents into the esophagus and potentially the pulmonary tree. Precurarization with a small dose of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent has been proposed to help decrease muscle fasciculation and the subsequent rise in intraabdominal pressure. Precurarization is not without risk since overdosage of the nondepolarizing agent may cause weakness, patient distress, difficulty breathing, gastroesophageal regurgitation, and even pulmonary aspiration. Furthermore, precurarization reduces the neuromuscular blocking potency of succinylcholine and it also delays the onset of action. The intubating dosage of succinylcholine should be increased from 1 mg/kg to 1.5 mg/kg when precurarization is used due to this antagonism from the nondepolarizing agent. An appropriate dosage for precurarization is 10% of the ED95. The recommended dosage is often inaccurately doubled or tripled in other specialty textbooks and even in some of the anesthesia literature. Alternatively, sometimes this is misunderstood to be 10% of the intubating dose. Understanding effective dose, ED50 and ED95, will help clarify the difference. Since there is response variability to any medication within a population, the effective dose (ED) is often used as a starting point for medication administration. The ED50 is the median effective dose that will produce an effect in 50% of the population that it is administered to. ED95 would refer to the median effective dose in 95% of the population, but unfortunately this terminology has a different meaning for nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs. The ED95 for nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs is the dose that causes 95% twitch suppression in 50% of the population. The dose used for tracheal intubation is typically twice the ED95, although this is variable and depends on the muscle relaxant used – see the chart below. There have been studies which show doubling the dose of rocuronium to 20% of the ED95 (i.e. 10% of intubating dose) can cause an unacceptable increase in the risk for side effects such as blurred vision, heavy eyelids, voice changes, difficulty swallowing, and dyspnea. Precurarization should be given approximately 3-5 minutes prior to administration of succinylcholine. Rocuronium is the most common medication to be used for precurarization in modern anesthesia practice since pancuronium, vecuronium, cisatracurium, and mivacurium are not as effective as defasciculants. Precuraization can also be used for other purposes such as speeding the onset of action of a nondepolarizing medication, helping to decrease the risk of muscle pain due to fasciculations, and potentially diminishing the increase in intracranial pressure that can be seen with fasciculations. Precurarization does not have any effect on the increase in intraocular pressure that is seen with fasciculations, nor does it seem to play a significant role in the increase in potassium that can be seen following succinylcholine administration. Example: for a 70kg adult the precurarization dose with rocuronium is approximately 2mg. Answers B & C & D: The ED95 for nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs is the dose that causes 95% twitch suppression in 50% of the population. The dose used for tracheal intubation is typically twice the ED95, although this is variable and depends on the muscle relaxant used – see the chart below. There have been studies which show doubling the dose of rocuronium to 20% of the ED95 (i.e. 10% of intubating dose) can cause an unacceptable increase in the risk for side effects such as blurred vision, heavy eyelids, voice changes, difficulty swallowing, and dyspnea. Precurarization should be given approximately 3-5 minutes prior to administration of succinylcholine. Rocuronium is the most common medication to be used for precurarization in modern anesthesia practice since pancuronium, vecuronium, cisatracurium, and mivacurium are not as effective as defasciculants.  The recommended precurarization dosage for a nondepolarizing agent is 10% of the ED95, given about 3-5 minutes prior to succinylcholine. Using 10% of the intubating dose (20% of the ED95) is associated with an unacceptably high rate of side effects, including dyspnea in an awake patient.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Rhabdomyolysis induced by succinylcholine is the most likely cause of the elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) in the patient described in this question with muscular dystrophy. There are numerous causes of rhabdomyolysis. Some causes include direct injury to the cell membrane from crushing, tearing, burning, positioning, and dissolving of the muscle. Muscle cell hypoxia can occur when anaerobic conditions persist secondary to shock states, vascular occlusion, and/or tissue compression. Other causes include medications, infection, temperature extremes, and myopathies. Rhabdomyolysis during and after surgery is rare, although it can occur secondary to trauma, positioning, or medication administration. Rhabdomyolysis consists of the dissolution of skeletal muscles, causing the intracellular contents from myocytes to gain access to the circulatory system. These contents include myoglobin, potassium, and creatinine kinase, which in large amounts can be toxic. This release can lead to electrolyte disturbances, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, and myoglobinuric renal failure. Rhabdomyolysis after administration of succinylcholine or volatile anesthetic can occur as a consequence of malignant hyperthermia. However, myoglobinemia and increased serum creatinine kinase have been reported after succinylcholine administration without the malignant hyperthermia picture. It has been hypothesized that this is caused by shearing forces that are set up by asynchronous contraction of adjacent muscle cells after their activation by succinylcholine. After it has been administered, succinylcholine causes massive changes in ion distribution, with contraction, swelling, and subsequent damage resulting in rhabdomyolysis. The risk of rhabdomyolysis is highest in patients with neuromuscular disorders including but not limited to myotonic dystrophy, central core disease, and Becker dystrophy. Volatile anesthetics have been implicated in causing rhabdomyolysis after malignant hyperthermia; however, there also have been cases of isolated rhabdomyolysis secondary to volatile anesthetic administration without evidence of malignant hyperthermia, especially in patients with muscular dystrophy. It is now thought that these patients do not have a higher risk of developing malignant hyperthermia compared with the general population. However, succinylcholine should be avoided in patients with muscular dystrophy because of risk of hyperkalemia and rhabdomyolysis. Some experts still recommend a nontriggering anesthetic in patients with dystrophinopathies, although many have received halogenated volatile anesthetics without complication. Among medications commonly administered perioperatively, halogenated volatile anesthetics have been associated with rhabdomyolysis in susceptible patients. Nitrous oxide is not a halogenated volatile agent.
Answer B: Propofol has been associated with rhabdomyolysis in the setting of propofol infusion syndrome (PRIS), which presents with metabolic acidosis, cardiac dysfunction, rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, or hypertriglyceridemia after initiation of propofol. The patient described in this question received a bolus, not an infusion, of propofol and would not be at risk of PRIS.
Answer C: Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker agents of either the aminosteroidal and benzylisoquinolinium type are less likely than succinylcholine to have been the cause of rhabdomyolysis. Rhabdomyolysis consists of the dissolution of skeletal muscles, causing the intracellular contents from myocytes, including myoglobin, potassium, and creatinine kinase, to gain access to the circulatory system, which in large amounts can be toxic and lead to electrolyte disturbances, metabolic acidosis, coagulopathy, and myoglobinuric renal failure. Rhabdomyolysis can occur after a multitude of clinical pictures. Among medications commonly administered perioperatively, halogenated volatile anesthetics, succinylcholine, corticosteroids, and long durations (days) of propofol infusions have been associated with rhabdomyolysis in susceptible patients. One of the most common side effects of fospropofol is paresthesias (D), which occur in >50% of patients. Paresthesias occur with propofol in 10-20% of patients. Fospropofol was approved by the FDA in 2008 for use in MAC sedation. It is a water-soluble prodrug that is hydrolyzed to propofol by endothelial and hepatic alkaline phosphatases. Metabolism also liberates phosphate and formaldehyde, but blood levels of both of these compounds do not become significantly elevated. Compared to propofol, fospropofol has a slower onset of action (approximately 4-10 minutes, depending on dose) since it must first be metabolized to propofol. Due to this slower onset of action, the incidence of respiratory depression, apnea, and hypotension is lower compared to propofol. Paresthesias are the most common side effect of fospropofol use occurring in approximately 50-70% of patients (D), typically within the first five minutes following the initial dose of drug. They include burning, tingling, and/or stinging sensations and usually occur in the perianal or genital regions. Other areas where paresthesias have been known to occur include the buttocks, chest, ears, and nose. The paresthesias resolve spontaneously and pretreatment with local anesthetics, NSAIDs, or opioids does not decrease their incidence. Paresthesias occur with propofol in approximately 10-20% of patients, usually occur at the site of injection, and the severity and incidence may be decreased with pretreatment, such as with local anesthetics. Pruritus is also a common side effect of fospropofol, occurring in 15-30% of patients. The pruritus is usually localized to the genitals, though it may be generalized. The incidence of pruritus associated with propofol is 1-3% and is more commonly generalized or localized to the area of injection. Bacterial contamination of or growth in fospropofol, and subsequent patient inoculation, is significantly less likely than with propofol since the former does not utilize a lipid-containing oil-water emulsion (B). The lipid base of propofol can allow bacterial growth; preservatives, such as EDTA, must be added to decrease this risk. At sedation doses, propofol causes apnea of ≥30 seconds in approximately 10-25% of patients whereas the incidence of apnea with fospropofol is < 10% (A). Significant hypotension occurs with propofol in 5-25% of patients and in approximately 5% of patients with fospropofol (C).  The most common side effects of the water-soluble propofol prodrug fospropofol are paresthesias (typically perianal or genital) and genital pruritus. Due to its slower onset of action, the incidence of respiratory depression, apnea, and hypotension are lower with fospropofol compared to propofol.  Bengalorkar GM, et al. Amiodarone treatment can result in sinus bradycardia (pulse < 60 bpm) primarily via the calcium channel-blocking properties of amiodarone. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic that functions by blocking voltage-gated potassium channels prolonging the repolarization of the cardiac action potential. A secondary mechanism of action is decreasing conduction via the atrioventricular and sinus nodes by blocking sodium and calcium channels and β-receptors. Amiodarone is the only antiarrhythmic with little to no negative inotropic effects, making it a good option for patients with a reduced ejection fraction. Amiodarone is commonly used to treat acute ventricular tachycardia, persistent ventricular fibrillation after defibrillation, and refractory atrial fibrillation. Side effects are numerous due to amiodarone accumulation in tissues and affect nearly every organ system. Various side effects of amiodarone • Hypotension • QT prolongation Liver • Hepatitis • Cirrhosis • Momentary elevation in AST/ALT • AST • ALT Lungs • Acute respiratory distress syndrome • Pulmonary fibrosis • Chronic interstitial pneumonitis • Organizing pneumonia • Chest radiography • Pulmonary function tests Thyroid* • Hypothyroidism/hyperthyroidism • Thyroid-stimulating hormone Skin • Blue discoloration • Photosensitivity • Physical examination Abbreviations: ALT, alanine aminotransferase; AST, aspartate aminotransferase. *Amiodarone contains 37% iodine by weight. Amiodarone can lead to QT prolongation, but rarely is this prolongation proarrhythmic. Prolonged QTc is > 440 ms in men and > 460 ms in women. The QT interval varies with heart rate. Increased heart rates have shorter QT intervals, and decreased heart rates have longer QT intervals. Thus, the QT interval can be corrected for heart rate (QTc = QT/√cardiac cycle in seconds). Bradycardia is more common than QTc prolongation.
Answer C: Severe abdominal pain is associated with digoxin toxicity and is not a common side effect of amiodarone. Bradycardia can be seen with amiodarone treatment primarily as a result of the calcium channel-blocking properties of amiodarone. Other significant side effects include hyperthyroidism/hypothyroidism, pulmonary fibrosis, chronic interstitial pneumonitis, atrioventricular block, blue discoloration of the skin, peripheral neuropathy, and corneal deposits. Because amiodarone is a cytochrome (CYP) P450 inhibitor, care must be taken when medications that are metabolized by the CYP system are given. One noteworthy interaction with amiodarone is warfarin. When warfarin is given with amiodarone, the effects of warfarin are potentiated because its degradation by CYP enzymes is inhibited, increasing the concentration of warfarin. Desflurane degradation in the presence of desiccated carbon dioxide absorbent results in carbon monoxide production. When a carbon dioxide absorbent is very low on water content, degradation of sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane produce carbon monoxide and heat. It is the result of an exothermic reaction between the absorbent and the anesthetic agent. Desflurane produces the most carbon monoxide while sevoflurane produces the most heat. There are rare cases of carbon monoxide poisoning and thermal injury to patients, usually associated with the first case on a Monday morning after the anesthetic machine has been left on all weekend with high gas flows, which dried out the absorbent. Normally the halogenated agents undergo oxidative metabolism in the liver with the cytochrome P450 system. Depending on the inhalational agent, varying amounts of fluoride are produced during metabolism, which can lead to nephrotoxicity; though with today’s newer agents, this is a theoretical risk. The order of fluoride production for volatile anesthetics is methoxyflurane > > sevoflurane > isoflurane > desflurane. Compound A is produced from sevoflurane degradation.
Answer C: Carbon dioxide and water are not produced from desflurane degradation with a desiccated carbon dioxide absorbent. Carbon monoxide and heat are produced from the degradation of anesthetic agents in the presence of desiccated carbon dioxide absorbent. Among today’s volatile anesthetics, degradation of desflurane produces the most carbon monoxide.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Pulmonary toxicity correlates most closely with total cumulative dose and occurs several months to years after the initiation of amiodarone therapy. Although acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) can occur in the acute period, interstitial pneumonitis takes several months to develop. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent, although it has properties of both class I and II antiarrhythmics. It is used for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and can be given intravenously or orally. It inhibits inactivated (phase 0) sodium channels, inhibits sympathetic activity by noncompetitive beta-receptor blockade, and blocks L-type (slow) calcium channels. Many of the adverse effects associated with oral amiodarone are due to tissue accumulation of the drug over long-term therapy and are not seen with short-term intravenous use. Intravenous amiodarone has a different electrophysiologic and pharmacologic profile from its oral counterpart. The intravenous form produces a smaller increase in action potential duration in the myocardium, has little effect on sinus cycle length, and it may have a more potent and rapid antiadrenergic activity. Intravenous amiodarone can cause hypotension, cardiac effects, acute respiratory distress syndrome, nausea, vomiting, abnormal liver function tests, and phlebitis when given through a peripheral intravenous line. The cardiac side effects include bradycardia, asystole, heart failure, and shock. Oral amiodarone therapy has well-known side effects that can cause dysfunction of almost every organ system. The pulmonary toxicity is likely the most severe and is the most common cause for death due to amiodarone therapy. Chronic interstitial pneumonitis occurs in up to 20% of patients and presents as a nonproductive cough and dyspnea. Cardiac disturbances also include prolonged QT interval and torsades de pointes. A transient rise in the aminotransferase concentrations may occur and the medication should be discontinued if a two-fold elevation is observed. Thyroid dysfunction is a common complication and can result in hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Chronic therapy has also been associated with a slate-blue/grey discoloration of the skin and abnormalities with color vision. Unlike digoxin, which causes yellow/green vision problems, amiodarone is associated with blue vision problems. Asystole is a potential acute response to amiodarone therapy.
Answer C: Nausea and vomiting are acute side effects of amiodarone administration. Adverse effects of acute amiodarone therapy include nausea, vomiting, phlebitis, hypotension, bradycardia, asystole, heart failure, shock, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Chronic therapy affects PFTs, LFTs, and TFTs (pulmonary, liver, thyroid) and can also cause a blue/grey skin discoloration.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Amiodarone: Side Effects (B)" Clinical Anesthesia. 6th edition. Pages 1543. Giardina, Elsa-Grace. Major side effects of amiodarone; Clinical uses of amiodarone. UpToDate. January 23, 2013.

Echothiophate inhibits pseudocholinesterase, thereby potentiating the effects of succinylcholine. Echothiophate is an anticholinesterase used to treat refractory glaucoma by causing miosis. Systemic absorption can cause up to a 95% decrease in plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) function. Patients using echothiophate eye drops have demonstrated prolonged neuromuscular block after succinylcholine administration. It may take up to 4-6 weeks after discontinuation of the drug for normal butyrylcholinesterase activity to return. Cyclopentolate is a topical anticholinergic ocular drug used to induce mydriasis for ocular procedures. Systemic absorption can occur and lead to central nervous system (CNS) signs and symptoms of anticholinergic toxicity. Signs and symptoms include dysarthria, tachycardia, disorientation, psychosis, and convulsions.
Answer C: Topical epinephrine is sometimes used for open-angle glaucoma treatment. Certain concentrations of topical epinephrine have been associated with anxiety, tachycardia, and hypertension.
Answer D: Timolol is a nonselective β-adrenergic blocking agent used topically for the treatment of glaucoma. Systemic absorption can occur and lead to severe bronchospasm and bradycardia. Betaxolol is a selective β-1 antagonist that is relatively oculospecific with minimal systemic side effects. Severe bradycardia may occur, however, when combined with other oral βreceptor antagonists. Despite its oculospecificity, betaxolol should be used with caution in patients who have severe obstructive pulmonary pathology. The use of topical echothiophate eye drops for greater than 1 month can be associated with up to a 95% decrease in the function of plasma butyrylcholinesterase. Normal activity returns within 4-6 weeks after discontinuation. Succinylcholine administration during this time may result in prolonged neuromuscular blockade.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Echothiophate: Pseudocholinesterase Effect" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 1328.

Intravenous famotidine (and cimetidine) has an onset of action of 30 minutes when it is administered intravenously (IV) and 60 minutes when it is administered orally. Parietal cells in the stomach have histamine-2 (H2) receptors and respond to histamine by secreting acid. Histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2 blockers), such as cimetidine and famotidine, can be used to reduce gastric acid secretion by blocking the effect of histamine on these receptors. The onset of action of the clinically used H2 blockers (primarily famotidine and cimetidine) are very similar, and they are typically given (IV or orally) 30 to 90 minutes before surgery. The duration of action of famotidine is longer (~10-12 hr) than that of cimetidine (~4-5 hr), independent of the route of administration. Cimetidine is associated with more adverse effects compared with famotidine, including the inhibition of the hepatic mixed-function oxidase system prolonging the half-lives of medications metabolized by this system, such as lidocaine, propranolol, and diazepam. Other side effects of chronic cimetidine use include gynecomastia and galactorrhea. Antacids, such as calcium carbonate, have an immediate onset of time, with peak effect within 15 to 30 minutes when they are taken orally.
Answer C: Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole have an onset of action of one to three hours when they are taken orally.
Answer D: Proton pump inhibitors such as pantoprazole have an onset of action of 15 to 30 minutes when they are administered IV. The onset of action of histamine-2 receptor blockers, such as famotidine, have an onset of action of 30 minutes when they are administered intravenously and 60 minutes when they are administered orally. Proton pump inhibitors have an onset of action of 15 to 30 minutes when they are administered intravenously and one to three hours when they are administered orally. The order of non-depolarizing muscle relaxant potentiation is desflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane > halothane > TIVA (e.g. propofol). All volatile anesthetic agents prolong the actions of the neuromuscular blocking drugs, likely by potentiating the medications’ effects postsynaptically at the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor in the neuromuscular junction. Desflurane (A) potentiates this block the most as it is the least potent volatile agent and therefore present in the highest aqueous concentration at equal levels of minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) as compared to isoflurane (B) and sevoflurane (D). Isoflurane and sevoflurane are both known to inhibit current through the nicotinic receptor in a dose dependent fashion. However, since they are more potent agents, less of the agent is present at the neuromuscular junction as compared to desflurane. As the MAC of isoflurane and sevoflurane are not markedly different, their aqueous concentration is not significantly different at the neuromuscular junction to have significant variation in their potentiation effects. Nitrous oxide (C), unlike the volatile agents, was not traditionally thought to prolong neuromuscular blockade. In fact, it was the agent used in the pharmacokinetic studies of the neuromuscular blockers. Some studies now suggest, however, that nitrous oxide may potentiate neuromuscular blockers to a small extent. This effect is not as pronounced as those of the volatile anesthetics.  The order of non-depolarizing muscle relaxant potentiation is desflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane > halothane > TIVA (e.g. propofol).  Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Pages 436, 504, 514. This patient is at low risk for anaphylaxis to cephalosporins despite their history of rash with penicillin. Cefazolin, a firstgeneration cephalosporin, should be administered to this patient. Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis is given for contaminated, clean-contaminated, and some clean procedures. Cephalosporins are the most common antibiotic given because of their coverage of skin microbes. Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins arises from the common beta-lactam ring and common R group side chains. About 2% or less of patients with skin-proven penicillin sensitivity will have a reaction to cephalosporins. Penicillin reactions should be classified as immediate or delayed. Immediate reactions occur within 1 hour of the last administered dose. Typical features include flushing, hives, pruritus, angioedema, urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension. Type 1 allergic reactions are IgE-mediated and are the cause of most immediate reactions. This is significant because it is this type of reaction that carries the risk of anaphylaxis on re-exposure to an inciting agent. Delayed reactions typically occur days to weeks following the medication administration. In a patient who reports a history of rash only, this is likely a delayed reaction but the patient should be questioned for other features of an immediate reaction. Anaphylaxis to cephalosporins is uncommon, with estimates ranging from 0.0001% to 0.1%. With a true allergy to penicillin or cephalosporins, vancomycin or clindamycin may be given instead. Patients who report a penicillin allergy should be risk-stratified on likelihood of a reaction to cephalosporins and treated accordingly. Reaction WITH likely IgE-mediated features Risk of anaphylaxis is very low High Hx of likely anaphylactic reaction to penicillins Alternate drug should be chosen Further work-up with skin-prick testing and cephalosporin desensitization Many providers will simplify this approach even further. They will only administer cephalosporins if all of the following are true: 1) The reaction to penicillin occurred > 10 years ago. 2) The reaction did not include any IgE-mediated symptoms. 3) The reaction did not include any severe reactions (e.g. TENS, DRESS syndrome). Answers B & C: Vancomycin and clindamycin are appropriate alternatives to cephalosporins in patients at increased risk for anaphylactic reaction. In this patient with history of rash, a cephalosporin should still be administered.  Patients with a history of a delayed reaction to penicillin can be given cephalosporins. In a patient reporting an immediate penicillin reaction with concerning features including flushing, hives, pruritis, angioedema, urticaria, bronchospasm, or hypotension, an alternate drug should be chosen. Medications with first-order kinetics have the potential to follow zero-order kinetics and vice versa. Drug metabolism via first-order or zero-order kinetics is not an inherent property of the drug but rather a way to describe mathematically how these drugs behave in vivo. Several medications such as warfarin, theophylline, heparin, aspirin, phenytoin, and alcohol reach zero-order kinetics faster than many other drugs, so the tendency is to think of these drugs as always following zero-order kinetics in therapeutic concentrations. However, after the metabolic capacity of the liver or metabolizing organ system is overwhelmed, all drugs will revert to being metabolized via zero-order kinetics until enough of the drug has been eliminated for the rate of clearance to again be proportional to drug plasma concentration. A basic pharmacology concept regarding drug metabolism or elimination is first vs zero-order pharmacokinetics. Elimination is the change in the plasma concentration of a drug divided by the change in time. First-order kinetics describes a situation in which drug elimination is proportional to drug concentration. As more drug is introduced into the system more enzymes are induced, and metabolism increases proportionally. The rate of elimination is not constant or linear; rather, it is exponential. As time goes on, progressively less drug leaves the body per time constant. Some drugs, such as propofol, are so highly extracted by their metabolizing organ, such as the liver, that their rate of metabolism is proportional only to liver blood flow. Progressively less drug is still eliminated per unit time because smaller amounts of the drug are present in the blood to be metabolized, which is the definition of first-order kinetics. A constant fraction of medication being eliminated per unit time describes first-order kinetics, not zero-order kinetics. Zero-order kinetics describes a situation in which the enzyme or enzymes involved in that particular drug’s metabolism are at maximum capacity (Vmax). In this situation, drug metabolism is independent of plasma concentration because the enzymes are saturated. This means that the rate of elimination is constant or linear. In other words, in zero-order kinetics, "a constant amount of medication is eliminated per unit time."
Answer B: Liver blood flow-dependent elimination is characteristic of first-order kinetics, not zero-order kinetics.
Answer D: If a drug is following zero-order kinetics, the plasma drug concentration could continue increasing while the rate of elimination is not able to be increased. The rate of drug metabolism is at Vmax, so any additional drug will not be metabolized and can lead to toxicity. However, many medications, even at toxic levels, are still following first-order kinetics. First-order kinetics describes a situation in which a constant proportion (percentage) of a drug is removed per unit time, whereas zero-order kinetics describes a situation in which a constant amount of a drug is removed per unit time, regardless of concentration. Drugs that typically follow zero-order kinetics are THE PAW: theophylline, heparin, ethanol, phenytoin, aspirin, and warfarin. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Zero-order Pharmacokinetics (B)" Gropper M, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. Ch. 18: Basic Principles of Pharmacology. Section: Zero Versus First-Order Kinetics. 9th ed.

Compared to morphine, tramadol has a decreased mu receptor binding. Tramadol is a centrally acting synthetic opioid analgesic that is used for acute and chronic pain management. Tramadol is available in multiple formulations and can be administered via multiple routes (oral, rectal, sublingual, intramuscular, and intravenous). The oral route is the most commonly used and is discussed here. After oral administration, peak plasma concentration occurs after 1.2 to 1.9 hours. Absorption is almost 100%, and bioavailability is approximately 70% as a result of first-pass metabolism. The plasma elimination half-life is approximately six hours. Tramadol is metabolized by several pathways, mostly via conjugation in the liver; conjugation of the parent compound along with metabolites occurs. Tramadol is mainly excreted via the kidneys (~90%), with very small amounts being excreted via the biliary system (~1%). Eleven metabolites are known, and their metabolism is similar to the parent compound, with most metabolism occurring in the kidneys. There is very little chance of accumulation of any of the metabolites, even after multiple administrations. Tramadol passes through the placental barrier; however, very small amounts are excreted in breast milk (~0.1%). Tramadol has a well-known mechanism of action. Tramadol has a weak affinity for the mu-opioid receptor, with no affinity for the delta or kappa receptors. The affinity for the mu receptor is 6,000 times less than that of morphine. Existence of a second nonopioid mechanism has been theorized because there is a lack of reversibility of the analgesia and few withdrawal symptoms after naloxone administration. This other mechanism of action involves tramadol’s ability to inhibit neuronal uptake of norepinephrine and serotonin. Both of these neurotransmitters are involved in the antinociceptive effects of descending inhibitory pathways of the central nervous system. The main advantage of tramadol compared with other opioid analgesics is its lower risk of respiratory depression, constipation, and potential for abuse. Because tramadol binds to the mu receptor, there is a potential for respiratory depression; however, it is unlikely to be clinically relevant. Additionally, tramadol has only a minor effect on gastrointestinal transit time, leading to a lower risk of ileus. The incidence of nausea and vomiting varies according to the results of one study. While no increased risk was found in some studies reported, an increased risk was found in other studies, with the results depending on the dose and circumstances surrounding the administration. Tramadol has no clinically relevant hemodynamic effects. Tramadol has been trialed for almost every type of postsurgical pain, including labor analgesia. It can also be used for some kinds of chronic pain, and some authors recommend it on step 2 of the World Health Organization guidelines for cancer pain treatment. Tramadol works partially by limiting serotonin reuptake in neurons. This is thought to aid in analgesia because serotonin is involved in the nociceptive pathways of the central nervous system.
Answer C: Tramadol has a much lower risk of respiratory depression, also secondary to its decreased mu receptor affinity. Tramadol is a synthetic opioid analgesic that binds weakly to the opioid mu receptors. It also inhibits neuronal reuptake of norepinephrine and serotonin, which is thought to mediate some of the analgesic effects. Review of opioid receptors and their influence on physiology. This list is not exclusive. • Delta receptor: analgesia, antidepressant, physical dependence • Kappa receptor: analgesia, dysphoria, miosis, sedation • Mu receptor: analgesia, physical dependence, respiratory depression, miosis, euphoria, decreased gastrointestinal motility American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Sugammadex is a synthetic, modified γ-cyclodextrin. Therefore, a patient with hypersensitivity to cyclodextrins is at significantly increased risk for an anaphylactic reaction to sugammadex, and its use is contraindicated. Sugammadex is a reversal agent for the steroidal neuromuscular blocking medications rocuronium and vecuronium. Sugammadex is an 8-member ring with a central core that encapsulates the steroid nucleus of rocuronium and vecuronium (intermediate-acting neuromuscular blocking agents). The binding to rocuronium (dissociation constant of 0.055 μmol/L) is 3 times as tight as vecuronium. Despite this, the effectiveness for both rocuronium and vecuronium are similar because the typical dose of vecuronium is about 6 times less than an equivalent dose of rocuronium. Typical doses of sugammadex are 2 mg/kg for a neuromuscular blockade reversal from rocuronium and vecuronium when the train-of-four count is at least 2, with reversal occurring in 2 to 4 min. When the block is deeper (train-of-four < 2 or post-tetanic twitches), 4 mg/kg is required. When there is a profound block, such as in a failed rapid sequence induction and intubation, doses of 16 mg/kg are required. The sugammadex-steroidal neuromuscular blocking drug complex is primarily eliminated via the renal system, with an elimination half-life of 100 min. Sugammadex is biologically inactive and binds to rocuronium and vecuronium. Sugammadex is relatively selective for steroidal neuromuscular blocking drugs but does additionally bind to the steroidal portions of toremifene, flucloxacillin, progesterone, and fusidic acid. Oral contraception has been known to be affected by sugammadex, with the administration of sugammadex being equivalent to missing 1 daily oral dose; thus, it is recommended to use alternative means of birth control for 1 week after sugammadex administration. One contraindication to the use of sugammadex is a history of hypersensitivity reaction to sugammadex or any of its components. The prevalence of anaphylactic reactions is estimated to be between 1:3,500 and 1:20,000, with most reactions occurring within 4 min of administration. Side effects of sugammadex include nausea, vomiting, pruritus, headache, dysgeusia, bradycardia, and bronchospasm. Myotonic dystrophy is not a contraindication to the use of sugammadex. It is actually advantageous to use sugammadex in these patients (including patients with spinal muscular atrophy) because these patients are at increased risk of complications with residual neuromuscular blockade. The use of sugammadex in these patients has been shown to provide rapid reversal without block reoccurrence.
Answer C: Oral contraceptive use is not a contraindication to the use of sugammadex. Sugammadex does affect the efficacy of oral contraception. It is recommended to use alternative means of birth control for 1 week after sugammadex administration because sugammadex can bind to progesterone. Sugammadex is a reversal agent for the steroidal neuromuscular blocking medications rocuronium and vecuronium. It is contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to sugammadex or its components. Sugammadex is physically incompatible with ondansetron and verapamil and should not be coadministered with these medications. If sugammadex and 1 of the above drugs are to be administered in the same IV line, the line should be adequately flushed with saline between the administration of the 2 drugs. Increasing attention is being paid to the fascinating subject of pharmacogenomics as it may account for the enormity of variable responses to medications. Polymorphisms are variants in DNA sequence that occur in at least 1% of the population. Various polymorphisms may make patients more or less susceptible to opioid pain medication effects. For example, a polymorphism in the OPRM gene may render morphine less effective in some patients, while polymorphisms in the melanocortin 1 receptor (MC1R) gene, which is also associated with red hair, may lead to increased analgesia. Cytochrome P450 3A4 (CYP3A4) is responsible for the metabolism of most anesthetics, lidocaine, and dexamethasone. For example, midazolam inhibits CYP3A4 which can prolong the effect of fentanyl. The cytochrome P450 enzymes display various polymorphisms that lead to altered drug metabolism. Cytochrome P450 2C19 (CYP2C19) is responsible for the metabolism of proton pump inhibitors, such as omeprazole, and antidepressants which may lead to therapeutic success or failure of these medications depending on if the enzyme is hyperactive or underactive.
Answer B: Cytochrome P450 2C9 (CYP2C9) metabolizes phenytoin, warfarin, and ibuprofen. Poor warfarin metabolism can have excessive anticoagulation.
Answer C: Cytochrome P450 2D6 (CYP2D6) is a particularly important P450 enzyme to anesthesiologists as it metabolizes many medications we administer such as codeine, beta-blockers, some antiarrhythmics, diltiazem, and tramadol. These medications rely on CYP2D6 for creation of active metabolites. Polymorphisms can lead to altered patient response to medications. Important enzymes to anesthetic practice are CYP2D6, CYP3A4, and MC1R.  Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Pages 128, 129 American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Flumazenil has the shortest duration of action at the benzodiazepine receptor of all the listed answer choices. Its plasma elimination half-life of 0.7-1.3 hours is significantly shorter than benzodiazepine agonists. This can lead to the recrudescence of sedation from benzodiazepines following the elimination of flumazenil. Therefore, when administering flumazenil, careful attention needs to be paid to its duration of action relative to that of the benzodiazepines taken by the patient, and additional doses of flumazenil should be available. Note that although flumazenil is generally considered a benzodiazepine antagonist, it exhibits a partial agonist effect. In one study, propofol was potentiated by giving high doses of flumazenil, suggesting flumazenil has a mixed or partial agonist effect. Answers A & B & D & E: The plasma elimination half-life of diazepam is 20-50 hours, alprazolam is 6-27 hours, lorazepam is 11-22 hours, temazepam is 10 hours, and midazolam is 1.7-2.6 hours.  Flumazenil has the shortest elimination half-life of all currently used benzodiazepines, which makes recrudescence of sedation after a single administration of flumazenil likely. Furosemide administration can cause a hypokalemic-hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis secondary to potassium excretion and contraction alkalosis. Metabolic alkalosis is common following the administration of loop and thiazide diuretics. When more diuresis occurs with those medications, the alkalemia that develops is more pronounced. When these agents are administered, a contraction alkalosis occurs due to a decrease in the extracellular volume around a constant extracellular HCO3- (bicarbonate). This combined with an increase in urinary hydrogen ion loss results in alkalosis. The mechanism is similar but the site of action is different. Loop diuretics work at the ascending loop of henle where they block the sodium-potassium chloride transporter resulting in a decreased sodium and chloride reabsorption. In certain loop diuretics, a hypokalemic-hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis will occur. Thiazide diuretics work primarily at the distal convoluted tubules where they inhibit sodium and chloride reabsorption. The same hypokalemic-hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis will occur. Acetazolamide can be given to correct the alkalemia. Acetazolamide is a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. It is a commonly used diuretic that causes noncompetitive inhibition of the carbon anhydrase enzyme. This enzyme usually catalyzes the reaction between water, carbon dioxide, carbonic acid, and bicarbonate. Inhibition of this enzyme causes an increase in renal bicarbonate with a resultant alkalization of the urine. Acetazolamide may cause a mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis due to bicarbonate excretion. Acetazolamide may impair carbon dioxide elimination in patients with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and should be used in caution with that patient population. Normal respiratory compensation of metabolic acidosis entails increasing minute ventilation to decrease CO2 to increase the pH back to the physiologic norm. Patients with severe COPD have difficulty in increasing their effective minute ventilation. Therefore the CO2 levels will remain higher and the pH will remain acidotic. Potassium-sparing diuretics act in the collecting ducts where they alter the transport of sodium resulting in decreased sodium reabsorption. Additionally, the potassium excretion is inhibited resulting in decreased excretion and potassium-sparing. A mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis can be observed when administering potassium-sparing diuretics. This is due to the lack of aldosterone effect on hydrogen ion secretion. Hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis can be seen with acetazolamide administration, not furosemide.
Answer C: Hyperchloremic metabolic alkalosis is typically not seen with diuretic administration. It would not be expected with furosemide administration as it can cause hypokalemic-hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.
Answer D: Hypokalemic metabolic acidosis is typically not seen with diuretic administration unless there is another concurrent metabolic disturbance. It would not be expected with furosemide administration as it can cause hypokalemic-hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. Diuretic administration can cause metabolic disturbances. The degree of disturbance often depends on the mechanism of action and specific diuretic. Thiazide and loop diuretics can cause an alkalosis. Acetazolamide and potassiumsparing diuretics can cause a metabolic acidosis.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Diuretic: Effects On Acid-Base Balance (B)" Miller's Anesthesia. 9th Edition. Etomidate causes adrenocortical suppression primarily through inhibition of 11β-hydroxylase, resulting in reduced cortisol (and aldosterone) production. Etomidate also inhibits the 17α-hydroxylase enzyme, which is a minor contributor to decreased production of cortisol and aldosterone compared to the inhibition of 11β-hydroxylase. Etomidate is an intravenous hypnotic agent used for the induction of anesthesia with minimal hemodynamic and respiratory effects compared to other induction agents. It has the less desirable side effects of pain on injection, nausea and vomiting, myoclonus, and thrombophlebitis. It was discovered in the 1980s that intensive care unit (ICU) patients who received etomidate infusions for sedation had higher mortality rates compared with other types of sedation. This led to the discovery of etomidate inhibiting 11β-hydroxylase, resulting in decreased cortisol production. Etomidate is no longer routinely used as a continuous infusion for sedation. Etomidate is a potent inhibitor of cortisol production for up to 72 hours after an induction dose. The significance of this is controversial, and there is no definitive evidence to support increased mortality with a single induction dose of etomidate in the ICU population. Etomidate is still used as an induction agent in select circumstances at the anesthesiologist's discretion, such as the need for hemodynamic stability during induction. The enzyme 11β-hydroxylase is responsible for the conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. Thus, administration of etomidate causes suppression of adrenal cortisol synthesis. Illustration © TrueLearn, LLC 5α-Reductase is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. 5α-Reductase inhibitors, such as finasteride, are used for benign prostatic hyperplasia and male pattern hair loss. Etomidate does not inhibit this enzyme.
Answer C: 18-Hydroxylase is an enzyme in the aldosterone synthesis pathway and is responsible for the conversion of corticosterone to aldosterone. Etomidate does not inhibit this enzyme.
Answer D: 21-Hydroxylase is the enzyme responsible for the conversion of progesterone and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone to deoxycorticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol, respectively. 21-Hydroxylase deficiency is the main cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. Etomidate does not inhibit this enzyme. Etomidate causes adrenocortical suppression primarily through inhibition of adrenal mitochondrial 11βhydroxylase, resulting in reduced cortisol (and aldosterone) production. Fentanyl can reduce MAC by up to 80%. Minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) is the concentration of inhaled anesthetics needed to prevent movement during surgical stimulus in 50% of the patients. Various factors and medications can decrease MAC requirements. Commonly used IV medications that reduce MAC ("MAC reducers") include opioids, lidocaine, benzodiazepines, and alpha-2 agonists. However, the degree of reduction among these medications varies. Opioids, specifically fentanyl, can produce up to an 80% reduction in MAC. The degree of reduction is based on the dose of the opioid and the type of opioid. There is a ceiling effect with the opioid MAC reduction where additional concentration does little to affect MAC, around 80% MAC reduction. Medications like nalbuphine and butorphanol, which are opioid agonist-antagonists, can also reduce MAC, but to a lesser degree. The fentanyl type opioids (fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil) seem to have the largest MAC reduction. In analgesic doses (e.g. fentanyl 3 mcg/kg), they reduce MAC by about 50%. They can also reduce propofol induction dose by 50% at this analgesic concentration. General anesthesia can be achieved with proper fentanyl dosing combined with propofol dosing that would only produce conscious sedation if given alone (e.g. 25-50 mcg/kg/min). Alfentanil can reduce propofol induction dose by 50%, even at small doses. An alfentanil dose of 3 mcg/kg is subanalgesic and subhypnotic alone but can reduce the midazolam ED50 by 50% when combined. As another example, fentanyl 50 mcg or alfentanil 500 mcg may have minimal hypnotic effects but can significantly potentiate other hypnotics when given in combination. It is worth noting that MAC reduction is not complete. Thus, general anesthesia cannot be obtained with opioids alone. Lidocaine requires high doses in humans to have any significant effect on MAC. Animal studies have shown a 10-30% reduction in MAC, but appropriate dosing is unknown. Ketamine has also been shown to reduce MAC by up to 40% in animal studies, though dosing seems higher than practical. Magnesium administration has a curious effect on anesthetic requirements. Studies have shown that it decreases anesthetic requirements during TIVA. However, the opposite has been shown with volatile anesthetics, where it increases MAC. To further confuse the picture, rats fed a low magnesium diet (hypomagnesemic) had higher MAC requirements. Midazolam has been shown to reduce MAC but high doses may be required in humans to have any significant effect. The reduction can be in the range of 40-70%, depending on the dose. Dexmedetomidine has been shown to reduce MAC by 35-50% in a human study, depending on the dose, and up to 100% in animal studies. Notably, it is not approved as a sole anesthetic agent (unlike propofol). Phenylephrine and gabapentin do not affect MAC. Ephedrine has been shown to increase MAC requirements by up to 50%. Ephedrine and dexmedetomidine modulate the release of norepinephrine, which may partially explain their effects on MAC. Lidocaine requires very high doses to have any significant effect on MAC
Answer C: Magnesium increases inhalational MAC requirements. The opioids, particularly fentanyl type, have significant MAC reducing properties at analgesic doses. Midazolam and dexmedetomidine can reduce MAC. Gabapentin does not affect MAC. Magnesium and ephedrine increase MAC requirements.  Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th Edition. Aprepitant is a neurokinin type 1 (NK1) receptor antagonist used to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) and has not been associated with any ECG changes. Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is the leading cause of delayed discharge from the postanesthesia care unit and for unexpected admissions after ambulatory surgery. Although many medications have shown great efficacy at preventing and/or treating PONV, they are not without side effects. Many of the antinausea, antiemetic medications target receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) of the brainstem. This area is also known as the area postrema and, along with the nearby nucleus tractus solitarius, is felt to contain dense quantities of emetogenic chemoreceptors. Receptors identified in this area so far include dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, histamine, and NK1 types. Aprepitant antagonizes the NK1 receptors in the CTZ, preventing nausea and vomiting. Early trials have shown equal efficacy between aprepitant and ondansetron for their effects on nausea; however, aprepitant has been shown to be more efficacious against vomiting. This data are supported by early trials of the not yet available casopitant, another NK1 receptor antagonist. Droperidol and haloperidol are butyrophenone neuroleptic medications. They antagonize dopamine receptors in the CTZ and have shown good efficacy against nausea and vomiting. Droperidol and haloperidol have been associated with prolongation of the QT interval on ECG, though these changes were primarily associated with the higher doses used for treatment of psychosis.
Answer C: Ondansetron is a 5-hydroxytryptamine receptor subtype 3 (serotonin, 5-HT3) antagonist. Numerous large studies have shown great efficacy for the prevention and treatment of PONV. However, 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are also associated with slight QT prolongation on ECG, bradycardia, and other cardiac conduction disorders. Aprepitant is a neurokinin type 1 (NK1) receptor antagonist and has shown good efficacy for the prevention of vomiting for up to 48 hours postoperatively. Aprepitant has not been shown to cause any changes in ECG, whereas several other antinausea medications such as droperidol, haloperidol, and ondansetron can cause QT prolongation. Glycopyrrolate decreases parasympathetic activity and therefore results in delayed gastric emptying. Glycopyrrolate is a synthetic quaternary ammonium anticholinergic. Parasympathetic activity is reduced by competitively blocking the acetylcholine receptor. Clinically, this results in decreased gastrointestinal motility (delayed emptying), tachycardia, bronchial smooth muscle relaxation, decreased salivary and gastric secretions, lowering of the lower esophageal sphincter tone, and urinary retention. Due to the quaternary structure of glycopyrrolate, it does not cross the blood brain barrier and will not result in sedation or mydriasis. The duration of action of glycopyrrolate is 2-4 hours so if given shortly before anesthetic induction, the risk of aspiration is slightly increased due to the gastrointestinal side effects discussed above. Glycopyrrolate results in decreased salivary and gastric secretions.
Answer C: Glycopyrrolate results in lowering of the lower esophageal sphincter tone.
Answer D: Glycopyrrolate does not significantly affect the upper esophageal sphincter. Glycopyrrolate delays gastric emptying, decreases salivary and gastric secretions, increases heart rate, relaxes bronchial smooth muscle, decreases lower esophageal sphincter tone, and causes urinary retention. Isoflurane > sevoflurane > desflurane > nitrous oxide is the correct sequence of inhaled anesthetic potency of the most commonly used inhaled anesthetics. Potency is defined as the amount of drug required to elicit a predefined effect; a more potent drug requires a lower dose. In 1960, Eger and colleagues defined the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) as the inhaled anesthetic required to prevent movement in response to an abdominal incision in 50% of subjects, and the MAC is now used to define the potency of inhalational anesthetics. Although MAC is usually expressed as volume percentage, its pharmacologic effect is actually determined by the partial pressure. Meyer and Overton discovered a strikingly elegant and simple linear relationship between anesthetic potency and lipid solubility. That is, a more lipid-soluble (higher oil:gas partition coefficient) inhalational anesthetic is a more potent (lower MAC) anesthetic. Because of the Meyer-Overton correlation, researchers were led to believe hat lipids' bilayers were the target site of the mechanism of action of inhalational anesthetics. Such lipid-based anesthetic theories were predominant from the 1960s to the 1980s before shifting to the more current, protein-target-based theories. Although MAC is usually expressed as volume percentage, its pharmacologic effect is actually determined by the partial pressure. For example, 1.2% of isoflurane at 1 atm (760 mmHg) is 9.12 mmHg, which produces 1 MAC. This distinction is significant under conditions in which atmospheric pressure is different from sea level, such as at high altitudes or in a hyperbaric chamber; 1.2% of isoflurane at 0.5 atm (360 mmHg) would only be 4.56 mmHg, which would produce only 0.5 MAC. Fortunately, variable bypass vaporizers, such as those for isoflurane and sevoflurane, hold partial pressure output constant at different atmospheric pressures, and an isoflurane vaporizer set to 1.2% would actually produce 2.4% (corresponding to 9.12 mmHg, or 1 MAC) at 0.5 atm.
Answer B: The MAC is defined as the inhaled anesthetic required to prevent movement in response to an abdominal incision in 50% of subjects. However, MAC derivatives exist to describe alveolar concentrations required to render 50% of subjects amnesic, unconscious, or with blunted autonomic responses (BAR); 0.25 × MAC is MACamnesia, 0.5 × MAC is MACunconscious, and 1.3 × MAC is MACBAR.
Answer D: The Meyer-Overton correlation describes the linear relationship between anesthetic potency and lipid solubility. Isoflurane > sevoflurane > desflurane > nitrous oxide is the correct sequence of inhaled anesthetic potency. The Meyer-Overton correlation describes the relationship between lipid solubility and anesthetic potency. A more lipid-soluble (higher oil:gas partition coefficient) inhalational anesthetic is a more potent (lower MAC) anesthetic. Ticlopidine has the longest elimination half-life of the drugs listed. Antithrombotic drugs fall into two classes with the ultimate effect of both being preventing clot formation and/or growth. Antiplatelet drugs primarily prevent platelet activation and/or aggregation while anticoagulants primarily reduce fibrin formation. These drugs may be used for blood clot prophylaxis or treatment of acute thrombi. Several different classes of antiplatelet drugs exist including, but not limited to: irreversible cyclooxygenase inhibitors (e.g. aspirin), adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor inhibitors (e.g. clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticlopidine, ticagrelor), phosphodiesterase inhibitors (e.g. cilostazol), and glycoprotein IIb-IIIa inhibitors (e.g. abciximab, eptifibatide, tirofiban). Several different classes of anticoagulant drugs exist including, but not limited to: antithrombin III activators (e.g. heparin, low molecular weight heparin), heparin-like factor Xa inhibitors (e.g. fondaparinux), direct factor Xa inhibitors (e.g. rivaroxaban, apixaban), direct thrombin inhibitors (e.g. bivalirudin, hirudin, argatroban, dabigatran), and vitamin K antagonists (e.g. warfarin). The duration of action of an antithrombotic drug is a result of the drug’s half-life and its mechanism of action (notably whether its effects are reversible or irreversible). For example, although the plasma half-life of aspirin is only 20 minutes, the duration of effect of the drug is approximately 7-10 days. This prolonged duration occurs since aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase and thus produces an inhibitory effect on platelet aggregation for the duration of the life of a platelet (7-10 days). The drug’s duration thus lasts until new platelets are formed which have not been exposed to aspirin. The ADP receptor inhibitors irreversibly inhibit the receptor which impairs the ADP-dependent activation of the GP IIb-IIIa complex (and thus impairs platelet aggregation and thrombus formation) for the duration of the life of the affected platelets. Among the drugs in this class, the elimination half-life of ticlopidine is significantly longer than the others: 4 days vs 7-8 hours. Ticlopidine accordingly has the longest antiplatelet effect (approximately 10-14 days) since the drug works for several days after administration. Accordingly, ticlopidine should be stopped two weeks prior to a surgical procedure whereas the other ADP receptor inhibitors may be stopped approximately one week prior to a procedure. Argatroban is a direct thrombin inhibitor that reversibly binds to the thrombin active site. Due to a short half-life, the duration of the drug is approximately 2-4 hours and should be held 4-6 hours prior to a surgical procedure. Tirofiban is a reversible GP IIb-IIIa receptor inhibitor with a rapid onset and short duration of action. Its duration of action is approximately 4-8 hours, though it is usually recommended to stop the drug at least 12 hours prior to a surgical procedure. The table below summarizes the plasma half-lives of several antithrombotic drugs as well as the recommendations for stopping these drugs prior to a surgical procedure. The time to stop the drugs directly relates to the duration of action of the drugs. Please note that specific time periods for discontinuation of these drugs may vary depending on institution, physician preference, procedure type, and other patient factors. The duration of effect of aspirin is approximately 7-10 days.
Answer B: The duration of effect of argatroban is approximately 2-4 hours.
Answer D: The duration of effect of tirofiban is approximately 4-8 hours. EMLA (eutectic mixture of local anesthetics) is a local anesthetic mixture applied transdermally to provide anesthesia for the skin. EMLA has been shown to cause methemoglobinemia, likely secondary to the prilocaine in the formulation, in some patients; therefore, it is contraindicated in patients with congenital methemoglobinemia. EMLA comprises a mixture of lidocaine and prilocaine. Adverse reactions are rare and include mild skin irritation, contact dermatitis, and methemoglobinemia. Prilocaine has a relatively rapid onset and moderate duration of action; however, its biotransformation produces aminophenols that oxidize hemoglobin to methemoglobin a characteristic of prilocaine that has limited its clinical use. EMLA cream should not be used in patients with G6PD deficiency or in patients taking other methemoglobin-inducing medications. Congenital methemoglobinemia is due to diminished enzymatic reduction of methemoglobin back to hemoglobin. Methemoglobin is an altered state of hemoglobin in which the ferrous (Fe2+) irons have been oxidized to ferric (Fe3+) irons, rendering them unable to carry oxygen. Patients with congenital methemoglobinemia are generally cyanotic but asymptomatic, and they should avoid all methemoglobin-inducing drugs such as prilocaine, benzocaine, quinine, metoclopramide, sulfonamides, dapsone, and chloral hydrate. Patients treated with class III antiarrhythmic drugs (eg, amiodarone, bretylium, sotalol, dofetilide) should be maintained under close surveillance and considered for electrocardiogram monitoring because cardiac effects may be additive. if it is possible, avoid EMLA in patients treated with class III antiarrhythmic drugs. EMLA contraindications include • Allergy to amide anesthetics • Concomitant class III antiarrhythmic drugs • Congenital or idiopathic methemoglobinemia • Infants (<12 months) receiving treatment with methemoglobin-inducing agents Satisfactory dermal analgesia is achieved one hour after application, reaches the maximum at two to three hours, and persists for one to two hours after removal. To provide sufficient analgesia for clinical procedures such as intravenous catheter placement and venipuncture, EMLA cream should be applied under an occlusive dressing for at least one hour. To provide dermal analgesia for clinical procedures such as split skin graft harvesting, EMLA cream should be applied under occlusive dressing for at least two hours. Additional topical anesthetic formulations • Benzocaine: 20% solution for mucosal anesthesia, risk of methemoglobinemia especially with repeated doses • Cocaine: 4% solution for topical anesthesia (sinus surgery, awake intubation) or 11.8% tetracaine, epinephrine (adrenalin), and cocaine for wound repair • EMLA: 2.5% lidocaine and 2.5% prilocaine eutectic mixture for minor procedures (pediatric IV placement), onset 45 to 60 minutes, duration two hours, typical adult dose is 2.5 to 10 g • J-Tip: 1% buffered lidocaine for minor procedures (pediatric IV placement), needle-free pressure-injection device • LET: 4% lidocaine plus 0.1% epinephrine and 0.5% tetracaine for minor procedures (laceration repair), as aqueous solution or methylcellulose gel • LMX: 4% liposomal solution for minor procedures (pediatric IV placement), onset 30 minutes, max 100 cm2 application area in children <10 kg Prilocaine (part of the EMLA formulation) is contraindicated in a patient with congenital methemoglobinemia.
Answer C: Morphine is not contraindicated in a patient with congenital methemoglobinemia. EMLA (eutectic mixture of local anesthetics) contraindications include allergy to amide anesthetics, concomitant class III antiarrhythmic drugs (eg, amiodarone, sotalol), congenital or idiopathic methemoglobinemia, and infants receiving treatment with methemoglobin-inducing agents. Both methadone and ciprofloxacin can prolong the QT interval putting a patient at risk for torsades de pointes. Methadone is a long-acting opioid agonist often used to treat chronic pain or opioid use disorder. One of the most significant side effects is a dose-dependent prolongation of the QT interval. Studies suggest this may be due to the drug’s effect on cardiac repolarization. The risk for prolonged QT intervals is greatest in patients taking greater than 120 mg daily, however, lower doses and acute use can still prolong the QT interval. Because methadone is metabolized by cytochrome p450, drugs inhibiting this enzyme may lead to increased methadone toxicity and further QT prolongation. Combining multiple drugs that prolong the QT interval, such as the antibiotic ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone), puts patients at greater risk for developing torsades de pointes. It is important to be aware that nearly all the commonly used antiemetics can prolong the QT interval. Dexamethasone, aprepitant, and palonosetron (a 5-HT3 receptor antagonist) are antiemetics that have not been shown to significantly prolong the QT interval. Dexamethasone and aprepitant are antiemetics that have not been shown to prolong the QT interval.
Answer C: Nitrous oxide has not been shown to prolong the QT interval but halogenated volatile anesthetics (e.g. sevoflurane) have been shown to prolong the QT interval. Patients taking methadone, especially at doses greater than 120 mg/day, are at risk of developing a prolonged QT interval. This places these patients at risk for developing lethal arrhythmias, such as torsades de pointes. Cytochrome p450 inhibiting medications should be used with caution in patients taking methadone to prevent unintentional elevations in serum methadone levels. Methadone has N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) antagonistic properties in addition to opioid receptor agonism. This promotes pain control and reduces tolerance in patients with chronic pain. Methadone may also be used in the intensive care unit (ICU) to reduce tolerance to opioids and maintain adequate pain control. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Cefazolin may be administered in as quickly as three to five minutes. Cefazolin is a first-generation cephalosporin. Cefazolin binds to penicillin-binding proteins found in the cell wall of bacteria. When cefazolin binds to the bacterial cell wall, bacterial cell wall synthesis and replication are inhibited, making the bacteria more susceptible to destruction. Cefazolin does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier. Cefazolin attains a peak plasma concentration five minutes after IV administration. Cefazolin can be administered via IV push for more than three to five minutes according to the package insert. The timing of cefazolin administration and tourniquet inflation time has been studied for orthopedic procedures. The inflation of a tourniquet after cefazolin administration attained a concentration difference in the extremity when the tourniquet was inflated at one minute vs at five minutes after cefazolin administration. However, even when the tourniquet was inflated one minute after administration, the tissue concentration of cefazolin was above the bacterial minimum inhibitory concentration. Additional antibiotics with slower infusion times include vancomycin, gentamicin, and caspofungin. Side effects of rapid infusion rates with certain antibiotics include local irritation at the IV site, hypotension, renal dysfunction, and drug toxicity. Histamine release is more common with fast administration of vancomycin, leading to vancomycin flushing syndrome, previously known as red man syndrome. Vancomycin is recommended to be administered no faster than over a duration of 60 minutes. Ciprofloxacin is a second-generation fluoroquinolone with a broad spectrum of activity. Ciprofloxacin acts by inhibiting topoisomerase type II and IV, preventing bacteria replication. According to the package insert, ciprofloxacin should be administered over 60 minutes. Side effects of ciprofloxacin include QT prolongation, tendonitis, and photosensitivity. Ciprofloxacin has been associated with local skin reactions when it has been administered faster than over a duration of 60 minutes. Histamine release has also been documented with ciprofloxacin in dogs.
Answer C: Metronidazole is a nitroimidazole antibiotic that causes the inhibition of bacterial replication by inhibiting the DNA synthesis of bacterial cells. Metronidazole works when partially reduced, which is the reason why metronidazole is effective in anaerobic bacteria. Metronidazole should be infused over a course of 30 to 60 minutes. Metronidazole often causes disulfiramlike effects when ethyl alcohol is taken after metronidazole. Cefazolin is a commonly used first-generation cephalosporin that can be administered relatively quickly. Many other antibiotics must be administered over longer durations of time. Meperidine is structurally similar to atropine and, accordingly, demonstrates atropine-like effects including tachycardia. Meperidine was initially studied as an anticholinergic agent before being discovered as an analgesic. The physiologic effects of meperidine differ from other opioids mainly due to two factors: atropine-like drug effects and weak local anesthetic properties. At standard analgesic doses, meperidine is associated with hemodynamic stability. However, high doses cause hypotension and tachycardia. The hypotension is likely attributed to histamine release. In addition, high concentrations of meperidine decrease cardiac contractility, an effect resistant to naloxone. This is due to the local anesthetic effects of meperidine. Clinically, opioids are routinely used to prevent tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. Tachycardia may occasionally be seen with morphine administration as histamine release can cause transient hypotension with reflexive tachycardia. Answers A & C: Hydromorphone, fentanyl, and remifentanil all produce dose-dependent bradycardia by both sympatholytic and parasympathomimetic properties.  Opioids are routinely used to prevent tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. However, high doses of meperidine can cause tachycardia due to its atropine-like effects.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Meperidine: anticholinergic effect" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 468-475.

Activation of the NMDA receptor increases intracellular calcium which in turn acts as a sort of second messenger for a variety of signaling pathways. The NMDA receptor is an ionotropic glutamate receptor that functions as a non-specific ion channel when activated. Unlike most other receptor types which are either voltage-dependent or ligand-gated, the NMDA receptor is both. The two primary receptor agonists are glutamate and glycine and the receptor contains specific binding sites for each. In addition, the receptor can only be activated when the cell is depolarized. At resting membrane potential (non depolarized state), the ion channel is blocked by magnesium. Depolarization removes the magnesium. Therefore, both of the following two conditions must be met for the NMDA receptor to become activated: 1) Glutamate (or glycine) must be bound (ligand-gated) and 2) The cell must be depolarized (voltage-gated) The receptor will not be active if only one of these conditions is met. When the receptor is activated, the ion channel opens and allows sodium and calcium entry into the cell and potassium out of the cell. However, it is the calcium influx (C) that is the primary mediator of the effects of NMDA receptor activation since it acts as a second messenger for a variety of signaling pathways. Important NMDA receptor antagonists include, but are not limited to, dextromethorphan, ketamine, memantine, methadone, nitrous oxide, and tramadol. Answers A & B: The NMDA receptor does not use cAMP or cGMP as second messengers. Insulin and glucagon receptors use cAMP while cGMP acts as a second messenger for nitroglycerin, sodium nitroprusside, nitric oxide, and sildenafil. At resting membrane potential, the ion channel is blocked by magnesium. The NMDA receptor is an ionotropic glutamate receptor that functions as a nonspecific ion channel when activated. Activation only occurs when glutamate is bound to the receptor AND the cell is depolarized. The receptor’s effects are primarily mediated via increased intracellular calcium. Administration of magnesium along with ketamine can potentiate the effects of ketamine. Chen HS, Lipton SA. The chemical biology of clinically tolerated NMDA receptor antagonists. J Neurochem. 2006; 97(6): 1611-1626. Johnson JW, et al. Recent insights into the mode of action of memantine and ketamine. Curr Opin Pharmacol. 2014; 20C: 54-63. Petrenko AB, et al. The role of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors in pain: a review. Anesth Analg. 2003; 97(4): 1108-1116. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Ketamine Receptor Effects"

A decrease in calcium can interfere with acetylcholine release. Hypocalcemia can decrease the amount of acetylcholine that is released from the nerve terminal. Acetylcholine is synthesized from choline and acetate and is stored in vesicles. Each vesicle contains about 5,000-10,000 acetylcholine molecules. As an action potential travels through the axon and reaches the nerve terminal, P-type calcium channels are activated. Calcium that enters through the P-channels interacts with vesicles containing acetylcholine. This allows for the binding of SNARE proteins (which stands for soluble NSF attachment proteins (SNAP) receptor proteins) that are involved in the fusion, docking, and release of acetylcholine. The acetylcholine molecule after being released from the nerve terminal diffuses across the synapse and binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Nicotinic receptors have 5-subunits, with two identical subunits named alpha. The acetylcholine molecule binds to the alpha subunit. In order to activate the nicotinic receptor, both the alpha subunits need to be bound. Factors that decrease release of acetylcholine: 1) Antibiotics (clindamycin, polymyxin) 2) Magnesium: antagonizes calcium 3) Hypocalcemia 4) Anticonvulsants 5) Diuretics (furosemide) 6) Eaton-Lambert syndrome: inhibits P-type calcium channels 7) Botulinum toxin: inhibits SNARE proteins Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, diltiazem) do not affect P-channels. These drugs affect L-type calcium channels. Myasthenia gravis is due to antibodies destroying post-synaptic acetylcholine receptors. Acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal is not affected.
Answer C: Calcium-channel blockers affect L-type channels, not P-calcium channels.
Answer D: Potassium channel blockers (4-aminopyridine) prolong the calcium present in the nerve terminals leading to increased acetylcholine release. A decrease in calcium can interfere with acetylcholine release. Hypocalcemia can decrease the amount of acetylcholine that is released from the nerve terminal. Both the botulinum and tetanus toxin inhibit SNARE proteins. However, botulinum toxin acts at the level of the peripheral nerve, and the tetanus toxin acts at the central nervous system. Botulinum --> inhibits SNARE --> decrease acetylcholine release (peripheral nerve) Tetanus --> inhibits SNARE --> inhibits GABA neurons (CNS) American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword.
