Alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonists (e.g. dexmedetomidine and clonidine) have been shown to reduce the incidence of perioperative myocardial ischemia, thereby reducing associated morbidity and mortality. Dexmedetomidine is a highly specific alpha2 agonist that provides sedation, anxiolysis, hypnosis, analgesia, and sympatholysis. Dexmedetomidine decreases heart rate (HR) and systemic vascular resistance (SVR) and indirectly decreases cardiac output (CO), systemic blood pressure (SBP), and myocardial contractility. It causes limited respiratory depression, as the hypercapnic ventilatory response remains unaffected even at high doses that produce pronounced sedation.
Answer C: When used for sedation, dexmedetomidine has been shown to reduce opioid requirements by greater than 50%.
Answer D: The specificity for the α2 receptor is higher for dexmedetomidine (α2:α1 = 1600:1) than clonidine (α2:α1 = 200:1). Dexmedetomidine has a high specificity for the α2 receptor and provides sedation, anxiolysis, hypnosis, analgesia, and sympatholysis. It decreases HR, SVR, CO, SBP, the incidence of perioperative myocardial ischemia, and reduces perioperative opioid requirements.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Dexmedetomidine: decreased ischemia risk" Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 284-285.

Curve D (red) represents remifentanil. Context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. “Context” refers to the length of an infusion. For most drugs, the longer the infusion runs, the longer it takes for the drug plasma concentration to decline by half after the infusion is stopped. The CSHT reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drug plasma clearance is the collection of processes (e.g., metabolism, excretion, biotransformation, etc.) that remove the drug from plasma and therefore decrease the drug plasma concentration. If all other factors are identical, a drug with a high plasma clearance will have a lower CSHT than a drug with a low plasma clearance. When an infusion of a drug is running, a portion of the drug moves or redistributes down its concentration gradient from the central (plasma) compartment into peripheral (tissue) compartments. Once the drug infusion stops, the plasma concentration will decrease and the concentration gradient reverses. Then, the drug that has accumulated peripherally redistributes back into plasma. A drug with a slower redistribution back to plasma will have a faster CSHT than an otherwise identical drug with a faster redistribution. This occurs because the drug is being cleared from the plasma faster than the drug is returning from the periphery, and thus the plasma concentration falls faster. Keep in mind that CSHTs are different from elimination half-lives since the latter are the result of metabolism and excretion from the whole body, not just plasma. The time to decrease the plasma concentration by half (CSHT) is NOT related to the time to eliminate half of the drug from the body (“terminal half-life”). Propofol (blue line) has a steadily rising though relatively short CSHT even with a long duration of infusion. Due to its lipophilicity, propofol has a very large volume of distribution (150-700 L) and readily redistributes from the central compartment to the periphery during an infusion. This contributes to a somewhat long elimination half-life of six hours. However, the CSHT of propofol is relatively short since the drug has a high metabolic clearance from plasma (1500-2200 L/min) and a slow redistribution from peripheral to central. Fentanyl (green line), like propofol, is highly lipophilic and has a large volume of distribution (335 L). However, it has a longer and more variable CSHT due to rapid redistribution. The rapid redistribution back to plasma prevents the plasma concentration from quickly falling after the infusion is stopped, even though fentanyl is rapidly cleared (1530 mL/min). Alfentanil (purple line) has a small volume of distribution (27 L) due to a lower lipid solubility and a high degree of protein binding (90%). Since much less of the drug redistributes into peripheral tissues, redistribution back to plasma does not significantly affect plasma concentration. This explains why the CSHT of alfentanil does not increase after about two hours of infusion time. Note however for short infusions, the CSHT of alfentanil is higher than for fentanyl. This occurs since the plasma clearance of alfentanil is significantly lower (240 mL/min) than fentanyl. Remifentanil (red line) has a flat and low CSHT curve. Remifentanil’s ester structure causes it to be very rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma and tissue nonspecific esterases. Accordingly, it has a very high plasma clearance (4000 mL/min) which keeps the CSHT low. The drug’s volume of distribution is also low (30 L) so redistribution does little to raise plasma concentration after the infusion is turned off. This causes the CSHT curve to remain flat even with long-running infusions. Although not depicted on the graph, the curve for sufentanil closely resembles the propofol curve. Sufentanil’s CSHT is lower than fentanyl and alfentanil because of a moderately high plasma clearance (900 mL/min) and because of its redistribution pharmacokinetics. Sufentanil has a moderately large volume of distribution (120-250 L) and the drug slowly equilibrates between the plasma and peripheral compartments. Due to this slow equilibration, even after the infusion is turned off, a slow redistribution INTO the peripheral compartments continues to occur. This causes the drug’s CSHT to be lower than might otherwise be expected. This curve represents fentanyl.
Answer B: This curve represents alfentanil.
Answer C: This curve represents propofol. Context-sensitive half-time describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. It reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drugs with rapid plasma clearance and a low rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a low CSHT while drugs with a slow plasma clearance and high rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a high CSHT. Prior administration of a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker (NDNB) does not blunt the rise in intraocular pressure (IOP) seen with succinylcholine administration. Succinylcholine is associated with multiple side effects including, but not limited to: cardiovascular rhythm changes, hyperkalemia, muscle fasciculations, myalgias, and increases in intracranial pressure (ICP), intragastric pressure, and IOP. Pretreatment with a NDNB 3-5 minutes before succinylcholine administration may reduce the incidence or severity of some, but not all, of these side effects. Pretreatment with NDNB does not alter the cardiovascular side effects of succinylcholine. The exact mechanism responsible for bradycardia with nodal or ventricular escape beats and asystole is unknown because succinylcholine has little effect on autonomic cholinergic receptors. Cardiac side effects are more often seen with repeat dosing in children and can be attenuated with the use of glycopyrrolate or atropine. Succinylcholine more commonly causes tachycardia, mediated by catecholamine release. The succinylcholine-associated increases in potassium may be blunted by very high dose NDNB administration, well outside the clinically acceptable range for pretreatment doses. Intraocular pressure following succinylcholine administration can increase 5-15 mm Hg despite pretreatment with a NDNB. The exact mechanism is unknown, but studies have shown that the increase in IOP occurs despite detachment of extraocular muscles. This has led to the belief that the mechanism most likely is intraocular. Currently, there is widespread recommendation to avoid succinylcholine in open-eye injuries. Importantly, inadequate anesthesia, elevated blood pressure, and insufficient neuromuscular blockade during tracheal intubation can elevate IOP higher than succinylcholine alone. There is minimal evidence that succinylcholine has led to extrusion of eye contents or blindness.
Answer B: Pretreatment with NDNB significantly decreases or prevents fasciculations. Although anecdotally thought to reduce the incidence of myalgias, there has been no definitive evidence that supports this.
Answer C: The rise in intragastric pressure caused by succinylcholine can be decreased with NDNB pretreatment.
Answer D: Administration of a NDNB can blunt the rise in ICP seen with succinylcholine use. Similar to IOP, inadequate anesthesia, elevated blood pressure, and insufficient neuromuscular blockade during tracheal intubation can elevate ICP higher than succinylcholine alone. The occurrence of succinylcholine-induced fasciculations and increases in ICP and intragastric pressure may be decreased by NDNB pretreatment. Increases in IOP will occur despite pretreatment and current recommendations are to avoid succinylcholine in open-eye injuries.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The mechanism of action of nitric oxide is shared with other nitrates (hydralazine, nitroglycerin). As these drugs are metabolized, they release nitric oxide. Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase, the enzyme responsible for synthesizing cyclic guanosine 3,5 -monophosphate, causing relaxation of arteriolar and venous smooth muscle. Nitric oxide is a naturally occurring vasodilator that is released by endothelial cells and plays a major role in vascular tone regulation. Nitric oxide has a short half-life of fewer than five seconds and provides sensitive endogenous control of regional blood flow. Inhaled nitric oxide is a selective pulmonary vasodilator (due to the short half-life in the blood) that is used for the treatment of pulmonary hypertension. Fenoldopam produces vasodilation through activation of D1 dopamine receptors.
Answer C: Nitrous oxide acts on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, u opioid receptors, and γ-aminobutyric acid A receptors. Nitric oxide’s anesthetic effect is through its inhibition of NMDA receptors. Sodium nitroprusside, hydralazine, and nitroglycerin release nitric oxide as they are metabolized. Nitric oxide is a naturally occurring vasodilator that is released by endothelial cells to produce arteriolar and venous smooth muscle dilatation. Nitric oxide activates guanylyl cyclase, which synthesizes cyclic guanosine 3,5 -monophosphate, producing vasodilatation. Nitric oxide can be administered via inhalation to cause pulmonary vasodilation.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "Nitric oxide: Mechanism of action" Butterworth JF, et al. Morgan and Mikhail’s Clinical Anesthesiology. Ch. 15: Hypotensive Agents. 7th edition.

Flumazenil is a short-acting competitive antagonist of benzodiazepines. Flumazenil has the shortest half-life of all benzodiazepines, with a duration of action of about 45 minutes to one hour. Therefore, any patient who has received flumazenil should be observed for recurrent sedation. Flumazenil has a high portion of a free drug when it is injected with little protein binding, resulting in a quick onset of action (~one to three minutes) and rapid clearance. A patient who has received sedation and antagonism with flumazenil should be observed to avoid the potential of resedation. Resedation can occur because flumazenil has a shorter half-life than any other benzodiazepine. Midazolam has the shortest duration of action of the commonly used agonist benzodiazepines, so, although it still may occur, resedation is less of a problem compared to other benzodiazepine medications. If resedation occurs, repeat bolus dosing or a continuous infusion of flumazenil can be used to maintain therapeutic levels until clearance of the benzodiazepine agonist occurs. Pulmonary edema is not associated with flumazenil use; it can be seen with naloxone administration, especially in larger bolus doses.
Answer C: In a patient who does not have γ-aminobutyric acid receptor upregulation from chronic alcoholism or benzodiazepine use, a flumazenil-induced seizure is uncommon. Because of the short half-life of flumazenil, recrudescence of benzodiazepine-induced somnolence is common after its use.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Flumazenil Typical Clinical Effect (B)" Miller RD, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Ch. 26: Intravenous Anesthetics. 7th Edition.

Intravenous regular insulin is helpful in decreasing the serum potassium level in severe hyperkalemia (> 6.5 mEq/L) by shifting potassium intracellularly. It can temporize hyperkalemia until a definitive treatment to decrease potassium levels takes effect. High doses of IV insulin (10 units of regular insulin) should be given with dextrose unless the serum glucose is ≥ 250 mg/dL for severe hyperkalemia. The onset of action is 10-20 minutes with peak effect at 30-60 minutes and a total duration of action of 4-6 hours. This high dose of insulin is much more effective at lowering potassium, (~0.5-1 mEq/L) than lower doses of insulin but often leads to hypoglycemia and the need for vigilant glucose monitoring 4-6 hours after the bolus of insulin. Overall, treatment for hyperkalemia includes calcium to stabilize the myocardium in the setting of ECG changes, shifting potassium intracellularly, and elimination of potassium from the body. Cardiac membrane stabilization: • Calcium gluconate 1g to antagonize the effects of potassium on cardiac membranes • Temporizing measure to prevent or treat cardiac arrhythmias which can be fatal in hyperkalemia • No effect on potassium levels Shifting: • Treatment for hyperkalemia to decrease serum potassium levels include insulin +/- dextrose to temporarily shift potassium intracellularly • Albuterol can also be given to temporarily shift potassium intracellularly. It is only recommended as an adjuvant to insulin due to additive effects rather than as a sole method for shifting. Elimination: • Diuresis, gastrointestinal loss, or removal via hemodialysis. • Loop diuretics, such as furosemide, are routinely used to eliminate potassium in patients who can produce urine. The onset of action of loop diuretics is generally faster than oral potassium binders or hemodialysis (due to time to initiate). Although classically taught that sodium bicarbonate is a mainstay of hyperkalemia treatment, its effectiveness has been called into question. Historic research suggesting its effectiveness was largely done in the single patient population of end-stage renal disease patients receiving hemodialysis. That research showed sodium bicarbonate may be effective at lowering potassium in patients with metabolic acidosis. This may not be generalizable to other patient populations, however. Furthermore, sodium bicarbonate can lower ionized calcium transiently, which could be deleterious in a patient at risk for malignant arrhythmias. The use of sodium bicarbonate to routinely treat hyperkalemia is no longer recommended. Loop diuretics, such as furosemide, are recommended in the treatment of severe hyperkalemia; however, in hyperkalemic emergencies, such as the patient presented in this question, rapid-acting therapies like calcium and insulin must occur first to prevent cardiovascular collapse.
Answer C: Patiromer, approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2015, and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, approved by the FDA in 2018, are oral potassium binders that can be used in the acute or chronic treatment of hyperkalemia. After a single oral dose, the potassium-lowering effects of patiromer can be seen after 7 hours, whereas sodium zirconium cyclosilicate’s effects can be seen after 1 hour. Side effects of patiromer include hypomagnesemia, transient constipation, and diarrhea. Side effects of sodium zirconium cyclosilicate include peripheral edema. Both can cause hypokalemia, and neither is known to cause bowel necrosis. Sodium polystyrene has fallen out of favor because its benefits are questionable and only supported by low-quality evidence. Its onset was slow, taking up to 24 hours or more to decrease serum potassium. Furthermore, its use was attributed to multiple cases of bowel necrosis. Considering the lack of good supporting evidence, risk of severe injury, and better agents now available, it would be difficult to recommend the continued use of sodium polystyrene. Overall, treatment for hyperkalemia includes calcium to stabilize the myocardium in the setting of ECG changes, shifting potassium intracellularly, and elimination of potassium from the body. In hyperkalemia emergencies (> 6.5 mEq/L with symptoms) calcium (myocardial stabilization) and insulin (shifting) should be administered first to prevent cardiovascular collapse followed by therapies to remove potassium from the body. Calcium is controversial for the treatment of hyperkalemia in the setting of digoxin use. Although it is given to hyperkalemic patients to prevent myocardial excitability, administering calcium to a hyperkalemic patient on digoxin could prove disastrous. Digoxin inhibits sodium-potassium ATPase, which leads to increased intracellular sodium that causes decreased activity of the sodium-calcium exchanger. This results in increased intracellular calcium to improve inotropy. Additional exogenous calcium that influxes into the cardiac myocyte can cause the lethal “stone heart.” This is a pathological noncontractile state of the myocardium due to a massive influx of calcium causing impaired diastolic relaxation from calcium-troponin C binding. This influx may also lead to a malignant arrhythmia. There have been multiple case reports since the 1930s of death after patients on digoxin therapy received calcium. Since that time, digoxin has become less commonly prescribed. A retrospective chart review of 2,220 subjects from 1989-2005 did not find, however, an association between calcium administration and death in patients on digoxin. It is advised that hyperkalemic patients on digoxin therapy be given potentially life-saving calcium, with caution that a malignant arrhythmia may develop. If hyperkalemia is thought to be due to digoxin toxicity, then definitive treatment requires a digoxin-specific antibody. Nevertheless, in patients with severe hyperkalemia who develop concerning ECG changes, calcium gluconate must be administered first and promptly to stabilize cardiac myocytes to avoid progression to a fatal arrhythmia. Low molecular weight heparin (LMWH) more selectively inhibits activated factor X when compared to unfractionated heparin (UFH). LMWH, such as enoxaparin and dalteparin, work similarly to UFH by binding the serine protease inhibitor ATIII. Binding of ATIII by UFH or LMWH induces a conformational change that increases ATIII’s activity by 1000-fold to inhibit activated factor X and thrombin. Inhibition of thrombin requires simultaneous binding of heparin to both ATIII and thrombin, but inhibition of factor Xa only requires heparin binding to ATIII. A longer polysaccharide chain (higher molecular weight) is required for the increased binding sites leading to thrombin inhibition. The shorter polysaccharide chains (lower molecular weight) of LMWH is more restricted in binding solely to ATIII, therefore more selectively inhibits Xa. While LMWH is more selective for factor Xa than UFH (in the case of enoxaparin almost 4 times more selective), inhibition of thrombin still occurs. Selective Xa inhibition can be desirable as factor Xa has limited function outside the coagulation system, unlike thrombin which also plays a role in the immune system and inflammatory pathways. LMWH is also less associated with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and platelet dysfunction than UFH, although LMWH is still contraindicated in a patient with a history of HIT. While UFH and LMWH are widely used for thromboprophylaxis, more selective inhibitors of the coagulation cascade are desirable in certain clinical scenarios. LMWH and UFH activate ATIII. This increases ATIII inhibition of the clotting cascade primarily involving factor Xa and thrombin.
Answer B: Both LMWH and UFH indirectly inhibit factor Xa and thrombin. This is not an advantage of LMWH over UFH.
Answer D: Direct thrombin inhibitors include argatroban, bivalirudin, lepirudin, and desirudin which are approved for use in HIT. Dabigatran is an oral direct thrombin inhibitor. LMWH is more selective for factor Xa inhibition than UFH, with less effect on thrombin inhibition.  Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Pages 438-440. St. John’s wort primarily induces P450 3A4 and P450 2C9 enzymes. St. John’s wort is a well-known inducer of the P450 system. Induction of enzymes causes increased metabolism of drugs. Therefore, the drug becomes less efficacious, and dose changes may be required. Induction of the 3A4 system increases the metabolism of alfentanil, midazolam, lidocaine, and oral contraceptives. Induction of the 2C9 system increases the metabolism of most nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Oral contraceptives and antiretroviral medications may be less effective when patients are taking St. John's wort. P450 2C19 is not affected by St. John’s wort. However, the 2C19 system is important in the metabolism of clopidogrel. Clopidogrel is a prodrug metabolized by the 2C19 system. Some patients are under metabolizers of clopidogrel because they have a genetic mutation in this system. Metabolism by the 2C19 system is not required for prasugrel, another ADP receptor antagonist, to become active.
Answer B: The P450 2D6 enzymes are not affected by St. John’s wort. However, the 2D6 enzymes play an important role in pain control. P450 2D6 is an important enzyme in the conversion of codeine to morphine. There is wide discrepancy concerning 2D6 enzyme efficacy. Some people have hypermetabolism and can metabolize more codeine to morphine. Patients with hypermetabolism are at risk of overdose from even small doses of codeine, and the US Food and Drug Administration has issued a safety alert recommending against codeine for children undergoing tonsillectomy and/or adenoidectomy. However, some people have minimal 2D6 activity and, therefore, do not process codeine into morphine. These patients experience no therapeutic effect from codeine. St. John’s wort is an herbal medication that is taken by patients to treat depression. St. John’s wort induces P450 3A4. This induction causes many anesthetic-related drugs, including alfentanil and midazolam, to be metabolized. St. John’s wort is a drug used to help treat anxiety and depression. St. John’s wort has mild sedative properties that can affect anesthesia, so it should be used with caution in patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors or selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Additionally, St. John’s wort has been associated with delayed arousal from anesthesia, and it has been argued that minimum alveolar concentration may be decreased in patients taking St. John’s wort. Benzodiazepines, propofol, and barbiturates can decrease ketamine-induced emergence delirium. An important consideration when using ketamine relates to the high incidence of psychomimetic reactions early in the recovery period. The most common reactions include hallucinations, nightmares, altered cognition, and altered short-term memory. Repeated doses of ketamine may decrease the severity and incidence of emergence delirium, but one of the most effective strategies for prevention of emergence delirium is the use of midazolam approximately five minutes prior to an induction with ketamine. Droperidol may increase the incidence of emergence delirium associated with ketamine use.
Answer C: The use of neostigmine has no correlation with the incidence of emergence delirium.
Answer D: Opioids have not been shown to decrease the incidence of emergence delirium. Ketamine is associated with a high incidence of psychomimetic reactions early in the recovery period. The incidence of these reactions can be decreased by coadministration of benzodiazepines, propofol, or barbiturates.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Ketamine Emergence Delirium: Rx" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 455.

Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) should not be combined with meperidine (C) due to the risk of serotonin syndrome. MAOIs were the first class of antidepressants discovered. They work by inhibiting the enzyme monoamine oxidase, which is responsible for breaking down serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. Meperidine is a synthetic opioid, which works by acting on the Mu-receptor and is widely used for treating pain and post anesthetic shivering. Meperidine is in a class of opioids known as phenylpiperidine opioids along with methadone and tramadol. These three opioids are all weak serotonin reuptake inhibitors. Decreased serotonin reuptake, especially when combined with the decreased serotonin breakdown which occurs with MAOIs, can lead to serotonin syndrome. In 1984, a patient named Libby Zion was given a combination of the MAO-I phenelzine and meperidine by a resident physician, leading to lethal serotonin syndrome. Her death led to creation of the Libby Zion Law in New York, which set a limit on resident physician work hours. Serotonin syndrome is a continuum that can present with subtle mild symptoms or overt life-threatening symptoms. Mild symptoms include akathisia, agitation, tremor, anxiety, tachycardia, sweating, diarrhea, and mydriasis. Moderate-to-severe symptoms include hyper-vigilance, hyperthermia, hypertension, symmetrical hyperreflexia with lower extremity predominance, inducible extremity clonus, myoclonus, and ocular clonus. Life-threatening symptoms include rigidity, autonomic instability, hyperthermia >40°C, disseminated intravascular coagulation, rhabdomyolysis, ataxia, confusion, tonic-clonic seizures, multiorgan failure, and coma. Serotonin syndrome is a clinical diagnosis and no laboratory test is confirmatory. The differential diagnosis includes anticholinergic toxicity, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and malignant hyperthermia. Clonus is the most important finding in confirming the diagnosis of serotonin syndrome. Ocular clonus is rarely seen in other conditions and can be elicited by having the patient fixate on a finger then rapidly moving it to midline. The most accurate diagnostic criteria currently are the Hunter Toxicity Criteria Decision Rules. To meet diagnostic criteria, the patient must be on a serotonergic agent and have one of the following: * Spontaneous clonus. * Inducible clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis. * Ocular clonus plus agitation or diaphoresis. * Tremor plus hyperreflexia. * Hypertonia plus temperature >38°C plus ocular clonus or inducible clonus. Multiple medications are associated with serotonin syndrome: Increase in serotonin synthesis: L-tryptophan Inhibition of serotonin metabolism: MAO-A inhibitors—moclobemide, MAO-B inhibitors—selegiline, MAO inhibitors—phenelzine, tranylcypromine, isocarboxazid. Increase in serotonin release: Amphetamines, Appetite suppressants—fenfluramine, Cocaine, MDMA (“ecstasy”), Mirtazapine, Reserpine Stimulation of postsynaptic receptors: Buspirone, Lithium, Lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), Trazodone Cyclic antidepressants: Amitriptyline, Clomipramine, Doxepin, Imipramine Serotonin specific reuptake inhibitors and related: Citalopram, Fluoxetine, Fluvoxamine, Paroxetine, Sertraline, Sibutramine, Tramadol, Trazodone, Venlafaxine Others: Antiemetics—metoclopramide, ondansetron, granisetron, Antimigraines—carbamazepine, ergot alkaloids, sumatriptan, valproic acid, Cyclobenzaprine, Dextromethorphan, Fentanyl, Linezolid, Meperidine, Panax ginseng, Ritonavir, St. John's wort  Meperidine is a weak serotonin reuptake inhibitor and can therefore lead to serotonin syndrome if given to patients taking MAO inhibitors. Indirect sympathomimetics, such as ephedrine, can produce exaggerated response in patients taking MAOIs as they trigger the release of accumulated catecholamines. Miller Anesthesia. Opioids cause dose-dependent ventilatory depression which can lead to acute respiratory acidosis, identified by elevated arterial PaCO2, low arterial pH, and minimally elevated serum bicarbonate. Opioid analgesics depress ventilation by activation of μ-receptors (particularly μ2) in the ventrolateral medulla and other areas of the brainstem. Higher PaCO2 and lower PaO2 levels are necessary to drive ventilation during opioid administration. As the PaCO2 climbs, arterial pH decreases. Renal compensation for respiratory acidosis occurs at a slow rate. In acute respiratory acidosis, serum bicarbonate levels increase 1 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2. If the respiratory acidosis is chronic, bicarbonate levels increase between 4-5 mEq/L for each 10 mm Hg rise in PaCO2. Hence, in this scenario, early compensation for the acute respiratory acidosis is seen with a bicarbonate level of 26 mEq/L for the PaCO2 level of 70 mm Hg. Patients with chronic respiratory acidosis, such as those with chronic hypercarbia from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), have a relatively normal pH, an elevated PaCO2, and a serum bicarbonate level that reflects a 4-5 mEq/L increase per 10 mm Hg increase in PaCO2.
Answer C: Although unusual, it is also possible to have a concurrent metabolic and respiratory acidosis (or concurrent alkalosis). For example, a patient may have diabetic ketoacidosis, uremia, or diarrhea resulting in a metabolic acidosis coupled with a respiratory acidosis from COPD or hypopnea due to postoperative pain. These patients can experience severe, lifethreatening acidemia if not promptly treated. Opioids produce a dose-dependent ventilatory depression which necessitates higher PaCO2 and lower PaO2 levels to activate the chemoreceptors responsible for ventilatory drive. As the PaCO2 increases, patients become increasingly acidotic in a predictable fashion according to the acuteness of their hypercapnia.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "ABG: opioid effect" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 291-293. Evers, Anesthetic Pharmacology, 2nd edition, p. 498.

Recurrence of respiratory depression or “renarcotization” is not uncommon after naloxone administration for reversal of the effects of morphine or hydromorphone. Naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist, has a short duration of action (30-60 minutes) relative to the duration of action of longer-acting opioids (e.g. morphine and hydromorphone), which can be up to several hours. Therefore, naloxone is ideally used to reverse shorter-acting opioids such as fentanyl or alfentanil. Repeated doses or an infusion may be needed for longeracting opioids. Naloxone has the greatest affinity for the µ-receptor but also has some activity at the δ- and κ-receptors. Onset of action for intravenous naloxone is 1-2 minutes and duration of action is 30-60 minutes. Side effects include increased heart rate, increased blood pressure, and potentially pulmonary edema. These effects are mediated by an increase in resultant pain and sympathetic stimulation. Hypothermic patients receiving naloxone for opioid reversal can experience a two or three-fold increase in oxygen consumption with the resultant increase in cardiac output and stress on the cardiovascular system. Many practitioners advocate the dilution of naloxone from 0.4 mg/mL to 0.04 mg/mL in non-emergent situations. Then, 40 mcg aliquots of naloxone may be titrated every 5 min until apnea or pronounced hypopnea has resolved. This can help minimize the detrimental side effects of complete opioid reversal and sympathetic stimulation (e.g. pulmonary edema). Naltrexone is a longer-acting opioid antagonist that is better suited for the longer acting opioids. Alternatively, partial opioid agonist-antagonists (e.g. nalbuphine) may be used to maintain analgesia while antagonizing opioid receptors. Onset of action for intravenous naloxone is 1-2 minutes.
Answer B: Opioid antagonists are most commonly used to restore a normal pattern of spontaneous ventilation in patients with opioid overdose. Opioid antagonists can also reverse opioid-induced nausea and vomiting, pruritus, and urinary retention. Naloxone, an opioid antagonist, has an onset of action of 1-2 minutes and duration of 30-60 minutes. Recurrence of respiratory depression can occur after naloxone administration if used to reverse a long-acting opioid overdose. Naloxone can also reverse opioid-induced nausea, vomiting, pruritus, and urinary retention. Side effects include an increase in sympathetic stimulation which can cause pulmonary edema and/or myocardial ischemia, particularly if a large bolus dose is given. Opioid agonist-antagonists (e.g. nalbuphine, pentazocine, butorphanol, and buprenorphine) have limited effects on smooth muscles of the bladder, biliary tree, and intestines, therefore causing less urinary retention, biliary colic, and constipation compared with pure opioid agonists. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Opioid Reversal” Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 810-812. Longnecker, Anesthesiology, 1st edition, pp. 890-892.

A position statement formulated by the American Pain Society, American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine, and the American Society of Anesthesiologists was published in 2016, titled “Guidelines on the Management of Postoperative Pain”. In these guidelines it was recommended that patient controlled analgesia (PCA) be administered whenever parenteral opioids are needed. This includes hospitalized patients who cannot take medications via the oral or enteral routes. These recommendations came from a review of the literature that found that IV PCA is more effective with higher patient satisfaction when compared to health care provider initiated intermittent bolus dosing of opioids. The panel recommended that IV PCA could be used in patients who were greater than six years of age and who were able to cognitively understand the concept of PCA. Furthermore, the panel recommended against basal infusion of opioids in opioid-naïve patients because the evidence does not show improved analgesia compared to PCA with no basal rate. Basal rates are associated with an increased risk of respiratory depression, nausea, and vomiting. The evidence of using a basal rate in patients who are opioid tolerant is lacking, however there may be a stronger rationale in that population because of the higher potential for under dosing and uncontrolled pain. Side effects from opioids are mostly the same regardless of the route of administration. In patients receiving opioids in the postoperative period, proper monitoring for sedation and respiratory depression is vital. Multiple studies have been conducted surrounding the best type of analgesia route/method in the perioperative period and no single type or modality has been shown to be superior. Multiple studies have been devoted to the concept of multi-modal analgesia and the benefits of providing different mechanisms to target different pain pathways. Most experts recommend using acetaminophen and/or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, and there is strong evidence to support this recommendation. These medications are well tolerated (in patients where a contraindication does not exist). Other agents which can be considered as part of a multi-modal approach to pain include celecoxib, ketamine, gabapentin, pregabalin, and lidocaine. Regional anesthesia can also play an important role when indicated. This patient is one day postoperative from a bowel resection. Although most ERAS protocols advise to start oral intake as soon as possible postoperative in patients having colorectal surgery, absorption of medications may not be predictable. Several studies have shown that stomach emptying time is delayed but the absorption from the small intestine may be intact. This patient is nauseated though and may vomit any oral medications administered, thus an intravenous route is more likely to control pain consistently until the patient's nausea can be better controlled.
Answer B: Basal rates for intravenous PCAs are not advisable because they are associated with an increased risk of respiratory depression, especially in a patient who is opioid naïve. The evidence is not strong for patients with opioid tolerance, however it may be more reasonable in that patient population.
Answer C: This would be the modality of choice in this patient who is one day postop from a major abdominal surgery. This is associated with better patient satisfaction and more constant plasma levels of medications, while also balancing the risk of respiratory depression (which is the most significant side effect that can occur, especially in basal rate infusions in opioid naïve patients).
Answer D: Patients as young as six years old may be able to control a PCA. PCA has been shown to be a superior way to administer pain medications because the patient is in control and there is no delay in administration, which often happens with nurse administered pain medications. Patients older than six are potentially able to understand cause and effect, and thus work a PCA. Even family controlled analgesia can work favorably in the correct circumstances. Intravenous patient controlled analgesia is an excellent form of pain management when a patient is unable to tolerate oral medications. It usually results in a more continuous plasma concentration of medication and also helps the patient became more able to be in control of their pain.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "PCA In Opioid-naive Pt" Chou, R. Guidelines on the Management of Postoperative Pain. Management of Postoperative pain: a clinical guidelines from the American Pain Society, the American Society of Regional Anesthesia and Pain Medicine, and the American Society of Anestheisologists’ Committee on Regional Anesthesia, Executive Committee, and Administrative Council. The Journal of Pain. 2016(17): 131-157. Kennedy, J. Drug absorption from the small intestine in immediate postoperative patients. British Journal of Anesthesia. 2006(97): 171-180.

Methadone has been associated with electrocardiographic abnormalities such as prolonged QT interval and torsades de pointes. Methadone is primarily metabolized via the cytochrome P450 system, especially CYP3A4. Concurrent use of medications that inhibit CYP3A4 activity can lead to higher serum levels and potentially lethal cardiac arrhythmias. Methadone is a highly bioavailable opioid with a long, unpredictable elimination half-life (19-58 hours). In addition to its opioid effects, methadone is also an NMDA receptor antagonist and serotonin reuptake inhibitor. These added effects help augment methadone’s analgesic properties. Ketorolac is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug that has no effect on QT interval. It can affect renal glomerular blood flow and cause or worsen preexisting renal failure. Ketorolac also inhibits platelet aggregation and thromboxane production, which can lead to increased bleeding.
Answer B: Meperidine is a synthetic opioid commonly used for pain management and treatment of shivering in the postoperative period. It does not prolong the QT interval. Normeperidine, meperidine’s toxic metabolite, is neuroexcitatory and high concentrations can cause seizures. Methadone can produce or worsen a preexisting prolonged QT interval, which can lead to the lethal arrhythmia, torsades de pointes. This risk is increased with concurrent use of CYP3A4 inhibitors.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Methadone: QT interval" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 475, 554-556, 1482-1483, 1520. Evers, Anesthetic Pharmacology, 2nd edition, pp. 516, 520, 525.

Activation of biliary smooth muscle is prevented by efferent innervation. This innervation is inhibited by opioid receptor activation. In patients with biliary disease, the frequent contractions induced can result in biliary colic. The pressure in the common bile duct can increase ten times baseline during these contractions. With morphine, increased biliary activity can last for more than two hours. Atropine, papaverine, and naloxone can relieve opioid-induced biliary colic. Answers A & B & C: Benzodiazepines, inflammation, peptic ulcer disease, and GERD would all be less likely in this clinical scenario than biliary colic. Flumazenil, NSAIDs, and H2 blockers are not implicated in biliary colic.  Opioids can induce biliary colic, particularly in susceptible patients. This can be alleviated by blocking opioid receptor activation or by blocking parasympathetic activation.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Opioids: Biliary Colic (B)" Katzung, Bertram G. Etomidate can cause adrenal suppression by inhibiting the enzyme 11-β hydroxylase. Etomidate is an intravenous anesthetic drug believed to function as a GABA-agonist. It is typically used for induction of anesthesia in hemodynamically unstable patients since it has minimal effects on cardiac function or vascular tone and does not cause histamine release. Etomidate also decreases cerebral metabolic oxygen demand, cerebral blood flow, and intracranial pressure (ICP), but maintains cerebral perfusion pressure. While etomidate otherwise appears to be an ideal agent to provide long-term sedation for neurosurgical patients with elevated ICP, it is avoided due to inhibition of adrenocortical synthetic function, especially in the setting of prolonged drug exposure. However, even a single dose can cause temporary adrenal suppression. Other side effects include pain on injection, myoclonus, and postoperative nausea and vomiting. Specifically, etomidate inhibits the adrenal enzyme 11-β hydroxylase, the downstream effects of which are inhibition of cortisol (and aldosterone) synthesis. The 11-β hydroxylase enzyme converts deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone and 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. Corticosterone can then be converted to cortisol or aldosterone by other enzymes. The enzyme 21-hydroxylase converts progesterone to deoxycorticosterone and 17α-hydroxyprogesterone to 11-deoxycortisol. Etomidate does not affect the function of this enzyme.
Answer C: Etomidate inhibits the adrenal enzyme 11-β hydroxylase. Etomidate inhibits adrenal steroidogenesis by inhibiting the enzyme 11-β hydroxylase which is responsible for cortisol and aldosterone production. Adrenal suppression is most pronounced with long-term use, but can also occur transiently after a single dose.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Etomidate: Adrenal suppression" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 15, 455.

Contact dermatitis represents a cutaneous T cell mediated immune reaction. Approximately 10% of the population reports a penicillin (PCN) allergy. When skin tests are performed, only 10-15% of patients who report an allergy will actually have IgE mediated reaction. Interestingly, there is a gradual loss of PCN IgE over time. Greater than 80% of patients with a prior history of adverse reactions will have negative skin test within 10 years, and resensitization is uncommon. In the United States, most allergy is related to the beta-lactam core which combines with lysine residues in proteins. Cephalosporins, carbapenems, and monobactams also have a beta-lactam core. Sensitivity to the R-group side chains is also possible. Sensitivity to penicillins and cephalosporins is responsible for approximately 70% of perioperative antibiotic anaphylactic reactions. Patients who had a penicillin reaction over 10 years prior and who had non IgE-mediated or severe symptoms have a less than 1% chance of reaction to cephalosporins. Without a skin test, the risk of a reaction when given a cephalosporin is between 0.17 and 8.4% depending on the prior reaction. An IgE mediated reaction is a Type I, anaphylactic reaction.
Answer C: Severe reactions that are not IgE-mediated are possible reactions to beta-lactam antibiotics. Examples of severe non IgE-mediated reactions are Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis. A Type II reaction results in hemolytic anemia and is IgG mediated. A type III reaction represents serum sickness, while a type IV reaction is contact dermatitis.
Answer D: IgM antibodies are responsible for the acute phase immune reaction to infection.
Answer E: A non-immune mediated reaction is a pseudoallergic or anaphylactoid reaction, which may be clinically indistinguishable from anaphylaxis at presentation. A skin rash represents a cutaneous T cell mediated immune reaction.  Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Pages 266, 278 Solensky, R. Up to Date: Allergy to Penicillins. Ebo DG, et al. Anaphylaxis during anaesthesia: diagnostic approach. Allergy 2007: 62: 471–487 American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Antibiotic Prophylaxis: PCN Reactions"

Remifentanil is an ultra-short acting opioid analgesic that is metabolized independent of the kidneys by plasma esterases. Fentanyl is relatively safe when used in patients with end stage renal disease (ESRD) because of its rapid redistribution, lack of metabolites, and unchanged free fraction. However, because remifentanil is metabolized independent of the liver and kidneys, it is considered ideal for patients with renal failure. Remifentanil is usually administered as a continuous infusion due to its short elimination half-life (0.17-0.33 hours) and steady context-sensitive half-time regardless of infusion duration. Methadone also needs little adjustment in patients with renal disease. Hydromorphone accumulates in patients with renal failure, so smaller doses are necessary. In addition, a toxic metabolite, hydromorphone-3-glucuronide, can accumulate. Like normeperidine, it also has neuroexcitatory and pro-convulsant properties.
Answer B: Morphine should be used with caution in patients with renal failure due to the accumulation of an active metabolite, morphine-6-glucuronide. Morphine-6-glucuronide can lead to prolonged sedation and respiratory depression. Many analgesics used perioperatively have toxic metabolites that can accumulate in patients with ESRD. Remifentanil is metabolized by esterases and is therefore safe in patients with renal disease. Additionally, fentanyl and methadone would be options in ESRD. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits the COX enzyme and is therefore effective for the duration of the life of the platelet (approximately 7 days). Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 469, 484-485, 492, 1482, 1357. Evers, Anesthetic Pharmacology, 2nd edition, pp. 516, 520, 525. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Opioids: Use In ESRD"

Infants have a higher initial uptake of volatile anesthetics than adults due to their minute ventilation to functional residual capacity (FRC) ratio. Infants have a lower FRC than adults, which provides less “air” to dilute the volatile anesthetic being breathed. However, the infant’s higher minute ventilation places more volatile anesthetic in the alveoli where it can be taken up. This increased minute ventilation is primarily why infants have a higher uptake and faster induction with volatile anesthetics compared to adults. Infants have a decreased metabolism because of immature organs; however, even with mature organs, there is little metabolism of volatile anesthetics. Additionally, the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) requirements are increased in infants, not decreased. The MAC requirements of infants often peak at 6 months of age.
Answer B: The increased oxygen consumption to FRC ratio has no effect on the speed of induction or rate of anesthetic uptake. The increased oxygen consumption to FRC ratio explains the rapid desaturation with apnea in infants. With a higher minute ventilation and cardiac output, the uptake of volatile anesthetic is greater in infants.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Uptake And Distribution: Infant Vs. Adult" Hines, Roberta L. and Marschall, Katherine. Stoelting's Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease. 6th edition. 2012.

Benzodiazepine metabolism occurs in the liver, involving either phase I metabolism (N-dealkylation or aliphatic hydroxylation) and/or phase II metabolism (glucuronidation or acetylation). Lorazepam has five metabolites but primarily undergoes glucuronide conjugation without any phase I metabolism and, because of this, is less affected by age and liver disease. The main metabolite of lorazepam is inactive and water-soluble, thus is excreted rapidly by the kidneys. Because the metabolite is inactive, renal failure has an insignificant effect on lorazepam. Oxazepam is the other benzodiazepine which undergoes glucuronidation without phase I metabolism, making it useful in patients taking medications that interact with the cytochrome p450 system. All benzodiazepines can be affected by liver disease if the disease is significant enough to reduce metabolism or to reduce the production of binding proteins. Since benzodiazepines are protein-bound, severe liver disease can increase the free fraction of available benzodiazepines in the blood. Benzodiazepine hydrolysis is used to extract benzodiazepines from biological specimens, such as urine. Hydrolysis is not used for lorazepam metabolism.
Answer C: Midazolam and diazepam undergo hepatic oxidation-reduction. The clearance of diazepam and midazolam decreases with age and smoking increases it; these two factors have little effect on the clearance of lorazepam.
Answer D: Midazolam and diazepam undergo hepatic oxidation-reduction. Oxidation-reduction is not used for lorazepam metabolism. Lorazepam undergoes glucuronidation metabolism in the liver without any phase I metabolism. Midazolam is metabolized to active forms called hydroxymidazolams, which have up to 30% the potency of the primary drug. Diazepam is metabolized to active forms called oxazepam and desmethyldiazepam. Sevoflurane produces the largest concentration of fluoride ions following hepatic metabolism. The clinical importance of metabolism of today’s volatile anesthetics is related to fluoride-induced nephrotoxicity. This is in contrast to halothane metabolism of the past which was related to hepatotoxicity. Fluoride-induced nephrotoxicity was described after methoxyflurane use for long cases. Once this was noted, the agent was immediately removed from the market. Fluoride accumulation currently remains a topic of interest in regards to sevoflurane. Sevoflurane undergoes 5-8% hepatic metabolism, resulting in an increase in serum fluoride concentrations. Sevoflurane does not, however, cause a renal concentrating effect due to decreased solubility in blood and tissue. Fluoride production rapidly declines once the anesthetic is no longer administered. In addition, the degree of renal metabolism of inorganic fluoride ions, a process known as defluorination, contributes to nephrotoxicity. Sevoflurane is minimally defluorinated within the kidneys. The nephrotoxicity described from inorganic fluoride ions is a high-output renal failure that does not respond to vasopressin. This results from direct fluoride ion toxicity to the collecting ducts which inhibits the effect of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). It is characterized by hypovolemia, polyuria, elevated blood urea nitrogen, elevated creatinine, serum hypernatremia, and serum hyperosmolality. Although sevoflurane creates more fluoride ions during administration as compared with enflurane, serum and tissue levels of fluoride ions slowly decline up to 72 hours following the cessation of enflurane administration. This was likely due to the increased solubility of enflurane in blood and tissue. Answers C & D: Isoflurane and desflurane yield the least amount of fluoride ions. Methoxyflurane created the largest concentrations of inorganic fluoride ions and fluoride-induced nephrotoxicity. Enflurane was related to renal concentration effects of fluoride ions causing nephrotoxicity. Sevoflurane produces more fluoride ions than enflurane while being administered, but the concentration of fluoride rapidly declines with cessation of administration, owing to its low blood and tissue solubility. Fluoride ion production: methoxyflurane > sevoflurane > enflurane > isoflurane > desflurane. Nephrotoxicity occurs when fluoride levels are >50 µmol/L. Moderate renal injury occurs between 50-80 µmol/L and severe injury occurs at >80 µmol/L. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Volatile Anesthetics: Fluoride Ion” Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 438-439. Miller, Basics of Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 81. Longnecker, Anesthesiology, 1st edition, pp. 760-761.

Cyanocobalamin is a nontoxic form of vitamin B12 formed when hydroxycobalamin (another form of B12 that can be used as an antidote for cyanide poisoning) chelates a cyanide ion. Metabolism of sodium nitroprusside produces five cyanide ions per nitroprusside molecule. Normally, these ions are eliminated before any significant toxicity can occur. However, following lengthy nitroprusside infusions, the cyanide ions accumulate and can lead to toxicity via three different mechanisms. Major signs and symptoms of nitroprusside toxicity are metabolic acidosis (with anion gap), elevated mixed venous oxygen, arrhythmias, and CNS disturbances. One mechanism of toxicity is the creation of cyanmethemoglobin which is unable to carry oxygen. This causes an anemic hypoxia. Nitroprusside metabolism results in conversion of hemoglobin to methemoglobin. Since methemoglobin has an extra positive charge it readily attracts the negatively charged cyanide ion to form cyanmethemoglobin. Note, however, that the enzyme methemoglobin reductase rapidly converts the methemoglobin that is formed back to hemoglobin, so large quantities of cyanmethemoglobin are not usually formed. Cyanmethemoglobin production is significantly increased when nitrates are used to treat cyanide toxicity since they greatly increase methemoglobin formation which is then converted to cyanmethemoglobin.
Answer C: The primary physiologic mechanism for cyanide ion elimination is metabolism in mitochondria (especially renal and hepatic cells) to thiocyanate, which is less toxic than cyanide. This reaction is catalyzed by rhodanese enzymes and requires thiosulfate as a substrate. Thiocyanate is eliminated renally but has an excretion half-life of ≥ 4 days. Thiocyanate toxicity can occur with long-term nitroprusside administration, in patients with impaired renal function, or in patients given sodium thiosulfate to treat cyanide poisoning. Symptoms include nausea, tinnitus, muscle spasm, visual changes, disorientation, psychosis, and seizures. Nitroprusside is metabolized to cyanide ions and toxicity can occur following lengthy infusions. The three major mechanisms for nitroprusside toxicity are 1) Cyanide ions bind to cytochrome c oxidase and inhibit cellular aerobic respiration. 2) Formation of cyanmethemoglobin which is unable to carry oxygen. 3) Thiocyanate production which causes CNS-related effects.  Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 910, 1077. Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, p. 2116. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Nitroprusside toxicity: blood chemistry"

As it has a remarkably short half-life, the site of production of nitric oxide has the most influence on its function. Nitric oxide (NO), also known as endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF), is produced in endothelial cells and has vasodilatory effects and anti-aggregating effects on platelets. It has a half-life of only a few seconds and is highly diffusible across cell membranes. It is involved in cellular signaling and homeostasis. NO is also produced by immune cells and in the bone marrow. It stimulates insulin release in the pancreas. It is also involved in neuronal transmission and can modulate the pain response. Production in vascular endothelium is important in the regulation of blood flow. Nitric oxide does bind with hemoglobin. Efficient binding of NO to hemoglobin is exploited when NO is administered via inhalation to promote pulmonary vasodilation whilst limiting systemic hypotensive effects. However, the function of the molecule is not altered by binding with hemoglobin, just attenuated. NO can also bind with myoglobin when filtered by the renal tubules leading to medullary vasoconstriction and ischemia.
Answer B: It is possible to increase NO levels from dietary consumption of nitrate rich leafy green vegetables. This may have health benefits for some patients (e.g. hypertensive patients) given NO’s vasodilatory properties, but the effect or function of NO is not changed if it is received from exogenous sources. Several medications also increase NO levels such as nitroglycerin and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors.
Answer C: Genetic polymorphisms of the three different isoforms of nitric oxide synthase and its modifiers are involved in many disease processes such as hypertension and renal disease. However, this does not determine function. It is the localized effects of nitric oxide at the specific site of production (neuronal, endothelial, cardiovascular) that determine the function of NO (neuronal transmission versus vasodilation versus immunomodulation). Site of production determines the function of nitric oxide. Production in vascular endothelium is important in the regulation of blood flow.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Sites Of NO Production" Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Pages 118, 123, 125, 281, 390, 1296, 1355, 1476

Fenoldopam is a selective dopamine-1 agonist that increases renal blood flow despite decreased systemic arterial blood pressure. Fenoldopam has little to no alpha, beta, or dopamine-2 receptor agonist activity. Nitroglycerin relaxes smooth muscle in the veins via the release of nitric oxide. However, nitroglycerin does not increase renal blood flow because it has selective vasodilatory effects on renal conductance but not on resistance of blood vessels.
Answer B: Sodium nitroprusside relaxes smooth muscle in the veins via the release of nitric oxide. When veins are dilated, arterial blood pressure decreases, which then releases renin and catecholamines. There is a decrease in renal perfusion but renal function is maintained.
Answer D: Adenosine is a vasodilator that affects vessels primarily in afterload. It also causes renal vasoconstriction and as such, there is a decrease in renal perfusion, urinary output, and glomerular filtration rate after administration. Fenoldopam is a selective dopamine-1 agonist that increases renal blood flow.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Vasodilators: Renal Blood Flow" Elkayam U, et al. Renal vasodilatory effect on endothelial stimulation in patients with chronic congestive heart failure. J Am Coll Cardiol. 1996; 28(1): 176-182. Morgan and Mikhail’s Clinical Anesthesiology, 4th edition. Pages 256-261.

The concentration effect explains why nitrous oxide has a more rapid rise of FA/FI than desflurane, despite the blood:gas coefficients (B). The concentration effect causes the rate of FA/FI rise to occur faster with nitrous oxide than with desflurane. When a very high concentration of anesthetic is used (e.g. 70% nitrous oxide) the concentration effect increases the rate of induction. With uptake of anesthetic and oxygen (due to the concentration gradient) the volume of the lung decreases and the remaining volume of gas in the alveoli has a higher relative concentration than originally inspired. The use of an anesthetic at 100% is an example, though not clinically feasible. If 100% nitrous oxide were given, uptake would occur into the pulmonary blood and lung volume would decrease. However, the concentration in the lung would remain 100%. This is similar to the mechanism for oxygeninduced atelectasis. The concentration effect is only effective for nitrous because it is the only agent administered in a high enough concentration for the effect to occur. Normally the rate of rise of FA/FI is related to the solubility or blood:gas coefficient of the anesthetic agent. However, nitrous oxide has a blood:gas coefficient of 0.47, which is higher than the blood:gas coefficient of 0.42 for desflurane. The blood:gas coefficient is often the most important factor in rise of FA/FI. The rise of FA/FI is related to the speed of inhalational induction. Solubility of commonly used anesthetics is: desflurane > nitrous oxide > sevoflurane > isoflurane from least soluble to most soluble.
Answer C: The oil:gas coefficient is a measure of lipophilicity. The oil:gas coefficient is related to anesthetic potency and minimum alveolar concentration (MAC). The higher the oil:gas coefficient the lower the MAC. Isoflurane has an oil:gas coefficient of 99 and a MAC of about 1. Whereas desflurane has an oil:gas coefficient of 19 and a MAC of about 6.
Answer D: The second gas effect occurs when nitrous oxide and a volatile anesthetic are used concurrently. Uptake of nitrous oxide is significant because of the high concentration used (the concentration effect). When a significant amount of nitrous oxide is removed from the alveoli into the blood the relative alveolar concentration of the volatile agent being used increases. This increase speeds up the anesthetic onset for the volatile agent, which is the second gas effect. The concentration effect occurs when a high concentration of anesthetic can be used. Currently the only anesthetic in clinical use in which the concentration effect can be demonstrated is nitrous oxide. This effect explains why nitrous oxide has a more rapid onset than desflurane. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet function by blocking the formation of thromboxane A2. When a dose is administered, even though the medication will be metabolized the effects will continue for the life of that platelet. Thus, in order for the effects to be reversed, new platelets must be synthesized. For each day after interruption of any agent which irreversibly inhibits platelet function (aspirin, clopidogrel), approximately 10% to 14% of normal platelet function is restored. Therefore it can take 7 to 10 days for an entire platelet pool to be replenished. Thrombogenesis (clot formation) includes two processes – platelet aggregation and coagulation. Platelet aggregation includes activation of platelets and subsequent attaching of fibrinogen strands. Coagulation is a complex cascade of events leading to formation of fibrin strands. Different antithrombotic agents work at different points in this complicated symphony. There are two main types of antithrombotic agents – the antiplatelet agents and the anticoagulants. They each have very different management strategies in the perioperative period that depend on the agent used and the reason the patient is taking that specific medication. In the perioperative period there is a balance between the risks of clot formation versus the risk of bleeding. Continuation of antithrombotic drugs certainly can tip that balance into a position where it increases the patient's risk of bleeding. However, cessation of the agents can increase the patient's risk for thrombosis, which can be catastrophic. In addition, other considerations need to be evaluated in regards to antithrombotic agents, specifically surrounding the proposed use of neuraxial anesthesia. This decision has become even harder to make since newer antithrombotic agents have not been studied extensively in the surgical population. There are several different governing bodies which have released guidelines regarding the use of antithrombotic agents; the following discussion attempts to summarize. Most patients are on antiplatelet agents to prevent initial thrombosis or re-thrombosis of the coronary/carotid arteries. There are several agents but the most commonly used are aspirin and clopidogrel. Aspirin works by blocking the formation of thromboxane A2 in platelets which in turn inhibits aggregation during the platelet's life span. The most often prescribed dose is 81mg per day however patients may be on much higher doses. Recently, the continuation of aspirin in the perioperative period has come into question. In patients considered high risk, aspirin was continued at the lowest dose except for in surgeries where compression is impossible (such as intracranial neurosurgery or posterior eye chamber surgery). A recent trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine questioned the continuation of even low dose aspirin but this still needs further studying. There are no contraindications to continuing aspirin therapy when planning neuraxial anesthesia, however the clinician must be aware that when administered in conjunction with other agents which also affect coagulation (such as NSAIDs), this may lead to an increased risk of neuraxial complications. Clopidogrel is the other commonly prescribed antiplatelet agent which blocks adenosine diphosphate receptors on the platelet membrane inhibiting expression of glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors that bind fibrinogen. Most surgeries require the discontinuation of clopidogrel, however case reports of continuation even for major surgery have been described. The decision to discontinue will really depend on the indication for clopidogrel and the urgency of surgery. If possible, discussion with the patient’s cardiologist should occur if coronary revascularization has recently been performed. Anticoagulant agents work via different mechanisms depending on the specific medication and the reason for prescription is vast. The most commonly used agents are warfarin, injectable anticoagulants, and the newer novel oral agents. The most common reasons patients are on these medications include mechanical heart valves, abnormal cardiac rhythms, previous pathologic thrombosis, or genetic defect causing hypercoagulable states. It is impossible to quickly summarize perioperative management of these agents since there are so many indications and the decision to continue/hold depends on why the patient is taking the agent and which specific agent they are using. When a patient presents for elective surgery who is on antithrombotic agents, the clinician should go through a perioperative management evaluation which includes what agent the patient is taking and the indication for that agent. It is ideal if patients can be seen at least seven days preoperative to give enough time to discontinue and allow recovery of the platelets prior to surgery if cessation is deemed necessary. Antiplatelet agents irreversibly inhibit platelet function, thus even though the medication is no longer present, the effect on the platelet persists. For each day after interruption of any agent, approximately 10% to 14% of normal platelet function is restored thus it can take 7 to 10 days for an entire platelet pool to be replenished. Providing patients with written documentation of instructions is also important so they are more likely to be followed. If a ‘bridge’ is required, it is especially important that the patient or caregiver understands how to provide the injection. Equally as important as preoperative management is resumption of patient’s antithrombotic agents in the postoperative period. Antiplatelet Agents: Aspirin Inhibits thromboxane A2 synthesis Clopidogrel (Plavix) Prasugrel (Effient) Ticagrelor (Brilinta) Inhibit ADP receptor activation Dipyridamole (Persantine) Cilostazol (Pletal) Lowers calcium by elevating cAMP Abciximab (ReoPro) Tirofiban (Aggrastat) Eptifibatide (Integrilin) Blocks GP IIb/IIIa receptors Anticoagulation Agents: Answers B & C & D: For each day after interruption of any agent, approximately 10% to 14% of normal platelet function is restored thus it can take 7 to 10 days for an entire platelet pool to be replenished which irreversibly inhibits platelet function.  Preoperative management of antithrombotic agents depends on several variables – what specific agent the patient is taking, why they are taking that agent, the surgery they are scheduled for, and the urgency of that surgery. When determining whether to stop the agent, it is important to weigh the risk of perioperative hemorrhage to that of thromboembolism formation. Breaking down the agents into those that inhibit platelet function versus those that exert effects on the coagulation system will help determine management.  Douketis, J. Hydrochlorothiazide works by inhibiting the Na-Cl co-transporter in the distal convoluted tubule. This causes inhibition of sodium reabsorption in the distal convoluted tubules, thereby increasing the excretion of both sodium and water. Thiazide diuretics, such as hydrochlorothiazide and chlorthalidone, are primarily used to treat hypertension. They have a weaker natriuretic and diuretic effect than loop diuretics as the distal convoluted tubule provides significantly less reabsorption than the loop of Henle. Thiazides are used in combination with loop diuretics for edema resistance to loop diuretics alone. Hydrochlorothiazide has the potential to cause several electrolyte disturbances such as hyponatremia, hypochloremic alkalosis, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, and hyperglycemia. Increased excretion of chloride can lead to hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis and increased excretion of sodium can lead to hyponatremia. It also increases potassium excretion leading to hypokalemia. Hydrochlorothiazide can also directly inhibit calcium excretion in the distal tubule and indirectly increase calcium reabsorption in the proximal tubes due to decreased extracellular volume leading to hypercalcemia. There is no Na+/Cl- transporter in the loop of Henle. The Na-Cl cotransporter is located in the distal convoluted tubule.
Answer C: This is the mechanism of action of loop diuretics which inhibit the Na-K-2Cl carrier in the loop of Henle.
Answer D: There is no Na-K-2Cl transporter in the distal convoluted tubule. The Na-K-2Cl carrier is located in the loop of Henle. Hydrochlorothiazide is a diuretic used primarily for hypertension that works by blocking the Na-Cl co-transporters in the distal convoluted tubules of the kidney, thereby decreasing Na+ and Cl- reabsorption. Curve A (green) represents fentanyl. Context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. “Context” refers to the length of an infusion. For most drugs, the longer the infusion runs, the longer it takes for the drug plasma concentration to decline by half after the infusion is stopped. The CSHT reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drug plasma clearance is the collection of processes (e.g., metabolism, excretion, biotransformation, etc.) that remove the drug from plasma and therefore decrease the drug plasma concentration. If all other factors are identical, a drug with a high plasma clearance will have a lower CSHT than a drug with a low plasma clearance. When an infusion of a drug is running, a portion of the drug moves or redistributes down its concentration gradient from the central (plasma) compartment into peripheral (tissue) compartments. Once the drug infusion stops, the plasma concentration will decrease and the concentration gradient reverses. Then, the drug that has accumulated peripherally redistributes back into plasma. A drug with a slower redistribution back to plasma will have a faster CSHT than an otherwise identical drug with a faster redistribution. This occurs because the drug is being cleared from the plasma faster than the drug is returning from the periphery, and thus the plasma concentration falls faster. Keep in mind that CSHTs are different from elimination half-lives since the latter are the result of metabolism and excretion from the whole body, not just plasma. The time to decrease the plasma concentration by half (CSHT) is NOT related to the time to eliminate half of the drug from the body (“terminal half-life”). Propofol (blue line) has a steadily rising though relatively short CSHT even with a long duration of infusion. Due to its lipophilicity, propofol has a very large volume of distribution (150-700 L) and readily redistributes from the central compartment to the periphery during an infusion. This contributes to a somewhat long elimination half-life of six hours. However, the CSHT of propofol is relatively short since the drug has a high metabolic clearance from plasma (1500-2200 L/min) and a slow redistribution from peripheral to central. Fentanyl (green line), like propofol, is highly lipophilic and has a large volume of distribution (335 L). However, it has a longer and more variable CSHT due to rapid redistribution. The rapid redistribution back to plasma prevents the plasma concentration from quickly falling after the infusion is stopped, even though fentanyl is rapidly cleared (1530 mL/min). Alfentanil (purple line) has a small volume of distribution (27 L) due to a lower lipid solubility and a high degree of protein binding (90%). Since much less of the drug redistributes into peripheral tissues, redistribution back to plasma does not significantly affect plasma concentration. This explains why the CSHT of alfentanil does not increase after about two hours of infusion time. Note however for short infusions, the CSHT of alfentanil is higher than for fentanyl. This occurs since the plasma clearance of alfentanil is significantly lower (240 mL/min) than fentanyl. Remifentanil (red line) has a flat and low CSHT curve. Remifentanil’s ester structure causes it to be very rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma and tissue nonspecific esterases. Accordingly, it has a very high plasma clearance (4000 mL/min) which keeps the CSHT low. The drug’s volume of distribution is also low (30 L) so redistribution does little to raise plasma concentration after the infusion is turned off. This causes the CSHT curve to remain flat even with long-running infusions. Although not depicted on the graph, the curve for sufentanil closely resembles the propofol curve. Sufentanil’s CSHT is lower than fentanyl and alfentanil because of a moderately high plasma clearance (900 mL/min) and because of its redistribution pharmacokinetics. Sufentanil has a moderately large volume of distribution (120-250 L) and the drug slowly equilibrates between the plasma and peripheral compartments. Due to this slow equilibration, even after the infusion is turned off, a slow redistribution INTO the peripheral compartments continues to occur. This causes the drug’s CSHT to be lower than might otherwise be expected. This curve represents alfentanil.
Answer C: This curve represents propofol.
Answer D: This curve represents remifentanil. Context-sensitive half-time describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. It reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drugs with rapid plasma clearance and a low rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a low CSHT while drugs with a slow plasma clearance and high rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a high CSHT. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH) binds to antithrombin III (ATIII), causing a conformational change and accelerating the degradation of activated factor Xa. Low-molecular-weight heparin indirectly inhibits factor Xa via activation of ATIII. There are two forms of heparin, unfractionated heparin (UFH) and LMWH. Heparin is a naturally occurring anticoagulant consisting of mucopolysaccharides ranging in weight from 5,000 to 40,000 Da, and is commonly referred to as UFH. Unfractionated heparin functions by indirectly inhibiting thrombin and factor Xa via binding to ATIII, causing a conformational change and enhancing the degradation of thrombin and factor Xa. Although UFH use has decreased in favor of LMWH, UFH is still used for immediate anticoagulation as an infusion for pulmonary embolism, cardiopulmonary bypass, and acute coronary artery syndrome. Unfractionated heparin can be monitored with activated partial thromboplastin time or activated clotting time and can be reversed with protamine. Low-molecular-weight heparin consists of heparin that is < 8,000 Da and has a mechanism of action similar to that of UFH. The action of LMWH is more specific in that, mainly, it degrades factor Xa, not thrombin. Low-molecular-weight heparin is preferred for deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis because it has a half-life that is longer than that of UFH, and monitoring is not required, although it can be monitored by following factor Xa levels. Monitoring is required only in patients with obesity or those with renal insufficiency. Unfractionated heparin is preferred in cases of renal insufficiency. Apixaban is a direct inhibitor of factor Xa.
Answer C: Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist. Low-molecular-weight heparin binds to antithrombin III, causing a conformational change and accelerating the degradation of activated factor Xa. Low-molecular-weight heparin indirectly inhibits factor Xa.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "LMWH: Mechanism Of Action (B)" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Low-molecular-weight fractions of heparin (LMWH) like enoxaparin can be used to prevent or treat deep vein thrombosis. Similar to unfractionated heparin (UFH), the mechanism of action of LMWH is through the actions of anti-thrombin (AT). However, unlike UFH, most of the effect is by inactivation of factor Xa activity rather than thrombin inhibition (factor IIa). Anti-Xa assay is the best answer as it is most specific for LMWH; it should be drawn 4 hours after the dose is administered. Partial thromboplastin time (PTT) is used to assess the intrinsic pathway (prekallikrein, high molecular weight kininogen, factors XII, XI, IX, VIII) and common pathway of the coagulation cascade. It is largely used to monitor anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin (UFH). While PTT may be prolonged with the use of LMWH, the increase is not clinically relevant, and therefore not the best answer.
Answer C: Prothrombin time (PT) is used to assess the extrinsic pathway (tissue factor and factor VII) and common pathway (factors II [prothrombin], V, X, and fibrinogen) of the coagulation cascade. The majority of the vitamin K dependent coagulation factors: II, VII, IX, X, Protein C, and Protein S are represented by the extrinsic and common pathways. For this reason it is largely used for monitoring of warfarin anticoagulation, a vitamin K antagonist. LMWH exerts its anticoagulation effect by inactivation of factor Xa. Although laboratory monitoring in nonpregnant patients is not necessary, the anti-Xa assay is the best test to document the adequacy of anticoagulation with LMWH.
