Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism (5-8%) followed by isoflurane (0.2%) then desflurane (< 0.2%). The clinical importance of volatile anesthetic metabolism is related to fluoride-induced nephrotoxicity. Initially this phenomenon was described after methoxyflurane use during long cases, but it currently remains a topic of interest particularly in regards to sevoflurane in the same setting. Sevoflurane undergoes 5-8% metabolism that results in increases in serum fluoride concentrations. However, sevoflurane does not cause a renal concentrating defect since it is associated with a more rapid decline in plasma fluoride concentrations. In addition, sevoflurane has minimal renal defluorination compared to the previouslyused enflurane which has been demonstrated to be a factor in toxicity. Enflurane-induced nephrotoxicity is a high-output renal insufficiency that does not respond to vasopressin. It is characterized by dehydration, dilute polyuria, elevated blood urea nitrogen, elevated creatinine, serum hypernatremia, and serum hyperosmolality. There was found to be a correlation between serum fluoride concentration and metabolism of enflurane (3%) which led to further investigations into sevoflurane and possible nephrotoxicity. Answers A & B & D: Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism (5-8%) followed by isoflurane (0.2%) then desflurane (< 0.2%).  Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism of the inhaled anesthetics used in clinical practice today. Despite demonstrated elevations in serum fluoride concentrations in long cases, it has not been shown to cause fluorideinduced nephrotoxicity.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Volatile anesthetics: metabolism" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 438-439. Miller, Basics of Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 81.

Sodium nitroprusside (SNP) toxicity is a direct effect of cyanide and thiocyanate toxicity that typically presents as a triad including elevated mixed venous oxygen (PVO2), SNP tachyphylaxis, and metabolic acidosis. Metabolism of the vasodilator SNP generates five cyanide molecules per SNP molecule. These are typically further metabolized in mitochondria by using thiosulfate as a substrate to thiocyanate, which is significantly less toxic. Thiocyanate has an excretion half-life of up to one week and can be prolonged by renal failure. Cyanide can also be converted by using vitamin B12 (cobalamin) to nontoxic and renally excreted cyanocobalamin. Accordingly, the risk of cyanide toxicity is higher in patients with diets deficient in sulfur or vitamin B12. Presenting signs of cyanide toxicity include metabolic acidosis, elevated PVO2, and flushing. Symptoms can include altered mental status, weakness, and headaches at low blood levels and loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, and death at high blood levels. Cyanide toxicity occurs at blood levels > 100 mg/dL, which can be achieved when > 1 mg/kg of SNP is administered in less than two hours or when > 0.5 mg/kg/hour is administered in 24 hours. Thiocyanate toxicity usually occurs with long-term (more than several days) SNP administration, particularly in those with renal failure or patients in whom cyanide toxicity was treated with sodium thiosulfate. Symptoms are typically central nervous system abnormalities and include hypoxia, nausea, tinnitus, muscle spasm, disorientation, and psychosis. These symptoms are usually seen when thiocyanate levels reach 5 to 10 mg/dL. Although SNP reacts with hemoglobin (Hb) to form methemoglobin (MetHb), the enzyme MetHb reductase rapidly converts MetHb back to Hb, preventing any appreciable accumulation.
Answer C: Skin often appears bright pink and flushed, not cyanotic, due to elevated levels of cyanide-hemoglobin complexes. Sodium nitroprusside (SNP) administration has the potential for causing toxicity due to the accumulation of its metabolic byproducts cyanide and thiocyanate. Common presenting signs of cyanide toxicity include elevated PVO2, tachyphylaxis to SNP, metabolic acidosis, and flushing. Symptoms of thiocyanate toxicity include hypoxia, nausea, tinnitus, muscle spasm, disorientation, and psychosis. Amyl nitrite works as an antidote for cyanide poisoning by converting hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which avidly binds cyanide, converting cyanide to the nontoxic cyanomethemoglobin. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Nitroprusside Toxicity: Dx" Gropper MA, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. 9th edition. Ch. 79: Pediatric and Neonatal Critical Care

Amiloride is associated with hyperkalemia. Amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone, and eplerenone are the four potassium sparing diuretics. They work by blocking sodium reabsorption in the cortical collecting tubule and simultaneously increasing potassium reabsorption. Amiloride is a well tolerated drug whose only major side effect is hyperkalemia (A). Hyperkalemia is associated with peaked T waves on ECG, with T wave amplitude often surpassing that of the QRS complex as shown in the image. Increasing hyperkalemia may be visualized as a shortened QT interval, widening of the QRS, and PR prolongation. Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors may increase the risk of hyperkalemia in patients on potassium sparing agents. Furosemide, and all loop diuretics (e.g. bumetanide, ethacrynic acid), inhibit the sodium/potassium/2-chloride receptor in the ascending tubule loop of Henle. Potassium excretion is increased along with sodium and hypokalemia can result. Hypokalemia is characterized by T wave flattening or inversion and U waves on the ECG. Hydrochlorothiazide works on the sodium/chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule increasing both sodium and potassium excretion. Thusly, hypo- and not hyperkalemia is an associated side effect. Thiazides also increase calcium reabsorption as electroneutrality is maintained. Hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyponatremia may be seen. Lithium toxicity is associated with hypermagnesemia. It is also associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which may be prevented or treated by blockade of the collecting tubule luminal sodium receptors with amiloride. Hypermagnesemia is characterized by PR interval prolongation and a widening QRS complex. Loop diuretics are associated with hypokalemia and are used in the treatment of hyperkalemia.
Answer C: Thiazide diuretics are associated with hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia, and hyperlipidemia.
Answer D: Lithium is not associated with hyperkalemia. Amiloride can be associated with hyperkalemia. The K+ STAys with Spironolactone, Triamterene, Amiloride. The Hofmann elimination reaction is a pH- and temperature-dependent reaction that proceeds more readily when pH and temperature are increased. Cisatracurium is a benzylisoquinolinium nondepolarizing neuromuscular-blocking drug. It is an isomer of atracurium that undergoes nonenzymatic Hofmann elimination in the plasma. This reaction is independent of renal or hepatic function and accordingly, renal and/or hepatic failure do not affect the duration of action of cisatracurium. Cisatracurium is, therefore, an ideal neuromuscular-blocking drug for patients with significant renal or hepatic disease. An intubating dose of cisatracurium (0.1-0.15 mg/kg) has a typical duration of action of 30-60 minutes, and the elimination half-life of the drug is 22-25 minutes. In the Hofmann elimination reaction, a quaternary ammonium group is converted to a tertiary amine by cleavage of a carbonnitrogen bond. A cisatracurium molecule can undergo this reaction at 2 different sites, leading to its rapid metabolism. The reaction occurs readily in plasma and is not catalyzed by an enzyme. The reaction speed is increased, however, as pH and/or temperature is increased. Therefore, the effects of cisatracurium will last longer in patients who are acidotic and/or cold and the drug will need to be re-dosed less frequently. Answers A & B: A higher temperature and higher pH increase Hofmann elimination reaction speed.  Cisatracurium undergoes nonenzymatic Hofmann elimination in plasma. The reaction speed is increased with higher pH and higher temperature. As the drug undergoes minimal renal or hepatic metabolism, it is safe to use in patients with significant kidney or liver disease.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cisatracurium: Hofmann Elimination" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th Edition. Pages 536, 1228. Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th Edition. Pages 867-869.

Natural licorice contains glycyrrhizic acid which inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase (11-BHD). This inhibition allows cortisol to activate Na-K-ATPase channels in the renal proximal tubules leading to hypokalemia. Glucocorticoids (cortisol) and mineralocorticoids (aldosterone) are released by the adrenal cortex and are involved in fluid and electrolyte homeostasis. Aldosterone stimulates Na-K-ATPase channels resulting in sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion. Excesses of aldosterone (e.g. Conn syndrome) lead to hypertension (sodium retention) and hypokalemia because of increased urinary potassium secretion. This is accompanied by increased urinary acid (H+) excretion by activation of Na+/H+ pumps resulting in metabolic alkalosis. The alkalosis is exacerbated by the creation of bicarbonate by carbonic anhydrase. Cortisol is metabolized to cortisone by 11-BHD in the kidneys. Cortisone does not activate the renal steroid receptors, thus preventing an inappropriate mineralocorticoid response. Inhibition of 11-BHD by licorice allows cortisol to act like aldosterone causing all of the symptoms of Conn syndrome, which may include hypokalemia, hypertension, hypernatremia, fluid overload, and metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic alkalosis will lead to reduced calcium availability, not hypercalcemia. Only natural licorice has this effect because it contains glycyrrhizic acid. Most of the licorice sold in the U.S. has artificial flavoring and rarely conveys risk. Answers A & C & D & E: Inhibition of 11-BHD by licorice allows cortisol to act like aldosterone causing all of the symptoms of Conn syndrome, which may include hypokalemia, hypertension, hypernatremia, fluid overload, and metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic alkalosis will lead to reduced calcium availability, not hypercalcemia.  Large quantities of natural licorice will induce hyperaldosterone-like effects including: hypokalemia, hypertension, hypernatremia, fluid overload, and metabolic alkalosis. Aminoglycoside antibiotics, including streptomycin, kanamycin, tobramycin, neomycin, and gentamicin may potentiate neuromuscular blockade when given with neuromuscular blocking drugs. Gentamicin inhibits prejunctional acetylcholine release and depresses postjunctional receptor sensitivity to acetylcholine, thus prolonging paralysis in a patient who received it along with a muscle relaxant. Aztreonam and other monobactams have not been reported to potentiate the effects of neuromuscular blocks drugs. Some of the penicillin class drugs (penams), however, have been shown to prolong blockade.
Answer B: Cefepime and other cephalosporin antibiotics have not been reported to potentiate the effects of neuromuscular blocks drugs.
Answer D: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and other sulfonamide antibiotics have not been reported to potentiate the effects of neuromuscular blocks drugs. Antibiotics including aminoglycosides, polymyxins, tetracyclines, lincomycin, and clindamycin can cause prolonged neuromuscular blockade when given in conjunction with a paralytic agent. It is believed that aminoglycoside antibiotics antagonize calcium ions by means of its involvement in the process of acetylcholine release by nerve impulses. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The median time to maximum plasma fentanyl concentration (i.e. peak effect) is approximately 30 hours following placement of a transdermal fentanyl patch (D). Transdermal fentanyl patches provide a convenient and moderately reliable way to deliver continuous and controlled amounts of fentanyl over a long period of time. They are most frequently prescribed for the management of severe chronic pain in patients who have developed some degree of opioid tolerance. The patches are designed to be worn for 72 hours during which time they release a nearly constant amount of drug per unit time. Onset of effect takes approximately 6-8 hours following patch placement while the peak effect occurs approximately 30 hours following placement in healthy patients. Perioperative management of patients with transdermal fentanyl patches requires several considerations (a full discussion of which is beyond the scope of this question) to prevent unintentional under- or overdosing of opioids. Generally, patches should be removed prior to an anesthetic and an equipotent intravenous infusion (e.g. morphine or fentanyl) be started and carefully titrated to effect. For minor or short surgeries, a patch may be left in place. Removal of fentanyl patches is recommended because physiologic changes that occur during an anesthetic alter drug release from the patch. The initial peripheral redistribution of blood flow during a general anesthetic increases skin perfusion (and transiently skin temperature), both of which are known to increase fentanyl uptake from the patch. Fentanyl patches are particularly sensitive to heat; delivery can more than double in the presence of heat. Care must be taken with active warming devices, since if placed on or very near a patch they can significantly increase fentanyl delivery and cause unintentional perioperative overdoses. A second factor to consider is timing of fentanyl patch placement and removal. Due to a long context-sensitive half-time and continued absorption from the skin and subcutaneous tissues, it takes approximately 24 hours for plasma fentanyl concentrations to decrease by 50% after a patch is removed. Thus it is important to inform those who will be taking care of the patient postoperatively to monitor the patient and administer additional opioids carefully since fentanyl is still being released into the circulation. If the patch is to be replaced postoperatively, recall that it will take at least 6-8 hours for an onset of effect, so additional opioids should be available during that time period.  The median time to peak plasma fentanyl concentration is approximately 30 hours following placement of a transdermal fentanyl patch. Onset is approximately 6-8 hours after placement. Volatile anesthetics decrease cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen but increase cerebral blood flow (C). Cerebral blood flow is very highly regulated in humans and can be altered by several mechanisms. One of the main determinants of CBF is the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen, which is the amount of oxygen utilized by the neurons. Because of the brain’s high O2 consumption (~20% of body’s total oxygen) and low oxygen reserves, the brain is highly reliant on continuous cerebral blood flow for oxygen supply. For this reason, CBF generally parallels CMRO2 and therefore can range widely from 10-300 mL/100 g/min based on the brain’s metabolic oxygen demands at the moment. Increased oxygen demands can occur with increased state of arousal, increased temperature, seizure, etc. CMRO2 generally decreases with hypothermia and sleep. Anesthetics also change CMRO2. All volatile anesthetics decrease CMRO2, thereby causing some decrease in CBF in response. However, the volatiles also have a direct cerebral vasodilating effect, therefore increasing CBF. This phenomenon is sometimes referred to as "uncoupling" because the CMRO2 decreases while the CBF increase. Nitrous oxide does not cause decoupling. Nitrous oxide both increases CMRO2 and CBF, thus is not a preferred agent in certain neurosurgical procedures. Additionally, an increase in CBF will lead to an increase in intracranial pressure (ICP). Thus, agents that increase CBF (e.g. nitrous oxide, volatile anesthetics, ketamine) will also increase ICP. With low levels of isoflurane (typically less than 1 MAC), the CBF effects balance out and the CBF remains essentially the same. However, with higher amounts of inhaled anesthetics, the CBF has a dose dependent increase and the overall effect is increased CBF. The term "uncoupling" is a bit of a misnomer as the CBF does decrease with a decrease in CMRO2, however it also increases due to the vasodilatory effect of the volatiles. Isoflurane essentially has two different and distinct effects on the brain, which at higher concentrations leads to an overall increase in CBF and decrease in CMRO2.  All volatile anesthetics are thought to cause an “uncoupling” of the CBF and CMRO2. They decrease CMRO2 while increasing CBF via a direct cerebral vasodilating effect. All intravenous anesthetics except ketamine cause a decrease in CMRO2 and a decrease in CBF. Fentanyl has no effect on CMRO2 or CBF. The rate of induction with isoflurane would be most improved with high minute ventilation. Agents with high blood:gas solubility (KB:G), such as isoflurane and halothane, are most affected by minute ventilation. The KB:G values for the commonly administered inhaled anesthetics are listed below. Recall that agents with low solubility have a more rapid onset and offset due to less blood and tissue uptake and more rapid equilibration of inspired and alveolar concentration (which equilibrates with the brain). The rate of FA/FI is dependent on the alveolar concentration of inhaled anesthetic. The highly soluble agents are rapidly swept away into the blood once they reach the alveoli, which causes the alveolar concentration to fall. In order to replace the agent that leaves the alveoli, the patient requires a higher minute ventilation for delivery. The figure below shows this concept. Spontaneous ventilation provides a negative feedback loop to prevent overdose. As the concentration of volatile anesthetic increases, there is decreased minute ventilation (increased respiratory rate and decreased tidal volume) which in turn slows the rate of rise in FA/FI. Hence, there is arguably a margin of safety in the spontaneously breathing patient. This is not the case for controlled ventilation. Figure. The FA/FI rises more rapidly if minute ventilation is increased. This effect is more pronounced in the agents with high solubility including halothane and isoflurane. Desflurane has a low blood:gas solubility. Although the FA/FI is increased with increased minute ventilation, this effect is small compared to isoflurane.

Answer D: Sevoflurane has a low blood:gas solubility. Although the FA/FI is increased with increased minute ventilation, this effect is small compared to isoflurane. The rate of inhaled anesthetic induction (FA/FI) is increased with increased minute ventilation. This effect is greatest with the agents with high solubility, including halothane and isoflurane. 2-chloroprocaine, along with all other ester local anesthetics, are broken down in the plasma by plasma cholinesterase. 2-chloroprocaine is a local anesthetic that blocks electrical conductivity in neurons by blocking the sodium channels. It is an ester-type local anesthetic and is broken down in the blood by plasma cholinesterase, just as all ester local anesthetics are. The amide local anesthetics undergo hepatic metabolism. 2-chloroprocaine is the most rapidly metabolized of all of the local anesthetics, having a plasma half-life of 12 seconds in adults. Its action on the neuron also has a quick onset of action of about 6-10 minutes, but it only blocks nerve conduction for 30-60 minutes, therefore necessitating frequent re-dosing. Liver metabolism is seen with amide local anesthetics such as lidocaine and bupivacaine.
Answer C: Hofmann elimination (also known as exhaustive methylation) is how cisatracurium is eliminated 2-chloroprocaine is an ester local anesthetic that is metabolized rapidly by plasma cholinesterase. Patiromer is an oral potassium binder which causes the elimination of potassium via the gastrointestinal tract with effects evident after about 7 hours. Treatment for hyperkalemia includes calcium chloride to stabilize the myocardium, insulin +/- dextrose (if blood glucose is > 250 mg/dL, then the administration of dextrose can be withheld) to temporarily shift potassium intracellularly, and elimination of potassium via diuresis, gastrointestinal loss, or removal via hemodialysis. Albuterol can also be given to temporarily shift potassium intracellularly, but it often is not used due to more pronounced side effects at the doses required. Loop diuretics, such as furosemide, are routinely used to eliminate potassium in patients who can produce urine. The onset of action of loop diuretics is generally faster than oral potassium binders or hemodialysis which is often slow to initiate in practice. Patiromer, approved by the FDA in 2015, and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, approved by the FDA in 2018, are oral potassium binders which can be used in the acute or chronic treatment of hyperkalemia. After a single oral dose, the potassium-lowering effects of patiromer can be seen after 7 hours whereas sodium zirconium cyclosilicate’s effects can be seen after 1 hour. Side effects of patiromer include hypomagnesemia, transient constipation, and diarrhea. Side effects of sodium zirconium cyclosilicate include peripheral edema. Both can cause hypokalemia, and neither is known to cause bowel necrosis. Furosemide is a loop diuretic that promotes potassium loss in the loop of Henle kidneys. It is generally a mainstay of potassium elimination when treating hyperkalemia, however, its use is based on the patient’s ability to produce urine. If the patient is anuric, it is unlikely to have any benefit.
Answer C: Sodium polystyrene has fallen out of favor because its benefits are questionable and only supported by low-quality evidence. Its onset was slow taking up to 24-hour or more to decrease serum potassium. Furthermore, its use was attributed to multiple cases of bowel necrosis. Considering the lack of good supporting evidence, risk of severe injury, and better agents now being available, it would be difficult to recommend the continued use of sodium polystyrene. The mainstays of treatment for hyperkalemia include calcium chloride to stabilize the myocardium, insulin +/dextrose to temporarily shift potassium intracellularly, and elimination of potassium via diuresis (usually loop diuretics such as furosemide), gastrointestinal loss (via the potassium binders patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate), or removal via hemodialysis. Intravenous insulin is the most rapid way to lower serum potassium, but this must be followed up by a method of eliminating the potassium, such as with furosemide, as the effects of insulin are only temporary. Hyperventilation lowers extracellular potassium levels by decreasing plasma CO2 levels, but it does not eliminate potassium from the body. This leads to a left shift in the bicarbonate buffer system (see below) which lowers extracellular hydrogen ion concentration. This causes potassium to shift into the cells in order to maintain electrical neutrality. CO2 + H2O ↔ H2CO3 ↔ H+ + HCO3- American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Acute Hyperkalemia: Rx" Lexicomp. Barbiturates are known to induce the cytochrome P450 enzyme system. Drugs that require the cytochrome system for degradation will have enhanced metabolism in patients taking barbiturates and therefore will require a dose increase. Other drugs known to induce P450 enzymes include phenytoin, rifampin, carbamazepine, and ethanol. Drugs known to inhibit P450 enzymes include fluconazole, metronidazole, valproic acid, and ciprofloxacin. Atracurium is metabolized by non-specific plasma esterases and via hofmann elimination and is therefore unaffected by alterations in P450 enzyme activity.
Answer C: Propofol is metabolized mostly by hepatic glucuronidation. Propofol dosing would most likely be the same. Due to possible P450 effects, the dose could potentially be increased, but not decreased with chronic phenobarbital use. Barbiturates are inducers of the cytochrome P450 enzyme system and therefore drugs that undergo elimination via this system will require increases in drug dosing. The codeine family of drugs will be less effective in patients taking fluoxetine as codeine requires conversion to the active drug, morphine, via CYP 2D6, which is inhibited by fluoxetine. The duration of action of the anticholinergic agent atropine is 15 to 30 minutes, with an onset of action of one minute when it is used for neuromuscular blockade antagonism. When a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker is antagonized with a cholinesterase inhibitor, the cholinesterase inhibitor should be paired with an appropriate anticholinergic such that the onset of action and duration of the two drugs are similar (table). The anticholinergic agent of choice for most pairings is glycopyrrolate because of its longer duration of action and lack of central nervous system penetration. If a cholinesterase inhibitor is chosen with an onset of action that is quicker and/or a duration that is longer than that of the paired anticholinergic, cardiac muscarinic effects, including significant bradycardia or other arrhythmias, may become pronounced. By contrast, if the cholinesterase inhibitor has an onset of action that is slower and/or a duration that is shorter than the paired anticholinergic, tachycardia and other arrhythmias may prevail. *Administered intravenously The duration of action of glycopyrrolate is two to four hours.
Answer C: The duration of action of neostigmine is 20 to 30 minutes.
Answer D: The duration of pyridostigmine is up to six hours. A cholinesterase inhibitor should be paired with an anticholinergic agent with similar time to onset and duration of action when nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade is antagonized to minimize side effects from either medication. The durations of action for the following medications are as follows when they are used for neuromuscular blockade antagonism: atropine (15-30 min), glycopyrrolate (2-4 hr), neostigmine (20-30 min), and pyridostigmine (6 hr). Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic that acts on the distal collecting ducts of the nephron and can cause hyperkalemia. The tubule lumen in this segment is negatively charged with respect to blood and positively charged potassium ions are secreted into the tubule. Potassium-sparing diuretics, such as amiloride and triamterene, block these tubular potassium channels. They exert their diuretic effects by preventing reabsorption of luminal sodium. Hydrogen ions are exchanged for intraluminal sodium ions in the proximal tubule of the nephron. Carbonic anhydrase converts carbonic acid to bicarbonate ions and hydrogen ions in the luminal cells. This creates more hydrogen ions to be exchanged and allows for greater reabsorption of luminal sodium. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide, are a class of diuretics that cause both sodium and bicarbonate ions to be lost in the urine, which can lead to metabolic acidosis. Metabolic acidosis may also cause hyperkalemia. Answers B & D: Other electrolyte abnormalities observed with thiazide diuretics include hyponatremia, hypokalemia, and hyperuricemia. Thiazide diuretics have also been associated with hyperlipidemia, hyperglycemia, pancreatitis, jaundice, and aplastic anemia. Hypokalemia and hyponatremia can be observed after administration of loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide. These medications exert their effect on the thick ascending loop (TAL) of Henle and prevent sodium reabsorption from the lumen. Hypercalcemia can be observed with thiazide diuretics through inhibition of the sodium-calcium exchanger. These medications act on the distal convoluted tubules and reduce the amount of excreted calcium (hence their utility in reducing calcium-containing kidney stones) and reabsorbed sodium. Potassium-sparing diuretics can cause hyperkalemia by blocking potassium secretion in the distal collecting ducts. Thiazide diuretics can cause hypercalcemia due to their effects on the sodium-calcium exchanger in the distal convoluted tubule. Loop diuretics can cause hypokalemia and hyponatremia by affecting the TAL. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors can cause metabolic acidosis, which may lead to hyperkalemia if untreated. Acetazolamide is the treatment of choice for high-altitude/mountain sickness due to its ability to eliminate CSF alkalosis. A mnemonic for the potassium-sparing diuretics is: "The K+ STAys," for Spironolactone, Triamterene, and Amiloride. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 1359-1360. Physostigmine is the treatment of choice for delirium associated with scopolamine. Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist in the same class as glycopyrrolate and atropine. Scopolamine may be administered preoperatively in the form of a transdermal patch as an antiemetic, particularly in patients with a history of motion sickness. Scopolamine should be included as part of the differential diagnosis for postoperative delirium because it can cause central anticholinergic syndrome. Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain are affected by scopolamine as a result of the uncharged tertiary amine structure that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier. Treatment for central anticholinergic syndrome must similarly involve medications that can cross the blood-brain barrier. Physostigmine has a tertiary amine structure, which gives it access to the central nervous system and allows it to act as an antidote to antimuscarinic drugs. Its duration of action is likely to be shorter than that of scopolamine, thus repeat doses may be required. Physostigmine would also be the treatment for atropine-induced delirium. Scopolamine may also be administered in intravenous (IV) form for amnesia. This is typically performed for hemodynamically unstable patients, such as during massive hemorrhage or trauma. Scopolamine IV may also be given preoperatively to reduce the risk of awareness in selected populations. The sedative effects may be desirable for premedication but can interfere with awakening after short procedures. Because of its pronounced ocular effects, scopolamine is best avoided in patients with closedangle glaucoma. Additionally, the surgical team should be aware that mydriasis and central nervous system depression may interfere with neurologic assessment after surgery (eg, in trauma patients). In addition to anesthetic uses, neostigmine is also used in the treatment of colonic pseudoobstruction (Ogilvie syndrome). Neostigmine is ineffective at crossing the blood-brain barrier, so it is not used for the management of scopolamineinduced delirium. However, neostigmine sufficiently crosses the placenta such that atropine can be considered for use in reversing nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade in pregnant patients. Glycopyrrolate does not cross the placenta enough to fully prevent fetal bradycardia that may be induced by neostigmine.
Answer C: Pyridostigmine is a quaternary amine and is, therefore, poorly absorbed in the gut and does not cross the blood-brain barrier. It is used in patients with myasthenia gravis and may also be used for prophylaxis against nerve agent exposure. Pyridostigmine bromide pills were given to military troops to protect against exposure to sarin and soman nerve agents. There is evidence that it is a possible causal factor of Gulf War syndrome. Physostigmine is an anticholinesterase with a tertiary amine structure that can be used as a treatment for central anticholinergic syndrome. Edrophonium (by the so-called “tensilon test”) is used to differentiate myasthenia gravis (MG) from cholinergic crisis and Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. In MG, the body produces autoantibodies that block, inhibit, or destroy nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the neuromuscular junction. Edrophonium, an effective acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, reduces muscle weakness by blocking the enzymatic effect of acetylcholinesterase enzymes, prolonging the presence of acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft. Edrophonium is ineffective at crossing the blood-brain barrier, so it is not used for treatment of scopolamine-induced delirium. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Etomidate is associated with pain on injection, which is a result of the venous irritation from the lower pH (6.9) of the propylene glycol solution in the etomidate formulation. Pain can be minimized from etomidate by injecting it into a larger vein, or lidocaine can be given before the etomidate. Several IV medications used in anesthesia have been associated with pain or irritation on injection, with the most common being propofol, etomidate, methohexital, diazepam, and rocuronium. Common methods to reduce the pain on injection include injecting into a larger or central vein and administration of opioids and/or lidocaine before the injection of the medication causing the pain on injection. Ketamine is an induction agent that does not cause pain on injection.
Answer C: Lidocaine can be used to decrease the pain on injection for propofol and etomidate. Lidocaine does not cause pain on injection. Pain on injection is common with some medications commonly used in anesthesia, with the most common being propofol, etomidate, methohexital, diazepam, and rocuronium. Methods to minimize the pain include injecting into a larger or central vein and the administration of lidocaine and/or opioids before the injection of the medication causing the pain on injection. Dexmedetomidine does not significantly depress respiratory drive. In addition, dexmedetomidine does not alter arterial oxygenation, pH, the ventilatory response to hypercarbia, or the slope of the CO2 response curve. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective alpha-2 agonist with greater selectivity for the alpha-2 receptor compared with clonidine. Dexmedetomidine has multiple important anesthetic implications, including hypnosis, analgesia, anxiolysis, and sedation. It also blunts the sympathetic response to surgery. Dexmedetomidine can be used perioperatively for analgesia or sedation for patients at risk for apnea, such as those with a history of obstructive sleep apnea or those who have undergone bariatric surgery. Dexmedetomidine is commonly used during awake craniotomies, carotid endarterectomy, and deep brain stimulation. Dexmedetomidine is neuroprotective after ischemic cerebral injury due to reduced cerebral catecholamine release. Dexmedetomidine's effects on the central nervous system include sedation and analgesia with a decrease in cerebral blood flow and the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen. There also appears to be no reduction in epileptiform activity with dexmedetomidine, so it can be used as an agent during surgical treatment of seizures. Effects of dexmedetomidine on the cardiovascular system include a variable effect on systemic blood pressure (with a greater tendency to decrease blood pressure, but dexmedetomidine can also increase blood pressure), a reduction in heart rate, and a reduction in cardiac output. There appears to be a potential improvement in cardiac outcomes with dexmedetomidine as a result of the reduction in oxygen consumption and blunting of the sympathetic response to surgery. Pharmacodynamics of dexmedetomidine Mechanism of action alpha-2 Receptor agonist at locus coeruleus and spinal cord CNS Sedation and analgesia Decreased CBF, CMRO2 Decreased MAC No reduction in epileptiform activity Cardiovascular Decreased HR and CO Variable effect on blood pressure (hypotension > hypertension) Pulmonary Decreased tidal volume, minute ventilation Respiratory rate: minimal to no change Ventilatory response to CO2: no change Abbreviations: CBF, cerebral blood flow; CMRO2, cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen; CNS, central nervous system; CO, cardiac output; HR, heart rate; MAC, minimum alveolar concentration. Dexmedetomidine preserves the patient’s native respiratory drive and does not alter the ventilatory response to hypercarbia. In addition, minute ventilation and tidal volume are decreased with a minimal change in respiratory rate.
Answer C: The sedative and analgesic effects of dexmedetomidine are through activation of alpha-2 receptors in the locus coeruleus and spinal cord, not through alpha-1 receptors. Dexmedetomidine produces its sedative and analgesic effects through alpha-2 agonism at the locus coeruleus and the spinal cord. Dexmedetomidine decreases cerebral catecholamine release, thereby reducing cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen and is neuroprotective after a neurological injury. Dexmedetomidine preserves the patient's respiratory drive; however, minute ventilation and tidal volume are decreased with a minimal change in respiratory rate. Regarding the cardiovascular system, there appears to be a potential improvement in cardiac outcomes with dexmedetomidine due to the reduction in oxygen consumption and blunting of the sympathetic response to surgery. Heart rate and cardiac output are decreased with dexmedetomidine, while there is a variable effect on blood pressure (hypotension > hypertension). Hypoventilation is the primary cause of hypoxemia in patients receiving intravenous (IV) patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) with opioids. Hypoxemia in this setting is due to shunting secondary to underventilated alveoli and alveolar collapse (e.g., atelectasis) and hypercapnia. Decreased diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) suggests impaired oxygen diffusion, which would not occur acutely. Further, significant reductions in DLCO are needed before hypoxemia occurs.
Answer C: Dead space occurs when there are areas of adequate ventilation but poor perfusion. Hypoventilation would not affect perfusion. Hypoventilation is the primary cause of hypoxemia in patients receiving intravenous patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) with opioids.  Miller’s Anesthesia 7th Edition. After a second dose of succinylcholine, the patient is likely to develop bradycardia. Bradycardia often occurs in children after they receive succinylcholine because of the activation of muscarinic receptors at the sinoatrial node, along with a high baseline vagal tone. Several different heart rhythms can be seen after the administration of succinylcholine. The most common arrhythmia in children is bradycardia. Bradycardia occurs most often in children because of a high vagal tone, which is associated with more acetylcholine receptors at the sinoatrial junction. Additionally, bradycardia is also seen in adults when a second dose of succinylcholine is given. The cause of heart sensitization is succinylmonocholine, which is a metabolic product of succinylcholine. Bradycardia can be prevented by preadministration of atropine. Hyperkalemia can be expected in patients with burns or muscular dystrophy, but significant hyperkalemia is not an expected side effect of re-dosing succinylcholine.
Answer C: Masseter spasm can be seen after succinylcholine administration. It is related to activation of the neuromuscular junction and is essentially a severe form of fasciculation. While masseter spasm after succinylcholine does not indicate malignant hyperthermia, spasm can be an initial sign of the condition. Bradycardia with succinylcholine administration is most likely to occur with repeated dosing and in children. Succinylcholine has a rapid onset (30-60 seconds) and is cleared very quickly by plasma cholinesterase. Succinylcholine should be used within 14 days of removal from refrigeration. It is the only muscle relaxant that can be reliably used by intramuscular (IM) injection, with the quickest IM absorption via lingual injection. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Hydrochlorothiazide use is associated with Hypokalemia (D). Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic that acts by inhibiting reabsorption of sodium in the distal convoluted tubule (DCT). Reduction of sodium reabsorption in the DCT via the Na+-Cl- co-transporter leads to natriuresis and subsequent osmotic diuresis. The increased concentration of sodium excreted in the collecting ducts causes hyperactivity of the Na+-K+ exchanger, which results in passive secretion of potassium ions into the collecting duct lumen, leading to hypokalemia. Preoperative correction of mild to moderate hypokalemia is not recommended due to risk of hyperkalemia with overcorrection and inability to correct total body potassium stores with rapid administration. Hydrochlorothiazide use is commonly associated with the following blood chemistry derangements: - Hypokalemia - Hypomagnesemia (A) - Hyponatremia - Hypercalcemia (B) - Hyperuricemia (leading to possible gout) - Hyperglycemia (C) - Hypercholesterolemia - Increased LDL production - Hypertriglyceridemia  Hydrochlorothiazide can cause hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia, hypercholesterolemia, increased LDL production, and hypertriglyceridemia. Hypocalcemia can occur with loop diuretics due to increased excretion of calcium into the urine (hypercalciuria). Diuretics act by diminishing sodium reabsorption at different sites in the nephron, increasing urinary sodium and water losses. Diuretics are divided into major classes distinguished by the site of their mechanism of action. Loop diuretics impact sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. Thiazide-type diuretics act in the distal tubule and potassiumsparing diuretics act in the cortical collecting tubule. Loop diuretics also have important effects on renal calcium handling. The reabsorption of calcium in the loop of Henle is primarily passive, driven by the sodium-chloride transport activity. As a result, inhibiting the reabsorption of sodium-chloride leads to a concurrent reduction in that of calcium, leading to increased calcium excretion. Calciuresis can lead to kidney stones and/or nephrocalcinosis. Thiazide diuretics inhibit sodium transport in the distal tubule and the cortical collecting tubule. These segments reabsorb a smaller proportion of the filtered load than the loop of Henle. Thiazide diuretics have a smaller natriuretic effect than loop diuretics and, when given in maximum dose, inhibit the reabsorption of up to 5% of filtered sodium. Thiazides also affect calcium handling. The distal tubule is the major site of active calcium reabsorption in the nephron. Although thiazides inhibit the reabsorption of sodium in this segment, they also increase the reabsorption of calcium. This can be useful in the treatment of recurrent kidney stones due to hypercalciuria. The magnesium-wasting effect of loop diuretics occurs in the loop of Henle, as this is the major site of magnesium reabsorption. The effects of thiazide diuretics on magnesium excretion are less well established than those of loop diuretics. Experimental studies suggest that thiazides have little direct effect on magnesium transport, while some clinical studies suggest that thiazide treatment may induce magnesium loss. This may be secondary to alterations in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system. Diuretic Electrolyte Changes Urine sodium Increased All diuretics Loop, thiazides, K+ sparing, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors Urine potassium Increased All diuretics except K+ sparing Urine calcium Increased Decreased Loop diuretics Thiazide diuretics Blood pH Decreased Increased Acidemia with carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, K+ sparing Alkalemia with loop diuretics, thiazides Thiazide and loop diuretics cause the excretion of magnesium, resulting in hypomagnesemia.
Answer C: Hypercalcemia occurs with thiazide diuretics, and thus these can be a treatment option for hypocalcemia. Loop diuretics are associated with hypocalcemia. Diuretics result in the excretion of sodium from the body. Calcium is excreted by loop diuretics and reabsorbed by thiazide diuretics. Volatile anesthetics lead to a rapid shallow breathing pattern, with an increase in respiratory rate and a decrease in tidal volume. Volatile anesthetics also attenuate the respiratory response to hypercarbia and hypoxia. To varying degrees, all volatiles anesthetics lead to a rapid shallow breathing pattern. When the increase in respiratory rate is not sufficient to compensate for the decrease in tidal volume, the minute ventilation decreases. Volatile anesthetics preserve minute ventilation to different degrees. While desflurane is able to preserve minute ventilation through tachypnea up to 1.6 minimum alveolar concentration (MAC), isoflurane has a less pronounced tachypnea and, therefore, a more significant drop in minute ventilation. In addition to hypoventilation, the increase in dead space ventilation produced by shallow tidal volumes also results in an increase in the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2). Volatile anesthetics also blunt the hypoxic and the hypercarbic respiratory drives. Volatile anesthetics act on central chemoreceptors to suppress hypercarbic respiratory drive and act on peripheral chemoreceptors to suppress hypoxic respiratory drive. Volatile anesthetics will blunt the respiratory response to hypoxia and hypercarbia and will result in an increase in PaCO2.
Answer B: Volatile anesthetics lead to a rapid shallow breathing pattern, with an increase in respiratory rate and a decrease in tidal volume.
Answer D: Volatile anesthetics preserve minute ventilation to different degrees. While desflurane is able to preserve minute ventilation through tachypnea up to 1.6 MAC, isoflurane has less pronounced tachypnea and, therefore, a more significant drop in minute ventilation. In addition to hypoventilation, the increase in dead space ventilation produced by shallow tidal volumes also results in an increase in PaCO2. Volatile anesthetics lead to a rapid shallow breathing pattern, with an increase in respiratory rate and a decrease in tidal volume. The combination of hypoventilation and dead space ventilation leads to increased partial pressure of carbon dioxide. Hypercarbic respiratory drive and hypoxic respiratory drive are also suppressed by volatile anesthetics.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Inhalational Anesthesia: Ventilatory Effects”. Propofol acts on gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA) receptors. Propofol increases the time that the GABAA receptors remain open after activation. GABAA receptors, when active, allow Cl- to enter neurons and hyperpolarize the cell. Propofol is a useful induction agent because it produces a quick, reliable onset of general anesthesia. Several other medications target the GABAA receptor including etomidate and benzodiazepines. Benzodiazepines directly activate the GABAA receptor. Alpha2 receptors are prejunctional receptors activated by norepinephrine (negative feedback loop). Alpha2 receptors are agonized by clonidine and dexmedetomidine. Dexmedetomidine is much more selective for the alpha2 receptor than clonidine. Agonism of the alpha2 receptor causes sedation without respiratory depression. Side effects of alpha2 receptor agonism include hypotension and bradycardia. In some instances, a bolus of dexmedetomidine can cause hypertension because of the activation of the sympathetic nervous system. GABAB receptors are linked to potassium channels. The most common GABAB receptor agonist medication is baclofen. Baclofen is used to treat muscle spasticity from spinal and supraspinal pathology.
Answer C: The N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor contains a calcium channel inhibited by several medications. Ketamine is the prototypical anesthetic agent that affects the NMDA receptor. Phencyclidine (PCP) and nitrous oxide also antagonize the NMDA receptor. Antagonism of the NMDA receptor can cause anesthesia without producing respiratory depression. NMDA is also related to the development of chronic pain. Propofol acts to potentiate GABAA receptors. To differentiate GABAA from GABAB, remember Baclofen for GABAB and Anesthetics for GABAA. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Propofol Mechanism Of Action" Miller, Ronald D. and Pardo, Manuel. Basics of Anesthesia. 6th edition. Propofol. Medscape.

The addition of fresh epinephrine to a plain local anesthetic does not significantly change the block onset time. Local anesthetics are weak bases that bind to the intracellular portion of voltage-gated sodium channels and prevent nerve conduction. Although the “active” form of local anesthetics is the ionized form [charged cation (BH+)], the speed of onset of effect is determined by the proportion of local anesthetic in the unionized [basic, uncharged (B)] form. Unionized molecules pass through the lipid membrane and reach their targets easier than ionized molecules. The onset of action of local anesthetics is primarily a result of lipid solubility and pKa. The more lipid soluble, the more quickly the molecule can pass through the cell lipid membrane and reach its sites of action. The pKa of a drug refers to the pH at which the drug exists in equal parts of ionized and unionized forms. A local anesthetic with a lower pKa will have a greater unionized fraction (and generally faster onset) at physiologic pH (7.4) than a local anesthetic with a higher pKa (greater ionized fraction at physiologic pH and generally slower onset). Local anesthetics are formulated as hydrochloride salts with a pH slightly <7, as the ionized molecule is more soluble and stable than the free base. Once injected, the local anesthetic solution is quickly buffered to the pH of the tissue. The addition of bicarbonate to a local anesthetic mixture speeds the onset of action by raising the pH of the anesthetic solution so that more of the unionized fraction is available. Note that bicarbonate should only be mixed just prior to injection as the mixture becomes less stable for storage.
Answer B: Epinephrine causes local vasoconstriction, which prolongs the duration of effect of local anesthetics. By decreasing local blood flow, local anesthetic is maintained in the area of injection. Epinephrine solutions must be acidic (pH 2-5) to preserve the epinephrine. The addition of typical amounts of fresh epinephrine to plain local anesthetics (pH ~6) has little effect on the speed of onset of local anesthetics. However, premixed local anesthetic solutions with epinephrine are significantly more acidic (pH 3-4); this drives the local anesthetic to its ionized form, thus potentially slowing speed of onset.
Answer C: Local anesthetic concentration also affects the speed of onset. The greater the concentration, the faster the speed of onset since there is a steeper concentration gradient to drive local anesthetics intracellularly. This is how chloroprocaine (pKa 9, which would predict a slow onset) has such a rapid onset: a 3% solution is highly concentrated compared to, for example, 0.25% bupivacaine (pKa 8.1).
Answer D: Tissue inflammation slows the onset of effect of local anesthetics. Inflammation leads to a localized acidic environment. This drives more local anesthetic into its ionized form (local pH is farther from local anesthetic pKa), thus decreasing the speed of onset. Additionally, increased blood flow associated with inflammation washes local anesthetics away from their site of action. The onset of effect of a local anesthetic is affected by its concentration (higher is faster), lipid solubility (higher is faster), pKa (lower is faster), and environment pH (higher is faster). Anything that increases the concentration or proportion of local anesthetic in its unionized form will speed the onset of analgesia.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Local Anes Onset: Factors Influencing" Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 914-916, 920, 924-925.

Volatile anesthetics decrease the sensitivity of the postjunctional skeletal muscle cell membrane to depolarization. This effect is more pronounced with longer duration of anesthesia as more volatile anesthetic is taken up by skeletal muscle. Volatile agents do not alter acetylcholine release.
Answer C: Acetylcholine is metabolized to acetate and choline in the neuromuscular junction and then choline is taken up by prejunctional neurons. Acetylcholine is not taken up prior to hydrolysis.
Answer D: Volatile agents may augment neuromuscular blockade by increased muscle blood flow via vasodilation, which may increase delivery of vecuronium to the muscle. Volatile anesthetics potentiate neuromuscular blockade by DECREASING sensitivity of the postjunctional membrane to depolarization and INCREASING skeletal muscle blood flow which both augment neuromuscular blockade. In addition, potentiation of neuromuscular blockade occurs by depression of upper motor neurons.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Lithium prolongs action of succinylcholine and non-depolarizing relaxants such as rocuronium and vecuronium. Lithium is a metal that, as a salt, is often used in the treatment of bipolar disorder and several other psychiatric conditions. Lithium is a cation with a charge of 1+. Lithium reduces excitatory neurotransmission while increasing GABA or inhibitory neurotransmission. Lithium has been shown to decrease acetylcholine release from alpha motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction. This causes lithium to prolong the duration of action of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents. Additionally, lithium activates potassium channels and thus inhibits neuromuscular transmission presynaptically and muscular contraction postsynaptically. The combination of lithium and nondepolarizing blockers results in a synergistic inhibition of neuromuscular transmission. The combination of lithium and succinylcholine results in additive inhibition. Antibiotics have different effects with regard to duration of neuromuscular blockade. Cephalosporins and penicillins do not affect neuromuscular blockade. However, aminoglycosides and clindamycin do have a significant effect on neuromuscular blockade.
Answer B: Pseudocholinesterase deficiency is a genetic autosomal recessive condition that affects the duration of depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents, but not most nondepolarizing agents. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency occurs in about 1 in 5,000 Caucasian individuals. Pseudocholinesterase is responsible for the metabolism of succinylcholine. Mivacurium is the only nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent that is metabolized by pseudocholinesterase, and therefore its duration of action is prolonged by pseudocholinesterase deficiency.
Answer C: Myasthenia gravis is a condition where nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers are prolonged. Depolarizing blockade in patients with myasthenia gravis is typically shortened because of the decreased number of receptors available for blockade. Succinylcholine works by binding to both alpha units of the acetylcholine receptor and causing activation. However, in myasthenia gravis many of the receptors are already occupied decreasing the efficacy of succinylcholine. Lithium prolongs action of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers. Lithium may decrease anesthetic requirements (lower MAC) because it blocks brainstem release of norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The order of recovery from neuromuscular blockade after nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent administration is, from first to last, diaphragm > laryngeal muscles > corrugator supercilii > abdominal muscles > orbicularis oculi > geniohyoid > adductor pollicis. The corrugator supercilii is the most resistant to neuromuscular blockers, and among the choices provided it will be the first to regain muscle function. Corrugator supercilii monitoring is reflective of laryngeal muscle paralysis and may be used to assess for adequate intubating conditions. The response to neuromuscular blockade of muscle groups to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA) occurs at different rates. When NMBAs are administered, the first muscle groups to become paralyzed are the central muscles, such as the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles, with response of the peripheral muscles such as adductor pollicis occurring later. This response is quicker for the central muscles due to the greater amount of blood flow and, as a result, NMBA delivery. Due to the higher density of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, the diaphragm is relatively resistant to nondepolarizing NMBAs and recovers much more quickly than any other muscle group despite being one of the first muscles to be paralyzed. At times, the adductor pollicis will be inaccessible due to positioning during surgery; in this case, the facial muscles may be used to assess for adequate intubating conditions because their recovery from neuromuscular blockade correlates well with the recovery of other muscle groups. For example, the recovery of the corrugator supercilii muscle at the eyebrow correlates well with the recovery at the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles, and the recovery of the orbicularis oculi correlates well with the adductor pollicis. Despite these correlates, it may be rather difficult clinically to distinguish between the responses of the two facial muscles. After the arms become accessible, it is advised to place the neuromuscular monitoring system back on the adductor pollicis. The adductor pollicis is more sensitive than the corrugator supercilii to neuromuscular blockade. Because the adductor pollicis is the most sensitive to the blockade, recovery of function provided evidence of greater recovery of more resistant muscles such as the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles. Recovery to a train-of-four (TOF) ratio of ≥ 0.9 at the adductor pollicis is recommended prior to extubation. A TOF ratio < 0.9 results in impairment of laryngeal muscles, pharyngeal muscles, and the response to hypoxia.
Answer C: The orbicularis oculi would recover after the rectus abdominis.
Answer D: The rectus abdominis would recover after the corrugator supercilii. The recovery of the corrugator supercilii muscle at the eyebrow correlates well with the recovery of the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles. It is one of the first muscles to recover from neuromuscular blockade after the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Recovery Of Neuromusc. Fun. In Different Muscles" Gropper MA, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. Ch. 28: Reversal (Antagonism) of Neuromuscular Blockade: Antagonism of Neuromuscular Blockade: Current Management Practices. 9th edition. UpToDate. Monitoring Neuromuscular Blockade. Literature review current through Apr 2022. This topic last updated Apr 22, 2022.

Alfentanil has the lowest pKa of all of the listed drugs with a pKa of 6.5. At a physiologic pH of 7.4, approximately 89% of the drug will be in its nonionized form. Commonly, fentanyl is considered a short-acting opioid while morphine is considered long-acting. However, the elimination halflives of the two drugs are similar and, surprisingly, fentanyl’s is longer (~3-6 hours for fentanyl and ~2-3 hours for morphine). The duration of effect of opioids, unlike many other drugs, is not primarily determined by drug elimination, but more importantly, by lipid solubility. Morphine has a longer onset time and duration of action because it has a more difficult time crossing and then leaving the blood-brain (or blood-spinal cord) barrier due to a lower lipid solubility. By contrast, the more lipid-soluble fentanyl has a shorter onset and duration of action since it readily crosses, and leaves, the blood-brain barrier. The lipid solubility of an opioid is a prime determinant of the onset and duration of action of the drug as it affects how easily the drug is able to cross cellular (lipid) membranes. In addition to a drug’s chemical composition, one of the most important physicochemical characteristics relating to lipid solubility is the fraction of the drug that is in a nonionized form. Ionized drugs are polar and do not readily pass through cell membranes whereas nonionized drugs are significantly more lipid soluble (often 103-104 times more soluble). The pKa of a drug refers to the pH at which it exists in equal parts of ionized and nonionized forms. An opioid with a pKa less than physiologic pH (~7.4) will have a much greater nonionized fraction whereas an opioid with a pKa >7.4 will have a greater ionized fraction. The table below lists the lipid solubility, pKa, and percent of drug in a nonionized form at physiologic pH of the four opioids in this question. Lipid solubility is represented by the octanol-water partition coefficient (λow); the higher the λow, the higher the lipid solubility. A unique characteristic of alfentanil relative to other opioids is its significantly lower pKa resulting in a very high fraction of the drug existing in the nonionized form. Coupled with its moderate lipid solubility, this allows alfentanil to very rapidly cross the blood-brain barrier and have an ultra-short onset of action. The plasma-brain equilibration half-time of alfentanil is 0.9-1.1 minutes compared to 6.2 minutes for sufentanil, 4.7-6.4 minutes for fentanyl, and 139 minutes for morphine. Answers B & C & D: See table above.  Alfentanil has the lowest pKa and highest fraction of nonionized drug at physiologic pH.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Opioids: pKa" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 468-469, 484. Silverstein, Geriatric Anesthesiology, 2nd edition, pp. 211-213.

Vecuronium is an intermediate-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drug (NMBD) that is primarily eliminated through the hepatobiliary system, but is partially cleared by the kidneys. Due to this, it has reduced clearance and increased half-life elimination in renal failure patients, likely due to build-up of a partially active metabolite 3-desacetylvecuronium. Renal failure does not affect the efficacy of NMBDs and initial dosing adjustments are not necessary, but renal failure does affect their clearance resulting in a longer duration of action. In general, it is best to avoid long-acting NMBDs, such as pancuronium. The commonly used intermediate-acting NMBD drugs, including cisatracurium, rocuronium, and vecuronium have important differences in duration of action in the setting of renal disease. Cisatracurium is degraded primarily by Hofmann elimination and its duration of action is unaffected by renal failure. Rocuronium's major route of elimination is the biliary system, but it is partially excreted unmetabolized in the urine. Because of this, the elimination half-life of rocuronium is slightly extended in renal failure; however, the duration of action of rocuronium has not been shown to be significantly different in renal failure patients in the clinical setting. Vecuronium's major route of excretion is also hepatobiliary, but it is secondarily cleared by the kidneys and has been shown to have an extended elimination half-life and an extended duration of action in renal failure patients. This is likely due to the buildup of 3-desacetylvecuronium, the primary metabolite of vecuronium, which has 80% of the neuromuscular blocking function of vecuronium and is excreted by the kidneys. The change in clearance and extended duration of action of vecuronium has been shown to have clinical significance in the intensive care unit (ICU) population. Succinylcholine is a short-acting depolarizing NMBD that has a half-life of fewer than 12 minutes in the absence of butyrylcholinesterase deficiency. Succinylcholine half-life is not prolonged in renal failure. Cisatracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination, which is independent of renal function, and is commonly chosen for use in patients with renal failure.
Answer B: Rocuronium is eliminated 70% by hepatic metabolism and only about 10% by renal elimination. It is generally considered safe to use in patients with renal failure with a minimal extended duration of action that is clinically insignificant. Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs (NMBDs) may be affected by renal disease. Of the commonly used intermediate-acting nondepolarizing NMBDs, vecuronium has the most prolonged duration of action in renal failure patients. Cisatracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination (independent of renal clearance) and the duration of action of rocuronium is largely unaffected by renal failure.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Renal Failure: Relaxants" Miller’s Anesthesia 9th Edition. Chapter 27: Pharmacology of Neuromuscular Blocking Drugs.

Mannitol is a sugar alcohol that acts as an osmotic diuretic as it is freely filtered at the glomerulus with poor reuptake back into the vasculature. Hyperglycemia may also act as an osmotic diuretic when glucose levels rise beyond the point of maximum transport through the glomerulus. Any poorly reabsorbed solute that is easily filtered at the level of the glomerulus can act as an osmotic diuretic by creating a gradient that causes fluid to remain within the renal tubule. Mannitol is the prototypical osmotic diuretic. Urea, glycerin, and isosorbide have also been used as osmotic diuretics. Mannitol draws fluid into the renal tubule, which allows for continued patency and flushing of debris from the tubule. Accordingly, mannitol can exert a renal protective effect. In addition, mannitol transiently creates an osmotic gradient within the vasculature and can maintain circulating plasma volume and renal perfusion via this effect, further eliciting protective properties. Angiotensin is part of the RAAS and is activated during systemic stress (e.g., hypovolemia, shock) to help retain fluid and maintain circulating plasma volume.
Answer B: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released in response to atrial stretch (generally due to volume overload). Atrial natriuretic peptide then induces diuresis via natriuresis, not via an osmotic effect. Atrial natriuretic peptide blocks the reabsorption of sodium from the distal tubule and collecting duct causing fluid to shift into the tubule. Hyperglycemia can mimic the effects of mannitol by acting as an osmotic diuretic. Mannitol is relatively contraindicated in patients with congestive heart failure (CHF) due to an initial increase in intravascular volume. Furosemide is the drug of choice when diuresis is recommended in this class of patients. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Mannitol Osmolarity Effects” Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 1349-1350, 1359-1360. Evers, Anesthetic Pharmacology, 2nd edition, pp. 790, 795.

This patient is taking St. John's Wort which induces cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoenzymes and increases the metabolism of cyclosporine. This can result in subtherapeutic drug levels and an increased risk of transplant rejection. There have been case reports of acute transplant rejection in patients taking St. John's Wort for depression, and its use should be stopped at least five days before surgery and not restarted after surgery in these patients. St. John's Wort has been used by patients to treat depression, and its mechanism of action is related to the inhibition of serotonin reuptake, dopamine reuptake, and norepinephrine reuptake. Previous thoughts were that its action was similar to a monoamine oxidase (MAO)inhibitor; however, the in vivo relevance has been invalidated. Primary surgical and anesthetic concerns include induction of CYP 3A4 resulting in enhanced metabolism of drugs such as lidocaine, alfentanil, and midazolam as well as CYP 2C9, which is involved in the breakdown of warfarin. Warfarin therapy is, therefore, unreliable in patients taking St. John's Wort and puts them at risk for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) and thromboembolism. St. John's Wort is not a substantial MAO inhibitor in vivo and therefore would not increase the risk of hypertensive crisis intraoperatively with the use of ephedrine.
Answer C: Warfarin breakdown will be enhanced and therefore the risk of DVT and thromboembolism will be increased. St. John's Wort is an herbal antidepressant that induces the CYP enzymes and can alter drug responses with antirejection medications, warfarin, and intraoperative anesthetics. It should be stopped at least 5 days prior to any surgical operation.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Herbal Supplements" Miller's Anesthesia. Anesthetic Implications of Complementary and Alternative Medications in 8th edition. Pages 1226-1239. Barone GW, et al. Drug interaction between St. John's wort and cyclosporine. Ann Pharmacother. 2000 Sep;34(9):1013-6.

The termination of action of a bolus dose of thiopental is primarily due to redistribution of the drug from the brain to peripheral tissues (C). After injection of a single bolus dose of a drug, it distributes at different rates to tissues based on their relative perfusion (see figure below). Thiopental rapidly diffuses to the brain (within 30-60 seconds from injection) due to the high proportion of cardiac output that goes to the brain. In addition, thiopental is lipophilic and easily crosses the blood brain barrier. Due to the brain’s low relative volume, the concentration of thiopental within the brain quickly equilibrates with the plasma concentration. It is during this time period where thiopental exerts its greatest anesthetic effects. In addition to the brain, thiopental is also being taken up by other body tissues (e.g. muscle, fat) albeit at a lower rate due to lower relative perfusion. As this happens, the drug plasma concentration falls and the concentration gradient between the brain and plasma reverses. The drug in the brain rapidly diffuses back into plasma and is subsequently redistributed to all the other tissues still taking up the drug. In this way, redistribution of thiopental from the brain to other body tissues is the primary mechanism for the drug’s termination of action (C). It is not due to metabolism and elimination which occurs much more slowly (elimination half-time of 11 hours). Other examples of drugs whose terminations of action are primarily due to redistribution (following a single bolus dose) include methohexital, propofol, and fentanyl; all of these drugs are highly lipophilic. Metabolism of most drugs occurs via two processes, phase I and phase II metabolism. Phase I includes oxidative and reductive reactions including hydrolytic reactions and those catalyzed by the hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes. Phase II reactions involve conjugation of the drug or its metabolite(s) with a substrate such as glucuronic acid. Once a drug is metabolized, it is much more efficiently eliminated from the body. During a prolonged thiopental infusion, peripheral tissue concentrations (e.g. muscle, fat) of the drug reach central compartment (blood and highly perfused tissues) concentrations and the termination of action of the drug becomes dependent on elimination by hepatic metabolism. The most important step in termination of action in this situation is side-chain oxidation (D). In the setting of large and prolonged thiopental dosing, a desulfurization reaction can occur which produces pentobarbital (A). Pentobarbital has long-lasting CNS-depressant activity and its production prolongs the effects of thiopental. A limited number of drugs, such as remifentanil, are primarily metabolized by ester hydrolysis (B) in the blood by plasma esterases. The termination of action of these drugs is due to this rapid metabolism instead of redistribution.  The termination of action of the effects of a bolus dose of thiopental is primarily due to redistribution of the drug from the brain to peripheral tissues rather than by metabolism. The same is seen with bolus doses of methohexital, propofol, and fentanyl.  Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 139-140, 450-451, 469. Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 728-734. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Thiopental termination of action"

Spironolactone, a potassium-sparing diuretic used to treat resistant hypertension, also has antiandrogenic effects that can lead to gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men. Potassium-sparing diuretics function at the distal convoluted tubules and collecting ducts. They consist of aldosterone receptor antagonists (spironolactone and eplerenone) and epithelial sodium channel blockers (triamterene and amiloride). Aldosterone leads to the synthesis and incorporation of Na+ channels and Na+/K+-ATPase into the distal convoluted and collecting duct cells. This results in increased Na+ absorption and K+ excretion. This process usually takes 24 to 48 hours, which is the reason antagonism of aldosterone takes time for its effect to be seen. Aldosterone receptor antagonists result in a mild natriuresis and retention of K+ by binding to aldosterone receptors, preventing the action of aldosterone. This also results in a decrease in H+ excretion. Side effects related to potassium-sparing diuretics include hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis. Additionally, spironolactone acts on sex hormone receptors acting as an antiandrogen. Because of the antiandrogen effects, additional side effects specific to spironolactone include gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men and amenorrhea in women. Amiloride shares many general side effects with spironolactone, such as hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis, but does not have antiandrogenic side effects.
Answer B: Side effects of furosemide include ototoxicity, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and hypocalcemia.
Answer C: Side effects of hydrochlorothiazide include hyperglycemia, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, hypercalcemia, hyponatremia, and hypomagnesemia. Side effects related to potassium-sparing diuretics include hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, and metabolic acidosis. Side effects specific to spironolactone include gynecomastia and erectile dysfunction in men and amenorrhea in women due to the additional antiandrogenic effect of spironolactone. The antiandrogenic side effects of spironolactone can be used clinically to treat androgenetic alopecia in women and moderate to severe acne vulgaris. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Aldosterone Antag: Side Effects (B)" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Ch. 50: The Renal System and Anesthesia for Urologic Surgery: Diuretic Drugs: Effects and Mechanisms. 8th edition. UpToDate. Mechanism of Action of Diuretics. Literature review current through Apr 2022. This topic last updated Nov 24, 2020.

Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic and will not cause hypokalemia. There are several types of diuretics that are differentiated by the mechanism of action which occurs at different sites in the nephron; the prominent property of most diuretics is a reduction of sodium chloride reabsorption resulting in increasing sodium and water losses. Diuretics are used to treat a variety of pathologic states: hypertension, heart failure, renal dysfunction, glaucoma, and various other edematous states. There are several common adverse effects of diuretics: volume depletion, azotemia, hypokalemia, hyponatremia, and acid-base disturbances. Volume depletion is most likely to occur at the start of treatment and it can result in depleted circulatory volume and reduction in tissue perfusion. Azotemia can occur from the decrease in renal perfusion resulting in an increase in BUN and creatinine (this is referred to as prerenal azotemia). Hyponatremia can occur, especially with thiazide diuretics, and is more common in patients with edematous states such as heart failure and cirrhosis. Metoclopramide is contraindicated in patients with bowel obstruction. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist centrally and a cholinergic agonist peripherally. It is used perioperatively as an antiemetic. By promoting gastric emptying and increasing gastroesophageal sphincter tone, it may decrease the risk of pulmonary aspiration. It is typically given in doses of 5-10 mg IV 15-30 minutes prior to induction to allow sufficient time for drug onset. However, drug combinations involving metoclopramide are not found to reduce PONV to a greater extent than monotherapy. It may be because at dosages commonly used perioperatively (e.g. 10 mg), metoclopramide only has mild antiemetic effects. Higher doses (25-50 mg) may be necessary to have discernible benefit, but carry the risk of more side effects such as extrapyramidal symptoms. Metoclopramide has little effect on gastric acidity. Per ASA guidelines, "Metoclopramide is a weak antiemetic and at a dose of 10 mg is not effective in reducing the incidence of nausea and vomiting." As it is a promotility agent, risk of bowel perforation exists if metoclopramide is given to a patient with a bowel obstruction. Aspiration risk is best mitigated in these patients with rapid sequence induction with or without preoperative administration of intravenous histamine receptor antagonists. While ASA practice guidelines do not recommend routine use of gastric stimulants to compensate for patients who are not sufficiently NPO, several subsets of patients stand to benefit from promotility agents such as metoclopramide. Diabetic patients who may have some degree of gastroparesis, as well as anyone undergoing an outpatient procedure could be considered for metoclopramide use.
Answer B: During pregnancy, progesterone-mediated relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) occurs as early as the first trimester. Metoclopramide can counteract this relaxation of the LES and decrease gastric volume in a parturient. This medication could be considered as an antiemetic adjunct, especially in urgent situations where ideal NPO time may not be feasible though routine use has not shown reduction in the incidence of pulmonary aspiration.
Answer D: Similarly to the first two scenarios, any trauma patient should be considered full stomach secondary to unknown length of time since last oral intake with massive sympathetic output decreasing gastrointestinal motility. Metoclopramide could be considered to decrease the risk of pulmonary aspiration though decreased gastric fluid volume is not guaranteed. Metoclopramide is a promotility antiemetic contraindicated in patients with complete bowel obstruction. Combinations involving metoclopramide are not found to reduce PONV to a greater extent than monotherapy. Metoclopramide is a weak antiemetic and at a dose of 10 mg is not effective in reducing the incidence of nausea and vomiting. Metoclopramide inhibits plasma cholinesterase and can increase the duration of action of succinylcholine. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword.
