There is high individual patient variability in pharmacokinetics for methadone dosing. The plasma half-life of methadone may range from 13 to 50 hours while the analgesic effects often last 4 to 8 hours. This high variability necessitates careful dose titration when starting a patient on methadone therapy to avoid dangerous side effects such as respiratory depression while providing adequate analgesia to patients. Methadone is a full agonist at mu receptors (it does also act as an NMDA receptor antagonist and as a monoamine transmitter reuptake inhibitor). Because it is a full agonist, there is no "ceiling dose" beyond which there is no further analgesic effect. Partial opioid agonists such as buprenorphine are limited by a ceiling effect dose in providing analgesia. Methadone is metabolized in the liver by cytochrome P450 and the metabolites are inactive. There is no concern with metabolites accumulating, so methadone dosage does not need to be adjusted in renal insufficiency until stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CrCl < 15mL/min). Fentanyl and methadone are the safest opioids in end-stage renal disease. For end-stage renal disease, a decrease in methadone dosing to 50-75% of the original dose is recommended. Methadone is a synthetic opioid that is a mu-receptor agonist, NMDA-receptor antagonist, and monoamine transmitter reuptake inhibitor. Methadone is especially useful in patients with opioid tolerance (due to NMDA blockade) and those with neuropathy (due to monoamine reuptake inhibition). Side-effects of methadone include respiratory depression, QTc prolongation, nausea/vomiting, constipation, and biliary spasms. Methadone has a Black Box warning for: 1) Death from respiratory depression 2) Cardiac effects 3) Arrhythmias (Torsades de Pointes) Respiratory depression is the chief hazard, which can occur at a later time than when methadone was dosed. Since methadone has a long half-life and a slow tissue release into the bloodstream, it has the potential for cumulative toxicity. For example, a patient who is started on methadone may have respiratory depression hours after they get home from their first dose. The QT prolongation can lead to arrhythmias such as Torsades de Pointes. Caution should be used if a patient has a QTc > 450 ms, and if it is > 500 ms consider discontinuing methadone. Methadone has numerous drug interactions that can increase or decrease its metabolism resulting in inadequate analgesia or toxicity, respectively. For example, alcohol and benzodiazepines can decrease methadone's metabolism (increase plasma concentration) leading to toxicity. Patients on methadone should be routinely screened to ensure that they are avoiding these drugs. Repeat ECG 30 days after methadone initiation. Then, repeat ECG annually or with changes in methadone dosing. - Routine urine drug screens Methadone is a full agonist at mu receptors and there is no ceiling effect analgesic dose.
Answer B: QTc prolongation is common with methadone therapy. Routine electrocardiogram surveillance is recommended to monitor for QTc prolongation.
Answer C: Renal dose adjustments are not needed for patients with renal insufficiency as there are no active metabolites from methadone breakdown. For patients with end-stage renal disease (CrCl < 15mL/min) a dose reduction is recommended. Patients on methadone therapy should have slow and careful titration of the drug during initiation of therapy, serial electrocardiograms, and routine urine drug screening. Dose adjustments are rarely needed for patients with renal disease. Inhalational anesthetics and ondansetron can also cause QT prolongation. Treatment of Torsades de Pointes is intravenous magnesium. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (NDNMBs) act as nicotinic receptor competitive antagonists. Rocuronium is an NDNMB commonly used for muscle relaxation during surgery. Muscle contraction occurs through a series of steps. The presynaptic neuron first undergoes depolarization via an influx of sodium ions. Depolarization of the nerve triggers the influx of calcium into channels at the nerve terminal. Calcium facilitates the release of acetylcholine molecules out of the presynaptic nerve and into the neuromuscular junction. The acetylcholine molecules then bind to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on the motor end plate, which leads to depolarization and then contraction of the muscle. Blocking the motor end plate acetylcholine receptor does not allow the muscle to contract. Because rocuronium is a competitive antagonist, its action can be overcome (in other words rocuronium can be displaced) by large numbers of the receptor agonist. This is the mechanism of neostigmine, the "reversal" agent. It is important to note that the term "reversal" does not imply antidote or a permanent (non-competitive) reversal. Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor. Acetylcholinesterase is the enzyme that degrades acetylcholine, and blocking this enzyme leads to increased numbers of acetylcholine molecules. The acetylcholine then displaces the rocuronium from the acetylcholine receptor, allowing muscle contraction. Neostigmine does not directly block the neuromuscular blockers or even directly block their effects. It reverses the paralysis indirectly by providing more agonist molecules to displace the neuromuscular blocker. If the neostigmine is given before enough of the NMB has been metabolized, there may still be too many molecules of NMB to adequately displace, and the patient will remain weak. They could alternatively appear strong initially only to weaken again later as the neostigmine is metabolized. This is the reason that NDNMBs must be carefully dosed and monitored with a nerve stimulator throughout surgery and with neostigmine administration. Unlike neostigmine, the drug Sugammadex is a selective relaxant binding agent (SRBA). Sugammadex is a modified γcyclodextrin, with a lipophilic core and a hydrophilic periphery. The negatively charged extensions electrostatically bind to the quaternary nitrogen of rocuronium as well as contribute to the aqueous nature of the cyclodextrin. Sugammadex's binding encapsulation of rocuronium is one of the strongest among cyclodextrins and their guest molecules. The rocuronium molecule bound within Sugammadex's lipophilic core is rendered unavailable to bind to the acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Here are several ways to reduce the risk of residual blockade: 1) Use of clinical tests (head-lift, hand grip, etc.), but only useful for detecting severe blockade 2) Use of shorter-acting NDNMBs 3) Use of qualitative neuromuscular monitoring (tetanus, TOF count) 4) Use of quantitative neuromuscular monitoring (TOF ratio) 5) Routine reversal of neuromuscular blockade 6) Early reversal of neuromuscular blockade (not immediately at extubation) 7) Reversal at a higher TOF count 8) Avoidance of total twitch suppression 9) Use of new pharmacologic agents (Sugammadex) If Rocuronium was a non-competitive antagonist it could not be displaced by larger numbers of acetylcholine molecules and neostigmine would therefore not work as a "reversal" agent.
Answer C: Succinylcholine, a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker, works as an acetylcholine receptor agonist. All non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers act as competitive antagonists at the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Despite giving a patient an appropriate dose of neostigmine to “reverse” their neuromuscular blockade, it is still possible for a patient to remain paralyzed or weak, or to develop weakness later in the recovery room. This phenomenon is referred to as recurarization, and can occur after neostigmine wears off and the neuromuscular blocker (NMB) has not yet been metabolized or removed from the system. Residual neuromuscular blockade is defined as a train-of-four (TOF) ratio < 0.9 measured at the adductor pollicis muscle. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Administration of norepinephrine results in intense vasoconstriction and increasing blood pressure and, resulting in reflex bradycardia. This vasoconstriction on the venous system leads to effects that maintain cardiac output. The decreased venous capacitance causes an increase in venous return and preload. Although the heart rate has decreased, the increased preload along with the β1-stimulation (positive ionotropic effect) results in an increased stroke volume maintaining or slightly increasing cardiac output. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter released by postganglionic sympathetic neurons and has an affinity for the following: α1 > α2 > β1. Because of its affinities, administration of norepinephrine results in intense vasoconstriction (with reflex bradycardia) and increased myocardial contractility. As a result, norepinephrine primarily elevates arterial blood pressure without significantly affecting cardiac output. Isoproterenol is a nonselective β-agonist; its use leads to an increase in heart rate and cardiac output via β1 and a decrease in blood pressure via β2.
Answer B: Administration of pure α1-agonists such as phenylephrine leads to an increase in blood pressure through α1 vasoconstricting effects, resulting in reflex bradycardia. Unlike norepinephrine, there is no β1 activity increasing myocardial contractility; thus, cardiac output often decreases.
Answer D: Unlike epinephrine, administration of norepinephrine does not lead to tachycardia due to the intense vasoconstriction-mediated reflex bradycardia. Administration of epinephrine does lead to increased heart rate and cardiac output. Administration of norepinephrine (α1 > α2 > β1) leads to intense vasoconstriction, causing slight reflex bradycardia. Despite the bradycardia, cardiac output is maintained via a decrease in venous capacitance, resulting in an increase in preload and stroke volume. The β1 increase in myocardial contractility further increases the stroke volume, and, despite a decrease in heart rate, cardiac output is maintained or slightly increased. Magnesium is commonly used in parturients as seizure prophylaxis for preeclampsia and as a tocolytic agent in pre-term labor as it causes tocolysis by relaxing uterine smooth muscle and vascular tone. ECG changes begin to occur when serum magnesium levels are between 7-12 mg/dL Normal serum magnesium levels are between 1.5-2.5 mg/dL. Hypermagnesemia is > 2.5 mg/dL and can result from kidney impairment, overuse of magnesium-based laxatives or enemas, over-infusion of magnesium in preeclampsia treatment, and disorders such as milk-alkali syndrome. Hypermagnesemia results in neurotoxicity by decreasing transmission of the impulse across the neuromuscular junction resulting initially in diminished deep tendon reflexes. As the magnesium levels rise (see table below), the reflexes disappear. Cardiotoxicity results from magnesium acting as a calcium and potassium channel blocker, disrupting cardiac function and leading to complete heart block and cardiac arrest (> 12 mg/dL). Due to its calcium channel blocker effects, magnesium can lead to hypotension, bradycardia, and ECG changes including prolonged PR interval and widened QRS. Treatment of hypermagnesemia begins by stopping the source of magnesium. If the patient is symptomatic, calcium gluconate can be administered. The elimination of magnesium can be further increased by adding a loop diuretic and increasing diuresis with normal saline. If the patient has renal failure, dialysis is indicated. Answer C: A serum magnesium level of 12-15 mg/dL may lead to muscle paralysis, respiratory failure, and complete heart block. Magnesium toxicity has multiple effects seen at different serum levels, most of which are caused by its action as a calcium channel antagonist. PR prolongation and QRS widening can be seen at serum magnesium levels of 7-12 mg/dL.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "MgSO4: Cardiac effects" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Terbutaline causes potassium to shift intracellularly which can potentially cause HYPOkalemia. Terbutaline, along with other β2-agonists such as epinephrine, causes potassium to shift intracellularly as a direct effect of β2-receptor stimulation. Nonselective β-blockers can prevent this side effect of β2-agonists. Overall, this effect is generally shortlived. In obstetric patients given terbutaline infusions for management of preterm labor, potassium levels were found to return to baseline within 30 minutes of discontinuation of the infusion1. Numerous medications and medication classes can cause hyperkalemia either by direct or indirect effects. See the table below for examples. ACE = angiotensin converting enzyme, NSAIDs = nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor (ACEi) that significantly decreases the release of aldosterone from the adrenal cortex. Since aldosterone causes secretion of potassium (by stimulating the Na+/K+ pumps in the renal distal tubules and collecting ducts), inhibition of its effects can lead to hyperkalemia.
Answer B: Losartan is an angiotensin receptor blocker (ARB) that has the same downstream effects on potassium (hypokalemia) as an ACEI
Answer C: Administration of mannitol can cause translocational hyperkalemia. Since mannitol is significantly hypertonic, intravascular administration causes water efflux from cells. Solvent drag then occurs by which intracellular potassium follows the water efflux and becomes intravascular. Over time, hypokalemia can occur with prolonged mannitol use as diuresis favors potassium loss. Terbutaline and other β2-agonists can cause hypokalemia. Multiple medications and medication classes, including ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, nonselective β-antagonists, NSAIDs, and potassium-sparing diuretics, can cause hyperkalemia. In the late 1800s, Charles Ernest Overton and Hans Horst Meyer independently observed a significant correlation between the potency of anesthetics and their solubility in olive oil. There are several theories of general anesthetic action. The Meyer-Overton correlation, also known as the lipid solubilityanaesthetic potency correlation, was part of a theory that related the fatty fraction in brain cells and anesthetic action. Although this has been useful for determining potency, it has not fully explained the mechanism of general anesthetics. Based on this correlation, another theory persisted for many years regarding hydrophobic anesthetic molecules accumulating inside the neuronal cell membrane, leading to membrane thickening and change in function. This theory was found to have several flaws. For example, stereoisomers of a volatile anesthetic have very different potency but their oil/gas partition coefficients are similar. Also, increases in body temperature can cause similar neuronal membrane changes without causing anesthesia. One of the issues with understanding the mechanism of anesthetics is the diversity of molecular structures between different anesthetics (e.g. chloroform, ethanol, ether, sevoflurane). This suggests to researchers that there is no specific structure-activity relationship, meaning there may not be a specific receptor that anesthetics are binding to. This led to the unitary hypothesis, which proposes that a common mechanism accounts for all anesthetic actions. A modern version of lipid hypothesis exists. With this theory, solubility of anesthetics in the lipid bilayer causes a redistribution of membrane lateral pressures. Other studies have shown that anesthetics can interact with proteins directly via hydrophobic binding sites, which can affect membrane proteins without interacting with the lipid bilayer. Regardless, the exact mechanism of general anesthetics remains unknown. Meyer-Overton correlation for the inert gases and nitrogen. Xenon is the most soluble inert gas in oil and thus the most potent. This is followed by krypton and argon. Answers A & B: The correct answer is olive oil.  The Meyer-Overton correlation related the potency of anesthetics with solubility in olive oil. The Meyer-Overton correlation led to the unitary hypothesis, which notes that a common mechanism accounts for all anesthetic actions. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. A reduction in myocardial contractility is seen with volatile anesthetics because of their ability to reduce calcium availability and/ or calcium sensitivity of the contractile apparatus. Volatile anesthetics affect both L-type and T-type calcium channels and depress contractile function by inhibiting sodium-calcium exchange, effectively reducing intracellular calcium concentration. Cardiovascular effects seen with volatile anesthetics include dose-dependent reductions in myocardial contractility, systemic vascular resistance, cardiac preload, and mean arterial pressure. Isoflurane, desflurane, and sevoflurane depress myocardial contractility in vitro and in vivo. Desflurane causes systemic and coronary hemodynamic effects that are similar to those produced by isoflurane; however, cardiovascular stimulation can be seen with rapid increases in inspired concentrations of desflurane, which leads to transient increases in contractility from stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system. Cardiovascular effects of inhaled anesthetics Abbreviations: MAC, minimum alveolar concentration; SVR, systemic vascular resistance. *Can cause tachycardia at concentration >1 MAC. Decreasing the rate of dissociation of the γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptor is the mechanism of action for barbiturates.
Answer B: Increasing the permeability of the neuronal cell membrane to chloride ions is one of the mechanisms of action for the sedative effects of propofol.
Answer C: Inhibiting intracellular sodium channels is the mechanism of action for local anesthetics. Cardiovascular effects seen with volatile anesthetics include dose-dependent reductions in myocardial contractility, systemic vascular resistance, cardiac preload, and mean arterial pressure. The negative inotropic effect seen with the use of volatile anesthetics is mainly due to the reduction of intracellular calcium in the myocardium. While volatile anesthetics mainly act as cardiac depressants, cardiovascular stimulation can be seen with rapid increases in inspired desflurane concentrations, which leads to transient increases in contractility. The effect of volatile anesthetics on sodium-calcium exchange and reducing intracellular calcium concentrations may be particularly important in the neonatal myocardium, which, compared to the adult myocardium, may be more sensitive to the negative inotropic actions of volatile anesthetics. Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions are both histamine-mediated reactions with signs and symptoms that are clinically indistinguishable. An anaphylactic reaction is a type I hypersensitivity reaction, an immunoglobulin E-mediated (IgEmediated) allergic response, that causes mast cell degranulation and histamine release. Anaphylactoid reactions are drug reactions that cause uncontrolled histamine release by a mechanism not involving IgE. Clinical features of these reactions include urticaria, bronchospasm, angioedema, and venodilation causing hypotension and cutaneous flushing. Common intraoperative triggers of anaphylactic reactions include muscle relaxants, latex, and antibiotics. Common triggers for anaphylactoid reactions include protamine, IV contrast dye, opioids, d-tubocurarine, and thiopental. Anaphylactic reactions are IgE-mediated and therefore require a sensitizing exposure to an allergen prior to the triggering exposure.
Answer B: Anaphylactoid reactions are not IgE-mediated; rather, they result from direct stimulation of histamine release.
Answer C: Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions result from profound endogenous histamine release. Serum tryptase levels therefore rise in both reactions. One study of mast cell tryptase levels found that their presence favors an IgE-mediated cause but does not always distinguish between anaphylactoid and anaphylactoid reactions; thus, patients in whom mast cell tryptase concentrations are not increased still require skin testing. Anaphylactic and anaphylactoid reactions are clinically indistinguishable histaminergic reactions with different triggering mechanisms.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Norepinephrine is the most effective treatment for refractory hypotension that is caused by ACE-I. ACE inhibitors (ACEi) and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) are usually withheld in the 24 hours prior to general anesthesia to prevent intraoperative hypotension. Furthermore, a recent study found that withholding ACEis or ARBs 24 hours before major non-cardiac surgery was associated with a lower risk of death and postoperative vascular events. In patients who continue ACEi/ARB, sometimes intraoperative hypotension can be refractory to first-line measures such as fluids, ephedrine, phenylephrine, and glycopyrrolate. In addition to preventing the direct actions of Angiotensin II, ACEis and ARBs decrease the response to catecholamines and the circulating levels of vasopressin. Because of this, many textbooks recommend the use of exogenous vasopressin as a treatment for ACEi/ARB-induced hypotension. On the other hand, a randomized clinical trial comparing terlipressin (a longer-acting vasopressin analog available in Europe) to norepinephrine found that although both agents corrected hypotension, terlipressin decreased cardiac output and gastric perfusion, and increased lactate levels, whereas norepinephrine restored blood pressure while maintaining cardiac output, with normal lactate levels, and without affecting gastric perfusion. Bolus doses of vasopressin are a relatively common for intraoperative hypotension associated with ACEi/ARB use. A typical vasopressin infusion for septic shock would be 0.03 units/min, so a 1 unit bolus of vasopressin would be equivalent to more than 30 minutes of a continuous infusion. Single bolus doses of 0.5 or 1 unit vasopressin are large doses with the potential to significantly decrease gastric perfusion and also decrease cardiac output. Both ACE-Is and ARBs act on the renin-angiotensin-system (RAS). Renin is secreted from the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney in response to sympathetic stimulation. Renin converts angiotensinogen, which is formed in the liver, to angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II in the lungs by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). Angiotensin II acts on AT1 receptors, resulting in catecholamine secretion, aldosterone secretion, vasoconstriction, and anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secretion. With the blockade of catecholamines and vasoconstriction, and decreased uptake of water from the kidneys, induction of anesthetic can result in hypotension. As previously mentioned, norepinephrine is preferred for refractory hypotension in this setting. In this case, ephedrine has already been tried and found ineffective. Also, ephedrine infusions are generally not recommended due to tachyphylaxis (acute tolerance that develops with indirect-acting sympathomimetics due to depletion of endogenous catecholamines at nerve endings).
Answer B: Methylene blue can block the vasodilatory effect of nitric oxide by inhibiting guanylate cyclase. However, it is usually considered a last-line medication for vasoplegic shock. Also it is contraindicated in patients receiving SSRIs because it is a MAO inhibitor and can cause serotonin syndrome. Intraoperative hypotension associated with perioperative continuation of ACEi/ARB therapy: IV hydration, phenylephrine, ephedrine, glycopyrrolate are the early treatments. Refractory hypotension can be reversed with either norepinephrine or vasopressin, but only norepinephrine will do so while maintaining cardiac output and gastric perfusion. Metoclopramide is used to treat gastroparesis, but has been utilized as nausea prophylaxis during surgery or with chemotherapy. It is a dopamine antagonist, which derives its anti-nausea effect from antagonizing dopamine in the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the CNS. At higher doses it also blocks serotonin receptors, which can also contribute to its antinausea effects. In addition, metoclopramide is a peripheral cholinergic agonist and enhances the response to acetylcholine in tissues of the upper GI tract. This action causes accelerated gastric emptying, reduced gastric fluid volume, increased tone and amplitude of gastric contractions, and enhanced peristalsis of the duodenum and jejunum. It causes relaxation of the pyloric sphincter, however increases lower esophageal sphincter tone. It has no effect on gastric pH. Due to its anti-dopaminergic effect, metoclopramide should be avoided in patients with Parkinson disease. It also has a risk of causing extra-pyramidal side effects such as tardive dyskinesia. Extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) include akinesia (inability to initiate movement), akathisia (inability to remain motionless or a feeling of severe restlessness), and muscle spasms such as torticollis (spasm of the neck) or oculogyric crisis (spasm of the eyes, typically upward). Treatment options include diphenhydramine and benztropine. Metoclopramide is a dopaminergic antagonist.
Answer B: Metoclopramide decreases gastric fluid volume.
Answer C: Metoclopramide accelerates gastric emptying.
Answer D: Metoclopramide has no effect on gastric pH. Of the items listed, perioperative anaphylaxis is most commonly associated with exposure to neuromuscular blocking agents. Studies have indicated that neuromuscular blocking agents and antibiotics are the classes of drugs most associated with perioperative anaphylaxis. Anaphylaxis is the result of a type 1 hypersensitivity reaction. Antigens bind to IgE antibodies on mast cells and basophils. The activation of these cells causes a significant histamine release resulting in hypotension, bronchospasm, and urticaria. Anaphylaxis occurs in 1 in 10,000-20,000 anesthetics and is associated with a 3.4% mortality rate. Most reactions occur within 5 minutes of administration of the causative medication or agent. Anaphylaxis to induction agents and opioids is rare. Some agents are associated with histamine release which can be confused for anaphylaxis. Tryptase is released from mast cells when IgE activates them, thus measurement of tryptase levels may be helpful in suspected anaphylaxis. Tryptase levels increase rapidly during anaphylaxis but also fall quickly, as the half-life is only 2 hours. Neuromuscular blockers are one of the most common agents associated with anaphylaxis (along with antibiotics). The incidence of anaphylaxis is thought to be 1 in 6,500, but this may be underreported. Quaternary ammonium ions found in NMB are the most likely culprit for causing IgE activation. Many household chemicals share similar quaternary ammonium to neuromuscular blocking drugs. Previous exposure to cough medicines containing pholcodine (previously used in Europe) has been associated with rocuronium anaphylaxis. Additionally, quaternary ammonium can be found in shampoo, soap, and toothpaste. Latex is a common allergen that may cause anaphylaxis. Latex often causes symptoms of anaphylaxis 30-60 minutes after exposure. However, anaphylaxis may occur immediately. People at higher risk of latex allergy include healthcare workers, atopic patients, and patients with spina bifida.
Answer B: Reactions to local anesthetics are rare but often suggested as a cause of anaphylaxis. Amino ester anesthetics are degraded into the metabolite para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA). PABA is the reason for reactions to most local anesthetics. Anaphylaxis to amino amide anesthetics occurs at an even lower frequency than amino ester anesthetics. Methylparaben, a common preservative, is often found in local anesthetics. Methylparaben is structurally similar to PABA, and therefore cross reactivity is possible. In the past, PABA was widely used in sunscreens as an ultraviolet filter. Water-insoluble PABA derivatives such as padimate O are currently used in some products. Neuromuscular blocking drugs and antibiotics are among the most common agents associated with perioperative anaphylaxis. Epinephrine is the drug of choice for anaphylaxis as it supports hemodynamics, promotes bronchodilation, and stabilizes mast cells. Serum mast cell tryptase levels can aid in diagnosis. Allergy to neuromuscular blockers is more common in women than men, which is believed to be due to cross-reactive tertiary or quaternary ammonium groups found in both neuromuscular blockers and a variety of topical cosmetics and personal products, as well as certain over-the-counter cough remedies. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) has a higher rate of pruritus compared to nurse-administered bolus doses of opioids for postoperative pain control. Patient-controlled analgesia is a relatively new technique that is made possible by sophisticated computer chip technology. Safety measures are programmed into the pump to prevent overdose that could cause death. In essence, PCA is an on-demand, intermittent administration of an opioid medication that is under the patient's control. The system can be set with or without a basal (continuous) rate, depending on patient characteristics and requirements. The provider sets several variables: the demand (bolus) dose, lockout interval (delay between doses), and, possibly, a background infusion (basal) rate. Several opioids have been used in PCA; commonly, hydromorphone, morphine, and fentanyl are used. Background rates were thought to improve analgesia; however, results of several studies have provided evidence that PCA increases the total dosage used and increases the risk of respiratory depression. Generally, basal rates are reserved for opioidtolerant patients. The incidence of opioid-related side effects other than pruritis from PCA vs intermittent dosing does not appear to differ significantly. The rate of respiratory depression is low for PCA without basal dosing (<0.5%) and is no different from intermittent or neuraxial opioid administration. Usually, respiratory depression is caused by errors in programming or administration (ie, operator error). Additionally, the rate of nausea, vomiting, sedation, and confusion are similar between PCA and intermittent dosing. The risk of pruritus was found to be higher in PCA dosing. Patient-controlled analgesia provides slightly improved analgesia and patient satisfaction; however, patients using PCA use slightly more opioids compared with those receiving bolus doses given by nursing staff.
Answer C: The rate of respiratory depression is low for PCA without basal dosing (<0.5%) and is no different from intermittent or neuraxial opioid administration. The incidence of opioid-related side effects other than pruritis from PCA vs intermittent dosing does not seem to differ significantly.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The intubating dose of rocuronium should be increased secondary to an increase in the volume of distribution of the drug. Neuromuscular blocking agents are highly water-soluble due to quaternary amine structures and thus an increase in body water, such as with cirrhosis, CHF, or renal failure, results in decreased plasma concentration of neuromuscular blockers requiring an increase in intubating dose. It is important to remember, however, that clearance of drugs dependent on hepatic metabolism is reduced and therefore they will have a prolonged duration of action. Rocuronium, vecuronium, and pancuronium will all have increased duration of action secondary to impaired hepatic metabolism (caveat: rocuronium is not metabolized but is cleared by the liver in the bile) and therefore maintenance dosing should be reduced and neuromuscular monitoring carefully followed. Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann elimination in the plasma and thus the duration of action is not affected by cirrhosis or renal disease. A breakdown product, laudanosine, is cleared by the liver but levels produced are insignificant clinically.
Answer C: Succinylcholine is metabolized in the plasma by pseudocholinesterase and the duration of action is prolonged with severe liver disease secondary to decreased pseudocholinesterase production. This is rarely of clinical significance unless used in a very short procedure as the apnea time is increased from 3 minutes to 9 minutes.
Answer D: Vecuronium is metabolized and cleared by the liver, thus clearance will be decreased. Liver disease decreases plasma protein concentration and results in an increase in free drug concentration. This would normally increase drug clearance, however the impaired ability of the liver to metabolize the drug outweighs the decreased plasma protein concentration and thus duration of action is prolonged. Intubating doses of neuromuscular blocking drugs are increased in cirrhosis because of the increase in volume of distribution. Maintenance doses of hepatically metabolized and/or cleared drugs should be reduced and neuromuscular function carefully monitored as duration of action is prolonged. Halothane decreases systemic blood pressure mainly by reducing cardiac output. A common effect of potent volatile anesthetics is dose-related decreases in arterial blood pressure. It is well documented that sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane decrease arterial blood pressure, systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and myocardial function comparably and in a dose-dependent manner. The drop in blood pressure caused by these agents is directly related to the decrease in SVR while cardiac output is relatively maintained. Nitrous oxide, in comparison, generally leads to no change or an increase in arterial blood pressure. Halothane decreases arterial blood pressure primarily by decreasing cardiac output. Halothane causes minimal changes to SVR. Answers A & B & C: The drop in blood pressure caused by these agents is directly related to the decrease in SVR while cardiac output is relatively maintained.  Sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane decrease arterial blood pressure, SVR, and myocardial function comparably and in a dose-dependent manner. Halothane decreases blood pressure primarily by decreasing cardiac output and causes minimal changes to SVR. Halothane is unlikely to be tested on the current American Board of Anesthesiologists exams. However, understanding the other volatile anesthetics allows for this question to be answered. Additionally, some physicians being trained in the U.S. travel for medical mission work to areas of the world where halothane is more commonly used. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Cyclosporine, along with its solvent polyethoxylated castor oil, can cause prolonged action of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs (NDNBDs). Transplant recipients require immunosuppressive agents to counteract the response of their intrinsic immune system to the foreign allografts. Cyclosporine is an immunosuppressant drug that inhibits calcineurin. Inhibition of calcineurin prevents Tlymphocyte differentiation and cytokine elaboration. Aside from prolonging the action of NDNBDs, cyclosporine also has nephrotoxic and neurotoxic effects. Answers A & C: Mycophenolate and azathioprine are antilymphoproliferative agents that have not been shown to prolong neuromuscular blockade. Azathioprine is metabolized to 6-mercaptopurine which inserts into DNA and arrests the cell cycle. Mycophenolate inhibits inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase and also leads to arrest of the cell cycle due to purine synthesis inhibition. Inhibition of the cell cycle most significantly affects immune cells that rapidly proliferate in response to transplanted tissues, but other proliferating cell lines, such as those of the gastrointestinal tract and bone marrow, are also affected. This can lead to gastrointestinal ulceration, anemia, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. Tacrolimus is also a calcineurin inhibitor, but has not been shown to prolong neuromuscular blockade. Like cyclosporine, tacrolimus is nephrotoxic and neurotoxic. Cyclosporine is an immunosuppressant drug that can prolong the action of NDNBDs. In addition, it has potentially neurotoxic effects, including generalized seizures, and is nephrotoxic. Use of St. John’s wort has been attributed to at least two cases of solid organ transplant rejection. St. John’s wort induces cytochrome CYP3A4, which is responsible for the metabolism of cyclosporine. Its use can lead to subtherapeutic cyclosporine levels. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Results of numerous studies have provided evidence that coadministration of drugs that contain N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) antagonistic properties (ketamine, butorphanol, buprenorphine, and nitrous oxide) can either prevent or reduce opioid-induced hyperalgesia caused by remifentanil. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH) is associated with the use of potent, high-dose opioids. Researchers found that, when potent opioids such as remifentanil or fentanyl were administered, there was a small yet significant increase in acute pain after surgery. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia was shown to be due to spinal sensitization to glutamate and substance P in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Results of additional studies provided evidence that activation of glycogen synthase-3β (GSK-3β) led to hyperalgesia by regulating NMDA receptor plasticity and that inhibition of GSK-3β prevented OIH. Additionally, abrupt cessation of potent opioids, such as remifentanil, is also associated with OIH. When remifentanil was withdrawn gradually, no OIH was observed. Results of studies have provided evidence that ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, can prevent OIH and acute opioid tolerance. Low-dose ketamine (10-30 mg/hour) infusion can be used to prevent OIH. When buprenorphine, an opioid with NMDA antagonist activity, was administered along with remifentanil, it prevented OIH. Other drugs that possess NMDA activity, such as nitrous oxide and butorphanol, reduced the risk of OIH when they were given along with remifentanil. Antagonism of the NMDA receptors, not α2-receptors, during remifentanil use may prevent or reduce the development of OIH.
Answer B: Antagonism of the NMDA receptors, not κ-opioid receptors, during remifentanil use may prevent or reduce the development of OIH.
Answer C: Antagonism of the NMDA receptors, not μ-opioid receptors, during remifentanil use may prevent or reduce the development of OIH. Results of studies have provided evidence that ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, can prevent opioid-induced hyperalgesia during remifentanil use. Pseudotolerance can be seen in patients with chronic pain as the underlying disease progresses, causing more pain. The increase in nociception/pain is a result of the destruction of nerves in the area of the pain. The resulting destruction leads to the development of neuropathic pain, which does not respond well to increases in opioids. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Mixing propofol with lidocaine has been shown to decrease the stability of the propofol emulsion and may cause pulmonary embolism. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) prescribing information (PI) for propofol recommends against mixing lidocaine prior to injection. "Propofol injectable emulsion should not be mixed with other therapeutic agents prior to administration." Propofol is a popular anesthetic medication used for the induction of anesthesia. Propofol is often distributed in a 10% lipid emulsion with 10 mg/mL (1%) of propofol. The reason propofol is distributed in a lipid emulsion is because it is highly lipid soluble. The lipid solution of propofol can support bacterial growth and strict aseptic technique should be used when handling the drug. Propofol should be administered or discarded within 12 hours of opening because of the risk of bacterial growth. Mixing propofol with 40 mg of lidocaine has been shown to decrease the stability of the propofol emulsion. Masaki and colleagues mixed varying amounts of lidocaine and propofol then examined the mixture, both macroscopically and microscopically, for coalescence of droplets. They found that when 20 mg or more of lidocaine was mixed with propofol lipid droplets began to form. These lipid droplets formed more quickly and were larger with a greater amount of lidocaine. When 40 mg of lidocaine was added, droplets of greater than 5 mcm were detected at 30 minutes. The theoretic human risk of embolism occurs at droplet sizes greater than 5 mcm. The FDA recommends against mixing propofol with any other therapeutic medications prior to administration. If lidocaine is mixed with propofol, it should be done immediately before injection and in a dose not exceeding 20 mg / 200 mg propofol. A modified Bier block is better at reducing pain on injection than the technique of mixing propofol and lidocaine. A modified Bier block involves venous occlusion for 30-120 seconds while a small dose (50-100 mg) of lidocaine is administered through the IV. The lidocaine anesthetizes nerves that innervate the vessel and can prevent pain with injection of propofol.
Answer C: Pain on injection with propofol is reported to be at about 70% of untreated patients. Pain on injection is reported by anesthesiologists as a common avoidable complication related to anesthesia. However, methods to reduce this complication are widely varied. Some practitioners do nothing, while others pre-administer lidocaine or an opioid. Some anesthesia providers perform a modified Bier block and others mix lidocaine with propofol.
Answer D: Administration of propofol in an antecubital vein has been reported to be the most effective method to reduce pain associated with the injection of propofol. The next most effective method to reduce pain on injection was the use of a modified Bier block. Mixing propofol with lidocaine has been shown to decrease the stability of the propofol emulsion and may cause pulmonary embolism. The FDA recommends against mixing propofol with any other therapeutic medications prior to administration. The most effective methods to reduce pain are propofol injections using an antecubital vein and a modified Bier block prior to injection.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. One of the most common side effects of dexmedetomidine is hypotension. Other potential cardiovascular effects include bradycardia and hypertension. All of the potential cardiovascular responses to dexmedetomidine are more likely with bolus or loading doses. Dexmedetomidine is a selective α2 agonist with sedative, anxiolytic, analgesic, hypnotic, and sympatholytic properties, with a selectivity that is 8 times greater than that of clonidine for the α2 receptor. It is commonly used for sedation in the intensive care unit in patients who are mechanically ventilated, for procedural sedation, and as part of total intravenous anesthesia. Dexmedetomidine acts on α2 receptors in the brain and the spinal cord primarily at the locus coeruleus. When an electroencephalogram is performed in patients receiving sedation via dexmedetomidine, the result resembles non–rapid eye movement sleep. The most common cardiovascular side effects of dexmedetomidine include bradycardia, hypotension, and hypertension. Classically, bolus or loading doses were associated with bradycardia and hypertension, while infusions were associated with bradycardia and hypotension. However, recent research has provided evidence that the most common response to bolus doses, loading doses, and infusions is bradycardia and hypotension. For unknown reasons, some patients develop initial hypertension with higher plasma concentrations of dexmedetomidine, while others do not. Extremes of hypertension, hypotension, and bradycardia all appear to be more likely with bolus or loading doses. When researchers examined the overall response in study groups, dexmedetomidine infusions resulted in a decrease in mean arterial pressure, heart rate, and cardiac output. Cardiac output is decreased with dexmedetomidine use. Because of the reduction in cardiac output, dexmedetomidine should be used with caution in patients who cannot tolerate bradycardia or a decreased cardiac output.
Answer C: Dexmedetomidine can cause bradycardia, not tachycardia. The most common cardiovascular side effects of dexmedetomidine are hypotension, bradycardia, and, to a lesser extent, hypertension. All of the potential cardiovascular responses to dexmedetomidine are more likely with bolus or loading doses.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Bradycardia may occur in patients treated with sugammadex. The incidence is approximately 1% with 2 mg/kg and 4 mg/kg doses, and 5% with 16 mg/kg doses. The bradycardia may be severe and cases of bradycardia with cardiac arrest have been reported. Anticholinergics (e.g. atropine) are the recommended treatment. Additional cardiovascular adverse effects include, but are not limited to tachycardia, hypotension, arrhythmias, and ST segment changes. Sugammadex is a modified γ-cyclodextrin capable of encapsulating steroidal neuromuscular blocking drugs (rocuronium and vecuronium) and rapidly reversing their effects. Sugammadex has two notable advantages over neostigmine: the ability to reverse even deep neuromuscular blockade (even in the absence of twitches on train-of-four monitoring) and more rapid recovery from neuromuscular blockade. Additionally, use of sugammadex allows many of the muscarinic side effects of neostigmine and anticholinergic side effects of glycopyrrolate to be avoided. However, sugammadex has its own side effect profile that should be understood. The most critical adverse effect of sugammadex is anaphylaxis or hypersensitivity reactions. The incidence of true anaphylaxis is low (0.3-1%), but the incidence of hypersensitivity reactions (most common symptoms include nausea, pruritus, and/or urticaria) may be as high as 7-9% and tend to be dose-dependent. Sugammadex may transiently increase the risk for coagulopathy or bleeding since it has been observed to prolong PT/INR and aPTT up to 25% for up to one hour after administration. Despite these findings, no studies to date have shown an increased risk of clinical bleeding or hematoma formation.
Answer C: Women who use hormonal contraceptives containing an estrogen and/or progesterone should be advised to use an additional non-hormonal contraception method (e.g. condoms or spermicides) for seven days after sugammadex administration. Sugammadex can potentially bind the birth control hormones and temporarily place a female patient at increased risk for an unintended pregnancy.
Answer D: Sugammadex is not known to cause urinary retention. This is a possible side effect of using anticholinergic medications (e.g. glycopyrrolate), which are given with cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. neostigmine) for nondepolarizing blockade antagonism. The use of sugammadex for reversal can help avoid urinary retention seen with these other agents. The two most important adverse effects of sugammadex include anaphylaxis/hypersensitivity reactions and potentially severe bradycardia. Other important adverse effects include, but are not limited to arrhythmias, tachycardia, hypotension, prolongation of PT/INR and aPTT, and increased risk of unintentional pregnancy due to inactivation of hormonal contraceptives. Sugammadex has no affinity for succinylcholine or benzylisoquinolinium neuromuscular blocking drugs (e.g. cisatracurium) and will not reverse their effects. Glucagon causes an inotropic response, which is not an effect of the alpha1-adrenergic properties of phenylephrine. Glucagon activates adenylyl cyclase to increase cyclic AMP levels, leading to a positive inotropic and chronotropic cardiac response. Glucagon is a single-chain peptide hormone, synthesized and secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreas. Glucagon activates G-protein coupled receptors, which stimulates adenylyl cyclase production leading to increased cAMP which leads to increased glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis while inhibiting glycogen synthesis in the liver. It is the major counterregulatory hormone to insulin. Glucagon is contraindicated in pheochromocytoma due to the risk for hyperglycemia and severe hypertension. It is also contraindicated in insulinoma due to the risk of severe hypoglycemia. Answers A & C: Glucagon also has cardiovascular effects that resemble the catecholamines epinephrine and norepinephrine. These neurotransmitters bind to adrenergic receptors, which are G-protein coupled receptors. Glucagon may be useful in the treatment of beta-blocker overdose by increasing cAMP in the myocardium while bypassing the second messenger system. It may also be useful in anaphylaxis in patients taking beta-blockers as they may be resistant to the beta-adrenergic effects of epinephrine. The cardiac effects of glucagon are also unaffected by catecholamine depletion. Isoproterenol is a nonselective beta-adrenergic agonist which works via a G-protein coupled receptor to increase cAMP levels leading to positive inotropy and chronotropy. It is arrhythmogenic, unlike glucagon. Glucagon activates adenylyl cyclase to increase cyclic AMP levels. Glucagon increases cardiac index, mean arterial pressure, and ventricular contractility. Butorphanol, unlike most opioids, does not cause biliary spasm as it does not cause sufficient sphincter of Oddi contraction to increase pressure in the common bile duct. Butorphanol is a synthetic mu agonist-antagonist opioid analgesic with partial agonist activity at the κ-opioid receptor. It may be the preferred opioid for relieving biliary colic. Butorphanol is more effective in reducing pain in women than in men, which is one of the reasons it is used for labor analgesia. When an opioid agent increases bile duct pressure, the effect can be reversed by naloxone. Naloxone alone has no significant effect on the sphincter of Oddi and effectively relieves opioid-induced biliary spasm. Answers B & C & D: Common bile duct pressures following infusion of morphine, fentanyl, and meperidine all become significantly elevated compared to butorphanol and placebo.  Butorphanol has minimal effect on sphincter of Oddi contraction and does not cause biliary spasm.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Epidural and intrathecal administration of morphine is associated with increased risk of nausea and vomiting compared to neuraxial lipophilic opioids (e.g. fentanyl and sufentanil). Use of opioids as adjuncts for neuraxial anesthesia and analgesia can significantly enhance block quality, density, and duration of analgesia. However, this comes at the price of an increased risk of side effects including sedation, respiratory depression, pruritus, and nausea/vomiting, compared to local anesthetics alone. Epidural morphine is associated with an increased risk of nausea and vomiting compared to epidural fentanyl in both obstetric and surgical populations. There is a general trend that the incidence of pruritus is higher with morphine compared to fentanyl, but not all studies show a statistically significant difference.
Answer B: Data from both obstetric and surgical cases suggest that postoperative opioid consumption may either be lower with epidural morphine compared to epidural fentanyl or that there is no significant difference between the two.
Answer C: Administration of epidural opioids can cause maternal hypotension even in the absence of co-administered local anesthetics. This is due to decreased maternal levels of catecholamines from pain relief. Among opioids, there is no significant difference in the overall incidence of intraoperative hypotension when dosing an epidural for cesarean section.
Answer D: Use of intrathecal lipophilic opioids may be associated with an increased risk of fetal heart rate abnormalities, notably bradycardia. The mechanism is thought to be an indirect effect of rapid pain relief. This can acutely drop maternal epinephrine levels and lead to increased uterine tone and decreased uteroplacental perfusion. Epidural opioid use, regardless of opioid type, does not appear to significantly affect fetal heart rate. Use of epidural lipophilic opioids (e.g. fentanyl) is associated with a decreased risk of nausea and vomiting and possibly pruritus compared to epidural use of more hydrophilic opioids (e.g. morphine). The ASA recommends a longer period of monitoring for respiratory depression following a single neuraxial dose of morphine compared to fentanyl. For lipophilic opioids: continual monitoring for at least 20 minutes following administration and then at least hourly monitoring for the next two hours. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-I) are contraindicated in pregnancy as they are teratogenic. Other absolute contraindications include ACE-I allergy and angioedema. Relative contraindications include hypotension and hyperkalemia. Renal artery stenosis was formerly a contraindication; however, recent literature shows a benefit to ACE-I therapy in these patients as long as they do not develop acute renal failure upon initiation. Dysfunction of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system is common in patients with essential hypertension. For these patients, an ACE-I (e.g. lisinopril, enalapril, captopril) may be prescribed. They are considered first-line therapy for patients with heart failure, myocardial infarction, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease with proteinuria. ACE-I work in the endothelium of the lungs, where ACE is active, to prevent the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. Angiotensin II leads to vasoconstriction, sodium retention, and release of aldosterone. Adverse effects of ACE-I include cough, hyperkalemia, angioedema, and acute renal failure. Hyperkalemia is predominantly due to lower levels of angiotensin II and, thus, lower aldosterone secretion which results in reduced urinary potassium excretion. In patients with normal renal function, ACE-I typically increases serum potassium by less than 0.5 mEq/L, but there are significant patient and co-morbidity variation in the development of hyperkalemia. ACE-I lower blood pressure primarily by decreasing peripheral vascular resistance, with little effect on heart rate and cardiac output. This makes ACE-I ideal agents in patients with coronary artery disease and heart failure. They also help prevent ventricular remodeling and reduce afterload. Some practitioners advise holding the ACE-I on the morning of surgery for fear of refractory hypotension, particularly if large fluid shifts are anticipated. As of 2020, this controversy still has not been resolved. Studies suggest holding for cases with the potential for large blood loss. Some studies have shown no increase in hypotension at induction nor refractory hypotension in elective surgery for patients on ACE-I medications. The decision to hold an ACE-I must be individualized based on the indication for the ACE-I and the patient’s response to therapy. Aortic insufficiency is not a contraindication to ACE-I therapy. Previously, antihypertensive medications were avoided in patients with severe aortic stenosis; however, literature is emerging that supports ACE-I use in aortic stenosis to reduce left ventricular remodeling.
Answer B: If proteinuria is present in chronic kidney disease, ACE-I therapy is indicated as a first line therapy. Without proteinuria, ACE-I appear to provide no additional benefit over other hypertensive agents but are not contraindicated. ACE-I are contraindicated in pregnancy, history of angioedema, and allergy to ACE-I. Relative contraindications include hypotension and hyperkalemia. There is controversy over the perioperative risks and benefits of withholding ACE-I on the day of surgery; however, ACE-I use on the day of surgery is associated with increased intraoperative hypotension. Succinylcholine is safe for use in normokalemic renal failure patients. Serum potassium increases approximately 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine administration. This increase is not prevented by a defasciculating dose of a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Patients with preexisting hyperkalemia, such as those with renal failure, do not have a greater than expected increase in potassium levels with succinylcholine but, depending on the potassium level before the administration of succinylcholine, the absolute level can still meet the toxic range. Other conditions in which an upregulation of extrajunctional receptors may result in life-threatening hyperkalemia following succinylcholine administration include neuromuscular disorders (e.g. Guillain-Barré syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, and Friedrich ataxia), stroke, major trauma (e.g. crush injury), and prolonged immobility with disease. Succinylcholine should be avoided after 24 hours and for up to one year following burns of >10% total body surface area. This is due to proliferation of extrajunctional receptors causing a potentially significant hyperkalemia which can lead to cardiac arrest.
Answer C: Hyperkalemia has been reported with myotonia and muscular dystrophies, including Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and cardiac arrests have been reported in children before the diagnosis of the disease has been made. This has led some clinicians to take the position that succinylcholine should not be used routinely in boys under the age of eight. Of note, rhabdomyolysis can occur in these patients after succinylcholine which is either the main cause or contributing cause of severe hyperkalemia.
Answer D: In spinal cord injury patients, the amount of potassium released correlates with the extent of the acquired motor deficit. It is considered safe to administer succinylcholine for the first 48 hours after an acute injury. The potassium increase is maximal between 4 weeks and 5 months after spinal injury. Serum potassium increases approximately 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine administration in most patients, even those with chronic renal disease. Severe hyperkalemia leading to cardiac dysrhythmias and arrest has been described in patients after spinal cord injuries, neuromuscular disorders (e.g. Guillain-Barré syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, and Friedrich ataxia), stroke, major trauma (e.g. crush injury), extensive burns, and prolonged immobility with disease. This hyperkalemia is a result of upregulation of extrajunctional receptors. There are few indications for chronic barbiturate therapy, essential tremor being one of them. Primidone is a barbiturate that is active in itself and also due to its active metabolite phenobarbital. Barbiturates are a class of drugs that act on gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors. These drugs stimulate GABAmediated inhibition of neurons. GABA is a neurotransmitter found in the central nervous system. When GABA binds to these GABA-receptors, chloride ion channels are opened. This allows chloride ions to enter the nerve cells and create a negative charge inside. In other words, the neuron becomes hyperpolarized. This prevents action potential formation. A barbiturate binds to these GABA-receptors, and enhances the effect of GABA on these receptors (i.e. increases the time chloride ion channel stays open). Some commonly used barbiturates in anesthesia are thiopental, pentobarbital, and methohexital. The cytochrome P450 is a superfamily of constitutive and inducible enzymes that catalyze most phase I biotransformations, with CYP3A4 accounting for nearly half of all cytochrome P450-mediated drug metabolism. Here are some commonly used drugs in anesthesia that are metabolized by cytochrome p450 3A4: Acetaminophen Alfentanil Alprazolam Bupivacaine Codeine Diazepam Diltiazem Fentanyl Lidocaine Midazolam Nicardipine Nifedipine Omeprazole Ropivacaine Statins Sufentanil Verapamil Warfarin Answers A & B: Chronic barbiturate use does not affect GABA-receptors, qualitatively or quantitatively. These changes are actually seen in patients who use benzodiazepines chronically. Chronic barbiturate use does not affect minimum alveolar concentration. Chronic administration of barbiturates decreases the duration of action of drugs metabolized by cytochrome p450, such as midazolam.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Neostigmine inhibits both acetylcholinesterase and pseudocholinesterase. When succinylcholine is administered after neostigmine, succinylcholine is not degraded, and the effects of succinylcholine are enhanced and prolonged, resulting in a phase II blockade. Succinylcholine is the only depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent used in clinical practice. Succinylcholine comprises two acetylcholine (ACh) molecules covalently bound together via the acetate methyl groups. The two ACh molecules will then bind to the two α-subunits on the ACh nicotinic receptor leading to depolarization. Because succinylcholine is not hydrolyzed by acetylcholinesterase, it results in prolonged activation of ACh nicotinic receptors leading to membrane hyperpolarization and desensitization, finally causing muscle paralysis. Two types of depolarization blockades can occur with succinylcholine, phase I and phase II. Phase I1 Phase II2 It occurs after • Regular single dosing • Large doses (>10x that of ED95) • Presence of pseudocholinesterase deficiency • Prolonged exposure (>30 min of infusion) • Succinylcholine administration after neostigmine3 Response to tetanus • Sustained contraction • Tetanic fade PTF • No • Yes Train-of-four fade • No • Yes Abbreviations: PTF, posttetanic fade. 1Phase I blockade is the normal response to a single dose of succinylcholine, resulting in desensitization and muscle paralysis. 2Phase II blockade results from extensive or continued doses of succinylcholine, leading to continuous activation of the receptor. Despite this continuous activation and an influx of sodium into the cell and potassium out, the Na+/K+-ATPase pump increases activity, driving the membrane potential back to normal. The receptor no longer responds normally, and the blockade is prolonged. The nerve stimulation with a phase II block is similar to that of a nondepolarizing blockade. 3One study provided evidence that the duration of succinylcholine (1 mg/kg) extended from 11 to 35 minutes after succinylcholine was administered 5 minutes after a 5-mg dose of neostigmine. The duration of action will be increased, not decreased.
Answer B: The duration of action will be increased due to a phase II block rather than a phase I block.
Answer D: The duration of action will be increased, not unchanged. Succinylcholine administration after neostigmine results in the enhancement of the effects of succinylcholine, prolonging the duration of the effects of succinylcholine and resulting in a phase II blockade. Neostigmine inhibits both acetylcholinesterase and pseudocholinesterase, leading to increased concentrations of acetylcholine and succinylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Clonidine decreases anesthetic requirements (B). Clonidine is a selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist with an affinity ratio of 220:1 for the alpha-2 receptor compared to the alpha-1 receptor (compared to 1600:1 for dexmedetomidine, another selective alpha-2 agonist). This selectivity decreases CNS stimulation making clonidine a useful antihypertensive medication while carrying risk of bradycardia, hypotension, and sedation. Oral clonidine reaches peak effect within 60 to 90 minutes with a half-life of 9 to 12 hours. Rebound hypertension from acute clonidine withdrawal typically takes 12 to 60 hours after the last oral dose of clonidine. It is unlikely that a patient would have acute hypertension due to clonidine withdrawal intraoperatively (A). Withdrawal syndrome characterized by tachycardia, hypertension, flushing, tremor, and sweating. Clonidine decreases mean alveolar concentration (MAC) requirements for inhalational anesthetics (B). It is a useful adjunct for general inhalational anesthesia as well as for total intravenous anesthesia. It has been shown to decreased MAC requirements without prolonging emergence from anesthesia. Clonidine is used as an adjunct medication for chronic pain patients (C). It may be particularly effective in chronic pain conditions where neuropathy is a predominant component. Intravenous clonidine produced significantly greater analgesia than epidural clonidine, but both routes are associated with significant side-effects. Transdermal clonidine patch and topical clonidine gel has been used in painful diabetic neuropathy. There is evidence that clonidine can reduce opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH). Clonidine has been shown to decreased post-operative shivering as well as post-operative nausea (D).  Clonidine decreases anesthetic requirements (decreased MAC), is a useful co-analgesic particularly in chronic pain patients, reduces post-operative shivering, and reduces post-operative nausea. The most likely cause of the laryngospasm was the intramuscular (IM) ketamine injection, which can be used to treat agitation. The risk of laryngospasm is higher with IM administration than with intravenous (IV) ketamine. Ketamine is an intravenous anesthetic that functions as an N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist. Ketamine is often used for agitation, anesthesia (IV and IM inductions), analgesia, bronchodilation, chronic pain, depression, and procedural sedation in children and in burn patients. Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia that can be described as a trance-like cataleptic unconscious state (eyes open, spontaneous respiration, unconscious, and nonresponsive to painful stimuli). It is useful in patients who are hemodynamically unstable because it leads to increases in heart rate and blood pressure (theorized to be due to activation of the sympathetic nervous system) but should be avoided in patients with severe coronary artery disease due to increased oxygen demand. Moreover, ketamine maintains spontaneous respiration and preserves airway reflexes, minimizing the risk of aspiration. Ketamine can be given via numerous routes such as IV (100%, bioavailability), IM (93%), transnasal (25%-50%), and rectal and oral (16%). With ketamine's high lipid solubility and low protein binding, the uptake into the brain and onset are rapid. Because of this rapid uptake, ketamine can be used for sedation in agitated patients. Lorazepam can be given for agitation because it is sedating and is often given with haloperidol to prevent acute dystonia from haloperidol.
Answer C: Second-generation antipsychotics such as olanzapine can be used for sedation in agitated patients. Unlike firstgeneration antipsychotics, second-generation antipsychotics have a significantly reduced incidence of acute dystonic reactions. Haloperidol, a first-generation antipsychotic, has a much higher rate of acute dystonic reactions that can lead to laryngospasm. Haloperidol for agitation is often given intramuscularly with diphenhydramine and lorazepam, which aid in sedation but also prevent acute dystonic reactions from the high dose of haloperidol (5 mg). Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that can be given through many routes, most commonly via the intravenous (IV) and intramuscular (IM) routes. A serious but rare side effect of ketamine is laryngospasm, possibly due to the increase in salivation. The risk of laryngospasm is higher with IM vs IV administration. Low-dose ketamine infusion has been used in chronic pain, with the most extensively studied condition being chronic regional pain syndrome (CRPS). When ketamine was given to patients with CRPS, there was a reduction in pain scores and opioid consumption, although this was short-lived. The reduction in chronic pain by ketamine is believed to be due to several factors: (1) reduction of neuropathic pain; (2) the analgesic effect of ketamine itself; (3) synergistic interaction with opioids at the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor; (4) prevention of the development of opioid-induced hyperalgesia; (5) reduction of nociceptive input to the brain at the spinal and supraspinal levels; and (6) NMDA receptor inhibition of presynaptic spinal dorsal horn neurons (most important for acute pain relief; activation of NMDA receptors leads to release of excitatory neurotransmitters such as glutamate and substance P). High-dose phenylephrine causes arterial and venous constriction which leads to decreased splanchnic perfusion. Splanchnic blood supply is controlled by systemic blood pressure, cardiac output, and sympathetic tone. There is minimal contribution from the parasympathetic system. Phenylephrine is a selective α1-receptor agonist with minimal β effects. Phenylephrine’s α1 effects cause arterial and venous vasoconstriction. In higher doses, cardiac output is commonly reduced due to increases in myocardial work and afterload. The reduced splanchnic perfusion is more a result of arterial constriction than a reduction in cardiac output. Answers C & D: In lower doses, the venous constriction results in improved preload from venous return and may improve cardiac output. This is not seen in patients who have systolic heart failure, as the increased afterload can worsen cardiac output. a1 receptor activation from high dose phenylephrine leads to decreased splanchnic perfusion from arterial and venous constriction. The patient is most likely experiencing residual neuromuscular blockade and ventilation should be assisted (D). Bilevel positive airway pressure (BPAP) is another option for assisting spontaneous respirations. Residual neuromuscular blockade can lead to airway obstruction, poor inspiratory effort, and atelectasis which leads to hypoxia if not treated. Oxygen alone can help with hypoxemia, but may mask worsening hypercarbia if the patient is unable to take deep breaths. There have been reports of hypoventilation in the PACU resulting in hypercapnia with PaCO2 > 200 mm Hg while oxygenation was maintained via passive oxygenation. The maximum dose of neostigmine is 70-80 mcg/kg at which point a "ceiling effect" takes place. This dose results in complete blockade of the acetylcholinesterase enzymes and occurs in approximately 10 minutes. If recovery does not occur by this time, repeated doses of neostigmine provide no additional benefit because the target is already blocked. At this point recovery takes place by elimination of the neuromuscular blocking agent from the neuromuscular junction. In some instances additional anticholinesterase medication may cause paradoxical weakening. The anticholinesterase effect increases the amount of acetylcholine release. In an overdose, depolarization of the endplate caused by the excess acetylcholine can lead to a depolarization block, similar to that seen with succinylcholine.
Answer B: While ordering a chest radiograph may be appropriate in a patient with COPD, the next most important step is assisting ventilation in a patient that is likely weak from neuromuscular blockade. Providing oxygen may transiently improve the saturation but if the patient is unable to adequately ventilate or protect their airway then hypercarbia or aspiration may occur. Patients with COPD are at risk for rupturing blebs which may lead to a pneumothorax. A tension pneumothorax is diagnosed clinically and requires immediate needle decompression and/or a chest tube.
Answer C: Once maximum acetylcholinesterase blockage has been achieved additional benefit is not gained even when switching to other anticholinesterase drugs. Edrophonium and neostigmine do not potentiate each other and may not even be additive. Choose one drug and give maximum dose if needed. The maximum dose of edrophonium is 1.5 mg/kg. Edrophonium has a quicker onset than neostigmine but is less effective at reversing deep neuromuscular blockade even at maximum doses. Additional doses of anticholinesterases provide no benefit once the acetylcholinesterases are completely blocked. Use of doses larger than maximum for anticholinesterase drugs can result in a depolarizing blockade.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Neostigmine: Max Dose Rationale (B)" Miller. Succinylcholine administration causes a transient increase in lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone. Succinylcholine simultaneously increases both intragastric pressure and LES tone. However, unless the LES is incompetent, there is no increased risk of aspiration because the increase in LES tone is greater than the increase in intragastric pressure. If there is concern for an incompetent LES, the increase in intragastric pressure can be offset by pretreatment with a priming dose of a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker. This priming dose should not exceed 10% of the drug's ED95. The muscarinic effects of succinylcholine may theoretically increase the risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting in susceptible patients, but clinical studies have not shown any clinically significant effect.
Answer B: Succinylcholine causes an increase in the intragastric pressure.
Answer D: Upper esophageal sphincter tone is generally reported to be decreased by succinylcholine. Succinylcholine increases both LES tone and intragastric pressure. The former effect is greater than the latter, so the risk of aspiration is not increased. The increase in intragastric pressure can be offset by a priming dose of a nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocker.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Morphine improves coronary perfusion through a reduction in preload and a reduction in end-diastolic pressures (EDP) in the ventricles. The EDV is proportional to the EDP generated within the ventricle. The RV is perfused during both systole and diastole whereas the LV is perfused during diastole only. Right-sided coronary perfusion pressure during systole is equal to the difference between aortic systolic pressure and RVEDP. Right-sided coronary perfusion pressure during diastole is equal to the difference between aortic diastolic pressure and RVEDP. Left-sided coronary perfusion pressure is the difference between aortic diastolic pressure and left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP). Coronary perfusion pressure is improved by REDUCING both RVEDP and LVEDP. The CO2-ventilatory response curve is noted as the black line. The linear curve is shifted to the right and the slope is reduced upon administration of morphine (red line). The point where the ventilation curve (dashed curve) meets each linear CO2 response curve represents the apneic threshold of that particular response curve (dotted lines perpendicular to the x-axis). The apneic threshold of PaCO2 at which the patient spontaneously ventilates is increased with morphine administration. Of note, the response curves are linear between PaCO2 of 20-80 mm Hg. Beyond 80 mm Hg, CO2 has a depressant effect on ventilation. Preload reduction and vasodilatation are due to morphine’s histamine release. This dose-dependent histamine release is the largest out of the commonly used opioids. This may lead to a decrease in SVR, hypotension, tachycardia, bronchospasm, and an increase in pulmonary vascular resistance. Of note, morphine also reduces afterload which also helps to reduce the myocardial fiber length and oxygen demand. This effect on coronary perfusion pressures is less pronounced than preload reduction.
Answer C: Morphine in large doses over a short period of time (like FENTANYL) can cause thoracic and abdominal wall rigidity.
Answer D: Preload is the ventricular volume at the end of diastole or the end-diastolic volume (EDV). The EDV of both ventricles determines the myocardial fiber length and the force of ventricular contraction required during ejection. The morphine-induced reduction in the force of contraction reduces the myocardial oxygen demand at doses of 0.1-0.3 mg/kg (C). Morphine typically does not cause a reduction in myocardial contractility when administered alone. Morphine may cause myocardial depression when combined with volatile anesthetics.
Answer E: All µ-opioid agonists cause dose-dependent respiratory depression by decreasing the sensitivity of central medullary chemoreceptors to elevated levels of carbon dioxide. This effect is represented by a rightward shift and slope reduction of the hypercapneic ventilatory response curve. Morphine reduces preload and afterload. This reduces myocardial oxygen demand and improves coronary perfusion pressures by reducing ventricular EDV and EDP. Morphine has minimal effect on myocardial contractility by itself but may cause myocardial depression when combined with volatile anesthetics. All µ-opioid agonists cause dose-dependent respiratory depression by decreasing the sensitivity of central chemoreceptors to elevated levels of CO2. Evoked Potential: Morphine and its active metabolites, morphine-6-glucuronide and morphine-3-glucuronide, are excreted via the kidneys. Morphine-6-glucuronide is a more potent and a longer-lasting opioid agonist than morphine itself. This makes morphine relatively contraindicated in renal failure. Patients who receive an excessive amount of acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibitor are at an increased risk of developing weakness. The recommended maximum dose of neostigmine is 0.07 mg/kg. Reversal of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade is achieved by administering an AChE inhibitor. Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs (NMBDs) are competitive antagonists and compete with acetylcholine (ACh) in the synaptic cleft. The chances that ACh will bind to ACh receptors (instead of the NMBD) increases with AChE inhibition. Excessive inhibition of AChE can lead to prolonged elevations in synaptic ACh concentrations. Prolonged exposure to ACh can lead to both presynaptic and postsynaptic inactivation of sodium channels. Inactivation of sodium channels prohibits depolarization from occurring. In addition, both presynaptic and postsynaptic ACh receptors become desensitized to ACh. Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors also inhibit plasma butyrylcholinesterase, which can prolong the effects of succinylcholine.
Answer B: Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors can exert effects at both nicotinic and muscarinic receptors. Increased muscarinic stimulation can lead to increased salivation, bradycardia, and an increased incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Reducing the dose of neostigmine is not an effective strategy for reducing PONV, though this was mentioned in older ASA Practice Parameter statements.
Answer C: Increased muscarinic stimulation can lead to increased salivation. Excessive dosing of AChE inhibitors can cause weakness by motor axon sodium channel inactivation and presynaptic nicotinic receptor desensitization. Postsynaptic sodium channel inactivation and acetylcholine receptor desensitization also occur. Combined, these can lead to significant muscle weakness.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword.
