Nitrous oxide is associated with megaloblastic changes and agranulocytosis due to its ability to decrease the activity of vitamin B12-dependent enzymes. Nitrous oxide decreases the activity of the vitamin B12-dependent enzymes methionine synthetase and thymidylate synthetase. The mechanism of action includes irreversible oxidation of the cobalt atom of vitamin B12. Inhibiting these enzymes can lead to bone marrow suppression and neurologic disturbances. Megaloblastic changes have been consistently observed in patients exposed to nitrous oxide for 24 hours, and four days of exposure has led to agranulocytosis. In humans who use nitrous oxide daily for recreational use, a sensory and motor polyneuropathy combined with signs of posterior lateral spinal cord degeneration has been described (subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord). When 70% nitrous oxide is administered to patients, 50% inactivation of methionine synthetase occurs in approximately 46 minutes. In healthy patients, the impact of enzyme inactivation may be subtle or subclinical, but in those with underlying vitamin B12 deficiency or critical illness, neurologic or hematologic sequelae can occur. Concern exists that nitrous oxide can affect a rapidly developing fetus because methionine synthetase and thymidylate synthetase are involved in formation of both myelin and DNA. Answers A & B: None of the volatile anesthetics have an effect on vitamin B12-dependent enzymes or an association with agranulocytosis.  Nitrous oxide inhibits the vitamin B12-dependent enzymes, methionine synthetase and thymidylate synthetase. This may lead to subclinical problems in relatively healthy patients, but may cause neurologic and hematologic sequelae in critically ill and vitamin B12-deficient patients. The liver extensively metabolizes nicardipine and, as a result, hepatic insufficiency can result in prolonged half-life (B). Nicardipine is a calcium-channel blocker; more specifically, it is an antagonist of calcium influx through the slow channels of cell membranes. It is an effective coronary and peripheral arterial dilator. Nicardipine can be used to relieve angina, especially those due to coronary artery spasms. It is also useful as an anti-hypertensive drug, particularly in neurosurgical patients. However, the advantage of nicardipine is that it does not decrease cardiac function. Nicardipine (intravenous and oral) can cause an increase in heart rate in about 25% of the people. This tachycardia is NOT due to baroreceptor response, rather due to sympathetic activation. Nicardipine decreases systemic vascular resistance, but also increases cardiac contractility (C). The exact mechanism of this positive inotropic effect is unknown. There seems to be no increased risk of bronchospasm in patients with lung diseases receiving nicardipine (A). In fact, some studies suggest that nicardipine may increase forced expiratory volume over one second (FEV1) and forced vital capacity (FVC). Nicardipine dosage is not affected by renal insufficiency (D). The use of nicardipine increases both renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate and also decreases renovascular resistance. Oral nicardipine is well absorbed, but has very low availability due to extensive liver metabolism. The first-pass effect reduces the concentration of nicardipine available for systemic circulation. The half-life of nicardipine is about 60-100 minutes. After being metabolized by the liver, nicardipine is eliminated via bile and feces. Patients with hepatic insufficiency will have decreased metabolism resulting in prolonged duration (B). Side-effects of nicardipine are mostly transient and are related to vasodilation: flushing, headache, and peripheral edema. Abrupt withdrawal of nicardipine after chronic use does not produce any side-effects.  Nicardipine is metabolized by the liver and eliminated via gastrointestinal tract. Renal insufficiency has no effect on nicardipine use. Severe hepatic insufficiency results in significantly prolonged nicardipine half-life.  Barash, P. Clinical Anesthesia. 6th Ed. 2009. The local anesthetic with the highest incidence of transient neurologic symptoms is lidocaine. When lidocaine is used for spinal anesthesia in the lithotomy position, the incidence increases up to 36%. Transient neurologic syndrome (TNS) is a complication of spinal anesthesia that can be seen after the use of lidocaine and other local anesthetics. The defining feature of TNS is paradoxical back pain radiating to the lower extremities without the presence of other neurological symptoms. Transient neurologic syndrome occurs 2 to 24 hours after the resolution of the spinal anesthesia. There are no long-term neurological sequelae with TNS. The estimated incidence is between 4% and 40%, depending on the risk factors present. Risk factors include the use of lidocaine, ambulatory anesthesia, and the lithotomy position; baricity and dose of local anesthetics do not increase the risk of TNS. Treatment for TNS includes the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and trigger point injections. The incidence of TNS with bupivacaine is 1%.
Answer C: The incidence of TNS with prilocaine is 1%.
Answer D: The incidence of TNS with ropivacaine is 1%. Risk factors associated with an increased incidence of transient neurologic symptoms after spinal anesthesia include the use of lidocaine (the local anesthetic with the highest incidence), ambulatory anesthesia, and the lithotomy position. Cardiac output is maintained with desflurane use. Desflurane increases heart rate and decreases both mean arterial pressure and systemic vascular resistance while maintaining cardiac output. Some studies have shown desflurane can better maintain blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance when compared to isoflurane. Invasive measurements of left ventricular indices demonstrate that desflurane does not alter regional or chamber stiffness and therefore, desflurane does not affect left ventricular diastolic function. The increase in heart rate at 1.0 MAC is comparable to that seen with isoflurane use at 1.0 MAC, though rapid changes of desflurane over 1.0 MAC tend to cause a more dramatic increase in heart rate. This change in heart rate is thought to be reflexively mediated via baroreceptors in response to decreased blood pressure. It is the rapid change in desflurane concentration that leads to increased heart rate, not the absolutely MAC value. Again, at 1.0 MAC the heart rate change is similar between desflurane and isoflurane.
Answer B: Desflurane decreases blood pressure primarily by decreasing afterload.
Answer C: Desflurane causes a dose-dependent depression of myocardial function, but due a reflexive increase in heart rate, cardiac output is maintained. Desflurane primarily decreases arterial pressure by decreasing afterload. Desflurane increases heart rate, particularly when the concentration is quickly increased, and also causes dose-dependent depression of myocardial function. Cardiac output is maintained and there is no significant effect on left ventricular diastolic function.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The image in the question stem shows peaked T waves, an ECG finding characteristic of hyperkalemia. Bumetamide is a treatment option for hyperkalemia (A). Hyperkalemia may be caused by many physiologic processes and pharmaceutical agents. ACE inhibitors and ARBs, mannitol, aldosterone antagonists, digitalis, and some beta-blockers can result in hyperkalemia through various mechanisms. Bumetanide (A), is a loop diuretic that inhibits the sodium/potassium/2-chloride receptor in the ascending tubule loop of Henle. A large salt load is delivered to the distal nephron that is greater than it is able to reabsorb leading to marked diuresis. Potassium excretion is increased along with sodium, and hypokalemia can result. Hypokalemia is characterized by T wave flattening or inversion and U waves on the ECG. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors (ACEIs) such as captopril, enalapril, and lisinopril prevent the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II (B). All ACEIs carry a risk of hyperkalemia as do angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) since inhibition of angiotensin II formation prevents the subsequent formation of aldosterone. Aldosterone acts on the distal tubules and collecting ducts of the nephron to increase sodium and fluid retention and increase potassium excretion. Blockade of this pathway can lead to hyperkalemia. The exact molecular mechanism for succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia is not known (C). It is a well-known risk nonetheless in certain patient populations such as burn victims, patients with spinal cord injury, stroke, multiple sclerosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Proliferation of extrajunctional receptors may play a role in increased potassium release with depolarization of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor. Spironolactone is an aldosterone antagonist (D). As aldosterone works to increase potassium secretion, blockade of this hormone can lead to hyperkalemia and its associated ECG findings and physiologic derangement.  ACEIs/ARBs, aldosterone antagonists, and succinylcholine administration may lead to hyperkalemia. Enalapril is one of many drugs that have been implicated in drug-induced lupus. Codeine is an opiate prodrug that requires conversion to its metabolites to exert its clinical effects (A). A prodrug is a drug that has reduced or no activity on its own and must be metabolized to its active form(s). The effects of the prodrug codeine are primarily dependent on metabolism via O-demethylation to morphine, which requires the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2D6. Other metabolic pathways are seen in the figure below. One of the codeine glucuronides, codeine-6-glucuronide, may also provide some degree of analgesia. Norcodeine provides little or no analgesia. Since the action of codeine is dependent on conversion to (primarily) morphine, genetic variability of the activity of the CYP2D6 enzyme determines a patient’s response to the drug. Patients who have little or no CYP2D6 function (“poor metabolizers”) will experience very limited or no analgesia from codeine since little or no morphine is produced. On the other end of the spectrum, patients who have multiple functional copies of the CYP2D6 gene (“ultrarapid metabolizers”) will convert codeine into significantly more than normal amounts of morphine. While these patients may experience excellent analgesia, morphine accumulates quickly and can result in morphine toxicity. There are rare reports of young children dying due to respiratory depression/arrest despite receiving normal doses of codeine. These children were later found to be ultrarapid metabolizers. In the middle of the spectrum are patients who have normal CYP2D6 function (“extensive metabolizers”) or moderately decreased function (“intermediate metabolizers”). Hydromorphone does not require metabolism to exert its primary clinical effect. is primarily metabolized to hydromorphone-3-glucuronide, which provides no analgesic effects. Buildup of renally-excreted hydromorphone-3-glucuronide can lead to neuroexcitatory effects including agitation, restlessness, and myoclonus.
Answer C: Oxymorphone does not require metabolism to exert its primary clinical effect. It is primarily metabolized to oxymorphone-3-glucuronide and 6-hydroxy-oxymorphone. The activity of the former metabolite is unknown, and the latter is known to provide less analgesic effect than oxymorphone. Oxycodone is metabolized to oxymorphone via CYP2D6. Codeine is an opiate prodrug whose effects are primarily dependent on metabolism to morphine, which requires the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2D6. Clonidine is an alpha2 agonist that has analgesic effects and can be administered into the epidural space. When injected into the epidural space, clonidine acts on adrenergic receptors located at the spinal cord. Studies have shown that clonidine was able to produce effective analgesia that is comparable to morphine. However, clonidine had a longer duration of action than morphine. In one study, some patients who received clonidine had analgesia for up to one month! Adrenergic receptors at the spinal cord seem to potentiate the effects of opioids, such as morphine. Giving morphine and clonidine together enhances the analgesic effect. The addition of clonidine increased both the duration and intensity of morphine's analgesic effect. This allowed for less re-dosing of morphine. This is not the case with fentanyl. Combining clonidine plus fentanyl showed no difference in analgesic effects compared to fentanyl alone. Epidural administration of clonidine can produce significant hypotension and causes more sedation than morphine. But the opioid side effects of pruritus, nausea, and vomiting are not seen with clonidine. The hypotension from clonidine was often resolved with fluids. Clonidine does not have the side effects commonly seen with opioids. When clonidine is combined with an opioid, it enhances analgesia and allows for the reduced dosing of the opioid. This further reduces the risk of nausea and vomiting. Several studies have shown that clonidine can reduce the risk of PONV and the mechanism is likely multifactorial, including the previously mentioned reduction on anesthetic requirements as well as a reduction in sympathetic tone and catecholamine release.
Answer C: Clonidine is more likely to produce significant hypotension.
Answer D: Morphine plus clonidine increases both the duration and intensity of the analgesia. Clonidine is an effective analgesic drug. It has a longer epidural effect duration than morphine. When given in combination with morphine, the analgesic effect is enhanced.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Epidural: Clonidine Vs Morphine (B)" Anzai Y, et.al. Aspirating a foreign body can result in the obstruction of the right mainstem or a smaller bronchus. This leads to a portion of the lung that is not ventilated but is perfused, causing an intrapulmonary shunt that will result in a slower inhalational induction. In normal patients without any ventilation or perfusion issues, the alveolar and arterial anesthetic partial pressures are assumed to be normal. However, this is not the case if V/Q (ventilation-perfusion) mismatch is present. When ventilation is normal but perfusion is reduced, it results in dead space. If ventilation is reduced, but perfusion is normal, it results in a shunt. When perfusion is affected (reduced cardiac output, pulmonary embolism), the speed of induction of inhalational agents is increased. The impact is more significant with soluble agents such as isoflurane. The rise of FA/FI is steeper with lower perfusion of the lungs. When ventilation is affected (intrapulmonary shunt), the speed of induction of inhalational agents is decreased. This is mainly due to the dilutional effect of the shunted blood. This occurs to a greater degree with insoluble agents (desflurane, sevoflurane). The alveolar partial pressure of the inhaled agent is not reduced by a foreign body (shunt). Even though an entire lung is no longer ventilating, the one lung that is being ventilated will have normal or even increased alveolar partial pressure of the anesthetic.
Answer C: The solubility of inhaled anesthetics is not altered by V/Q mismatch. The solubility of an inhaled anesthetic is based on its blood-gas coefficient and it is affected by temperature. Intrapulmonary shunt reduces the speed of inhalational induction.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Uptake Of Inhaled Anesthetics: VQ Mismatch" Miller’s Anesthesia 7th Edition. Higher doses of dopamine will result in beta-1 receptor binding which will cause release of norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals. Dopamine is a naturally occurring catecholamine that stimulates beta-1 and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors as well as D-1 dopamine receptors, which are primarily located in the renal and mesenteric vasculature. The response to exogenously administered dopamine depends on the dose given. At lower concentrations, dopamine primarily acts on the D-1 dopamine receptors to produce vasodilation of the renal, mesenteric, and coronary vasculature. The main result is an increase in the glomerular filtration rate and renal blood flow. Furthermore, low dose dopamine will result in sodium excretion which will increase urine output. Higher doses will stimulate the beta-1 receptors to increase release of norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals. The end result is an increase in heart rate, systolic blood pressure, and pulse pressure. Diastolic blood pressure is minimally affected however pulmonary vascular resistance may increase. At the highest doses, dopamine administration will stimulate alpha-1 receptors which results in peripheral vasoconstriction. Dopamine was previously first line therapy for shock states, although norepinephrine has replaced this recommendation. Dopamine, when compared with norepinephrine for treatment of shock, was associated with a higher incidence of arrhythmias and a higher mortality in patients with cardiogenic shock. Side effects of dopamine depend on the dose and the patient's comorbid conditions. Dopamine can cause tachyarrhythmias and myocardial ischemia. Furthermore, at higher doses a decrease in splanchnic blood flow may occur with resultant gut ischemia. Dopamine infusions may alter endocrine and immune functions including decreased secretion of thyroid stimulating hormone, prolactin, and growth hormone. Dopamine decreases the ventilatory response to hypoxemia and hypercarbia secondary to exertion of a depressive effect on the carotid bodies. Furthermore, dopamine may impair regional ventilation/perfusion matching in the lung, potentially causing or worsening hypoxemia. If dopamine is extravasated, it can result in skin necrosis and sloughing thus administration into a central line is recommended. If extravasation does occur, prompt infiltration of the area with phentolamine and/or application of topical nitroglycerin should be considered to counter the vasoconstriction. General Dosing Guidelines: Low dosing: 0.5 to 3 mcg/kg/min Moderate dosing: 3 to 10 mcg/kg/min High dosing: >10 mcg/kg/min Note that these are general guidelines and sometimes the desired effect will occur within different dosing parameters for individual patients. Higher doses of dopamine will result in beta-1 receptor binding which will cause release of norepinephrine, not epinephrine, from sympathetic nerve terminals.
Answer C: Stimulation of dopamine D-1 receptors results in vasodilation of the renal, mesenteric, and coronary vasculature.
Answer D: D-1 dopamine stimulation will result in sodium excretion. This will augment urine output. Low dose dopamine, also referred to as renal dopamine, is no longer recommended to treat or prevent acute renal failure. Although low doses will increase renal blood flow, numerous studies have failed to show it decreases the incidence of renal failure. Dopamine causes its effects through stimulation of beta-1 receptors and release of norepinephrine.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Somatic motor neurons are myelinated, fast-conducting nerves. As the nerve axons progress to nerve endings, the myelin sheath is lost before branching into the terminal fibers. Each terminal fiber supplies a muscle fiber via the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). The NMJ consists of the presynaptic motor neuron nerve terminal and its Schwann cells, the synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic muscle fiber. Lower motor neuron cell bodies are located in the ventral horn of the spinal cord or in the motor nuclei of cranial nerves. The axons travel via the ventral roots to muscles. The axons end as terminal fibers at the NMJ. When an action potential reaches the nerve terminal, sodium from outside the nerve terminal flows inside. This depolarization opens voltage-gated calcium channels, which allows the entry of calcium ions into the nerve terminal and causes acetylcholine to be released into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine then binds to the nicotinic muscle-type acetylcholine receptors, leading to an influx of sodium ions into the muscle and an efflux of potassium out of the muscle, causing depolarization and resulting in muscle contraction. Before birth, each muscle cell has contact with several nerves and has several NMJs. However, after birth, all but one of the nerves retract, and only one NMJ remains. A motor unit consists of the motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates. The innervation ratio is the number of muscle fibers that each neuron innervates. The innervation ratio changes depending on the function of the muscle group. For groups that require fine control, such as eye or facial muscles, the innervation ratio is 1:2 (one nerve innervating two muscle fibers). For large muscles with coarse, powerful movements, such as the thigh or back, the innervation ratio is much higher, approaching 1:2,000. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptors of muscle fibers are highly concentrated at the synapses. At birth, these receptors are immature and consist of five protein subunits (α2βγδ). After birth, the receptors mature by replacing the γ subunit with an ε subunit. Outside of the junctional area, there are far fewer receptors. Lower motor neurons originate in the ventral horn of the spinal cord or the motor nuclei of cranial nerves. The dorsal horn contains the ascending sensory pathways and interneurons that make connections within the spinal cord.
Answer B: Nicotinic muscle-type acetylcholine receptors consist of five protein subunits. The mature receptor contains two α subunits and one each of the β, δ, and ε subunits.
Answer D: The innervation ratio changes, depending on the function of the muscle group. For groups that require very fine control, the innervation ratio is 1:2. For large muscles that have coarse, powerful movements, the innervation ratio is much higher, approaching 1:2,000. The neuromuscular junction consists of the presynaptic motor neuron, the synaptic cleft, and the postsynaptic muscle fiber. Axons end as unmyelinated terminal fibers. Action potentials cause the release of acetylcholine molecules from the terminal fibers, which then bind to the five-subunit nicotinic muscle-type acetylcholine receptors, leading to depolarization and contraction of the muscle. Spironolactone is a competitive aldosterone antagonist that is a potassium-sparing diuretic. It works in the distal tubule of the nephron segments in the kidney. Inhibition of aldosterone will cause a mild retention of potassium and excretion of sodium. The most commonly described side effects of spironolactone are hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, gynecomastia, and impotence. Other potassium sparing diuretics, such as eplerenone, triamterene, and amiloride, all possess similar side effects as spironolactone. Spironolactone may be added to a medical regimen to treat edema, specifically in those with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, or nephrotic syndrome. It is not likely to cause edema. In fact, spironolactone improves survival in patients with volume overload and heart failure.
Answer B: Spironolactone may be added to a medical regimen to treat hypokalemia. It is not likely to cause it. Instead, hyperkalemia and hyperkalemic, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis are more likely to occur. The most commonly described side effects of spironolactone are hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, gynecomastia, and impotence.  Barash’s Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Page 1415. Just as with all calcium channel blockers (CCB), nicardipine predominantly causes arteriolar vasodilation compared to venous vasodilation, resulting in decreased arterial blood pressure. Calcium channel blockers inhibit the firing of L-type voltagedependent Ca2+ channels. Calcium channel blockers can be generally divided into two chemical groups with unique pharmacodynamic profiles: dihydropyridine-type CCB (eg, nifedipine, nicardipine, nimodipine, clevidipine) and nondihydropyridine-type CCB (diltiazem and verapamil). Both groups of CCBs reduce left ventricular afterload and maintain preload because they preferentially dilate the arterial smooth muscle compared to venous smooth muscle, but dihydropyridine-type CCBs do not have a negative inotropic or dromotropic effect on the heart, while the nondihydropyridine-type CCBs have a negative inotropic and dromotropic effect on the heart. Calcium channel blockers are particularly useful for postoperative coronary artery bypass graft patients because they cause coronary arterial vasodilation and inhibit coronary artery vasospasm. These actions may enhance coronary blood flow if it is assumed that coronary perfusion pressure is not substantially reduced due to arterial vasodilation. Nondihydropyridine CCBs reduce myocardial oxygen demand by decreasing both heart rate and contractility. On the other hand, dihydropyridines may increase myocardial oxygen demand via reflex tachycardia, but they do not have a negative inotropic effect. Sodium nitroprusside causes both arterial and venous dilation, resulting in a decreased afterload and preload. Because of its rapid onset, sodium nitroprusside is frequently used in a hypertensive emergency.
Answer C: Diltiazem predominantly decreases chronotropy through inhibition at the level of the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Diltiazem also decreases inotropy but to a lesser degree.
Answer D: Nitroglycerin is predominantly a venodilator, which results in a decreased preload. Decreased preload is useful in patients with decompensated heart failure from ischemia because it reduces myocardial oxygen demand. Patients with hypovolemic or inferior myocardial infarction should not be treated with nitroglycerin because it may result in dramatic hypotension. Calcium channel blockers (CCB) inhibit the firing of L-type voltage-dependent Ca2+ channels. Calcium channel blockers predominantly cause arteriolar vasodilation compared to venous vasodilation, resulting in decreased arterial blood pressure. Dihydropyridine-type CCBs do not have a negative inotropic or dromotropic effect on the heart, while nondihydropyridine-type CCBs (diltiazem, verapamil) have a negative inotropic and dromotropic effect on the heart. Concurrent administration of neuromuscular blocking drugs (NBDs) and calcium channel blockers (CCBs) to a CCB-naïve patient can cause mild potentiation of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs. Calcium ions play important roles in both smooth and skeletal muscle contraction. Calcium channel blockers alter calcium’s ability to cross the cellular membrane resulting in less excitation-contraction. Most studies examining this effect on skeletal muscle have been conducted with animal models and have revealed that CCBs cause a progressive dose-related reduction in twitch height. Additional studies (again, primarily in animal models or in-vitro) have examined the interactions of CCBs and NBDs. Most studies show the effects of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs muscle relaxants are augmented by CCBs. The exact mechanism behind this is unclear but it may be due to one or more of the following: alterations in presynaptic variables reducing calcium conduction, alteration of intracellular calcium pools, or inhibition of the calcium membrane pump mechanisms. All of these could result in a decrease of acetylcholine mobilization and modification of muscle relaxation. Additionally, there are case reports of patients who were given CCBs for cardiovascular disease in the perioperative period and then had severe weakness after muscle relaxation was administered. Given the information discussed above, careful titration of NBDs should be considered when given to patients who are also being administered CCBs in the perioperative period. Note that CCBs, when taken chronically, have only a very mild minor potentiation effect on both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs (generally only observed in in-vitro or animal study models). This effect is considered to be clinically insignificant and no changes in dosing to CCBs or NBDs are generally necessary. Answers B & C & D: Concurrent administration of NBDs and CCBs to a CCB-naïve patient can cause mild augmentation of both depolarizing and nondepolarizing NBDs.  Calcium channel blockers can augment depolarizing and nondepolarizing muscle relaxants, particularly when the two drugs are administered concurrently to CCB-naïve patients. Consider the careful titration of NBDs in this setting. In patients taking chronic CCBs, the augmentation effect is clinically insignificant. During treatment of malignant hyperthermia, CCBs should not be given in combination with dantrolene because it can lead to life-threatening hyperkalemia and myocardial depression. However, if a patient on a chronic CCB develops malignant hyperthermia, dantrolene should always be given as withholding dantrolene can significantly worsen mortality. Diarrhea is a side effect of the administration of the anticholinesterase agent neostigmine. The primary side effects of anticholinesterase administration are bradycardia and increased gastrointestinal activity. Glycopyrrolate is an antimuscarinic that can be administered before neostigmine administration to block the effects of neostigmine at muscarinic sites. Neostigmine is an anticholinesterase that functions by increasing the amount of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by competitively inhibiting cholinesterase. Neostigmine increases acetylcholine, which competes with nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking (NMB) agents for nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Neostigmine is often the preferred anticholinesterase used for reversal because of its quick onset of action, strong affinity for the cholinesterase enzyme, and fewer muscarinic side effects compared with other agents. It is a common reversal agent for NMB, but its use for reversal is declining with the rise of the use of sugammadex for the reversal of rocuronium and vecuronium. Because neostigmine blocks cholinesterase found at nicotinic and muscarinic sites, the addition of an antimuscarinic agent such as atropine or glycopyrrolate is used to prevent the side effects of bradycardia, nausea, increased peristalsis, and diarrhea. Other side effects of neostigmine include complete heart block, asystole, and bronchoconstriction. It is important to note that neostigmine does not cross the blood-brain barrier. Anhidrosis is an anticholinergic side effect, not a side effect of neostigmine.
Answer C: Mydriasis is an anticholinergic side effect, not a side effect of neostigmine.
Answer D: Urinary retention is an anticholinergic side effect, not a side effect of neostigmine. Neostigmine competitively inhibits cholinesterase enzymes found at nicotinic and muscarinic sites, which increases the amount of acetylcholine. The addition of an antimuscarinic such as atropine or glycopyrrolate is used to prevent the side effects of bradycardia, nausea, increased peristalsis, and diarrhea caused by neostigmine administration. A mnemonic to remember the symptoms of anticholinergic syndrome is "red as a beet, dry as a bone, blind as a bat, mad as a hatter, hot as a hare, and full as a flask." The mnemonic correlates with the following symptoms: flushing, anhidrosis, dry mucous membranes, mydriasis, altered mental status, hyperthermia, and urinary retention. Although patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) may have higher baseline serum potassium concentrations than healthy patients, ESRD by itself does not affect the rise in potassium following succinylcholine administration. Transient serum potassium elevation is a side effect of succinylcholine due to skeletal muscle depolarization, which leads to cation influx and potassium efflux. In healthy patients, succinylcholine can transiently raise serum potassium as much as 0.5 mEq/L as a result of this potassium efflux. Patients with certain conditions can experience more profound succinylcholineinduced hyperkalemia (serum potassium increase up to nearly 3.5 mEq/L) due to nicotinic extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor upregulation. This can lead to cardiac arrhythmias and potential cardiac arrest. Answers A & C: Patient populations at risk for more profound succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia include those who are >24 hours status post burn injuries, major denervation injuries, peripheral denervation, spinal cord transection, or trauma that leads to prolonged immobilization. It is still appropriate to use succinylcholine to safely secure the airway in these patients if their injury is < 24 hours old, as there has not been enough time to experience nicotinic extrajunctional acetylcholine receptor upregulation. Succinylcholine has a Black Boxed warning specifically for this reason. Caution should also be used in patients with muscular dystrophies (especially in children who can have potentially undiagnosed disorders), stroke patients, patients with neuromuscular disorders, or intensive care patients with prolonged immobilization. In some patients, such as muscular dystrophy, hyperkalemia can occur secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Other patients are also subject to upregulation of extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors and are therefore more prone to significant succinylcholine-induced hyperkalemia. Succinylcholine administration transiently raises serum potassium approximately 0.5 mEq/L in healthy patients. Succinylcholine is contraindicated in patients with neuromuscular disorders, prolonged immobility, and those >24 hours status post burns, trauma, or denervation injuries. This is due to an upregulation of extrajunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, leading to an increase in serum potassium up to 3.5 mEq/L following succinylcholine administration. In children, there is a risk of cardiac arrest from hyperkalemia rhabdomyolysis.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Overall, allergic reactions to local anesthetics are uncommon. Most untoward reactions to local anesthetics are non-allergic, and most patients who report allergies to local anesthetics are in fact not allergic when tested by skin testing. For example, a patient who recalls pounding in the chest when injected local anesthetic by their dentist is more likely to have had a physiologic (nonallergic) reaction to the epinephrine content of that formulation. In cases of true allergy, aminoester local anesthetics (procaine, chloroprocaine, etc) are more likely to elicit allergic reactions compared to aminoamides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine, etc) because the aminoesters are derivatives of paraaminobenzoic acid (PABA), a known allergen (hapten to be precise). Although allergic reactions to aminoamides are very rare, patients may occasionally react to preservatives such as methylparaben contained in the aminoamide formulation. Multiple-dose vials of lidocaine typically contain 0.1% of methylparaben added as preservative, whereas single dose solutions are typically methylparaben free. Methylparaben is the methyl ester of para-hydroxybenzoic acid, which is structurally similar to para-aminobenzoic acid (PABA), differing only in having a hydroxyl group vs amino group in the para position. Thus, cross-sensitivity between these compounds can occur. Answers A & D: Aminoester local anesthetics are derivatives of paraaminobenzoic acid, which is known to be allergenic. Lidocaine is an amino-amide, not an amino-ester. Sulfites such as sodium metabisulfite are added as antioxidants for the catecholamine content. Lidocaine vials with epinephrine will typically contain metabisulfite, which may also elicit allergic responses. This vial did not contain epinephrine. True allergic reactions to local anesthetics are rare. Aminoester local anesthetics are more likely to elicit allergic reactions compared to aminoamides because they are derivatives of para-aminobenzoic acid, a known allergen. Also potential allergens are the preservatives included in some formulations, methylparaben (structurally related to PABA) and sulfites. Injectable 1% diphenhydramine, in addition to its antihistamine effect, is a safe, inexpensive, and effective local anesthetic for simple dermal procedures (e.g. sutures) in patients who report “-caine” allergies. Methohexital lowers the seizure threshold and may trigger seizures in susceptible patients. Methohexital is a short-acting barbiturate anesthetic. It binds to GABAA receptors which leads to neuronal hyperpolarization and inhibition of neurotransmission. Methohexital remains the drug of choice for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) because of longer seizure times (versus propofol), shorter awakening times (versus thiopental), and fewer side effects (versus etomidate). For ECT, methohexital is considered to cause no change in seizure duration overall. However, compared with saline it will decrease seizure duration during ECT. Methohexital is also commonly used as an induction agent for anesthesia for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) since, unlike many other IV anesthetics, it does not raise the seizure threshold and can increase ictal activity at low doses (e.g. 0.75 - 0.9 mg/kg). Administration of methohexital to patients with a history of seizures or epilepsy can trigger a new-onset seizure. However, methohexital has not been known to trigger a seizure in patients without any other risk factors. Similarly, there have been no reports of recurrent spontaneous seizures following methohexital administration for ECT. See the table below for other side effects of methohexital. Note that the excitatory side effects (e.g., hiccups, muscle twitches) are more prominent than those seen in most other IV anesthetics. The three commonly used barbiturates for induction of anesthesia are methohexital, thiopental, and thiamylal. However, methohexital is the only one commonly used in the United States. The complications of injecting barbiturates include a garlic or onion taste (40% of patients with thiopental or thiamylal), allergic reactions, local tissue irritation, and rarely tissue necrosis. The sulfur molecule in thiopental and thiamylal is the likely cause of the abnormal taste with induction, and the lack of this molecule explains why the abnormal taste is not seen with methohexital. Thiopental and thiamylal produce fewer excitatory symptoms with induction than methohexital, which produces cough, hiccough (hiccups), tremors, and twitching approximately five times more often. Hiccups with methohexital can be severe and cause distress for patients in the post-anesthesia recovery unit. Tissue irritation and local complications may occur more frequently with the use of thiopental and thiamylal than with methohexital. In comparative studies, pain on injection was shown to be greater with methohexital (12%) than with thiopental (9%). Results also show phlebitis occurs more frequently with methohexital use (8%) than with thiopental use (1%). Tissue and venous irritation are more common if a 5% solution is used, rather than the standard 2% solution. Answers A & B & C: Methohexital is not known to cause atrial fibrillation, diarrhea, or QT prolongation.  Unlike most other IV anesthetics, methohexital has epileptogenic activity and can induce seizures in at-risk patients. See the table above for other side effects of methohexital. Reconstituted vecuronium, which has an acidic pH, should not be mixed with alkaline solutions (e.g. barbiturate solutions such as methohexital) in the same syringe or administered simultaneously during intravenous infusion through the same needle or same intravenous line as they will precipitate and could occlude the intravenous line. Airway reflexes under ketamine anesthesia are maintained. Ketamine has been used frequently for procedural sedation in the emergency department. Airway reflexes have been found to be maintained in multiple studies. Further, aspiration is unlikely even when used for procedural sedation in an unsecured airway. Quoted from a review on the topic, "Despite 30 years of widespread ketamine use, there are no documented cases of clinically significant ketamine-associated aspiration in a patient lacking established contraindications to this drug." That being said, there is significant controversy regarding whether these reflexes are "protective" or not. The general consensus is that airway reflexes are preserved but these should not be assumed to be protective. Ketamine maintains better airway protective reflexes than many other anesthetics, but they are dose related (higher doses means less protective airway reflexes). Although an induction dose will likely preserve reflexes in a non-fasted patient without issue, it is not 100% protective against aspiration in a non-fasted patient. Ketamine, even at low serum levels, can produce powerful analgesia. The mechanism includes mu opioid receptor agonism and NMDA receptor antagonism. At higher doses, ketamine can produce hallucinations, amnesia, and increased sympathetic tone. Ketamine produces “dissociative amnesia,” in which protective reflexes and respiratory drive are relatively preserved in comparison to a similar anesthetic depth with other intravenous anesthetic agents.
Answer B: Ketamine increases CMRO2.
Answer C: The predominant hemodynamic effect of ketamine is indirect myocardial stimulation. Some direct myocardial depression is seen, however this is almost never clinically significant due to the indirect stimulation effects, even in critically ill patients. Ketamine is unique when compared to many other intravenous anesthetics: airway reflexes and respiratory drive are relatively preserved, significant analgesia is produced, and sympathetic tone is increased. Ketamine's analgesic effect is present even with relatively small doses.  Miller’s Anesthesia 7th Edition. Chapter 26: Intravenous Anesthetics. Page 742-747. Miller’s Anesthesia 7th Edition. Extravasated propofol is associated with minimal local tissue injury. Many IV medications administered perioperatively are considered irritants, meaning they cause pain and/or slight damage to local tissue when extravasated. This may be an effect of the medication itself, or more commonly, due to a solvent or preservative. Despite even small amounts of propofol causing substantial pain with intravascular injection or upon extravasation, it is an irritant associated with minimal local tissue injury. Medications are considered vesicants if they cause extensive tissue injury or destruction. Most commonly, these medications fall into one of several categories including chemotherapeutics, vasoactive substances, concentrated electrolyte solutions, and hyperosmolar solutions. Mechanisms of tissue injury include direct cytotoxic effects, severe vasoconstriction, and increased osmotic pressure leading to compartment syndrome and ischemia. Answers A & B & C & E: Diazepam, phenytoin, promethazine, and thiopental are vesicants. Extravasation of each of these medications has been associated with severe local tissue necrosis, gangrene, or amputation.  Multiple specific drugs or drug classes are associated with severe local tissue injury and necrosis if extravasation occurs. Care should be taken to administer these drugs through easily visible, reliable peripheral or central intravenous access. Ketorolac inhibits afferent renal artery vasodilation. Ketorolac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID). Ketorolac inhibits cyclooxygenase and prevents the formation of prostaglandins and thromboxane. Prostaglandins have protective effects on the gastrointestinal and renal systems. Thromboxane is produced by platelets and increases platelet activation. NSAIDs, therefore, have reversible anti-platelet activity. Prostaglandins cause vasodilatation of the afferent renal artery, increasing renal blood flow. Inhibition of prostaglandins will therefore prevent the increase in renal blood flow. For short-duration therapy, ketorolac has not been shown to affect renal function to any clinical significance. However, after 5 days of maximal therapy, ketorolac has been associated with renal dysfunction. This is a result of the prostaglandin inhibition of ketorolac resulting in decreased renal blood flow. Ketorolac has anti-platelet effects, which can increase the incidence of bleeding when co-administered with warfarin. Ketorolac does not affect the prothrombin time (PT)/international normalized ratio (INR). Ketorolac also has no effect on the free fraction of warfarin in the bloodstream. Warfarin is highly protein bound, so any drug that displaces it from albumin will effectively increase the potency of warfarin with a subsequent increase in INR.
Answer C: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors will inhibit efferent renal artery vasoconstriction, which can lead to renal dysfunction in the proper setting. Ketorolac can decrease the glomerular filtration rate, especially when administered for greater than 5 days, via inhibition of afferent renal artery vasodilation. Chloroprocaine (2-chloroprocaine) has a very fast onset of action because it is used in relatively high concentrations (eg, 3%) compared to other local anesthetics. 2-Chloroprocaine is a local anesthetic that blocks electrical conductivity in neurons by blocking the sodium channels. It is an ester-type local anesthetic and, just as other esters, is broken down by plasma cholinesterases. The amide local anesthetics undergo hepatic metabolism. 2-Chloroprocaine is the most rapidly metabolized of all of the local anesthetics, having a plasma half-life of 12 seconds in adults. The onset time of all local anesthetics is dependent on many factors, including lipid solubility, pKa, concentration, and injection site. It has been frequently stated that the onset time of a local anesthetic is correlated to the pKa. Only the nonionized base penetrates the nerve cell membrane and has a physiologic effect. The pKa of a local anesthetic is the pH at which the fraction of ionized and nonionized drug is equal. Local anesthetics with a pKa closer to a physiologic pH will have more drug in the nonionized form and, therefore, more drug available for use. 2-Chloroprocaine has a pKa of ~9 but works faster than bupivacaine, which has a pKa of ~8. The time of onset is also highly dependent on the concentration of a particular local anesthetic. A solution of 0.75% bupivacaine will have a much faster onset than a solution of 0.25% bupivacaine. 2-Chloroprocaine is so rapidly metabolized and has such low systemic toxicity that it can be delivered in much higher concentrations, up to 3%. For this reason, 2-chloroprocaine has a very rapid onset of action despite its high pKa. Lipid solubility is the primary determinant of potency in local anesthetics.
Answer C: Although 2-chloroprocaine has a relatively high pKa, it has a fast onset of action due to its high concentration. It has been frequently stated that the onset time of a local anesthetic is correlated to the pKa. Only the nonionized base penetrates the nerve cell membrane and has a physiologic effect. The pKa of a local anesthetic is the pH at which the fraction of ionized and nonionized drug is equal. Local anesthetics with a pKa closer to a physiologic pH will have more drug in the nonionized form and, therefore, more drug available for use. While pKa is generally closely related to the onset time of local anesthetics, 2-chloroprocaine has a very rapid onset despite a high pKa. This is due to the high concentration of 2-chloroprocaine that can be safely given secondary to its rapid metabolism and low systemic toxicity.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "2-chloroprocaine Onset" Gropper. Miller's Anesthesia. 9th edition. Ch. 29: Local Anesthetics.

Nitrous oxide is not contraindicated for short abdominal operations such as a laparoscopic cholecystectomy or appendectomy. One study found that nitrous oxide had no clinically apparent deleterious effects during laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Another study found that nitrous oxide did not cause noticeable bowel distention during laparoscopic bariatric procedures of relatively short duration. The amount of time using nitrous oxide during abdominal surgery is more important than the type of surgery being performed. Nitrous oxide is greater than 30 times more soluble in blood than nitrogen, so it readily diffuses into gaseous areas of the body, such as the gut, faster than nitrogen can diffuse out. Increasing the length of time that nitrous oxide is administered and the concentration at which it is delivered contributes to increasing bowel distention. There is a linear relationship with time administered to increase in bowel distension with up to a 200% increases in volume after 4 hours. A 50% concentration of nitrous oxide can double bowel gas, a 75% concentration can quadruple the volume, whereas an 80% mixture can lead to a fivefold increase after several hours of administration. It is worth noting that at 75% nitrous oxide there may be a much more rapid increase in volume when referring to a pneumothorax. Pneumothorax may double in volume by 10 minutes and may triple it by 30 minutes. Equilibration and volume increase may occur within seconds in the case of air embolism. Because of its ability to distend bowel, nitrous oxide is normally avoided in situations where the bowel is already distended or during long abdominal operations since it can lead to ischemia and poor operating conditions. A patient with adhesions leading to small bowel obstruction would likely already have inflamed, distended bowel and may require a lengthy operation.
Answer C: Nitrous oxide is not recommended for laparoscopic donor nephrectomy since bowel distention can lead to poor surgical visualization. In one study, nitrous oxide had to be discontinued in 1/4th of these because the surgical team could not continue with the operation secondary to bowel distention.
Answer D: Whether the operation is accomplished laparoscopically or via laparotomy does not, in itself, determine the appropriateness of nitrous oxide use. Rather, the length of the operation and presence of obstruction, cancer, or diverticulitis, for example, lead to preexisting bowel distention that nitrous oxide has the potential to exacerbate. Nitrous oxide should be avoided in situations where bowel distention could be particularly hazardous. Both the length of time administered and the concentration of nitrous oxide lead to increasing bowel distention. An air-filled endotracheal tube cuff is susceptible to expansion by nitrous oxide. At 75% nitrous oxide a cuff can double or triple in volume causing pressure on the tracheal mucosa. Similarly, nitrous oxide may expand the cuffs of balloon-tipped (e.g. pulmonary artery) catheters. The air expansion is rapid and a doubling of catheter volume may occur within 10 minutes. Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Pages 1226, 1227, 1396 Singh P, et al. Isoflurane is the most lipid soluble of the three commonly used volatile anesthetics in the United States (desflurane, sevoflurane, and isoflurane) and is also the most potent of the three. There is a correlation between lipid solubility, or oil:gas partition coefficient, and potency of volatile anesthetic agents. This was first discovered by Meyer and Overton in the early 1900s and termed the Meyer-Overton correlation. The Meyer-Overton correlation attempted to explain the mechanism of action of volatile anesthetics which has been proven to be overly simplistic; however, the fact that there is a correlation between lipid solubility and potency of the common volatile agents remains true. The blood-gas partition coefficient of inhalational anesthetics correlates with the speed of onset and offset, not the potency. Isoflurane has the highest blood-gas partition coefficient of desflurane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane. The order of bloodgas partition coefficient is isoflurane >> sevoflurane > desflurane, which is also inversely proportional to their speed of onset and offset, desflurane > sevoflurane >> isoflurane.
Answer C: Isoflurane is more potent than sevoflurane and desflurane. Nitrous oxide is even less potent than desflurane with a MAC of >100%; however, it is technically an inhalational anesthetic and not a volatile anesthetic as it is a gas at standard ambient conditions compared to the volatile anesthetics which are volatile liquids under the same ambient conditions. Of note, halothane is even more potent than isoflurane and although not used in the United States, is still used throughout the world.
Answer D: The MAC is a measure of potency of an inhaled anesthetic, with a lower number indicating a lower percentage of partial pressure of the agent needed to prevent movement to a surgical stimulus in 50% of the population. The MAC of isoflurane is generally cited around 1.1%, while the MAC of sevoflurane is usually cited around 1.8% (1.7%-2.2%). The MAC of desflurane is approximately 6.6% Isoflurane is a potent volatile anesthetic with a MAC near 1.1%. In terms of inhalational anesthetic potency, isoflurane (MAC ~1%) > sevoflurane (MAC ~2%) >> desflurane (MAC ~6%) >>> nitrous oxide (MAC ~104%). The Tec 9 Datex-Ohmeda vaporizer heats desflurane to 2 atmospheres in order to ensure reliability of the dialed concentration. This is because desflurane is near boiling point at room temperature, which means an unpredictable amount is in liquid form, while the rest of it may be in gaseous form. This heated vaporizer reliably converts desflurane to the gaseous form. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Epidural 2-chloroprocaine has an onset time of approximately 6-12 minutes, as a result of the high concentration of local anesthetic that is used. The ester local anesthetic 2-chloroprocaine is most frequently used in the setting of obstetric epidural analgesia. Compared to other commonly used local anesthetics, is has the fastest onset of action time. 2-chloroprocaine has an onset time of 6-12 minutes, and that may be shortened slightly when high volumes are used. It is available in a 2% and 3% concentration. Duration of action is 45-60 minutes plain and 60-90 minutes when mixed with epinephrine (1:200,000 dilution). Chloroprocaine is hydrolyzed rapidly by plasma cholinesterases (half-life elimination of 21 seconds). However, metabolism is decreased in patients with a pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Chloroprocaine is commonly used to obtain rapid analgesia for an emergency cesarean section, when a working epidural catheter is already in place. Answers A & C: The onset of action for chloroprocaine via the epidural route is 6-12 minutes.  Chloroprocaine has the fastest onset of action time among commonly used epidural local anesthetics at 6-12 minutes. It has the shortest duration of action of all the local anesthetics. Administration of 2-chloroprocaine may decrease the efficacy of subsequently administered neuraxial drugs including bupivacaine, morphine, and fentanyl. Chloroaminobenzoic acid (the metabolite of 2-chloroprocaine) may be responsible for decreasing the efficacy of subsequent bupivacaine administration. Chloroaminobenzoic acid may also act as an antagonist of the µ-opioid receptor, leading to reduced efficacy of subsequent opioid neuraxial administration. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), specifically fluoxetine and paroxetine, significantly inhibit CYP2D6 and slow the conversion of hydrocodone to hydromorphone within the liver. While oral hydrocodone itself has an analgesic potency that is comparable to morphine when it is administered orally, its metabolite hydromorphone has roughly 4 times greater analgesic efficacy. Inhibition of the CYP2D6 enzyme may, therefore, result in less clinical analgesic effect than otherwise might be gained from the ingestion of hydrocodone. Codeine, hydrocodone, and oxycodone are all medications converted by the cytochrome P450 system (specifically CYP2D6) into metabolites with greater analgesic potency (morphine, hydromorphone, and oxymorphone respectively). It should be noted that codeine itself is a prodrug and has minimal to no intrinsic analgesic properties and only exerts its clinical effect through these conversions. Both hydrocodone and oxycodone have similar intrinsic analgesic properties to morphine, with hydrocodone tending to be a slightly weaker analgesic and oxycodone tending to be slightly stronger than morphine itself. The conversion of hydrocodone to hydromorphone increases its analgesic potency by a factor of 4, and the conversion of oxycodone to oxymorphone increases its analgesic potency by a factor of 2. Drug interactions involving the cytochrome P450 isoforms generally result from one of two processes: enzyme inhibition or enzyme induction. The CYP2D6 enzyme is responsible for the metabolism of many psychotherapeutic agents. Inactive forms of this enzyme can increase requirements for opioid prodrugs since conversion to the active forms is significantly reduced. For example, 7-10% of Caucasians express an inactive homozygous form of CYP2D6, which does not facilitate the O-methylation of codeine into morphine, producing a minimal clinical effect from the ingestion of this drug. Conversely, a small proportion of the population possesses a CYP2D6 phenotype that causes rapid metabolism of this same drug, resulting in potentially dangerous clinical levels of morphine following the ingestion of a routine dose of codeine. It is for this reason that codeine is has received a Food and Drug Administration (FDA) warning for its use in pediatric patients undergoing tonsillectomy. Hydrocodone is not significantly metabolized by CYP3A4 or CYP1A2.
Answer C: Tolerance is the state in which increased doses of the same substance are needed to achieve the desired effect. In this question, the acute rise in drug consumption following the initiation of a drug that has been shown to improve symptoms of their pain syndrome should alert the clinician to a possibly undesirable drug interaction. SSRIs inhibit CYP2D6 which reduces the activation of many opioids (e.g. codeine, hydrocodone, oxycodone) to more potent forms (eg, morphine, hydromorphone, oxymorphone). Nitrous oxide is a mixed competitive/noncompetitive antagonist at the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor (NMDA) receptor. Although nitrous oxide interacts at multiple receptor types (including, but not limited to, glycine, nicotinic acetylcholine, and serotonin receptors), it is via its NMDA antagonism that most of its anesthetic effects are thought to be mediated. The NMDA receptor is a class of glutamate-activated ion channels that conducts sodium, potassium, and calcium ions. It is involved in the long-term modulation of synaptic responses and is associated with synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory. Activation of the receptor increases the intracellular concentration of calcium that then functions as a second messenger via multiple pathways. Activation also results in sodium influx and potassium efflux. Some examples of drugs that act on the NMDA receptor: • Dextromethorphan is an over-the-counter cough suppressant with NMDA antagonist properties. It can be abused recreationally in large doses because it acts as a dissociative anesthetic. • Ketamine is a potent, selective NMDA inhibitor that binds to the phencyclidine site on the receptor. Antagonism results in (dissociative) anesthesia, analgesia, amnesia, bronchodilation, and maintenance of protective airway reflexes. Side effects include hallucinations or other psychomimetic reactions (improved or prevented with benzodiazepines or propofol), salivation (improved or prevented with antisialagogues such as glycopyrrolate), and increases in intraocular pressure, intracranial pressure, and cerebral metabolic rate. • Magnesium has NMDA antagonist activity. Physiologically, it blocks the NMDA ion channel at resting membrane potential. Depolarization must occur to remove the magnesium and allow calcium, sodium, and potassium to cross the ion channel. • Phencyclidine, also known as angel dust, is a dissociative drug that acts via NMDA antagonism with no known medical use. It is abused as a recreational drug, and patients may present after intoxication. These patients may be agitated, be violent, and have nystagmus. Despite agitation and possible violence, they likely have reduced minimum alveolar concentration requirements. • Nonhalogenated inhalational anesthetics (eg, nitrous oxide and xenon) are thought to act primarily through NMDA antagonism. Halogenated volatile anesthetics (eg, sevoflurane, isoflurane, and desflurane) result in NMDA antagonism at very high doses, but this is not thought to be of significant clinical importance. Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that does not have any effects at the NMDA receptor. Opioids that do exhibit some NMDA antagonism include propoxyphene (no longer available in the United States), methadone, and tramadol.
Answer C: Propofol is a γ-aminobutyric acid agonist, not an NMDA antagonist. Multiple medications commonly used perioperatively function as N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonists. Examples include but are not limited to ketamine, magnesium sulfate, nitrous oxide, and certain opioids including methadone and tramadol.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. An object lodged in the right mainstem bronchus will prevent ventilation to a lung that is perfused, creating an intrapulmonary shunt. In the presence of a right-to-left shunt, inhalational induction will be slower. In other words, the rate of rise for the alveolar concentration to inspired concentration (FA/FI) of desflurane will decrease. A right to left shunt, both intrapulmonary and intracardiac, slow inhalational induction. This is due to the dilution of the anesthetic agent when venous blood that has bypassed the lungs mixes with arterial blood. This delay is more obvious with the less soluble agents, such as desflurane and nitrous oxide. Comparing the two, nitrous oxide will be more affected than desflurane due to the concentration effect. The concentration effect explains why the rate of rise of FA/FI is faster for nitrous oxide even though the blood-gas coefficient is lower for desflurane. Soluble agents such as isoflurane may see minimal or no delay in induction. Intravenous induction is mainly affected by right to left intracardiac shunts (eg, Eisenmenger syndrome) and results in faster induction since the lungs are bypassed. More common intracardiac shunts (eg, ventricular septal defect with left to right shunting) will have minimal effect on either IV or inhalational induction. An intrapulmonary shunt will not affect the speed of intravenous induction. The chart below shows a summary of the various shunts and how anesthetic agents are affected. A right to left shunt, both intrapulmonary and intracardiac, slow inhalation induction.
Answer B: An intrapulmonary shunt will not affect the speed of intravenous induction. Right to left shunt slows the speed of inhalational induction. This is more obvious in less soluble agents. In the presence of an intrapulmonary shunt, the speed of induction will affect (most to least): Nitrous Oxide > Desflurane > Sevoflurane > Isoflurane > Halothane. Endobronchial intubation is another situation that produces a right to left intrapulmonary shunt. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Inhalant Anes Uptake: R To L Shunt (B)" Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 8th Edition.

With an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 1.3, hydromorphone has the lowest lipophilicity of any of the listed opioids. All of the other opioids listed are considered lipophilic, while hydromorphone and morphine are considered hydrophilic. The physiological effects of intrathecal use of opioids depend on many factors, such as lipid solubility. Fentanyl and sufentanil, both highly lipid soluble, have a rapid onset and short duration compared to less lipid-soluble opioids such as morphine. Increased lipid solubility leads to increased uptake into neurons, blood vessels, and fatty tissue. The spread of opioids within the cerebrospinal fluid is more extensive with the less lipid-soluble (ie, hydrophilic) opioids, such as morphine, compared to the more lipid-soluble opioids. The spread is more extensive with the hydrophilic opioids due to the slower uptake into blood vessels and elimination from the cerebrospinal fluid and epidural space. Because hydrophilic opioids spread more extensively and persist longer within the cerebrospinal fluid or epidural space, they have a higher risk of respiratory depression after intrathecal injection hours after use. Approximate values of the octanol/H2O partition coefficient of various opioids Alfentanil has an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 145, making it more lipophilic.
Answer B: Fentanyl has an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 813, making it one of the most lipophilic.
Answer D: Sufentanil has an octanol/H2O partition coefficient of 1778, making it the most lipophilic of the opioids listed. When opioids are used for neuraxial anesthesia, hydrophilic opioids spread more extensively and persist longer within the cerebrospinal fluid or epidural space. The order of the least to the most lipophilic opioids based on the octanol/H2O partition coefficient is hydromorphone (1.3) > morphine (1.4) > alfentanil (145) > fentanyl (813) > and sufentanil (1778). Meperidine has its effect upon the kappa (κ) opioid receptor. Meperidine use has become less common due to its wide side effect profile and long half-life of its active metabolites (14-21 hours). This becomes particularly important in renal failure patients where metabolites can accumulate, notably normeperidine, which is proconvulsant. Despite these limitations, meperidine is still used today primarily to treat shivering from multiple causes including general anesthesia, epidural anesthesia, fever, transfusion reactions, and following the administration of amphotericin B. Studies show that this anti-shivering effect occurs without affecting the mu (µ) opioid receptor, but rather is a multimodal effect that focuses upon the κ receptor. Meperidine does have analgesic properties (potency 1/10 that of morphine) mediated by both mu and κ receptors. The major subtypes of opioid receptors include µ, κ, and delta (δ). The µ receptor is responsible for the most commonly recognized properties of opioids and has three subclasses. The µ1 receptor produces the analgesic and physical dependence properties of most opioids while stimulation of the µ2 receptor results in respiratory depression, miosis, euphoria, decreased gastrointestinal motility, and physical dependence. The actions of µ3 receptors are unknown but may mediate some anti-inflammatory activity. The κ receptor mediates analgesia but also dysphoria, sedation, miosis, and inhibits antidiuretic hormone release. The δ receptor is responsible for analgesia, physical dependence, and perhaps antidepressant effects. Partial agonists and mixed agonist-antagonist agents, such as nalbuphine, have differential effects at each receptor site. Nalbuphine works as a kappaagonist/mu-antagonist analgesic. Methadone exerts significant effects on the mu opioid receptor. Methadone also acts on the NMDA receptor as an antagonist. NMDA receptor antagonism explains methadone's effect for neuropathic pain and in opioid tolerance. Methadone does prolong the QT interval and should be monitored.
Answer C: Morphine has its main effect on the mu opioid receptor. Morphine is metabolized by the liver to morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G) and morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G). More morphine is metabolized to M3G than M6G. However M6G is an active metabolite of morphine.
Answer D: Remifentanil has its main effect upon the mu opioid receptor. Remifentanil is unique with a very short half-life which is not affected by the infusion time. Remifentanil is metabolized by nonspecific plasma and tissue esterases. Meperidine’s beneficial effects are multimodal and center around the kappa opioid receptor. Meperidine has structural similarities to atropine. Which is why meperidine is the only opioid associated with increases in heart rate following administration. Meperidine also has some weak local anesthetic effects. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Tachycardia is the most common side effect associated with albuterol. Albuterol is the most common beta-agonist that is used perioperatively. Albuterol is selective for the beta-2 receptors and causes relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle. Albuterol can be used to treat bronchospasm, asthma, or wheezing, or it can be used prophylactically to reduce postoperative respiratory complications in high-risk patients (eg, recent respiratory infection, smoking, etc). Albuterol can be administered to the patient before the induction of anesthesia, intraoperatively through the endotracheal tube, or after extubation. The most common side effect of albuterol is tachycardia from the beta effect on the heart. Premature ventricular contractions are also commonly seen with albuterol use. Diastolic hypotension can be seen after large doses of albuterol. Central nervous system beta receptor stimulation from albuterol can lead to agitation and tremors. Beta-agonists also cause a decrease in potassium, which can result in hypokalemia because beta-adrenergic agonists cause potassium to shift intracellularly. Burst suppression pattern on electroencephalography (EEG) tracing is seen because the depth of anesthesia is increased after volatile or intravenous anesthetic use. This burst suppression pattern is initially observed at bispectral index scale values between the range of 20 and 40. Albuterol has not been shown to alter EEG results.
Answer B: Albuterol and beta-adrenergic agonists are associated with hypokalemia, not hyperkalemia, due to the intracellular shift of potassium.
Answer C: Diastolic hypotension, not hypertension, can be seen after albuterol use. Tachycardia is the most commonly observed side effect of inhaled albuterol. Beta-adrenergic drugs, such as albuterol, can also cause hypokalemia due to the intracellular shift of potassium. Mivacurium is metabolized by butyrylcholinesterase (BCHE) and therefore its effect is prolonged in patients with BCHE deficiency. Butyrylcholinesterase (alternately pseudocholinesterase or plasma cholinesterase) is the enzyme responsible for degradation of succinylcholine and mivacurium. Administration of either of these medications to patients with BCHE deficiency therefore results in prolonged neuromuscular blockade and the potential for prolonged apnea. Butyrylcholinesterase deficiency is an inherited trait that may be homozygous or heterozygous. The incidence of the heterozygous atypical type is approximately 1:500. Individuals with this genotype may experience an increase in duration of effect of succinylcholine by 50-100% (typically 20-30 minutes). The incidence of homozygous atypical is 1:3000, and this causes an increase in duration of effect by 4-8 hours. Approximately 20 genetic variants of the BCHE gene exist with the A- and K-variants being the most common. The A and K variants are the most common.
Answer B: Duration of action is prolonged. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency prolongs the duration of action of succinylcholine and mivacurium, which can lead to prolonged neuromuscular blockade and apnea. Echothiophate is an anticholinesterase used to treat refractory glaucoma by causing miosis. Since it inhibits BCHE, systemic absorption can cause up to a 95% decrease in BCHE function, thereby potentiating the effects of succinylcholine. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Butyrylcholinesterase Deficiency" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 127, 511.

After administration of mannitol, an increase in plasma volume will occur which will result in an increase in blood pressure and cardiac output. This may lead to an increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, especially in patients with heart failure. This increase may lead to pulmonary edema in certain patients. The term diuretic typically is applied to a medication that can decrease the extracellular fluid volume by increasing urinary water or solute excretion. Mannitol produces diuresis by increasing osmotic pressure in the proximal tubule and loop of Henle, causing a decrease in passive reabsorption of water and thus an increase in renal blood flow. Following the administration of mannitol, the excretion of sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, and chloride is increased. In the interstitial space, the increased osmotic pressure draws water from the cells to increase extracellular fluid which will further increase total plasma flow. There is a decrease in hematocrit and blood viscosity secondary to the hemodilution that occurs from solute extraction. Following intravenous administration of mannitol, several physiologic responses occur. Plasma volume will increase which leads to an increase in cardiac output and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. An increase in blood pressure may also be seen depending on the systemic vascular resistance. Following the diuresis, a decrease in plasma volume and overall total body water may cause the patient to become hypovolemic with potential decreases in cardiac output and blood pressure. Acute overzealous administration can result in a dilutional metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia. Accumulation of mannitol can produce hyperkalemia and an increase in plasma osmolality. Mannitol is administered via the intravenous route – it is not readily absorbed from the intestine thus an oral form is not available. After an injection less than 10% is reabsorbed by the renal tubule and, in a patient with a normal GFR, the half-life of mannitol is approximately 2.2 hours. However this can be prolonged to over 30 hours in patients with abnormal GFR. Mannitol is used for a variety of clinical reasons; the most common indication is neurologic and neurosurgical conditions where elevated intracranial pressure is seen. When administered as a bolus, in the presence of an intact blood brain barrier, mannitol decreases cerebral edema and thus intracranial pressure (ICP). A rapid bolus can transiently increase ICP. Prolonged infusions of mannitol have been shown to reverse the osmotic gradient and increase ICP. Mannitol has been proven to be more effective at reducing water brain content compared to loop diuretics or hypertonic saline. Blood pressure is typically increased following acute administration of mannitol.
Answer B: Cardiac output is increased following mannitol administration.
Answer C: A transient elevation in ICP can be seen with a rapid bolus. This is not likely to be seen with an appropriate bolus dose (0.25-1 g/kg) given over at least 10-15 minutes. After administration of mannitol, an increase in plasma volume will occur which will result in an increase in blood pressure and cardiac output. This may lead to an increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, especially in patients with heart failure.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Nalbuphine, a mixed opioid agonist-antagonist, lowers the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of volatile anesthetics by less than 10%, even at high doses (C). Unlike volatile anesthetics and certain IV anesthetics such as propofol, opioids have ceiling effects that prevent them from being used safely as sole anesthetic agents. This is evidenced by reports of recall and awareness in cases using high-dose fentanyl and even combinations of opioids and nitrous oxide. Administration of opioids with volatile anesthetics can significantly decrease the MAC. Still, there is a sub-MAC ceiling effect at which there is no further reduction in MAC despite increases in dose. This is further evidenced by monitoring the effects of opioid administration using EEG. Progressive changes are initially seen on EEG with increasing doses of opioids, but eventually, a ceiling effect occurs, and no further EEG changes are observed. By contrast, increasing concentrations of volatile anesthetics result in progressive EEG changes, ultimately inducing burst suppression and then an isoelectric EEG. Fentanyl and remifentanil (at equipotent doses) are very effective at lowering MAC, with up to an approximately 80% reduction observed at higher (but still clinically relevant) doses. Morphine can lower volatile anesthetic MAC by approximately 20-60%, depending on the dose. Partial opioid agonists and mixed agonist-antagonist agents, such as nalbuphine and butorphanol, do not have nearly as significant an effect on lowering MAC as pure opioid agonists. For example, despite having an analgesic potency nearly equivalent to morphine, nalbuphine lowers MAC by no more than 10%, even at high doses. Butorphanol lowers MAC only slightly more than 10%. Morphine can lower volatile anesthetic MAC by approximately 20-60%, depending on the dose.
Answer C: Fentanyl and remifentanil (at equipotent doses) are very effective at lowering MAC, with up to an approximately 80% reduction observed at higher (but still clinically relevant) doses. Most opioids significantly lower volatile anesthetic MAC requirements when administered concurrently. However, partial opioid agonists and mixed agonist-antagonists have a greatly reduced, and nearly clinically insignificant, effect on MAC.  Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 777-780. Murphy MR, Hug CC Jr. The enflurane sparing effect of morphine, butorphanol, and nalbuphine. Anesthesiology. 1982; 57(6): 489-492. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Opioids: MAC effect"

The ED95 of a neuromuscular blocking drug is the effective dose required to achieve 95% block of a single twitch in 50% of individuals. In general pharmacology, ED95 refers to the effective dose needed to get the desired effect for 95% of the population. Unfortunately, this term has a different meaning specifically for neuromuscular blocking agents. For these agents, ED95 refers to the median dose required to achieve a 95% reduction in the maximal twitch response from baseline, in 50% of the population. A more appropriate term would be ED5095, however the terminology ED95 has stuck for this context. The ED95 for rocuronium is 0.3 mg/kg, which means that half of patients will achieve at least a 95% blockade of a single twitch if they receive this weight-based dose. For effective relaxation during intubation, one to two times the ED95 is typically needed. This is why most practitioners use, for example, at least 0.6 mg/kg of rocuronium for intubation. The rapid sequence intubation dose of rocuronium is therefore four times ED95 (1.2 mg/kg). Dose response curves are used to determine potency of neuromuscular blocking agents. The relationship is plotted between twitch depression and weight-based dose. The ED95 is the median dose corresponding to a 95% single twitch depression. ED95 doses are used to compare potency between drugs. For example, the ED95 for vecuronium is 0.05 mg/kg and the intubating dose is 0.1 mg/kg. This indicates that vecuronium has a potency 6 times that of rocuronium. Therefore, six times the dose of rocuronium should be administered to achieve the same effect as vecuronium (i.e. 6 x 0.05 mg/kg = 0.3 mg/kg). Answers A & B: This is an incorrect description of the meaning of an ED95 dose.  ED95 is the effective dose of a neuromuscular blocking drug required to achieve 95% block of a single twitch in 50% of individuals who receive this drug and dose. For effective relaxation during intubation, one to two times the ED95 is typically administered. Potency of neuromuscular blockers is best described by their ED95.
