The rate of rise of the alveolar concentration (FA)/ inspired concentration (FI) ratio is more rapid for nitrous oxide compared to desflurane because of the concentration effect, despite nitrous oxide having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient (0.47) than desflurane (0.45). In general, the blood/gas solubility, measured as the blood/gas partition coefficient, is what determines the speed of onset and rate of rise of FA/FI with the lower the blood/gas partition coefficient, the faster the onset and rate of rise of FA/FI. However, nitrous oxide has the fastest rate of rise of any of the inhalational anesthetics despite having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient than desflurane. The reason that nitrous oxide has a faster onset of action than desflurane is due to the concentration effect. At equiamnestic inspired concentrations, the percentage of inspired nitrous oxide is far higher than that of desflurane. As the relatively large concentration (and therefore volume) of nitrous oxide is absorbed at the level of the alveoli, the remaining gas occupies a smaller volume. Therefore, mixed inspired gas from the conducting airways will replace this volume. This gas has the same high concentration of nitrous oxide, so this effect is perpetuated. In this way, ventilation is augmented above the minute ventilation. This makes a greater quantity of agents available to the lung for absorption for a given time period. This image illustrates the concentration-effect during a single inhalation. Much more nitrous oxide is absorbed than what would be expected as the concentration-effect draws more nitrous oxide into the alveoli from the conducting airways as large volumes of nitrous oxide already in the alveoli are absorbed. Illustration © TrueLearn, LLC Nitrous oxide exists as a gas at standard temperature and pressure, so vapor pressure is not relevant in this comparison.
Answer C: Nitrous oxide has a higher (0.47) blood/gas partition coefficient than desflurane (0.45).
Answer D: The second gas effect describes why the FA/FI ratio of a second anesthetic equilibrates more rapidly when nitrous oxide is used. This effect is not relevant when the rate of uptake of desflurane is compared to the rate of rise of nitrous oxide. The absorption of nitrous oxide is augmented by the concentration effect, making the rate of absorption faster than that of desflurane despite having a higher blood/gas partition coefficient. Of all the answer choices, intravenous fentanyl would cause the largest decrease in MAC values. It has been shown that fentanyl will decrease MAC by 50% when 3 mcg/kg is used and up to 80% when 10 mcg/kg is used. Alfentanil, sufentanil, and remifentanil also possess the capability to decrease MAC. Anesthesia often consists of multiple agents that act synergistically to improve surgical conditions. Opioids are often added to volatile anesthetics to smooth the course and decrease the amount of volatile required. Often the combination of an opioid and volatile anesthetic is better tolerated hemodynamically than a volatile used alone. Animal data have shown that a significant reduction in MAC occurs with administration of opioids. The synthetic opioids (fentanyl, remifentanil, alfentanil, and sufentanil) result in a more significant decrease when compared with morphine and hydromorphone. Opioid partial agonists (nalbuphine and butorphanol) produce an even smaller reduction in MAC. Two studies indicate that “MAC awake” is much less affected by opioids than standard MAC. Factors that increase MAC: drugs (amphetamines, cocaine, ephedrine, chronic ethanol use), electrolytes (hypernatremia), and hyperthermia. Factors that decrease MAC: drugs (propofol, etomidate, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, ketamine, alpha-2-agonists, acute ethanol intoxication, local anesthetics, opioids, chronic amphetamine use, lithium, verapamil), elderly age, electrolytes (hyponatremia), anemia, hypercarbia, hypothermia, hypoxemia, and pregnancy (controversial). Intravenous lidocaine does decrease MAC in humans, however intravenous fentanyl would cause a larger decrease. In animal studies 1.5 mg/kg of lidocaine has been shown to decrease MAC by 10% to 30%.
Answer C: Gabapentin has not been shown to alter MAC values. Intravenous opioids result in a decreased minimum alveolar concentration (MAC). The synthetic opioids cause a higher reduction in MAC compared to morphine. Gabapentin has not been shown to alter MAC values.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Factors Affect Anes Depth: Opioids" Clinical Anesthesia. 7th edition. Drug Interactions. Page 560. Basics of Anesthesia. 6th edition. Inhaled anesthetics. Pages 81-82.

Oral famotidine has an onset time of action of ~1 hr, while intravenous famotidine has an onset time of ~30 minutes. Parietal cells in the stomach have histamine-2 (H2) receptors and respond to histamine by secreting acid. Histamine-2 receptor antagonists (H2 blockers), such as cimetidine and famotidine, can be used to reduce gastric acid secretion by blocking the effect of histamine on these receptors. Histamine-2 receptor blockers are occasionally used in the perioperative period to prevent sequelae from aspiration in high-risk patients. Recommendations for elective Cesarean section include pharmacologic prophylaxis for aspiration with a nonparticulate antacid, H2 blocker, metoclopramide, and/or a proton pump inhibitor in all patients because of the elevated risk of aspiration associated with pregnancy. The onset of action of the clinically used H2 blockers (primarily famotidine and cimetidine) are very similar, and they are typically given (IV or oral) 30 to 90 min before surgery. The duration of action of famotidine is longer (~10-12 hr) than that of cimetidine (~4-5 hr), independent of the route of administration. Cimetidine is associated with more adverse effects compared with famotidine, including the inhibition of the hepatic mixedfunction oxidase system prolonging the half-lives of drugs metabolized by this system, such as lidocaine, propranolol, and diazepam. Other side effects of chronic cimetidine use include gynecomastia and galactorrhea. Antacids have a near-immediate onset, with the peak effect seen within 15 to 30 min of oral administration. Antacids work by neutralizing acid in the stomach. Sodium citrate is the most common nonparticulate antacid used in Cesarean deliveries.
Answer B: The onset of IV famotidine is ~30 min. The onset is ~60 min via the oral route.
Answer D: The onset of proton pump inhibitors (PPI) is 1 to 3 hr when administered orally, but peak response may take up to 5 days. Proton pump inhibitors act by binding to hydrogen-potassium ATPases in the stomach and cause a permanent inhibition. Synthesis of new pumps takes about 24 hr, which explains the duration of action of PPIs. The onset of action of the clinically used histamine-2 receptor blockers (primarily famotidine and cimetidine) are ~30 min (IV) and ~60 min (oral). The duration of action of famotidine is longer (~10-12 hr) than that of cimetidine (~4-5 hr), independent of the route of administration. In 2011, the American Society of Anesthesiologists task force found insufficient evidence to support the effect of administering histamine-2 receptor blockers (or other drugs such as proton pump inhibitors, antacids, antiemetics, and gastrokinetic agents) in the perioperative period on the incidence of pulmonary aspiration, emesis, or reflex; thus, they do not recommend their use in patients who do not have an increased risk of aspiration. At 20ºC and 1 atm, the vapor pressures of the four most commonly used inhaled anesthetics from lowest to highest are sevoflurane (157 mmHg), isoflurane (238 mmHg), desflurane (669 mmHg), and nitrous oxide (38,770 mmHg). At a temperature of 20°C and 1 atm, all inhalational anesthetics exist in the liquid form except for nitrous oxide, which has a boiling point of −88°C. Although most of the inhalational anesthetics may be liquid in form, they equilibrate between the liquid and gas phases in a closed container. The molecules in the gaseous state exert a pressure, known as vapor pressure, on the closed container because of the kinetic energy of the molecules colliding with the container. Vapor pressure is proportional to temperature. As the temperature rises, the kinetic energy of the liquid increases, which raises the number of molecules in the gaseous state and increases the vapor pressure. After the temperature is raised sufficiently such that the vapor pressure exceeds the atmospheric pressure in an open container, it will have reached its boiling point. Boiling points and vapor pressures at 20ºC of inhalational anesthetics Answers A & B: Sevoflurane < isoflurane < desflurane < nitrous oxide is the order from the lowest to the highest vapor pressures. Nitrous oxide < desflurane < isoflurane < sevoflurane is the order from the highest to the lowest vapor pressures. At 20ºC and 1 atm, the vapor pressures of the four most commonly used inhaled anesthetics from lowest to highest are sevoflurane (157 mmHg), isoflurane (238 mmHg), desflurane (669 mmHg), and nitrous oxide (38,770 mmHg). Milrinone causes smooth muscle vasodilation by increasing intracellular cAMP levels. Normal myocardial pressure-volume loop. LVESV = left-ventricular end-systolic volume, LVEDV = left-ventricular end-diastolic volume, LVESP = left-ventricular end-systolic pressure, LVEDP = left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure, CPP = coronary perfusion pressure, AoDP = aortic diastolic pressure, AoSP = aortic systolic pressure, SV = stroke volume. The diastolic filling phase occurs as the LV fills from the LVESV towards the LVEDV. Isovolumetric contraction within the LV occurs as the pressure increases from LVEDP to the AoDP. The ejection period occurs once the aortic valve opens. The pressure within the LV then increases until it becomes equal to the AoSP. The heart no longer ejects at this point, there is a drop in pressure, and isovolumetric relaxation occurs. The drop in pressure is proportional to the pressure that was generated by the myocardium. Hence, the steeper the slope of pressure reduction, the more contractility generated by the myocardium. Positive lusitropy and increased contractility with inodilator therapy. The solid black lines represent the normal myocardial P-V loop. The positive lusitropic effect is illustrated as a reduction in the slope and a rightward shift (red arrow) of the diastolic filling phase. This shift results in a reduction in the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP’) and left ventricular end-systolic pressure (LVESP’) and an increase in both the coronary perfusion (CPP’) and stroke volume (SV’). Stroke volume increases as a result of isovolumetric contraction occurring at a larger left ventricular end-diastolic volume (LVEDV’). The aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP’) may remain the same or be mildly reduced. Aortic systolic pressure (AoSP’) will be appreciably reduced, owing to the vasodilatory effect. The contractility is displayed as the slope of the systolic pressure-volume relationship. It is increased (Contractility’) due to the inotropic effect. Left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV’) will be reduced, further increasing the resultant SV’. Answers A & C: Milrinone is a selective phosphodiesterase (PDE) III inhibitor that is often used in the treatment of severe congestive heart failure. Inhibiting PDE III impairs cAMP breakdown, therefore allowing increased intracellular levels of cAMP. This leads to an increased influx of intracellular calcium stores, thereby enhancing cardiac ionotropy. Additionally, increased cAMP levels lead to smooth muscle vasodilation and decreased peripheral vascular resistance. Milrinone is also a potent pulmonary vasodilator leading to its use in the treatment of pulmonary hypertension. Phosphodiesterase III inhibitors promote diastolic relaxation (positive lusitropy), ventricular filling, and reduction in the myocardial wall tension. Milrinone acts to increase cardiac output via enhanced myocardial contractility and peripheral vasodilation (see images above). Milrinone is, however, associated with the potential for cardiac arrhythmias. Milrinone, a PDE III inhibitor, increases cardiac inotropy and causes peripheral and pulmonary vasodilation via increased intracellular cAMP levels and calcium stores. Milrinone is also referred to as an inodilator for these reasons. The effects of an inodilator may be illustrated on the myocardial P-V loop. These include a reduction in the slope of the diastolic filling phase, LVEDP, AoDP (mild), AoSP, LVESV, and the LVESP. There is also an increase in lusitropy (ventricular relaxation), SV, CPP, and myocardial contractility.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Dexamethasone is associated with perineal itching and pain when given as a bolus to an awake patient. This side-effect is more common in females, the young, and with bolus administration. The cause of perineal itch is unknown though it may be related to the phosphate esters in the chemical structure. These symptoms are also seen in other steroids such as hydrocortisone. For PONV prophylaxis during general anesthesia, these symptoms can be avoided (i.e. masked) by administering dexamethasone after induction of anesthesia. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha2 agonist medication used for sedation and analgesia. Dexmedetomidine is typically given with a bolus dose followed by an infusion. Side-effects include hypotension and bradycardia. Additionally, bolus administration of dexmedetomidine is associated with paradoxical hypertension.
Answer C: Fentanyl is a commonly used opioid that has been used to decrease the incidence of steroid induced perineal pruritus. Fentanyl has been associated with chest wall rigidity when high doses are used in bolus form.
Answer D: Phenytoin is an antiseizure medication that blocks voltage gated sodium channels. Intravenous phenytoin should not be given as a rapid push because it can cause severe hemodynamic effects as well as arrhythmias. Arrhythmias caused by phenytoin are a result of sodium channel blockade and phenytoin can be considered a 1b-antiarrhythmic medication. Phenytoin is associated with intrauterine growth restriction and fetal abnormalities.
Answer E: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that is very effective against gram positive organisms. Vancomycin is a large molecule that is not orally bioavailable. Additionally, administration should not exceed 10mg/min because of the risk of vancomycin infusion syndrome (i.e. "red man syndrome"). Vancomycin infusion syndrome is characterized by hypotension, tachycardia, generalized pruritus, and red rash. Histamine release is non-immune mediated and related to the fast administration of a larger molecule drug. Bolus administration of intravenous steroids, particularly dexamethasone, to an awake patient can cause intense perineal itching. Risk factors include female gender and young age. Fospropofol is also associated with genital burning and itching. Fospropofol is a prodrug of propofol in phosphate ester form, which is where the "fos" in the name comes from. Kuczkowski, K.M. Studies have shown that patients who report penicillin allergy and do not have a history of severe reactions (whether IgEmediated or non-IgE-mediated) can safely receive cephalosporin antibiotics. Cefazolin should be given to this patient even after having a rash with a previous penicillin reaction. A study showed that the risk of similar allergic reaction with prior reaction to penicillin after administration of both cephalosporins and sulfonamide antibiotics argues against the idea of "cross-reactivity" with beta-lactam antibiotics. This same study also showed that the risk of anaphylaxis is less than 0.001% and that the absolute risk of allergic-type reactions with a history of penicillin reaction is exceedingly rare. IgE-mediated symptoms include urticaria, angioedema, dyspnea, dysphagia, bronchospasm, and anaphylaxis. Severe non-IgE-mediated reactions include Stevens-Johnson syndrome or toxic epidermal necrolysis (mucosal lesions, bullous or exfoliative skin lesions, evidence of other organ involvement such as renal failure or hepatic failure), DRESS (Drug Rash with Eosinophilia and Systemic Symptoms) syndrome, interstitial nephritis, and hemolytic anemia. Higher Risk If the patient’s penicillin reaction was any of the following, it is recommended to not give a cephalosporin: - less than 10 years ago - they had IgE-mediated symptoms after receiving penicillin - they had a severe non-IgE-mediated reaction Recommend skin testing to the patient before future surgical procedures. If unsure about the reaction and timing, recommend skin testing prior to the administration of penicillins. Skin testing should not be recommended for patients who had a severe exfoliative past reaction to penicillin, such as toxic epidermal necrolysis. Low Risk If a patient’s penicillin reaction is more than 10 years ago AND they had no IgE-mediated symptoms AND they had no severe non-IgE-mediated reactions, then they are low risk (< 1%) for having a reaction if they receive cephalosporins. The risk of anaphylaxis is very small in these patients. Gentamicin is most effective against Gram-negative organisms, not Gram-positive skin flora.
Answer C: Cefazolin should still be given because the risk of anaphylaxis or serious allergic-type reaction is low in this patient. Also, vancomycin is associated with reactions (e.g. Red Man syndrome) and antibiotic-related infections. Studies have shown that patients who report penicillin allergy and do not have a history of severe reactions (whether IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated) can safely receive cephalosporin antibiotics. Factors that can result in variable activated clotting time include: hemodilution, hypothermia, platelet counts below 30-50 k/mL, and concomitant administration of other medications which affect platelets. Anticoagulants act on a variety of different processes in the human body and are integral to modern medicine and surgery. In the operating room, anticoagulants are most often used in the cardiothoracic rooms although they are routinely administered in smaller doses for deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis in the perioperative period. Many institutions now administer anticoagulants for DVT prophylaxis prior to induction of anesthesia. For this discussion we will focus on monitoring anticoagulants in the cardiothoracic room, specifically heparin monitoring. Proper anticoagulation is vital to cardiac surgery because the patient is often placed on the cardiopulmonary bypass circuit; if proper anticoagulation is not present, catastrophic clotting can occur. Adequate monitoring of heparin activity has been associated with less bleeding and more accurate titration. Heparin's effect was first measured using whole-blood clotting time which involved putting blood into a glass tube and manually tilting it until blood fluidity is no longer detected – this required undivided attention of the tester and could take up to 30 minutes. The activated clotting time (ACT) was developed in the 1960s and is still the most common test used to detect heparin's effect in the operating theater. Whole blood is added to a test tube that contains an activator, diatomaceous earth (celite) or kaolin, which stimulates the intrinsic coagulation pathway. Most ACT machines are automated and they all work slightly differently but the two most common laboratory devices use cartridges or cylinders that are heated to 37 degrees. When clot is formed, it will slow the rate of descent of a plunger that is detected and reads a number – the longer the clot takes to form, the higher the number. There are some differences in results that are measured between the different systems, and in particular at lower heparin concentrations and in pediatric patients who have greater heparin consumption rates. ACT use has been questioned because there is sometimes extreme variability and there is not a direct correlation with plasma heparin levels. Factors that can result in variable ACT include: hemodilution, hypothermia, platelet counts below 30-50 k/mL, concomitant administration of other medications which affect platelets (e.g. prostacyclin, aspirin, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors), general anesthesia, and surgery which alters coagulation in general but also affects the ACT. Point of Care (POC) ACT systems use disposable cards that contain particles that move in response to a magnetic field within the device. When clot forms, the movement is decreased and the end of the test is heralded. These are called “heparin management test” (HMT). Quick review on other tests of anticoagulation effects: The standard tests are PT and the PTT. PTT tests the integrity of the intrinsic and final coagulation pathways and is more sensitive to lower levels of heparin than the ACT. PTT uses a phospholipid substance to stimulate the interaction of platelet membrane in activating factor XII. PTT will be prolonged when deficiencies of factors XII, XI, IX, or VIII are present. The PT measures the extrinsic and common coagulation pathways. PT will be prolonged when a deficiency of factor VII is present. Thromboelastography (TEG) allows the clinician to obtain information on the integrity of the coagulation cascade, platelet function, platelet-fibrin interactions, and fibrinolysis. It attempts to quantitate the viscoelastic properties of the clot formation along with its break down. If whole blood is used, the specimen must be run quickly, usually within 3-4 minutes. Otherwise, a citrate anticoagulant can be added and activated with kaolin allowing longer transit times. The blood is placed in a tube that has a suspended pin inside. This pin is attached to a torsion wire that is coupled to an amplifier and recorder. The curve oscillates and when blood is in the liquid form the pin becomes coupled to the motion of the cuvette and a signal is recorded. The tracing is recognizable and has certain key characteristics - reaction time (R value), coagulation time (K value), alpha angle, maximal amplitude (MA), and amplitude 60 minutes after maximal amplitude (A60). The R time represents the time for initial fibrin formation. It is the period between when the test is started and when initial fibrin formation occurs. R time measures the level of clotting factors (the intrinsic coagulation pathway, extrinsic coagulation pathway and final common pathway). Although age can alter heparin metabolism, pediatric patients are more likely to have variable ACTs because of the increased consumption of heparin, not elderly patients.
Answer C: The ACT is more likely to be variable with low plasma levels of heparin.
Answer D: Usually, variability with ACT is seen in extreme thrombocytopenia below 30-50 k/mL. Factors that can result in variable ACT include: hemodilution, hypothermia, platelet counts below 30-50 k/mL, and concomitant administration of other medications which affect platelets (e.g. prostacyclin, aspirin, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors). Remifentanil is metabolized by nonspecific tissue and blood esterases (also known as red cell esterase), and thus, of all of the drugs listed above, only remifentanil would not be affected (C). Esmolol would also be unaffected. Pseudocholinesterase (PChE), also known as plasma cholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase (BChE), is a glycoprotein enzyme produced by the liver, circulating in the plasma. It specifically hydrolyzes exogenous choline esters; however, it has no known physiologic function. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency is typically an inherited enzyme abnormality that results in abnormally slow metabolic degradation of exogenous choline ester drugs such as succinylcholine, mivacurium, ester local anesthetics, cocaine, and heroin. A variety of pathologic conditions, physiologic alterations, and medications also can lower plasma pseudocholinesterase activity (e.g. severe liver disease, plasmapheresis, AChE inhibitors, pregnancy). Genetic analysis may demonstrate a number of allelic mutations in the pseudocholinesterase gene, including point mutations resulting in abnormal enzyme structure and function with frameshift or stop codon mutations resulting in absent enzyme synthesis. Partial deficiencies in inherited pseudocholinesterase enzyme activity may be clinically insignificant unless accompanied by a concomitant acquired cause of pseudocholinesterase deficiency; for example, pregnancy. Clinically significant effects generally are not observed until the plasma cholinesterase activity is reduced to less than 75% of normal. Dibucaine inhibits normal pseudocholinesterase to a far greater extent than the abnormal enzyme. This observation led to the development of the test for dibucaine number (DN). Under standardized test conditions, dibucaine inhibits the normal enzyme about 80 percent and the abnormal enzyme about 20 percent, thus the DN is the percent of PChE enzyme activity that is inhibited by dibucaine. Normal typical PChE enzyme activity yields a DN of 70-80; heterozygous atypical yields a DN of 50-60, homozygous atypical yields a DN of 20-30. Together, the DN and the PChE enzyme activity results can help to identify individuals at risk for prolonged paralysis following the administration of succinylcholine. Decreased PChE enzyme activity in conjunction with a DN less than 30 suggests high risk for prolonged paralysis. Normal to decreased PChE enzyme activity in conjunction with a DN 30-79 suggests variable risk. Although decreased PChE activity in conjunction with DN greater than or equal to 80 suggests variable risk, these results may be caused by exposure to organophosphates, the presence of liver disease, pregnancy, or circulating succinylcholine. Specimens should be collected 48 hours after the administration of succinylcholine. A dibucaine number is not an expensive test and some feel routine ordering is cost-effective. Choloroprocaine is an ester local anesthetic. All ester local anesthetics are metabolized via hydrolysis by pseudocholinesterase, thus 2-choloroprocaine’s metabolism and duration of action would be affected. Remember, ester local anesthetics have only one “i”, whereas amides have more than one (e.g. lidocaine, bupivacaine).
Answer B: Mivacurium, a benzylisoquinolinium short-acting nondepolarizing skeletal muscle relaxant, is also metabolized via hydrolysis by pseudocholinesterase. Metabolism can therefore be very slow in people with pseudocholinesterase deficiency, resulting in prolonged paralysis. Mivacurium is available worldwide, although its use in the United States has declined in favor of alternative agents that also offer a rapid onset of action but with a safer cardiovascular profile when administered in a rapid bolus dose. It is far more commonly used in Europe and the United Kingdom.
Answer D: Of the answers listed above, perhaps the most clinically important substrate is the depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent, succinylcholine. Pseudocholinesterase hydrolyzes succinylcholine to succinylmonocholine and then to succinic acid. In individuals with normal plasma levels of normally functioning pseudocholinesterase enzyme, hydrolysis and inactivation of approximately 90-95% of an intravenous dose of succinylcholine occurs before it reaches the neuromuscular junction. The remaining 5-10% of the succinylcholine dose acts as an acetylcholine receptor agonist at the neuromuscular junction, causing prolonged depolarization of the postsynaptic junction of the motor-end plate. In normal subjects, skeletal muscle function returns to normal approximately 5-10 minutes after a single bolus injection of succinylcholine as it passively diffuses away from the neuromuscular junction. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency can result in higher levels of intact succinylcholine molecules reaching receptors in the neuromuscular junction, causing the duration of paralytic effect to continue for as long as 8 hours or more. This condition is recognized most often when respiratory paralysis unexpectedly persists for a prolonged period of time following administration of standard doses of succinylcholine. This also highlights that neuromuscular monitoring should be used every time a muscle relaxant is administered, including with succinlycholine. The mainstay of treatment in these cases is ventilatory support until diffusion of succinylcholine from the myoneural junction permits return of neuromuscular function of skeletal muscle. Remifentanil and esmolol are metabolized by nonspecific blood and tissue esterases and would not be affected by a pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Succinylcholine, mivacurium, ester local anesthetics (2-chloroprocaine, tetracaine, procaine), cocaine, and heroin are metabolized via hydrolysis by pseudocholinesterase, also known as plasma cholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase. A deficiency or defect in this enzyme would result in decreased metabolism and prolonged effects of the substance. Patients who have been receiving echothiophate eye drops are at risk for significant prolongation of succinylcholine's effects for up to 2 weeks after therapy is discontinued. Multiple blood transfusions in the setting of liver dysfunction may lead to citrate accumulation and calcium chelation by citrate resulting in hypocalcemia. This may be observed as QT prolongation on electrocardiogram (ECG) due to ST segment prolongation. Citrate is a preservative used in stored blood products and is metabolized in the liver. Citrate is of little consequence in patients with normal hepatic function but can cause citrate toxicity when high volumes of blood products are used in patients with liver dysfunction. Alterations are observed on ECG due to variations in the depolarization and repolarization processes within the myocardium. The concentrations of electrolytes, both inside and outside the cells, play a vital role in influencing the ECG patterns. These electrolyte imbalances can have noticeable effects on the heart's electrical activity as recorded by an ECG (table). Hypocalcemia can lead to a diverse range of clinical manifestations affecting various systems in the body. These include neuromuscular symptoms such as peripheral numbness, tingling, weakness, fatigue, muscle spasms, and seizures. Respiratory manifestations may involve laryngeal or bronchial spasms, potentially leading to respiratory failure. Psychiatric symptoms such as depression, anxiety, and psychosis can arise, alongside smooth muscle effects such as abdominal cramps and increased urinary frequency. Hypocalcemia classically causes prolongation of the QT interval by slowing ventricular repolarization. In severe cases, this can result in heart block and predispose to torsades de pointes. This patient's electrocardiogram and symptoms provide evidence of digoxin toxicity. Electrolyte abnormalities, including hypercalcemia, hypokalemia, and hypomagnesemia, can promote conditions that make digoxin toxicity more likely. The only medication listed as an answer choice in this question that may cause those abnormalities is hydrochlorothiazide, a thiazide, potassium-wasting diuretic that can cause hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hypokalemia. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside used for supraventricular tachycardia and heart failure. Its mechanism of action relies on selective binding and reversible inhibition of the α subunit of the Na+/K+ ATPase in the cardiac sarcolemma, causing an increase in intracellular sodium and a reduction in intracellular potassium. As a result, the intracellular Na+ gradient favors less extrusion of Ca2+ from the cell via the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, providing a greater intracellular concentration of Ca2+. This improves cardiac contractility and reduces conduction via the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes. Unfortunately, digoxin is characterized by a low therapeutic threshold and narrow therapeutic window, creating conditions easily suited to toxicity. The therapeutic serum concentration of digoxin is 0.8 to 2 ng/mL, and toxicity can be seen at any level outside of the therapeutic range. In addition to the electrolyte disturbances listed, toxicity is also more likely in the setting of renal insufficiency if doses are not adjusted because 70% to 80% of digoxin is excreted unchanged via the kidneys. Digoxin toxicity is characterized by cardiac arrhythmias (eg, bradycardia, premature ventricular complexes, atrioventricular block), gastrointestinal disturbances, and/or neurologic disturbances (eg, confusion, visual changes, weakness, delirium). Treatment of toxicity includes an initial survey (eg, assessment of airway, breathing, circulation) and initiation of digoxin-specific antibodies. Electrocardiogram results illustrate the classic downsloping (scooping) ST-segment depression in a patient taking digoxin Amlodipine may cause edema or side effects related to vasodilation (eg, headaches, reflex tachycardia) but is not typically associated with any of the major conditions that may promote digoxin toxicity.
Answer C: If it is untreated, hypothyroidism may promote digoxin toxicity, but adjustments to levothyroxine dose would be less likely to promote digoxin toxicity. Digoxin is a cardiac glycoside with a narrow therapeutic window and low therapeutic threshold. Several conditions can promote digoxin toxicity, including electrolyte abnormalities (eg, hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia), renal insufficiency, and hypothyroidism. Toxicity is manifested by cardiac, gastrointestinal, and neurologic disturbances and should be treated with stabilization and digoxin-specific antibodies. Ethacrynic acid is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na+-K+-Cl2−triple transporter in the thick ascending loop of Henle. Diuretics are essentially medications that increase the production of urine. They can be subdivided on the basis of the part of the nephron they interact with and the effects they cause. The most common diuretics are carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, loop diuretics, thiazides, potassium-sparing diuretics, and osmotic diuretics. The order of recovery from neuromuscular blockade after nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent administration is, from first to last, diaphragm > laryngeal muscles > corrugator supercilii > abdominal muscles > orbicularis oculi > geniohyoid > adductor pollicis. The adductor pollicis would be the last muscle to recover from neuromuscular blockade. The response to neuromuscular blockade of muscle groups to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA) occurs at different rates. When NMBAs are administered, the first muscle groups to become paralyzed are the central muscles such as the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles, with response of the peripheral muscles such as adductor pollicis occurring later. This response is quicker for the central muscles due to the greater amount of blood flow and, as a result, NMBA delivery. Due to the higher density of nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, the diaphragm is relatively resistant to nondepolarizing NMBAs and recovers much more quickly than any other muscle group despite being one of the first muscles to be paralyzed. The recovery of the corrugator supercilii muscle at the eyebrow correlates well with the recovery at the diaphragm and laryngeal muscles and would be one of the first muscles to recover. The recovery of the orbicularis oculi, a muscle near the corrugator supercilii, correlates well with the adductor pollicis.
Answer C: The cricothyroid is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle and would recover quickly.
Answer D: The diaphragm would be the first muscle to recover from neuromuscular blockade. The first muscle to recover from neuromuscular blockade is the diaphragm, and the last muscle is the adductor pollicis. Thus, if the adductor pollicis has recovered from neuromuscular blockade as assessed by train-of-four monitoring, the diaphragm will have recovered as well.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Milrinone is a selective PDE III inhibitor and decreases the hydrolysis of cyclic AMP. Inotropic medications increase cardiac output via increased contractility of the heart. Some inotropic medications may also increase systemic vascular resistance in addition to increasing inotropy. These medications are also classified as vasopressors. CO is a product of stroke volume and heart rate. Increasing the heart rate increases inotropy through the Treppe (or Bowditch) effect. Increased heart rate causes a buildup of intracellular calcium, due to the inability of the Na+/K+ ATPase to keep up with the sodium influx at higher heart rates. Dobutamine is a synthetic catecholamine which acts on beta-adrenergic receptors. This leads to an increase in cAMP via Gprotein-coupled receptors (GPCR). Stimulation of beta-1 receptors causes an increase in heart rate and contractility, which increases CO. Dobutamine does have slight vasodilating properties, which can result in a decrease in systolic blood pressure and mean arterial pressure. In cardiogenic shock, dobutamine is a good choice of inotropic agent. The common problem with dobutamine is tachyarrhythmias. Isoproterenol is a beta agonist medication, which increases heart rate. A slight increase in CO is seen as a result of the Treppe effect. Isoproterenol is often considered the drug of choice to increase heart rate in a denervated heart. A denervated heart cannot respond to antimuscarinic medications and needs direct agonism. Isoproterenol and epinephrine can provide direct beta agonism in these situations. Levosimendan is a calcium sensitizing medication. Levosimendan increases cardiac sensitivity to calcium, thus increasing inotropy and CO. Levosimendan has a short half-life, but produces active metabolites with longer half-lives. Levosimendan is not currently available in the United States. Side-effects of levosimendan include tachyarrhythmias and hypotension. Milrinone is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that acts mainly on PDE3. By inhibiting phosphodiesterase there is an increase in cyclic AMP (cAMP) inside cardiac cells. Beta-adrenergic receptors use cAMP as a second messenger to increase phosphorylation of calcium and potassium channels in the cells. Increased levels of cAMP causes increased contractility (inotropy), heart rate (chronotropy), and conduction velocity (dromotropy). This leads to an increase in intracellular calcium and increases inotropy. Milrinone is also a potent vasodilator, which leads to a decrease in afterload. The decrease in afterload also promotes and increase in cardiac output. It has been shown to improve pulmonary blood flow and left ventricular filling, thus is useful in the management of pulmonary hypertension. Milrinone as an IV medication has a half-life of several hours. Oral milrinone was used as a treatment for CHF patients until it was shown to increase mortality. Milrinone Effects: 1) Cyclic AMP Effect: Inotropy - Increases contractility (inotropy), heart rate (chronotropy) and conduction velocity (dromotropy). - Increased cardiac output. 2) Cyclic AMP Effect: Vasodilation - Smooth muscle relaxation. - Decreased left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. - Improves pulmonary blood flow and left ventricular filling. Answers A & B: This drug activates beta adrenergic receptors, which will increase cAMP via GPCR. Levosimendan is a calcium sensitizing medication. Milrinone is a phosphodiesterase 3 inhibitor that increases contractility of the heart. Milrinone also causes vasodilatation and decreased afterload. Milrinone is often used as an inotropic medication following cardiopulmonary bypass, for pulmonary hypertension, and during acute CHF exacerbation. However, chronic milrinone treatment has been associated with increased mortality.  Kaplan, Joel A. Essentials of Cardiac Anesthesia. 2008. Levosimendan. Medscape. Drug Ther Perspect. 2001;17(20). Symptomatic hyponatremia will decrease minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of inhaled anesthetics as it results in CNS depression. In general, agents that decrease cerebral metabolic rate, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and neurotransmission will decrease MAC, whereas the opposite is true in regards to increasing MAC. Therefore, other anesthetics such as opioids, propofol, ketamine, and benzodiazepines will decrease MAC whereas stimulants such as ephedrine and acute cocaine use will increase MAC. Chronic use of ethanol will increase MAC whereas acute intoxication will decrease MAC. Chronic methamphetamine or cocaine use will decrease MAC whereas acute use will increase MAC. Other things that decrease MAC include severe hypotension (SBP < 50 mm Hg), severe metabolic acidosis, hypothermia, increasing age, pregnancy, and severe anemia. Red hair females are reported to have an increase in MAC of 19% compared to dark-haired counterparts. Notable factors that do not alter MAC include thyroid function (unless there are alterations in temperature), hypo- or hypercapnia, duration of anesthesia, gender, type of surgical stimulus, metabolic alkalosis, and hyperkalemia. Acute stimulant intoxication, such as cocaine or methamphetamine, will increase central neurotransmitter levels and thus increase MAC.
Answer B: Chronic ethanol use results in an increase in MAC.
Answer C: The melanocortin-1 receptor gene, seen in patients with red hair, increases MAC requirements. Additionally, redheads are more sensitive to thermal pain and are resistant to the analgesic effects of subcutaneous lidocaine. Factors that decrease MAC are those that decrease neurotransmission, decrease CNS neurotransmitter levels, or decrease cerebral metabolism including hyponatremia. Magnesium administration has a curious effect on anesthetic requirements. Studies have shown that it decreases anesthetic requirements during TIVA. However, the opposite has been shown with volatile anesthetics where it increases MAC. To further confuse the picture, rats who were fed a low magnesium diet (hypomagnesemic) had higher MAC requirements. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "MAC Reducers (B)" Clinical Anesthesia. Nalbuphine is a mu-opioid receptor partial antagonist and a kappa receptor agonist. It is classified as a mixed opioid agonistantagonist. The partial antagonistic activity against the mu-opioid receptor results in a ceiling effect for respiratory depression. Nalbuphine has a plateau or ceiling effect, which is a useful property. Increasing the dose of nalbuphine above a certain threshold will not increase respiratory depression. Because pain is mediated by both kappa and mu receptors, nalbuphine will not reverse analgesia to the same extent as naloxone. Nalbuphine can, however, still induce withdrawal in patients who are opioid-dependent. A dose of 5 to 10 mg of nalbuphine may be useful to treat pruritus from neuraxial anesthesia. Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist with possible (controversial) kappa activity. It dissociates from the mu receptor very slowly, which makes antagonism with naloxone difficult. Buprenorphine also exhibits a ceiling effect for respiratory depression, similarly to nalbuphine. Nalbuphine is a kappa-opioid receptor agonist.
Answer C: Nalbuphine is a mu-opioid receptor partial antagonist, not an agonist. Nalbuphine is a mu-opioid receptor partial antagonist and kappa-opioid receptor agonist. The partial antagonism of the mu-opioid receptor results in a ceiling effect on respiratory depression.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Nalbuphine: Plateau Effect Mech" Barash PG, et al. Doxorubicin is typically associated with severe cardiac toxicity but can also cause pulmonary infiltrates, myelotoxicity, and toxicity to the gastrointestinal, hepatic, and renal systems. Doxorubicin is toxic to numerous organs including the liver and kidneys. Doxorubicin is a chemotherapeutic agent, classified as an anthracycline antibiotic. The most severe complication of doxorubicin therapy is cardiomyopathy. Risk factors predisposing to a higher chance of cardiac toxicity include active or prior cardiovascular disease, prior or concomitant radiation therapy to the mediastinum/pericardial area, and previous or concomitant use other cardiotoxic agents. Preoperative anesthetic assessment in patients with prior documented doxorubicin therapy may include an ECG, echocardiogram, and/or multigated acquisition (MUGA) scan. Definitive diagnosis of doxorubicin-induced cardiotoxicity may be obtained through endomyocardial biopsy. Chronic, potentially fatal doxorubicin-induced heart failure is cumulative and risk is increased with higher doses. For this reason, the total cumulative dose of doxorubicin is limited to 300 mg/m2.
Answer B: Heart failure can occur during treatment or up to several months after termination of therapy.
Answer D: Acute doxorubicin toxicity may manifest with abnormal conduction patterns, acute ST segment changes on ECG, and supraventricular or ventricular dysrhythmias. ECG monitoring should be employed if acute toxicity is suspected. Doxorubicin is a chemotherapeutic agent that is potentially toxic to the cardiac, pulmonary, GI, hepatic, and renal systems. It is also potentially myelotoxic. The most severe complication is doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy with heart failure that is cumulative, dose-related, and may occur during or after termination of therapy. Acute cardiac toxicity may manifest on ECG as ST segment changes or dysrhythmias.  Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 1132, 2610. Longnecker, Anesthesiology, 1st edition, p. 1248. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Doxorubicin: Complications"

Buprenorphine has a ceiling effect at higher doses, such that further increases in dosing produce little or no additional effects. At higher doses, it has a partial agonist ceiling effect, more so for respiratory depression than analgesic effect. This offers a degree of safety against abuse potential and respiratory depression. Buprenorphine has a high affinity for the μ-receptor with a half-life for dissociation from the receptor between 2-3 hours (compare to fentanyl’s 7 minutes). This leads to a low-level of physical dependence and prolonged clinical effects, up to 6 hours, despite a metabolic and elimination half-life of 3 hours. Buprenorphine is available in multiple routes of administration. Since buprenorphine has low oral bioavailability, it is commonly produced in sublingual formulations with and without added naloxone. Sublingual formulations with naloxone help protect against opioid abuse and respiratory depression if misused intravenously. Buprenorphine is a thebaine derivative with mixed agonist-antagonist activity. It functions as a μ-opioid partial agonist and κ-antagonist.
Answer C: Indications for buprenorphine include treatment of opioid dependence, opioid detoxification and maintenance, and chronic pain syndromes. It may also be used for acute pain in patients intolerant or allergic to morphine and can prolong the analgesic effect of nerve blocks when added to the local anesthetic. One of the major benefits of buprenorphine for opioid detoxification is that it is typically associated with a relatively symptom-free withdrawal period.
Answer D: Buprenorphine has an analgesic potency at low doses that is 25-40 times that of morphine. Buprenorphine is a partial μ-agonist and κ-antagonist with 25-40 times the potency of morphine. There are ceiling effects, particularly for respiratory depression, at high doses. Cessation of buprenorphine is typically associated with only mild withdrawal symptoms.  Malinoff, et al. Anticholinergic agents such as atropine, glycopyrrolate, cyclopentolate, and scopolamine can cause mydriasis (pupillary dilation), leading to blurry vision. They may be used therapeutically as ophthalmic agents to induce mydriasis and cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation). Anticholinergic/antimuscarinic medications such as atropine act as competitive antagonists of acetylcholine on its receptors. Cholinergic receptors may be further categorized as either nicotinic or muscarinic, and most anticholinergic medications act highly selectively at muscarinic receptors. The sensitivity of end organs to anticholinergic blockade varies so that lower doses may inhibit salivation and sweating, but larger doses are required for exerting cardiovascular and gastrointestinal effects. Anticholinergics have antisecretory properties, decreasing nasal and bronchial secretions, salivation, lacrimation, sweating, and gastric acid production. They increase heart rate, which can be useful for the treatment of bradycardia. Anticholinergics relax smooth muscles in the lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and bladder., resulting in dilation of the bronchi and bronchioles, a decrease in peristalsis leading to constipation, and urinary retention. Some anticholinergic agents (eg, scopolamine) also act as antiemetics and can be used prophylactically for postoperative nausea and vomiting. The effects on the central nervous system (CNS) can vary, and both CNS excitation (eg, agitation, confusion, restlessness, delirium, hallucinations) and depression (eg, amnesia, sedation, somnolence, stupor, coma) can occur in central anticholinergic syndrome. These effects on the CNS can be reversed with physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor that can cross the blood-brain barrier. Anticholinergics lead to bronchial smooth muscle relaxation, resulting in bronchodilation. In addition, bronchial secretions are also decreased. Causing these bronchial effects and the prevention of bradycardia are important reasons to administer anticholinergics when providers seek to reverse neuromuscular blockade with cholinesterase inhibitors.
Answer B: Anticholinergics lead to decreased peristalsis and secretions in the gastrointestinal tract.
Answer D: Anticholinergics lead to decreased sweating. Even though eccrine sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic nervous system, their activity at the postganglionic neuron axon terminal is activated by acetylcholine. Anticholinergics induce mydriasis, tachycardia, bronchodilation, decreased sweating, and, potentially, central nervous system effects. Isoflurane at a MAC of 1.0 increases heart rate by about 10-15 beats/min, and decreases systemic vascular resistance (SVR) leading to a reduction in blood pressure. There is little to no change in central venous pressure (CVP) at 1.0 MAC isoflurane, but it can decline at higher MAC values. Moreover, CVP is a function of many complex factors governing pressures within the venous system. These may include the compliance within the splanchnic system, intravascular volume status, and the effects of medications on the venous system. When there is vasodilation and sudden increase in compliance of the splanchnic venous system from inhaled anesthetic, a relative hypovolemia occurs. There is a reflexive vasoconstriction of the splanchnic venous system in order to increase preload to the heart. The central venous pressure, therefore, is minimally altered assuming a patient is not critically ill and not confounded by profound capillary leakage and circulating toxins. Isoflurane may theoretically cause coronary steal phenomenon, in which coronary vasodilation redirects blood flow away from fixed stenotic coronary branches. Coronary steal physiology may, in theory, occur with any medication that causes coronary vasodilation in the setting of coronary anatomy that lends itself to redirection of blood flow away from stenotic lesions. Coronary steal phenomenon may also occur due to collateral flow within the same layer, see figures below. Arterioles closest to the stenosis may have increased vasodilatory reserve as compared with those further away. In the setting of stenosis and hypotension, flow can be increased through the vascular beds close to the stenosis but not through those further away. Collateral steal therefore occurs as a result. There have been no significant studies, however, supporting the contraindication of isoflurane in patients with coronary artery disease. Coronary autoregulation in transmural coronary blood flow with coronary artery stenosis. Despite a higher original flow (Q1), flow to the endocardial, myocardial, and subendocardial layers becomes dependent on the lower flow distal to an area of stenosis (Q2). Arteriolar smooth muscles, however, also control blood flow within the vascular beds of each layer within the heart. In the setting of coronary artery stenosis, arteriolar vasodilation occurs to maintain adequate flow, Q3, Q4, and Q5 to the myocardial, endocardial, and subendocardial layers, respectively. Whereas the myocardial and endocardial layers are only partially vasodilated with further vasodilatory reserve, the subendocardial layer is maximally dilated in order to ensure adequate blood flow in the setting of proximal stenosis. Coronary steal phenomenon in transmural blood flow in the presence of coronary artery stenosis and hypotension. Coronary steal occurs as a result of blood being “stolen” from the maximally vasodilated vessels and distributed to the vessels which have vasodilatory reserve and preserved autoregulation. This phenomenon may be exemplified through subendocardial ischemia during hypotension in the setting of coronary artery stenosis. Blood flow to the coronary vascular bed may therefore be increased, preserved, or reduced depending on the degree of vasodilation provided by the arterioles within each region distal to the stenosis. Normally, the arterioles within the layers above the subendocardium are not maximally dilated, retaining vasodilatory reserve in the setting of hypotension while promoting blood flow to the subendocardium. As flow proximal to the stenosis, Q1, is reduced due to hypotension, arteriolar vasodilation occurs within the vascular beds of the myocardial and endocardial layers. This vasodilation increases blood flow, Q3 and Q4, to these layers despite reduced blood proximal to the stenosis. Arteriolar vasodilation to the subendocardium, however, was maximally dilated in the setting of an already-present stenosis. Further reduced flow to the subendocardium does not result in further vasodilation, and the flow to this vascular bed becomes wholly pressure-dependent. Hypotension will therefore cause ischemia and/or infarction as a result of blood being “stolen” by vasodilation at the myocardial and endocardial layers. This phenomenon has teleological advantages as ventricular contractility is sustained by ensuring adequate blood supply to the myocardium. There is little to no change in central venous pressure (CVP) at 1.0 MAC isoflurane, but it can decline at higher MAC values.
Answer B: There have been no significant studies, however, supporting the contraindication of isoflurane in patients with coronary artery disease. Answers D & E: Isoflurane at 1.0 MAC decreases the response to PaCO2, increases respiratory rate, and reduces tidal volume. These effects combine to yield a mild reduction in minute ventilation. At 1.0 MAC of isoflurane, cardiovascular effects include increased heart rate (10-15 beats/min), decreased SVR and blood pressure, and minimal changes in CVP. Respiratory effects include a mild reduction in minute ventilation, a reduced tidal volume, and an increased respiratory rate.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Angiotensin converting enzyme catalyzes the degradation of bradykinin. Under normal conditions, bradykinin promotes vasodilation by increasing production of arachidonic acid metabolites and nitric oxide. ACE inhibition will increase levels of bradykinin, promoting its effect in reducing blood pressure. Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors are a class of drugs developed for the treatment of hypertension. They work by inhibiting the vasoconstrictive and sodium-retentive properties of angiotensin II (ATII) and promoting the vasodilatory and natriuretic properties of bradykinin. Specifically, ACE inhibitors decrease the formation of ATII and decrease the degradation of bradykinin. ACE is an enzyme present in vascular and pulmonary endothelial cells and is pivotal to the renin-angiotensin system (RAS). Initially in this pathway, renin is released by the juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney in response to reduced sodium delivery at the macula densa, decreased renal perfusion pressure, or sympathetic activation. Renin cleaves angiotensinogen to angiotensin I. ACE then cleaves ATII from angiotensin I. ACE inhibitors block this conversion step. Under normal conditions ATII increases sodium retention via aldosterone stimulation and via renal vasoconstriction. It also increases fluid retention with stimulation of antidiuretic hormone release from the posterior pituitary. Thus, a decrease in angiotensin II by ACE inhibitors will decrease volume expansion and decrease fluid retention. ACE also catalyzes the degradation of bradykinin. Under normal conditions, the effect of bradykinin on the kidney is to increase natriuresis through direct tubular effects. Bradykinin also affects vascular endothelium by increasing production of arachidonic acid metabolites and nitric oxide promoting vasodilation. ACE inhibition will therefore increase levels of bradykinin, further promoting its effects in reducing blood pressure. Figure: Angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) converts angiotensin I (Ang I) to angiotensin II (Ang II), which then binds to its receptors leading to increased volume expansion. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor (Inh) decreases the conversion of Ang I to Ang II and thus decreases the hypertensive effects of Ang II. ACE inhibitors promote an increase in natriuresis through direct tubular effects of bradykinin, as well a decrease in the sodium retentive effects of the RAS and a decrease in action of aldosterone.
Answer B: Bradykinin stimulates the production of arachidonic acid metabolites, nitric oxide, and endothelium-derived hyperpolarizing factors in the vascular endothelium. The effects of these mechanisms causes vasodilation. ACE inhibitors decrease the degradation of bradykinin and thus the production of arachidonic metabolites would increase.
Answer C: ATII has the ability to increase vascular permeability and increase smooth muscle contraction. Thus, inhibition by ACE inhibitors would have an opposite effect.
Answer D: Aldosterone release is a final step in the RAS pathway which promotes sodium and water retention in the kidney via activation of sodium/potassium pumps within the distal tubule. ACE inhibitors reduce the amount of ATII which normally stimulates aldosterone release. The antihypertensive effects of ACE inhibitors are the result of decreasing the action of aldosterone within the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and increasing bradykinin’s vasodilatory and kidney natriuretic effects. ACE inhibitors can cause a decrease in glomerular filtration in the setting of hypoperfusion because of a decrease in efferent arteriolar resistance. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Mivacurium, due to its degradation by pseudocholinesterase (levels of which are decreased in burn patients), requires the smallest increase in dosage for burn patients. Patients with massive burns demonstrate resistance to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs (NDNMBs) based on the size of and time elapsed since the burn. Compared with normal patients, the number of acetylcholine (ACh) receptors is increased in muscles close to the burn and, to a smaller degree, away from the burn site. This effect may be seen as soon as 24-48 hours after the burn and usually resolves with healing. Since NDNMB's drug effect is produced by competitively inhibiting ACh receptors, the presence of more receptors means a higher dose of free drug is required to produce neuromuscular blockade manifesting as twitch depression. Burn patients also have increased protein binding, meaning less free drug is available to bind ACh receptors, further increasing dose requirements. Atracurium, despite some metabolism by pseudocholinesterase, may require 4x ED95 to overcome the resistance seen in burn patients.
Answer B: Mivacurium is different from most NDNMBs because it is metabolized by pseudocholinesterase alone. Burn patients have decreased levels of pseudocholinesterase, making them more sensitive to the effects of mivacurium. However, increased ACh receptors still contributes to some resistance to the drug. The net result of these two effects is that the required dose of mivacurium in burn patients is 1-2x the dose used in healthy patients. Answers C & D: Doses of most NDNMBs must be increased 2-5x in burn patients to achieve the same intubating conditions in the same time period as in healthy patients due to drug resistance. Patients with massive burns demonstrate resistance to NDNMBs, resulting in increased dosing requirements, due to upregulation of ACh receptors and increased plasma protein binding. Mivacurium’s dosing requirements are only slightly increased relative to other NDNMBs as it is metabolized by pseudocholinesterase, the levels of which are decreased in burn patients. Doxorubicin is an anthracycline antineoplastic agent that at intermittent, high-dose administrations, has been shown to cause chronic cardiomyopathy. Doxorubicin is one of several antitumor antibiotics that causes single strand DNA breaks or cross-links by causing the formation of free radicals in proximity to DNA. Cyclophosphamide, an alkylating drug, and 5-fluorouracil, an antimetabolite, are also capable of causing cardiotoxicity, which can result in heart failure and intolerance to excessive fluid administration. Bleomycin is an antibiotic antineoplastic that can cause interstitial pneumonitis. This can lead to decreased tolerance of excessive fluid administration, though not generally to the extent of a patient with doxorubicin-induced cardiomyopathy. More importantly, inspired oxygen concentrations should be limited in patients receiving bleomycin as high oxygen concentrations can aggravate the pneumonitis. Lidocaine has also been shown to enhance bleomycin’s cytotoxic effects. The specific mechanism is unknown but may be related to enhanced DNA strand breakage by bleomycin and/or impaired DNA strand repair by native cellular mechanisms. Answers C & D: Vincristine and vinblastine are both vinca alkaloid antineoplastic agents that have been linked to peripheral neurotoxicity. Documentation of preexisting peripheral neuropathies in patients receiving vinca alkaloids is important before performing regional anesthesia. They do not increase the risk for side effects from excessive fluid administration. Several antineoplastic drugs, including doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, 5-fluorouracil, paclitaxel, and rituximab, are capable of causing cardiac toxicity with resultant heart failure. As with any patient with cardiomyopathy, careful attention must be paid to fluid administration to avoid the complications associated with heart failure, such as pulmonary edema. A dose of 2 mg/kg actual body weight is recommended for routine reversal of neuromuscular blockade (NMB) from rocuronium or vecuronium when the patient has two twitches in response to train-of-four (TOF) stimulation. Sugammadex is a synthetic, modified γ-cyclodextrin (an 8-glucose ring) that has a large lipophilic core and eight hydrophilic side chains. It functions as a reversal agent for steroidal neuromuscular blocking drugs (rocuronium and vecuronium) since each molecule of sugammadex is capable of encapsulating and noncovalently binding one molecule of neuromuscular blocker. Neuromuscular blockers bind to sugammadex with a high affinity and dissociate at a very low rate, therefore sugammadex allows for reversal of potentially all levels of NMB. Unlike neostigmine, there is no ceiling effect with sugammadex and NMB can be rapidly reversed even in the absence of twitches on TOF monitoring. Currently, there are three recommended doses for sugammadex in adults (not currently FDA approved for pediatric patients) based on the clinical indication and the degree of NMB. It is important to note that sugammadex dosing is based on actual body weight. Dosing based on ideal body weight can result in under-dosing in overweight/obese patients and can place them at risk for residual neuromuscular blockade. See the table below for details. Answers A & B: Sugammadex dosing is based on actual body weight, not ideal body weight. Both doses (especially the 100 mg dose) will likely be inadequate to fully reverse the neuromuscular blockade and the patient could be at risk for residual neuromuscular blockade. A dose of 2 mg/kg actual body weight is the recommended dose in this patient based on the presence of two twitches from TOF stimulation.
Answer D: A dose of 4 mg/kg actual body weight would be appropriate if the patient had no twitches with TOF stimulation and 1-2 post-tetanic counts. There are three recommended doses for sugammadex in adults based on the clinical indication and the degree of NMB. Use of a 16 mg/kg dose of sugammadex following rapid sequence intubation with rocuronium cannot be relied upon as a rescue solution for an unanticipated cannot intubate, cannot ventilate scenario. The management of a cannot intubate/ventilate scenario should primarily focus on facilitating airway patency, oxygenation, and ventilation per the American Society of Anesthesiologists’ difficult airway algorithm. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (ACE-Is) have been shown to improve survival after myocardial infarction. Enalapril is an ACE-I that blocks the conversion of angiotensin 1 to angiotensin 2. ACE-Is decrease afterload and effectively block angiotensin and aldosterone. Ventricular remodeling is decreased with the use of ACE-Is. Most importantly, ACE-Is have been shown to reduce mortality after STEMI. The mortality benefits of an ACE-I are additive to the mortality benefit of aspirin and beta-blockers. Ischemic heart disease occurs when oxygen or blood supply is inadequate to ensure the metabolic needs of the heart. Risk factors for coronary atherosclerosis development include: tobacco use, diabetes, age, high LDL, and low HDL. Atherosclerotic plaques can become unstable and rupture revealing a highly thrombogenic material. A STEMI often occurs when a plaque becomes disrupted and a clot forms on the plaque causing total vessel occlusion. The goal of STEMI therapy is to limit infarct size and establish reperfusion to ischemic tissue as soon as possible. Following reperfusion there are several recommendations for medical therapy. By instituting medical therapy the goal is to minimize further risk and complications. The institution of antiplatelet therapy can have a 25% reduction in risk of stroke or cardiovascular mortality. Following a myocardial infarction patients should be placed on several medications that help reduce complications and decrease risk factors for an additional myocardial infarction. Following a myocardial infarction lifestyle modification and control of systemic disease should occur. Medications to be initiated following a myocardial infarction should be beta-blocker, ACE-I, statin, and aspirin. Additional medications may also be given to special populations of patients. Spironolactone should be given to patients with an ejection fraction of 35% or less. Alogliptin is a dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitor that causes the inactivation of incretin hormones. The SAVOR and EXAMINE trials looked at patients with diabetes plus acute MI. Studies have found no increase in cardiovascular outcomes over placebo. Additionally, alogliptin has not been shown to improve mortality benefit following myocardial infarction.
Answer C: Nicardipine is a calcium channel blocker of the dihydropyridine class. Nicardipine blocks the inflow of calcium into vascular smooth muscle, and effectively promotes vascular relaxation. Nicardipine is used to treat hypertension, angina, and Raynaud syndrome. Beta-blockers have been shown to have a greater benefit than calcium channel blockers with regard to myocardial infarction. There may be some benefit of verapamil and diltiazem by decreasing myocardial oxygen demand, however the dihydropyridines do not have the same effects. ACE inhibitors reduce mortality after myocardial infarction.  Fauci AS, et. al. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine. 17th edition. 2008. pages 1514-1543. O'Riordan M. Ketamine is contraindicated as the sole anesthetic in patients with ischemic heart disease (B). Ketamine is an anesthetic agent that is structurally similar to PCP or phencyclidine. Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia by reducing or blocking signals to the conscious mind from other parts of the brain. Ketamine works as an NMDA receptor antagonist and is a chiral molecule with an S(+) and R(-) enantiomers. The S(+) enantiomer is the more potent anesthetic agent. Metabolism of ketamine occurs via the liver and the cytochrome P450 system. Norketamine is produced by the liver and is an active metabolite of ketamine with less potency. Ketamine possesses significant analgesic activity. It has been shown to decrease opioid requirements in patients even at low doses. A dose of 10-20 mg preoperatively can provide preemptive analgesia. Ketamine is effective for both nociceptive and neuropathic pain. Higher doses of ketamine are associated with hallucinations, vivid dreams, and emergence reactions. If administered alone the incidence is higher than if co-administered with a benzodiazepine. Ketamine acts as a sympathomimetic, which causes an increase in heart rate and blood pressure. The sympathomimetic effects of ketamine increase myocardial oxygen demand as well as increase myocardial workload (B). These effects are not optimal in a patient with significant coronary artery disease. The sympathomimetic effects of ketamine may be beneficial in a hypotensive trauma patient. Increased pulmonary pressures can occur because of pulmonary vasoconstriction with the use of ketamine. Patients who are catecholamine depleted may succumb to the cardiosuppressive effects of ketamine. Ketamine is unique amongst anesthetic induction agents in that respiratory status is preserved and not significantly depressed. Ketamine is also unique in that it is one of the few induction agents that can be administered via multiple routes: IV, PO, and IM. This make it an acceptable agent to preserve respirations and induce anesthesia prior to IV access (A, D). Ketamine has bronchodilator properties and has been used effectively in bronchospasm (C). An increase in secretions can be noted after ketamine administration, which can be counteracted by administration of an antisialagogue. Possible Contraindications To Ketamine: - Increased ICP with spontaneous ventilation - Intracranial mass lesion with spontaneous ventilation - Open eye injury or other ophthalmologic disorder (increased IOP) - Ischemic heart disease (as sole anesthetic agent) - Vascular aneurysms (as sole anesthetic agent) - Psychiatric disease such as schizophrenia  Ketamine causes dissociative anesthesia, can be administered by several different routes, and has analgesic properties. Hypertension, tachycardia, and hypersalivation are associated with ketamine administration. Ketamine may be neuroprotective in head-injured patients who are mechanically ventilated. Many of the negative CNS effects of ketamine can be blunted by the co-administration of other anesthetic agents. Barash, Paul G. et. al. Clinical Anesthesia. 6th edition. 2009. Reves JG, et al. The use of oral long-acting opioids to decrease sedation requirements in the setting of drug shortages is an accepted practice in the critical care environment. During major pandemics or mass-casualty incidents, drug shortages are common. Unfortunately, the medications that tend to become scarce are the medications that are most commonly used, thus these situations often require the modification of practice to accommodate for this decreased availability of certain medications. In situations where there is an excessive number of patients requiring mechanical ventilation, such as a viral respiratory pandemic, it is common for hospital systems to have shortages of the commonly used sedative including propofol, midazolam, dexmedetomidine, and fentanyl. In these situations, practitioners must turn to adjunctive and alternative medications to fulfill that sedation need, while taking into account the entirety of the clinical situation both within the hospital system and in some cases, outside of the hospital as well. Sedation in the intensive care unit (ICU) tends to require a lower level of sedation that anesthesiologists are accustomed to in the operating room. Indeed, the majority of the time sedation is being provided to facilitate the patient's tolerance of an endotracheal tube that would otherwise be intolerable. Typical sedation regimens in the ICU include propofol, dexmedetomidine, or a combination of fentanyl and midazolam, all run as infusions. Intravenous opioids, such as fentanyl, are sometimes used instead of sedation. A basic understanding regarding the reasons that each of these might be selected in turn can help to guide their use in periods of drug shortages. Propofol is used to provide hypnosis and amnesia in the ICU and is rapidly titratable with a relatively short context-sensitive halflife compared to some other agents. A major downside to the use of propofol includes its cardiodepressant and vasodilatory effects, though these are often of less clinical significance at the low doses used in the ICU. Another downside to propofol is its respiratory depressant effect which may interfere with weaning from mechanical ventilation. Possibly the most well-known cause of switching from propofol is the risk of propofol infusion syndrome which presents as triglyceridemia, lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, and acute fatty liver injury. Rising triglycerides tend to herald the onset of these other symptoms, and will typically prompt providers to switch to another sedation strategy. Dexmedetomidine is being increasingly used for ICU sedation due to promising research into its ability to mimic native sleep cycles and decrease ICU delirium. One of the primary benefits of dexmedetomidine is the fact that it does not interfere with a patient's respiratory drive, and also provides a type of sedation that is characterized by an ease in waking patients up for neurologic checks followed by them falling back into apparent sedative sleep. Major side effects include hypotension and bradycardia, though these are relatively uncommon if administered as an infusion without a loading dose. Fentanyl and midazolam are the most hemodynamically stable sedation combination used in the ICU, though the contextsensitive half-life for both of these drugs is very long and they both impair the ventilatory response to hypercarbia. That said, fentanyl is extremely effective at allowing a patient to tolerate an endotracheal tube by providing profound analgesia. Special considerations in the setting of infectious pandemics that require many patients to be sedated for mechanical ventilation include decreasing the nursing contact with the patient in order to mitigate the spread of a contagion, as well as minimizing and preserving the supply of intravenous sedatives. A common way that this is accomplished is through the use of readily available and inexpensive oral opioids that are given via a gastric tube (NG/OG). Either morphine or hydromorphone will have a distinct and lasting effect to decrease the amount of sedation that a patient requires, as well as minimize the amount of time that a nurse needs to make direct contact with an infectious patient. The primary benefits of dexmedetomidine are its preservation of a patient's native respiratory drive, as well as the ease of arousability from sedation while sedated with this drug. Neuromuscular blockade effectively eliminates these advantages, and dexmedetomidine should be reserved for patients who are not paralyzed and able to interact with the ventilator during periods of drug shortages. This drug combination creates a scenario where a patient can be awake (or arousable) but unable to move.
Answer C: Etomidate infusions have been shown to significantly impair adrenal function and are no longer recommended in critically ill patients, even in the setting of drug shortages.
Answer D: While the use of intermittent doses of midazolam from smaller vials may help preserve the larger volumes of solutions that are used for continuous infusions, hourly nursing contact with a patient in the setting of a viral respiratory pandemic is less than ideal and other strategies could help to mitigate this contact and the potential for infectious spread. Drug shortages during periods of exceptional medical need force providers to consider alternate means of providing safe and effective care. A common way to decrease sedative requirements in the intensive care unit is to administer oral opioids through a gastric tube to provide a baseline level of analgesia that facilitates the patient's tolerance of an endotracheal tube. Lidocaine toxicity tends to present in a very specific pattern of central nervous system (CNS) findings. Numbness around the lips and tongue are the first signs/symptoms. Visual and auditory disturbances (tinnitus) then follow. The clinical scenario then progresses to dizziness/lightheadedness, muscular twitching, unconsciousness, and seizure activity. These clinical signs may then be followed by cerebral edema, increased intracranial pressure, coma, respiratory arrest, and ultimately cardiovascular depression and death. Patients who are premedicated with anticonvulsants, such as benzodiazepines or barbiturates, may have masked CNS symptoms and develop cardiovascular depression before other signs are apparent. The most common cause of lidocaine toxicity is dosing error. The maximum recommended dose of lidocaine without epinephrine is 5 mg/kg. The maximum recommended dose with epinephrine is 7 mg/kg. Note that these maximum doses are commonly cited but are not absolute as studies are lacking. The rate of systemic absorption of local anesthetics is dependent on the blood supply at the site of injection. Areas of regional anesthesia from highest to lowest vascularity include: intravenous > tracheal > intercostal > caudal/paracervical > epidural > brachial plexus > sciatic/femoral > spinal > subcutaneous. Lidocaine has been linked to cauda equina syndrome, causing urinary and fecal incontinence as well as gait disturbances. This association has been documented in the setting of high concentration (5%) intrathecal lidocaine administered via narrow lumen (e.g. 27 gauge) catheters. The slow administration of 5% lidocaine through these catheters allows for pooling of the drug in the region of the cauda equina. This form of local neural toxicity may be due to demyelination. Seizure is one of the last signs/symptoms of local lidocaine toxicity.
Answer C: Neuromuscular excitation is not an early sign/symptom of lidocaine toxicity. Lidocaine toxicity is dependent on dose and site of injection. The most common cause is dosing error. The maximum dose (commonly cited) of lidocaine with and without epinephrine is 7 mg/kg and 5mg/kg, respectively. Central nervous system toxicity is first noted by circumoral and tongue numbness. Areas of regional anesthesia from highest to lowest vascularity include: intravenous > tracheal > intercostal > caudal/paracervical > epidural > brachial plexus > sciatic/femoral > spinal > subcutaneous.
