Mepivacaine has an octanol:buffer partition coefficient (a measure of hydrophobicity) of 136. Among the answer choices, it is the least hydrophobic local anesthetic, and, as a result, it has the lowest potency. The most important property related to the potency of local anesthetics is lipid solubility. Typically, lipid solubility is measured as a partition coefficient in a laboratory setting by determining how much local anesthetic partitions into a hydrophobic solvent such as octanol. When the octanol:buffer partition coefficient is high, the local anesthetic has a higher lipid solubility and potency. Lipid solubility is important because more lipid-soluble local anesthetics have an easier time crossing the hydrophobic lipid membrane. After it is inside the cell, the local anesthetic must bind to a hydrophobic pocket within the voltage-gated sodium channel. Thus, local anesthetics that have a higher lipid solubility will be able to permeate the cell membrane and bind the site of action more easily compared with less lipid-soluble local anesthetics. The size of the local anesthetic molecules also affects potency; larger molecules are more potent compared with smaller molecules. The size of the molecule also correlates with lipid solubility; larger molecules are more lipid-soluble compared with smaller molecules. Local anesthetics and their octanol:buffer partition coefficients Bupivacaine has the highest octanol:buffer partition coefficient (3,420) and is the most potent of the local anesthetics, based on hydrophobicity.
Answer B: Chloroprocaine has an octanol:buffer partition coefficient of 810, making it the second most potent of the local anesthetics, based on hydrophobicity.
Answer C: Lidocaine has an octanol:buffer partition coefficient of 366, making it the second least potent of the local anesthetics, based on hydrophobicity. The most important property related to the potency of local anesthetics is lipid solubility, which can be measured by the octanol:buffer partition coefficient. The octanol:buffer partition coefficient of commonly used local anesthetics are mepivacaine (136), lidocaine (366), chloroprocaine (810), and bupivacaine (3,420). The order of potency, based on hydrophobicity, is also the same order from least (mepivacaine) to most (bupivacaine) potent. The pKa of local anesthetics affects the potency, although to a lesser degree compared with lipid solubility. Only the uncharged form of the local anesthetic is able to cross the lipid membrane and exert its action. At a physiologic pH of 7.4, nearly all local anesthetics will be predominantly in the ionized, charged form unable to cross the lipid membrane. Thus, local anesthetics with a lower pKa will have a greater percentage in the uncharged form. For anesthetics with higher pKas such as chloroprocaine (pKa 8.7), sodium bicarbonate can be added to the solution to alkalinize it and form more of the uncharged form of the local anesthetic, increasing the percentage that is able to cross the lipid membrane. Milrinone is excreted in the urine primarily in unconjugated form and dosage should be adjusted in the setting of renal failure. Milrinone is a second generation phosphodiesterase III (PDE III) inhibitor. Both PDE I and PDE II hydrolyze all cyclic nucleotides, but PDE III acts on cAMP specifically. Milrinone, therefore, increases cAMP levels which causes its inodilator properties.
Answer C: Common side effects of milrinone include tachycardia and hypotension. Thrombocytopenia was a clinical concern with the use of amrinone (renamed inamrinone) but is not significant with milrinone use after 48 hours of infusion. Higher doses of milrinone have been associated with atrial fibrillation.
Answer D: Since it does not act on the adrenergic alpha and beta receptors, milrinone has been proven effective as an inotrope in the setting of beta blockade and in the setting of beta receptor down-regulation (e.g. CHF). Milrinone is commonly used synergistically with adrenergic agents (e.g. epinephrine, norepinephrine). Milrinone is unique in its ability to increase cardiac index without increasing myocardial oxygen demand. It also improves myocardial relaxation (lusitropy) and augments coronary circulation.
Answer E: Milrinone increases cardiac index while reducing systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance. Milrinone is excreted via the kidneys in its unconjugated form and therefore dosage should be adjusted in the setting of renal failure.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Norepinephrine should not be administered intramuscularly (IM) as it can cause local ischemia and tissue necrosis. A number of cardiovascular medications can be given IM. This can be beneficial when patients are hemodynamically unstable but intravenous access is either lost or cannot readily be obtained. In addition, IM doses of some medications can be used prophylactically to prevent anticipated hemodynamic changes. Examples of cardiovascular medications that can be given IM include, but are not limited to atropine, glycopyrrolate, ephedrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, and hydralazine. Vasopressin can also be administered IM but exerts minimal vasoactive effects by that route. Norepinephrine is a direct α1, α2, and β1 agonist. It significantly increases blood pressure but its effects on heart rate and cardiac output are dependent on systemic vascular resistance. Adrenergic stimulation is α >> β leading to potent vasoconstriction. Accordingly, central line administration is preferred. Administration via a small vein, IM administration, or accidental extravasation can lead to localized ischemia which can progress to tissue necrosis. Should this occur, the degree of necrosis can potentially be decreased by infiltration of the affected area with a phentolamine solution (5-10 mg in 10-15 mL saline). Ephedrine is an indirect-acting sympathomimetic. It stimulates α and β adrenergic receptors primarily by triggering release of norepinephrine. Since the drug does not have any direct vasoactive effects, it is safe to administer IM and will not cause localized ischemia. An IM dose of 0.5-0.6 mg/kg will produce modest increases in blood pressure and heart rate within 10-15 minutes from the time of injection.
Answer B: Epinephrine is a direct agonist at α1, α2, β1, and β2 adrenergic receptors. It increases contractility, heart rate, and cardiac output. Although a potent vasoconstrictor, epinephrine is rapidly absorbed after an IM dose and its β effects prevent significant localized α-mediated vasoconstriction and ischemia. An IM dose of 0.1-0.5 mg increases heart rate, blood pressure, and produces bronchodilation within 5 minutes from injection.
Answer D: Phenylephrine is a direct-acting α1 agonist. It improves blood pressure via increased preload and afterload but typically causes a reflexive bradycardia. Although phenylephrine mimics many of the effects of norepinephrine, it is less potent and causes venoconstriction > arterial constriction and is accordingly safe for IM administration. An IM dose of 2-5 mg will raise blood pressure and lower heart rate typically within 10-15 minutes from injection. Cardiovascular medications that can be given intramuscularly include, but are not limited to atropine, glycopyrrolate, ephedrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, and hydralazine. Volume of Distribution (Vd) = Drug dose / Plasma concentration The volume of distribution does not have an actual physical correlate in plasma volume. Rather, it is the theoretical size of the plasma compartment that would explain the observed plasma concentration if all of the drug given was only distributed in the plasma. Because of this, it is sometimes referred to as the "apparent" volume of distribution. The volume of distribution depends on the affinity of the drug for tissue components (tissue proteins, tissue lipids) relative to its affinity for plasma components (plasma proteins). Tissue proteins may include high-affinity receptor sites. Tissue lipids are an important binding site, depending on the partition coefficient of the drug in fat (and the individual's fat volume). In summary, the following statement was released from the ABA regarding this topic: "The volume of distribution is the total drug within the body divided by the drug plasma concentration. It is directly proportional to the unbound drug in the plasma and inversely proportional to the unbound drug in the tissue. As such, drugs that are lipophilic have a higher Vd than drugs that are hydrophilic. Also, having greater tissue binding will decrease the unbound proportion in the tissue, thus increasing the volume of distribution." Answers A & B & C: Drugs with high degree of plasma protein binding, low degree of tissue protein binding, and hydrophilic nature have a smaller Vd.  Lipophilic drugs with high affinity for tissue components (tissue proteins, tissue lipids) have a large volume of distribution.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Chronic carbamazepine does not prolong the effect of vecuronium, but may shorten the effect instead. Vecuronium is an aminosteroid neuromuscular blocking medication. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents act by competitively inhibiting acetylcholine on the nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents are large and therefore unable to cross barriers like the blood-brain barrier and blood placental barrier. Carbamazepine is an anti-seizure medication that acts on voltage-gated sodium channels. Acute use of anticonvulsants can potentiate neuromuscular blockade while chronic use can attenuate neuromuscular blockade by reducing the duration of action of the blockade. Carbamazepine is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 system and induces the P450 system. The P450 system is also involved in the metabolism of vecuronium. Patients treated with carbamazepine have an increased metabolism of vecuronium. Prolong Non-Depolarizing Blockade: - Acute use of anticonvulsants (e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine) - Antibiotics (e.g. streptomycin, clindamycin, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides) - Antiarrhythmics (e.g. calcium channel blockers) - Dantrolene - Ketamine - Local anesthetics (high doses only) - Lithium - Magnesium - Volatile anesthetic agents Shorten Non-Depolarizing Blockade: - Chronic use of anticonvulsants (e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine) - Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. neostigmine) Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic. The aminoglycoside antibiotics prolong the effects of aminosteroidal neuromuscular blocking agents. Aminoglycosides inhibit the release of acetylcholine from alpha motor neurons. Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic that has pre- and post-junction effects that prolong blockade at extremely high doses. Antibiotics like penicillin and cephalosporins have no effect on neuromuscular blockade. Aminoglycosides, polymyxins, lincomycin, and clindamycin primarily inhibit the prejunctional release of acetylcholine and also depress postjunctional nAChR sensitivity to acetylcholine. Tetracyclines, on the other hand, have postjunctional activity only. When combined with non-depolarizing blockers, they can potentiate neuromuscular blockade.
Answer C: Hypocalcemia potentiates neuromuscular blockade because calcium is important for the release of vesicles containing acetylcholine from nerves at the neuromuscular junction. When calcium levels are low, less acetylcholine is released. With less acetylcholine being released there is less competition at the acetylcholine receptor and neuromuscular blockers have a greater effect. Hypermagnesemia acts similarly by blocking calcium from entering alpha motor neurons and preventing the release of some of the acetylcholine containing vesicles.
Answer D: Desflurane is a volatile anesthetic with a low blood:gas partition coefficient of 0.42. The low blood gas coefficient means that very little desflurane is dissolved in tissues, but that desflurane is able to rapidly equilibrate with tissues resulting in quick onset and termination of effects. This rapid equilibration into tissues including muscle is the reason why desflurane potentiates neuromuscular blockade more than other volatile anesthetics. The location of potentiation is likely at the neuromuscular junction and occurs in a dose-dependent fashion. Potentiation from greatest to least for volatile anesthetics is desflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane. The presence of volatile anesthetics potentiates neuromuscular blockade as does hypocalcemia, hypothermia, and hypokalemia. Desflurane causes greater blockade potentiation than sevoflurane or isoflurane. Lithium and magnesium potentiate neuromuscular blockade by antagonizing calcium, as do calcium channel blocking medications.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Rescue antiemetics of the same class as prophylactic antiemetics are typically not recommended. Ondansetron is a 5HT3 receptor antagonist with an anti-vomiting efficacy that is more pronounced than the anti-nausea efficacy. It is best used as a prophylaxis medication. In patients who fail ondansetron prophylaxis, rescue use of the medication is not more effective than placebo thus should not be given. If post-operative nausea and vomiting (PONV) occurs within six hours postoperatively, patients should not receive a repeat dose of the prophylactic medication and a medication from a different class should be used such as droperidol, promethazine, diphenhydramine, or "sub hypnotic" low dose propofol. Of note, metoclopramide in particular is not recommended for rescue therapy in these patients. Following anesthesia, postoperative nausea and vomiting are the two most common unpleasant side effects. The incidence has decreased significantly however in certain patients at high risk the incidence is up to 70%. Vomiting can increase costs through longer recovery room stays and decreased patient satisfaction. Postoperative nausea and vomiting has a complex physiologic mechanism with multiple receptors and pathways involved. The cholinergic receptors are found in the vomiting center and vestibular nuclei. The area postrema has dopamine and serotonin receptors (5HT3). Opioids affect the area postrema directly at the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ). The risk of postoperative nausea and vomiting begins at the age of three and children are more likely to have postoperative vomiting compared to adults who have reached puberty. Risk factors for PONV can be broken down into anesthetic, patient factors, and surgical factors which are debated and controversial. PONV Receptors & Antagonists: Agonist Antagonist Serotonin (5-HT3) Ondansetron Palonosetron Histamine Promethazine Dimenhydrinate Diphenhydramine Muscarinic Scopolamine Dopamine (D2) Droperidol Neurokinin (NK1) Aprepitant Others Dexamethasone Propofol Midazolam Since there are multiple receptors involved in the production of postoperative nausea and vomiting, combination antiemetic therapy has been proven more effective than single-agent therapy. Furthermore, a multimodal approach to those with high risk is also effective. Avoidance of nitrous oxide, neuromuscular blockade, generous intravenous hydration, avoidance of long acting opioids when possible, and a total intravenous anesthetic with propofol are options to reduce PONV. It is also important to mention that several therapies have been proven ineffective for PONV prophylaxis - one of these is metoclopramide when given at the standard dose of 10mg. Doses of 25 mg or 50 mg of metoclopramide are needed for a reduction in PONV, although there is a risk of extrapyramidal side effects with increasing doses. Anesthesia related risk: use of volatile anesthetics, use of nitrous oxide during the maintenance phase, use of opioids especially post-operatively, and use of neostigmine especially higher doses. Patient related risk factors: female, history of PONV, history of motion sickness, and nonsmoker. Surgical related risk (controversial): longer surgical procedures, laparoscopic surgery, major gynecologic surgery, “open” gastrointestinal surgery, breast surgery, eye surgery, and ENT surgery. There are several PONV scoring systems, Apfel et al developed the most common one used which gives the following risk factors: female, history of motion sickness or PONV, nonsmoker, and use of opioids for postoperative analgesia. The risk of PONV with 1 risk factor is 20%, 2 is 40%, 3 is 60% and 4 is 80%. Answers A & B & D: Metoclopramide or ondansetron are not recommended for rescue therapy in patients who previously received ondansetron.  In patients who received ondansetron intraoperatively, metoclopramide as well as ondansetron are not recommended for rescue therapy. Use of a medication from a different class is most effective. The total dose of local anesthetic is an important factor in determining the spread of local anesthetic within the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the spread of local anesthetics within the CSF affects the height of the spinal anesthetic block. Block spread from spinal anesthesia refers to the number of dermatomes covered. Drug factors that impact the block height include the total dose of local anesthetic used and the baricity of the solution, while the total volume of injection makes little impact. Isobaric solutions produce a block spread that is, on average, lower than hyperbaric solutions but with greater variability. The greater variability in block height is thought to be, in part, due to variable CSF density in specific patients and the influence of temperature on solution baricity. Volume, drug concentration, speed of injection, and positioning do not affect block height for isobaric solutions. However, increasing the dose of isobaric solutions does increase block spread. Isobaric solutions are those that have a density that is the same as CSF and, thus, remain at the level they are injected, while hypobaric solutions have a lower density, and hyperbaric solutions have a higher density, causing them to rise and fall, respectively. Hypobaric solutions are prepared by mixing the local anesthetic solution with distilled water, while hyperbaric solutions are prepared by mixing local anesthetic with dextrose 5% to 8%. Baricity determines gravity's effect on solution spread in CSF. Hypobaric solutions will rise in CSF, isobaric solutions will not be affected by gravity, and hyperbaric solutions will fall to dependent areas. Hyperbaric solutions, followed by isobaric and hypobaric solutions, are used most commonly. With hyperbaric solutions, baricity and patient positioning are the most important factors determining spread. Dose, volume concentration, and injection site have a much smaller impact on block height. With hypobaric solutions, positioning is the most important factor. Body mass index (BMI) has been found to be a poor predictor of spinal anesthetic spread. While CSF volume has been found to be inversely correlated with block spread in isobaric spinal anesthetics, factors such as age, weight, height, and BMI have been found to be poorly correlated with CSF volume.
Answer B: Patient height has minimal impact on the block height because patient height correlates poorly with total CSF volume, and the length of the vertebral column does not increase linearly with height.
Answer D: The total volume of solution injected has minimal impact on the block height. The total dose of local anesthetic and baricity of the solution are important factors that affect the spread of local anesthetic within the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and the spinal anesthetic block height. Cerebrospinal fluid volume is inversely correlated with block spread, but the clinical utility of this is limited because factors such as age, weight, height, and body mass index have been found to be poorly correlated with CSF volume. In hyperbaric and hypobaric solutions, patient positioning plays the most important role in the spread of spinal anesthetic. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Alfentanil has a high unionized fraction due to low pKa. This leads to a very fast onset of action compared to other opioids. Additionally, alfentanil has moderate lipid solubility, which also decreases onset time. Alfentanil has a pKa of 6.5, which places 90% of the drug in the unionized form at physiologic pH. Additionally, alfentanil is highly protein bound. The protein binding and lower lipid solubility (compared to fentanyl) makes the volume of distribution for alfentanil smaller than most other opioids (30 L). The blood-brain equilibration time of alfentanil is 1.1 minutes. This is significantly faster than many other opioids. Fentanyl has a pKa of 8.4 and takes about 6.8 minutes for serum and brain levels to equilibrate. Despite having a lower unionized fraction than morphine, the high lipid solubility leads to a much faster onset of action.
Answer C: Sufentanil has a pKa of 8.0 and equilibrates with the brain slightly faster than fentanyl, at 6.2 minutes due to very high lipid solubility despite low unionized fraction. Opioid onset of action is related to unionized fraction (e.g. pKa) and lipid solubility. Opioid duration of action is related to lipid solubility, with low solubility leading to longer action. Alfentanil has rapid onset due to very high unionized fraction (low pKa) and moderate lipid solubility. Remembering "4" will get you in the appropriate range for differences between alfentanil and fentanyl. Alfentanil has about 4 times faster onset. Alfentanil lasts about 1/4 the duration. Alfentanil is about 1/4 the potency (requires 4x the dose of fentanyl for the same effect). American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Systemic absorption of topical cyclopentolate can cause anticholinergic toxicity. Cyclopentolate is a topical anticholinergic drug used to induce mydriasis (i.e. mydriatic drug) for ocular procedures. Systemic absorption can occur and lead to central nervous system signs and symptoms of anticholinergic toxicity. These include dysarthria, tachycardia, disorientation, psychotic reactions, and convulsions. Central toxicity is more likely to follow use of the 2% solution as opposed to the 1% mixture. Acetylcholine causes miosis (i.e. miotic drug), facilitates the flow of aqueous humor, and lowers intraocular pressure. It is sometimes used intraocularly after lens extraction. Systemic absorption can lead to bradycardia, increased salivation, and bronchospasm. Atropine or glycopyrrolate may be used to correct these side effects.
Answer C: Echothiophate is an anticholinesterase used to treat refractory glaucoma by causing miosis. Systemic absorption can inhibit plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase), the enzyme responsible for succinylcholine metabolism. Patients using echothiophate eye drops have demonstrated prolonged neuromuscular blockade after succinylcholine administration.
Answer D: Timolol is a nonselective β-adrenergic blocking drug used topically for glaucoma treatment. Systemic absorption can occur and lead to severe bronchospasm and bradycardia. Cyclopentolate is an anticholinergic drug often used during ocular surgery to induce mydriasis that can lead to CNS toxicity, including convulsions, if absorbed systemically. Cessation of ocular globe manipulation is the first step in treating life-threatening bradycardia caused by the oculocardiac reflex during ocular surgery. The time constant (t) is calculated by dividing the volume or capacity of the circuit (Vc) by the fresh gas flow (FGF). Therefore, in order to decrease the time constant, we can either decrease the capacity of circuit or increase the fresh gas flow. Following first order kinetics, 63%, 84%, 95%, and 99% of equilibrium will be reached after 1, 2, 3, and 4 time constants, respectively. Decreasing the time constant will therefore reach equilibrium at a faster rate. Time constants also apply to the tissue-blood partition coefficients, meaning the amount of inhaled anesthetic that can be dissolved in the tissues divided by tissue blood flow. The time constant for isoflurane is about 3-4 minutes. Complete equilibrium of isoflurane with any tissue, including the brain, would take 3 time constants (10-15 minutes). For nitrous oxide, desflurane, and sevoflurane, the time constant is about 2 minutes. Brain equilibrium then would take about 6 minutes. Increasing the circuit capacity would increase the time constant.
Answer B: Decreasing minute ventilation will not alter the time constant and will decrease the Fa/Fi ratio, decreasing anesthetic uptake.
Answer D: While increasing the volatile concentration may increase the rate of anesthetic uptake by increasing the Fa/Fi ratio, it will not decrease the time constant. The time constant is the volume or capacity of the circuit (Vc) divided by the fresh gas flow (FGF).  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Time Constant Definition" Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Chapter 17: Inhaled Anesthetics. Page 417.

Neostigmine indirectly increases acetylcholine muscarinic bronchial stimulation, which can result in bronchospasm and increased respiratory secretions. Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, so it increases the amount of acetylcholine in the body by blocking the enzyme that breaks it down. Its primary clinical use is in the reversal of neuromuscular blocking agents. Increasing the amount of acetylcholine available at the motor end plate reverses the relaxant effect because neuromuscular blockers are competitive antagonists that can be displaced by large amounts of the receptor agonist. Acetylcholine is the neurotransmitter for the entire parasympathetic nervous system, parts of the sympathetic nervous system, and the motor end plates of skeletal muscles. There are two types of receptors for acetylcholine, nicotinic (present on skeletal muscle and autonomic ganglia) and muscarinic (end organ receptors on salivary/gastric glands, smooth muscle [bronchial, gastrointestinal, bladder, and vascular], and the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes of the heart). Neuromuscular blockers block only the nicotinic receptors on the skeletal muscles, thereby causing paralysis. Neostigmine, however, causes an increase in acetylcholine throughout the body, with several resulting side effects. The side effects are generally related to the activation of the parasympathetic nervous system. Because most of these effects are due to acetylcholine activity at the muscarinic receptors, patients are frequently cotreated with glycopyrrolate or atropine, which are muscarinic receptor antagonists. Neostigmine causes an increase in acetylcholine, which would act on the parasympathetic neuron receptors in the eye to produce miosis (pupillary constriction), not mydriasis.
Answer C: Neostigmine increases acetylcholine muscarinic stimulation of the heart, causing bradycardia, not tachycardia. Neostigmine causes an increase in acetylcholine by inhibiting the enzyme that degrades it, acetylcholinesterase. Muscarinic side effects are generally those caused by the activation of the parasympathetic nervous system. The maximum recommended dose of neostigmine is 0.08 mg/kg, up to a maximum of 5 mg in an adult. Excessively high doses of neostigmine can potentiate neuromuscular blockade. This phenomenon has been theorized to result from several different mechanisms. Excessive neostigmine may lead to a depolarizing block, similar to succinylcholine, because of excessive motor end plate depolarization by acetylcholine. In addition, results of some animal studies have provided evidence that neostigmine might directly block the acetylcholine receptors in high doses. Finally, neostigmine can potentiate the effect of succinylcholine by inhibiting pseudocholinesterase. Because of these potential side effects, care must be taken to properly dose neostigmine. Milrinone is a phosphodiesterase III (PDE3) inhibitor which increases inotropy. Both milrinone and inamrinone (formerly known as amrinone) act by inhibiting the PDE3 isoenzyme which is responsible for the cleavage of intracellular cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). This allows for greater diastolic storing of calcium (which is facilitated by cAMP) by the sarcoplasmic reticulum which improves diastolic relaxation, a physiologic effect known as lusitropy. Lusitropy may be depicted on the myocardial pressure-volume loop as a rightward shift of the diastolic filling phase as seen in Figure 1 below. Increased cAMP also causes increased calcium release during systole. Therefore, once cellular depolarization and calcium-dependent calcium release occurs within cardiac myocytes, the large stores of calcium within the sarcoplasmic reticulum are released leading to an increase in systolic contractility. Figure 1: The effect of improved lusitropy (black dotted line) on the myocardial P-V loop. The PDE3 inhibitors also decrease systemic and pulmonary vascular resistance through their effects on vascular smooth muscle. Milrinone acts as both an arterial- and venodilator. Venodilation decreases preload while pulmonary and systemic arterial dilation lead to both right and left ventricular afterload reduction. Increased inotropy and vascular dilation has led to the PDE3 inhibitors being known as inodilators. Milrinone has largely replaced the use of inamrinone due to the latter’s effects on platelet count (e.g. thrombocytopenia). Milrinone also has a 20-fold increased inotropic activity compared to its predecessor, and a short half-life. In Figure 2 below, the solid black lines represent the normal myocardial P-V loop while the dashed black line shows the changes due to inodilator therapy. The positive lusitropic effect is illustrated as a reduction in the slope and a rightward shift (red arrow) of the diastolic filling phase. This shift results in a reduction in the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP’) and left ventricular end-systolic pressure, and an increase in both the coronary perfusion (CPP’) and stroke volume (SV’). Stroke volume increases since the left ventricular end-systolic volume (LVESV’) is reduced more than the reduction in left ventricular enddiastolic volume (LVEDV’). The aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP’) may remain the same or be mildly reduced. Aortic systolic pressure (AoSP’) will be appreciably reduced, owing to the vasodilatory effect. The contractility is displayed as the slope of the systolic pressure-volume relationship. It is increased (Contractility’) due to the inotropic effect. Figure 2: The effect of positive lusitropy and increased contractility with inodilator therapy. Normal P-V loop is solid black curve. Dashed black curve demonstrates effects of inodilator. Milrinone increases contractility.
Answer B: Milrinone improves diastolic relaxation also known as lusitropy.
Answer D: Milrinone causes venodilation, which decreases preload. The cardiovascular effects of milrinone can be summarized as: increased inotropy, increased lusitropy, increased ejection fraction, increased stroke volume, increased cardiac output, decreased afterload, decreased preload, pulmonary vasodilation, and systemic vasodilation. Milrinone has been shown to improve mixed venous admixture through its reduction in myocardial oxygen consumption. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 356. Glucagon improves cardiac contractility via a nonadrenergic mechanism. Glucagon has multiple physiologic effects including inhibition of gastric motility, promotion of hepatic gluconeogenesis, and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi. In addition, glucagon also acts as a cardiac inotropic and chronotropic agent. It increases intracellular cAMP through a specific nonadrenergic receptor and results in increased myocardial contractility. Glucagon is useful for treatment of β-blocker toxicity because it does not utilize α- or β-adrenergic receptors. Stimulation of the latter is generally ineffective in the setting of β-blocker toxicity. Glucagon is generally not considered a first line therapy for low cardiac output (CO) states, but may be beneficial in the following situations after conventional therapies have failed: (1) low CO following cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), (2) low CO following myocardial infarction, (3) chronic congestive heart failure, (4) low CO from excess β-blockade, and (5) anaphylactic shock with refractory hypotension. Glucagon does cause relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, but this has not been shown to decrease the incidence of shock liver as a result of CPB or low CO states.
Answer C: Glucagon increases intracellular cAMP through a specific nonadrenergic receptor. Glucagon increases intracellular cAMP which results in increased inotropy and chronotropy in cardiac myocytes. This effect is mediated through a specific, nonadrenergic receptor. Myoclonus is seen with several induction agents but is not typically seen with midazolam (C). Myoclonus describes sudden jerking movements, such as those sometimes observed during induction of anesthesia. It likely results from inhibition of descending cortical inhibitory pathways. Myoclonus can resemble seizures but EEG evidence of seizures is lacking during these episodes. It may also be associated with jaw clenching, which can complicate airway management. Etomidate (A) is frequently (50-80% incidence) associated with myoclonic movements on induction. The incidence is dose dependent. Methohexital (B) is associated with more excitatory side effects than propofol including a higher incidence of myoclonus and hiccups. Induction doses of propofol result in myoclonic-like movements in some patients (D) though this is less common as it typically produces myorelaxation. Ketamine is also associated with myoclonic movements. Lorazepam and to a lesser extent diazepam may facilitate if not induce some forms of myoclonus. However, midazolam (C) has not been implicated as a cause of myoclonus. Pretreatment with midazolam reduces the incidence of myoclonus associated with etomidate. There are rare case reports of midazolam causing myoclonus in neonates, but this has not been seen in adults.  Etomidate, ketamine, and methohexital are associated with myoclonus. Propofol, although less common, is also associated with myoclonic movements. Midazolam has not been associated with myoclonus.  Barash Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition. Phenytoin is an anticonvulsant that also has properties as a class Ib antiarrhythmic drug whose mechanism, like lidocaine, is to prolong phase 0 (ventricular depolarization) of the cardiac action potential by binding to voltage-gated sodium channels (INa) to terminate ventricular arrhythmias. Class Ib antiarrhythmics affect ventricular myocytes predominantly and have minimal effect on the atria and AV node. Because of this, their use is reserved for ventricular arrhythmias. Class I drugs are also sodium channel blockers, and class Ib is characterized by rapid binding to and detaching from the sodium channel and an increased affinity for the depolarized sodium channel (rather than the resting sodium channel), making them especially useful in tachyarrhythmias. Class I antiarrhythmics decrease the slope of phase 0 (INa) which prolongs the QRS complex and also shortens repolarization, resulting in a shorter QT interval, although this effect is clinically insignificant. Other drugs in this class Ib include mexiletine and tocainide. Phenytoin is a classic antiepileptic drug with action at the voltage-gated sodium channel and many other effects, including termination of ventricular arrhythmias, induction of microsomal P450 enzymes in the liver, gingival hyperplasia, enhancement of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade with the initiation of therapy, and diminished nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade with chronic use. The drugs of certain classes affect only 1 aspect of the cardiac action potential, while other classes affect multiple aspects, compounding its effects. Sotalol is a class III antiarrhythmic (potassium channel blocker) and is a strong nonselective beta blocker. Phenytoin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels.
Answer C: Verapamil is a class IV antiarrhythmic and is a nondihydropyridine calcium channel blocker used to prevent nodal arrhythmias and rate control in atrial fibrillation by decreasing conduction velocity across nodal tissue. Phenytoin blocks voltagegated sodium channels. Phenytoin is an antiepileptic drug with antiarrhythmic properties mediated by the blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels. Among commonly used antiemetics (including steroids and dopamine, histamine, and serotonin antagonists), scopolamine has the highest incidence of visual disturbances (typically blurry vision) as they occur in up to 20% of patients. Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist that, when administered in a sustained release transdermal patch, is effective for the prevention or treatment of PONV. Since scopolamine is a tertiary amine, it is able to pass through the blood brain barrier and antagonize M1 muscarinic receptors (and to a lesser extent, H1 histamine receptors) in the cerebral cortex, pons, hypothalamus, and area postrema/vomiting center. Action at these sites leads to its ability to reduce nausea and vomiting. Scopolamine is particularly effective at blocking the M1 and H1 receptors activated by the vestibular system and accordingly, is highly effective at preventing motion sickness. This characteristic also applies towards preventing PONV since opioid administration increases vestibular sensitivity. The transdermal patch allows for controlled, sustained release of scopolamine with approximately 1 mg of the drug delivered over 72 hours. After application, it typically takes four hours for therapeutic plasma levels of scopolamine to be reached. Peak plasma concentration occurs 24 hours after application. After 72 hours, drug elution from the patch is minimal and the patch should be removed. Since scopolamine is a centrally-acting antimuscarinic, it can be associated with several side effects. The most common include blurred vision, dry mouth, dizziness, and agitation. It is particularly important to recognize that scopolamine can cause mydriasis (pupil dilation) and cycloplegia (paralysis of accommodation) which can place patients with glaucoma at risk for increased intraocular pressure (IOP). Accordingly, use of scopolamine is relatively contraindicated in patients with known or suspected glaucoma or those in whom an elevation of IOP would be dangerous. Although less likely with the transdermal formulation (relative to IV or IM bolus dosing), scopolamine may also lead to CNS depressant effects including amnesia, dysphoria, and sedation. Optimally, the patch should be placed at least four hours prior to when the antiemetic effect is needed and some advocate placing the patch the night prior to surgery. If surgery is short, placing the patch 30-60 minutes prior to surgery may not initially reduce the patient’s risk for PONV.
Answer B: Use of a scopolamine patch is not recommended in pediatric patients since a safe and effective dose has not been established. Also, children are more susceptible to the drug’s antimuscarinic side effects including amblyopia, mydriasis, hallucinations, and delirium. Additionally, and perhaps more importantly, the patch should never be cut since cutting the patch damages the layer that promotes slow, controlled delivery of the drug. As a result, scopolamine delivery will be unpredictable and the risk for an overdose is greatly increased. Scopolamine is an antimuscarinic drug that, when applied as a transdermal patch, can help prevent or treat PONV for up to 72 hours. The patch should be applied at least four hours prior to the need for its antiemetic action. The patch should never be cut or otherwise damaged as this can alter drug delivery. Common side effects include blurred vision, dry mouth, and agitation. Scopolamine is relatively contraindicated in patients with glaucoma since the drug’s mydriatic and cycloplegic effects can raise IOP. Scopolamine can cause paradoxical bradycardia when given in low doses (0.1-0.2 mg). Remifentanil is the only opioid metabolized via hydrolysis by nonspecific plasma esterases. Remifentanil is unique among opioids as it is rapidly metabolized by ester hydrolysis in the serum by nonspecific plasma esterases into a significantly less active compound. Since remifentanil’s short duration of action is due to metabolism instead of redistribution, a 60-minute or 600-minute infusion will have the same elimination half-life of 10-20 minutes. Answers A & B: All other opioids are metabolized in the liver. Opioids are first biotransformed in the liver by phase I reactions involving the cytochrome P450 system (oxidative and reduction reactions) and then phase II reactions (conjugation). The metabolized and conjugated opioids are then renally excreted.  Remifentanil is the only opioid hydrolyzed in the serum by nonspecific plasma esterases; the liver metabolizes all other opioids.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Remifentanil: metabolism" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 469, 484-488.

The defining feature of alfentanil is its quick onset of action, primarily due to its low pKa. Opioid bolus front-end kinetics, or onset of action after a bolus dose, follow general pharmacologic principles and are mainly dependent on lipid solubility, pKa, and the concentration of the drug. In general, the more lipid-soluble the opioid is the quicker the onset of action. This explains why fentanyl, which is very lipid-soluble (partition coefficient 813), has an earlier onset of action than morphine, which is much less lipid-soluble (partition coefficient 1.4). This trend is generally true with opioids, with the exception of alfentanil which has a shorter onset time than fentanyl while being significantly less lipid-soluble (partition coefficient 145). Alfentanil has a pKa of 6.5 meaning that it is primarily non-ionized at physiologic pH (approximately 90%) which allows it to move across membranes very rapidly providing a very fast onset and offset with a bolus dose. Other opioids with higher pKa values have more molecules in the ionized form which are not able to cross membranes and access the opioid receptors, making the relative effective concentration of these drugs at the site of action lower. Alfentanil also has a significant protein binding and a modest clearance. It is metabolized by the CYP3A4 and 5 system in the liver which shows considerable variability amongst patients and thus response can be highly variable. The context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) is another important pharmacokinetic principle with opioids, which is the offset of action after an infusion. CSHT is defined as the time required for a 50% decrease in concentration after stopping a continuous, steadystate infusion. Below is a chart comparing the CSHT between alfentanil with other opioids and intravenous anesthetic agents. Alfentanil can be used as an infusion and has a context-sensitive half time that is lower than fentanyl but higher than remifentanil. Fentanyl is much more lipid-soluble (partition coefficient 813) than alfentanil (partition coefficient 145).
Answer C: Sufentanil is the most potent of the clinically used opioids due to its high affinity for the opioid receptors. Fentanyl and remifentanil are of comparable potency (about 10x less than sufentanil), followed by alfentanil. Morphine is significantly less potent than the synthetic opioids.
Answer D: Remifentanil has the shortest context-sensitive half-time of the clinically used opioids due to its metabolism by plasma esterases. Alfentanil and sufentanil have a longer context-sensitive half-time than remifentanil but shorter than fentanyl, making them suitable for use in infusions. Alfentanil is an opioid with rapid onset and offset due to its lower pKa of 6.5 resulting in higher un-ionized fraction at physiologic pH. The clinical pharmacokinetics of alfentanil can be estimated by "4". Compared to fentanyl: alfentanil has 4x faster onset, is 1/4th as potent, and lasts about 1/4th the duration. Meperidine is metabolized in the liver to normeperidine, which is then further metabolized and eliminated via the liver and kidneys. Normeperidine has minimal analgesic activity and is a CNS stimulant. It can produce tremors, muscle twitches, and even seizures. Meperidine is a synthetic opioid, which works by acting on the Mu receptor and is widely used for treating pain and post anesthetic shivering. Its half-life is 2.5-4 hours, and it is metabolized in the liver to normeperidine. In patients with liver failure, the half-life of both meperidine and normeperidine are prolonged. The half-life of normeperidine is quite long, lasting 15-30 hours before it is further broken down and eliminated by both the liver and kidneys. Unlike meperidine, normeperidine has no activity on the Mu opioid receptor, but it does have CNS excitatory effects which can lead to nervousness, tremors, muscle twitches, and seizures. For this reason, meperidine should be used cautiously in patients with liver or kidney disease, and its doses and duration of use should be limited even in healthy patients. Additionally, this medication is not typically recommended for patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) due to the potential for neurotoxicity. The maximum daily dose recommended is 10mg/kg/day for no more than 3 days. Meperidine PCAs should be avoided in elderly patients and those with renal failure. Meperidine use should also be limited in patients taking MAO inhibitors. Meperidine blocks the reuptake of serotonin, and when combined with MAO inhibitors can lead to serotonin syndrome, which is characterized by delirium, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, rigidity, convulsions, and coma. In addition, MAO inhibitors have an inhibitory effect on the hepatic enzymes, therefore prolonging the duration of action of meperidine and leading to symptoms of narcotic overdose. There are rare case reports of SNRIs causing seizures. In a placebo-controlled trial, they occurred in 0.02% of adult patients. Seizures are much more common with discontinuation of these medications.
Answer B: Although the hydromorphone-3-glucuronide metabolite has neuroexcitatory effects, meperidine is a much more likely cause of seizure.
Answer D: Benzodiazepines are a common treatment for seizure and would be unlikely to lead to seizure. Withdrawal from these medications is associated with seizures. Some benzodiazepines, such as lorazepam, may be mixed with preservatives like propylene glycol or benzyl alcohol, which can cause lead to serious side effects in infants. Meperidine is metabolized in the liver to normeperidine, which can cause seizures. The death of Libby Zion, an 18-year-old college student, in a New York hospital in 1984, led to a highly publicized court battle over the lack of supervision of inexperienced and overworked young doctors. Libby was given a combination of the antidepressant/MAO-I phenelzine with meperidine, leading to serotonin syndrome. Sugammadex, a γ-cyclodextrin, is the reversal agent for the steroidal neuromuscular blocking drugs rocuronium and vecuronium. Sugammadex can be given at a dose of 2 mg/kg for moderate blockade (train-of-four [TOF] count of 2-4), 4 mg/kg for deep blockade (a posttetanic count of at least 1-2), and 16 mg/kg if no posttetanic twitches are present such as immediately after a large dose of rocuronium is given for a rapid-sequence induction and intubation. The patient described in this question would require 1,600 mg of sugammadex because they were given a rapid-sequence induction dose of rocuronium and have zero twitches on TOF monitoring and zero twitches on posttetanic count. Monitoring neuromuscular blockade is helpful because it provides a method for quantifying the level of blockade. One of the most common methods is TOF stimulation, in which four consecutive 2-Hz stimuli are given to the adductor pollicis muscle. Muscle twitches are then produced, depending on the level of neuromuscular blockade. The number of twitches is referred to as the TOF count. The number of twitches can be used to assess the level of blockade, how much and when reversal agent can be given, and what percentage of the acetylcholine receptors are blocked. If no TOF twitches are present, posttetanic twitches can be assessed by applying a 50-Hz stimulus for five seconds (tetanus), followed three seconds later by consecutive stimuli at 1 Hz. The number of twitches present after tetanus is called the posttetanic count. The TOF ratio (TOFR) is another measure to assess the level of blockade. The TOFR is calculated by dividing the amplitude of the fourth twitch by the first. When the TOFR is < 0.9, there is residual neuromuscular blockade, and reversal is required. Reversal can be achieved through various methods, such as allowing sufficient time for the neuromuscular blockade to dissipate or using neostigmine (an anticholinesterase) or sugammadex. Sugammadex can be given at a dose of 2 mg/kg for moderate blockade (TOF count of 2-4).
Answer B: Sugammadex can be given at a dose of 4 mg/kg for deep blockade (a posttetanic count of at least 1-2). When a large dose of rocuronium (1.2 mg/kg) is given for rapid-sequence induction and zero posttetanic twitches are present, a dose of 16 mg/kg of sugammadex is required for the reversal of neuromuscular blockade. Ginger, garlic, ginkgo, and vitamin E are all associated with an increased risk of bleeding. Use of vitamins, herbals, and supplements has become increasingly common and should be identified during any preoperative evaluation. Ginger supplements may combat nausea and ease muscle spasms. They may also inhibit thromboxane synthetase. This enzyme is responsible for the production of thromboxane, a potent platelet aggregator and vasoconstrictor. Ginkgo can inhibit platelet-activating factor (PAF) in vitro. Both garlic and vitamin E have been shown to decrease platelet aggregation. Echinacea may be taken by patients as prophylaxis against the common cold. It may stimulate T-lymphocyte and interferon production and may have mild antibacterial properties. Echinacea interacts with certain cytochrome P450 enzymes (e.g. CYP 3A4). It may alter plasma levels of drugs dependent on these enzymes for metabolism. Warfarin is dependent on multiple cytochrome P450 enzymes, including CYP 3A4. Echinacea by itself does not increase the risk of bleeding, but risk of bleeding may increase if combined with warfarin.
Answer C: Kava has been used as an anxiolytic. It can cause sedation through its presumed activation of the γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptor. Case reports have linked the herb to hepatotoxicity. Kava by itself also does not increase bleeding risk.
Answer D: The commonly used intraoperative sympathomimetic ephedrine was derived from the Ephedra plant genus. The herbal supplement of this plant is called Ma-huang. Oral ephedra taken for weight loss has published adverse CNS and cardiac events such as hypertension, palpitations, tachycardia, cerebral vascular accidents, and seizures. Ephedra is not associated with increased bleeding. Garlic, ginger, ginkgo, and vitamin E are all associated with an increased risk of bleeding. A history of herbal and supplement use should be obtained preoperatively as supplements can have a number of adverse side effects and/or drug interactions.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Herbal Meds: Anticoag Effects" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 561-562. Kumar, Pathologic Basis of Disease, 7th edition, p. 68.

Curve B (purple) represents alfentanil. Context-sensitive half-time (CSHT) describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. “Context” refers to the length of an infusion. For most drugs, the longer the infusion runs, the longer it takes for the drug plasma concentration to decline by half after the infusion is stopped. The CSHT reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drug plasma clearance is the collection of processes (e.g., metabolism, excretion, biotransformation, etc.) that remove the drug from plasma and therefore decrease the drug plasma concentration. If all other factors are identical, a drug with a high plasma clearance will have a lower CSHT than a drug with a low plasma clearance. When an infusion of a drug is running, a portion of the drug moves or redistributes down its concentration gradient from the central (plasma) compartment into peripheral (tissue) compartments. Once the drug infusion stops, the plasma concentration will decrease and the concentration gradient reverses. Then, the drug that has accumulated peripherally redistributes back into plasma. A drug with a slower redistribution back to plasma will have a faster CSHT than an otherwise identical drug with a faster redistribution. This occurs because the drug is being cleared from the plasma faster than the drug is returning from the periphery, and thus the plasma concentration falls faster. Keep in mind that CSHTs are different from elimination half-lives since the latter are the result of metabolism and excretion from the whole body, not just plasma. The time to decrease the plasma concentration by half (CSHT) is NOT related to the time to eliminate half of the drug from the body (“terminal half-life”). Propofol (blue line) has a steadily rising though relatively short CSHT even with a long duration of infusion. Due to its lipophilicity, propofol has a very large volume of distribution (150-700 L) and readily redistributes from the central compartment to the periphery during an infusion. This contributes to a somewhat long elimination half-life of six hours. However, the CSHT of propofol is relatively short since the drug has a high metabolic clearance from plasma (1500-2200 L/min) and a slow redistribution from peripheral to central. Fentanyl (green line), like propofol, is highly lipophilic and has a large volume of distribution (335 L). However, it has a longer and more variable CSHT due to rapid redistribution. The rapid redistribution back to plasma prevents the plasma concentration from quickly falling after the infusion is stopped, even though fentanyl is rapidly cleared (1530 mL/min). Alfentanil (purple line) has a small volume of distribution (27 L) due to a lower lipid solubility and a high degree of protein binding (90%). Since much less of the drug redistributes into peripheral tissues, redistribution back to plasma does not significantly affect plasma concentration. This explains why the CSHT of alfentanil does not increase after about two hours of infusion time. Note however for short infusions, the CSHT of alfentanil is higher than for fentanyl. This occurs since the plasma clearance of alfentanil is significantly lower (240 mL/min) than fentanyl. Remifentanil (red line) has a flat and low CSHT curve. Remifentanil’s ester structure causes it to be very rapidly hydrolyzed by plasma and tissue nonspecific esterases. Accordingly, it has a very high plasma clearance (4000 mL/min) which keeps the CSHT low. The drug’s volume of distribution is also low (30 L) so redistribution does little to raise plasma concentration after the infusion is turned off. This causes the CSHT curve to remain flat even with long-running infusions. Although not depicted on the graph, the curve for sufentanil closely resembles the propofol curve. Sufentanil’s CSHT is lower than fentanyl and alfentanil because of a moderately high plasma clearance (900 mL/min) and because of its redistribution pharmacokinetics. Sufentanil has a moderately large volume of distribution (120-250 L) and the drug slowly equilibrates between the plasma and peripheral compartments. Due to this slow equilibration, even after the infusion is turned off, a slow redistribution INTO the peripheral compartments continues to occur. This causes the drug’s CSHT to be lower than might otherwise be expected. This curve represents fentanyl.
Answer C: This curve represents propofol.
Answer D: This curve represents remifentanil. Context-sensitive half-time describes the time required for the plasma concentration of a drug to decrease by 50% after stopping an infusion of the drug. It reflects primarily two opposing processes: drug plasma clearance and drug redistribution. Drugs with rapid plasma clearance and a low rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a low CSHT while drugs with a slow plasma clearance and high rate of tissue to plasma redistribution will have a high CSHT. Norepinephrine can cause tachycardia, reducing time in diastole. Tachycardia increases the metabolic rate of the myocardium and decreases coronary perfusion to the left ventricle, putting patients with coronary disease at risk for myocardial ischemia. In the surgical intensive care unit (SICU), cardiovascular failure is the leading cause of death. The primary goal of treating these patients is maintaining sufficient perfusion to the vital organs through adequate cardiac output and mean arterial pressure. This goal is generally obtained through the administration of fluids with inotropic agents and/or vasopressors. Commonly used vasopressors are dopamine, norepinephrine, epinephrine, phenylephrine, ephedrine, and vasopressin. Unfortunately, these medications can cause negative side effects. The most common side effects are ventricular ectopy and tachyarrhythmia, which is of no surprise because of the location of stimulation. Medications that have a high degree of alpha stimulation may cause an increase in pulmonary artery pressure. Dopamine can decrease gastrointestinal mucosal perfusion, and prolonged infusion can lead to a reduced serum concentration of many hormones (prolactin, human growth hormone, and thyroid hormones). In one study, patients who developed adverse cardiac events had higher catecholamine vasopressor loads. The incidence of development was almost 50% of patients studied, and the most common adverse cardiac events were new onset tachyarrhythmia, prolonged elevated heart rate, and myocardial cell damage. In this study, epinephrine and phenylephrine were associated with an increased number of adverse cardiovascular events. Adding vasopressin to the treatment plan has been shown to decrease the dose of norepinephrine required and also to decrease the risk of serious adverse events in ventilatory shock. A desired effect of vasopressor therapy is an increase in systemic vascular resistance, which results in an increased, not decreased, afterload. In patients with reduced cardiac function, increased afterload may lead to an increased myocardial demand that can result in ischemia and infarction. This can be difficult in patients with vasodilatory shock. The requirement to increase the mean arterial pressure to ensure adequate perfusion must be weighed against the requirement to not increase afterload above what the myocardium can tolerate.
Answer B: Norepinephrine increases both the left ventricular end-diastolic volume and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP) through increased venous blood return and left ventricular contractility. An increase in LVEDP can decrease coronary perfusion pressure and reduce coronary perfusion (depending on the concurrent changes in the aortic diastolic pressure). The deleterious side effects of vasopressors may result in significant morbidity and, possibly, mortality in certain patient populations. In patients with preexisting cardiac dysfunction, medication-induced tachycardia may result in increased myocardial oxygen demand and decreased supply, resulting in myocardial ischemia. Tirofiban is a glycoprotein (GP) IIb-IIIa receptor inhibitor. Ordinarily, platelets do not bind to vascular endothelium. However, following vascular damage in which the extracellular matrix (ECM) of vascular endothelium is exposed, platelets undergo adhesion, activation, and aggregation. Platelet GP Ib-factor IXfactor V receptor complexes bind to vascular ECM proteins (especially von Willebrand factor, vWF) leading to platelet adhesion. Following adhesion, platelets undergo a series of biochemical and physical changes leading to platelet activation. Storage granules release a large variety of proteins (e.g. factors V and VIII, vWF, fibrinogen, ADP, ATP, calcium) that aid in hemostasis by recruiting and activating additional platelets and helping propagate the coagulation cascade. Platelets also undergo physical changes that increase their surface area and expose additional membrane phospholipids and GP platelet surface receptors. Newly exposed GP IIb/IIIa receptors are then activated by thromboxane A2. Once activated, they bind fibrinogen and allow for cross-linking with nearby platelets thus leading to platelet aggregation and, coupled with the coagulation cascade, thrombus formation. Antiplatelet drugs work primarily by decreasing platelet aggregation via one of several different mechanisms. See the table below for information on several common antiplatelet drugs. Abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban are GP IIb-IIIa receptor inhibitors and thus prevent platelet aggregation and thrombus formation. Unlike the other drugs listed above, these are only administered IV since oral forms were associated with increased mortality. Each drug has a different duration of platelet inhibition: 24-48 hours for abciximab, 2-4 hours for eptifibatide, and 4-8 hours for tirofiban. Dipyridamole is phosphodiesterase (PDE) inhibitor and adenosine reuptake inhibitor. Platelets are unable to aggregate properly when intracellular levels of cAMP are high (due to thromboxane A2 inhibition). Since PDE breaks down cAMP, its inhibition will lead to increased cAMP levels. In addition, binding of adenosine to extracellular platelet adenosine receptors leads to an elevation of intracellular cAMP concentrations. Dipyridamole blocks adenosine reuptake by platelets, erythrocytes, and vascular endothelium leading to increased extracellular concentrations which then bind to platelet receptors, impairing aggregation.
Answer B: Clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, and ticlopidine are adenosine diphosphate (ADP) receptor inhibitors which impair the ADP-dependent activation of the GP IIb-IIIa complex.
Answer C: Aspirin prevents platelet aggregation by irreversibly inhibiting cyclooxygenase (COX). This enzyme is responsible for producing prostaglandins from which thromboxane A2 is derived. Therefore, COX inhibition leads to the downstream effect of impaired aggregation due to decreased GP IIb-IIIa activation. Abciximab, eptifibatide, and tirofiban are GP IIb-IIIa receptor inhibitors that prevent platelet aggregation and thrombus formation.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Ondansetron is a serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonist with an extremely low incidence of development of extrapyramidal side effects (EPS). Postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) is the leading cause of delayed discharge from the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) and for unexpected admissions after ambulatory surgery. Although many medications have shown great efficacy at preventing and/or treating PONV, they are not without side effects. Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 receptor blocker. An abundance of this receptor was identified in the area postrema and the nucleus tractus solitarius of the brainstem. These areas are emetogenic and the inhibition of serotonin receptor binding has shown great efficacy in both preventing and treating PONV. The most common side effects of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are headache, dizziness, and constipation. As of 2014, there have been only a few case reports of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists being associated with QT prolongation on ECG when administered at usual doses. The FDA has issued a warning regarding QT prolongation with an IV bolus larger than 16 mg, and the manufacturer has removed the 32 mg single-dose formulation. Although EPS were not observed in initial clinical trials (whereas they were with droperidol, metoclopramide, and promethazine), a very small number of case reports have since implicated ondansetron in causing EPS, though the incidence is extremely low. Ondansetron has no known affinity for dopamine receptors, but animal studies suggest that it may play a role in dopaminergic transmission and therefore produce dopamine receptor-mediated side effects in certain patients. Previous history of dystonic reactions or EPS with other antiemetics appears to be the biggest risk factor for development of EPS with ondansetron. Dopamine receptors are also found in the area postrema of the brainstem and antagonism of these receptors has led to improvement and prevention of PONV. Extrapyramidal side effects can be observed after central dopamine antagonism and can manifest as acute dystonia, akinesia, or akathisia, and often resemble the signs of Parkinsonism. Metoclopramide is a benzamide structurally related to procainamide but lacks the local anesthetic or antiarrhythmic properties. Metoclopramide antagonizes dopamine and may lead to EPS.
Answer C: Prochlorperazine is a phenothiazine neuroleptic medication. This class of medications has anti-nausea properties similar to metoclopramide and the butyrophenones via inhibition of dopamine receptor activation in the area postrema. They too are prone to producing EPS. The area postrema of the brainstem, also known as the chemoreceptor trigger zone, contains dopamine, serotonin, acetylcholine, histamine, and neurokinin type 1 receptors. Antagonism of these receptors can help treat and prevent nausea. However, any medication leading to central antagonism of dopamine receptors can potentially cause EPS. A pneumothorax, which can rapidly grow in size with nitrous oxide use, can cause difficulty with ventilation and increased peak airway pressures in intubated patients. Subclavian vein central line placement is associated with a 1-2% risk of pneumothorax. Classically, a pneumothorax can be suspected if the syringe fills with air when venous access is being attempted, indicative of lung puncture. Most patients who develop a pneumothorax due to subclavian central line placement remain asymptomatic. However, concurrent or subsequent nitrous oxide use at 75% can expand a pneumothorax to double its size in 10 minutes and triple its size in 30 minutes. This can lead to difficulty ventilating with increased peak airway pressures. In severe cases, a tension pneumothorax can develop, in which the increased intrathoracic pressure may also impede venous return, causing reduced cardiac output and hypotension. A primary concern of nitrous oxide use is its ability to expand air-filled spaces because of its greater solubility in blood compared to nitrogen. Several closed air spaces, such as the bowel and middle ear, exist in the body. Other closed cavities may occur as a result of disease or surgery, such as a pneumothorax or a craniotomy. Nitrogen in air-filled spaces cannot be removed readily via the bloodstream, but nitrous oxide easily diffuses from the blood into these spaces. Diffusion of nitrous oxide continues into these spaces until the partial pressure equals that of the blood and alveoli (i.e. until equilibrium is reached between all three compartments). Although an expanding pneumothorax can cause hypoxia, hypoxic gas mixtures are unlikely to occur since most anesthesia machines have proportioning systems which require a minimum amount of oxygen dialed into the total fresh gas flow (FGF). For example, if oxygen falls below 25% of FGF, the proportioning system is activated in order to reduce N2O and to maintain O2 above this safety threshold.
Answer C: A suspected air embolus would cause a large drop in end tidal CO2. Central venous access was not obtained in this case and therefore introduction of intravascular air is highly unlikely. Tension pneumothorax can decrease cardiac return and thus decrease end tidal CO2, but this would not occur acutely. A gas mixture of 75% N2O can expand a pneumothorax to double its size in 10 minutes and to 3 times its size in 30 minutes. The volume of an air embolus causing cardiovascular collapse during the concomitant administration of N2O is less than the volume of an air embolus causing cardiovascular collapse in the absence of N2O. Aprepitant functions by blocking the action of substance P and neurokinin 1 and 2 preventing these substances from activating the neurokinin receptor. There are five neurotransmitters involved in meditating nausea and vomiting which include neurokinin 1/substance P, muscarinic M1, dopamine D2, histamine H1, and 5-hydroxytryptamine (HT)-3 serotonin. Aprepitant is a neurokinin-1 antagonist that blocks the action of substance P and neurokinins 1 and 2 which act centrally and peripherally. It is used to preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting as defined by nausea or vomiting within the post-anesthesia care unit or within 24 hours of surgery. It has a half-life of 40 hours and has been found to be more effective than ondansetron alone. Dopamine is antagonized by haloperidol which is a D2 receptor antagonist. A common side effect of haloperidol is the prolongation of the QT interval and the medication should be avoided in patients with a prolonged QT. It should also be avoided in patients with Parkinson disease as it can worsen symptoms due to the dopamine antagonism.
Answer B: Histamine is antagonized by antihistamines, most commonly used for PONV is diphenhydramine which is an H1 antagonist. It has been found to be equally efficacious as ondansetron.
Answer C: Serotonin is antagonized by ondansetron which is a 5-HT3 antagonist. It is commonly used for the prevention and treatment of PONV especially as it does not have any sedating effects. Similar to haloperidol, a common side effect of ondansetron is the prolongation of the QT interval. Aprepitant is a neurokinin-1 antagonist that blocks the action of substance P and neurokinins 1 and 2 which act centrally and peripherally to suppress nausea and vomiting. Acupuncture can be used as PONV prophylaxis by targeting the pericardium-6 (P6) acupuncture point. The P6 point is located a few inches above the wrist on the anterior surface of the forearm between the palmaris longus and flexor carpi radialis tendons. Though the quality of evidence is low, it has been demonstrated that targeting the P6 point was as effective as using anti-emetics. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. A decrease in calcium can interfere with acetylcholine release. Hypocalcemia can decrease the amount of acetylcholine that is released from the nerve terminal. Acetylcholine is synthesized from choline and acetate and is stored in vesicles. Each vesicle contains about 5,000-10,000 acetylcholine molecules. As an action potential travels through the axon and reaches the nerve terminal, P-type calcium channels are activated. Calcium that enters through the P-channels interacts with vesicles containing acetylcholine. This allows for the binding of SNARE proteins (which stands for soluble NSF attachment proteins (SNAP) receptor proteins) that are involved in the fusion, docking, and release of acetylcholine. The acetylcholine molecule after being released from the nerve terminal diffuses across the synapse and binds to the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Nicotinic receptors have 5-subunits, with two identical subunits named alpha. The acetylcholine molecule binds to the alpha subunit. In order to activate the nicotinic receptor, both the alpha subunits need to be bound. Factors that decrease release of acetylcholine: 1) Antibiotics (clindamycin, polymyxin) 2) Magnesium: antagonizes calcium 3) Hypocalcemia 4) Anticonvulsants 5) Diuretics (furosemide) 6) Eaton-Lambert syndrome: inhibits P-type calcium channels 7) Botulinum toxin: inhibits SNARE proteins Calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, diltiazem) do not affect P-channels. These drugs affect L-type calcium channels. Myasthenia gravis is due to antibodies destroying post-synaptic acetylcholine receptors. Acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal is not affected.
Answer C: Calcium-channel blockers affect L-type channels, not P-calcium channels.
Answer D: Potassium channel blockers (4-aminopyridine) prolong the calcium present in the nerve terminals leading to increased acetylcholine release. A decrease in calcium can interfere with acetylcholine release. Hypocalcemia can decrease the amount of acetylcholine that is released from the nerve terminal. Both the botulinum and tetanus toxin inhibit SNARE proteins. However, botulinum toxin acts at the level of the peripheral nerve, and the tetanus toxin acts at the central nervous system. Botulinum --> inhibits SNARE --> decrease acetylcholine release (peripheral nerve) Tetanus --> inhibits SNARE --> inhibits GABA neurons (CNS) American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Mivacurium is metabolized by pseudocholinesterase, which is the same enzyme that metabolizes succinylcholine. Mivacurium is a short-acting nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent with an onset time of 3 to 4 minutes and a duration of 15 to 20 minutes. Mivacurium is degraded by pseudocholinesterase (also known as plasma cholinesterase or butyrylcholinesterase) at 70% of the succinylcholine degradation rate. It is metabolized into inactive metabolites. In pseudocholinesterase deficiency, the action of mivacurium will be prolonged. The duration can be as long as 2 to 6 hours if the patient is homozygous for the deficiency. Mivacurium has side effects of histamine release it is administered at doses used for intubation. Reversal of mivacurium is either spontaneous with sufficient time or by antagonism by using anticholinesterases such as neostigmine. Neostigmine inhibits the enzymes that degrade mivacurium, but this effect is less than the effect of inhibition of acetylcholinesterases. Mivacurium had been withdrawn from the market in the USA with a subsequent return in 2017, but it is not used routinely in clinical practice in the USA. Atracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis with a small amount (<5%) excreted by the kidneys.
Answer B: Cisatracurium is degraded by Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis.
Answer D: Rocuronium is primarily excreted by the hepatic (70% via the biliary system) and the renal (30%) systems unchanged, with only a very small amount metabolized by the liver. Mivacurium is degraded by pseudocholinesterase (also known as plasma cholinesterase or butyrylcholinesterase), which is the same enzyme that degrades succinylcholine. Mivacurium is degraded at 70% of the succinylcholine degradation rate. When depolarizing and nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents are combined, they result in mutual antagonism. If a nondepolarizing neuromuscular agent is given before succinylcholine, the dose of the succinylcholine must be increased. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. The required initial dose of barbiturates for the induction of anesthesia in older adults (>65 years of age) is decreased compared to that in younger adults because of an age-related decrease in the initial volume of distribution. In older adults, there is generally a decrease in the dose required to achieve the desired anesthetic effect for both inhaled and intravenous anesthetics. Although barbiturates are not often used in modern anesthesia, certain pharmacologic principles exist. This age-related decrease in the dose of barbiturates is due to pharmacokinetics and is related to an age-related decrease in the initial volume of distribution due to a lower total body water content and muscle mass. The pharmacodynamics, or the sensitivity of the central nervous system to a hypnotic agent, of thiopental and etomidate are relatively unchanged in older adults, while the central nervous system sensitivity to propofol, opioids, and inhaled anesthetics is increased. Age-related effects involving the liver and kidney include a decrease in hepatic metabolism and renal function resulting in altered pharmacokinetics and a prolonged duration of action and decreased drug clearance, respectively. The minimum alveolar concentration decreases by about 6% per decade for most inhaled anesthetics. Pharmacodynamic agerelated changes in ion channels, synaptic activity, and receptor sensitivity account for the increased brain sensitivity to inhaled anesthetics seen in older adults. The circulating levels of albumin decrease with age, whereas alpha acid glycoprotein levels increase.
Answer C: In older adults, the brain becomes more sensitive (enhanced pharmacodynamic response) to propofol, opioids, and inhaled anesthetics. The pharmacodynamic responses to thiopental and etomidate are relatively unchanged in older adults.
Answer D: Hepatic metabolism is generally decreased in older adults. Factors that affect the pharmacologic responses of older patients (>65 years of age) include pharmacokinetic changes in plasma protein binding, body composition, drug metabolism, and pharmacodynamics. Changes in body composition with aging include a decrease in lean body mass, an increase in body fat, and a decrease in total body water. In older adults, the brain becomes more sensitive to propofol, opioids, and inhaled anesthetics; however, the brain's sensitivity to thiopental and etomidate is relatively unchanged in this population. While inhaled and intravenous anesthetics generally require a decreased dose in older adults, the decrease in the dose of barbiturates is secondary to a decrease in the initial volume of distribution. Age does not significantly affect the pharmacodynamics of muscle relaxants but does affect pharmacokinetics. The duration of action may be prolonged if the drug depends on hepatic or renal metabolism. Pancuronium clearance would be decreased in older adults because of its dependence on renal excretion. Cisatracurium undergoes Hofmann degradation and is unaffected by age. Vecuronium is associated with a prolonged duration of action in older adults secondary to an age-related decrease in hepatic metabolism and renal function.
