Ketamine is an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist. Ketamine is a selective NMDA receptor antagonist that binds to the phencyclidine site on the receptor. The NMDA receptor is an inotropic glutamate receptor that functions as a non-specific ion channel when activated and plays numerous roles including synaptic plasticity, learning, memory, and pain transmission. Ketamine is often considered a “complete” anesthetic as it produces dissociative anesthesia, analgesia, amnesia, bronchodilation, and (except at high doses) preserves respiratory drive and protective airway reflexes. However, it is rarely used as a sole anesthetic due to numerous sided effects including hallucinations or other psychomimetic reactions (improved or prevented with benzodiazepines or propofol), salivation (decreased with antisialagogues such as glycopyrrolate), and increases in intraocular pressure, intracranial pressure, and cerebral metabolic rate. Although primarily an NMDA receptor antagonist, ketamine interacts with a wide variety of other receptor classes. It is a weak opioid receptor agonist (especially mu and k), dopamine (D2) receptor agonist, and muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonist. Its affinities for these receptors are typically 10-20 times less than its NMDA receptor affinity. Additionally, ketamine inhibits nitric oxide synthase and is a dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Ketamine is an NMDA receptor antagonist. Answers C & D: Ketamine is a weak k-opioid receptor agonist. Ketamine is primarily an NMDA receptor antagonist, although it has weaker activity at a variety of other receptor classes. Ketamine provides anesthesia, analgesia, and amnesia. It also causes bronchodilation and, except at high doses, preserves respiratory drive and protective airway reflexes. Other drugs with primary or secondary NMDA receptor antagonism activity include amantadine, dextromethorphan, ethanol, memantine, methadone, nitrous oxide, tramadol, and xenon gas. After administration of mannitol, an increase in plasma volume will occur which will result in an increase in blood pressure and cardiac output. This may lead to an increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, especially in patients with heart failure. This increase may lead to pulmonary edema in certain patients. The term diuretic typically is applied to a medication that can decrease the extracellular fluid volume by increasing urinary water or solute excretion. Mannitol produces diuresis by increasing osmotic pressure in the proximal tubule and loop of Henle, causing a decrease in passive reabsorption of water and thus an increase in renal blood flow. Following the administration of mannitol, the excretion of sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, bicarbonate, and chloride is increased. In the interstitial space, the increased osmotic pressure draws water from the cells to increase extracellular fluid which will further increase total plasma flow. There is a decrease in hematocrit and blood viscosity secondary to the hemodilution that occurs from solute extraction. Following intravenous administration of mannitol, several physiologic responses occur. Plasma volume will increase which leads to an increase in cardiac output and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. An increase in blood pressure may also be seen depending on the systemic vascular resistance. Following the diuresis, a decrease in plasma volume and overall total body water may cause the patient to become hypovolemic with potential decreases in cardiac output and blood pressure. Acute overzealous administration can result in a dilutional metabolic acidosis with hyponatremia. Accumulation of mannitol can produce hyperkalemia and an increase in plasma osmolality. Mannitol is administered via the intravenous route – it is not readily absorbed from the intestine thus an oral form is not available. After an injection less than 10% is reabsorbed by the renal tubule and, in a patient with a normal GFR, the half-life of mannitol is approximately 2.2 hours. However this can be prolonged to over 30 hours in patients with abnormal GFR. Mannitol is used for a variety of clinical reasons; the most common indication is neurologic and neurosurgical conditions where elevated intracranial pressure is seen. When administered as a bolus, in the presence of an intact blood brain barrier, mannitol decreases cerebral edema and thus intracranial pressure (ICP). A rapid bolus can transiently increase ICP. Prolonged infusions of mannitol have been shown to reverse the osmotic gradient and increase ICP. Mannitol has been proven to be more effective at reducing water brain content compared to loop diuretics or hypertonic saline. Blood pressure is typically increased following acute administration of mannitol.
Answer B: Cardiac output is increased following mannitol administration.
Answer C: A transient elevation in ICP can be seen with a rapid bolus. This is not likely to be seen with an appropriate bolus dose (0.25-1 g/kg) given over at least 10-15 minutes. After administration of mannitol, an increase in plasma volume will occur which will result in an increase in blood pressure and cardiac output. This may lead to an increase in pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, especially in patients with heart failure.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Droperidol and haloperidol cause central nervous system depression and are used, at times, specifically for this effect. Butyrophenones are fluorinated derivatives of phenothiazines. Their mechanism of action is quite complex with binding at dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin, and acetylcholine receptors. There are also postulated anti-histamine and anti-adrenergic (alpha 1) receptor binding sites. CNS depression is a documented side effect.
Answer B: Facial flushing is not a documented side effect.
Answer C: Medications in this class have anti-muscarinic properties, suggesting they would promote constipation.
Answer D: Medications in this class have anti-muscarinic and anti-histamine properties, suggesting they would prove antiemetic. The side effect profiles of haloperidol and droperidol can be derived by understanding their mechanisms of action. Both are anti-dopaminergic, anti-histamine, and anti-muscarinic. Isoflurane results in an increase in heart rate starting at 0.25 minimum alveolar concentration (MAC). Other cardiovascular effects of the commonly used volatile anesthetics (desflurane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane) include decreased systemic vascular resistance, decreased mean arterial pressure, decreased contractility, a near neutral effect on cardiac output, and prolongation of the QT interval. Inhalational anesthetics exert several effects on the cardiovascular system. All inhalational anesthetics cause a dose-dependent reduction in mean arterial pressure as a result of decreasing systemic vascular resistance. Nitrous oxide is the exception as it does not affect mean arterial pressure. Cardiac output is unchanged or only slightly reduced as the increase in heart rate can nearly compensate for any decrease in preload or contractility caused by a volatile anesthetic. This increase in heart rate is also dose-dependent and is different for each anesthetic. Tachycardia is induced at a MAC of 0.25 for isoflurane, 1.0 for desflurane, and 1.5 for sevoflurane. Rapid increases in the concentration of desflurane (and not other volatile anesthetics), such as from 4% to 8%, results in a significant increase in heart rate and blood pressure. It is speculated that this is due to catecholamine release due to irritation of the airway mucosa. Isoflurane has coronary vasodilating properties.
Answer B: The mean arterial pressure decreases with all inhalational anesthetics mainly by decreasing systemic vascular resistance.
Answer D: All inhalational anesthetics depress myocardial contractility. Inhalational anesthetics increase the heart rate in a dose-dependent manner. Tachycardia is induced at a MAC of 0.25 for isoflurane, 1.0 for desflurane, and 1.5 for sevoflurane. Other cardiovascular effects of the commonly used volatile anesthetics (desflurane, isoflurane, and sevoflurane) include decreased systemic vascular resistance, decreased mean arterial pressure, decreased contractility, a near neutral effect on cardiac output, and prolongation of the QT interval. Nitrous oxide does not reduce systemic vascular resistance and mean arterial pressure like volatile anesthetics. Sevoflurane, desflurane, and isoflurane prolong the QT interval. Care should be taken when using these inhalational anesthetics on patients with congenital or acquired long QT interval syndrome. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Donepezil is a reversible, non-competitive inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase which can cause increased availability of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Patients on donepezil should be monitored for prolonged relaxation after succinylcholine. Acetylcholine is important for learning and memory. In Alzheimer patients, acetylcholine concentration is diminished and the effect of acetylcholine is reduced. Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, galantamine, rivastigmine) are commonly prescribed because they block acetylcholinesterase and increase the availability of acetylcholine. Because of the increased presence of acetylcholine, patients on donepezil will have prolonged relaxation after succinylcholine and show increased resistance to nondepolarizing muscle relaxants. Some sources recommend that donepezil be held 2-3 weeks prior to surgery. Levodopa is converted into dopamine and is used to alleviate the symptoms of Parkinson disease. It does not increase acetylcholine.
Answer C: Memantine is an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist used to treat Alzheimer disease by regulating glutamate activity. It does not increase acetylcholine.
Answer D: Venlafaxine is a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) that is used as an antidepressant. It can cause serotonin syndrome, but not prolonged muscle blockade. Donepezil is a reversible, non-competitive inhibitor of acetylcholinesterase which can cause increased availability of acetylcholine at neuromuscular junctions. Patients on donepezil should be monitored for prolonged relaxation after succinylcholine.  ABA Gaps In Knowledge Report, ITE 2018. Barbiturates target the reticular activating system in the brainstem. They exert their effect primarily by binding to the γaminobutyric acid type A (GABA) receptor. Barbiturates enhance the action of GABA by increasing the duration of opening of chloride ion channels. The anesthetic effect of barbiturates involves both the enhancement of inhibitory transmission and the inhibition of excitatory neurotransmission. Barbiturates cause CNS depression in a dose-dependent manner ranging from when administered as bolus injections. They do not produce analgesia. The cardiovascular effects of barbiturates vary depending on the rate of administration, dose, volume status, baseline autonomic tone, and preexisting cardiovascular disease. Hemodynamic responses to barbiturates are blunted by slower rates of induction. Bolus induction doses decrease blood pressure and increase in heart rate. Tachycardia is due to a central vagolytic effect and reflex responses to the decrease in blood pressure. The reduction in blood pressure causes a proportional reduction in renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate. Barbiturates depress the ventilatory center in the brainstem, blunting the ventilatory response to hypercapnia and hypoxia. Decreased minute ventilation encountered with barbiturates occurs through reduced tidal volumes and respiratory rate. Return of spontaneous breathing after an induction dose of a barbiturate is characterized by a slow breathing rate and decreased tidal volume. Barbiturates decrease cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, and intracranial pressure (ICP). This is due to the constriction of the cerebral vasculature. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) increases with barbiturate therapy. The ability of barbiturates to decrease ICP and cerebral metabolic rate (CMRO2) makes these drugs beneficial in the management of patients with spaceoccupying intracranial lesions. Barbiturates cause a decrease in hepatic blood flow. Chronic exposure to barbiturates has opposing effects on drug biotransformation. Induction of hepatic enzymes increases the rate of metabolism of some drugs, whereas binding of barbiturates to the cytochrome P-450 enzyme system interferes with the biotransformation of other drugs. Barbiturates depress the ventilatory center in the brainstem, decreasing the response to hypercapnia and hypoxia. Decreased responsiveness means hypercapnia and hypoxia are more likely to occur prior to compensatory ventilation.
Answer C: Barbiturates decrease renal blood flow and glomerular filtration rate in proportion to the fall in systemic blood pressure.
Answer D: Hepatic blood flow is decreased with barbiturate administration. Barbiturates cause a decrease in cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, and intracranial pressure (ICP). They decrease renal and hepatic blood flow. Barbiturate-mediated reductions in cerebral metabolic rate (CMRO2) and ICP make them useful in the anesthetic management of patients with space-occupying intracranial lesions. The CO2 response in this patient has been preserved with only a mild decrease in minute ventilation. Of the choices given, the most likely drug being administered is dexmedetomidine. Dexmedetomidine is a central alpha-2 receptor agonist with multiple effects including sedation, anxiolysis, mild analgesia, and hypnosis. Dexmedetomidine is said to emulate normal sleep as is evidenced by the fact that patients will usually respond to things that would awaken them from normal sleep and they have a normal EEG pattern. Dexmedetomidine does this by stimulating the locus coeruleus which ultimately leads to a decrease in histamine release from the tuberomammillary bodies and induces a sleep state. A major advantage of dexmedetomidine is that respiratory drive is preserved, and awakening for neurologic evaluation or commands in the ICU or during operations is maintained. Dexmedetomidine, like clonidine, also reduces opioid consumption and reduces MAC. Negative side effects include bradycardia and hypotension or hypertension (if bolused quickly or combined with anticholinergic medications); these are dose dependent. Rapid bolus creates hypertension by stimulation of peripheral alpha-2 receptors. Studies have outlined that with low dose infusions (< 0.1 mcg/kg/hour) generally there is a reduction in SVR, heart rate, and blood pressure with little effect on cardiac output. However when doses are increased to 2-3 mcg/kg/hour then an increase in SVR, PVR, and MAP with a decrease in heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure is seen, thus dose needs to be titrated accordingly. Dexmedetomidine cessation is not associated with a withdrawal syndrome like its counterpart clonidine. Benzodiazepines like midazolam are known to cause a decrease in response to CO2 and hypoxia even at sedative doses and this effect is augmented when combined with other CNS depressants, particularly opioids. Propofol is a significant respiratory depressant and decreases the ventilatory response to CO2 and oxygen and often induces apnea with induction doses. Opioids like, remifentanil significantly reduce the response to CO2 and oxygen and produces apnea that is dose related. Midazolam diminishes CO2 and hypoxic ventilatory responsiveness which is exacerbated by administration of other CNS depressants.
Answer C: Propofol causes a significant depression of ventilatory response to hypoxia and CO2.
Answer D: Opioids, like remifentanil, have a significant depressive effect on ventilatory response to CO2 and hypoxia. Respiratory effects of dexmedetomidine include a decrease in minute ventilation with a preserved carbon dioxide response curve and no change in arterial oxygenation. When hydrophilic opioids are administered via epidural route, they have a slower onset of analgesia, extensive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) spread, and longer duration of action and can produce delayed respiratory depression and a higher incidence of side effects as a result of their cephalic spread to the medulla. Opioids synergistically enhance the analgesic effects of epidural local anesthetics without prolonging the motor blockade. Epidural opioids cross the dura mater and arachnoid membrane to eventually reach the CSF and dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Lipophilic opioids partition into the epidural fat and are therefore found in lower concentrations in the CSF compared with hydrophilic opioids. Hydrophilic opioids (eg, morphine, hydromorphone) have a higher degree of solubility within the CSF, allowing for significant cephalad spread. Epidural-administered hydrophilic opioids have a slow onset and prolonged duration of action. Because of their slow onset of action, hydrophilic opioids are less suitable than lipophilic opioids for patient-controlled epidural analgesia. Lipophilic opioids (eg, fentanyl) have a rapid onset and a much shorter duration of action. When they are administered through the epidural route, lipophilic opioids are rapidly taken up by the epidural fat and redistributed into the systemic circulation, resulting in poor bioavailability to the spinal cord. Clinical pharmacology of epidural opioids Characteristics Disadvantages Hydrophilic opioids Slower onset Longer duration Higher CSF solubility Extensive CSF spread Delayed respiratory depression Delayed onset of analgesia Higher incidence of side effects Lipophilic opioids Faster onset Shorter duration Low CSF solubility Systemic absorption Brief single-dose analgesia Limited thoracic analgesia with lumbar administration Minimal CSF spread Lower incidence of side effects Rapid analgesia Abbreviation: CSF, cerebrospinal fluid. Delayed respiratory depression is seen with hydrophilic opioids administered through the epidural route. This is because of their slow cephalic spread compared to lipophilic opioids, which have minimal CSF spread.
Answer C: Hydrophilic opioids have a higher incidence of side effects compared to lipophilic opioids. Side effects of neuraxial opioids are dose-dependent and occur as a result of extensive rostral spread of the opioids, which directly stimulates the medullary vomiting and respiratory centers, resulting in a delayed onset of respiratory depression and vomiting.
Answer D: Hydrophilic opioids have a slower onset of action due to their low lipid solubility. Epidural-administered hydrophilic opioids (eg, morphine, hydromorphone) have a slower onset, a longer duration of action, a higher incidence of side effects, a delayed respiratory depression, an extensive cerebrospinal fluid spread, and a delayed onset of analgesia compared to lipophilic opioids (eg, fentanyl). This is mainly due to their low lipid solubility of hydrophilic opioids.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "Epidural Opioids: Pharmacokinetics" Gropper M, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Fade is described as a progressive decrease in the evoked response during prolonged or repeated nerve stimulation. The occurrence of fade after prolonged or repeated nerve stimulation is most characteristic of a phase II depolarizing block or a nondepolarizing block. Phase I depolarizing block is a typical depolarizing neuromuscular block seen in patients with normal pseudocholinesterase activity who are given a normal induction dose of succinylcholine (0.5-1 mg/kg). A phase I depolarizing block is characterized by no fade in response to a train-of-four (TOF) or tetanic stimulation, and no posttetanic facilitation or transmission occurs. However, patients who have genetically abnormal pseudocholinesterase levels can undergo a phase II depolarizing block, commonly referred to as dual, mixed, desensitizing block. Phase II depolarizing block can also occur in patients with genetically normal pseudocholinesterase levels after prolonged infusions or repeated bolus doses of succinylcholine. The presence of fade during prolonged or repeated nerve stimulation is characteristic of a nondepolarizing block or of a phase II depolarizing block if succinylcholine has been given. A phase II depolarizing block is also characterized by fade in the response to tetanic stimulation and the occurrence of posttetanic facilitation of transmission. Evoked responses during depolarizing (phase I and phase II) blocks Abbreviation: TOF, train-of-four. A phase I depolarizing block does not exhibit fade during repeated nerve stimulation; rather, a phase I depolarizing block exhibits a constant but diminished response to TOF or tetany.
Answer C: Tetany is a pattern of electrical stimulation used to monitor neuromuscular function defined as a sustained stimulus of 50 to 100 Hz lasting approximately five seconds. Tetany is not characterized by a fade in the response to repeated nerve stimulation.
Answer D: Upregulation of acetylcholine receptors can occur in stroke, spinal cord injuries (seen only at >24 hours, peaking at 7-10 days after injury), prolonged immobilization (patients immobilized for more than two weeks), burn injuries, and certain neurologic disorders (multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barre syndrome). Downregulation of acetylcholine receptors occurs in patients with myasthenia gravis, organophosphate poisoning, and anticholinesterase poisoning. A single dose of succinylcholine would not cause proliferation or upregulation of acetylcholine receptors and is not associated with fade. A phase II depolarizing block is characterized by the fade in response to prolonged or repeated nerve stimulation. A phase I depolarizing block is characterized by no fade in response to train-of-four or tetanic stimulation. Phase II depolarizing blocks can be seen with succinylcholine after repetitive bolus doses or a prolonged infusion. Echothiophate inhibits pseudocholinesterase, thereby potentiating the effects of succinylcholine. Echothiophate is an anticholinesterase used to treat refractory glaucoma by causing miosis. Systemic absorption can cause up to a 95% decrease in plasma butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) function. Patients using echothiophate eye drops have demonstrated prolonged neuromuscular block after succinylcholine administration. It may take up to 4-6 weeks after discontinuation of the drug for normal butyrylcholinesterase activity to return. Cyclopentolate is a topical anticholinergic ocular drug used to induce mydriasis for ocular procedures. Systemic absorption can occur and lead to central nervous system (CNS) signs and symptoms of anticholinergic toxicity. Signs and symptoms include dysarthria, tachycardia, disorientation, psychosis, and convulsions.
Answer C: Topical epinephrine is sometimes used for open-angle glaucoma treatment. Certain concentrations of topical epinephrine have been associated with anxiety, tachycardia, and hypertension.
Answer D: Timolol is a nonselective β-adrenergic blocking agent used topically for the treatment of glaucoma. Systemic absorption can occur and lead to severe bronchospasm and bradycardia. Betaxolol is a selective β-1 antagonist that is relatively oculospecific with minimal systemic side effects. Severe bradycardia may occur, however, when combined with other oral βreceptor antagonists. Despite its oculospecificity, betaxolol should be used with caution in patients who have severe obstructive pulmonary pathology. The use of topical echothiophate eye drops for greater than 1 month can be associated with up to a 95% decrease in the function of plasma butyrylcholinesterase. Normal activity returns within 4-6 weeks after discontinuation. Succinylcholine administration during this time may result in prolonged neuromuscular blockade.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Echothiophate: Pseudocholinesterase Effect" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 1328.

Abciximab is a platelet aggregation inhibitor mainly used during and after coronary artery procedures like angioplasty. It functions as a glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor blocker. Antiplatelet therapy is indicated for patients at risk of cerebral vascular accident, myocardial infarction, or other vascular thrombosis complications. There are several mechanisms for platelet dysfunction including COX inhibition, PDE inhibition, ADP receptor antagonism, and GP IIb/IIIa receptor antagonism. GP IIb/IIIa receptor blockers inhibit the cross-linkage of fibrinogen, the final step in the common hemostatic pathway for platelet aggregation. They include abciximab, tirofiban, and eptifibatide. These agents are administered only intravenously and primarily used for management of acute coronary syndrome. Their effects can be monitored with ACTs and are reversible with the clearance of the drug. Most of these agents have renal excretion and have half-lives around 2.5 hours except for abciximab which has a significantly longer half-life (12 hours) and clinical effects that last for approximately 48 hours. All of these drugs cause thrombocytopenia, but the effect is strongest with abciximab with an incidence of about 2.5% as opposed to 0.5% with the other receptor antagonists. Direct thrombin inhibitors are a class of medication that act as anticoagulants by directly inhibiting the enzyme thrombin. Lepirudin and desirudin are recombinant forms of hirudin, a naturally occurring anticoagulant. Argatroban and bivalirudin are synthetic agents in the same class. All four of these drugs directly inhibit thrombin in its free and fibrin-bound states. None of them are immunogenic and so there is no risk of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), although antibodies to lepirudin can cause bleeding complications. Clinical effects can be monitored with ACT or aPTT measurements. They are all approved for use in the United States, in particular for the treatment of HIT.
Answer C: P2Y12 ADP receptor antagonists, such as clopidogrel, prasugrel, and ticlopidine, prevent the expression of GP IIb/ IIIa on the surface of activated platelets, thereby inhibiting platelet adhesion and aggregation. These drugs are used for patients with coronary artery disease to prevent myocardial infarction, in-stent thrombosis, or for patients with cerebrovascular or peripheral artery disease to inhibit thromboembolism. Clopidogrel is the most commonly prescribed agent in this class and acts as a noncompetitive and irreversible antagonist. It is an inactive prodrug that requires oxidation to its active metabolite. Recently, a genetic polymorphism was discovered that results in the inability to metabolize clopidogrel making it ineffective and putting patients at risk of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality. The FDA put a black box warning on the medication to remind clinicians to monitor the activity.
Answer D: PDE inhibitors are primarily used for stroke prophylaxis since they increase the production of cAMP, which is an active inhibitor of platelet aggregation. These medications are rarely the first-line drug of choice for patients with cerebrovascular disease, but rather used in conjunction with aspirin therapy. Dipyridamole is the prime therapeutic agent in this class, but caffeine, aminophylline, and theophylline also result in reversible platelet dysfunction. Abciximab is a GP IIb/IIIa receptor blocker mainly used during and after coronary artery procedures like angioplasty. Mnemonic: abciximab can be remembered as abCIX (six) imab, where II(b) * III(a) = CIX (six). ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Anti-Platelet Drugs: Mechanism of Action" Barash Clinical Anesthesia. 7th Edition. Pages 437-441. Miller's Anesthesia. 7th Edition. Pages 1771-1773.

Chronic carbamazepine does not prolong the effect of vecuronium, but may shorten the effect instead. Vecuronium is an aminosteroid neuromuscular blocking medication. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents act by competitively inhibiting acetylcholine on the nicotinic receptor at the neuromuscular junction. Non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents are large and therefore unable to cross barriers like the blood-brain barrier and blood placental barrier. Carbamazepine is an anti-seizure medication that acts on voltage-gated sodium channels. Acute use of anticonvulsants can potentiate neuromuscular blockade while chronic use can attenuate neuromuscular blockade by reducing the duration of action of the blockade. Carbamazepine is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 system and induces the P450 system. The P450 system is also involved in the metabolism of vecuronium. Patients treated with carbamazepine have an increased metabolism of vecuronium. Prolong Non-Depolarizing Blockade: - Acute use of anticonvulsants (e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine) - Antibiotics (e.g. streptomycin, clindamycin, tetracyclines, aminoglycosides) - Antiarrhythmics (e.g. calcium channel blockers) - Dantrolene - Ketamine - Local anesthetics (high doses only) - Lithium - Magnesium - Volatile anesthetic agents Shorten Non-Depolarizing Blockade: - Chronic use of anticonvulsants (e.g. phenytoin, carbamazepine) - Cholinesterase inhibitors (e.g. neostigmine) Gentamicin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic. The aminoglycoside antibiotics prolong the effects of aminosteroidal neuromuscular blocking agents. Aminoglycosides inhibit the release of acetylcholine from alpha motor neurons. Clindamycin is a lincosamide antibiotic that has pre- and post-junction effects that prolong blockade at extremely high doses. Antibiotics like penicillin and cephalosporins have no effect on neuromuscular blockade. Aminoglycosides, polymyxins, lincomycin, and clindamycin primarily inhibit the prejunctional release of acetylcholine and also depress postjunctional nAChR sensitivity to acetylcholine. Tetracyclines, on the other hand, have postjunctional activity only. When combined with non-depolarizing blockers, they can potentiate neuromuscular blockade.
Answer C: Hypocalcemia potentiates neuromuscular blockade because calcium is important for the release of vesicles containing acetylcholine from nerves at the neuromuscular junction. When calcium levels are low, less acetylcholine is released. With less acetylcholine being released there is less competition at the acetylcholine receptor and neuromuscular blockers have a greater effect. Hypermagnesemia acts similarly by blocking calcium from entering alpha motor neurons and preventing the release of some of the acetylcholine containing vesicles.
Answer D: Desflurane is a volatile anesthetic with a low blood:gas partition coefficient of 0.42. The low blood gas coefficient means that very little desflurane is dissolved in tissues, but that desflurane is able to rapidly equilibrate with tissues resulting in quick onset and termination of effects. This rapid equilibration into tissues including muscle is the reason why desflurane potentiates neuromuscular blockade more than other volatile anesthetics. The location of potentiation is likely at the neuromuscular junction and occurs in a dose-dependent fashion. Potentiation from greatest to least for volatile anesthetics is desflurane > sevoflurane > isoflurane. The presence of volatile anesthetics potentiates neuromuscular blockade as does hypocalcemia, hypothermia, and hypokalemia. Desflurane causes greater blockade potentiation than sevoflurane or isoflurane. Lithium and magnesium potentiate neuromuscular blockade by antagonizing calcium, as do calcium channel blocking medications.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Prolonged NMB Risk Factors" Miller, Ronald D. Miller’s Anesthesia. 9th edition. Ch. 27: Pharmacology of Neuromuscular Blocking Drugs. UpToDate. Hormonal changes during pregnancy, mediated primarily via progesterone, lead to greater sensitivity to the nerve conduction blockade by local anesthetics. However, the half-life of aminoamide local anesthetics remains unchanged. Congestive heart failure is a state known to decrease hepatic blood flow, thus resulting in slowed degradation of aminoamide local anesthetics.
Answer B: The enzymatic degradation of aminoamide local anesthetics is impaired in end-stage liver disease.
Answer C: The half-life of aminoamide local anesthetics is prolonged in neonates due to their immature hepatic enzyme systems. Aminoamide local anesthetics such as lidocaine, bupivacaine, and ropivacaine are principally metabolized by enzymatic degradation in the liver, and their half-lives are prolonged in states of impaired liver function. Tizanidine is often prescribed for musculoskeletal pain, but its mechanism of action is via alpha-2 receptor agonism. Endothelin receptor antagonists include bosentan, ambrisentan, and tezosentan. Bosentan, which is often prescribed for pulmonary hypertension, causes vasodilation by blocking the action of endothelin. Endothelin is a peptide produced by the endothelium that normally binds its receptor and causes vasoconstriction. Endothelin is critical for vascular hemostasis, but its overexpression can contribute to hypertensive disorders. Beta-2 agonists include drugs like terbutaline, ritodrine, and albuterol. Smooth muscle beta-adrenergic receptors are coupled with G proteins. When stimulated, intracellular cAMP is increased leading to a cascade that ultimately results in smooth muscle relaxation. This mechanism is manifested by vasodilation, bronchial smooth muscle relaxation, and decreased uterine tone. Tizanidine, clonidine, and dexmedetomidine are alpha-2 receptor agonists. Alpha-2 receptor stimulation causes inhibition of norepinephrine release at the vascular prejunctional terminals. This form of negative feedback leads to vasodilation. Yohimbine is an alpha-2 antagonist that generally does not cause vasodilation and has been marketed as a dietary supplement or for sexual dysfunction (not approved by FDA). It is used in veterinary medicine to reverse sedation caused by alpha-2 agonists like xylazine. Bosentan is prescribed for pulmonary hypertension as it causes pulmonary vasodilation via endothelin receptor blockade.
Answer B: Terbutaline is a tocolytic that can cause vasodilation via beta-2 receptor agonism.
Answer D: Yohimbine is an alpha-2 receptor antagonist and may cause vasoconstriction. Tizanidine is an alpha-2 agonist.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Vasodilators: Others." Basics of Anesthesia. Autonomic Nervous System in 6th Edition. Pages 73-74.

After the age of 30 years, the minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) decreases with age by approximately 6% per decade for inhaled anesthetics. The MAC of sevoflurane would decrease by 6% from the age of 64 to 74 (one decade) for a woman. Minimum alveolar concentration is the alveolar concentration of an inhaled anesthetic that will prevent movement to a surgical stimulus in 50% of patients. The higher the MAC the lower the potency, and the lower the MAC the higher the potency. Each inhaled anesthetic has its own MAC value. Loss of consciousness will often occur well before the MAC value, typically at 0.4-0.5 MAC. Factors can increase or decrease the MAC (see table below). Other MAC values include MAC-awake, the alveolar concentration in which patients opens their eyes to command (MAC 0.15-0.5), and MAC-BAR, the alveolar concentration that blunts the adrenergic response, which is typically 50% higher than 1 MAC. Factors affecting MAC* Increase MAC Decrease MAC • Drugs that increase central neurotransmitters1 • Hyperthermia • Hypernatremia • Chronic ethanol abuse • Drugs that decrease central neurotransmitters2 • Older age • Metabolic acidosis • Hypoxia • Hypothermia • Hyponatremia • Acute ethanol ingestion • Lithium • Pregnancy • Administration of other anesthetics Abbreviation: MAC, minimum alveolar concentration. *This is not an exhaustive list; many more factors will decrease MAC. 1Acute amphetamine use, cocaine, ephedrine, levodopa, and monoamine oxidase inhibitors. 2Chronic amphetamine use, α-methyldopa, and reserpine. The MAC decreased by 6% for each decade.
Answer C: The MAC would decrease by 24% from 40 to 80 years of age.
Answer D: Because MAC decreases 6% per decade after the age of 30 years, a 27% reduction would occur over 40 to 50 years beyond the age of 30 (between 70 and 80 years of age). The minimum alveolar concentration decreases with age and decreases by approximately 6% per decade after the age of 30 years for inhaled anesthetics. Red-haired women have a 19% increase in MAC compared to other dark-hair women in addition to the altered pain threshold. This may be due to mutations in the melanocyte-stimulating hormone receptor (MC1R) allele. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "MAC: Age Effects (B)" Gropper M, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. Fibrinolysis (fibrin breakdown), a normal hematologic activity that leads to removal of thrombus when endothelium heals, is conducted mostly by the enzyme plasmin, the product of cleavage of plasminogen by tissue plasminogen activator (tPA). Plasmin is not normally freely circulating in the plasma; rather, it is bound to the surface of fibrin clots. The reasons for this are 1) that plasmin is produced when a ternary complex is formed between fibrin, tPA, and plasminogen (this increases the activity of tPA as well as the local concentration of plasminogen); and 2) that any circulating plasmin is quickly inhibited by α2 antiplasmin. Fibrinolysis can be excessive and lead to bleeding, e.g., after cardiopulmonary bypass (cardiopulmonary bypass causes the endothelium to release tPA). Currently available antifibrinolytic agents (aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid) are analogs of the amino acid lysine, and as such they competitively inhibit the binding of plasmin(ogen) lysine binding sites to the lysine residues in fibrin. In other words, they prevent the formation of the ternary complex noted above. Antifibrinolytic agents have been shown to reduce total perioperative blood loss and the number of patients transfused in major cardiac, orthopedic, or liver surgery. Currently, the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) guidelines give a recommendation to "use" such agents for prevention of bleeding in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass, but only of "consider using" for other indications. Fibrinogen replacement, in the form of cryoprecipitate, is indicated according to the 2015 ASA Practice Guidelines for Perioperative Blood Management in the following situations: fibrinolysis, massive transfusion, and low fibrinogen concentration (definitions of "low" vary and are typically higher in pregnancy).
Answer C: Thrombin has many prothrombotic actions. It activates factors I, V, VIII, XI, and XIII, as well as platelets. Thrombin is inhibited by argatroban, dabigatran, and bivalirudin. Aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid are lysine analogs that prevent the formation of the ternary complex between plasminogen, tPA, and fibrin, thus inhibiting plasmin formation and fibrin degradation. The 2015 American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) guidelines recommend the use of antifibrinolytic therapy for prophylaxis of the use of allogeneic blood transfusion in patients undergoing cardiopulmonary bypass. 2-Chloroprocaine is rapidly metabolized by plasma cholinesterase, leaving very little drug available to cross the placenta. Local anesthetics cross the placenta via passive diffusion, but the rate and degree of their transfer are dependent on several factors. More highly protein-bound drugs cross less because only the unbound portion of the drug is able to cross the placenta. More fat-soluble drugs also cross more readily as do those with a higher percentage of the drug in the nonionized form. Nonionized drugs cross more easily than ionized drugs. Fetal pH is also usually less than maternal pH, which can lead to ion trapping and greater drug concentrations in the fetus (H+ ions bind to non-ionized form, trapping drug in fetal circulation). Chloroprocaine does not participate in ion trapping and, thus, is a useful agent in the presence of a decompensated (eg, acidotic) fetus. 2-Chloroprocaine is an ester-type local anesthetic and is broken down in the blood by plasma cholinesterase, just as all ester local anesthetics are. The amide local anesthetics undergo hepatic metabolism. 2-Chloroprocaine is the most rapidly metabolized of all of the local anesthetics, having a plasma half-life of ~12 seconds in adults. Its action on the neuron also has a quick onset of action of about 6 to 10 minutes, but it blocks nerve conduction for only 30 to 60 minutes; therefore, frequent redosing is required. 2-Chloroprocaine is thought to be safe for use in obstetric patients because its rapid plasma metabolism leaves little to no drug available for placental transfer. In addition, its rapid metabolism allows doses with higher concentrations (eg, 3%) compared with other local anesthetics, leading to a very rapid onset. A surgical block for an emergency cesarean section can therefore be obtained very quickly and with little concern for the placental transfer of the drug. Disadvantages of 2-chloroprocaine include apparent antagonistic effects on subsequently administered local anesthetics and opioids (although some of these findings have been challenged) and neurotoxicity reported after accidental intrathecal injection of older formulations of 2-chloroprocaine. Bupivacaine crosses the placenta but to a lesser extent than lidocaine because of the high degree of protein binding of bupivacaine. In general, the more protein-bound amide-type local anesthetics (eg, bupivacaine and ropivacaine) less readily cross the placenta compared with less protein-bound local anesthetics (eg, lidocaine). Amide anesthetics cross the placenta more than ester-type anesthetics (eg, 2-chloroprocaine).
Answer C: Lidocaine crosses the placenta and can become "ion trapped" in the fetal circulation. Ion trapping occurs when the local anesthetic becomes charged in the more acidic fetal blood and begins to accumulate in the fetal blood. Fetal-maternal lidocaine ratio can reach 1.2 during fetal acidosis, which increases the risk of fetal local anesthetic toxicity. This effect can become more important with large epidural doses, obstetrical blocks (eg, pudendal, paracervical), or intravenous lidocaine used at intubation. This effect is most likely to be clinically significant in the premature fetus, which has increased blood-brain barrier permeability. Administration of 2-chloroprocaine results in the least amount of placental transfer of all local anesthetics because 2-chloroprocaine is rapidly metabolized in the plasma by plasma cholinesterase. Atropine or glycopyrrolate is an antimuscarinic that can be given alongside neostigmine to prevent the side effects associated with neostigmine. In the absence of atropine or glycopyrrolate, neostigmine will increase peristalsis, which can lead to nausea and diarrhea. Atropine can prevent these undesirable side effects. Neostigmine is an anticholinesterase that functions by increasing the amount of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by competitively inhibiting the cholinesterase enzyme. Neostigmine increases acetylcholine, which competes with nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents for nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Neostigmine is often the preferred anticholinesterase used for reversal because of its quick onset of action, strong affinity for the cholinesterase enzyme, and fewer muscarinic side effects compared with other agents. The primary side effects of anticholinesterase administration are bradycardia and increased gastrointestinal activity (nausea and diarrhea), but other side effects include increased salivation and mucous secretion, miosis, increased urination, and increased sweating. Giving atropine can prevent the increase, not the decrease, in airway secretions that can be seen when only neostigmine is given.
Answer B: Giving atropine can prevent the increase, not the decrease, in sweating which can be seen when only neostigmine is given.
Answer C: Giving atropine can prevent the decrease, not the increase, in heart rate (bradycardia) that is often seen when only neostigmine is given. Atropine and glycopyrrolate are antimuscarinics that can be given alongside neostigmine for the reversal of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade to prevent the primary side effects associated with neostigmine such as bradycardia and increased peristalsis (nausea and diarrhea). Pulmonary toxicity correlates most closely with total cumulative dose and occurs several months to years after the initiation of amiodarone therapy. Although acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) can occur in the acute period, interstitial pneumonitis takes several months to develop. Amiodarone is a class III antiarrhythmic agent, although it has properties of both class I and II antiarrhythmics. It is used for atrial and ventricular arrhythmias and can be given intravenously or orally. It inhibits inactivated (phase 0) sodium channels, inhibits sympathetic activity by noncompetitive beta-receptor blockade, and blocks L-type (slow) calcium channels. Many of the adverse effects associated with oral amiodarone are due to tissue accumulation of the drug over long-term therapy and are not seen with short-term intravenous use. Intravenous amiodarone has a different electrophysiologic and pharmacologic profile from its oral counterpart. The intravenous form produces a smaller increase in action potential duration in the myocardium, has little effect on sinus cycle length, and it may have a more potent and rapid antiadrenergic activity. Intravenous amiodarone can cause hypotension, cardiac effects, acute respiratory distress syndrome, nausea, vomiting, abnormal liver function tests, and phlebitis when given through a peripheral intravenous line. The cardiac side effects include bradycardia, asystole, heart failure, and shock. Oral amiodarone therapy has well-known side effects that can cause dysfunction of almost every organ system. The pulmonary toxicity is likely the most severe and is the most common cause for death due to amiodarone therapy. Chronic interstitial pneumonitis occurs in up to 20% of patients and presents as a nonproductive cough and dyspnea. Cardiac disturbances also include prolonged QT interval and torsades de pointes. A transient rise in the aminotransferase concentrations may occur and the medication should be discontinued if a two-fold elevation is observed. Thyroid dysfunction is a common complication and can result in hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Chronic therapy has also been associated with a slate-blue/grey discoloration of the skin and abnormalities with color vision. Unlike digoxin, which causes yellow/green vision problems, amiodarone is associated with blue vision problems. Asystole is a potential acute response to amiodarone therapy.
Answer C: Nausea and vomiting are acute side effects of amiodarone administration. Adverse effects of acute amiodarone therapy include nausea, vomiting, phlebitis, hypotension, bradycardia, asystole, heart failure, shock, and acute respiratory distress syndrome. Chronic therapy affects PFTs, LFTs, and TFTs (pulmonary, liver, thyroid) and can also cause a blue/grey skin discoloration.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Midazolam is a benzodiazepine which should be avoided during pregnancy, especially early in pregnancy when anatomical structures are developing. Use during the third trimester is associated with floppy infant syndrome and significant neonatal withdrawal symptoms. Midazolam is pregnancy category D. This means it should be used only in life-threatening emergencies when no safer drug is available and there exists positive evidence of human fetal risk. Benzodiazepines have been associated with cleft lip and palate in animal studies, however, the association in humans is controversial and a single dose has not been associated with teratogenicity. Perinatal use of diazepam has been associated with hypotonia, hypothermia, and respiratory depression. The teratogenic risk of benzodiazepines appears small at most. There may be a small risk of preterm birth and low birth weight. It is recommended that long-term use of benzodiazepines be avoided due to the association with neonatal withdrawal. Benzodiazepines are used in anesthesia as anxiolytics, sedatives, and hypnotics. Their actions are exerted through GABAa receptors. The four benzodiazepines commonly used in anesthesia are midazolam, lorazepam, temazepam, and diazepam. Benzodiazepines are metabolized in the liver; therefore, caution should be used with these medications in patients with liver dysfunction. Also, benzodiazepines are excreted through the kidneys and caution should be used with these medications in patients with renal insufficiency. For example, midazolam is metabolized by hepatic enzymes resulting in active and inactive metabolites. The active metabolite is subsequently cleared by the kidneys. This process may cause high concentrations of this metabolite if a patient has renal insufficiency. Etomidate has been used in pregnant women who are hemodynamically unstable. Potential side effects include pain on injection, postoperative nausea, myoclonus, and adrenal suppression. Etomidate is pregnancy category C.
Answer C: Propofol is used to produce a rapid and smooth induction of anesthesia. It has not been shown to be associated with any teratogenicity. Propofol is pregnancy category B.
Answer D: Rocuronium is a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent which acts by competitively blocking the binding of acetylcholine to its postsynaptic receptors. Rocuronium has not been associated with teratogenicity. Rocuronium is pregnancy category C. Benzodiazepines should be avoided in pregnancy. Chronic use of acetazolamide leads to hypokalemic metabolic acidosis. Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, preventing the resorption of sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate in the proximal tubule. Carbonic anhydrases maintain a proton gradient that increases hydrogen ion availability for secretion into the tubular lumen and are integral for converting bicarbonate and hydrogen ions into water and carbon dioxide, promoting bicarbonate reabsorption. Inhibition by acetazolamide, therefore, leads to a decrease in sodium bicarbonate reabsorption. A metabolic acidosis ensues from the loss of bicarbonate in the urine. Potassium excretion is increased indirectly via increased sodium and water delivery to the collecting ducts, where sodium within the collecting duct is exchanged for potassium to recover a portion of the high sodium concentration within the collecting duct. Acetazolamide also increases urinary calcium excretion to a small extent. Calcium excretion increases indirectly through reduced sodium reabsorption, which leads to decreased water reabsorption and, ultimately, inhibition of calcium reabsorption in the proximal tubule. This set of lab findings is most consistent with loop diuretics administration. Loop diuretics, such as furosemide, act on Na+K+2Cl−cotransporters in the loop of Henle to decrease sodium chloride reabsorption. Loop diuretics lead to increased potassium excretion, partially because increased delivery of sodium to the cortical collecting ducts leads to more reabsorption of sodium by principal cells there, which must be balanced by increased potassium efflux to preserve electroneutrality within the tubular fluid. Loop diuretics also result in urinary loss of both calcium and magnesium, but overall loss may depend on dosing and preexisting deficits. Because total body calcium concentrations are generally more tightly regulated than magnesium concentrations, hypocalcemia is less common compared with hypomagnesemia.
Answer B: This set of lab findings is most consistent with thiazide administration. Thiazides blocks Na+Cl−cotransport at the distal tubule. This leads to hyponatremia more significant than that with loop diuretics because thiazides do not lead to water excretion to the same degree as loop diuretics. By increasing distal sodium and water delivery, thiazides also increase potassium excretion, partially for the same reason that loop diuretics lead to increased potassium excretion. Decreased distal sodium reabsorption from thiazides leads to increased proximal and distal calcium reabsorption. Because they promote hypocalciuria and, possibly, hypercalcemia, thiazides are useful for treating nephrolithiasis and hypocalcemia, with increased bone mineralization and reduced incidence of hip fractures observed from long-term use. Chronic use of thiazides may lead to hypomagnesemia from renal wasting.
Answer C: This set of lab findings is most consistent with potassium-sparing diuretics administration. Potassium-sparing diuretics block the epithelial sodium channel (eg, amiloride, triamterene) or the mineralocorticoid receptor (eg, spironolactone, eplerenone) distally at the collecting tubules. Potassium-sparing diuretics are weak diuretics that are often used in combination with other diuretics to minimize hypokalemia. They cause hyperkalemia due to blocking sodium transport in the principal cells of the collecting ducts. Potassium-sparing diuretics in the cortical collecting tubule inhibit the reabsorption of sodium while increasing that of calcium accordingly. The effect on calcium transport is mild or minimal. There is evidence that potassiumsparing diuretics lead to magnesium retention, but serum magnesium changes may be minimal. Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase, preventing the resorption of sodium, chloride, and bicarbonate in the proximal tubule. Chronic administration of acetazolamide leads to metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Acetazolamide: Effects on ion conc (A)” Gropper M, et al. The fat compartment has the largest effective volume (eg, 620 L for sevoflurane) due to a large fat:bood partition coefficient (48:1). In contrast, the central nervous system (CNS) has a much smaller effective volume (eg, 2.4 L for sevoflurane). A larger effective volume requires a higher amount of anesthetic to raise the partial pressure in that compartment. In a four-compartment model for pharmacokinetics of the inhaled anesthetics, the compartments are the alveoli (central compartment), the vessel right group (VRG), the fat group, and the muscle group. The intercompartment rate constants (k) and the effective volume of each compartment are the key characteristics of each compartment. When a tissue group receives a larger amount of blood, the communication between two compartments and the equilibration in partial pressures with the alveoli (a larger k) is faster. • The VRG includes the CNS, liver, and kidney. Despite only accounting for 10% of the human body mass, this group receives 70% of the cardiac output under resting conditions. Because the CNS resides here, general anesthetic action depends on the partial pressure in the VRG. • The fat group receives only 10% of the cardiac output and thus equilibrates with the alveoli slowly, rarely equilibrating before any normal length procedure is concluded. The other reason for the slow equilibration is the large effective volume due to the fat solubility of volatile anesthetics. • The muscle group is intermediate between the VRG and the fat groups, having both a moderate capacity to absorb anesthetics and a moderate speed to equilibrate with the alveoli. When cardiac output increases, the k increases for all three compartments, allowing faster equilibration between compartments. A result of this is the persistent draining of volatile anesthetics from the alveoli compartment to the large fat compartment, slowing the rise in alveoli partial pressure, which leads to a slowed induction speed and alveolar concentration (FA) to inspired concentration (FI) rise. The four-compartment model also describes the changes in FA at emergence. Just as with intravenous medications, with inhaled anesthetics, there are distribution, elimination, and terminal phases. In the distribution phase, because the partial pressure of the VRG is higher than that of the muscle and fat groups, diffusion moves anesthetics toward the muscle and fat groups. In the elimination phase, the partial pressure in the muscle group equalizes with that of the VRG, and anesthetics move from the muscle group to the fat group. In the terminal phase, the fat group slowly releases its large store of anesthetics to the other compartments, including the alveoli, to be eliminated. Anesthetic partial pressures most quickly equilibrate between alveoli and the VRG and most slowly equilibrate between alveoli and fat. This difference is primarily due to differences in the fraction of cardiac output received and is represented by the k.
Answer B: Increased cardiac output increases the k for all three compartments, allowing faster equilibration between compartments. A result of this is the persistent draining of volatile anesthetics from the alveoli compartment to the large fat compartment, slowing the rise in alveoli partial pressure, which leads to a slowed induction speed and FA:FI rise.
Answer C: In the initial distribution phase immediately after an inhaled anesthetic is discontinued, the anesthetic agent diffuses from the alveoli and VRG to the muscle and fat groups (in addition to being exhaled). In the terminal phase, long after an inhaled anesthetic has been discontinued, the anesthetic agent diffuses from the fat group to the alveoli group, which then gets exhaled. In a four-compartment model for pharmacokinetics of the volatile anesthetics, the intercompartment rate constants and effective volume of each compartment are the key characteristics of each compartment. Tramadol’s inhibition of serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake may lower the seizure threshold. Tramadol is an opioid medication with some serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibition as well. It is considered low-potency, 10% that of morphine. Although available in other formulations, it is conventionally prescribed as an immediate-release tablet with a one-hour onset time and peak effect in 2-4 hours. As a mu-agonist opioid, tramadol can cause constipation, itching, and nausea. In contrast to other opioid medications, however, it can cause seizures. Tramadol is more likely to cause seizure at high doses or when given to patients with a pre-existing seizure disorder such as epilepsy. Answers A & B: These opioids do not lower the seizure threshold. Although meperidine’s metabolite normeperidine is neurotoxic and can cause seizures when the metabolite accumulates, it does not lower the seizure threshold. Tramadol is an opioid medication that lowers the seizure threshold.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Opioids: Seizure Threshold (B)” Clinical Anesthesiology. Succinylcholine is safe for use in normokalemic renal failure patients. Serum potassium increases approximately 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine administration. This increase is not prevented by a defasciculating dose of a non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocker. Patients with preexisting hyperkalemia, such as those with renal failure, do not have a greater than expected increase in potassium levels with succinylcholine but, depending on the potassium level before the administration of succinylcholine, the absolute level can still meet the toxic range. Other conditions in which an upregulation of extrajunctional receptors may result in life-threatening hyperkalemia following succinylcholine administration include neuromuscular disorders (e.g. Guillain-Barré syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, and Friedrich ataxia), stroke, major trauma (e.g. crush injury), and prolonged immobility with disease. Succinylcholine should be avoided after 24 hours and for up to one year following burns of >10% total body surface area. This is due to proliferation of extrajunctional receptors causing a potentially significant hyperkalemia which can lead to cardiac arrest.
Answer C: Hyperkalemia has been reported with myotonia and muscular dystrophies, including Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and cardiac arrests have been reported in children before the diagnosis of the disease has been made. This has led some clinicians to take the position that succinylcholine should not be used routinely in boys under the age of eight. Of note, rhabdomyolysis can occur in these patients after succinylcholine which is either the main cause or contributing cause of severe hyperkalemia.
Answer D: In spinal cord injury patients, the amount of potassium released correlates with the extent of the acquired motor deficit. It is considered safe to administer succinylcholine for the first 48 hours after an acute injury. The potassium increase is maximal between 4 weeks and 5 months after spinal injury. Serum potassium increases approximately 0.5 mEq/L after succinylcholine administration in most patients, even those with chronic renal disease. Severe hyperkalemia leading to cardiac dysrhythmias and arrest has been described in patients after spinal cord injuries, neuromuscular disorders (e.g. Guillain-Barré syndrome, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, and Friedrich ataxia), stroke, major trauma (e.g. crush injury), extensive burns, and prolonged immobility with disease. This hyperkalemia is a result of upregulation of extrajunctional receptors. The incidence of opioid-induced pruritus appears to be higher in pregnant women, possibly due to an interaction of estrogen with opioid receptors. Pruritus is one of the most common side effects after administering epidural or intrathecal opioids. While the underlying cause of pruritis is uncertain, it is possibly related to the activation of opioid receptors in the trigeminal nucleus or nerve roots with cephalad migration of the opioid. Multiple medications, including intravenous naloxone, naltrexone, nalbuphine, and droperidol, have been studied for the prevention and treatment of neuraxial opioid-induced pruritus. Results of additional studies have provided evidence that serotonin receptor antagonists (eg, ondansetron) may also be effective in the prophylaxis and treatment of opioid-induced pruritis. There is a shorter duration of opioid-induced pruritus with lipophilic opioids (eg, fentanyl, sufentanil) compared to that with hydrophilic opioids (eg, morphine, hydromorphone). Pruritis from intrathecal hydrophilic opioids is of longer duration, often includes the head and neck (pruritus with lipophilic opioids is generally limited to the trunk), and is more difficult to treat compared to the pruritus associated with lipophilic opioids. There is a higher incidence of pruritus in pregnant women after neuraxial opioid administration compared to that in nonpregnant patients. The incidence of pruritus is approximately 80% in peripartum patients, while the incidence of pruritus after intrathecal opioid administration for orthopedic surgery has been observed to be as low as 30%. The increased occurrence in pregnant women is hypothesized to be attributed to an interaction of estrogen with opioid receptors. When neuraxial opioids are administered with local anesthetics, there is a lower incidence of pruritus than with neuraxial opioids alone.
Answer B: Ondansetron may reduce the incidence and severity of opioid-induced pruritus; however, data on the benefits of ondansetron are conflicting.
Answer C: Opioid-induced pruritis is dose-dependent, with higher doses having a higher incidence and increased severity of pruritus. Pregnant patients are at an increased risk for the development of pruritus following intrathecal or epidural opioid administration. Lipophilic opioids have a slower duration of pruritus, while hydrophilic opioids have a longer duration and more involvement of the head and neck. Coadministration of neuraxial local anesthetic with neuraxial opioids can decrease the incidence of pruritus compared to that with neuraxial opioids alone. Amiloride is associated with hyperkalemia. Amiloride, triamterene, spironolactone, and eplerenone are the four potassium sparing diuretics. They work by blocking sodium reabsorption in the cortical collecting tubule and simultaneously increasing potassium reabsorption. Amiloride is a well tolerated drug whose only major side effect is hyperkalemia (A). Hyperkalemia is associated with peaked T waves on ECG, with T wave amplitude often surpassing that of the QRS complex as shown in the image. Increasing hyperkalemia may be visualized as a shortened QT interval, widening of the QRS, and PR prolongation. Concomitant use of ACE inhibitors may increase the risk of hyperkalemia in patients on potassium sparing agents. Furosemide, and all loop diuretics (e.g. bumetanide, ethacrynic acid), inhibit the sodium/potassium/2-chloride receptor in the ascending tubule loop of Henle. Potassium excretion is increased along with sodium and hypokalemia can result. Hypokalemia is characterized by T wave flattening or inversion and U waves on the ECG. Hydrochlorothiazide works on the sodium/chloride cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule increasing both sodium and potassium excretion. Thusly, hypo- and not hyperkalemia is an associated side effect. Thiazides also increase calcium reabsorption as electroneutrality is maintained. Hypercalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and hyponatremia may be seen. Lithium toxicity is associated with hypermagnesemia. It is also associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which may be prevented or treated by blockade of the collecting tubule luminal sodium receptors with amiloride. Hypermagnesemia is characterized by PR interval prolongation and a widening QRS complex. Loop diuretics are associated with hypokalemia and are used in the treatment of hyperkalemia.
Answer C: Thiazide diuretics are associated with hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia, hyperuricemia, hyperglycemia, and hyperlipidemia.
Answer D: Lithium is not associated with hyperkalemia. Amiloride can be associated with hyperkalemia. The K+ STAys with Spironolactone, Triamterene, Amiloride. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist. Adrenergic receptors are broadly divided into alpha and beta. There are then further classified into subtypes numbered 1 and 2. The effects of adrenergic agonists and antagonists depend on which receptors they bind. Alpha-1 receptors are found primarily in smooth muscle where they cause vasoconstriction. Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist. Alpha-2 receptors are found presynaptically and inhibit norepinephrine release. Clonidine and dexmedetomidine are alpha-2 agonists. They cause a decrease in sympathetic outflow from the central nervous system, leading to sedation and bradycardia. Clonidine has a 200:1 selectivity for alpha-2 compared to alpha-1. Dexmedetomidine preferentially binds alpha-2 with a ratio of 1600:1. Beta-1 receptors are located in the heart where they cause increased inotropy and chronotropy. Dobutamine acts primarily on beta-1 causing increased cardiac output. Beta-2 receptors are distributed in smooth muscle where they cause dilation. Bronchodilators such as albuterol and tocolytics such as terbutaline are beta-2 selective. Clonidine is an alpha-2 agonist but is less selective (1:200) than dexmedetomidine (1:1600).
Answer C: Epinephrine is a mixed alpha and beta agonist.
Answer D: Phenylephrine is a selective alpha-1 agonist. Dexmedetomidine is a highly selective alpha2-adrenoceptor agonist. The Meyer-Overton correlation describes the linear relationship between anesthetic potency and solubility in oil, such as olive oil. The striking elegance of the relationship between anesthetic potency and lipid solubility as described by Meyer and Overton led to the erroneous conclusion that “all chemically indifferent substances that are soluble in fat are anesthetics. Their relative potency as anesthetics will depend on their affinity to fat on one hand and water on the other hand, that is, on the fat/water partition coefficient.” The thought was that the lipid molecules of nerve membranes were the principal site of action of anesthetic agents. The appeal of a single unified mechanism mediated by lipid targets to explain the mechanism of action of anesthetics was intellectually appealing, and alternative targets were largely neglected by the scientific community. Evidence against lipid-based theories was recognized subsequently when it was discovered that there is a cutoff in increasing anesthetic potency in homologous series of long-chain anesthetic alcohols, and hydrophobic drugs that do not obey the MeyerOverton correlation. In addition, the enantiomeric selectivity of several anesthetics-supported protein binding sites as principal targets as stereoselectivity is difficult to reconcile with lipid targets. Today, there is widespread acceptance that signaling proteins such as ion channels and ligand-gated receptors are the principal anesthetic targets. However, the specific protein targets of volatile anesthetics continue to be elusive, as the scientific community continues to investigate potential target sites and relevant neural circuits underlying the anesthetic state. The enantiomeric selectivity of several anesthetics supported protein binding sites as principal targets, as stereoselectivity is difficult to reconcile with lipid targets.
Answer B: The hypotheses of inhaled anesthetics with lipid membrane target sites were predominant from the 1960s to the 1980s, before shifting to the more current protein-target-based theories.
Answer D: There is a cutoff in increasing anesthetic potency in homologous series of long-chain anesthetic alcohols, and hydrophobic drugs that do not obey the Meyer-Overton correlation. The Meyer-Overton correlation describes the linear relationship between anesthetic potency and solubility in oil such as olive oil. The hypotheses of inhaled anesthetics with lipid membrane target sites were predominant from the 1960s to the 1980s, before shifting to the more current protein-target-based theories. The specific protein targets of volatile anesthetics continue to be elusive, as the scientific community continues to investigate potential target sites. Etomidate is an imidazole derivative with an ester linkage which is hydrolyzed in the liver to produce an inactive carboxylic acid metabolite that is renally excreted. It is formulated in a 0.2% solution in 35% propylene glycol. An initial induction dose of 0.2-0.3 mg/kg provides hypnosis for 5-15 minutes. Like other induction agents, its hypnotic effect is terminated by redistribution. In the geriatric population, etomidate has a smaller initial volume of distribution and decreased clearance. A typical induction dose for geriatric patients is 0.15-0.2 mg/kg. In hemorrhagic trauma, 0.3 mg/kg is the minimum dose. Etomidate produces hypnosis through the GABAA receptor and has no analgesic effect. Cerebral blood flow and cerebral metabolic rate are reduced resulting in a decrease in intracranial pressure. Cerebral perfusion pressure is preserved or increased due to the maintenance of mean arterial pressure. Etomidate has been associated with seizure activity and can activate epileptogenic foci on EEG; however, a BIS monitor can be used reliably. Etomidate has less effect on ventilation than propofol and the barbiturates but can cause transient apnea upon induction of anesthesia. Typical induction doses result in very little effect on arterial or venous tone or cardiac contractility and this hemodynamic stability is preserved in unstable patients. In animal models, hemorrhage induced hypotension did not affect pharmacodynamics or pharmacokinetics of etomidate. Transient inhibition of 11β-hydroxylase can result in decreased synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone. This has not been shown to have deleterious effects in the general surgical population. Controversy exists on whether this quality of etomidate influences outcomes in the ICU and in trauma patients. Etomidate modulates the GABAA receptor.
Answer C: No reduction in dose is required in renal insufficiency or hepatic disease. In fact, higher doses are needed in some situations such as hemorrhagic trauma.
Answer D: Cerebral perfusion pressure is maintained or increased with the use of etomidate because intracranial pressure decreases while mean arterial pressure is preserved. CPP = MAP – ICP (or CVP whichever is greater). Etomidate induces anesthesia via modulation of the GABAA receptor, and is metabolized by hepatic ester hydrolysis. Etomidate is known for cardiovascular stability, maintenance of cerebral perfusion pressure, and adrenal suppression.  Miller’s Anesthesia. Intravenous Anesthetics in 8th Edition. Pages 850-854. One of the most common side effects of fospropofol is paresthesias (D), which occur in >50% of patients. Paresthesias occur with propofol in 10-20% of patients. Fospropofol was approved by the FDA in 2008 for use in MAC sedation. It is a water-soluble prodrug that is hydrolyzed to propofol by endothelial and hepatic alkaline phosphatases. Metabolism also liberates phosphate and formaldehyde, but blood levels of both of these compounds do not become significantly elevated. Compared to propofol, fospropofol has a slower onset of action (approximately 4-10 minutes, depending on dose) since it must first be metabolized to propofol. Due to this slower onset of action, the incidence of respiratory depression, apnea, and hypotension is lower compared to propofol. Paresthesias are the most common side effect of fospropofol use occurring in approximately 50-70% of patients (D), typically within the first five minutes following the initial dose of drug. They include burning, tingling, and/or stinging sensations and usually occur in the perianal or genital regions. Other areas where paresthesias have been known to occur include the buttocks, chest, ears, and nose. The paresthesias resolve spontaneously and pretreatment with local anesthetics, NSAIDs, or opioids does not decrease their incidence. Paresthesias occur with propofol in approximately 10-20% of patients, usually occur at the site of injection, and the severity and incidence may be decreased with pretreatment, such as with local anesthetics. Pruritus is also a common side effect of fospropofol, occurring in 15-30% of patients. The pruritus is usually localized to the genitals, though it may be generalized. The incidence of pruritus associated with propofol is 1-3% and is more commonly generalized or localized to the area of injection. Bacterial contamination of or growth in fospropofol, and subsequent patient inoculation, is significantly less likely than with propofol since the former does not utilize a lipid-containing oil-water emulsion (B). The lipid base of propofol can allow bacterial growth; preservatives, such as EDTA, must be added to decrease this risk. At sedation doses, propofol causes apnea of ≥30 seconds in approximately 10-25% of patients whereas the incidence of apnea with fospropofol is < 10% (A). Significant hypotension occurs with propofol in 5-25% of patients and in approximately 5% of patients with fospropofol (C).  The most common side effects of the water-soluble propofol prodrug fospropofol are paresthesias (typically perianal or genital) and genital pruritus. Due to its slower onset of action, the incidence of respiratory depression, apnea, and hypotension are lower with fospropofol compared to propofol.  Bengalorkar GM, et al. Meperidine is structurally similar to atropine and, accordingly, demonstrates atropine-like effects including tachycardia. Meperidine was initially studied as an anticholinergic agent before being discovered as an analgesic. The physiologic effects of meperidine differ from other opioids mainly due to two factors: atropine-like drug effects and weak local anesthetic properties. At standard analgesic doses, meperidine is associated with hemodynamic stability. However, high doses cause hypotension and tachycardia. The hypotension is likely attributed to histamine release. In addition, high concentrations of meperidine decrease cardiac contractility, an effect resistant to naloxone. This is due to the local anesthetic effects of meperidine. Clinically, opioids are routinely used to prevent tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. Tachycardia may occasionally be seen with morphine administration as histamine release can cause transient hypotension with reflexive tachycardia. Answers A & C: Hydromorphone, fentanyl, and remifentanil all produce dose-dependent bradycardia by both sympatholytic and parasympathomimetic properties.  Opioids are routinely used to prevent tachycardia and reduce myocardial oxygen demand. However, high doses of meperidine can cause tachycardia due to its atropine-like effects.
