Dexmedetomidine produces its sedative-hypnotic effect by acting on alpha2 receptors in the locus ceruleus, involving endogenous sleep pathways that allows the generation of natural sleep patterns in patients. It exerts its analgesic effects via the dorsal horn. Dexmedetomidine exerts its analgesic effects by stimulating alpha-2 receptors in the dorsal horn.
Answer C: Ketamine exerts its sedative-hypnotic effect by acting on the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor.
Answer D: Dexmedetomidine has not been demonstrated to have an effect on receptors in the ventral horn. Dexmedetomidine is an alpha2-agonist that produces a sedative-hypnotic effect in a unique manner by involving endogenous sleep pathways through alpha2 receptors in the locus ceruleus.  Miller. Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism (5-8%) followed by isoflurane (0.2%) then desflurane (< 0.2%). The clinical importance of volatile anesthetic metabolism is related to fluoride-induced nephrotoxicity. Initially this phenomenon was described after methoxyflurane use during long cases, but it currently remains a topic of interest particularly in regards to sevoflurane in the same setting. Sevoflurane undergoes 5-8% metabolism that results in increases in serum fluoride concentrations. However, sevoflurane does not cause a renal concentrating defect since it is associated with a more rapid decline in plasma fluoride concentrations. In addition, sevoflurane has minimal renal defluorination compared to the previouslyused enflurane which has been demonstrated to be a factor in toxicity. Enflurane-induced nephrotoxicity is a high-output renal insufficiency that does not respond to vasopressin. It is characterized by dehydration, dilute polyuria, elevated blood urea nitrogen, elevated creatinine, serum hypernatremia, and serum hyperosmolality. There was found to be a correlation between serum fluoride concentration and metabolism of enflurane (3%) which led to further investigations into sevoflurane and possible nephrotoxicity. Answers A & B & D: Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism (5-8%) followed by isoflurane (0.2%) then desflurane (< 0.2%).  Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism of the inhaled anesthetics used in clinical practice today. Despite demonstrated elevations in serum fluoride concentrations in long cases, it has not been shown to cause fluorideinduced nephrotoxicity.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Volatile anesthetics: metabolism" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 438-439. Miller, Basics of Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 81.

Glucocorticoids agonize nuclear receptor subfamily 3, group C, member 1 (NR3C1), also known as the glucocorticoid receptor (GCR). Corticosteroids also inhibit prostaglandin synthesis at phospholipase A2 at the beginning of the arachidonic acid pathway; thus, they have similar analgesic effects to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, which block cyclooxygenase at the next step in the pathway. Steroid medications are often used for their anti-inflammatory effects. Corticosteroids, in particular, are effective in treating inflammation due to their agonism of GCR. The glucocorticoid receptor regulates metabolism and immunity in most cells. In macrophages, upregulation of GCR leads to increased expression of anti-inflammatory proteins and inhibition of the expression of pro-inflammatory proteins. Diphenhydramine and loratadine are examples of antihistamines. Dexamethasone does not have direct antihistaminic activity.
Answer B: Biologic agents such as monoclonal antibodies infliximab and adalimumab directly bind and inhibit tumor necrosis factor-α and its pro-inflammatory effects.
Answer D: Although inflammatory mediators play a role in peripheral vasodilation, glucocorticoids themselves do not cause peripheral vasoconstriction. Dexamethasone is a glucocorticoid that agonizes the nuclear receptor subfamily 3, group C, member 1 receptor to upregulate anti-inflammatory proteins and repress inflammatory mediator production. Steroids also inhibit prostaglandin synthesis at the beginning of the arachidonic acid pathway.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline 2014. "Anti-inflammatory: Steroid Medications." Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology. Anesthesia for Patients with Respiratory Disease in 5th Edition. Page 536. Abraham SM, et al. Antiinflammatory effects of dexamethasone are partly dependent on induction of dual specificity phosphatase 1. The J Exp Med. 2006 Aug;203(8):1883-1889.

Decreased central compartment volume contributes most to the high initial plasma concentration of a drug following intravenous injection into an elderly patient. Physiologic changes occur as we age that affect all organ systems. This has numerous anesthetic implications, including altering the sensitivity of geriatric patients to most of the drugs used by anesthesiologists. In general, geriatric patients are more sensitive to anesthetic drugs, including propofol, benzodiazepines, and opioids. Geriatric patients thus require a decrease in the dose necessary to achieve a desired clinical effect. There are several factors that contribute to the need for decreased dosing in geriatric patients. Geriatric patients tend to have a reduced cardiovascular reserve. Total body water decreases by approximately 10-15% as patients age, leading to a decrease in the volume of the central compartment. This causes higher initial plasma concentrations of drugs administered via the intravenous route. Geriatric patients also have decreased lean body mass, another important factor requiring a reduction in drug doses. Providing specific calculations for dose reduction in geriatric patients is difficult and highly dependent on patient comorbidities and clinical context. Volatile anesthetic requirements decrease by approximately 6% per decade of life after age 40. Propofol may require at least a 20-50% dose reduction, although again this is highly dependent on patient comorbidities and clinical context. Opioid doses should be reduced, and reduction in benzodiazepine dose has been recommended by as much as 75% in geriatric patients. Geriatric patients have up to a 30-40% reduction in clearance of drugs metabolized by the P450 enzymes, primarily due to a reduction in hepatic flow. Renal function tends to decline as well, leading to decreased clearance of renally excreted compounds. These effects can impact duration and toxicity, however, they are not the most important factor in determining initial drug concentration following injection.
Answer C: The levels of the serum proteins change with age. Albumin levels decrease and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein levels increase. While this could theoretically contribute to higher plasma levels of medications, these changes are thought to have a clinically insignificant impact on drug concentration and effect.
Answer D: The percentage of body fat in elderly patients increases while muscle mass decreases. This results in an increased, rather than a decreased, volume of distribution and may result in prolonged clinical effects of lipid-soluble drugs. Geriatric patients require a reduced dose of most medications used by anesthesiologists. Decreased central compartment volume contributes to high initial concentrations. Increased body fat percentage can increase the volume of distribution for lipid-soluble drugs, causing an increased duration of action. Hepatic and renal clearance is decreased, increasing the duration of action. Albumin levels are reduced, although this is not thought to significantly contribute to plasma concentration differences. Midazolam is a benzodiazepine that undergoes hepatic metabolism via hepatic cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzymes and glucuronide conjugation. Nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors and protease inhibitors (ritonavir) inhibit the activity of the CYP450 system, prolonging the effects/half-lives of benzodiazepines and opioids. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) involves using a combination of classes of antiviral therapies to treat the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). Classic therapy for HIV treatment involves using at least three classes of medications. Nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) are associated with anemia, thrombocytopenia, lactic acidosis, and hepatotoxicity. Zidovudine, an NRTI, is also associated with bone marrow suppression, severe myopathy, and respiratory muscle dysfunction when administered simultaneously with corticosteroids. Nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors are associated with hepatotoxicity and alteration of the metabolism of the hepatic CYP450 system. Protease inhibitors (eg, ritonavir) are inhibitors of the CYP450 system, impairing the metabolism of benzodiazepines, opioids, and many other drugs. Drugs such as etomidate, cisatracurium, remifentanil, and desflurane, do not rely on metabolism by the CYP450 system and, therefore, can be safely administered at standard doses in patients receiving HAART. Protease inhibitors are also associated with premature coronary artery disease, hyperlipidemia, and cardiac conduction abnormalities (most notably PR interval prolongation). Lipodystrophy is the redistribution of body fat to the neck and abdomen, a complication of protease inhibitor therapy. This fat redistribution can lead to complications during intubation, increase the risk for aspiration, and potentially lead to respiratory complications. Classes of antiretroviral medications NRTIs Abacavir Didanosine Emtricitabine Lamivudine Zidovudine NNRTIs Delavirdine Efavirenz Etravirine Nevirapine Protease inhibitors Atazanavir Darunavir Indinavir Ritonavir INSTIs Bictegravir Dolutegravir Ratlegravir Note: Fusion inhibitors and coreceptor antagonists are also used Abbreviations: INSTI, integrase strand inhibitor; NNRTI, nonnucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor; NRTI, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor. Cisatracurium and atracurium undergo Hoffman elimination, independent of hepatic metabolism.
Answer B: Desflurane is not dependent on CYP450 metabolism and is not significantly impacted by the concomitant use of medications that inhibit the CYP450 system. Sevoflurane undergoes the most extensive metabolism of all the inhaled volatile anesthetic agents.
Answer D: Remifentanil undergoes metabolism via ester hydrolysis and is not dependent on the CYP450 system. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) can significantly alter the metabolism and clearance of many anesthetic drugs, including benzodiazepines and opioids. Drugs such as desflurane, etomidate, remifentanil, cisatracurium, and atracurium are not dependent on hepatic metabolism or the CYP450 system and, therefore, can safely be administered at standard doses in patients on HAART. Dermatomal spread of hyperbaric local anesthetic injections (such as the one in this question) into the intrathecal space is primarily determined by the baricity of the medication. The spread of hypobaric and isobaric local anesthetic mixtures is primarily determined by the total dose of local anesthetic administered. The spread of local anesthetic within the intrathecal space following a subarachnoid injection is highly variable. However, there are multiple factors that an anesthesia provider can modulate to more reliably predict the pharmacokinetics of these medications within that space. In general, these factors can be considered in three separate groups: drug, patient, and procedural factors. Drug factors that influence the spread of local anesthetic in the intrathecal space include the baricity, concentration, and volume of the injectate, as well as the total dose of local anesthetic that is administered. Hyperbaric solutions, in general, must be denser than cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) at physiologic temperature and have either a baricity of greater than 1.0000 or a density of greater than 1.00059 mg/mL. Hypobaric solutions have baricities and densities less than these values. Most often, dextrose is added to solutions in order to achieve hyperbaricity and sterile water is added to achieve hypobaricity. In hyperbaric solution, the baricity of the solution is the primary determinant of spread, with a more hyperbaric solution resulting in a more dependent spread of the anesthetic effect. Anesthesia providers can leverage this effect to modulate the site of action of the anesthetic, either through an understanding of the natural curvature of the spine or through positioning following drug administration. The dermatomal spread of hypobaric and isobaric solutions are more reliant on the overall dose of medication that is administered to exert a clinical effect, with little independent correlation found between the dermatomal spread of large volumes of dilute injectate or small volumes of concentrated injectate. Major patient factors that influence the dermatomal spread of local anesthetics include the overall CSF volume, the age of the patient, and the presence of pregnancy. Height has a minimal effect within "normal ranges" of adult height, as the primary determinant of height differences in this population is lower extremity limb length and much less difference is seen in the size of a spinal column. Increases in body habitus can decrease CSF volume and have been shown to increase the variability of spread in hypobaric solutions, though this has not been demonstrated when hyperbaric solutions are utilized. Advanced age is also associated with increased block height, likely due to the decreased CSF volume, and increased specific gravity in this population, as well as a baseline increased sensitivity to local anesthetic agents. Increased dura mater permeability in the elderly speeds the onset of epidural blockade. Pregnant women experience engorgement of their epidural venous plexus due to mass effect on the vena cava and other major vessels. This results in decreased CSF volume and consequently an increased block height with all other factors held constant. Procedural factors that affect dermatomal spread include primarily patient position and the use of an epidural injection following intrathecal injection. The intrathecal local anesthetic spread appears to diminish after 20-25 minutes following injection, and thus patient positioning in this time is potentially important for achieving an appropriate block. A combined spinal-epidural technique where a subarachnoid injection is made and then either an epidural catheter or injection is performed also influences the height of the subarachnoid block, both due to compression of the spinal canal due to epidural mass effect following an epidural injection, as well as possible intrathecal migration of medication administered in the epidural space through the dural defect from the subarachnoid injection. This has not been shown to be significantly correlated with the dermatomal spread of intrathecal local anesthetics.
Answer C: The overall dose of local anesthetic is most highly correlated with dermatomal spread when either hypobaric and isobaric solutions are utilized. Baricity is the most correlated with dermatomal spread when hyperbaric solutions are utilized.
Answer D: This has not been shown to be significantly correlated with the dermatomal spread of intrathecal local anesthetics. Volume is an important determinant of spread for epidural medication administration. A variety of factors influence dermatomal spread following intrathecal administration of local anesthetics. Baricity is most correlated with the spread of hyperbaric solutions, while the total dose of medication administered is most correlated with the spread of isobaric or hypobaric solutions. Other factors that influence dermatomal spread include patient position and factors that decrease cerebrospinal fluid volume such as pregnancy, obesity, or advanced age. Plain (isobaric) tetracaine can be mixed with dextrose to create a hyperbaric subarachnoid anesthetic. Mixing 1:1 with D10 (10% dextrose) is the manufacturer's recommendation to create a hyperbaric solution. For example, 1 mL from the tetracaine vial is 10 mg then adding 1 mL of D10 creates a total of 2 mL hyperbaric 0.5% tetracaine. Typical dosing for saddle anesthesia is 5-10 mg. For a typical cesarean section, 15 mg is an appropriate dose. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Pharmacokinetics: Subarachnoid Drug Administration" Miller Anesthesia. Hyperthyroidism in a patient presenting for an emergency procedure often necessitates the use of intravenous beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, and propylthiouracil in the perioperative period. Beta-adrenergic antagonists do not affect the underlying thyroid abnormality but may relieve signs and symptoms. However, propranolol does offer the added benefit of impairing the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. T4 and T3 are the major thyroid hormones. Often T4 is considered a prohormone and T3 is a more potent thyroid hormone produced by the deiodination of T4. Hyperthyroidism is a frequent problem associated with thyroid hyperactivity. Complications include thyrotoxicosis and thyroid storm. Multiple stressors including surgery can trigger thyrotoxicosis or thyroid storm. Treatment consists of supportive care, control of autonomic dysfunction, blocking peripheral conversion of T4 to T3, and decreasing thyroid hormone production. The first line treatment of hyperthyroidism is the use of an antithyroid agent such as methimazole and propylthiouracil. The goal prior to any elective surgery is a euthyroid state which can take about 6 to 8 weeks. In emergency cases, the use of beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, and/or propylthiouracil is often needed. The anesthesiologist should be prepared to manage thyroid storm, especially in patients with poorly controlled disease. Patients presenting for emergency surgery can also have hypothyroidism that is not controlled. Patients with hypothyroidism appear to have an increased sensitivity to anesthetics. These patients can be extremely sensitive to opioids and sedatives. Therefore, preoperative sedation should be undertaken with caution. Glucocorticoids such as dexamethasone are often administered to decrease hormone release and reduce the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
Answer C: Propranolol impairs the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
Answer D: Propylthiouracil interferes with the synthesis of thyroid hormones and inhibits the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3. Propylthiouracil is not available intravenously. Therefore, the drug must be taken orally through a nasogastric tube. For emergency procedures involving hyperthyroid patients, medication options include beta-blockers, glucocorticoids, and propylthiouracil. Beta-adrenergic antagonists do not affect the underlying thyroid abnormality but may relieve signs and symptoms. However, propranolol does offer the added benefit of impairing the peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Premedication: Thyroid Disorders” Birch et. al. Complications in Anesthesia. 3rd Edition. Pages 43-47. Hines, et al. Stoelting’s Anesthesia and Co-Existing Disease. 6th Edition. Pages 386-389.

Meperidine, given its atropine-like structure, will most likely cause an increased heart rate upon administration. Anesthesiologists frequently administer opioids preoperatively, intraoperatively, and postoperatively to provide analgesia or as part of a balanced anesthetic. A predominantly opioid-based anesthetic may be selected for hemodynamically unstable patients because, compared with other classes of anesthetic drugs, opioids usually cause fewer unwanted changes in the hemodynamic profile. Nonetheless, opioids, especially in large doses, can alter hemodynamics. Changes in heart rate, cardiac conduction, blood pressure, and myocardial contractility are possible. Whether these effects are beneficial or detrimental depends on the clinical setting. The administration of opioids generally results in a decreased heart rate. Opioid-induced bradycardia is primarily mediated by the CNS. The reduction in heart rate that typically accompanies the use of opioids is seen in conjunction with reduced sympathetic tone and may be desirable in some patients, such as those at risk for developing coronary ischemia. When compared with the use of fentanyl and sufentanil, the use of alfentanil less reliably prevents increases in heart rate and blood pressure in response to surgical stimulation during cardiac operations. Alfentanil is more commonly used at induction to reduce intubation effects, given its rapid onset of action. Additionally, opioids directly stimulate mu receptors in medullary vagal nuclei, an effect that can be attenuated by bilateral vagotomy. Some investigators have also noted decreases in heart rate with the use of remifentanil, even in the absence of enhanced parasympathetic tone, suggesting a direct effect on cardiac conduction tissue. Severe bradycardia and even asystole have been reported following the administration of opioids. Meperidine, a phenylpiperidine, is a synthetic mu opioid receptor agonist with a short half-life. Meperidine has structural similarities to atropine, an anticholinergic. Atropine causes tachycardia by acting as a muscarinic receptor antagonist that inhibits the effects of excessive vagal activity on the heart. Given the structural similarity, meperidine would lend itself to causing tachycardia over bradycardia. Opioids can produce bradycardia upon administration. However, the exception is meperidine, which is more likely to induce a tachycardia.
Answer B: Opioids appear to have no significant effect on coronary vasculature tone or myocardial metabolism; they do not produce steal phenomena, and they do not diminish the ability of large coronary arterioles to respond to vasoactive agents.
Answer C: Besides causing bradycardia, opioid administration can also lower blood pressure. Decreased sympathetic tone probably accounts for most of the blood pressure reduction (as opposed to decreased SVR seen with anesthetic agents). The tone of both venous capacitance vessels and arteriolar resistance vessels may decrease. Hypotensive effects are most prominent in patients with increased sympathetic tone, such as those with congestive heart failure or hypovolemia. In addition to reducing sympathetic tone and direct vascular effects, morphine and meperidine also activate mast cells and trigger histamine and tryptase release, which can contribute to vasodilatation and hypotension. The use of fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil, and remifentanil does not promote histamine release. Hypertension is occasionally observed in patients receiving opioid medications intraoperatively. Most frequently seen in patients with preserved left ventricular function, hypertensive responses probably result from either too low of an opioid dose or inadequate administration of other types of anesthetic agents. The predominant and usual effect of opioids on heart rate is bradycardia resulting from stimulation of the central vagal nucleus. Blockade of sympathetic actions may also play a role in opioid-induced bradycardia. Meperidine, in contrast to other opioids, rarely results in bradycardia, but it can cause tachycardia given its structural similarities to atropine.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Opioids: Circulation Effects." Faust Anesthesiology Review. 4th Edition. Pages 170-172. Miller's Anesthesia. 8th Edition. Pages 879-881. Barash Clinical Anesthesia. 7th Edition. Page 1621.

Spironolactone is a competitive aldosterone antagonist that is a potassium-sparing diuretic. It works in the distal tubule of the nephron segments in the kidney. Inhibition of aldosterone will cause a mild retention of potassium and excretion of sodium. The most commonly described side effects of spironolactone are hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, gynecomastia, and impotence. Other potassium sparing diuretics, such as eplerenone, triamterene, and amiloride, all possess similar side effects as spironolactone. Spironolactone may be added to a medical regimen to treat edema, specifically in those with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis of the liver, or nephrotic syndrome. It is not likely to cause edema. In fact, spironolactone improves survival in patients with volume overload and heart failure.
Answer B: Spironolactone may be added to a medical regimen to treat hypokalemia. It is not likely to cause it. Instead, hyperkalemia and hyperkalemic, hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis are more likely to occur. The most commonly described side effects of spironolactone are hyperkalemia, hyponatremia, gynecomastia, and impotence.  Barash’s Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition. Page 1415. Heterozygous pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase) deficiency occurs in ~ 1/30 individuals (leading to slight prolongation of succinylcholine duration ~15 min), and homozygous deficiency in ~ 1/3600 (leading to marked prolongation of succinylcholine duration ~ 2 hours). There are several abnormal alleles described in addition to the normal or U (usual), including the A allele (atypical), S (silent), F (fluoride), etc. Unlike the U allele, in which >80% of its activity is inhibitable by dibucaine, the A allele is characterized by resistance to dibucaine inhibition, resulting in a "dibucaine number" (i.e. percentage of activity that can be inhibited by dibucaine) of 20% for homozygotes and 50% for heterozygotes. A phase II block (train-of-four fade) is expected to develop when these patients receive succinylcholine. Similar to the development of fade with non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers, fade during a phase II blockade has been attributed to the blockade of presynaptic acetylcholine receptors, but other mechanisms have been postulated too, including electrolyte imbalances across the junctional membrane. This patient is at risk for awareness while paralyzed, a sensation described as suffocation or "being buried alive". Therefore, sedation should be continued until neuromuscular function has recovered enough that the patient can be extubated.
Answer B: Family counseling for pseudocholinesterase deficiency consists mostly of reassurance that the patient can live a normal, healthy life, and that prolonged paralysis is expected with succinylcholine. Potentially, the patient would have a high sensitivity to cocaine, and a lower sensitivity to heroin.
Answer C: The duration of succinylcholine can be somewhat prolonged in severe liver disease, as well as other physiological or pathological conditions, including pregnancy, renal disease, malnutrition, and burns. However, the apnea time would not be expected to exceed 20 or 30 minutes at the most. When butyrylcholinesterase activity is reduced to 20% of normal by severe liver disease, the duration of apnea increases from normal duration of 3 minutes to only 9 minutes. Succinylcholine can cause a phase II block that resembles the block caused by non-depolarizing neuromuscular blockers (including train-of-four fade, tetanic fade, and post-tetanic potentiation) when administered to patients with butyrylcholinesterase deficiency, or when given in high cumulative doses (e.g. 5 mg/kg). Because ultrashort half-life leads to a lack of deposition in tissues, remifentanil's context-sensitive half-time is independent of infusion duration. The context-sensitive half-time is the time for a drug that is infused to decrease by 50% in the plasma from a steady-state concentration after the infusion has stopped. The reason for the difference in context-sensitive half-times of different drugs is the varying degrees the drugs distribute among the different compartments in the body. For drugs that are highly lipophilic, the drug initially redistributes into the adipose tissue and accumulates until it saturates that compartment. Different drugs accumulate in different amounts. After the infusion stops, the drug then begins to diffuse out of the adipose tissue (or another compartment) into the blood. This is why elimination takes longer than when it solely remains in the blood. Fentanyl is one opioid in which the context-sensitive half-time increases with increasing duration of infusion. Remifentanil is an opioid that is independent of infusion duration mainly because of its ultrashort half-life of 2 minutes. Alfentanil's context-sensitive half-time initially increases but plateaus and does not increase with increased duration after it has plateaued.
Answer B: Fentanyl is a highly lipophilic opioid that has a significant rise in its context-sensitive half-time associated with a longer duration of infusion.
Answer D: Sufentanil's context-sensitive half-time linearly increases with increased duration, but its slope is not as significantly steep as that of fentanyl. It also does not have a plateau, as in the case of alfentanil. The context-sensitive half-time is the time for a drug that is infused to decrease by 50% in the plasma from a steady-state concentration once the infusion has stopped. A longer infusion results in a longer context-sensitive half-time for most drugs because of deposition in tissues. Remifentanil's context-sensitive half-time is independent of the duration of the infusion because its ultrashort half-life prevents deposition in tissues. Sufentanil is a derivative of fentanyl, with a potency 10 times and lipophilicity 2 times greater than fentanyl. It is primarily metabolized by the liver into inactive compounds and one active compound called desmethylsufentanil, which has 10% of the activity of sufentanil, although it has little clinical significance because it is produced in minute quantities. Sufentanil is primarily used as analgesia during anesthesia, resulting in stable hemodynamics and cardiac output. Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Opioids. 8th ed. E-book. Page 511. Ocular phenylephrine causes pupillary dilation. Phenylephrine is an agonist of the alpha-1 receptor in the autonomic nervous system. Alpha-1 receptor agonism generally causes smooth muscle contraction resulting in the following effects: - Vasoconstriction - Mydriasis (pupillary dilation) via contraction of the radial muscle in the iris - Increased salivary and sweat gland secretion - Piloerection of hair follicles - Increased ureter, bladder trigone, and bladder sphincter contraction - Vas deferens contraction Phenylephrine ocular drops typically come in 1%, 2.5%, and 10% concentrations, although the 2.5% concentration is most commonly used and the 1% concentration is typically reserved for neonates. Phenylephrine ocular drops are often used in combination with tropicamide, an antimuscarinic, to create a temporary state of mydriasis (pupillary dilation) and cycloplegia (loss of accommodation via ciliary muscle paralysis). Phenylephrine also causes blanching of the episcleral blood vessels. Phenylephrine drops may cause a transient elevation in blood pressure. Phenylephrine causes pupillary dilation, which can cause acute angle-closure glaucoma and increased intraocular pressure.
Answer B: Pupillary constriction occurs from parasympathetic stimulation of the M3 muscarinic receptor causing contraction of the iris and miosis.
Answer C: Ptosis can result from the inactivation of the superior tarsal muscle, a smooth muscle innervated by the sympathetic nervous system. Inactivation of the superior tarsal muscle occurs with the sympathetic antagonism that causes Horner’s syndrome. This does not occur with phenylephrine, which is a sympathetic agonist. Phenylephrine ocular drops may actually cause an improvement of ptosis depending on the underlying cause of the ptosis. Ocular phenylephrine causes pupillary dilation as an agonist of the alpha-1 receptor in the sympathetic nervous system. Opioids have a direct effect on the respiratory centers in the medulla, producing a dose-dependent depression of the ventilatory response to CO2. The respiratory depressant actions of opioids represent their most serious adverse effects. By decreasing pain and central ventilatory drive, opioids are effective agents in preventing hyperventilation induced by pain or anxiety. Because the lack of adequate pain relief can also cause postoperative respiratory dysfunction, opioids can be used as postoperative analgesics to prevent respiratory dysfunction. The respiratory depressant effects of opioids may be divided into two components: (1) suppression of the ventilatory drive (i.e., true respiratory depression from the inactivation of respiratory neurons in the brain stem) and (2) occlusion of the upper airways either from a direct suppression of neurons in the brainstem involved in maintaining the upper airway muscle tone or from the loss of muscle tone related to sedation. While opioids clearly affect respiratory neurons in the brainstem, the direct effect of opioids on the upper airway musculature is less clear. The drive to breathe is generated in multiple respiratory centers in the brainstem. Respiratory neurons receive inputs from various sites in the CNS (cortex, limbic system, hypothalamus, spinal cord), a set of receptors located in the brainstem (central chemoreceptors), and in the carotid bodies (peripheral chemoreceptors). These sensors send information - changes in pH, PCO2, and PO2 of the CSF and arterial blood - to the brainstem respiratory centers, which appropriately adjust breathing rate and pulmonary tidal volume. For example, acidosis, hypercapnia, and hypoxia will cause hyperventilation, while hypocapnia and alkalosis will reduce minute ventilation. Morphine-6-glucuronide, not morphine-3-glucuronide, is an active metabolite of morphine that leads to analgesia and possible respiratory depression. Morphine-3-glucuronide can accumulate in renal failure patients and lead to seizures.
Answer B: Opioids cause a reduction in respiratory rate, while a reduction in tidal volume is caused by the decreased input from the chemosensors.
Answer D: The respiratory depressant effects of opioids are increased or prolonged (or both) when these drugs are administered with other CNS depressants, including potent inhaled anesthetic agents, alcohol, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, most intravenous sedatives, and hypnotics. However, droperidol, scopolamine, and clonidine do not enhance the respiratory depressant effects of fentanyl or other opioids. Opioid administration leads to a number of effects on the respiratory system including decreased respiratory rate and a dose dependent depression of ventilatory response to CO2. In renal failure patients, metabolites can accumulate and ultimately lead to seizures or respiratory arrest. Mannitol is a sugar alcohol that acts as an osmotic diuretic as it is freely filtered at the glomerulus with poor reuptake back into the vasculature. Hyperglycemia may also act as an osmotic diuretic when glucose levels rise beyond the point of maximum transport through the glomerulus. Any poorly reabsorbed solute that is easily filtered at the level of the glomerulus can act as an osmotic diuretic by creating a gradient that causes fluid to remain within the renal tubule. Mannitol is the prototypical osmotic diuretic. Urea, glycerin, and isosorbide have also been used as osmotic diuretics. Mannitol draws fluid into the renal tubule, which allows for continued patency and flushing of debris from the tubule. Accordingly, mannitol can exert a renal protective effect. In addition, mannitol transiently creates an osmotic gradient within the vasculature and can maintain circulating plasma volume and renal perfusion via this effect, further eliciting protective properties. Angiotensin is part of the RAAS and is activated during systemic stress (e.g., hypovolemia, shock) to help retain fluid and maintain circulating plasma volume.
Answer B: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released in response to atrial stretch (generally due to volume overload). Atrial natriuretic peptide then induces diuresis via natriuresis, not via an osmotic effect. Atrial natriuretic peptide blocks the reabsorption of sodium from the distal tubule and collecting duct causing fluid to shift into the tubule. Hyperglycemia can mimic the effects of mannitol by acting as an osmotic diuretic. Mannitol is relatively contraindicated in patients with congestive heart failure (CHF) due to an initial increase in intravascular volume. Furosemide is the drug of choice when diuresis is recommended in this class of patients. Volatile anesthetics inhibit postganglionic cholinergic transmission. Volatile anesthetics have the ability to reduce neuromuscular transmission especially with deep anesthesia. These agents also can potentiate neuromuscular blocking drugs. More insoluble agents (e.g. desflurane) cause more relaxation than the soluble agents. This difference in relaxing effect is related to the insoluble volatile agent equilibrating more quickly at the neuromuscular junction. It also depends on the concentration used, where desflurane would have a higher concentration of agent. The mechanism by which volatile anesthetics cause muscle relaxation occurs on several levels. The volatile anesthetics affect alpha-motor neurons making them hyperpolarized through interneurons in the spinal cord. Additionally, volatile anesthetics cause nicotinic receptors to become less sensitive to acetylcholine. It is possible there is inhibition of acetylcholine release in addition to the direct muscle action. Through these mechanism, volatile anesthetics cause some degree of muscle relaxation and will potentiate neuromuscular blockade. Volatile anesthetic agents do not compete with acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction. Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (e.g. vecuronium, atracurium) act by competitive inhibition of acetylcholine at nicotinic receptors. Competitive antagonism involves two different drugs that bind to the same receptor. The drug with the larger concentration will have more effect because it outcompetes the drug with a smaller concentration.
Answer B: Calcium entry into muscle cells remains the same in the presence of volatile anesthetic agents. Calcium entry causes a release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Calcium also binds to troponin and allows for actin and myosin crosslinking. Calcium can be antagonized by magnesium, which at elevated doses can cause hypotonus and decrease tendon reflexes. The treatment for hypermagnesemia is calcium administration.
Answer C: Volatile anesthetics do not affect the metabolism of neuromuscular blocking agents. The half-life of different neuromuscular blocking agents can be affected by hepatic and renal dysfunction which causes a prolongation of effect. The metabolism of succinylcholine can be affected if an anticholinesterase medication is given. Succinylcholine and mivacurium have decreased metabolism in patients with pseudocholinesterase deficiency. Volatile anesthetics cause muscle relaxation through inhibition of acetylcholine receptor sensitivity and through hyperpolarization of motor neurons. Insoluble anesthetics cause more relaxation than soluble anesthetics.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Muscle Relaxation: Anes Agents (B)" Miller, Ronald D. The action of succinylcholine at the neuromuscular junction is terminated by simple diffusion of succinylcholine away from the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent with an onset of 1 to 1.5 minutes, with a duration of 7 to 12 minutes. Because the molecular structure of succinylcholine is similar to that of acetylcholine, succinylcholine is capable of depolarizing postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, and its use results in a longer depolarization. This leads to hyperpolarization, desensitization, and flaccid paralysis after the initial depolarization, which can be seen by the muscular fasciculations. Unlike acetylcholine, succinylcholine is not degraded by acetylcholinesterases within the synaptic cleft but rather by butyrylcholinesterase (also known as plasma cholinesterase or pseudocholinesterase) in the plasma. Succinylcholine is degraded into succinylmonocholine, which has minimal activity. The termination of action is a result of diffusion away from the NMJ. After succinylcholine moves back into the blood, it is degraded by the aforementioned enzymes. Unlike cisatracurium, which undergoes autodegradation by the Hoffmann elimination reaction, succinylcholine does not autodegrade.
Answer B: After succinylcholine diffuses away from the NMJ, it is then degraded by butyrylcholinesterase (also known as plasma cholinesterase or pseudocholinesterase). The mechanism of action for the termination of blockade of succinylcholine is diffusion away from the NMJ, not metabolism by butyrylcholinesterase.
Answer C: Pseudocholinesterase is another name for butyrylcholinesterase. The mechanism of action for the termination of blockade of succinylcholine is diffusion away from the NMJ, not metabolism by pseudocholinesterase (butyrylcholinesterase). After succinylcholine diffuses away from the NMJ, it is then degraded by pseudocholinesterase. The mechanism of action for the termination of blockade by succinylcholine occurs via diffusion away from the neuromuscular junction.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Antifibrinolytic therapy aims to decrease the risk of bleeding during many types of surgery and it has become commonplace in anesthesia practice. Antifibrinolytics work mechanistically by inhibiting fibrinolysis, which is the breakdown of clots. In other words, antifibrinolytics work to stabilize clots by inhibiting the fibrinolytic pathway. It is known that increased bleeding and the administration of blood transfusions increases a patient’s morbidity and mortality, thus any means to decrease this can improve patient outcomes. In cardiac surgery, fibrinolysis plays an important role in clot resolution and healing. However, increased fibrinolytic activity during cardiopulmonary bypass has been correlated with increased bleeding. There are many types of antifibrinolytic agents; the most well-known include the serine protease inhibitor (aprotinin) and the synthetic lysine analogues, E-aminocaproic acid (EACA) and tranexamic acid (TXA). Aprotinin is thought to act by inhibiting plasmin and is extracted from bovine lung. The synthetic antifibrinolytics bind to plasminogen, preventing its activation to plasmin and thereby stopping the lysis of polymerized fibrin. Cardiac surgery ranks high on the list of surgeries associated with blood transfusions, with approximately 50-60% of patients receiving a transfusion. In cardiac surgery, use of antifibrinolytics has been shown to decrease bleeding and the need for transfusion. When the blood contacts the cardiopulmonary bypass circuitry, the fibrinolytic system is ramped up in an attempt to prevent forming of huge clots since the body views the extracorporeal membranes as foreign. Antifibrinolytics are used prior to the start of cardiothoracic surgery in an attempt to prevent this activation. In the United States, aprotinin is no longer administered because large trials found an increase in morbidity, however this is debated and still being studied. The currently available options in the United States are EACA and TXA. The dosage of antifibrinolytic therapy is anything but standard and depends on the agent used, the type of surgery, and the goals of therapy. For both EACA and TXA, a loading dose followed by an infusion is recommended. TXA is 6 to 10 times more potent than EACA and it also has a longer half-life. Contraindications depend on the agent used and the dose administered. Both EACA and TXA should be avoided in patients with upper urinary tract bleeding because they are renally excreted and elevations of the drug in renal failure could cause thrombosis and obstructive nephropathy. TXA has been shown to increase the risk of seizure-like events in certain patients undergoing cardiac surgery when compared to other agents. There is controversy if exaggerated thrombosis occurs with antifibrinolytic agents and it appears to be dependent on the type of agent used and the dose administered. There is not an increased requirement for heparin when antifibrinolytics are given. Heparin activates antithrombin III which is not affected by administration of antifibrinolytics.
Answer C: An increase in the amount of time a patient remains on cardiopulmonary bypass is not caused by the administration of antifibrinolytics.
Answer D: Aprotinin was removed from the United States market due to an increase in morbidity and mortality that was found in several large studies thus it is not the agent of choice currently. The fibrinolytic system plays an integral part during cardiac surgery to maintain vascular patency. This system works in concert with clot formation. Following cardiac surgery, the equilibrium shifts and increased fibrinolysis leads to bleeding with the need for blood transfusion. Using antifibrinolytic therapy to move this equilibrium back can help decrease transfusion requirements and improve patient outcomes. Surgery results in tissue damage which activates the inherent hemostatic mechanisms that attempt to control bleeding and initiate wound healing. These mechanisms include clot formation and stabilization. The fibrinolytic system helps to prevent huge clots forming which would occlude vessels and result in organ damage. In an ideal world, these two systems (clot formation and fibrinolysis) would work in parallel and bleeding would stop without any intravascular thrombosis. The degree of fibrinolytic system activation depends on the type and length of surgery. Activation is more pronounced in orthopedic and cardiac surgeries. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. When the β2 receptor, a G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR), is activated, it increases cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP), leading to bronchodilation (table). Activation of the β2-adrenergic receptor leads to the release of guanosine diphosphate (GDP) from the Gs α subunit (Gsα) with the subsequent binding of guanosine triphosphate (GTP). The binding of GTP results in the dissociation of Gsα from the GPCR. The GTP-bound Gsα then activates adenylyl cyclase, producing the second messenger, cAMP, via hydrolysis of adenosine triphosphate. The increased cAMP levels activate cAMP-dependent protein kinase A (PKA), which phosphorylates various proteins, such as myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) and myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP), throughout the cell. The increase in cAMP and PKA activation inhibits MLCK, which is required for smooth muscle contraction because it phosphorylates smooth muscle myosin. Thus, there is smooth muscle relaxation with inhibition of MLCK. Phosphorylation of MLCP results in the activation of MLCP and removal of the phosphate group on myosin, leading to smooth muscle relaxation. Additionally, PKA activates ion channels that lead to the efflux of calcium out of the cell and into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, reducing the concentration of intracellular calcium required for smooth muscle contraction. Although the exact mechanism for this process remains to be fully elucidated and is rather complex, the combination of decreased calcium within the smooth muscle cell, MLCK inhibition, and MLCP activation result in bronchodilation. When the α1 receptor is activated, it increases IP3,leading to vasoconstriction.
Answer B: When the α2 receptor is activated, it decreases cAMP, leading to a decrease in insulin secretion.
Answer C: When the β1 receptor is activated, it increases cAMP, leading to an increase in heart rate. Activation of the β2-adrenergic receptor results in the activation of adenylyl cyclase, increasing the concentration of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) and subsequently activating protein kinase A (PKA). The rise in cAMP and PKA activation leads to intracellular calcium reductions and smooth muscle relaxation, producing bronchodilation.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Local anesthetic infiltration may alleviate this patient's post-operative pain. Postoperative pain is a concern in any surgical setting. Beyond patient satisfaction, uncontrolled postoperative pain can have significant physiologic consequences in exacerbating baseline cardiopulmonary issues. Pain may elicit a sympathetic response in a patient with ischemic disease, which could propagate worsening ischemia. Pain may also lead to respiratory distress, which is problematic especially after general anesthesia where a patient may be at risk of atelectasis and aspiration. Pain also limits functionality and could contribute to deconditioning and the development of deep venous thromboses. Uncontrolled acute pain can lead to chronic pain, which may involve opioid tolerance and dependence as well as central sensitization. Many options exist in treating post-operative pain. A pharmacopeia of acute medical analgesics exists including (most commonly) opioids and their non-opioid adjuncts such as acetaminophen and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. A multimodal analgesic approach is progressively more favored to prevent the side effects of opioids including hyperalgesia. Regional anesthesia provides elegant ways to perform surgery either as a supplement or as an alternative to general anesthesia. Regional anesthesia, administered in the neuraxiom or peripherally, involves the injection of local anesthetic to chemically block nerve signaling in order to provide adequate surgical settings and/or prevent pain. The use of regional techniques has been shown to decrease post-operative pain scores and the rate of opioid consumption in both the intraoperative and post-operative periods. Study results are mixed in some of the additional benefits of regional techniques, such as cancer prevention and decreased mortality. What is known, rather, is that a regional sympathectomy decreases the physiologic cascade of inflammatory processes to significantly alter the pain experience, possibly improve blood flow, and even inhibit the development of thrombosis. Peripheral nerve blockade for amputations can reduce phantom limb pain as well. The motor blockade that accompanies some of these techniques, however, can be concerning to some patients. Motor block also poses a fall risk that is especially relevant to the frail, elderly, and obese patients. Local anesthetic infiltration involves the injection of local anesthetic around the surgical site to prevent and/or treat pain. The injection may be administered as a single shot or continuously via a catheter subcutaneously at the wound site as well as intraor peri-articularly. There are surgeries that can be performed purely under local anesthetic such as superficial mass excisions, operating on digits, and inguinal hernia repair. Much of the data on local anesthetic infiltration revolves around the peri-operative care of lower extremity joint surgeries where it has been found superior to placebo in pain control and in decreasing opioid consumption. Local anesthetic infiltration is often compared to peripheral nerve blockade, but the heterogeneity of what solution drug mixtures are used and how they are administered is widely variable. Argued advantages include ease of administration since an ultrasound or peripheral nerve stimulator are not required. The lack of motor blockade is favored as this allows a patient earlier mobility and avoids the fall risk of peripheral nerve blockade. Disadvantages are centered around the variability in administration and outcome, the lack of a peripheral sympathectomy, and the short duration of analgesia. Answers A & D: Although these peripheral nerve blocks, especially in conjunction, could alleviate this patient's surgical pain, the patient would experience limb weakness. Although the adductor canal blockade causes less motor block than a femoral nerve block at the proximal though, it still affects the vastus medialis. Compared to placebo, adductor canal block significantly reduces quadriceps strength. The patient is actively vomiting and likely cannot tolerate oral medications. Opioids, in general, could also exacerbate this patient's nausea. Local anesthetic infiltration may alleviate this patient's post-operative pain without worsening nausea or causing a motor block. This should be considered as an option for post-operative pain relief. Intravenous lidocaine is another analgesic modality that can be administered in the post-operative period. It is best suited for sympathetically mediated pain, but has a role in general post-operative pain as well. Although it does not produce a motor block, it must be administered continuously under medical supervision to survey for signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity. Hypnosis after a usual 2.5 mg/kg bolus of propofol occurs quickly, peaks at 90-100 seconds, and lasts 5-10 minutes. The onset of decreasing arterial blood pressure is much slower (double the time on average). The onset of EEG effect with propofol seems to be independent of age, but the onset of decreasing arterial blood pressure is delayed with advanced age (up to triple the time required for the hypnotic effect). Older individuals have decreased clearance rates and a smaller central compartment volume. This causes a greater concentration for any given dose. They also have increased sensitivity to any given concentration. Thus an 80-year-old patient may require half as much propofol compared to a 20-year-old.
Answer B: Propofol is known as a CYP3A4 inhibitor. Propofol blood concentrations in the middle of its therapeutic range reduce CYP3A4 activity by ~37% and increase the concentration of drugs metabolized by this cytochrome (e.g. midazolam).
Answer C: Time to awakening is usually shorter than context-sensitive half time because the decrease in plasma concentration required for awakening is generally less than 50%. Propofol's effect on the CNS causes loss of consciousness very quickly (peak < 2 min) but its effects on the cardiovascular system are delayed, especially in older adults.  Miller's Anesthesia, 8th edition, Chapter 30, 821-863.

Nitrous oxide is the oldest anesthetic currently still in clinical use despite its toxic effects. Nitrous oxide irreversibly inhibits enzymes involved in DNA synthesis, specifically methionine synthetase, causing reduced DNA and purine synthesis, resulting in megaloblastic anemia. Megaloblastic changes have been observed in patients exposed to nitrous oxide for 24 hours, and agranulocytosis has been observed at up to four days of exposure. Additional results of this inhibition include impaired endothelial function, enhanced platelet aggregation, and oxidative stress. In combination, these effects can lead to significant damage to the pulmonary vascular system. Long-term nitric oxide exposure, especially in individuals who inhale it as a recreational drug, can lead to megaloblastic anemia, myelopathy, neuropathy, and encephalopathy. Risk factors that predispose patients to nitric oxides' toxic effects include gastrointestinal malabsorption syndromes (eg, pernicious anemia), extremities of age, alcoholism, malnutrition, and a strict vegan diet (which can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency). Medications that inhibit the metabolism of folate (eg, methotrexate) can also predispose patients to nitric oxide toxicity. Therefore, careful recognition and consideration of the patient's past medical history and medications are essential when nitrous oxide use. is considered. Accelerated neuronal cell death (apoptosis) and degeneration is the proposed mechanism by which prolonged exposure to inhaled anesthetics can lead to long-term learning and memory impairment and other neurocognitive problems.
Answer B: Nitrous oxide does not inhibit folate metabolism. However, patients taking folate metabolism inhibitors (such as methotrexate) are at an increased risk of developing nitrous oxide toxicity and subsequent megaloblastic anemia.
Answer C: Although nitrous oxide acts on N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, this mechanism of action would not lead to megaloblastic changes. Anesthesia providers should carefully screen patients to identify any risk factors for nitric oxide toxicity. These risk factors include gastrointestinal malabsorption syndromes (eg, pernicious anemia), extremities of age, alcoholism, malnutrition, and a strict vegan diet (which can lead to vitamin B12 deficiency). Nitrous oxide irreversibly inhibits enzymes involved in DNA synthesis, specifically methionine synthetase, leading to reduced DNA synthesis, and, ultimately, megaloblastic anemia. Although nitrous oxide does not inhibit folate metabolism, patients taking medications that inhibit folate metabolism are predisposed to nitrous oxide toxicity and megaloblastic anemia. Diffusion hypoxia can also occur from nitrous oxide use. This occurs when nitrous oxide is rapidly discontinued. This rapid elimination of nitrous oxide from the blood in addition to slower nitrogen diffusion leads to a reduced alveolar oxygen concentration, resulting in hypoxemia. If hypoxemia is observed at the end of surgery when nitrous oxide was rapidly discontinued, diffusion hypoxia should be considered and managed with 100% fraction of inspired oxygen until the hypoxemia is resolved. Airway reflexes under ketamine anesthesia are maintained. Ketamine has been used frequently for procedural sedation in the emergency department. Airway reflexes have been found to be maintained in multiple studies. Further, aspiration is unlikely even when used for procedural sedation in an unsecured airway. Quoted from a review on the topic, "Despite 30 years of widespread ketamine use, there are no documented cases of clinically significant ketamine-associated aspiration in a patient lacking established contraindications to this drug." That being said, there is significant controversy regarding whether these reflexes are "protective" or not. The general consensus is that airway reflexes are preserved but these should not be assumed to be protective. Ketamine maintains better airway protective reflexes than many other anesthetics, but they are dose related (higher doses means less protective airway reflexes). Although an induction dose will likely preserve reflexes in a non-fasted patient without issue, it is not 100% protective against aspiration in a non-fasted patient. Ketamine, even at low serum levels, can produce powerful analgesia. The mechanism includes mu opioid receptor agonism and NMDA receptor antagonism. At higher doses, ketamine can produce hallucinations, amnesia, and increased sympathetic tone. Ketamine produces “dissociative amnesia,” in which protective reflexes and respiratory drive are relatively preserved in comparison to a similar anesthetic depth with other intravenous anesthetic agents.
Answer B: Ketamine increases CMRO2.
Answer C: The predominant hemodynamic effect of ketamine is indirect myocardial stimulation. Some direct myocardial depression is seen, however this is almost never clinically significant due to the indirect stimulation effects, even in critically ill patients. Ketamine is unique when compared to many other intravenous anesthetics: airway reflexes and respiratory drive are relatively preserved, significant analgesia is produced, and sympathetic tone is increased. Ketamine's analgesic effect is present even with relatively small doses.  Miller’s Anesthesia 7th Edition. Chapter 26: Intravenous Anesthetics. Page 742-747. Miller’s Anesthesia 7th Edition. Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that is used for multiple purposes. Ketamine induces a “dissociated anesthesia” where the patient appears to be awake but is actually anesthetized. Ketamine provides intense analgesia and some degree of amnesia, depending on the dosage. Ketamine antagonizes the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. It also interacts with a variety of other receptors, some of these include the mu, kappa, and sigma opioid receptors as well as muscarinic receptors. Ketamine possesses a chiral center and thus is a mixture of two stereoisomers, S(+) and R(-). The S(+) enantiomer has greater analgesia potency and shorter duration of action where the R(-)enantiomer has higher affinity for the NMDA receptor. In the US, the most commonly administered form of ketamine is a combination of the two-enantiomer mixture. In some other countries, a single preparation with only the S(+) enantiomer is available. The single enantiomer S(+) preparation has a potency that is three to four times that of the racemic mixture. The single preparation also has fewer side effects and shorter recovery time because smaller doses are required. Ketamine is highly lipid soluble that lends to its ability to quickly cross the blood-brain-barrier. When administered intravenously, ketamine will rapidly cross the blood-brain barrier and peak effect is seen within one minute. Ketamine has a very rapid onset of action and a low protein binding. Ketamine is metabolized in the liver via the cytochrome CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 pathways into norketamine, a weaker but still active metabolite. Norketamine is approximately one-third as potent as ketamine and this metabolite is excreted in the urine. Ketamine has an elimination half-life of 2-3 hours in adults. Ketamine is a racemic mixture of two enantiomers, R(-) and S(+). Most preparations include both enantiomers, however, a preparation of the S(+) only is available. The S(+) enantiomer is more potent than the R(-).
Answer C: Ketamine is not highly protein bound, which is different from many other IV anesthetics.
Answer D: Norketamine is the metabolite of ketamine and is physiologically active. Its potency is about one-third its parent compound. Ketamine is a phencyclidine derivative that acts primarily as a NMDA receptor antagonist to produce intense analgesia and dissociative anesthesia. Ketamine is metabolized in the liver and excreted by the kidneys. Ketamine can be administered via almost every route possible – oral, rectal, transnasal, epidural, intramuscular, and most commonly intravenous. Following intravenous administration, approximately 90% is bioavailable. When administered via the oral or rectal routes, only approximately 15% is bioavailable. The smaller bioavailability is secondary to incomplete gastro-intestinal absorption and first pass metabolism. Ketamine has been used as an adjunct to other local anesthetic and narcotic epidural solutions. It is thought to act on receptors in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord via NMDA receptor blockade. Initially, neurotoxicity occurred with epidural ketamine and this was thought to be secondary to the preservative used in the preparation. Preservative free is now available and can be used to enhance epidural analgesia. Nitrous oxide is a colorless, odorless gas at room temperature. It does not cause suppression of respiratory drive in spontaneously breathing patients. Generally, nitrous oxide has weak anesthetic effects, but significant analgesic effects. Nitrous oxide is insoluble in blood. This characteristic allows for rapid induction and emergence as a result of equilibration between the delivered and alveolar anesthetic concentrations. Desflurane is a highly volatile liquid at room temperature and must be stored in tightly-sealed bottles. It causes a concentration-dependent decrease in respiratory drive. It is a bronchodilator, but a strong airway irritant that can increase respiratory secretions.
Answer B: Isoflurane is a volatile liquid at room temperature. It is the most commonly used inhalational anesthetic worldwide. It is typically used for the maintenance of anesthesia after induction with other agents because of its pungent odor. Isoflurane produces concentration-dependent depression of ventilation. It particularly depresses the ventilatory response to hypercapnia and hypoxia. Although it is a bronchodilator, it is an airway irritant and can produce laryngospasm upon induction.
Answer D: Sevoflurane results in concentration-dependent depression of respiratory drive. It does not cause airway irritation and is used in outpatient settings due to its rapid recovery profile. Nitrous oxide is a colorless, odorless gas at room temperature. It does not cause suppression of respiratory drive in spontaneously breathing patients. Administration of norepinephrine results in intense vasoconstriction and increasing blood pressure and, resulting in reflex bradycardia. This vasoconstriction on the venous system leads to effects that maintain cardiac output. The decreased venous capacitance causes an increase in venous return and preload. Although the heart rate has decreased, the increased preload along with the β1-stimulation (positive ionotropic effect) results in an increased stroke volume maintaining or slightly increasing cardiac output. Norepinephrine is a neurotransmitter released by postganglionic sympathetic neurons and has an affinity for the following: α1 > α2 > β1. Because of its affinities, administration of norepinephrine results in intense vasoconstriction (with reflex bradycardia) and increased myocardial contractility. As a result, norepinephrine primarily elevates arterial blood pressure without significantly affecting cardiac output. Isoproterenol is a nonselective β-agonist; its use leads to an increase in heart rate and cardiac output via β1 and a decrease in blood pressure via β2.
Answer B: Administration of pure α1-agonists such as phenylephrine leads to an increase in blood pressure through α1 vasoconstricting effects, resulting in reflex bradycardia. Unlike norepinephrine, there is no β1 activity increasing myocardial contractility; thus, cardiac output often decreases.
Answer D: Unlike epinephrine, administration of norepinephrine does not lead to tachycardia due to the intense vasoconstriction-mediated reflex bradycardia. Administration of epinephrine does lead to increased heart rate and cardiac output. Administration of norepinephrine (α1 > α2 > β1) leads to intense vasoconstriction, causing slight reflex bradycardia. Despite the bradycardia, cardiac output is maintained via a decrease in venous capacitance, resulting in an increase in preload and stroke volume. The β1 increase in myocardial contractility further increases the stroke volume, and, despite a decrease in heart rate, cardiac output is maintained or slightly increased. Patients who smoke have a lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) compared with nonsmokers. In addition, nicotine causes vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle by action on alpha-adrenergic receptors. This vasoconstriction effect can contribute to impaired wound healing. Nonsmokers are more likely than smokers to have PONV. The mechanism by which smoking reduces the risk of PONV is unclear; however, this reduced risk may be attributed to the fact that smokers are desensitized to nausea. Nicotine stimulates indirect γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-mediated cerebral dopamine release, and nicotine withdrawal in the perioperative period may lead to low postoperative cerebral dopamine levels, reducing activation of dopaminergic circuits in the chemotactic trigger zone in the medulla. Nicotine is known to constrict blood vessels, including coronary blood vessels. Vasoconstriction of the skin results in reduced skin blood flow and reduced temperature at the fingertips. This reduced blood flow in microvascular beds secondary to nicotine can contribute to impaired wound healing, renal disease, and, potentially, placental dysfunction during pregnancy. Nicotine can decrease coronary blood flow by acting on alpha-adrenergic receptors in vascular smooth muscle, leading to vasoconstriction of the coronary arteries. Nicotine releases norepinephrine from adrenergic neurons and also increases the adrenal release of epinephrine. This release in epinephrine increases cardiac work, contractility, and blood pressure.
Answer B: Nicotine stimulates indirect GABA-mediated cerebral dopamine release and does not inhibit GABA receptors.
Answer D: Nicotine acts on vascular smooth muscle alpha-adrenergic receptors, leading to vasoconstriction. Patients who smoke have a lower incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV) compared with nonsmokers. This lower incidence of PONV is potentially attributed to the reduction of dopaminergic circuits in the chemotactic trigger zone in the medulla. Nicotine also produces vasoconstriction of vascular smooth muscle and increases norepinephrine and epinephrine release, thereby increasing heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure. Vasoconstriction also results in reduced wound healing.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "Nicotine: Anesthesia implications" Gropper MA, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. The data plotted on the graph of medication concentration (y-axis) vs time (x-axis) illustrate first-order elimination, which is a constant fraction of the drug eliminated per unit of time. Each hour, 50% of the medication is eliminated. Drugs can be eliminated by either zero-order or first-order kinetics. Zero-order kinetics will eliminate a constant amount of drug per unit time regardless of the plasma concentration. The drug concentration decreases linearly with time. First-order kinetics will eliminate a constant fraction of the drug per unit of time. The drug concentration decreases exponentially with time. The elimination will increase proportionally as the plasma concentration increases. Thus, higher concentration results in faster clearance, whereas zero-order elimination is independent of concentration. Most medications in use are eliminated by first-order kinetics. The few drugs that are eliminated by zero-order kinetics are ethanol, cisplatin, phenytoin, and salicylates (at high doses). Zero-order elimination would result in a constant amount of medication eliminated per unit of time.
Answer C: Second-order elimination does not exist.
Answer D: Third-order elimination does not exist. First-order elimination of medication will result in a constant fraction of medication eliminated per unit of time. Zero-order elimination will result in a constant amount of medication eliminated per unit of time.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Pharmacokinetics: 1st order elim (B)" Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. Ch. 11: Basic Principles of Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetic Concepts. 8th edition. Gropper M, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. Ch. 18: Basic Principles of Pharmacology: Zero Versus First-Order Kinetics. 9th edition.

Propofol decreases the rate of dissociation of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and its receptor. Propofol (2,6-disopropylphenol), an alkylphenol compound, is virtually insoluble in aqueous solution. Because thiopental is no longer available in the United States, propofol has become the most commonly used intravenously administered anesthetic induction agent; its advantages include a rapid onset and offset, a rapid redistribution such that little of the drug accumulates even with continuous infusions, and a very low rate of postoperative nausea and vomiting associated with its use. A widely accepted theory of anesthetic action is that both IV and inhalational anesthetics exert their primary sedative and hypnotic effects through an interaction with the inhibitory GABA neurotransmitter system. When the GABA receptor is activated, transmembrane chloride conductance increases, resulting in hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic cell membrane and functional inhibition of the postsynaptic neuron. Sedative-hypnotic drugs interact with different components of the GABA-receptor complex. The interaction of barbiturates and propofol with specific membrane structures appears to decrease the rate of dissociation of GABA from its receptor, thereby increasing the duration of the GABA-activated opening of the chloride ion channel. The noncompetitive antagonism of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors is the mechanism of action of ketamine. Ketamine is not a particularly selective drug, with multiple sites of action, including those in the central and peripheral nervous systems. The properties of ketamine are primarily mediated by noncompetitive antagonism at NMDA receptors, but the drug also has local anesthetic properties. N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors have been implicated in the mechanism of anesthesia, pain transmission, morphine tolerance, memory and cognitive function, long-term potentiation, long-term depression, neuronal toxicity, and chronic neurologic diseases (e.g., Alzheimer disease and major depression), as well as inflammatory responses.
Answer C: The efficiency of coupling between the GABA receptor and the chloride ion channel is the mechanism of action of benzodiazepines. The binding of benzodiazepines to their receptor site increases the efficiency of coupling between the GABA receptor and the chloride ion channel.
Answer D: The inhibition of adenylate cyclase through binding of α2 receptors is the mechanism of action for dexmedetomidine. Various hypnotic agents exert their primary sedative and hypnotic effects through an interaction with the γaminobutyric acid (GABA) neurotransmitter system. Propofol exerts its effect by decreasing the rate of dissociation of GABA from its receptor, thereby increasing the duration of GABA-activated opening of the chloride ion channel. Halogenated anesthetic agents can undergo chemical degradation in the setting of carbon dioxide absorbents. This degradation can create potentially dangerous levels of carbon monoxide in certain clinical settings. Carbon dioxide absorbents that contain greater quantities of strong bases like KOH or NaOH will tend to produce greater quantities of carbon monoxide in the setting of volatile anesthetics than those that contain weaker bases like Ba(OH)2 and Ca(OH)2. Of the commercially available carbon dioxide absorbents, Sodalime has the highest proportion of KOH and therefore has the potential to produce the greatest potential of carbon monoxide. Table adapted from Miller's Anesthesia, 8th Edition. Table 26-4 Composition of Base Chemicals and Water Content of Carbon Dioxide Absorbents The strong bases that are present in carbon dioxide absorbents can cause halogenated anesthetic agents to degrade into carbon monoxide, trifluoromethane (CF3H), and the acid hydrogen fluoride (HF). This incidence of the degradation reaction is increased in the presence of stronger bases (KOH > NaOH >> Ba(OH)2 and Ca(OH)2), the dryness of the absorbent, as well as the concentration and chemical structure of the anesthetic agent that is being degraded. As can be seen in by the table above, Baralyme is the carbon dioxide absorbent that has the greatest concentration of KOH, and therefore produces the greatest carbon monoxide concentrations, all other factors being equal. It is for this reason that Baralyme was withdrawn from the market in 2004. Soadalime I remains the absorbent that is currently in use with the greatest risk of producing carbon monoxide. Typically, the above-described degradation of volatile anesthetics into carbon monoxide only occurs in the setting of a desiccated carbon dioxide absorbent. Typically, the water content of the absorbent must be less than 5% in order for carbon monoxide to be produced. In general, this can only happen if high-flow flushing of an anesthesia circuit occurs for 1-2 days (over a weekend). Anesthetics that contain a difluoromethyl group are much more susceptible to this degradation reaction as it involves the production of a trifluoromethane group. Desflurane is the volatile anesthetic that is most prone to undergoing this degradation reaction, followed by enflurane and then isoflurane. Sevoflurane will degrade in the setting of strong bases, but will not produce carbon monoxide. Instead, sevoflurane will degrade in a highly exothermic reaction and sevoflurane use in a circuit connected to a desiccated carbon dioxide absorbent can potentially result in an airway fire. Answers A & B & D: Of the answers provided, Sodalime has the highest concentration of KOH and therefore will produce the highest quantity of carbon monoxide in the setting of a halogenated anesthetic agent.  Factors that increase the production of carbon monoxide by carbon dioxide absorbents due to the degradation of halogenated anesthetic agents include decreased water content of the absorbent material, increased strong base concentration within the absorbent, concentration of the volatile anesthetic, and the chemical structure of the volatile anesthetic (desflurane > isoflurane). The degradation of sevoflurane does not produce carbon monoxide but instead produces very large quantities of heat that could potentially result in an airway fire. Changing FiO2 to 100% without significantly changing fresh gas flow is an appropriate method to reduce the risk of diffusion hypoxia. This will allow a more steady decline in nitrous oxide levels as there will be some rebreathing in the anesthesia circle system. Nitrous oxide is a weak anesthetic agent that has significant analgesic effects. Surgical anesthetic depth is only achieved under hyperbaric conditions. However, analgesia is produced at concentrations as low as 20%. When nitrous oxide is discontinued, it is eliminated rapidly. This rapid elimination results in the dilution of oxygen and carbon dioxide concentrations within the alveolus. Nitrous oxide cannot be used at concentrations above 80% as it limits the delivery of adequate oxygen. To avoid hypoxia, 100% oxygen should be administered when nitrous oxide is discontinued. Nearly 99.9% of absorbed nitrous oxide is eliminated unchanged by the lungs. Nitrous oxide is very insoluble in blood and other tissues. An increase in the respiratory rate will not prevent diffusion hypoxia. Upon discontinuation of nitrous oxide administration, nitrous oxide can diffuse from blood to alveoli and subsequently dilute oxygen in the lungs. A similar effect is seen with carbon dioxide concentrations within the alveolus.
Answer C: An increase in PEEP will not prevent diffusion hypoxia that results from discontinuation of nitrous oxide. Rapid elimination of nitrous oxide results in dilution of oxygen and carbon dioxide concentrations within the alveolus. The rapid equilibration between delivered and alveolar anesthetic concentrations provides for rapid induction and emergence from anesthesia. The rapid uptake of nitrous oxide from alveolar gas serves to concentrate coadministered halogenated anesthetics resulting in the second gas effect.
Answer D: Nitrous oxide is very insoluble in blood and other tissues. This characteristic allows for rapid equilibration between delivered and alveolar anesthetic concentrations. When co-administered with halogenated agents, there is a second gas effect. When nitrous oxide administration is rapidly discontinued, it can result in dilution of oxygen in the lung. High fresh gas flows will create a gradient between the anesthesia circuit (very low nitrous oxide level) and the alveolus, which promotes nitrous oxide washout into the lungs. Having FiO2 below 90% will increase the risk of hypoxia as well in this setting. Rapid elimination of nitrous oxide results in dilution of oxygen and carbon dioxide concentrations within the alveolus. To reduce the risk of hypoxia, 100% oxygen should be administered when nitrous oxide is discontinued.
