Labetalol undergoes hepatic oxidative biotransformation and glucuronidation. Labetalol is a non-selective competitive antagonist at both the β1 and β2 receptors as well as a selective antagonist at the α1 receptors. Labetalol also exhibits intrinsic sympathetic activity via partial β2 agonism and inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine. The ratio of α:β blockade varies depending on the route of administration, with a 1:3 ratio for oral administration and a 1:7 ratio for intravenous administration. The heart rate is typically maintained or reduced and there is little effect on cardiac output. Systemic vascular resistance decreases while maintaining cerebral, renal, and coronary blood flow. Following intravenous administration, the hypotensive effects are typically seen within 2-5 minutes, with a peak in activity at 5-15 minutes. These effects typically last for 2-4 hours. The most common side effects of labetalol are orthostatic hypotension, nausea, dizziness, and fatigue. There is no accumulation in renal disease and no dosing changes are necessary.
Answer B: The elimination half-life of labetalol is 6 hours.
Answer C: Labetalol is poorly lipid soluble and does not cross the placenta, which allows its use during pregnancy-induced hypertension. Labetalol has a half-life of 6 hours and undergoes hepatic oxidation and glucuronidation.  Goodman & Gilman, The Pharmacologic Basis of Therapeutics. Chapter 12 in 12th Edition. Pages 328-329. At plasma concentrations achieved by an induction dose of etomidate, inhibition of 11β-hydroxylase results in reduced cortisol and aldosterone synthesis. 11β-hydroxylase is responsible for the conversion of 11-deoxycorticosterone to corticosterone (precursor to aldosterone) and the conversion of 11-deoxycortisol to cortisol. An induction dose (0.3 mg/kg) of etomidate can inhibit the adrenal response to adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol synthesis for up to 72 hours. Although this inhibition has not been shown to be deleterious in the general population undergoing surgery, etomidate infusions in the ICU have been shown to increase mortality. Etomidate will also inhibit the action of 17α-hydroxylase but with minimal effect at clinically relevant concentrations. Etomidate is associated with 30-40% incidence of nausea and vomiting as well as a 70% incidence of myoclonus and hiccoughs. These excitatory movements can be decreased by pretreatment with midazolam, magnesium, or low-dose etomidate (0.03 mg/ kg). Pain on injection is common and likely due to the 35% propylene glycol formulation. This pain on injection can be decreased by pretreatment with intravenous lidocaine. Etomidate has also been associated with up to a 30% incidence of thrombophlebitis particularly if administered via a small vein in the hand. 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase is not inhibited by etomidate.
Answer C: Etomidate is associated with minimal inhibition of 17α-hydroxylase; however, not at clinically relevant plasma concentrations.
Answer D: 21α-hydroxylase is not inhibited by etomidate. Etomidate inhibits 11β-hydroxylase resulting in decreased synthesis of cortisol and aldosterone.  Miller’s Anesthesia. The vapor pressure of sevoflurane at 20ºC is 157 mm Hg and is the lowest among the answer choices. At a temperature of 20°C and 1 atmosphere of pressure, all inhalational anesthetics exist in the liquid form except for nitrous oxide, which has a boiling point of −88°C. Although the inhalational anesthetics may be liquid in form, they equilibrate between the liquid and gas phases in a closed container. The molecules in the gaseous state exert a pressure, known as vapor pressure, on the closed container due to the kinetic energy of the molecules colliding with the container. Vapor pressure is proportional to the temperature. As the temperature rises, the kinetic energy of the liquid increases, raising the number of molecules in the gaseous state, increasing the vapor pressure. After the temperature is raised sufficiently such that the vapor pressure exceeds the atmospheric pressure in an open container, it will have reached its boiling point. The boiling point of desflurane at 24ºC is near room temperature (20ºC) and, thus, requires a closed storage container and a pressurized and heated vaporizer to prevent boiling and unpredictable vapor concentrations. Boiling points and vapor pressures at 20ºC of inhalational anesthetics Table adapted from Barash PG, et al. Clinical Anesthesia. 8th ed. Table 18.1 Page 461. The vapor pressure of desflurane at 20ºC is 669 mm Hg.
Answer B: The vapor pressure of isoflurane at 20ºC is 238 mm Hg.
Answer C: The vapor pressure of nitrous oxide at 20ºC is 38,770 mm Hg. Vapor pressure is the pressure generated in a closed system by the gaseous phase of a substance at equilibrium between a gaseous and condensed (liquid or solid) state. The 3 main volatile anesthetics in clinical use have a boiling point above room temperature and, thus, exist as a liquid with vapor pressure. Sevoflurane has the lowest vapor pressure at 157 mm Hg, followed by isoflurane at 238 mm Hg and desflurane at 669 mm Hg. The difference between volatile and gaseous anesthetics is that volatile anesthetics (eg, sevoflurane) have a vapor pressure less than 1 atmosphere at 20ºC and a boiling point above 20ºC, whereas gaseous anesthetics (eg, nitrous oxide) have a vapor pressure greater than 1 atmosphere at 20ºC and a boiling point below 20ºC. The sedative effects of midazolam and dexmedetomidine are synergistic or supra-additive, meaning that the total effect is greater than the sum of the effect size when either drug is given alone. Drugs may have additive, synergistic, or antagonistic effects when they are combined. Additive drugs have a combined effect that is equal to the sum of the effect of each agent given alone. A classic example of this is inhaled anesthetics. For example, sevoflurane at a concentration of 0.5 minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) combined with desflurane at a concentration of 0.5 MAC has the same effect on the brain as either drug alone at a concentration of 1 MAC. Drugs that act by different mechanisms are typically not additive but instead act synergistically, meaning that the total effect is greater than the sum of the effect size when either drug is given alone. Examples of synergy include administration of propofol and remifentanil together, which has synergistic effects on respiratory depression, and administration of midazolam and dexmedetomidine together, which works synergistically for sedative effects. However, there are exceptions to this rule, including administration of ketamine and midazolam together, which has additive, not synergistic, hypnotic effects. While propofol and remifentanil have synergistic effects on respiratory depression, because both drugs induce respiratory depression by different mechanisms (γ-aminobutyric acid and opioid receptors, respectively), remifentanil does not have any effect on the bispectral index (BIS) value, so adding remifentanil to propofol does not further decrease the BIS reading. Drugs with antagonistic, or infra-additive effects, will have a total effect that is less than the sum of the effect size when either drug is given alone. An example of an antagonistic interaction is the effect on immobility when ketamine and propofol are combined. Opioids do affect the BIS value, so adding remifentanil to propofol does not affect the BIS value.
Answer B: Propofol and remifentanil has synergistic, not additive, effects on respiratory depression when they are administered together.
Answer C: Ketamine and midazolam have additive, not synergistic, hypnotic effects. When anesthetic drugs are combined, the effects may be additive, synergistic, or infra-additive. For most intravenously administered drugs, combining drugs with different mechanisms of action causes a synergistic effect. The exception to this rule is ketamine, which may cause additive, infra-additive, or synergistic effects depending on the drug combination. Glucagon improves cardiac contractility via a nonadrenergic mechanism. Glucagon has multiple physiologic effects including inhibition of gastric motility, promotion of hepatic gluconeogenesis, and relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi. In addition, glucagon also acts as a cardiac inotropic and chronotropic agent. It increases intracellular cAMP through a specific nonadrenergic receptor and results in increased myocardial contractility. Glucagon is useful for treatment of β-blocker toxicity because it does not utilize α- or β-adrenergic receptors. Stimulation of the latter is generally ineffective in the setting of β-blocker toxicity. Glucagon is generally not considered a first line therapy for low cardiac output (CO) states, but may be beneficial in the following situations after conventional therapies have failed: (1) low CO following cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), (2) low CO following myocardial infarction, (3) chronic congestive heart failure, (4) low CO from excess β-blockade, and (5) anaphylactic shock with refractory hypotension. Glucagon does cause relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, but this has not been shown to decrease the incidence of shock liver as a result of CPB or low CO states.
Answer C: Glucagon increases intracellular cAMP through a specific nonadrenergic receptor. Glucagon increases intracellular cAMP which results in increased inotropy and chronotropy in cardiac myocytes. This effect is mediated through a specific, nonadrenergic receptor. Both ferrous and ferric iron will readily bind with a variety of drugs that contain a catechol moiety. As the amount of freely circulating iron in the body is absolutely minimal, the main site of these interactions is within the gut where large amounts of free iron can exist, especially in a patient taking iron supplementation. Both levodopa and carbidopa contain a catechol moiety, and iron will bind to these drugs and inhibit their absorption from the intestinal lumen. This results in a clinically impactful decline in the effectiveness of the levodopa/carbidopa combination drug in treating the symptoms of Parkinson's disease. Given the nature of anesthesia practice, drug-drug interactions are commonly encountered. The majority of these interactions come in the form of pharmacokinetic or pharmacodynamic interactions. In pharmacokinetic interactions, the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination of a drug are somehow modified by the presence of another medication. In pharmacodynamic interactions, there may be a direct additive or opposed effect at the effector organ or there may be an upstream or downstream effect on a physiological control process by one drug that alters the effect of a medication. In general, interactions that impact the absorption of medications is not something that is often considered in the practice of anesthesia. The vast majority of medications that are given are via either the inhaled or parenteral route, and in the case of parenterally administered medications, the bioavailability is 100%. When caring for critically ill patients either in the operating room or in the ICU itself, consideration must be given to the bioavailability and absorption of medications that are given via the enteral route. In general, the formation of complexes through drug-drug binding represents a major cause of impaired absorption of medicines. Enteral metal ions such as calcium, magnesium, aluminum, and iron commonly form complexes with certain classes of antibiotics including tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline) and fluoroquinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin). As stated above, iron will also readily bind with the catechol moiety in both levodopa and carbidopa. This drug-metal complex will reduce enteric absorption of the drug and decrease its clinical effectiveness. For this reason, it is recommended that all metal-containing medications (antacids, laxatives, iron supplements) be given at least 2 hours from the time that these other drugs are given. Cholestyramine is a medication that is also commonly taken to help treat the pruritis associated with intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. This drug is designed to bind bile acids, and can also form complexes with other acidic drugs. Examples of these include warfarin, aspirin, phenytoin, and furosemide. In a similar fashion to the metals above, complexes formed by cholestyramine with other drugs will have decreased absorption and clinical effectiveness. Intravenous dexamethasone solution that is prepared with benzyl alcohol as a preservative will react when combined with ondansetron to form precipitates. This reaction is mediated by the preservative in the dexamethasone solution alkalinizing the solution and causing ondansetron to precipitate out of solution.
Answer B: Both diclofenac and warfarin bind to the same site (Site I) on albumin and have a similar protein-binding affinity. The coadministration of these medications may cause an increased clinical effect of the warfarin with significant hemorrhagic sideeffects.
Answer D: Mixing lidocaine and propofol within the same syringe will result in eventually layering and coalescing of the soybean oil and egg lecithin vehicle within which the lipid-soluble propofol is carried. This effect is due to the acidic nature of commercial local anesthetic preparations which modifies the characteristics of the emulsion. Because of this, lidocaine and propofol mixtures should be immediately administered once formulated, or simply administered separately. Drug-drug interactions where one drug binds the other are relatively rare, and primarily occur when two medications are administered via the enteric route. Most commonly these occur when enteric metals chelate with another medication and impair the medicine's ability to be absorbed.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. The proinflammatory action of volatile anesthetics can potentially exacerbate acute lung injury. Volatile anesthetics have many widespread systemic effects and their influence on the respiratory system is profound. Volatile anesthetics have bronchodilator actions due to a reduction in intracellular calcium and sensitivity. Inhaled anesthetics also decrease the rate of mucus clearance and the main lipid component of surfactant. Respiratory changes seen in the operating room include an inhibition of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, a reduction in tidal volume and minute ventilation with an increase in respiratory rate, a depression in the central ventilation response to hypercapnia or hypoxia, and potential proinflammatory actions worsening acute lung injury. Rapid shallow breathing is seen with inhalational volatile anesthetics.
Answer B: Diminished mucus clearance is seen with inhalational volatile anesthetics.
Answer C: Volatiles cause depression of the central response to hypercapnia and hypoxia. Volatile anesthetics decrease the rate of mucus clearance, increase respiratory rate, decrease tidal volumes, cause a depression of the central response to hypercapnia and hypoxia, and have the potential to exacerbate acute lung injury with their proinflammatory actions. The effect of anesthetics often dissipates rapidly as a result of redistribution, particularly when single-bolus kinetics are considered. Eventually, the fate of most intravenous anesthetics is like that of non-anesthetic drugs, meaning they mostly end up being hepatically metabolized and/or renally excreted. Drug metabolism is the single most important pharmacokinetic process that is responsible for many of the inter-individual variations seen in therapeutic drug responses. It is usually the slowest of the four traditional pharmacokinetic processes. Renal elimination terminates the actions of relatively few drugs. This includes drugs small in size, those that remain fully or nearly fully ionized at physiological pH, and those that are not protein bound. However, most pharmacologically active molecules tend to be lipophilic and remain unionized or only partially ionized at physiological pH. Often times, lipophilic drugs are bound strongly to plasma proteins. These molecules are not ideal candidates for renal elimination and would remain in the body for prolonged periods if some alternate process did not terminate their actions. For example, thiopental is a short-acting lipophilic agent and would exert its pharmacological effect for 100 years if it were not for alternative methods of drug action termination. The kidney is the most important organ for the excretion of drugs and/or their metabolites. Some compounds are also excreted via bile, sweat, saliva, exhaled air, or breast milk. Metabolism is the most important mechanism of drug action termination for most drugs. Drug action terminates by enzymecatalyzed conversion to inactive or less active compounds in a process known as biotransformation. Biotransformation is a major mechanism for drug elimination. Most drugs undergo biotransformation to produce more polar metabolites than the originally administered drug. Excretion of compounds through renal and hepatic systems largely depends on lipophilicity or fat solubility. More lipophilic compounds tend to be reabsorbed back into circulation, either following renal glomerular filtration or through hepatic biliary excretion. Therefore, biotransformation of compounds into more polar (hydrophilic) structures is essential for complete removal of the drug. In addition, decreased drug lipophilicity limits a drug’s capacity to redistribute and accumulate in highly lipophilic areas, such as fat or brain tissue. Biotransformation reactions are classified into two types: phase I (nonsynthetic) and phase II (synthetic) reactions. Phase I reactions include the process of oxidation, reduction, and hydrolysis. These reactions introduce functional groups (–OH, –SH, –NH2) that serve to promote the following phase II reactions. Some enzymes catalyzing phase I reactions include cytochrome P450, alcohol dehydrogenase, monoamine oxidase, esterases, and amidases. Phase II reactions are conjugation reactions, linking the functional groups from phase I reactions to other endogenous compounds. Enzymes catalyzing phase II reactions include glucuronyl transferase and sulfotransferase, among others. Cytochrome P450 enzymes catalyze phase I reactions.
Answer C: Metabolism is the more important mechanism of action termination for most drugs. Renal elimination terminates the actions of relatively few drugs.
Answer D: The kidney is the most important organ for the excretion of drugs and/or their metabolites. Some compounds are also eliminated via bile, sweat, saliva, exhaled air, or breast milk. Metabolism via biotransformation is the most important means of drug action termination. Renal elimination will terminate drug action for small, non-protein-bound and hydrophilic drugs. Redistribution plays a role in very lipophilic anesthetics.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Action Termination: Elimination" Goodman & Gilman’s The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics. The baricity of the local anesthetic solution (hyperbaric bupivacaine) is the most important factor affecting the level of blockade for spinal anesthesia. Baricity is important because it can influence the spread of the local anesthetic on the basis of gravity and the position of the patient. Because the patient is placed in the Trendelenburg position after injection, the only spinal anesthesia mixture that will travel is the 1.5 mL hyperbaric 0.75% bupivacaine, which will follow the force of gravity because it has a higher density than the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). In the Trendelenburg (head down) position, the hyperbaric solution will spread cephalad. Baricity is defined as the ratio of two densities, such as the density of the CSF to the density of the local anesthetic. Local anesthetics are made hyperbaric to CSF by adding a dextrose solution to them. When hyperbaric solutions are injected into the subarachnoid space, the hyperbaric local anesthetics will flow with gravity, depending on the position of the patient. When it is injected in the sitting position, the hyperbaric anesthetic will flow toward the sacral vertebra. When the patient is laid supine, the hyperbaric anesthetic will flow to the dependent areas of the spine reaching the midthoracic dermatomes. In the Trendelenburg position, the hyperbaric solution will spread cephalad. In contrast, hypobaric anesthetics will flow against gravity. Some factors, such as weight, height, body mass index, and vertebral column, have no clinically significant effect on the spread of the local anesthetic in average-sized adults. Under extreme conditions such as in much older patients (>65 years) or very tall patients, altering the dose can be considered. Older age is associated with an increased level of sensory block. In older patients, the CSF volume decreases, while the specific gravity of the CSF increases. In addition, the nerves are more sensitive to local anesthetics in older age. Cerebrospinal fluid and 1.5 mL isobaric 0.5% bupivacaine have a similar density. When 1.5 mL isobaric 0.5% bupivacaine is injected, the spread will stay at the level of injection and will not change on the basis of positioning.
Answer B: Cerebrospinal fluid and 1.2 mL isobaric 0.5% bupivacaine + 25 mcg fentanyl have a similar density. When 1.2 mL isobaric 0.5% bupivacaine + 25 mcg fentanyl is injected, the spread will stay at the level of injection and will not change on the basis of positioning.
Answer C: Cerebrospinal fluid and 1.2 mL isobaric 0.5% bupivacaine + 250 mcg morphine have a similar density. When 1.2 mL isobaric 0.5% bupivacaine + 250 mcg morphine is injected, the spread will stay at the level of injection and will not change on the basis of positioning. The baricity of the local anesthetic (hyperbaric local anesthetics) is the most important factor affecting the level of blockade for spinal anesthesia. Baricity is important because it can influence the spread of the local anesthetic on the basis of gravity and the position of the patient. Other factors that can affect the level of blockade include medication (total dose), patient (cerebrospinal fluid volume, older age, and pregnancy), and procedural factors (patient position, and epidural injection before or after spinal injection). A pneumothorax, which can rapidly grow in size with nitrous oxide use, can cause difficulty with ventilation and increased peak airway pressures in intubated patients. Subclavian vein central line placement is associated with a 1-2% risk of pneumothorax. Classically, a pneumothorax can be suspected if the syringe fills with air when venous access is being attempted, indicative of lung puncture. Most patients who develop a pneumothorax due to subclavian central line placement remain asymptomatic. However, concurrent or subsequent nitrous oxide use at 75% can expand a pneumothorax to double its size in 10 minutes and triple its size in 30 minutes. This can lead to difficulty ventilating with increased peak airway pressures. In severe cases, a tension pneumothorax can develop, in which the increased intrathoracic pressure may also impede venous return, causing reduced cardiac output and hypotension. A primary concern of nitrous oxide use is its ability to expand air-filled spaces because of its greater solubility in blood compared to nitrogen. Several closed air spaces, such as the bowel and middle ear, exist in the body. Other closed cavities may occur as a result of disease or surgery, such as a pneumothorax or a craniotomy. Nitrogen in air-filled spaces cannot be removed readily via the bloodstream, but nitrous oxide easily diffuses from the blood into these spaces. Diffusion of nitrous oxide continues into these spaces until the partial pressure equals that of the blood and alveoli (i.e. until equilibrium is reached between all three compartments). Although an expanding pneumothorax can cause hypoxia, hypoxic gas mixtures are unlikely to occur since most anesthesia machines have proportioning systems which require a minimum amount of oxygen dialed into the total fresh gas flow (FGF). For example, if oxygen falls below 25% of FGF, the proportioning system is activated in order to reduce N2O and to maintain O2 above this safety threshold.
Answer C: A suspected air embolus would cause a large drop in end tidal CO2. Central venous access was not obtained in this case and therefore introduction of intravascular air is highly unlikely. Tension pneumothorax can decrease cardiac return and thus decrease end tidal CO2, but this would not occur acutely. A gas mixture of 75% N2O can expand a pneumothorax to double its size in 10 minutes and to 3 times its size in 30 minutes. The volume of an air embolus causing cardiovascular collapse during the concomitant administration of N2O is less than the volume of an air embolus causing cardiovascular collapse in the absence of N2O. The axon, which is the long slender projection of the nerve responsible for conducting impulses, is wrapped by a delicate connective tissue layer call the endoneurium. A local anesthetic traveling from outside the peripheral nerve to the axon would pass through epineurium, perineurium, and finally the endoneruium. A peripheral nerve is composed of three main connective tissue sheathes: the endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium. The endoneurium is the innermost connective layer. Each individual axon is surrounded by the delicate endoneurium. Individual axons wrapped in endoneurium are bundle together to form a fascicle. Each fascicle is wrapped in a second connective tissue layer called the perineurium. The perineurium is a thin dense multilayered connective tissue sheath. Multiple fascicles wrapped in perineurium are contained within a peripheral nerve. The matrix of connective tissue outside of the perineurium functioning to hold the fascicles together is called the inner or interfascicular epineurium. The outer, or epifascicular epineurium, refers to the connective tissue sheath on the very outside of the peripheral nerve and encasing all of its contents. This is the outermost layer of the peripheral nerve itself. The outermost epineural tissue is loosely bound to a sheath of connective tissue outside of the nerve and this tissue sheath is referred to as the adventitia, paraneurium, mesoneurium, or gliding apparatus. The nerve encased in epineurium has mobility within this tissue sheath and can be thought of as a potential space for deposition of local anesthetic. From inside out the layers are: endoneurium, perineurium, and epineurium. At this time, it is generally accepted that avoiding needle placement and injection within the nerve is the safest approach. This means keeping the needle outside of the epineurium. This is referred to as an extraneural block. On ultrasound, placement of the needle and injection of local anesthetic within the adventitia, but outside of the epineurium may produce a doughnut sign where the local anesthetic surrounds the nerve within the connective sheath. Placement of the needle and injection within the nerve can potentially cause nerve injury. There are generally two types of intraneural injections. Needle placement within the epineurium, but outside of perineurim avoids puncture of the fascicle. This has been referred to as an extrafascicular block or an epineural intraneural injection. On ultrasound, this may be seen as nerve swelling and separation of the fascicles. Extrafascicular injections within the epineurium may or may not cause nerve damage depending on a variety of factors. Intentional injection within the epineurium is controversial and currently being studied. Puncture of epineurium and the perineurium places the needle within the fascicle, and has been referred to as an intrafascicular block or subepineural intraneural injection. It is well accepted that intrafascicular injection can lead to permanent nerve damage and should be avoided. Most blocks are performed by placing the needle close to the nerve but outside of the epineurium, which is the outermost layer of the peripheral nerve. Penetration of the perineurium would mean the needle is within the nerve and permanent damage could occur.
Answer B: The epineurium is the outer most layer of the peripheral nerve and an extraneural block would avoid penetration of this layer.
Answer D: The epineurium is the outer-most connective tissue layer of a peripheral nerve. Peripheral nerve anatomy from the inside-out is endoneurium, perineurium, epineurium. The endoneurium wraps individual axons. Most blocks are performed by placement and injection of local anesthetic outside of the epineurium. The maternal administration of midazolam during the third trimester and also during labor has been associated with the development of fetal hypotonia, also called floppy baby syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by a constellation of symptoms that include a laxity in the neonate's muscles when lying supine as well as sedation, apnea, impaired responses to cold stress, and a reluctance to suck. For this, as well as the common maternal preference to avoid amnestic agents around the time of delivery, midazolam is rarely administered prior to cesarean delivery. The anesthetic management of a patient undergoing an emergency cesarean delivery is complicated by the concerns of the anesthetic agents that are utilized on the neonate following delivery. Considerations for these anesthetics include the rapid securement of the maternal airway as well as optimization of oxygen delivery to the uterus and therefore the fetus prior to delivery. These anesthetics are typically performed in critical situations where the well-being of the newborn neonate, as well as the mother, depends on the rapid and efficient induction and maintenance of anesthesia. Given the risk for aspiration near the time of delivery, rapid sequence induction and intubation (RSII) is commonly performed for an emergency cesarean section. Medications used to safely perform this induction of anesthesia include propofol, etomidate, ketamine, as well as either a depolarizing or non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking agent such as succinylcholine or rocuronium respectively. Aspiration risk is maintained in the post-partum period for the first 48 hours after delivery, which has implications on procedures such as tubal ligation. Propofol has not been shown to affect neonatal Apgar scores and is the most rapidly acting induction agent that is in common use today, inducing anesthesia in as little as 45 seconds. While hypotension, especially in this patient population, is its most common side effect, when administered at typical induction doses umbilical vein concentrations of this drug are minimal, and no clinical effect of neonatal depression has been demonstrated. Higher or repeat dosing of this medication may result in neonatal depression, however, and care should be taken with repeat dosing if difficulty obtaining an airway occurs during the induction of anesthesia. Etomidate is another fast-acting IV induction agent that clinically differs from propofol in its minimal effects on maternal hemodynamics. When the peripartum course is complicated by hemodynamic instability, such as due to blood loss, this medication may be considered for rapid induction of anesthesia. This medication has not been shown to adversely affect neonatal Apgar scores when used for induction of cesarean sections, however, it does potentially lower the maternal seizure threshold, and fetal cortisol levels may be decreased for up to 6 hours following a single maternal dose. This hypocortisolism is of uncertain clinical significance, however, and etomidate is considered safe to use in this patient population. Ketamine is another IV induction agent with minimal hemodynamic effects following induction. When administered at typical induction doses it has not been shown to decrease neonatal Apgar scores. This medication inhibits the reuptake of norepinephrine in the peripheral system, and in doing so maintains an arterial blood pressure and cardiac output. Because of this effect, this medication is useful for inducing a patient who is suffering a large volume hemorrhage causing hemodynamic instability, or in a patient with sepsis. Repeat or increased dosing above standard induction doses can result in decreased uterine blood flow and a lowered maternal seizure threshold, though normal induction doses are thought to be safe to use for induction of cesarean section deliveries. Neuromuscular blocking agents administered at typical doses used during induction of anesthesia are not detectable in the umbilical blood samples. In the case of succinylcholine, this is likely due to its rapid metabolism. In the case of the nondepolarizing agents, their low lipophilicity greatly inhibits their transfer across the placental barrier. Regardless, administration of these medications in standard practice does not generate neonatal effects. Inhaled anesthetics do exert profound depressive effects on the fetus and neonate. While still intrauterine, volatile halogenated anesthetics decrease fetal heart rate and fetal heart rate variability, though the long-term effects of this exposure are largely unknown. At the time of delivery, maternal exposure to volatile anesthetics results in an anesthetized neonate as these medications rapidly equilibrate across the placenta with the fetal circulation. As these medications are eliminated through the expiration of the anesthetic gasses themselves, the neonate may require respiratory support following delivery in order to facilitate elimination of these drugs. In addition to the neonatal effects of halogenated agents, their use has profound effects on maternal physiology. Halogenated agents are potent uterine relaxants, and their use has been associated with increased blood loss during cesarean delivery. In the case of nitrous oxide, its use as a maternal anesthetic is recommended in order to minimize the amount of halogenated agent that is required to maintain anesthesia. While a theoretical risk of neonatal diffusion hypoxia and persistent pulmonary circulation due to persistent pulmonary hypertension exists with the administration of maternal nitrous oxide, these effects have not been observed clinically. Chronic opioid administration can result in an opioid dependant neonate, while acute administration of opioids in the peripartum period can result in a depressed neonate with a diminished heart rate and respiratory drive. This depression may be rapidly corrected by neonatal administration of naloxone, however, this is not typically recommended as it carries with it a high risk of placing the neonate into acute opioid withdrawal. Instead, treatment of newborn children of mothers who chronically abuse opioids is primarily supportive. Ketamine, when used in normal induction doses, has not been shown to impact Apgar scores following delivery.
Answer C: Propofol, when used in normal induction doses, is not detectable in neonatal circulation and does not impact Apgar scores following delivery.
Answer D: Rocuronium does not cross the placenta in clinically significant doses, and thus has not been shown to affect neonatal physiology to an extent that is clinically relevant. The majority of anesthetic agents may be used at normal doses in emergency cesarean deliveries. Inhaled anesthetic agents exert the most powerful negative effect on the neonate, and exposure in-utero should be minimized immediately prior to delivery through communication with the surgical team and rapid delivery of the fetus following induction of anesthesia. Benzodiazepines have been associated with fetal hypotonia ("floppy baby syndrome") when administered during labor and may have detrimental effects for hours to weeks following delivery. Results of numerous studies have provided evidence that coadministration of drugs that contain N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) antagonistic properties (ketamine, butorphanol, buprenorphine, and nitrous oxide) can either prevent or reduce opioid-induced hyperalgesia caused by remifentanil. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH) is associated with the use of potent, high-dose opioids. Researchers found that, when potent opioids such as remifentanil or fentanyl were administered, there was a small yet significant increase in acute pain after surgery. Opioid-induced hyperalgesia was shown to be due to spinal sensitization to glutamate and substance P in the dorsal horn of the spinal cord. Results of additional studies provided evidence that activation of glycogen synthase-3β (GSK-3β) led to hyperalgesia by regulating NMDA receptor plasticity and that inhibition of GSK-3β prevented OIH. Additionally, abrupt cessation of potent opioids, such as remifentanil, is also associated with OIH. When remifentanil was withdrawn gradually, no OIH was observed. Results of studies have provided evidence that ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, can prevent OIH and acute opioid tolerance. Low-dose ketamine (10-30 mg/hour) infusion can be used to prevent OIH. When buprenorphine, an opioid with NMDA antagonist activity, was administered along with remifentanil, it prevented OIH. Other drugs that possess NMDA activity, such as nitrous oxide and butorphanol, reduced the risk of OIH when they were given along with remifentanil. Antagonism of the NMDA receptors, not α2-receptors, during remifentanil use may prevent or reduce the development of OIH.
Answer B: Antagonism of the NMDA receptors, not κ-opioid receptors, during remifentanil use may prevent or reduce the development of OIH.
Answer C: Antagonism of the NMDA receptors, not μ-opioid receptors, during remifentanil use may prevent or reduce the development of OIH. Results of studies have provided evidence that ketamine, an NMDA antagonist, can prevent opioid-induced hyperalgesia during remifentanil use. Pseudotolerance can be seen in patients with chronic pain as the underlying disease progresses, causing more pain. The increase in nociception/pain is a result of the destruction of nerves in the area of the pain. The resulting destruction leads to the development of neuropathic pain, which does not respond well to increases in opioids. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Cisatracurium undergoes degradation by Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis, which is independent of the liver and the kidney and is not affected by age, so, the pharmacodynamics should not be significantly altered in older patients (>65 years of age). Cisatracurium exhibits a slightly delayed onset of effect in older patients due to a slower biophase equilibration (the time for the drug to reach the effect site). In addition, there is also a slight prolongation of the elimination half-life of the drug in older patients secondary to an increased volume of distribution, but this is not of clinical significance. Pharmacodynamics of neuromuscular blocking drugs (NMBD) may be altered in older patients. Physiologic changes that occur in the older adult population include decreases in total body water and lean body mass, increases in total body fat, decreases in hepatic and renal blood flow, and hepatic enzyme activity. Physiological and anatomic changes at the neuromuscular junction also occur, including an increase in the distance between the junctional axon and the motor endplate, decreased release of acetylcholine from the preterminal axon, and decreased concentration of acetylcholine in each vesicle in the prejunctional axon. Butyrylcholinesterase activity is decreased in older adults compared to younger patients (by ~25%). Because mivacurium is metabolized by butyrylcholinesterase, its clearance is reduced, resulting in a longer duration of action in older patients.
Answer C: Pancuronium is the most dependent on renal clearance of the medications listed in the question, and prolongation is seen in renal impairment. Pancuronium has delayed recovery in older patients because of decreased plasma clearance secondary to delayed urinary excretion.
Answer D: Vecuronium is dependent on hepatic metabolism and on hepatic and renal clearance. Vecuronium dose requirements are decreased in older patients, and spontaneous recovery is significantly longer. The prolongation of vecuronium action is secondary to decreased drug elimination consistent with age-associated decreases in hepatic and renal blood flow. Pharmacodynamics of neuromuscular blocking drugs may be altered in older patients (>65 years of age). The choice of drug and monitoring the depth of blockade are important in older adults because recovery of neuromuscular function is generally delayed. Cisatracurium and atracurium undergo degradation by Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis, which is independent of the liver and the kidney and is not affected by age. St. John's wort is a cytochrome P450 (CYP) 3A4 inducer that can increase the metabolism of many different medications. Cyclosporine is a substrate of cytochrome P450 3A4, and its levels can be decreased if taken with St. John's wort. Between 22-32% of patients undergoing surgery have been reported to use herbal medications. Given the large number of patients taking herbal medications, care should be taken as many herbal medications can result in perioperative adverse events and even reduce the level of other medications. St. John's wort, otherwise known as Hypericum perforatum, is an herbal medication used for its ability to improve mental health. The compounds associated with the mental health benefit of St. John's wort include hypericin and hyperforin which inhibit the reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine, and dopamine. If St. John's wort is taken with other medications that inhibit the reuptake of serotonin, serotonin syndrome may occur due to the excess serotonin. Additional care must be taken with St. John's wort as it is a known CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 inducer which can interfere with the metabolism of other medications. The induction of CYP3A4 can interfere with other substrates such as indinavir, ethinylestradiol, alfentanil, midazolam, lidocaine, and cyclosporine. The reduction of cyclosporine levels is especially important for transplant patients as transplant rejection can occur. The induction of CYP2C9 can result in a decrease in warfarin levels since it is also a substrate. It is advised to stop taking St. John's wort 5 days before surgery. Ginkgo inhibits, not activates, platelet-activating factor. Inhibition of platelet-activating factor is a concern in the perioperative period. Though clinical trials have not demonstrated bleeding complications, four case reports have demonstrated bleeding complications while taking ginkgo. It is recommended to discontinue ginkgo intake at least 2 weeks before surgery to avoid bleeding.
Answer B: Ginseng decreases, not increases, blood sugar. Ginseng is an herbal medication called an adaptogen due to its ability to protect the body against stress and restore homeostasis. Its actions are mainly due to heterogeneous and opposing effects of the ginsenosides resulting in an incompletely understood pharmacologic profile. One effect of ginseng is the ability to decrease postprandial blood glucose which could potentially result in hypoglycemia in patients fasting before surgery. It is advised to stop taking ginseng 7 days before surgery.
Answer C: Kava increases, not decreases, sedation by anesthetics. Kava functions as an anxiolytic and sedative which are due to the compounds called kavalactones. The sedative-hypnotic ability of kava is mediated through its ability to potentiate the inhibition of the neurotransmission of GABA resulting in an increase in sedation with anesthetics. It is advised to stop taking kava 24 hours before surgery St. John's wort is an herbal medication used for its ability to improve mental health, but it is also a known CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 inducer which can interfere with the metabolism of other medications. St. John's wort can decrease the serum levels of another cytochrome P450 3A4 substrate cyclosporine which can result in transplant rejection if levels become subtherapeutic and it can decrease warfarin levels. Ephedra, otherwise known as ma huang, was an herbal remedy used to promote weight loss, increase energy, and treat asthma and bronchitis. It was banned by the FDA in 2004 due to severe side effects such as fatal cardiac and central nervous system complications, but it can still be found on the internet. It contains ephedrine, pseudoephedrine, norephedrine, methylephedrine, and norpseudoephedrine. In a dose-dependent manner, ephedra causes an elevation of blood pressure and heart rate mediated mainly by the ephedrine resulting in indirect sympathomimetic activity causing vasoconstriction and vasospasm of coronary and cerebral arteries leading to myocardial infarction and stroke. Ephedra can also cause hypersensitivity myocarditis and tachyphylaxis from chronic use. If monoamine oxidase inhibitors are used concomitantly, it can cause life-threatening hyperpyrexia, hypertension, and coma. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. An acute rise is plasma osmolality from a large bolus of mannitol can increase circulatory volume and precipitate pulmonary edema in patients with underlying ventricular dysfunction. Mannitol has been used to decrease intracranial pressure (ICP). It does so by two mechanisms, in a biphasic fashion. First, it causes a sudden rise in the osmolality of the extracellular compartment leading to volume expansion. This volume expansion reduces the hematocrit, blood viscosity, and cell rigidity. These changes increase flow of the red blood cells through intracranial blood vessels. The intravascular volume expansion also increases cardiac output which then also increases cerebral blood flow (CBF). When auto-regulation of the brain is intact, this increase in CBF causes reflexive vasoconstriction and ultimately lowers the ICP. The second phase of ICP reduction is a result of the osmotic gradient created by mannitol. Mannitol does not cross the BBB and therefore increases the osmolality in the intracranial vasculature. This creates an osmotic gradient between the vasculature and the brain parenchyma. Water is then drawn out of the parenchyma and into the cerebral vasculature leading to an overall decrease in ICP. This requires an intact blood brain barrier. Overall, the decrease in ICP from a slowly given mannitol bolus starts to occur within 30 minutes, takes maximal effect in 1-2 hours, and lasts about 6 hours. It is important to note that in patients without elevated ICP, a transient rise in ICP lasting about 10 minutes can occur. This occurs when the cerebral vasculature has a vasodilatory reaction when a rapid bolus of mannitol is given and plasma osmolality has a sudden and dramatic increase. This phenomena does not appear to occur in patients with elevated ICP. Other potential side effects of mannitol include acute hypotension, volume overload, metabolic and electrolyte derangements, and renal failure. Hemodynamic effects of mannitol can be significant and vary over time. Rapid administration of mannitol can have a direct vasodilatory effect on the systemic vasculature causing a sudden but brief drop in blood pressure. As mannitol increases the circulating blood volume by drawing water into the intravascular compartment, stroke volume, cardiac output, and blood pressure increase. Patients with heart failure may not tolerate the acute increase in blood volume and this could precipitate pulmonary edema. As mannitol is freely filtered by the glomerulus and unable to be reabsorbed distally in the kidney, it begins to exert its diuretic effect. Patients can become hypovolemic leading to decreased cardiac output and blood pressure. The effect of mannitol on electrolytes can vary. A large bolus mannitol or preexisting renal dysfunction can lead to accumulation in the vasculature. The increase in plasma osmolality draws water and potassium out of cells. This can cause a dilutional hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis (dilution of bicarbonate). When the kidney filters mannitol, it acts as an osmotic diuretic and large volumes of dilute water are lost. There is an excess loss of water compared to sodium which leads to hypovolemic hypernatremia. The osmotic diuretic effect of mannitol can also lead to renal losses of potassium, phosphate, and magnesium. If dehydration is severe enough, a contraction alkalosis may be seen. Interestingly, mannitol can cause renal failure by a largely unknown mechanism if given in high repeated doses. Renal failure is more likely to occur in patients with baseline renal dysfunction. Mannitol is not known to cause hypoglycemia.
Answer C: Mannitol is not known to cause rhabdomyolysis.
Answer D: Mannitol does not cause increased systemic or pulmonary vasoconstriction. Adverse side effects of mannitol may include: transient increase in ICP (in patients without elevated ICP), hypotension, volume overload/pulmonary edema, hypovolemia, hypernatremia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, metabolic acidosis, metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, hypophosphatemia, and acute renal failure. Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) is contraindicated in disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC), also known as factor IX complex, is a medication made up of blood clotting factors II, IX, and X. PCCs have been available for treatment of patients with hemophilia B for several decades. It was first used as a source of factor IX in the 1970s prior to the advent of specific factor concentrates. Subsequently, it provided bypass treatment for hemophiliacs with factor inhibitors. Over the years, the safety and efficacy of PCCs have improved dramatically, and now, although they are only FDA approved for use in hemophilia, they are mainly given for reversal of vitamin K antagonists and in the management of critical bleeding associated with major surgery, trauma, or liver failure. PCCs are now a therapy of choice for emergent reversal of oral anticoagulants in place of recombinant factor VIIa (rFVIIa) and fresh frozen plasma (FFP), the previous standard of care. Recombinant factor VIIa failed to show significant outcome improvements for treatment of warfarin-related intracerebral hemorrhage in various trials. This is likely because it only replaces one of the vitamin K–dependent factors and, although the INR and PT decrease, this did not translate into meaningful survival benefits. PCCs are now preferred over FFP as well, for several reasons. First of all, they provide faster correction of coagulopathy compared to FFP. The factors in plasma are relatively dilute and a large volume (at least 10 to 15 mL/kg) is required for clinical reversal of oral anticoagulants. It takes extra time to match the patient’s blood type and thaw plasma. Furthermore, PCCs stem from human plasma, but they are treated with at least one viral reduction process, whereas transfusion of several units of FFP carries a significant risk of infectious and noninfectious transfusion reactions. The hemostatic benefits of PCCs will likely translate to treatment of critical surgical bleeding, liver failure, and trauma, although the literature support for these indications is lacking. It is important to remember that PCCs provide factor replacement for thrombin generation, their action still depends on adequate concentrations of platelets and fibrinogen. The potential for PCCs to generate a significant thrombin burst puts the patients at risk for thrombotic complications. The exact pathogenesis for thrombosis remains unclear, but animal models indicate that the accumulation of prothrombin, inactive factor II, and/or factor X after PCC administration is correlated with thrombogenesis. Furthermore, this risk is associated with patients with thrombotic tendencies, such as those on anticoagulation and elderly patients who have a history of stroke. There are very few studies in trauma patients, but no significant reports of thrombotic complications in volunteers or those treated with PCCs for critical bleeding. Considering PCCs contain various coagulation factors, giving PCC to a patient in DIC would be detrimental as this would only worsen the thrombogenic nature of the pathology. PCC is not contraindicated in factor X deficiency. In fact, PCC actually contains factor X within its formulation. Factor X has one of the longer half-lives in the PCC concentration, being present for about 30 hours. This is in contrast with the labile factor VII which only has a half-life of approximately 6 hours.
Answer C: PCC was originally developed for the treatment of patients with hemophilia B; however, due to the availability in the last years of plasma-derived high purity factor IX concentrates and, more recently, of a recombinant factor IX product, their indications have progressively shifted from this bleeding disorder towards the replacement therapy of congenital or acquired deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.
Answer D: A major indication for PCC is the urgent reversal of over-anticoagulation with warfarin. Vitamin K antagonists act through the inhibition of vitamin K-dependent gamma-carboxylation of coagulation factors II, VII, IX, and X and also of the endogenous anticoagulation factors proteins C and S, which are synthesized in the liver. The primary complication of oral anticoagulant therapy with coumarins is bleeding. There is general agreement that major or life-threatening bleeding requires rapid and complete warfarin reversal, which can be obtained with FFP or PCC. PCC is contraindicated in patients with disseminated intravascular coagulation, a pathological activation of coagulation, because giving clotting factors would only further fuel this process. Chronic administration of phenytoin will decrease the duration of neuromuscular blockade by most nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBA). The shortened duration of action of nondepolarizing NMBAs with chronic anticonvulsant use is thought to be caused primarily by increased clearance (likely from increased liver metabolism). It has also been discovered that, in addition to increased clearance, there is increased binding of NMBAs to α1-acid glycoproteins and the upregulation of neuromuscular acetylcholine receptors, which may also contribute to the decreased duration of action. The duration of action of mivacurium and atracurium are unaffected by phenytoin use. Conversely, acute administration of anticonvulsant medications will result in potentiation of the neuromuscular blockade because it has a depressant effect on acetylcholine release. This likely explains the upregulation of neuromuscular acetylcholine receptors with chronic use. Many factors such as neuromuscular disease, extremes of age, burns, obesity, hepatic/renal dysfunction, physiological derangements (hypothermia, electrolyte disturbances, and acidosis), and medications can affect the duration of neuromuscular blockade by nondepolarizing NMBAs. Medications can either potentiate (increase) or attenuate (decrease) the duration of neuromuscular blockade by nondepolarizing NMBAs. Dosage changes may be required, depending on the medication given. The following changes can be seen in the chart below. Effects of various agents on the duration of neuromuscular blockade by NMBAs Medication Effect on duration of blockade Combination of 2 nondepolarizing NMBAs • Same class: additive • Different class: synergistic Cefepime is a cephalosporin that has no effect on neuromuscular blockade by NMBAs. Another antibiotic class that does not interfere with neuromuscular blockade is penicillins.
Answer B: Mannitol has no effect on neuromuscular blockade by NMBAs. Neuromuscular blockade may be prolonged if furosemide is given.
Answer C: Dantrolene is a US Federal Drug Administration (FDA)-approved medication for the treatment of malignant hyperthermia. Other FDA-approved indications for dantrolene include its use in muscle spasticity disorders such as in stroke, spinal cord injury, cerebral palsy, and multiple sclerosis. It functions as a postsynaptic muscle relaxant. Although dantrolene does not block neuromuscular transmission, the response to stimulation is depressed, and, as a result, it potentiates the blockade. Chronic administration of anticonvulsants (phenytoin and carbamazepine) will result in a decrease in the duration of neuromuscular blockade by nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents. Acute administration will result in the prolongation of neuromuscular blockade. Tetanic stimulation is a technique used to monitor neuromuscular blockade. It involves repetitive stimulation at a frequency of 50 Hz for 5 sec, leading to a sustained muscle contraction. The sustained contraction will begin to fade as the blockade by nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking agents increases. The fade seen in tetanic stimulation is equivalent to that seen in train-of-four stimulation. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. ""Muscle relaxants: Drug interactions (B)"" Barash PG, et al. Etomidate’s actions on pulmonary vascular tone are similar to the actions observed with ketamine and propofol; that is, they attenuate the bronchoconstrictive responses to acetylcholine and bradykinin. Tracheal intubation can cause bronchoconstriction with increased resistance of the respiratory system. The ability of induction agents to blunt this response is a consideration for the anesthesiologist. The first report of etomidate was published in 1965 with an introduction to clinical practice in 1972. The unique properties of etomidate include hemodynamic stability and minimal respiratory depression. Etomidate is a sedative-hypnotic medication chemically unrelated to any other agent. Due to its rapid onset and rapid recovery, minimal effects on cardiovascular and respiratory parameters, and safety margin, etomidate has been suggested as the optimal sedative-hypnotic for rapid sequence induction and intubation (RSII) in the emergency medicine literature. Ketamine, however, may be a more appropriate agent in shock patients. Etomidate has a minimal or nonexistent effect on blood pressure, pulmonary artery pressure, pulmonary artery wedge pressure, central venous pressure (CVP), stroke volume, cardiac index, systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and pulmonary vascular resistance. It is widely believed that etomidate depresses airway reflexes less than propofol (unless co-administered with another sedative/ analgesic agent). Etomidate also relaxes the smooth muscle of the pulmonary vasculature system to a similar degree as propofol. Etomidate is a reasonable choice for procedural sedation because of the preservation of airway reflexes. Ketamine may be selected for procedural sedation for similar reasons as well. Etomidate has less effect on ventilation than do other anesthetics used to induce anesthesia. It does not induce histamine release in healthy patients or in patients with reactive airway disease. Induction of anesthesia with etomidate produces a brief period of hyperventilation, sometimes followed by a similarly brief period of apnea, which results in a slight increase in PaCO2. Ventilatory response to carbon dioxide is depressed by etomidate. Propofol significantly depresses airway reflexes, and etomidate depresses airway reflexes less than propofol.
Answer C: Etomidate relaxes the smooth musculature of the pulmonary vasculature system to a similar degree as propofol. Etomidate is a sedative-hypnotic medication that has less effect on ventilation compared to propofol. It depresses airway reflexes (less so than propofol), relaxes smooth muscle in the pulmonary vascular system, and does not induce histamine release in patients with reactive airway disease. Aspirin should be continued until surgery for patients who are taking aspirin and are scheduled for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery. Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet cyclooxygenase, increasing intraoperative blood loss and hemorrhagic complications. However, the perioperative benefits of aspirin help prevent vascular complications, including cardiac and thromboembolic complications. Traditionally, aspirin has been discontinued seven to ten days before surgery because of concerns about increased bleeding risks. This withdrawal period is excessive because new platelets formed after the discontinuation of aspirin are not inhibited. These benefits and risks of antiplatelet therapy depend on the patient’s indication for aspirin and the type of surgery planned. All patients with cardiovascular disease should receive lifelong aspiring to prevent ischemic cardiovascular events. Therefore, most patients scheduled for CABG take aspirin daily, and this is continued until surgery. For patients with a new diagnosis of cerebrovascular disease (and are not taking aspirin) who require CABG, the decision to start aspirin preoperatively should be individualized and dependent on the duration of the surgery delay and the bleeding risk of surgery. All patients with peripheral artery disease should be started on antiplatelet therapy (aspirin and/or clopidogrel) and continued indefinitely. Antiplatelet therapy is associated with a lower incidence of early stent-graft thrombosis after endovascular repair of popliteal artery aneurysms. Additionally, patients with lower extremity bypass also benefit from antithrombotic therapy. Aspirin 325 to 650 mg should be started at least 48 hours before the procedure, or, if aspirin is started within 48 hours of the surgery, a loading dose of 650 mg should be given at least four hours before the procedure. Patients undergoing noncardiac surgery who are being treated with long-term antiplatelet therapy for primary or secondary prevention should consult the prescribing provider and surgeon to decide whether the risks vs benefits support continuing aspirin or holding aspiring therapy five to seven days before surgery. For patients not receiving antiplatelet therapy, aspirin should not be started before noncardiac surgery. Aspirin should be continued in patients with a prior percutaneous coronary intervention and patients undergoing carotid endarterectomy unless the risk of bleeding outweighs the benefit of preventing myocardial infarction. Furthermore, aspirin can be safely continued in patients undergoing minor surgery. Patients undergoing elective CABG who are taking clopidogrel or any other platelet P2Y12 receptor blocker should discontinue the agent five to seven days before surgery. The patient described in this question is taking only aspirin; adding a second antiplatelet agent would increase the risk of intraoperative bleeding.
Answer C: Patients with coronary artery disease scheduled for CABG who are taking aspirin should continue aspirin until the day of surgery. If patients are not taking aspirin preoperatively, the decision to initiate antiplatelet therapy should be individualized and dependent on the duration of the delay of surgery, bleeding risk, and length of surgery. For patients receiving dual antiplatelet therapy with a P2Y12 receptor blocker (eg, clopidogrel), the agent should be discontinued five to seven days preoperatively.
Answer D: Aspirin should be continued until the day of surgery in patients with coronary artery disease who are scheduled for elective CABG. For patients who are taking antiplatelet medications, the continuation or discontinuation of these medications depends on the duration of therapy, type of surgery, bleeding risk of surgery, and the duration of the delay of surgery. For patients scheduled for elective coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery who are taking aspirin for either primary or secondary prevention, the patient is recommended to continue taking aspirin until the day of surgery. Additionally, aspirin can be safely continued in patients undergoing minor surgery.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "Antiplatelet Drugs: Perioperative Use" Gropper MA, et al. Bicarbonate administration lowers serum potassium levels. In the setting of acidosis, excess hydrogen ions enter cells, resulting in the extracellular movement of potassium to maintain electrical balance, thus increasing the measured serum [K+]. Conversely, during alkalosis, extracellular potassium ions move into cells to balance the extracellular movement of hydrogen ions, resulting in decreased plasma [K+]. This is the mechanism underlying bicarbonate administration in the setting of severe hyperkalemia. Intravenous sodium bicarbonate combines with a hydrogen ion to produce carbonic acid that dissociates into CO2 and water (50 mEq of bicarbonate produces approximately 1,250 mL of CO2). The partial pressure of CO2 in the blood is temporarily elevated until it is eliminated via the lungs. Theoretically, this increase in CO2 would cause cerebral vasodilation and increase intracranial pressure, although direct clinical evidence for this has not been found.
Answer B: Sodium bicarbonate can transiently lower blood calcium levels. Calcium binding to albumin is dependent on serum pH. In states of acidosis, the excess hydrogen ions displace calcium bound by albumin and thus ionized levels of calcium increase. This process is reversed in the setting of alkalosis and should be considered before administering sodium bicarbonate to a patient with preexisting hypocalcemia.
Answer C: Sodium bicarbonate is converted by carbonic anhydrase to water and CO2. After sodium bicarbonate administration, it is common to see an increase in end-tidal CO2. Sodium bicarbonate administration is associated with transient increases in partial pressure of CO2, end-tidal CO2, and intracranial pressure, with transient decreases in serum calcium and potassium. The proximal tubule reabsorbs anywhere from 65-75% of the ultrafiltrate formed by the Bowman capsule. Sodium is actively reabsorbed by membrane-bound Na-K adenosine triphosphate (Na-K-ATPase), which is found on the capillary side of the tubular cells. The resulting low intracellular sodium concentration allows for the passive movement of sodium down its gradient from luminal fluid into the tubular cells. This accounts for the majority of sodium reabsorption and subsequently water reabsorption. In the proximal tubule, luminal reabsorption of sodium is coupled with hydrogen ion secretion. This accounts for 90% of bicarbonate ion reabsorption. Bicarbonate joins with the hydrogen ions in the presence of carbonic anhydrase intraluminally to form carbonic acid. Carbonic acid dissociates into carbon dioxide and water, which are reabsorbed into the tubular cells. H + HCO3 --> H2CO3 --> H2O + CO2 The distal convoluted tubule accounts for only 5% reabsorption of the filtered sodium. As in other parts of the nephron, the energy is derived from Na-K-ATPase activity on the capillary side, but on the luminal side, Na is reabsorbed by a Na-Cl carrier.
Answer B: The loop of Henle is responsible for reabsorbing 15-20% of the filtered sodium. Specifically, this occurs in the thick ascending limb through the action of the Na-K-ATPase pump. Of the nephron tubular segments, the proximal tubule accounts for 65-75% reabsorption of ultrafiltrate formed by the Bowman capsule.  Morgan and Mikhail's Clinical Anesthesiology, 5th Edition. Within the uteroplacental circulation, the intervillous space has the lowest intravascular pressure (around 10 mmHg) allowing for high volumes of flow through the low resistance circulation as well as continued circulation of the fetal blood through the umbilical artery and vein. The placenta is a unique organ in that it receives blood flow from two separate organisms and their respective blood supplies. The uteroplacental and the fetoplacental circulations are independent, and no commingling of the blood supplies occurs during its transit. The maternal blood flow through the intervillous space is around 600-700 mL/min. This large blood volume is responsible for carrying nutrient-rich and oxygenated blood to interface with the villous core fetal vessels as well as carrying deoxygenated and nutrient-depleted blood away from the fetus. Uteroplacental circulation is not fully established until the beginning of the second trimester. At that time, the circulation is established that will remain in place throughout the remainder of the pregnancy. The vast majority of uterine blood flow to the spinal arteries arrives through the uterine arteries which maintain systemic maternal blood pressures (80-100 mmHg). The ovarian artery also contributes a small amount (5-10%) of blood supply to the fundus of the uterus. The spiral arteries are fed by the uterine arteries, and maintain pressures slightly lower than systemic (around 70 mmHg). These arteries pool into the intervillous space when interfaced with the placenta, which has a circulating pressure around 10 mmHg. The pressure within the intervillous space is lower than both the umbilical artery and veins (50 and 20 mmHg respectively). This prevents their collapse during normal circulation and allows nutrient and oxygen transfer between the maternal and fetal circulations. Spiral arteries have a slightly lower than systemic intravascular pressure (around 70 mmHg).
Answer C: The umbilical artery within the fetoplacental circulation experiences intravascular pressures around 50 mmHg.
Answer D: The uterine artery experiences maternal systemic blood pressures (80-100 mmHg). The intervillous space has the lowest intravascular pressures within the uteroplacental and fetoplacental circulation. This allows for both large volumes of blood to be moved through this space to allow adequate maternofetal nutrient and oxygen transfer, as well as prevents the collapse of umbilical veins as they return to this space. Immature extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors are unique because of the γ (gamma) subunit type they contain. Both mature and immature receptors contain α1 (alpha 1), β1 (beta 1), and δ (delta) subunit types. Postjunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors have three forms: mature junctional receptors, immature extrajunctional receptors, and neuronal α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Junctional receptors are considered mature, while extra junctional receptors are considered immature or fetal. All acetylcholine receptors have five subunit proteins arranged in a cylindrical shape. Mature receptors consist of two α1 subunits and one each of β1, δ, and ε subunits. Immature extra junctional receptors consist of two α1 subunits and one each of β1, δ, and γ. Neuronal α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors consist of five α7 subunits. The binding site of acetylcholine is the α1 and α7 subunits. Immature extrajunctional receptors have long open times and lowamplitude channel currents, in contrast to mature junctional receptors that have shorter open times and high-amplitude channel currents. The immature extra junctional form is present in states of decreased muscle activity such as the fetal state prior to muscle innervation as well as immobilization, burns, upper motor neuron injury, lower motor neuron injury, or sepsis. This immature receptor can be present anywhere on the muscle membrane, and synthesis begins within hours of inactivity. These receptors have a half-life of less than 24 hours, compared to 2 weeks for mature receptors, and the immature receptors are sensitive to succinylcholine while having relative resistance to non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs. The immature receptors have opening times up to 10 times longer than mature receptors, allowing for efflux of significant amounts of potassium resulting in hyperkalemia. The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is a more recently discovered receptor that also is present in skeletal muscle that has been immobilized or denervated. The α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor can also have a robust hyperkalemic response to succinylcholine and resistance to non-depolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs. The α1 (alpha 1) subunit is present in both junctional and extrajunctional receptors.
Answer B: The β1 (beta 1) subunit is present in both junctional and extrajunctional receptors.
Answer C: The ε (epsilon) subunit is present in only junctional receptors, not in extrajunctional receptors. Immature extrajunctional acetylcholine receptors contain a γ subunit rather than the ε of the mature form. The other four subunits: two α1 subunits one β1, and one δ are the same. Immature subunits are present in the fetal state and states of immobilization, burns, upper or lower motor neuron injury, and sepsis and are associated with increased efflux of potassium and hyperkalemia following activation by depolarizing drugs such as succinylcholine. Transpulmonary pressures are highest in patients with restrictive lung disease, such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Diseases that decreases the volume of air the lungs are able to hold are known as restrictive lung diseases. They are often a result of a decrease in the elasticity of the lungs themselves or caused by a problem with the expansion of the chest wall. Examples of restrictive lung diseases include asbestosis, sarcoidosis, and pulmonary fibrosis. Lung compliance is defined as the ease with which the lungs can expand under pressure; essentially it is a measure of the lung’s distensible nature. Lung compliance is reduced by factors that produce resistance to distension such as restrictive lung disease. In pulmonary fibrosis, connective tissue proteins have infiltrated lung tissue resulting in lungs that are not able to stretch as well as they normally do, thus reducing pulmonary compliance. Because pulmonary compliance is reduced, greater transpulmonary pressures are required to generate normal tidal volumes. In other words, the chest wall must work harder to move a volume of gas into the lungs. Because of this, patients breath at more rapid rates with smaller tidal volumes. Chronic bronchitis is an obstructive lung disease caused by inflammation of the bronchial mucosa and generally has no effect pulmonary compliance.
Answer B: COPD is an obstructive lung disease, not a restrictive lung disease. COPD may be associated with an increase, not decrease, in pulmonary compliance due to loss of alveolar and elastic tissue.
Answer C: Cystic fibrosis results in severe bronchiectasis in nearly all cases due to chronic cough, purulent sputum, and scarring of the bronchial airways; this produces an obstructive, not restrictive, lung disease pattern. Transpulmonary pressures are highest in patients with restrictive lung disease due to a reduction in lung compliance. An action potential, propagated by sequential voltage-gated sodium channel depolarization along the axon, arrives at the axon terminal boutons and opens voltage-gated calcium channels to allow calcium influx, which in turn triggers the exocytosis of acetylcholine into the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). Acetylcholine molecules are synthesized in the cytoplasm and transported inside intracellular vesicles, where they are stored. Electron microscopy has revealed two distinct pools of vesicles that release acetylcholine, a readily releasable pool and a reserve pool (named VP1 and VP2, respectively). The surface of these vesicles and the cell membrane contain soluble Nethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor (SNARE) proteins, which are a series of proteins that together allow acetylcholine release into the synaptic cleft. In particular, synaptotagmin and synaptobrevin are found on vesicles, and syntaxin and synaptosomal-associated protein 25 (SNAP-25) are found on the junctional cell membrane. When it is triggered by an action potential arriving from the axon, calcium enters the nerve through voltage-gated calcium channels. In particular, P-type and L-type calcium channels seem to be the subtypes involved in the nerve terminal associated with neurotransmitter release. These calcium channels are attacked by antibodies in Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. As vesicles migrate close to the nerve terminal membrane, synaptobrevin on the vesicles bind to a syntaxin and SNAP-25 complex on the cell membrane, “docking” the vesicle onto the cell membrane. During the docked state, synaptotagmin on the vesicles act as a calcium sensor, and calcium influx causes fusion of the vesicles to the cell membrane, leading to exocytosis and acetylcholine release. Botulinum neurotoxin digests some or all of these SNARE proteins to block acetylcholine release, causing flaccid paralysis. Calcium-triggered acetylcholine release acts through exocytosis of acetylcholine rich vesicles, not through active transport.
Answer C: Posttetanic potentiation occurs after a patient receives high-frequency tetanic stimulation. Calcium enters the nerve with each stimulus during tetanic stimulation and accumulates in the cytoplasm because it cannot exit as quickly as it can enter. Due to the elevated amount of calcium in the cytoplasm, a train-of-four stimulus applied during this time causes the release of large amounts of acetylcholine. In the setting of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade, the abnormally large amount of acetylcholine temporarily outcompetes the neuromuscular blocker and increases the train-of-four response.
Answer D: Calcium plays an integral role in NMJ signaling. If calcium is not present (or is less present) in the extracellular fluid, depolarization of the nerve will not produce the release of acetylcholine. In comparison, doubling the extracellular calcium can lead to a 16-fold increase in acetylcholine quantal content. An action potential, propagated by sequential voltage-gated sodium channel depolarization along the axon, arrives at the axon terminal boutons and opens voltage-gated calcium channels to allow for calcium influx, which in turn triggers the exocytosis of acetylcholine into the neuromuscular junction. In particular, synaptotagmin of the SNARE (soluble Nethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) proteins acts as a calcium sensor that triggers fusion in docked vesicles.
