Ketamine has shown to increase the bispectral index (BIS) in anesthetized patients and may confound the BIS as a guide to administering hypnotic agents. The BIS was proposed as a measure of the effects of anesthetic agents on the brain and can be used to assess the depth of hypnosis. The BIS is considered a processed electroencephalography (EEG), which provides a numerical output of 0 to 100 via a proprietary analysis of raw EEG signals. Values of 65 to 85 have been advocated as a measure of sedation, whereas values of 40 to 65 have been recommended for general anesthesia. Ketamine does not follow the basic anesthesia-related EEG pattern. Electroencephalography activity may be disorganized and variable at all doses. This disorganization of the EEG with ketamine is responsible for the failure of the BIS to be useful in examining the effect of ketamine on consciousness. Ketamine has its primary effect by blocking excitatory glutamatergic input to inhibitory interneurons. Impaired control over pyramidal neurons is why increases in cerebral metabolism and the appearance of altered behavioral states, including hallucinations, dissociative states, euphoria, and dysphoria, are seen. Barbiturates, propofol, and etomidate produce similar EEG patterns. These drugs follow the basic anesthesia-related EEG pattern, with initial EEG activation followed by dose-related depression. At very high doses, EEG silence ensues. Results of EEG studies of patients undergoing sedation with dexmedetomidine have revealed patterns similar to those seen in normal human sleep, with increased slow wave activity and prominent sleep spindles. Burst suppression or an isoelectric EEG pattern cannot be produced even with high doses of dexmedetomidine. Bispectral index values at comparable levels of sedation are lower with dexmedetomidine than with propofol. BIS values and associated levels of anesthesia Abbreviation: BIS, bispectral index. Administration of dexmedetomidine results in an EEG pattern similar to that seen in human sleep and allows accurate monitoring of sedation on the BIS.
Answer C: Administration of propofol results in an EEG pattern similar to barbiturates and etomidate. Using a BIS monitor in a patient who was given propofol would provide accurate prediction of the level of sedation.
Answer D: Administration of barbiturates does not increase BIS values and would not confound the BIS as a guide to administering hypnotic agents. Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that can increase the bispectral index (BIS) in anesthetized patients. Therefore, patients being treated with ketamine may not have accurate BIS values, and this index would not provide accurate results for monitoring of the level of sedation. Oxytocin is synthesized in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus, transported to the posterior pituitary gland through the infundibular stalk, and, ultimately, released by the posterior pituitary gland. The pituitary gland is composed of an anterior portion and a posterior portion. The posterior portion is connected to the hypothalamus by the infundibular stalk. Axons and nerve terminals ending in the posterior pituitary originate in the hypothalamus, specifically in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei. Oxytocin and vasopressin are synthesized within these nuclei and are then transported down the infundibular stalk bound to inactive carrier proteins called neurophysins. These neurophysins transport these molecules down the axons in the hypothalamo-hypophyseal tract to membrane-bound vesicles in the posterior pituitary. When these hormones are ready to be released, they are secreted into the inferior hypophyseal veins that drain the posterior pituitary into the system circulation. Figure 1 The hypothalamic-pituitary axis Oxytocin (OT) and vasopressin (otherwise known as anti-diuretic hormone [ADH]) are released from the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei. Vasopressin is a peptide that functions to regulate extracellular fluid volume and regulation of plasma osmolality. Oxytocin causes uterus contractions during pregnancy and promotes milk secretion and ejection from the mammary glands. Growth hormone is synthesized in the anterior pituitary. Oxytocin and vasopressin are the only 2 hormones synthesized in the hypothalamus (paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei) and released by the posterior pituitary.
Answer B: Oxytocin and vasopressin, not luteinizing hormone, are transported from the hypothalamus to the posterior pituitary via the infundibular stalk to be secreted. The anterior pituitary gland is not connected to the infundibular stalk.
Answer D: Vasopressin is not synthesized in the posterior pituitary but is merely stored there until release. Vasopressin is synthesized in the hypothalamus, specifically in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei. The posterior pituitary secretes oxytocin and vasopressin, which are both synthesized in the hypothalamus in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei. They are then transported down the infundibular stalk to the posterior pituitary for release.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. ""Post-pituitary hormones: Synthesis"" Barash PG, et al. Ketamine exerts its dissociative effects by affecting the thalamus, not through direct depression of the reticular activating system. The reticular activating system is a collection of brain pathways that affect consciousness and wakefulness. The thalamus is responsible for transmission of signals from the reticular activating system to the cerebral cortex. Almost all anesthetics directly depress the RAS, thereby altering consciousness. Conversely, ketamine affects the thalamus, preventing fluid transmission of signals to the limbic cortex and producing its distinct dissociative effects, while also causing hyperexcitability and functional disorganization within the RAS. Etomidate mimics the inhibitory effects of the GABA neuromodulator and directly depresses activity in the RAS.
Answer B: Volatile anesthetics have a wide variety of target sites and produce their effects through multiple mechanisms of action. Most of these agents will depress the RAS, rendering the patient unconscious.
Answer D: Barbiturates are another class of anesthetics which directly depress the RAS, leading to unconsciousness in the patient. Unlike most anesthetics which directly depress the RAS, ketamine exerts its effects on the thalamus, causing dissociation of the reticular activating system from the cerebral and limbic cortices. The acute hemodilution of the patient's blood with the large volume of crystalloid solution is the most common etiology of hypotension following initiation of CPB. Other common causes may be related to the dilution of the patient's plasma catecholamine levels, pH, and electrolyte concentrations by the large crystalloid bolus. The flow of a liquid through a tube was characterized by Dr. J. L. M. Poiseuille in the mid-19th century. Poiseuille's law relates the flow rate (Q) of a fluid with a given viscosity (μ) traveling through a tube with a given diameter (D) and length (L) under a given driving pressure (Δp) in the following relationship: Q = (π * Δp * D4) / (128 * L * μ). This equation is typically referenced in the practice of anesthesia for its establishment of the fourth-power dependence of flow rate on the diameter of a tube, a principle that is vital to safe and effective airway and ventilation management, as well as fluid administration among other topics in anesthesia practice. This equation also establishes the indirect linear relationship between flow and the viscosity of a fluid. Viscosity is a measure of the internal friction of a fluid and is more colloquially referred to as its "thickness." The more viscous a fluid is, the more it resists flowing. As seen in the image below, when referenced to water, plasma has only a slightly higher viscosity (1.8 times the relative viscosity of water). This is due to the cellular component of plasma, as well as the various proteinaceous components and other molecules. Blood, at normal physiological levels, is made up of approximately 45% red blood cells (RBCs). Given this large composition, it stands to reason that the viscosity of RBCs will have a significant effect on the total viscosity of blood. At a physiological hematocrit of about 40, blood is approximately 3 times as viscous as water. As the hematocrit drops to about 25-30%, however, the blood becomes only about twice as viscous relative to water. This decrease in the cellular component of blood results in a decrease in viscosity, which will, in turn, allow for more blood flow, according to Poiseuille's law. Cases where the blood is acutely hemodiluted, such as in this patient, can result in profound decreases in systemic vascular resistance due to the thinning of the blood and the improved flow characteristics. This commonly leads to hypotension following the initiation of CPB. It is important to note that this improved flow characteristic is countered by the decrease in the oxygen-carrying capacity that comes with hemodilution, and care should be taken in clinical settings to assess for and correct any deficiency in oxygen delivery that is identified. Image adapted from equations stated in Cinar, 2001. Illustration © TrueLearn, LLC In reality, the viscosity of blood in the microvasculature is much more complicated than Poiseuille's law describes. When the blood vessels shrink to sizes approaching that of the diameter of an RBC (about 8 μm), as they do in the capillary beds, the viscosity of the blood may actually tend to decrease, in a phenomenon known as the Fåhræus-Lindqvist effect. This effect is due to the progression of blood cells through this circulation in sequence, rather than in parallel, resulting in novel microvascular flow dynamics. The clinical importance of these findings is uncertain, however, and in general, hematocrit should be considered to be directly related to the blood viscosity and inversely related to flow through the blood vessels. Arterial plaque embolization is most likely to occur during the placement of the aortic cardiopulmonary bypass cannula, and would not likely explain acute hemodynamic instability following initiation of cardiopulmonary bypass.
Answer B: This patient becomes hypotensive after initiating cardiopulmonary bypass, effectively bypassing the cardiac and pulmonary circulation. Cardiogenic shock in this instance would have no impact on hypotension, as the cardiopulmonary bypass is ongoing with full cardiac output support.
Answer C: Cardiopulmonary bypass with 4.5 L/min of bypass flow is sufficient flow to replicate a normal adult's cardiac output. In this case, the patient's heart function was depressed at baseline, and his systemic circulation had likely compensated for this chronic low-cardiac output state. Acute increase of his cardiac output through the use of cardiopulmonary bypass would likely result in hypertension and not the hypotension seen in this patient. In any case, the bypass flows used in this case are very unlikely to be inadequate, and hemodilution is a much more likely cause of this patient's hypotension. Hemodilution can result in a decreased blood viscosity. This decreased viscosity can improve the flow characteristics of blood through the systemic circulation, resulting in a decreased systemic vascular resistance and, possibly, hypotension if this normovolemic hemodilution occurs too rapidly. Caution should be taken to ensure that adequate oxygen delivery is maintained because while hemodilution improves the flow characteristics of blood, it also decreases its oxygencarrying capacity. Epidural infusions containing local anesthetics have been shown to reduce the incidence of postoperative ileus. Surgical insult leads to the release of many inflammatory mediators, including histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins, and catecholamines. These inflammatory mediators activate peripheral nociceptors, leading to signal transduction via pain fibers that ultimately cause the release of substances such as substance P, calcitonin gene-related peptide, and γ-aminobutyric acid in the central nervous system. Control and manipulation of nociception in the perioperative period have important implications in managing not just short-term outcomes but long-term outcomes as well. Acute postoperative ileus is likely secondary to uncontrolled sympathetic nervous system activation, direct manipulation of the intestines, and the stress response associated with acute postoperative pain. The sympathectomy provided by epidural infusion of local anesthetic has been demonstrated to decrease the time to return of gastrointestinal function when compared to other modes of analgesia, such as systemic opioids and single-dose neuraxial opioids. While intravenous opioids delivered via patient-controlled analgesia have shown improved patient satisfaction over intermittent bolus of opioids, intravenous only regimens do not reduce incidence of ileus Answers C & D: Single-dose neuraxial opioids provide quality analgesia but do not address the sympathetic element causing decreased bowel motility. Epidural infusions containing local anesthetic have been shown to reduce the incidence of postoperative ileus.  ABA Keywords: "Postop Analgesia: GI Function" Mark LO, et al. Electroencephalography is produced by measuring excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials produced by the cortex. Signal transmission through the internal capsule is not measured in this form of neuromonitoring as it only measures signal within the grey matter of the cortex. The internal capsule is a bilateral structure, situated in the inferomedial part of each cerebral hemisphere. It acts in essence as an anatomic bypass route past the basal ganglia, allowing both ascending and descending axons to interface with the cerebral cortex. The corticospinal tract makes up the largest portion of the internal capsule and is the structure responsible for carrying motor signals from the motor cortex to the lower motor neurons of the spinal cord and eventually to the muscles themselves. Multiple other pathways between distal anatomic sites and the cortex exist within the internal capsule. Only a few of these are relevant to anesthesia providers and are described here. The internal capsule is divided into two limbs, the anterior and posterior limbs. The pathways within the anterior limb are not of significant concern in anesthetic practice. The majority of the posterior limb of the internal capsule is comprised of the corticospinal tract which is a relevant pathway in motor evoked potential monitoring. There are three other structures of note within this posterior limb. Sensory fibers pass posterior to the corticospinal tract and represent the connection between the spinothalamic tract and the somatosensory cortex. This connection is crucial when monitoring somatosensory evoked potentials. Acoustic fibers between the lateral lemniscus and the temporal lobe pass through this limb and are a crucial component of auditory evoked potentials. The fibers of optic radiation also pass through this limb from the lower visual centers to the visual cortex in the occipital lobe. This pathway is required for intact visual evoked potentials to be seen. Infarcts of the posterior limb of the internal capsule cause pure motor hemiparesis. It is supplied by the lateral striate (lenticulostriate) arteries, which are divisions of the middle cerebral artery. These arteries are affected by chronic hypertension, leading to stroke (e.g. lacunar stroke). Brainstem auditory evoked potentials are generated at the cochlea, pass along the cochlear nerve, through the cochlear nucleus, on to midbrain nuclei and the medial geniculate body, and eventually through the posterior limb of the internal capsule along the acoustic radiations to the cortex. Damage to this last step would impair auditory evoked potentials.
Answer C: Motor evoked potentials (MEPs) are most commonly generated by applying a transcranial electrical stimulus to the motor cortex. This stimulus then proceeds along descending motor pathways, through the internal capsule, decussating at the medullary pyramids, and down the spinal cord along the lateral corticospinal tract. The signal leaves the spinal cord, travels to a peripheral motor neuron, and eventually stimulates the muscle itself.
Answer D: Visual evoked potentials are generated at the retina, and proceed along the optic nerve, through the optic chiasm, and eventually along the optic radiations through the posterior limb of the internal capsule before arriving at the occipital cortex. The internal capsule acts as a bridge for multiple ascending and descending pathways to interface between the cortex and their distal signaling pathways. The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains the corticospinal tract, sensory pathways, acoustic radiations, and optic radiations, all of which are involved in the various evoked potential monitoring that is used in anesthesia practice. Some centers monitor both motor and somatosensory evoked potentials during surgical clipping of cerebral aneurysms. The addition of motor evoked potential monitoring to the more standard somatosensory evoked potential monitoring more effectively monitors the integrity of the subcortical pathways within the internal capsule. Because the motor pathways run anterior to the sensory pathways in the internal capsule, it is at greater risk if the anterior choroidal artery or perforator vessels are injured during dissection and clipping. Patients experiencing prolonged hypoxia will have a dominance of low-frequency waves, the lowest of which is delta waves that can be seen in the states of deep coma and encephalopathy. The electroencephalogram (EEG) is a monitor of cerebral function. Surface electrodes placed on the scalp detect electrical activity created by depolarization of cortical neurons. Electrical activity is measured between two points and signals common to the electrodes at these points are filtered to minimize interference from other sources such as cardiac muscle. The EEG can be used for intraoperative monitoring for functional assessment of the brain, detection of ischemia, assessment of seizure activity, patterns indicating suppression of activity, and potentially depth of anesthesia. The EEG is used in a more robust manner with numerous channels for evaluation and diagnosis of conditions such as epilepsy, however, intraoperative monitoring typically consists of 2-4 channels. Raw EEG data can be viewed, although for less experienced users it is more practical to employ programs for processing the raw data using Fourier analysis into wave frequencies creating an overall pattern. A spectral array can be derived by determining the power (amplitude squared) for each frequency in an EEG, and changes to this array are interpreted as a change in the condition of the patient. Waves of particular frequencies that are seen on EEG can be categorized as follows: *Table modified from Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th Edition Hypoxia can lead to inadequate oxygen delivery to the cerebral cortex, causing electroencephalogram changes similar to ischemia. The brain will attempt to compensate for decreased O2 levels by increasing cerebral blood flow to an upper limit. The changes seen on EEG include nonspecific global changes of “slowing.” First, there is a loss of fast frequencies, in particular, loss of alpha waves. This is followed by an increase in slow waves (theta), and then an increase in even slower waves (delta) as the ischemic threshold is crossed. If inadequate oxygen delivery persists, the EEG will become silent while any remaining oxygen becomes exclusively diverted to functions preserving cellular integrity as cell death occurs. Effects of carbon dioxide levels on EEG are less clear. Hypocarbia can lead to activation of seizure foci on EEG. Rapid decreases in carbon dioxide causes decreased cerebral blood flow and hypocarbia has been shown in rare cases to cause EEG changes consistent with ischemia. Hypercarbia tends to cause increased cerebral blood flow and thus EEG changes are indirectly related to hypercarbia via these changes in blood flow. The effect of hypercarbia in anesthetized patients may be similar to that seen with an increase in end-tidal volatile anesthetic concentrations. Answers A & B & D: Faster, higher frequency waves such as beta, alpha, and theta waves are less likely present in the setting of prolonged hypoxia as the brain progresses to suppression of electrical activity.  As a patient becomes hypoxic and the brain becomes ischemic, the following electroencephalogram changes take place: decrease in fast waves, increase in slow waves, suppression of activity, complete silence of activity. While a total intravenous anesthetic (TIVA) technique using propofol as the primary hypnotic agent is commonplace during surgeries requiring monitoring of motor evoked potentials (MEPs), excessive serum concentrations of propofol will tend to increase the latency and decrease the amplitude of an MEP signal in a similar fashion to what would be seen during spinal cord injury. If an MEP is generated during a surgical case immediately following the bolus administration of propofol, it is very possible that the neuromonitoring could reveal the above-mentioned changes, even if a propofol infusion had been used throughout the entire case. The intraoperative use of electrophysiologic monitoring such as somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs), MEPs, and electromyography (EMG) has vastly increased the safety of performing complex spine surgeries. Prior to their use, some societies quoted the risk of spinal injury following scoliosis surgery at as high as 4%. This decreased to around 0.5% with the widespread use of SSEP monitoring, however, there was still a proportion of patients with "falsely negative" SSEP monitoring during surgery that developed perioperative spinal cord injury. The proposed mechanism for these injuries came from the fact that the SSEP monitoring only assesses for intact conduction through the dorsal column of the spinal cord. This left essentially 2/3 of the spinal cord unmonitored by SSEPs. Because the vascular supply for the dorsal column differs from that of the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord which, is supplied by the anterior spinal artery, a loss of blood flow through the anterior spinal artery could result in spinal cord injury without evidence of such on SSEP monitoring. This anomaly led to the development of MEP monitoring. While a number of MEP monitoring techniques have been developed, transcranial electrical MEPs tend to be the most commonly used in clinical practice. In this technique, multiple electrodes are placed in the scalp and electrical stimulation is provided in sufficient quantity to stimulate the motor cortex that underlies the electrode through the skull. This stimulation will then proceed along the descending motor pathways in the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord which will eventually cause motor activity following stimulation of the neuromuscular junction. These muscular contractions can be detected by intramuscular needle electrodes that are placed throughout the bilateral upper and lower extremities. Because these intramuscular electrodes are in place, neurotonic discharges can be instantaneously detected by these electrodes when the surgeon manipulates structures such as nerve roots in the surgical field. This immediate feedback can also help to mitigate nervous injury during surgery. In general, a 50% increase in the stimulus intensity required to generate a transcranial electrical MEP is taken to be a significant change and is considered especially significant if a surgical event matches the change in MEP monitoring. Motor evoked potential monitoring has the primary advantage of being able to rapidly and immediately monitor the integrity of descending motor pathways, and when combined with SSEP monitoring, allows for a comprehensive evaluation of the integrity of practically the entire spinal cord. The major disadvantage of this technique is that it produces movement of the limbs and axial muscles, thus it cannot be performed continuously during surgery as with SSEP monitoring. Instead, it must be intermittently performed during spinal manipulation to assess anterior spinal integrity. Cortical stimulation also causes masseter muscle contraction, and a soft bite block is useful when this technique is used. Because this technique involves the direct stimulation of the cerebral cortex, it is relatively contraindicated in patients with epilepsy, brain lesions, increased intracranial pressure, or who have implanted devices that may be negatively affected by the stimulation. Also, MEP monitoring is more sensitive than SSEP monitoring to certain anesthetic agents. Because MEP monitoring requires an intact neuromuscular junction, neuromuscular blockade is contraindicated in the patients. It is common to induce with a nondepolarizing agent and then be required to reverse neuromuscular blockade prior to the surgical start in order to facilitate MEP monitoring. In myelopathic patients undergoing posterior spinal surgery, the surgeon may request an MEP to be obtained prior to positioning in order to ensure that no spinal injury occurs simply from positioning these patients. In these cases, the use of a short-acting neuromuscular blocking agent such as succinylcholine may be considered to allow an MEP to be rapidly obtained after the induction of anesthesia. Halogenated anesthetics will significantly reduce the amplitudes of MEP monitoring at 1.0 MAC however this effect is mitigated at 0.5 MAC or below. Many providers choose to avoid halogenated agents altogether for this reason and prefer instead to perform a TIVA technique. Propofol is the primary hypnotic agent that is used in these cases. It does cause a dose-dependent reduction in the amplitude of MEP signals, however, it has no effect on the latency of the signal and reduces the amplitudes to a lesser extent than do the halogenated agents. As mentioned above, a bolus of propofol in close temporal proximity to the generation of an MEP may result in a marked reduction in signal amplitude that could be mistaken for spinal cord injury and any bolus doses or changes in anesthetic should be communicated openly with the technologist that is performing the electrophysiologic monitoring. Most opioids have minimal impact on MEP monitoring when administered in typical doses and represent a mainstay in the perioperative management of the patients. Other adjunctive agents such as lidocaine or dexmedetomidine have minimal impact on MEP monitoring when administered in typically used clinical doses. Ketamine is an outlier from these medications as it has the potential to enhance the signals seen on electrophysiologic monitoring. Both severe hypothermia, as well as hypoxia and anemia, can also impair transmission through the spinal cord and can result in a decreased MEP signal response. It should be noted that SSEP and MEP monitoring will typically compare the evoked potentials from different portions of the case in order to determine if a surgical intervention may have caused an injury to the spinal cord. Because of the impact of many anesthetics on electrophysiologic, the administration of medications by way of continuous infusions instead of intermittently administering boluses of medications is preferred. This allows for a continuous plane of anesthesia to be maintained and any change in the SSEP or MEP signals to be better attributed to surgical changes and not changes in the anesthetic. As mentioned before, any bolus administrations of medications during a case where SSEP or MEP monitoring is being performed should be communicated to the electrophysiologic monitor technologist. Answers A & C: When administered at typical clinical doses, adjunctive medications such as dexmedetomidine and lidocaine have minimal impact on the signal amplitude of motor evoked potential monitoring. While high doses of sufentanil may cause some decrease in signal amplitude during motor evoked potential monitoring, a constant infusion of sufentanil will cause minimal perturbations in evoked potential monitoring during a surgical case. Transcranial electric motor evoked potentials are used to assess the integrity of the descending motor pathways of the anterior 2/3 of the spinal cord during major surgeries on the spine. When combined with somatosensory evoked potentials they allow monitoring of practically the entire spinal cord and have been shown to decrease the incidence of postoperative spinal cord injury. Many anesthetic agents attenuate the intensity of evoked potentials and in general infusions of medications are preferred to intermittent boluses of these drugs in order to provide a stable anesthetic and ensure that any changes in evoked potential monitoring are properly attributed to surgical changes. Hyperglycemia in patients with diabetes who undergo surgery is associated with increased rates of surgical site infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, and death. Intraoperative hyperglycemia is an independent risk factor for perioperative complications in cardiac surgery patients. Glucagon and insulin are secreted by the alpha and beta cells of the pancreas, respectfully. Glucagon’s primary action is to stimulate hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Glucagon promotes glycogenolysis by increasing hepatocyte cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP). Conversely, insulin has the opposite effect by decreasing intracellular cAMP levels, thereby preventing gluconeogenesis. Insulin is an anabolic hormone responsible for increasing glucose transport across cell membranes of adipocytes and myocytes. This hormone promotes glycogenesis and glucose oxidation and inhibits lipolysis in adipose tissue and skeletal muscle. It also inhibits fatty acid oxidation and hepatic and muscle ketogenesis and increases the rate of amino acid transport and protein synthesis in muscle, adipose tissue, and the liver. In response to surgical stress, insulin secretion is suppressed by increased catecholamine concentrations, while glucagon secretion is increased. The increased glucagon to insulin ratio results in the promotion of gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis. The ultimate result is insulin resistance and hyperglycemia. Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) levels are increased in response to surgical stress. In septic shock patients, there is an initial increase in ADH concentrations, followed by a significant decrease in ADH levels. These decreased concentrations are partially responsible for the persistent vasodilation in sepsis and hemodynamic instability after cardiac surgery.
Answer B: Growth hormone levels are increased in response to surgical stress.
Answer C: Although the level of serum catecholamine is increased in response to surgical stress, this increase has not been associated with adverse perioperative complications. Hyperglycemia is a metabolic derangement in response to surgical stress and is associated with adverse perioperative complications, particularly in patients with diabetes. CBF increases linearly with PaCO2 between 20 to 80 mm Hg. In order to maintain adequate cerebral oxygenation, CBF undergoes extensive regulation in the human body. In healthy adults, CBF is autoregulated with respect to MAP between a MAP range of 60 to 160 mm Hg. The cerebral autoregulation curve is right-shifted in chronic hypertension. Long term antihypertensive therapy can reverse the right shift towards a normal cerebral autoregulation curve. CBF increases linearly with PaCO2 between 20 to 80 mm Hg. Beyond 80 mm Hg, CBF tends to plateau. Hypoxia has minimal effect on CBF above tensions of 50 mm Hg, but below that level CBF rises dramatically. Hyperoxia has relatively little (roughly 10%) effect on decreasing CBF. Temperature changes CBF by 5% to 7% for every 1 degree Celsius. CBF decreases in hypothermia and increases in hyperthermia. Hyperoxia has relatively little (roughly 10%) effect on decreasing CBF.
Answer C: Temperature changes CBF by 5% to 7% for every 1 degree Celsius. CBF decreases in hypothermia and increases in hyperthermia. CBF increases linearly with PaCO2 between 20 to 80 mm Hg. Other factors in CBF regulation include MAP, oxygen levels, and temperature. Normal CBF is 50 mL/100 g/min. Normal cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) is 80 to 100 mm Hg. Normal ICP is less than 10 mm Hg. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Blood Flow: Cerebral And Spinal Cord” Morgan and Mikhail. Clinical Anesthesiology, 5th ed. Pages 577-578.

Negative pressure pulmonary edema (NPPE) has been proposed to be caused by the development of a strong negative intrathoracic pressure that increases preload and left ventricular afterload with a decrease in cardiac output. An increased afterload with a decrease in cardiac output leads to a decrease in pulmonary interstitial pressure and an increase in the pulmonary hydrostatic pressure gradient, causing a transudation of fluid resulting in pulmonary edema. Negative pressure pulmonary edema is commonly seen after an upper airway obstruction in a spontaneously breathing patient. Two separate mechanisms have been proposed to explain the pathophysiology behind the development of NPPE. Young, healthy patients are at an increased risk for NPPE because they can generate very high levels of negative inspiratory pressure. Forced respiration against a closed glottis increases left ventricular (LV) afterload by increasing LV pressure, raising LV wall tension. The increase in afterload depresses LV ejection. The resulting hypoxemia also decreases myocardial contractility and increases pulmonary arterial resistance. The combination of increased preload and afterload with a decrease in pulmonary interstitial pressure leads to an increase in the hydrostatic pulmonary pressure gradient. This increase in pulmonary hydrostatic pressure allows for a transudation of fluid out of the pulmonary capillaries into the interstitium, resulting in pulmonary edema. This upper airway obstruction creates a hyperadrenergic state leading to peripheral vasoconstriction and an increase in venous return, which further increases pulmonary blood flow contributing to edema. Another proposed physiological mechanism of NPPE is secondary to the mechanical stress from respiration against a closed glottis that induces breaks in the alveolar epithelial and pulmonary microvascular membranes, resulting in increased pulmonary capillary permeability. Treatment for NPPE should be initially focused on securing the airway and providing supplemental oxygen with noninvasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV). In patients who fail to respond to NIPPV, mechanical ventilation should be considered. Additional treatment strategies include diuresis to encourage the mobilization of pulmonary edema fluid. Negative pressure pulmonary edema Risk factors Men Airway obstruction Young age Physically fit Otolaryngology surgery Signs/symptoms Hypoxia Pink frothy fluid Bilateral patchy infiltrates on chest x-ray Treatment Relieve airway obstruction and correction of hypoxemia Supportive with 100% O2 PEEP ventilation by ETT or CPAP Diuretics Abbreviations: CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure; ETT, endotracheal tube; PEEP, positive end-expiratory pressure. Cytokine-induced increase in capillary permeability is the mechanism of acute respiratory distress syndrome, not NPPE. In NPPE, stress from respiration against a closed glottis creates breaks in the alveolar epithelial and pulmonary microvascular membranes, resulting in increased pulmonary capillary permeability.
Answer B: Negative pressure pulmonary edema is caused by an increase, not a decrease, in left ventricular afterload.
Answer C: An increase, not a decrease, in venous return is seen in NPPE, due to the increase in intrathoracic pressure. There are two proposed physiological mechanisms of negative pressure pulmonary edema. One mechanism is the development of increased intrathoracic pressure from a forced expiration against a closed glottis that increases venous return, preload, and left ventricular afterload, resulting in a decrease in pulmonary pressures creating an increased pulmonary hydrostatic pressure gradient. The second mechanism is that the upper airway obstruction leads to mechanical stress, creating breaks in the pulmonary microvascular membranes and alveoli, resulting in increased pulmonary capillary permeability.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "Negative press pulmonary edema: Physiology" Gropper M, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. Ch. 55: Airway Management in the Adult. Section: Extubation. 9th edition. Redistribution of heat from the core to the periphery is the largest contributor to the initial reduction in core temperature during general anesthesia. This does not result in loss of body heat content or mean body temperature, but instead shifts flow of heat to the periphery. The major thermoregulatory defenses in humans include sweating, arteriovenous shunt vasoconstriction, and shivering. General anesthetics substantially reduce the body’s thresholds for vasoconstriction and shivering. Anesthetized patients are thus poikilothermic over a broader range of core temperatures. Instead of core temperature regulation to within tenths of a degree, the body’s inter-threshold range increases by 10-20 fold during general anesthesia. Redistribution of heat to the peripheral tissues via vasodilation is responsible for the first 0.5-1.5 degrees Celsius drop in core body temperature. Prevention or reduction of this can be accomplished by pre-warming the patient’s extremities, especially the lower extremities, for at least 30 minutes prior to the induction of general anesthesia. This will decrease the temperature gradient between the body's core and the periphery, therefore decreasing the redistribution of heat. The two mechanisms of undesired heat loss in the operating room are: 1. Impaired thermoregulation secondary to anesthesia. 2. Low ambient temperature of the operating theater. The four types of heat loss that occur from a patient to the relatively cold operating environment are: 1. Radiation 2. Evaporation 3. Conduction 4. Convection The main mechanism of heat loss is radiation, accounting for approximately 67%. Radiative heat losses occur anytime an object is above absolute zero. The magnitude of the radiation is proportional to the fourth power of the temperature difference between the two sources. This heat loss typically follows redistributive heat loss in a linear fashion depending on ambient temperature, size of the operation, and efficacy of warming devices. Evaporation accounts for approximately 17% of heat loss. Patients under general anesthesia typically do not sweat, which is the main way that heat is lost due to evaporation. Together, conduction and convection account for approximately 16% of heat loss from a patient to the cold operating environment. Conduction refers to the transfer of heat from direct contact with objects. It is less important in the operating room because the patient is usually lying on foam or rubber which is well insulated. Convection can play an important role since air turnover constantly removes heat as the patient’s body exists in an equilibrium of heat transfer between itself and the surrounding air. However, this does not account for the initial reduction in core temperature. Conduction contributes little to heat loss in the operating room and refers to heat loss through direct contact with objects.
Answer B: Radiative heat loss to surroundings is the main mechanism for heat loss following an initial decrease in core temperature due to redistribution. Redistribution of heat from the core to the periphery is the largest contributor to the initial reduction in core temperature during general anesthesia. Prevention or reduction of this can be accomplished by pre-warming the patient’s extremities prior to the induction of general anesthesia. Radiation is the main mechanism for patient heat loss in the operating room following this initial redistribution of heat.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Hypothermia: Cold OR Mechanism (B)" Miller's Anesthesia, 7th Edition. Pages 1537-38. Sessler DI. Perioperative thermoregulation and heat balance. Lancet. 2016; 387: 2655-64. Sessler DI. Mild perioperative hypothermia. N. Engl. J. Med. 1997; 336(24):1730-7.

The gravid uterus in pregnancy increases the intraabdominal and gastric pressure above that of the lower esophageal sphincter. This decreased pressure gradient causes an increase in gastroesophageal reflux. Prophylaxis can include a non-particulate antacid, H2 receptor blocker, and/or a proton pump inhibitor. Answers B & C & D: This is untrue; the uterus pushes the stomach cephalad and increases overall intra-abdominal pressure.  The gravid uterus pushes the stomach cephalad and increases intragastric pressures above that of the lower esophageal sphincter, resulting in gastroesophageal reflux.  Barash Anesthesia. Obstetrical Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Page 1147. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Gastric Anatomic Position"

After 20 weeks' gestation, uterine vessel resistance decreases. During pregnancy, uterine blood vessels are maximally dilated and uterine blood flow is entirely pressure-dependent. Autoregulation plays no role in uterine blood flow maintenance during pregnancy. Anesthetics have the ability to greatly affect uterine blood flow; e.g., volatile anesthetics at high concentrations can cause both systemic vasodilation and myocardial depression, which alter uterine blood flow. Volatile anesthetics can cause myocardial depression with systemic vasodilation, which could significantly affect uterine blood flow.
Answer C: Autoregulation of uterine blood flow is absent in pregnancy, and uterine blood flow is entirely pressure-dependent.
Answer D: Uterine blood flow is increased in pregnancy, with decreased uterine vessel resistance. During pregnancy, uterine blood flow is governed by pressure changes and does not have autoregulatory control. Anesthetics and hemodynamic alterations can affect uterine blood flow. These changes need to be addressed to maintain optimal oxygenation of both the mother and fetus.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Regulation Of Uterine Blood Flow" Miller's Anesthesia. 9th edition. Ch. 62: Anesthesia for Obstetrics.

The available evidence suggests that neonates and infants express lower densities of postjunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) at the neuromuscular endplate. This may account for their relatively greater intrinsic sensitivity to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs compared to adults. Neuromuscular junctions (NMJs) are highly specialized regions of association between primary motor neurons and skeletal (striated) muscle cells. They consist of presynaptic nerve terminals aligned by basal laminae with deeply corrugated muscle cell membranes, each lined with millions of nAChRs. The NMJ also varies in structure and function with age. In the newborn, the motor endplate is relatively bland with minimal synaptic invaginations and relatively few nAChRs. However, the NMJ matures rapidly--becoming more corrugated with a narrower synaptic cleft and a higher density of nAChRs--during early postnatal development, gradually resembling its adult counterpart by approximately 30 days of life. In addition, the neonatal NMJ contains uniquely polyinnervated nerve terminals, which are gradually modified to singly innervated adult junctions through retraction of all but one motor neuron from the endplate. Ongoing NMJ maturation likely continues until at least 2 years of age. Nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs such as rocuronium function as competitive antagonists of the nAChR, reducing the sensitivity of the NMJ to depolarization in response to acetylcholine release from the nerve terminal. Their clinical effects are thus amplified in states of lower relative postjunctional nAChR densities such as those observed in neonates and patients with myasthenia gravis, and reduced plasma and synaptic concentrations will be required to achieve neuromuscular blockade. In addition, neonates may exhibit decreased net acetylcholine release from the motor nerve terminal, which further increases their sensitivity to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockade. Though neonates and young children do exhibit larger volumes of distribution compared to adults, this does not account for their greater sensitivity to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs at a given plasma concentration. In fact, due to their larger relative volumes of distribution, higher intravenous doses of drugs such as rocuronium may be required to achieve clinically significant plasma concentrations in children.
Answer C: Upregulation of extrajunctional (or fetal) nAChRs chiefly occurs in states of denervation or demyelination as well as other pathologies associated with decreased neuromuscular transmission (including burns, muscular crush injuries, and prolonged immobilization or neuromuscular blockade). While this phenomenon increases the risk of significant hyperkalemia with the administration of succinylcholine, sensitivity to nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs may be reduced. However, neonates do not typically express larger numbers of extrajunctional nAChRs, which are not usually detected in skeletal muscle after 31 weeks of gestational age. Neonates and infants are more sensitive to given plasma concentrations of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blocking drugs in part because of a lower density of postjunctional nicotinic acetylcholine receptors relative to adults. It has been suggested that the relatively crude, polyinnervated NMJ and the increased expression of extrajunctional nAChRs in the fetus may play a significant developmental role. These differences enable the developing fetus to compensate for reduced stores of acetylcholine in immature synaptic terminals, thus allowing the fetus to move its growing muscles spontaneously. Such movements (e.g. “kicks” in utero) allow for appropriate neuromuscular development. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Neuro Transmission: Morphology” Gropper MA et al. (Ed.). Diffuse systemic vasodilation—accompanied by a net reduction in systemic vascular resistance (SVR)—is common in the first few hours after the onset of acute hypoxia. However, compensatory sympathetic activation may ultimately produce an increase in the blood pressure, resulting from an increased heart rate and cardiac output after the initial acute period. The vasodilatory response is also present with localized oxygen deficiency (such as ischemia) in an attempt to restore adequate oxygen delivery. Rapid-onset hemodynamic changes in the setting of decreased systemic oxygen availability include a peripheral chemoreceptormediated increase in sympathetic tone—with a resulting increase in heart rate and cardiac output—as well as global systemic vasodilation as a direct response to hypoxia. While a rise in circulating catecholamine levels may partially offset the initial vasodilatory response, a net decrease in SVR is often observed in the acute of hypoxia while it may start to increase in the subacute phase. The responses of the pulmonary and systemic vascular networks to hypoxia are generally opposed. When the peripheral arterial oxygen tension is low, the vascular tone in the systemic circulation decreases due to increased local nitric oxide production, while pulmonary vascular tone tends to increase in the setting of hypoxia. The latter phenomenon, termed hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV), may arise from an increase in intracellular calcium in the absence of oxygen and is a largely beneficial response in various states of focal lung disease because HPV may shunt blood away from hypoxic to well-oxygenated alveoli. Diffuse alveolar hypoxia, however, may cause global pulmonary vasoconstriction and pulmonary hypertension. In general, alkalemia (an increase in blood pH) is not strongly associated with systemic vasodilation. Conversely, a decreased arterial pH may cause vasodilation. This is because protons themselves may act as vasodilatory metabolites in the systemic arteriolar tree and capillary networks. This phenomenon is perhaps best illustrated by the finding that severe acidemia (ie, pH <7.2) may be associated with catecholamine-refractory vasoplegia.
Answer B: Hyperoxia, particularly when it is prolonged, does not produce systemic vasodilation and is instead increasingly recognized as a source of morbidity in acutely ill patients. This is because excess oxygen may both cause systemic vasoconstriction and precipitate the formation of free radicals (more specifically termed reactive oxygen species), which are toxic to sensitive tissues. For this reason, there is evidence that hyperoxia may lead to neurotoxicity, retinopathy, tracheobronchitis, lung injury, and even myocardial ischemia due to paradoxical coronary vasoconstriction.
Answer C: Hypocapnia produces systemic vasoconstriction, not vasodilation. Because carbon dioxide serves as a potent vasodilatory metabolite in the systemic circulation, a reduction in the arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2) may produce relative vasospasm. This effect may predispose patients to ischemic injury, although induced hypocapnia may also be harnessed to therapeutic effect, as in patients with elevated intracranial pressure who benefit from controlled hyperventilation to promote cerebral vasoconstriction and a reduced intracranial blood volume. In the systemic circulation, hypoxia causes vasodilation in the acute phase. In the pulmonary circulation, hypoxia causes vasoconstriction.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Hypoxia: Vascular Effects." Gropper M, et al. Miller’s Anesthesia. 9th Edition. Philadelphia, PA: Elsevier; 2020:2313-2315. Bärtsch P, et al. Effect of altitude on the heart and the lungs. Circulation. 2007 Nov 6;116(19):2191-202.

The cerebellum is responsible for filtering large amounts of information from many sources to help coordinate muscle movements in agonist-antagonist muscle groups. Lack of cerebellar coordination may lead to characteristic findings such as intention tremor (a tremor that worsens with movement), dysmetria (inability to coordinate muscle movements to approximate distances), or nystagmus (due to vestibulocerebellar pathway disruption). The cerebellum is composed of an anterior lobe, posterior lobe, and flocculonodular lobe. These lobes contain functional parts responsible for interacting with specific sections of the brain. The vestibulocerebellum, spinocerebellum, and cerebrocerebellum interact with the vestibular system, spinal cord, and cerebral cortex, respectively, for the coordination of movements in those areas. The largest contributor to the cerebellum is the cerebrocerebellum, which receives afferent information from the cerebral cortex. The cerebrocerebellum is approximately 90% of the cerebellar volume. The spinocerebellum receives information from the spinal cord coordinating sensory input from the body and muscle movements peripherally. The vestibulocerebellum receives input from the vestibular system to maintain proprioception and balance in space. All of these systems are routed through the cerebellum for processing environmental and internal information, which the cerebellum filters to provide better coordination between muscle groups, improve the timing of movements, and assist with motor learning tasks. Disruption of the cerebellum can lead to specific injury patterns that are important to recognize during a neurological exam. Classically, cerebellar dysfunction can lead to problems with motor coordination. Cerebellar dysfunction and symptoms Nystagmus Disrupted vestibulocerebellar pathways lead to a saccadic or beating movement of the eye with a fast and slow component Many of the symptoms present in cerebellar dysfunction can overlap with cerebral dysfunction. Without performing imaging, a purely clinical diagnosis of cerebellar dysfunction may be difficult or impossible to determine. Studies have not provided clear evidence identifying the cause of a benign tremor, also known as essential tremor. The cerebellum has been suspected as the source of essential tremor, but neuroimaging studies have not provided evidence clearly identifying anatomical lesions in the cerebellum responsible for this pathology.
Answer C: A pill-rolling tremor is characteristic of Parkinson disease, which affects the substantia nigra in the midbrain.
Answer D: The resting tremor that improves with activity is more classically found in Parkinson disease. In Parkinson disease, the destruction of dopamine-producing cells in the substantia nigra of the midbrain causes a tremor when the muscles are at rest. The cerebellum receives large quantities of information from the brain, spinal cord, and vestibular system, supporting proper coordination of movements in agonist-antagonist muscle groups for appropriate balance and fine motor function. Disruptions in cerebellar functions, as in a stroke or congenital ataxic disease (ie, Friedreich's ataxia) can lead to a variety of symptoms including intention tremor, nystagmus, and dysarthria. Overshooting targets, as in the finger-to-nose examination during a field sobriety test, assesses cerebellar function in the presence of alcohol intoxication. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Brain Physiology: Cerebellum” Brodal P. The Central Nervous System. Ch. 6: Parts of the Nervous System. Section: Cerebellum. 5th ed. Campbell WW, et al. DeJong's The Neurologic Examination. Ch. 43: Cerebellar Function. 8th ed.

Glycosuria is common in pregnancy and should not cause alarm. It is due to the increased glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and the decreased renal tubular resorption capacity. During pregnancy, mechanical compression of the renal system and the effects of progesterone cause many alterations in the renal system. The GFR and the renal plasma flow are increased primarily due to a larger cardiac output. The GFR increases by about 50%, and when combined with the dilutional effect from the increased plasma volume, the plasma creatinine, and urea decrease. Creatinine and BUN levels should be lower than prepregnant levels, and values consistent with the pre-prepregnancy baseline should alert the provider of potential renal dysfunction. The increased GFR and decreased renal tubular resorption capacity make glycosuria a common occurrence in pregnancy. Due to the increase of GFR of about 50% and the dilutional effect of the increase in the plasma volume, both the blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and creatinine should be decreased. A level consistent with prepregnancy values could indicate severe renal impairment.
Answer B: Urea, uric acid, and creatinine all decrease in pregnancy as the GFR rises by about 50%. Pregnancy-induced changes to the renal system include an increased GFR by about 50% with concomitant decreases in urea, uric acid, and creatinine and an increase in glycosuria.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Renal" Miller's Anesthesia. Anesthesia for Obstetrics in Seventh Edition. Page 2206-2207.

Retinopathy of prematurity is seen in preterm infants, especially those with a birth weight of under 1200 grams. Blood vessels normally form from the macula towards the retina, which is normally complete at birth. In the preterm infant, this process proceeds for a longer period of time with risk of vasoconstriction, neovascularization, and hemorrhage. The most common cited cause is hyperoxia with sepsis, intraventricular hemorrhage, hypotension, and hypoxemia, having been implicated as well. Most will spontaneously regress and progress to normal vision. In the more advanced cases, retinal detachment and vision impairment may occur. Cryotherapy and laser procedures have been used with success and a general anesthetic is needed as a still surgical field is of extreme importance. During the anesthetic, a pulse oximetry reading of 96-99% should be obtained since the use of supplemental oxygen with readings in this range have not been implicated to cause additional progression of the disease. Most treatments require a still operating field and therefore a general anesthetic.
Answer C: While hypoxemia has been implicated, hyperoxia (too much oxygen) is the most cited cause of retinopathy of prematurity.
Answer D: Most cases result in spontaneous regression while some with the severe form have the potential for permanent blindness. Retinopathy of prematurity is most common in infants less than 1200 grams with a most cited cause of hyperoxia. Most of those affected have spontaneous regression and a general anesthetic is necessary for treatment as a still surgical field is needed.  Barash Anesthesia. Neonatal Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Pages 1200-1201. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neonatal Physiology: Retinopathy Of Prematurity"

Diaphoresis is mediated by sympathetic stimulation via release of acetylcholine and stimulation of muscarinic receptors and is the only symptom that may be seen in a patient who is hypoglycemic and on beta blockers. The normal response to hypoglycemia is an increase in sympathetic discharge, cortisol release, and glucagon release with symptoms of diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, altered mental status, and possibly even seizures. The sympathetic nervous system is composed of preganglionic neurons located in the lateral horn of the spinal cord from T1-L2. The preganglionic axons are short and synapse quickly in the sympathetic or prevertebral ganglia and the signal transmitted to the postganglionic neuron is through the neurotransmitter acetylcholine and nicotinic receptors. The postganglionic neuron then projects axons to effector organs and releases norepinephrine with stimulation of alpha or beta receptors. The exception is with sweat glands and the chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, both of which are stimulated by acetylcholine via muscarinic (sweat glands) and nicotinic (chromaffin cells) receptors. The adrenal medulla is essentially a modified postganglionic sympathetic neuron. This patient is taking the nonselective beta blocker propanolol which will block both beta-1 mediated tachycardia and hypertension along with beta-2 mediated relaxation of the ciliary muscle of the lens which improves distance, not near vision. The parasympathetic nervous system originates from the brainstem and sacral spinal cord and uses acetylcholine at all synapses. Acetylcholine binds to nicotinic receptors at the autonomic ganglia and muscarinic receptors at the effector site. Answers B & C: This will be blocked by propranolol.  Sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic nervous system and utilize acetylcholine with muscarinic receptors, therefore beta blockade will not prevent sweating with hypoglycemia which may be the only symptom seen in this setting.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Autonomic Neurotransmitters" Miller's Anesthesia. The Autonomic Nervous System in 8th edition. Pages 346-386.

The Haldane effect explains the increased ability of hemoglobin to carry carbon dioxide (CO2) from the tissues to the lungs for exhalation. Deoxygenated hemoglobin has 3.5 times more capacity for CO2 compared with oxygenated hemoglobin. Therefore, in the presence of low oxygen (O2) concentrations, hemoglobin binds more strongly to CO2, and, in areas of high O2 concentration, hemoglobin binds less strongly to CO2. Deoxygenated hemoglobin is a strong base that binds to hydrogen ions. In the tissue, O2 is released, and CO2 enters the erythrocyte. The CO2 combines with water to form carbonic acid by way of carbonic anhydrase and then ionizes to form hydrogen ions and bicarbonate. The hydrogen ion binds to the histidine residue on hemoglobin, while the bicarbonate (HCO3-) diffuses outside the erythrocyte. To maintain electric neutrality, chloride replaces the HCO3- (chloride shift). After it is in the lungs, hemoglobin is exposed to high concentrations of O2, causing it to have less affinity for the hydrogen ion, which is then released. The hydrogen ion then binds with bicarbonate to form CO2 and water. The CO2 is then exhaled and eliminated. The increased delivery of O2 at the tissue level can be partly explained by the Bohr effect. According to the Bohr effect, an increase in the CO2 and hydrogen ion concentrations will cause hemoglobin to have a decreased affinity for O2. This is seen as a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. As a result, hemoglobin will release O2 to the tissues that are metabolically active and are producing CO2. It is the complementary action to the Haldane effect. Whereas the Haldane effect provides an explanation for increased binding of CO2 for delivery to the lungs, the Bohr effect provides an explanation for decreased binding of O2 for delivery to the tissues. When hydrogen ions are in abundance, the hemoglobin has less affinity for O2 (Bohr effect and occurs in tissue), and, when oxygen is in abundance, the CO2 has less affinity for hemoglobin (Haldane effect and occurs in lungs).
Answer C: Helium helps deliver O2 to asthmatic patients in relation to the Reynolds number and the increase in laminar vs turbulent flow. When a patient has an asthma attack, obstruction to airflow results in turbulence and restricted flow to the lungs. Laminar flow is more efficient, and the Reynolds number helps predict whether airflow will be turbulent or laminar. The Reynolds number is determined by inertial forces (velocity, density, and length) divided by viscous forces. Flow is more likely to be turbulent and ineffectual when the Reynolds number is greater. Helium is less dense than nitrogen, and, by combining helium with oxygen, the density of the gas decreases. As the Reynolds number decreases, the airflow is more likely to be laminar, thus improving ventilation in the lungs. The Bohr and Haldane effects are complementary principles that help explain the efficient delivery of O2 to the tissue and of CO2 to the lungs. According to the Bohr effect, in areas of high CO2, the hemoglobin has less affinity for O2, which is more readily released for consumption by the tissues. According to the Haldane effect, deoxygenated hemoglobin has a higher affinity for CO2. After the deoxygenated hemoglobin reaches the lungs, the high O2 concentration decreases this affinity, and the CO2 is released.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Haldane Effect" Miller RD, et al. Miller's Anesthesia. Page 1563. 7th edition. Conlon CE. High frequency jet ventilation. World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists. Oct. 8th 2012.

Most currently available balanced crystalloid solutions, including lactated Ringer solution, have an osmolality of around 260 - 270 mOsm/kg which is slightly lower than a normal plasma osmolality (285 mOsm/kg). Administration of these hypotonic solutions to a patient will transiently decrease the plasma tonicity and therefore suppress anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secretion. This results in a temporary increase in diuresis in response to the increased intravascular volume. The term "Balanced Crystalloid Solution" refers to a crystalloid solution that attempts to mimic the normal physiologic makeup of plasma. This is typically done through the use of more physiologically normal levels of sodium and chloride (the major strong ions in plasma), as well as the other strong ions including potassium, calcium, magnesium, and lactate. In general, a strong ion difference is calculated as the difference between the serum cations and anions. Specifically, it is the difference of (Sodium + Potassium + Calcium + Magnesium) and (Chloride + Lactate). A physiologic strong ion difference is around positive 40 to 45. All balanced salt solutions leverage a combination of these ions to produce a similar strong ion difference. This is in stark contrast to 0.9% sodium chloride solution that has a strong ion difference of 0 (154 mEq/L sodium - 154 mEq/L chloride). Excessive administration of this hypertonic solution results in a hyperchloremic acidosis as the plasma strong ion difference is brought down. Balanced salt solutions do not have this issue and instead tend to promote a physiologically neutral acid-base status when administered. A characteristic of most balanced crystalloid solutions is the use of an organic anionic buffer to generate bicarbonate ions in the plasma. While the use of the physiologic buffer bicarbonate would be ideal in these solutions, its use is limited from two standpoints. The first is that bicarbonate will react with water to form carbon dioxide that diffuses through most IV solution bags, and the second is that bicarbonate can cause pH shifts that result in the precipitation of calcium or magnesium if present. Instead, balanced sal solutions utilize either lactate or acetate, both of which are oxidized in the body to form bicarbonate. Lactate primarily undergoes hepatic oxidation, while acetate is oxidized in the liver, heart, and muscles to form bicarbonate. Balanced crystalloid solutions are normally mildly hypotonic, which must be considered in disease states such as traumatic brain injury where plasma osmolality is of clinical concern. In these states, a higher serum osmolality might be beneficial to draw interstitial water out of the brain and decrease intracranial pressure, a process that could be reversed with excess administration of a hypotonic balanced salt solution such as lactated Ringer solution. In general, however, this modest hypoosmolarity is oftentimes desired as it allows for replenishment of the subglycocalyceal fluid space as well as promotes diuresis through a transient inhibition of ADH as described above, especially when compared with 0.9% sodium chloride solution. While most balanced salt solutions contain an organic anionic buffer, they tend to include either lactate or acetate which are oxidized in the body to form bicarbonate.
Answer C: Balanced salt solutions universally contain a more physiologic amount of chloride than 0.9% sodium chloride, with chloride ranges between 90 and 110 mEq/L, compared to the 154 mEq/L of chloride used in 0.9% sodium chloride solution.
Answer D: Balanced salt solutions tend to be mildly hypoosmolar (260 - 270 mOsm/kg) when compared to a typical plasma osmolarity (285 mOsm/kg). This is much less than the mildly hyperosmolar sodium chloride solution that has an osmolarity of 308 mOsm/kg. Balanced crystalloid solutions such as lactated Ringer's solution tend to be mildly hypoosmolar, have lower sodium and chloride concentrations than 0.9% sodium chloride, have a physiologic strong ion difference, and contain an anionic buffer that is metabolized into bicarbonate following administration. Balanced Crystalloid Solutions in 8th Edition. Pages 1781 - 1782.

The ganglia in which the presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons of both the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems synapse contain exclusively nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. As a rule, the autonomic nervous system (ANS) exerts its effects throughout the body through the neurotransmission of only three substances: acetylcholine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine. Depending on the tissue in which these substances are deposited, the ANS can have an inhibitory or excitatory effect which is mediated by the specific type and characteristics of the conjugate receptors within these tissues. Muscarinic and adrenergic receptors are coupled directly to G-proteins that allow these neurotransmitters to exert their end-organ effect through second-messenger signaling. Nicotinic receptors on the other hand directly cause an increase in the permeability of a cell membrane to sodium and calcium ions due to their direct association with the relevant ion channels and result in the rapid depolarization of the postsynaptic cell. Given these characteristics, it follows then that nicotinic receptors tend to be found in the postsynaptic membrane synapses when the effect of the postsynaptic tissue is to rapidly depolarize. An example of this is within the autonomic ganglia where the binding of acetylcholine that is released from presynaptic neurons to the postsynaptic nicotinic receptors results in depolarization of the postsynaptic neuron. Another example of where nicotinic receptors cause depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane is at the motor-end plate where their activation results in depolarization and contraction of the muscle tissue. Muscarinic acetylcholine receptors tend to be found in the effector tissues that respond to the release of acetylcholine from postsynaptic parasympathetic neurons. The notable exception to this is that eccrine sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic nervous system and are stimulated through activation of sympathetically released acetylcholine that activates muscarinic receptors in these sweat gland tissues. Due to their association with G-proteins, the downstream effects that are caused by the activation of muscarinic receptors are varied. In some tissues this effect is excitatory (e.g. muscarinic activation of the bronchospasm reflex) and in some tissues it is inhibitory (e.g. bradycardia from muscarinic stimulation of the sinoatrial node). The release of the catecholamines epinephrine and norepinephrine from postganglionic sympathetic neurons tend to have predictable effects based upon the receptors that are being stimulated in the effector organ. Muscarinic receptors are found primarily in the parasympathetic nervous system, however, the sympathetically innervated sweat glands also utilize these receptors.
Answer C: The parasympathetic postganglionic neurons exclusively release acetylcholine at the site of their effector tissues which will bind to muscarinic receptors on those tissues.
Answer D: The parasympathetic nervous system can have either an inhibitory or excitatory effect depending on the effector tissue that it is innervating. For instance, an increase in parasympathetic tone in the lungs results in bronchoconstriction while the same results in bradycardia and myocardial depression in the heart. Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are found within the autonomic ganglia and at the neuromuscular end-plate and allow for rapid depolarization of the post-synaptic tissue. The effects that occur following the stimulation of muscarinic acetylcholine receptors are much more varied and depend on the second-messenger G-protein coupled reactions that are triggered by their stimulation.  ABA Gaps In Knowledge Report, BASIC 2018. "Post-synaptic nicotinic cholinergic receptors are found in the sympathetic ganglia" American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. “Acetylcholine Receptor: Physiology (B)” Miller's Anesthesia. Postjunctional Acetylcholine Receptor in 8th Edition. Pages 431 - 432. McCorry LK. Physiology of the autonomic nervous system. Am J Pharm Educ. 2007;71(4):78.

The left ventricle (LV) is more sensitive than the right to ischemia due to an imbalance of oxygen supply/demand to the myocardium. Decreased diastolic time mostly affects the LV, which is perfused primarily during diastole. Coronary blood flow is directly proportional to coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) and inversely proportional to vascular resistance. Resistance is defined by the Hagen-Poiseuille Equation, R = (8 * L * η ) / (π * r^4), where R = resistance, L = length, η = blood viscosity, and r = vessel radius. This law explains the marked influence of the radius on coronary flow (e.g. atherosclerosis). Left ventricle coronary perfusion occurs primarily during diastole because this is when aortic blood pressure is greater than left ventricular (LV) pressure. During systole, left ventricular pressure is higher than aortic pressure and there is absence or even reversal of flow in the coronary arteries. Because of this LV CPP is defined as diastolic arterial pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure. Increased time in diastole (e.g. with beta-blockers) will, therefore, increase left ventricle coronary perfusion. Right ventricle (RV) coronary perfusion normally occurs throughout the cardiac cycle because right ventricle pressure does not normally exceed systemic pressures. In an individual with aortic pressures of 120/70 mmHg and RV pressures of 25/5 mmHg, the CPP will be greater in systole (120-25 = 95) than in diastole (70-5 = 65). Because of this, coronary flow to the right ventricle, measured in mL/min, is greater during systole than diastole. Answers B & C: Higher filling pressures and lower diastolic blood pressure would decrease diastolic coronary perfusion to both ventricles, not just the left ventricle. Granted, this would be less taxing to the right ventricle because it is also perfused during systole, and also because it has a greater ability to increase its oxygen extraction ratio and to downregulate its metabolic demand compared to the left ventricle. The right coronary artery and its branches have the highest incidence of vasospasm. Thus, Prinzmetal angina would not be likely to affect the LV while sparing the RV. Coronary perfusion occurs primarily during diastole and is dependent on coronary perfusion pressure and vascular resistance. Coronary perfusion pressure is defined as diastolic aortic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Preganglionic nerve fibers of the upper extremity originate from the first four or five thoracic spinal segments. The cervical spinal roots do not contribute to the sympathetic nervous system. Nerves of the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) arise from the thoracolumbar segments (T1-L3) of the spinal cord. Preganglionic fibers exit the spinal cord via the ventral horn and form the white communicating rami to enter one of 22 paired paravertebral ganglia. After entering their respective ganglion, fibers can either synapse with postganglionic fibers at that level, travel up or down the SNS chain to synapse at a different level, or they can travel a variable distance to a visceral collateral ganglion. Sympathetic nerve fibers of the upper extremity originate from the first four or five thoracic spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers enter three different ganglia termed the superior cervical, middle cervical, and the stellate ganglia. The stellate ganglion is also known as the cervicothoracic ganglion as it is formed by fusion of the inferior cervical and the first thoracic SNS ganglia. Within these ganglia, preganglionic fibers synapse at nicotinic receptors utilizing the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. The postganglionic fibers then travel with afferent pain fibers to the head, neck, upper extremities, heart, and lungs. The widespread sympathetic distribution of fibers accounts for pain in the neck and upper extremity that can be experienced with myocardial ischemia. This also accounts for the efficacy of stellate ganglion block in conditions involving sympathetically mediated pain such as complex regional pain syndrome of the upper extremity. Answers A & B & D: This is a correct statement.  The sympathetic nervous system of the upper extremity originates from the first four or five thoracic spinal segments. These preganglionic fibers synapse via acetylcholine-mediated nicotinic receptors in the superior cervical, middle cervical, and stellate ganglia. Postganglionic fibers then travel with afferent pain fibers to the head, neck, upper extremity, heart, and lungs. Sweat gland activation by the sympathetic nervous system is unique in that neurotransmission occurs via postganglionic fibers utilizing acetylcholine instead of norepinephrine. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th Edition. Pages 364-366. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Autonomic Innervation: Upper Extremity (B)"

When the presynaptic terminal is depolarized by an action potential, calcium channels open, resulting in an influx of calcium that triggers acetylcholine release. Potassium channels then open which allow for an efflux of potassium which rapidly restores the membrane potential. Meanwhile, the released acetylcholine travels across the cleft to bind to acetylcholine receptors on the postsynaptic membrane which results in depolarization of the endplate. This depolarization opens sodium channels which generate an action potential in the muscle. Figure: The action potential travels along the presynaptic neuron to the presynaptic terminal, which leads to intracellular calcium influx. The influx of calcium causes acetylcholine vesicles to adhere to the presynaptic terminal membrane. After the acetylcholine molecule is released across the synaptic cleft, it binds to the central ion channel, which causes a net inward flux of sodium, which then allows for muscle contraction to occur. Potassium ions restore the membrane potential of the presynaptic terminal and are less closely associated with generation of the postsynaptic membrane end plate potential that triggers an action potential than sodium.
Answer C: Calcium ions trigger acetylcholine release and are less closely associated with generation of the postsynaptic membrane end plate potential that triggers an action potential than sodium. The opening of sodium channels on the postsynaptic terminal triggers an action potential. The voltage gated sodium channel can be in one of three states: open (excited), inactivated (desensitized), or closed (resting). American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Action Potential: Ion Channels (B)" Neuromuscular Transmission: Basic and Applied Concepts, 1st edition. Page 82-84. Open Image. National Library of Medicine, National Institute of Health.
