Tissue hypoxia from carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning can occur due to a left shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. This occurs as a result of hemoglobin’s (Hb) increased affinity for CO as compared with oxygen. This leftward shift therefore increases oxygen binding to the Hb molecule. Carbon monoxide poisoning is commonly associated with burn victims due to smoke exposure during a fire. Carbon monoxide has an affinity for Hb that is 200-300 times stronger than oxygen. Hemoglobin preferentially binds to CO (carboxyhemoglobin, or COHb) leaving less Hb available for oxygen to bind. In addition, oxygen that binds with Hb tends not to dissociate from Hb, resulting in a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve. CO disrupts mitochondrial function, which leads to less adenosine triphosphate (ATP) production as a result of uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation. The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production. Combined, these factors result in tissue hypoxia and a metabolic acidosis (with an anion gap). Clinically, CO poisoning is difficult to discover without an adequate history because oxygen saturation is usually normal. Standard pulse oximetry is unable to distinguish between COHb and oxyhemoglobin as they both absorb light at similar frequencies. The diagnosis of carbon monoxide poisoning is made by co-oximetry, when elevated levels of COHb (> 15%) are found on arterial or venous blood gas analysis. Treatment includes high FiO2 which helps displace CO. Hyperbaric oxygen is reserved for patients with COHb > 30% and/or severe symptomatology (e.g., obtundation, delirium, bradyarrhythmia, etc.). CO disrupts mitochondrial function, leading to less ATP production due to uncoupled oxidative phosphorylation.
Answer C: The inability to utilize the electron transport chain shifts cellular metabolism towards glycolysis and lactate production. Carbon monoxide poisoning causes tissue hypoxia and acidosis by decreased coupling of oxidative phosphorylation, a leftward shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, decreased ATP production, and increased lactate production.  Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 909-910. Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 2671. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Carbon Monoxide: Tissue Hypoxia"

This patient’s systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is calculated to be 1520 dynes * sec/cm^5. First, mean arterial pressure (MAP) must be calculated since it is not given directly: MAP = [(1/3) * systolic pressure] + [(2/3) * diastolic pressure] = [(1/3) * 120 mm Hg] + [(2/3) * 90 mm Hg] = 100 mm Hg Next, SVR can be calculated using the following formula: SVR = [80 * (MAP – RAP)] ÷ CO = [80 * (100 – 5)] ÷ 5 = 1520 dynes * sec/cm^5 Where: MAP = mean arterial pressure (mm Hg) RAP = right atrial pressure (mm Hg), central venous pressure is commonly substituted for RAP CO = cardiac output (L/min) 80 = conversion factor which changes mm Hg/L/min (Woods unit) to dynes * sec/cm^5 Answers A & C & D: This patient’s systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is calculated to be 1520 dynes * sec/cm^5.  Systemic vascular resistance in dynes * sec/cm^5 = [80 * (MAP – RAP)] ÷ CO. Central venous pressure is commonly substituted for RAP. Conversion of dynes * sec/cm^5 to Woods units may be achieved by dividing SVR by 80. For example, 1520 / 80 = 19 Woods units.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Pulmonary vs SVR calculation" Marino, The ICU Book, 3rd edition, pp. 10-11, 174.

This patient’s pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is calculated to be 128 dynes * sec/cm^5. First, mean pulmonary arterial pressure (MPAP) must be calculated since it is not given directly: MPAP = [(1/3) * systolic pressure] + [(2/3) * diastolic pressure] = [(1/3) * 24 mm Hg] + [(2/3) * 12 mm Hg] = 16 mm Hg Next, PVR can be calculated using the formula below: PVR = [80 * (MPAP – PAOP)] ÷ CO = [80 * (16 – 8)] ÷ 5 = 128 dynes * sec/cm^5 Where: MPAP = mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mm Hg) PAOP = pulmonary artery occlusion pressure or pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (mm Hg) CO = cardiac output (L/min) 80 = conversion factor which changes mm Hg/L/min (Woods unit) to dynes * sec/cm^5 Answers B & C & D: This patient’s pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) is calculated to be 128 dynes * sec/cm^5.  Pulmonary vascular resistance in dynes * sec/cm^5 = [80 * (MPAP – PAOP)] ÷ CO. Conversion to Woods units may be achieved by dividing by the conversion factor of 80. For example, 128 / 80 = 1.6 Woods units (mm Hg/L/min).  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Pulmonary vs SVR calculation" Marino, The ICU Book, 3rd edition, pp. 10-11, 174.

ECT is known to cause an increase in intracranial pressure (ICP) and cerebral blood flow (CBF), which is of concern in patients with space-occupying lesions. Intracranial lesions are a relative contraindication to ECT. ECT involves placement of scalp electrodes to deliver an electrical stimulus to induce a seizure of at least 25-second duration. Physiologic effects of ECT include an increase in CMRO2, CBF, and ICP initially, followed by a return to baseline in the post-ictal period. There is also autonomic stimulation with initial bradycardia followed by hypertension and tachycardia, which can induce cardiac ischemia. In fact, cardiac-related events are the leading cause of death after ECT, though this is rare. Side effects of ECT include headache, myalgia, nausea, status epilepticus (though it is also used to treat this), fractures, emergence agitation, and neurocognitive impairment. Both long- and short-term memory loss have been produced by ECT and can persist. However, short-term memory loss is more common. Studies have suggested that technical implementation of ECT can affect neurocognitive side effects notably that the use of short pulse, right-unilateral, non-sine wave pulses result in a more favorable side effect profile. Answers A & D: Both bradycardia and tachycardia commonly occur during ECT. Initial short-lived bradycardia is commonly followed by tachycardia. Short-term memory loss is common. Long-term memory loss is also seen with ECT, though it is uncommon. Physiologic responses to ECT include elevations in CBF and ICP, long and short-term memory loss, and autonomic stimulation with initial bradycardia, followed by hypertension and tachycardia. Hypoxic patients (SpO2 < 94%) presenting with an ischemic stroke should receive supplemental oxygen to increase oxygen delivery to the affected area and also because these patients are at high risk for airway compromise. Hyperoxia should be avoided as well, thus oxygen should be titrated to maintain SpO2 < 100%, giving a goal range of 94-99%. Strokes or cerebrovascular accidents (CVAs) are a leading cause of death in the United States. Important steps for stroke survival include adequate public education, prehospital early recognition of stroke symptoms, and adequate emergency medical services with appropriate transport. Well-equipped stroke centers should be established and health care professionals such as anesthesiologists should be well-versed in the management of these patients. These patients may be encountered after rapid emergency department triage and often require urgent care and decision-making. Per the American Heart Association (AHA) Adult Basic Life Support (BLS) recommendations, the following key points must be considered in the management of strokes: • The presence and severity of a stroke should be rapidly assessed. The National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is recommended by the AHA and may be encountered in the patient history during handover of care from the emergency department to the perioperative teams. • Laboratory studies may or may not be available. Only a blood glucose is needed prior to fibrinolytic administration per AHA guidelines. • Baseline electrocardiogram and troponins are recommended in patients presenting with acute ischemic stroke, however, this should not delay fibrinolytic therapy. Chest radiographs are noncontributory in this setting and should not delay fibrinolytic administration. • Brain imaging is critical to the timely evaluation of these patients. Radiologists should assess brain imaging findings including the size, location, vascular distribution of the infarction, as well as the presence of bleeding. • Administration of fibrinolytic therapy within the first few hours of onset of neurologic injury to improve outcome. The AHA suggests placing institutional protocols in place to facilitate the evaluation of a stroke and initiation of fibrinolytic treatment within 60 minutes of patient arrival. In taking a history of a patient with recent ischemic stroke, anesthesiologists should look for any fibrinolytic administration including the timing and signs of hemorrhagic conversion which can occur. • Supplemental oxygen to hypoxemic patients (SpO2 < 94%) should be provided since patients with acute stroke are at risk for respiratory compromise. Additionally, poor perfusion combined with hypoxemia will worsen ischemic brain injury. Respiratory compromise may occur due to partial airway obstruction, dysregulation of ventilation, aspiration, atelectasis, and pneumonia. Patients with decreased consciousness or bulbar dysfunction may have lost airway reflexes, and central periodic breathing (Cheyne-Stokes respiration) may be seen. Hyperoxia should also be avoided, thus titrate oxygen for a goal SpO2 < 100%. • Temperature regulation is key. These patients can present with hyperthermia soon after stroke onset. Hyperthermia is associated with poor neurologic outcome and should be addressed by treating the cause and monitoring temperature closely. • Extremes of systemic blood pressure in these patients can be detrimental and, in the absence of strong recommendations, values close to baseline blood pressure should be maintained, especially since these patients may have disturbed brain autoregulation. Pharmacologic interventions to lower as well as increase blood pressure should be available. • Fluid management goals should be to achieve euvolemia. These patients are often hypovolemic on presentation and this may lead to hypoperfusion and worsening of the brain injury. Conversely, hypervolemia may exacerbate brain edema due to ischemia and inflammation and may increase stress on the heart. • Glucose levels should be carefully monitored and kept within normal range. Hypoglycemia is rare and may lead to permanent brain damage. Conversely, hyperglycemia, which is more common in acute ischemic stroke due to stress, have been associated with worse clinical outcomes in multiple studies. • Close cardiac monitoring and continuous rhythm monitoring should be employed to screen for atrial fibrillation and other arrhythmias which are at highest risk of occurring during the first 24 hours since acute stroke onset. These patients present for endovascular intervention in the interventional radiology suite. Even if intra-arterial treatments are being considered, eligible patients should receive recombinant tissue plasminogen activator (rTPA) therapy prior to arrival. Patient eligibility for rTPA is out of the scope of this question but can be found in the references below. The AHA's statements on endovascular interventions for the management of acute stroke include: • Similarly to intravenous fibrinolytic therapy, reduced time to reperfusion is associated with improved clinical outcomes • The usefulness of emergent intracranial angioplasty or stenting is not well-known Stroke patients frequently present with hyperthermia which can be detrimental for neurologic outcomes due to increased inflammation and metabolism. Patients should be maintained at normothermia.
Answer B: Overly aggressive reduction in glucose may lead to hypoglycemia and permanent neurological damage. It is appropriate to leave the current glucose level as is and recheck at a later interval. Per the American Heart Association, "Avoiding hypoglycemia was considered more important than the unproven benefits of treating moderate hyperglycemia."
Answer D: This hypertensive patient under stress and with a new stroke has risk factors for elevated blood pressure. She also may have an elevated baseline systemic blood pressure. It is appropriate to avoid extremes of blood pressure especially in stroke patients who may no longer have intact cerebral autoregulation. Extremes of blood pressure can be detrimental to neurologic outcomes. Goals for patients presenting with acute stroke include normothermia, normotension, euvolemia, normal blood glucose levels, avoidance of hypoxemia (SpO2 < 94%), avoidance of hyperoxia (SpO2 100% on oxygen), and, most importantly, rapid fibrinolysis. The total arterial blood oxygen content in a patient with a hemoglobin (Hb) of 10 g/dL, partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) of 100 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation (SaO2) of 100% would be 13.9 mL/dL. The total arterial blood oxygen content is 13.9 mL/dL = (10 g/dL × 1.36 mL O2/g Hb × 100%) + (100 mm Hg × 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg). The total oxygen content in arterial blood is the sum of the oxygen bound to Hb and the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma. Each gram of normal Hb can bind ~1.36 mL of oxygen. Some texts reference 1.34 O2/g Hb because 1.36 is the carrying capacity under ideal conditions, and there are often small quantities of less effective forms of hemoglobin such as carboxyhemoglobin or methemoglobin in the blood. If all available sites of Hb are bound to oxygen, then the SaO2 will be 100%. Thus, the equation for the oxygen content bound to Hb is 1.36 mL O2/g Hb × Hb value of the patient × SaO2. The other source of oxygen is the amount dissolved in the plasma. According to Henry's law, the amount of dissolved oxygen is related to the partial pressure of oxygen and the solubility coefficient. The solubility coefficient of oxygen is 0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg, so the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma is 0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg × PaO2. By combining these 2 equations, the total oxygen content in arterial blood is (1.36 mL O2/g Hb × Hb value of the patient × SaO2) + (0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg × PaO2). The amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma is 0.3 mL/dL. The PaO2 is 100 mm Hg, and the solubility coefficient of oxygen in blood is 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg. Thus, 0.3 mL/dL = 100 mm Hg × 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg.
Answer B: The amount of bound oxygen to Hb with an SaO2 of 100% is 13.6 mL/dL. Hemoglobin is 10 g/dL, SaO2 is 100%, and the Hb can carry 1.36 mL O2/g Hb. The amount of bound oxygen to Hb is 13.6 mL/dL = 10 g/dL × 1.36 mL O2/g Hb × 100%.
Answer D: The value of 20.7 mL/dL would be the total oxygen content in arterial blood for a healthy individual with an Hb of 15 g/dL, a PaO2 of 100 mm Hg, and an SaO2 of 100%. The total oxygen content in arterial blood is 20.4 mL/dL = (15 g/dL × 1.36 mL O2/g Hb x 100%) + (100 mm Hg × 0.003 mL O2/dL blood/mm Hg). The total oxygen content in arterial blood is the sum of the oxygen bound to hemoglobin (Hb) and the amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma. The total oxygen content in arterial blood can be calculated with the equation (1.36 mL O2/g Hb × Hb value of the patient × oxygen saturation) + (0.003 mL O2/dL/mm Hg × partial pressure of oxygen). Water moves freely across the blood-brain barrier (BBB) based on the tonicity of intravascular fluid. The BBB forms a boundary between the central nervous system (CNS) and the rest of the body. It is a semipermeable membrane made up of the nearly fused junctions of vascular endothelial cells. The pores of this wall are lipophilic and small, thereby repelling hydrophilic molecules, such as charged ions, and large molecules. The relative osmolarity or oncotic pressure of the intravascular space determines the inward or outward flow of water across the BBB. The nature of the BBB is clinically relevant to the anesthesia provider for several reasons. The integrity of the BBB reflects neuroprotectivity. Disruption of the BBB, such as in cases of trauma or extreme hypertension, may lead to brain edema and CNS damage. While oncotic pressure generally drives the fluid gradient across a healthy BBB, hydrostatic pressure becomes the dominant factor once it is disrupted. The lipophilicity of the BBB also makes it a strategic drug target. Part of the reason volatile anesthetics induce general anesthesia is due to the lipid solubility of these gases across the BBB. Certain drugs with the same function may differ in CNS permeability because of the BBB, including the anticholinergic medication glycopyrrolate (does not cross BBB or cause sedation) and atropine (crosses the BBB and causes sedation). Fluid movement across the BBB is dependent on osmotic gradients. With the pathologic disruption of the BBB, hydrostatic pressure becomes more central to intracranial fluid movement.
Answer B: Mannitol is a sugar alcohol with osmotically active properties. It is given to promote diuresis during the oliguric phase of acute renal failure and in cases of elevated intraocular pressure and elevated intracranial pressure. Mannitol is also useful in flushing out harmful toxins. Its utility in elevated intracranial pressure stems from its large molecular weight, which makes it unable to penetrate the BBB. Mannitol then draws fluid from the brain into the intravascular space, which is then excreted as urine.
Answer C: The BBB is hydrophobic, which prevents the transit of ionized compounds. Its lipophilicity contributes to the penetration of volatile anesthetic into the CNS. The blood-brain barrier (BBB) protects the central nervous system from pathogens and rapid fluctuations in its electrolyte fluid balance. Water moves freely across the BBB based on the tonicity of intravascular fluid. With the pathologic disruption of the BBB, hydrostatic pressure becomes more central to intracranial fluid movement. Surgical stimulus and heightened states of arousal (e.g. fear or anxiety) cause hyperventilation. This typically causes a leftward shift and increased slope of the carbon dioxide ventilatory response curve (VRC). A VRC illustrates how changes in a patient’s arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) will alter minute ventilation. The VRC is typically linear between PaCO2 values of 20-80 mmHg, such that increasing PaCO2 levels correspond to resultant increases in minute ventilation. Various factors can shift the PaCO2 baseline of a minute ventilation response. This baseline is illustrated as the PaCO2 at which a VRC intersects a ventilation curve (grey dotted line in these figures). The slope of the VRC represents the sensitivity of the ventilatory centers to elevated PaCO2. See the figure below for more details. MAC: minimum alveolar concentration. Volatile anesthetics at ≤1 MAC cause a rightward, parallel shift of the VRC. Volatile anesthetics >1 MAC reduce sensitivity to elevated PaCO2, cause a rightward shift, and reduce the slope of the VRC.
Answer C: Opioid, barbiturate, and other sedative-hypnotic medication administration shift the VRC to the right and depress the slope, in a dose-dependent manner. The result is a reduced minute ventilation and higher baseline PaCO2 therefore reducing minute ventilation.
Answer D: A change in end-tidal oxygen concentration from 20% to 60% will generally have no significant effect on a patient’s VRC. If the change represents correction of arterial hypoxemia, however, the curve may shift to the right with a decrease in the slope. Factors that cause a leftward shift and an increased slope of a carbon dioxide ventilatory response curve include arterial hypoxemia, metabolic acidemia, surgical stimuli, and certain central nervous system pathologies. Factors that cause a rightward shift and a reduced slope of the curve include opioids, barbiturates, and sedative-hypnotic drugs. Volatile anesthetics ≤1 MAC cause a rightward, parallel shift of the VRC.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Co2-Vent Response Curve: Left Shift" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 271-273.

When adenosine triphosphate (ATP) binds the myosin head during the muscle contraction cycle, the myosin head detaches from the actin filament. Muscle contraction begins when the muscle cell is polarized when acetylcholine (ACh) binds to postsynaptic receptors. The depolarization spreads across the sarcolemma and into the t-tubules, activating the voltage-sensitive dihydropyridine receptors that are mechanically coupled to the ryanodine receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The ryanodine receptors release the stored Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm, increasing the intracellular Ca2+ concentration. The increased intracellular Ca2+ binds to troponin C on tropomyosin, leading to a conformational change such that the tropomyosin moves away, revealing a binding site on the actin filament for the myosin head to bind. The myosin head then binds the actin, forming a cross-bridge at a 90° angle. The myosin head releases a phosphate (Pi), and myosin pulls itself along the actin, decreasing the angle, causing the muscle to shorten and releasing the remaining adenosine diphosphate (ADP) molecule. Because the ATP binding site is now available, another ATP molecule binds to the site on the myosin head, releasing the myosin head from the actin filament. As the ATP is hydrolyzed on the detached myosin head, the myosin head returns to the cocked 90° angle state. The ADP and Pi remain on the myosin head. The myosin head is now ready to bind actin again. As long as the Ca2+ remains elevated, additional cross-bridging will occur, and muscle contraction ensues. When the level of Ca2+ is elevated, it binds to troponin C, leading to a conformational change such that the tropomyosin moves, revealing a binding site on the actin filament for the myosin head to bind. The myosin head then binds the actin, forming a cross-bridge at a 90° angle.
Answer B: The myosin head releases a Pi, and myosin pulls itself along the actin, decreasing the angle, causing the muscle to shorten, releasing the remaining ADP molecule.
Answer D: As the ATP is partially hydrolyzed on the detached myosin head, the myosin head returns to the cocked 90° angle state. During the muscle contraction cycle, when adenine diphosphate is released from the myosin head, the adenine triphosphate (ATP) binding site is available to bind another molecule of ATP. When ATP binds the myosin head, it detaches from the actin filament. Mutations in the gene for the ryanodine receptor can result in the opening of the receptor after exposure to trigger agents such as volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. This life-threatening condition is called malignant hyperthermia. This activation by triggering agents results in an uncontrolled release of Ca2+ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, leading to continued contraction of the muscles, causing increased oxygen consumption, carbon dioxide generation, and lactic acid production. The management of negative pressure pulmonary edema (NPPE) involves starting supplemental oxygen and positive endexpiratory pressure (PEEP), which can be via non-invasive methods or endotracheal intubation. Pulmonary edema following an airway obstruction can occur due to different mechanisms, but the predominant one involves creating a negative pressure in the presence of a closed glottis. This is an uncommon complication that occurs in about 0.1% of patients. When negative pressure is initiated while the glottis is closed or obstructed, a large intrapleural pressure is generated. The negative transpulmonary gradient favors the shifting of fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the interstitium. The fluid accumulates so rapidly that the lymphatic system is unable to clear it. Situations that can create an occluded or obstructed glottis include laryngospasm, upper airway mass, or biting down on the endotracheal tube (simulates a closed glottis). These present with stridor, increased work of breathing (use of accessory muscles), paradoxical breathing (chest wall moves in with inspiration), and difficulty/inability to mask ventilate. The effects of negative pressure pulmonary edema are seen within 1-90 minutes. Hypoxia and diffuse interstitial/alveolar infiltrates on chest radiograph are noted, though radiographic findings may take time. Negative pressure pulmonary edema is self-limited, but it does prolong hospital stay. Management of negative pressure pulmonary edema involves improving respiratory function and avoiding further damage to the lungs. This includes supplemental oxygen and positive-pressure ventilation (non-invasive or endotracheal). Administering albuterol may help with bronchospasm or wheezing, however, in patients with negative pressure pulmonary edema the mainstay treatment involves supplemental oxygen and PEEP.
Answer B: Corticosteroids do not have a role in negative pressure pulmonary edema (also known as post-obstructive pulmonary edema).
Answer C: Diuretics are a possible option for NPPE, however, only after upper airway obstruction and hypoxemia are addressed. A bolus of furosemide is not likely to rapidly relieve hypoxemia, in comparison to PEEP. Negative pressure pulmonary edema occurs in any setting where the patient has an occluded or obstructed airway and they then try to take a deep breath. The effects of the pulmonary edema (hypoxia, crackles on auscultation) can be noticed immediately or shortly after. Management involves supportive care with supplemental oxygen. Positive end-expiratory pressure can be useful and diuretics may be considered.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Pulmonary Edema Due To Laryngospasm (B)" Ghofaily L, et.al. Surgical stress, trauma, extensive burn injuries, and sepsis can lead to alterations in hormones, including an increase in adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) release. The nervous system activates the stress response after surgical stimuli through impulses sent from the operative site to the hypothalamus. Hypothalamic activation increases the activity of the sympathetic nervous system, which stimulates the adrenal medulla to secrete epinephrine and the pancreas to secrete glucagon. Hypothalamic activation also increases the output of the cardiovascular system and stimulates the release of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). The posterior pituitary gland is also stimulated during surgical stress, resulting in the release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). Plasma ADH concentrations are elevated after stresses, such as surgery, pneumonia, and myocardial infarction. The magnitude and duration of elevated ADH levels are proportional to the degree of stress. In septic shock, there is an initial increase in ADH concentrations, followed by a decrease to critically low concentrations. These extremely low concentrations are partially responsible for the persistent vasodilation in septic shock and hemodynamic instability after cardiac surgery. The release of CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to release corticotropin (ACTH), which stimulates the adrenal glands to release cortisol. Cortisol mobilizes energy stores and promotes gluconeogenesis in the liver, leading to hyperglycemia. The serum concentration of catecholamines, norepinephrine, epinephrine, and dopamine increase after surgical stress. Additional stressors include anxiety, hypotension, hypothermia, burn injuries, and hypercarbia. In addition to their cardiovascular effects, catecholamines induce significant metabolic effects. Beta-2 adrenergic stimulation increases glycogenolysis, hepatic gluconeogenesis, and glucagon release while decreasing glycogen synthesis. Lipolysis is further increased by beta-2 adrenergic stimulation. The surgical stress response can also result in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. The pituitary gland is less responsive to gonadotropin-releasing hormone (Gn-RH), decreasing the release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Follicle-stimulating hormone and LH concentrations are minimally changed during surgery but decrease on the first postoperative day. The subsequent increase in CRH and cortisol levels contributes to the suppression of reproductive function. Testosterone concentrations significantly decrease in men after stress due to decreased production and increased clearance. Estrogen concentrations were shown to be decreased in premenopausal women during surgical stress, at times resulting in amenorrhea. Antidiuretic hormone is increased in response to surgical stress because it acts on V2 receptors in the kidney, leading to the insertion of aquaporin channels in the renal wall.
Answer B: Similarly to LH, FSH is decreased during the stress response.
Answer D: After surgical stimuli, the pituitary is less responsive to Gn-RH, resulting in the decreased release of LH and folliclestimulating hormone. This produces hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. The stress response to surgical stimuli can lead to various metabolic and physiologic alterations through impulses sent from the operative site to the hypothalamus. This response subsequently increases the activity of the sympathetic nervous system and the secretion of hormones from the anterior and posterior pituitary, most notably antidiuretic hormone, cortisol, and catecholamines. Reproductive hormones such as luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone decrease, resulting in hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. The induction of hypothermia reduces the actual arterial partial pressures of dissolved gases such as carbon dioxide and oxygen. This occurs chiefly because the blood solubility of a gas increases with decreasing temperature. Arterial blood gas analysis has become a fundamental practice in perioperative and critical care settings because it facilitates the rapid assessment of several key metabolic parameters. Values obtained through direct gas analysis include the arterial pH, partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2), and PaO2. The arterial bicarbonate concentration can also be derived indirectly from these parameters. When they are considered together, these values provide a snapshot of the patient’s oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base balance that may guide active clinical management. The PaCO2 is primarily a function of effective alveolar ventilation, the proportion of minute ventilation that participates in gas exchange. As alveolar ventilation increases, more carbon dioxide is released into the environment, and PaCO2 falls proportionally. By contrast, decreased alveolar ventilation, whether due to reduced total minute ventilation or increased dead space fraction, results in an increased PaCO2. However, several other factors also directly influence the PaCO2, including tissue-level metabolic rate as well as body temperature. Hypothermia is associated with a reduced PaCO2. This is because of the well-recognized connection between temperature and the solubility of gases in the blood. Gas solubility increases with decreasing temperature because a greater number of gas molecules shift into a dissolved (aqueous) phase and thus reduce the partial pressure of the gas “remaining” above the liquid solvent. When hypothermia is induced for therapeutic purposes—as is often performed during procedures requiring cardiopulmonary bypass or circulatory arrest—a patient will develop a relative respiratory alkalosis with reduced PaCO2 and increased arterial pH. For every 1°C reduction in core temperature, the patient’s PaCO2 can be expected to fall by ~2 mm Hg. During cardiopulmonary bypass, gas exchange is controlled by the bypass machine and can be manipulated by the perfusionist. Hypothermia is associated with a state of relative insulin resistance and reduced insulin release. This may produce significant hyperglycemia, requiring close glycemic monitoring and correction of elevated serum glucose concentrations with exogenous insulin administration.
Answer C: The effects of temperature on dissolved gases were described for CO2 in the question explanation, but these effects also apply to all dissolved gases, including oxygen. As the temperature falls, the blood solubility of oxygen also increases significantly, and PaO2 is reduced. With every 1°C decrease in core temperature, the patient’s PaO2 will fall by ~5 mm Hg.
Answer D: Because of slowed central nervous system activity and altered pharmacokinetics during hypothermia, lower doses of most anesthetics are required to maintain a state of general anesthesia. Using volatile anesthetics, such as isoflurane, notably results in substantially lower minimum alveolar concentrations for surgical anesthesia with significant temperature reductions. This trend correlates with the electroencephalographic changes produced by hypothermia itself. For instance, burst suppression without additional sedation may begin in patients cooled to 25°C, and electrical silence may be observed between 15°C and 20°C. Hypothermia reduces both the arterial partial pressure of carbon dioxide and the arterial partial pressure of oxygen because a decreased temperature causes an increase in gas solubility in the blood. Because arterial blood gas (ABG) is almost always interpreted at or near a physiologic body temperature (37°C), controversy persists regarding the question of whether ABG values should be corrected to the patient's actual body temperature during periods of hypothermia. In addition, a patient’s acid-base status during hypothermic cardiopulmonary bypass may be targeted toward a pH-stat or alpha-stat strategy, with pH-stat management involving the addition of carbon dioxide to a patient's blood to maintain a corrected partial pressure of carbon dioxide (PaCO2) near 40 mm Hg and a pH near 7.40 during the hypothermic phase. Because a reduced PaCO2 predictably causes cerebral vasoconstriction, pH-stat management may better preserve cerebral blood flow and homogenous brain cooling, although this advantage comes at the expense of increased embolic risk. One of the important pathways in the development of reactive oxygen species (ROS) involves pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. interferon-gamma, inflammatory protein 2). These cytokines lead to activation of NADPH oxidase (NOX) reactions in the electron transport chain of cellular mitochondria and lead to oxygen free radicals. Oxygen free radicals cause a variety of damage both at the microscopic and macroscopic level. Hyperoxia is defined as a state of excess supply of oxygen in tissues and organs that leads to ROS formation. After ROS form, tissue damage begins, most notably in the lung and the central nervous system. Exposure to 100% fractional inspired oxygen (FIO2) for as little as 4-6 hours has been shown to cause tracheobronchitis and decreased vital capacity. Critically ill patients and neonates have been shown to be deficient of anti-oxidant mechanisms and thus are more susceptible to oxygen toxicity. A devastating complication seen specifically to premature infants from high inspired oxygen concentrations is retinopathy, more specifically known as retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). Hyperoxia produces free radical oxygen species that cause vasoconstriction of the retinal vessels, which leads to scarring and possible retinal detachment. ROP may be mild and resolve spontaneously; however, more serious cases can lead to blindness. A systematic approach should be used when administering oxygen to every neonate: • Only use O2 when clinically indicated. Always start with a low amount of O2 (usually FiO2 of 0.3 or 0.4), and titrate to maintain oxygen saturation (SpO2) > 94% or to an arterial PaO2 > 100 mm Hg • Use protective lung volume ventilation strategies (i.e. tidal volumes 4-6 mL/kg) when able to, and consider using positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to minimize further increases in FIO2 • Consider lower flows on the anesthesia circuit as high O2 flows can lead to desiccation of the airway (especially in neonates and young children) and increases the risk for lung barotrauma Two large randomized controlled trials studied FIO2 values and their effects on long-term chronic lung disease, duration of hospitalization, and neurodevelopmental measures in neonates. The Supplemental Therapeutic Oxygen for Pretheshold Retinopathy of Prematurity (STOP-ROP) trial concluded that there was no significant difference in the rate of progression to the threshold of ROP in the group of newborns cared for with lower O2 saturation range (89-94%) versus the higher group (96-99%). As a secondary outcome, the authors noticed an increased incidence of chronic lung disease and longer durations of hospitalizations, both which occurred at higher rates in the higher FIO2 group. In the Benefits of Oxygen Saturation Targeting (BOOST) trial, no differences were found in their primary outcomes, which were defined as growth and neurodevelopmental measures by 12 months corrected age. In the group who received higher O2 saturations (95-98%), these babies required oxygen for a longer period of time, had a higher dependence on oxygen at 36 weeks post-conceptual age, and needed home O2 therapy with higher frequencies compared to the infants in the lower O2 saturation group (91-94%). The goal when providing oxygen to a neonate is to start low and titrate FIO2 levels in order to maintain SpO2 levels > 94% or a PaO2 > 100 mm Hg. Hyperoxia can lead to unwanted complications including retinopathy.
Answer C: Hyperoxia and reactive oxygen species have been implicated in the pathophysiology of a variety of diseases, particularly chronic lung disease, central nervous system damage (i.e. retinopathy), and red blood cell damage.
Answer D: Metabolic conditions such as diabetes mellitus and increased FiO2 levels have been shown to increase the rate of reactive oxygen species formation, resulting in an imbalance between antioxidants and oxidants and damage to macromolecules such as nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids. Thus, the rate of reactive oxygen species formation is related to metabolic conditions and oxygenation, not cardiac output (if anything it would be indirectly linked to cardiac output). Hyperoxia is defined as a state of excess supply of oxygen in tissues and organs. High fractional inspired concentrations of oxygen (FIO2) lead to formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS). An important pathway involved in ROS formation is activation of NADPH oxidase (NOX) reactions in cellular mitochondria which cause cellular damage. Oxygen toxicity of the neonate usually manifests as chronic lung disease and central nervous system diseases (i.e. retinopathy of prematurity). When administering oxygen to a neonate, always start with the lowest possible amount of oxygen and titrate FIO2 levels to maintain SpO2 > 94% or PaO2 > 100 mg Hg. In newborn resuscitation, the algorithm always starts by providing positive pressure ventilation with room air. If the neonate’s oxygen level does not stay above 90%, FIO2 is gradually titrated up until the desirable saturation level (usually at least 90-92%) is achieved. Increased cardiac output during pregnancy increases maternal oxygen consumption. Overall, pregnancy increases oxygen consumption by 40-75% as a result of increased metabolic demand. In fact, two-thirds of this increase is attributed to fetal, placental, and uterine metabolism increase. Both at rest and during exercise, maternal oxygen uptake and consumption are increased in pregnant patients. The fetus, uterus, and placental tissues increase oxygen consumption at a higher rate than the mother per unit of weight. Each kilogram of maternal tissue consumes oxygen at a rate of approximately 4 mL/minute, while the fetoplacental unit consumes oxygen at a rate of approximately 12 mL/minute. During labor, oxygen consumption increases by up to 40% during the first stage and up to 75% during the second stage. The cause of maternal respiratory alkalosis is likely multifactorial, but mainly due to progesterone-induced central respiratory stimulation. Alkalosis leads to a left-shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, which would result in oxygen retention in the blood rather than release and consumption.
Answer C: Two-thirds of the increase in maternal oxygen consumption is accounted for by the combined metabolism of the fetus, placenta, and uterus.
Answer D: Functional residual capacity (FRC) increases after delivery, however, it remains below pre-pregnancy values for up to 1 to 2 weeks postpartum. Meanwhile, oxygen consumption, tidal volume, and minute ventilation remain elevated for up to 6 to 8 weeks postpartum. Pregnancy increases oxygen consumption by 40-75% as a result of progressively increased tissue metabolism, especially that of the fetus, placenta, and uterus. ACE inhibitors are known to inhibit the process of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. During one-lung ventilation, this could potentially result in an increase in shunt flow through the non-ventilated lung and eventually cause systemic hypoxia. During one-lung ventilation, the physiologic process of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) is able to decrease blood flow to the non-ventilated lung by around half, resulting in a decrease in shunt fraction through that lung and prevention of systemic hypoxemia. Decreases in alveolar oxygen concentration stimulate this response, which is primarily mediated by precapillary vasoconstriction. This local increase in pulmonary vascular resistance results in a preferential diversion of blood to areas of the lung that are adequately ventilated. This response will take around 2 hours to fully exert itself, however, the majority of the vasoconstriction will tend to occur in the first 20-30 minutes of local alveolar hypoxia. This is clinically relevant because acute hypoxia at the initiation of OLV could potentially take up to 20-30 minutes to reach the optimum effect of HPV. Thus, waiting and supporting the patient through a transient period of hypoxia may be necessary in order to allow surgery to proceed. There are many medications that have the effect of inhibiting HPV include vasodilators such as nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers. Even in patients who are not undergoing one-lung ventilation, these medications can induce clinically significant shunting that results in systemic hypoxia and could prompt their discontinuation. Physiologic states such as acidosis and hypercarbia will tend to induce pulmonary vasoconstriction, so it follows that alkalemia and hypocarbia act to inhibit hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, though the clinical effect of these states on HPV is of questionable significance. In addition to these physiologic states, any increase in pulmonary artery pressure will tend to increase the arteriovenous shunt fraction as the increased pulmonary pressures force blood through areas of the lung that would otherwise not receive perfusion. These states include pulmonary embolism, mitral stenosis, and potentially the use of certain vasopressors. It is important to note that pulmonary embolism primarily causes dead space ventilation through V/Q mismatching, but it also induces some degree of A/V shunting due to the increases in pulmonary artery pressures. It is traditionally taught that inhaled anesthetics are inhibitors of HPV. This teaching is however based on older studies utilizing enflurane and halothane, neither of which are in common use today. While the modern volatile anesthetics (isoflurane, sevoflurane, desflurane) are all indeed inhibitors of HPV, their actual effect is minimal and most anesthetics that involve the use of one-lung ventilation still utilize one of these agents for anesthetic maintenance. At 1 MAC, these agents will tend to inhibit HPV by about 20%. While this may seem like a large amount, this equates to only a 4% increase in the net shunt fraction during one-lung ventilation, a difference that is of questionable clinical significance. On another note, the HPV inhibitory effect of volatile anesthetics seems to be greater when the anesthetic is delivered to the alveolar capillaries via the alveolus itself and not the pulmonary circulation. Because the volatile anesthetic is not being delivered to the alveolus in the non-ventilated lung, the effect of volatile anesthetics on inhibiting HPV is mitigated. Because of these facts, there has been no evidence that the use of a totally intravenous anesthetic technique is beneficial for the sake of oxygenation than the use of a volatile anesthetic technique when performing surgery with one-lung ventilation. Answers A & C: Beta-blockers have not been shown to have a significant impact on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Thiazide diuretics have not been shown to have a significant impact on hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction. Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is an autoregulatory pulmonary reflex that causes precapillary vasoconstriction to preferentially divert the pulmonary circulation away from areas of alveolar hypoxia. All of the volatile anesthetics attenuate this reflex but to a mild and likely clinically insignificant degree. Propofol does not appear to have a significant effect on this reflex. Other vasodilating drugs such as nitroglycerin, nitroprusside, ACE-inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, and calcium channel blockers all attenuate this reflex to varying degrees. Hepatic encephalopathy is theorized to be due to hyperammonemia, which results from the accumulation of protein metabolism waste products. Therefore, procedures, such as a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS), that shunt blood away from the liver are likely to worsen hyperammonemia by reducing the hepatic conversion of ammonia to urea. Ammonia is the primary byproduct of protein metabolism. Protein metabolism occurs largely in the liver via deamination and transamination of amino acids. The liver is also responsible for a critical, final step in protein catabolism, the conversion of the relatively insoluble ammonia into the more water-soluble compound urea via the urea cycle which allows for renal excretion. Without sufficient conversion of ammonia to urea, hyperammonemia ensues, which is suspected to be a large contributor to the altered mental status associated with hepatic encephalopathy. For patients with liver disease, significant portal hypertension leads to a substantially increased risk of developing portosystemic collateral vessels and reversal of portal venous flow. This ultimately increases the risk of varices, ascites, and overt hepatic decompensation. Placing a low-resistance channel between the hepatic vein and the portal vein via the TIPS procedure can effectively offload the portal vein, reduce portal hypertension, and reduce the risk of developing these complications of portal hypertension. However, by diverting blood flow away from the portal vein, substances that require liver metabolism are also diverted away, including protein breakdown products such as ammonia. If ammonia is not delivered to the liver for conversion to urea, ammonia will accumulate, and hepatic encephalopathy may develop or worsen. Therefore, in a patient with signs of hyperammonemia such as hepatic encephalopathy, alternative treatments to first manage the hyperammonemia (ie, lactulose and rifaximin) may be more appropriate initially before the procedure. Recurrent esophageal varices are one of the indications for TIPS.
Answer B: Refractory ascites are an indication to perform TIPS. Reduction of portal hypertension and ascites after a TIPS procedure may improve hepatic function and reduce the risk of acute decompensation
Answer C: Patients with ascites related to end-stage liver disease are at an increased risk of aspiration; however, this is not a contraindication to the TIPS procedure or general anesthesia. Ammonia is the primary byproduct of protein metabolism and must be converted to urea to be excreted. This occurs primarily in the liver, and therefore, shunting blood away from the liver is likely to worsen hyperammonemia by reducing the hepatic conversion of ammonia to urea. Therefore, hepatic encephalopathy is a relative contraindication to a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt procedure.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. During focal ischemia, residual blood flow through collateral circulation results in a small but significant delivery of oxygen to the area of decreased flow downstream from the blood flow obstruction and allows for the generation of some adenosine triphosphate (ATP). The generation of a small amount of ATP helps to prevent catastrophic and irreversible membrane failure that would otherwise occur within minutes of the onset of ischemia. Clinically, therefore, focal ischemia appears to be more welltolerated compared with global ischemia. Cerebral ischemia results from impaired blood flow to the brain and is a common mechanism of acute brain injury. There are two types. Focal ischemia occurs when blood flow to restricted parts of the brain is insufficient, usually from thrombosis or embolism, and is confined to a specific region of the brain. Global ischemia typically results from systemic hypotension and encompasses wide areas of brain tissue. Compared to other organs, the brain has a very high rate of energy utilization. However, it has minimal energy storage capacity and is thus extremely vulnerable to a decrease in the blood flow that otherwise delivers a continuous supply of the oxygen and glucose required to create ATP. In a review of cerebral ischemia, the first focus must be on the critical cerebral blood flow thresholds that correspond to various levels of cerebral injury that occur if this blood flow is disrupted. Normal cerebral blood flow is approximately 50 mL/100 g/min, and a decrease in that flow will result in a gradual decline of cerebral function, eventually leading to catastrophic and irreversible membrane failure. When normal cerebral blood flow is 20 mL/100 g/min, the brain will begin to demonstrate electroencephalography (EEG) slowing, which corresponds to the dysfunction of the cortical neurons. When normal cerebral blood flow is 15 mL/100 g/min, the cortical EEG will be isoelectric. When normal cerebral blood flow is between 10 and 15 mL/ 100 g/min, there will be a gradual decrease in the energy supply that will eventually lead to neuronal death over the course of hours. When normal cerebral blood flow is between 6 and 10 mL/100 g/min, the neuronal injury will be temporarily reversible, but neuronal death will result if the flow is not rapidly restored. Neuronal injury and death can be attenuated through the slowing of the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen through the use of hypothermia and is how cases that use deep hypothermic circulatory arrest are possible without lasting cerebral injury. In focal ischemia, some residual collateral circulation to the area downstream of the blood flow obstruction will typically keep the neurons supplied with at least a small amount of oxygen and glucose. This allows focal ischemia to be much better tolerated compared to the global ischemia that occurs during circulatory arrest. The primary event that occurs during cerebral ischemia is the failure of ATP production due to decreased oxygen and glucose delivery to the neuron. This energy failure will result in rapid depolarization, the release of intracellular potassium into the extracellular space, an influx of both sodium and potassium, and the release of a very large amount of excitatory neurotransmitters, including glutamate. In both focal and global ischemia, activation of glutamate reactors will result in an increased influx of sodium and calcium that will eventually result in marked neuronal edema that occurs rapidly after neuronal depolarization. Neuronal ischemia, in general, will lead to depolarization and the influx of a large amount of extracellular sodium resulting in neuronal edema. This occurs in both focal and global ischemia.
Answer C: Both global and focal ischemia can induce changes in EEG, although focal ischemia will induce EEG changes only over the cortical area that is downstream to the area of blood flow obstruction. Focal slow-wave activity on EEG may be intermittent or persistent and is indicative of focal cerebral pathology of the underlying brain region; more persistent or consistently slower activity generally is indicative of more severe cerebral dysfunction. This intermittent or persistent focal slowing seen consistently over one head region or persistent, unvarying, and unreactive focal or generalized slow-wave activity is distinct from the generalized background slowing in the theta and delta frequencies, which is a normal finding on EEG during developmental slowing in children, adolescents, and some young adults or in the onset of drowsiness and sleep activity. Generalized background slowing indicates diffuse cerebral dysfunction, which, similarly to focal slowing, does not specify a cause.
Answer D: The neuronal injury in both global and focal ischemia is attenuated by decreasing the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen in the ischemic area through the use of therapeutic hypothermia. Cerebral ischemia results from impaired blood flow to the brain and is a common mechanism of acute brain injury. There are two types. Focal ischemia occurs when blood flow to restricted parts of the brain is insufficient, usually from thrombosis or embolism, and is confined to a specific region of the brain. Global ischemia typically results from systemic hypotension and encompasses wide areas of brain tissue. Focal cerebral ischemia is more well-tolerated compared with global cerebral ischemia because of the preservation of some residual collateral flow to the ischemic region of the brain. Neonatal interstitial fluid is proportionally three times larger than in adults contributing to a proportionally larger extracellular fluid volume. In a healthy human adult, total body water (TBW) comprises approximately 55-60% of lean body mass in men and 45-50% in women. Although most body tissue is 70-80% water, this is offset by bone (20% water) and fat (10-15% water). TBW is made up of 1/3 extracellular fluid and 2/3 intracellular fluid. Extracellular fluid volume is further subdivided into 3/4 interstitial fluid and 1/4 plasma fluid. Meanwhile, in neonates, TBW is 70-80% with a greater proportion of extracellular fluid compared to adults. In fact, premature babies have an extracellular fluid compartment that exceeds intracellular fluid volume. The proportionally greater volume of distribution warrants higher doses per kilogram compared to older children and adults. TBW percentage decreases up until around age 12 where it normalizes at adult values. This percentage then begins to decrease again with aging due to an increase in fat content although TBW volume remains the same. The proportionally reduced distribution for hydrophilic drugs leads to greater plasma concentrations. Conversely, these physiologic changes lead to a decrease in the plasma concentration of lipophilic drugs. % TBW by age Age TBW (%) Table adapted from Miller's Anesthesia, 9th Edition Total body water comprises 70-80% of lean body mass in neonates as opposed to ~60% in adults.
Answer C: Total body water is the sum of extracellular volume and intracellular volume. The extracellular volume consists of interstitial fluid and plasma fluid volumes.
Answer D: The proportion of total body water (% water per kg body mass) is significantly lower than lean individuals because adipose tissue contains much less water compared to other tissues. Total body water (TBW) is an important factor in assessing a patient's fluid status, assessing fluid requirements, and in the context of administering anesthetic drugs. The % TBW is highest as a neonate, normalizes by teenage years, and decreases again in old age. Men have a higher % TBW (~60%) compared to women (~50%) and obese individuals have lower % TBW than lean individuals due to the low amount of water in adipose tissue. The kidney is able to reabsorb and excrete numerous compounds. The chemical structure, delivery of metabolites, and available transport proteins contribute to the overall function of the renal system. The kidney is able to excrete unchanged hydrophilic molecules as well as metabolites from hepatic breakdown via Phase I and Phase II reactions (recall Phase I is reductionoxidation reactions and Phase II is conjugation). Should the kidney have been designed to excrete in a passive manner, simply dependent on drug delivery via blood flow, there would be complete inefficiency in drug excretion. Located in the proximal renal tubules are active protein transporters or organic acids and bases that allow for the elimination of the metabolites. This allows for the kidneys to filter and excrete metabolites more efficiently despite receiving a large cardiac output. Nevertheless, this system is still subject to dysfunction due to factors such as decreased cardiac output and intrinsic renal disease that allow for metabolites to increase in concentration. This form of reaction is done in the liver. Recall Phase I is reduction-oxidation reactions and Phase II is conjugation.
Answer C: Drug ionization does lead to decreased elimination and its mechanism is unrelated to increasing efficiency.
Answer D: This is the mechanism by which some drugs cross the blood-brain barrier. Renal disease can lead to an increase in drug metabolites. It is the kidney’s active protein transporters in the proximal renal tubules that increase the efficiency with which these drugs are eliminated. Common anesthetic drugs that are associated with significant renal excretion include aminoglycosides, cephalosporins, digoxin, neostigmine, rocuronium, and sugammadex. Tidal volumes in the neonate are similar to the adult on a volume per kg basis. They have increased respiratory rates which thereby increases the neonate's minute ventilation as compared to the adult. The neonate's closing volume is higher and can approach their normal tidal volume which can result in premature closure of small airways. The neonate has a higher minute ventilation due to their higher oxygen consumption. With a similar functional residual capacity compared to the adult but a higher minute ventilation, the neonate's ratio of minute ventilation to FRC is two to three times higher. This leads to a decreased oxygen reserve but a faster inhalation induction in the neonate. Closing volumes are high in the neonate and may be near the normal tidal volume.
Answer B: While the tidal volume is comparable to the adult on an mL/kg basis, the neonate's respiratory rate is increased, therefore increasing their minute ventilation as well.
Answer C: The neonate's respiratory rate is increased as compared to the adult. Tidal volume in the neonate is comparable to an adult on a volume/kg basis while their closing volume, respiratory rate, and minute ventilation are increased.  Barash Anesthesia. Neonatal Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Page 1181. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neonatal Physiology: Lung Volumes Vs Adult"

The extracellular fluid compartment (ECF) is one-third of the total body water. The intravascular compartment is one-fourth of the ECF. Thus, the intravascular fluid compartment is 1/4 × 1/3 = 1/12 ≈ 8% of total body water. If total body water is 50 L, then the amount contained intravascularly is 4 L (50 L × 8%). Total body water (percentage of total body water) is divided into extracellular (33%) and intracellular (ICF; 67%) fluid compartments, and each is further subdivided into smaller compartments. The ECF comprises interstitial (25%) and intravascular (5%) compartments. The interstitial fluid compartment is the fluid around cells and outside the vasculature. The intravascular fluid compartment is bound by the vascular endothelium, which allows for the free passage of small ions into the interstitium. Although small ions may pass into the interstitium freely, the tight junctions between the endothelial cells prevent the movement of larger molecules such as albumin. As a result, these proteins are osmotically active and capable of drawing in water intravascularly. The composition of total body water The interstitial fluid compartment is 25% of the total body water, 12.5 L for the patient described in this question.
Answer C: The ECF is 33% of the total body water, 16.6 L for the patient described in this question.
Answer D: The ICF is 67% of the total body water, 33.3 L for the patient described in this question. The intravascular fluid compartment is 8% of total body water. Colloid solutions tend to remain intravascularly for a longer duration than crystalloids and have equal efficacy in fluid resuscitation when given in proper amounts. Colloids are typically indicated in fluid resuscitation in severely intravascularly depleted patients such as those with hemorrhagic shock (while awaiting the transfer of blood) or severe hypoalbuminemia or burn patients. Notably, colloid solutions such as albumin are prepared in normal saline; thus, they have a chloride concentration between 145 and 154 mEq/L. Colloids such as dextrans are limited by side effects, such as a reduction in blood viscosity, platelet adhesion, red blood cell aggregation, and von Willebrand factor levels. Due to their side effects, dextrans can improve blood flow and reduce thrombus formation. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Intravascular fluids: Distribution (B)" Barash PG, et al. The induction of a pharmacologic burst suppression utilizing anesthetic agents has been shown to improve mortality in patients with status epilepticus that is refractory to all other abortive therapies. Pharmacologic burst suppression is an electroencephalographic (EEG) finding where the EEG will display a rhythmic alternation between prolonged periods of flat-line EEG alternating with a short period of with bursts of electrical activity. The practice of inducing this electroencephalographic state is controversial due to limited evidence that demonstrates benefit in only a select few clinical scenarios. The theory behind burst suppression is that by inducing a largely electrically quiet brain state, the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen (CMRO2) can be decreased by up to 50%. This is preferable to an entirely silent EEG as the presence of brief periods of activity allow for monitoring of the depth of anesthesia. By allowing for brief bursts of electrical activity, the provider is able to ensure that they are not providing an excessive amount of anesthetic agent to achieve a largely flat EEG. If it were entirely quiet, there would be no way to know just how much extra agent was being administered to ensure this EEG state, and emergence from the pharmacologic coma would be difficult to accurately predict. No specific guidelines exist as to the optimal ratio of burst to suppression on an EEG in this state, and many providers utilize a goal of 1:10 burst to suppression when targeting this EEG state though this is a largely arbitrary value. In theory, periods of decreased cerebral perfusion might benefit from a pharmacologically decreased CMRO2, however, this has not been largely borne out in practice. For instance, no benefit has been shown in surgeries for cerebral aneurysms nor in patients recovering following a cardiac arrest. In cases where the electrical activity of the brain is unable to be controlled, such as in refractory status epilepticus, there does exist some benefit for the pharmacologic induction of a burst suppression EEG, and there may also be some benefit both in traumatic brain injury and in carotid endarterectomies when shunting is not performed. Agents that are typically used to induce burst suppression include propofol, halogenated anesthetics (typically isoflurane), or barbiturates. Clinically, the amount of barbiturate that is needed to induce burst suppression will result is an extremely protracted emergence from the anesthetic over the course of days. Propofol and the halogenated anesthetics allow for a much more titratable EEG and more rapid emergence. Severe hypothermia will eventually induce burst suppression and eventual EEG silence, though the temperature at which this occurs is variable in patients and insufficient evidence exists as to whether targeting this EEG finding should be the goal of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest in patients undergoing surgeries requiring this level of cerebral blood flow disruption. Insufficient evidence exists to determine if there is a benefit to targeting an EEG with burst suppression during surgeries that involve cerebral flow disruption (e.g. deep hypothermic circulatory arrest). Answers B & C: Pharmacologic burst suppression has been shown to not improve outcomes in patients undergoing cerebral aneurysm surgeries or following a cardiac arrest. Pharmacologic burst suppression is an EEG finding induced by anesthetic agents which displays long periods of electrical silence punctuated by brief bursts of electrical activity. In this state, the cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen decreases by up to 50%, and it may be protective in pathologic states of poor cerebral perfusion though this is controversial. Anesthetic agents that are utilized to induce burst suppression include propofol, halogenated anesthetic gasses, and barbiturates. Burst suppression is typically avoided in most anesthetic settings but has been shown to improve mortality in status epilepticus. Surfactant plays an indispensable role in the pulmonary development of the neonate. It acts to expand alveoli and maintain the functional residual capacity at exhalation. Preterm neonates who are deficient in surfactant are at risk of respiratory distress syndrome which can result in atelectasis, hypoxia, decreased lung compliance, and an increase in the work of breathing. Exogenous surfactant should be utilized as both prophylaxis and treatment for respiratory distress syndrome. It can be administered through an endotracheal tube and can be used to improve gas exchange in neonates with heart failure, sepsis, or other systemic illness. Decreased surfactant has been associated with respiratory distress syndrome in the neonate.
Answer B: A decrease in surfactant causes atelectasis with subsequently decreased lung compliance and an increased work of breathing.
Answer C: Exogenous surfactant can be given through an endotracheal tube for both prophylaxis and treatment of respiratory distress syndrome. Surfactant plays an important role in preventing atelectasis and increasing lung compliance while decreasing the work of breathing. It acts to maintain the functional residual capacity at exhalation and can be given through the endotracheal tube to prevent or treat respiratory distress syndrome in the neonate.  Barash Anesthesia. Growth hormone-secreting tumors result in acromegaly and are most likely to be associated with difficult airway management. Acromegaly occurs as a result of excess growth hormone. This leads to a number of anatomic and physiologic effects, many of which are relevant to the practice of anesthesia. The excess growth hormone causes enlarged connective tissue, bones, and visceral organs. This includes macrognathia (enlarged jaw), macroglossia (enlarged tongue), as well as enlargement of the nose, epiglottis, pharyngeal tissue, and laryngeal tissue. Due to the soft tissue enlargement, many patients with acromegaly have obstructive sleep apnea and it is also common to have a component of central sleep apnea. Patients may also experience subglottic stenosis. All of these factors can impact the ability of a provider to adequately mask ventilate and intubate. The literature supports a rate of difficult intubation ranging from 2-5% in large population studies of patients without acromegaly. While the literature on patients with acromegaly is limited, there is at least one prospective trial and several retrospective publications describing difficulties with intubation of acromegalic patients, with an incidence of difficult intubation in 10-30% of patients. Successful intubation of acromegalic patients in these studies was aided by the use of external laryngeal pressure and gum elastic bougies (tracheal tube introducers). As with any patient, a thorough airway exam should be performed including assessment of Mallampati score, neck mobility, and jaw mobility. Alternatives to direct laryngoscopy such as awake fiberoptic intubation should be considered for these patients, especially if providers have had prior difficulty with intubation. Acute pituitary deficiency in the perioperative setting is associated with hypotension. This is not known to be associated with difficult airway management.
Answer B: Adrenocorticotropic hormone-secreting tumors in the anterior pituitary cause the condition of glucocorticoid excess known as Cushing’s disease. While these patients often have obesity and obstructive sleep apnea, their anatomy does not pose the same difficulties in airway management as the patient with acromegaly.
Answer D: Syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone (SIADH) is a condition in which the body produces too much antidiuretic hormone. This results in hyponatremia and reduced serum osmolarity. SIADH is not known to be associated with difficult airway management. Patients with acromegaly are at increased risk of difficult airway management due to enlargement and distortion of tissues in the face, oropharynx, and larynx. Thorough airway assessment should be performed preoperatively and providers should have a low threshold for using techniques such as awake fiberoptic intubation to secure the airway. This patient likely has Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) with resultant hypoxemia from shunting. Increasing FiO2 is the least likely intervention to improve the patient's PaO2. ARDS is highly prevalent in the ICU population and accounts for 10-15% of all ICU admissions. ARDS can arise from direct lung injury (ie pneumonia) or in association with extrapulmonary infection (sepsis) and is characterized by inflammatory infiltration of the lung resulting in diffuse alveolar damage. This pulmonary edema and alveolar collapse can result in severe ventilationperfusion mismatch (low V/Q ratio aka shunt). The Berlin Definition of ARDS (see table below) characterizes the severity of disease based on the degree of hypoxemia. Treatment of ARDS is largely supportive and includes treatment of inciting events, avoidance of complications, and mechanical ventilation. Mechanical ventilation strategies are primarily directed towards optimizing gas exchange while minimizing additional lung injury (lung-protective ventilation with tidal volumes of 4-6 mL/kg and plateau pressure < 30 mm Hg). Lung recruitment strategies are often utilized and include increasing PEEP, recruitment maneuvers, and prone positioning. These methods help improve FRC and maintain the patency of available alveolar units for gas exchange. Because ARDS is characterized by significant intrapulmonary shunting, the hypoxemia is relatively unresponsive to oxygen therapy and therefore increasing the FiO2 is unlikely to improve gas exchange. Berlin Definition of ARDS Timing Within 1 week of known clinical insult OR new/worsening respiratory symptoms Imaging* Bilateral opacities - not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse, or nodules Origin of Edema Not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload** Oxygenation (with PEEP or CPAP ≥5 mmHg) Mild: PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 201-300 mm Hg Moderate:PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 101-200 mmHg Severe: PaO2/FiO2 ratio ≤100 mmHg *via chest radiography or CT scan **often requires objective assessment (eg echocardiography) Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) would bypass the diseased lungs and provide mechanical support of gas exchange thus improving PaO2. The use of ECMO to support patients with severe ARDS became prominent during the influenza pandemic of 2009. A multicenter randomized control trial demonstrated that patients randomized to ECMO consideration had increased likelihood of disability-free survival at 6 months. However, widespread use of this treatment option is limited by its invasive nature, cost, and the need for specialized treatment centers.
Answer C: PEEP helps to improve FRC and maintain the patency of available alveolar units for gas exchange. Improved gas exchange (ie less V/Q mismatch) would improve PaO2.
Answer D: Prone positioning for treatment of ARDS has been rigorously studied. Justification for this method centers around the idea that there is A) less alveolar collapse due to gravity and B) more even distribution of perfusion in the prone position as compared to the supine position. A 2010 meta-analysis of seven RCTs found a mortality benefit to prone positioning in patients with a severe ARDS (ie PaO2/FiO2 ratio of ≤100). However, because this treatment method is associated with additional complications (endotracheal tube dislodgement, pressure ulcers, etc.), it is often used as a rescue therapy when conventional ventilation strategies have failed. Oxygen therapy is of limited value with large intrapulmonary shunts due to limitation of gas exchange and requires alternative therapies to improve V/Q matching.  Clinical Anesthesia. Atelectasis (A) is associated with an increased alveolar arterial (Aa) gradient. The alveolar arterial oxygen gradient is a calculation used to help determine ventilation-perfusion abnormalities. The equation compares the relationship between alveolar oxygen tension and arterial blood oxygen level. When the gradient is increased, a V/Q mismatch or diffusion problem is occurring. A normal Aa gradient occurs in hypoventilation and when the FIO2 is decreased. A normal A-a gradient is 5 - 10 mm Hg for a young adult nonsmoker. The A-a gradient increases about 1 mm Hg per decade of life, so a 40-year-old would have a normal A-a gradient of < 14 mm Hg. A conservative estimate of A-a gradient can be calculated with the same equation as pediatric endotracheal tube size: (Age / 4) + 4. A-a gradient is then A-a = PA – PaO2 Atelectasis is the collapse of alveoli which results in shunting of blood. Atelectasis can be caused by compression due to increased abdominal pressure or increased closing capacity. Atelectasis can also occur from loss of surfactant, which increases alveolar collapse as a result of increased surface tension across the alveoli. Additionally, absorption atelectasis occurs from diffusion of all gas from out of the alveoli and into the blood. Critical illness myopathy (B) is a syndrome of global muscle weakness and destruction that develops in some critically ill patients. These patients have severe muscle weakness and hypoventilate as a result. Hypoventilation does not cause an increase in the Aa gradient. Myasthenia gravis (C) is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies to acetylcholine receptors are produced. Myasthenia gravis causes a progressive weakness which leads to hypoventilation. An opioid overdose (D) causes central hypoventilation because of a right shift and down slope of the CO2 response curve. Treatment for an opioid overdose primarily involves support of ventilation. Pickwickian syndrome (E) is also known as obesity hypoventilation syndrome. Patients with Pickwickian syndrome hypoventilate at night and become hypercarbic and hypoxic. Many patients with Pickwickian syndrome also have obstructive sleep apnea, but Pickwickian syndrome is a central form of hypoventilation. As stated earlier hypoventilation does not affect the Aa gradient because gas diffusion in the lungs is not significantly changed. Pickwickian syndrome is associated with right-sided congestive heart failure and pulmonary hypertension from hypoxia.  The A-a gradient is increased (> 15 mm Hg) with shunting, dead space ventilation, and diffusion defects. The A-a gradient is not increased (5 - 10 mm Hg) with hypoventilation or low FiO2 in isolation.  Miller, Ronald D. Miller’s Anesthesia. 7th edition. 2010. Marino, Paul L. Coagulation factors are the single best measure to provide an assessment of hepatic protein synthesis function. This is because clotting factors have a short half-life. For example, factor VII has a half-life of only four to six hours – this is compared to albumin which has a half-life of approximately 21 days. Because approximately 20 to 30 percent of normal coagulation activity is necessary for appropriate coagulation, coagulation dysfunction tests suggest severe liver dysfunction. An excellent indicator of such dysfunction is measurements of prothrombin time. Nevertheless, prothrombin times may be high because of vitamin K deficiency, disseminated intravascular coagulation, congenital clotting factor deficiencies, and certain drugs. Evaluation of protein synthesis by the liver can be determined by evaluating the serum levels of proteins synthesized by the liver. In this respect, serum albumin levels can make assessments of the liver protein synthetic capacity. Serum albumin is synthesized by hepatocytes, but because it has a half-life of 21 days in the serum, its correlation to the protein synthetic function of the liver should be assessed over several weeks. However, hypoalbuminemia is not a reliable indicator of hepatic synthetic function because it can occur with protein-losing enteropathies, increased vascular permeability, fluid retention, nephrotic syndrome, chronic infections, increased catabolism, and malnutrition. Thus, it has a long half-life. Additionally, acute hepatic dysfunction will only affect albumin levels mildly.
Answer C: Serum Gamma-Glutamyl transferase (GGT) is an enzyme that is found in hepatic as well as other tissues. GGT is the most sensitive indicator of biliary tract disease, but because it is found in other tissues as well it is not as useful as 5’NT measurements to determine if an elevated alkaline phosphatase is due to liver damage. Nevertheless, the evaluation of GGT is not better than the evaluation of coagulation factors in determining the function of hepatic protein synthesis. Hepatic protein synthesis is best assessed by measuring coagulation factors.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword: "Hepatic Protein Synthesis" Barash’s Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition.
