Acetylcholine is used by both the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous systems at the ganglia to transmit signals from the preganglionic to the postganglionic neurons. The parasympathetic nervous system uses acetylcholine at the postganglionic neurons and the target organ to produce an effect. The sympathetic system utilizes primarily norepinephrine. The autonomic nervous system is composed of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems. The sympathetic nervous system lies within the lateral gray column of the spinal cord where its cells bodies are located spanning from T1-L2. The nerves housed within the spinal cord that then synapse at the ganglia are the preganglionic neurons. They then activate postganglionic neurons by releasing acetylcholine. The postganglionic neurons then release norepinephrine at most target sites to activate the adrenergic receptors with the exception of epinephrine at the adrenal medulla and acetylcholine at sweat glands. The parasympathetic nervous system contains a cranial and pelvic portion. The cranial portion consists of cranial nerves III, VII, IX, and X, and the pelvic portion consists of the pelvic splanchnic nerves from S2-4. The parasympathetic neurons are similar to the sympathetic neurons as they both utilize acetylcholine at the ganglia to transmit the signal. Parasympathetic neurons release acetylcholine at their target organs to produce an effect. A difference between the two systems is that the parasympathetic preganglionic neurons synapse on the ganglia close to the organs they innervate resulting in short postganglionic neurons. Epinephrine is used by the postganglionic cells of the sympathetic nervous system at the adrenal medulla.
Answer C: Glycine is not used by either system but is an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain and spinal cord.
Answer D: Norepinephrine is used by the postganglionic cells of the sympathetic nervous system to produce an effect at the target sites. Acetylcholine is utilized by both the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system to transmit signals from preganglionic to postganglionic neurons.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Renin is released from the kidneys in response to a decrease in blood pressure. It cleaves the peptide angiotensinogen to create angiotensin I (C). Renin is created and stored by the cells in the afferent arterioles of the kidney. Renin secretion can be caused by 3 different mechanisms: a decrease in serum NaCl concentration sensed by the kidneys, a decrease in blood pressure sensed by kidney baroreceptors, or activation of renal B1 receptors by norepinephrine. Decreases in blood pressure, such as that displayed by the patient above, would cause a release of renin into the serum by at least one of these mechanisms. Renin then acts by cleaving the peptide angiotensinogen to create angiotensin I. Angiotensin I is then converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE). Angiotensin II (Ang II) has several effects, which combine to increase systemic perfusion in patients. The most immediate response to Ang II is an increase in blood pressure caused by an increase in systemic vascular resistance. Ang II activates the angiotensin1 (AT1) receptors on vascular smooth muscle cells, causing constriction of the arterioles. Ang II also augments the sympathetic nervous system by inhibiting norepinephrine reuptake into nerve terminals. It also stimulates the release of catecholamines from the adrenal medulla. In addition, Ang II causes a centrally mediated increased thirst and enhances the release of vasopressin. These effects are almost immediate, but are not long-lasting. Ang II also has longer lasting effects in the body. In addition to its effects on blood pressure, it stimulates remodeling of the cardiovascular system, causing hypertrophy of cardiac cells and increased collagen deposition. It also has profound effects on the kidney, causing a decrease in the urinary excretion of both sodium and water. Lastly, Ang II stimulates the adrenal cortex to synthesize and release aldosterone. Aldosterone also acts on the kidneys to decrease the urinary excretion of sodium and water. This ultimately leads to an increase in blood volume and therefore blood pressure. Angiotensin II leads to the increased release of aldosterone. Angiotensin II also increases blood pressure by direct vasoconstriction.
Answer B: Angiotensin I is converted to angiotensin II by angiotensin converting enzyme.
Answer D: Both angiotensin II and aldosterone act on the kidneys to decrease the urinary excretion of sodium and water. A decrease in blood pressure stimulates the release of renin into the serum from the renal tubules. Renin converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, which is then converted to angiotensin II by ACE. Angiotensin II causes an increase in blood pressure by direct vasoconstriction, enhancing the sympathetic nervous system, and causing an increase of aldosterone.  Brunton, LL. et. al. Goodman & Gilman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 12th edition, Chapter 26 American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Hypovolemia: Renin-angiotensin Response"

Stretching of aortic baroreceptors occurs due to increased blood pressure, causing a reflexive inhibition of vasoconstrictor centers in the medulla and vagal parasympathetic stimulation. This results in decreased vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate. Several mechanisms exist for regulating circulation peripherally via receptors and reflexes. The main receptor targets for regulation are the autonomic nervous system, which includes the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems. Sympathetic nerve fibers innervate both blood vessels and the heart with the overall function of increasing resistance via vasoconstriction and increasing cardiac activity, although sympathetic nervous system activation does have some vasodilatory function. Vasoconstriction is accomplished by activating alpha-1 receptors, while increased cardiac activity takes place by activating beta-1 receptors. Vasoconstriction takes place in both arteries and veins in order to increase peripheral resistance and transfer of blood from peripheral venous pools to heart. The parasympathetic system impacts circulation primarily via innervation to the heart, with activation of parasympathetic muscarinic receptors causing decreased heart rate and slightly decreased contractility. Reflexes within the circulatory system primarily utilize negative feedback mechanisms. The major circulatory reflexes are the baroreceptor reflexes. Baroreceptor reflexes utilize stretch receptors in large systemic arteries that are activated with increased arterial blood pressure, sending signals to the central nervous system which then provides feedback via the autonomic system to reduce blood pressure. The main baroreceptors are located in the aortic arch wall, as well as the carotid sinuses which are above the carotid bifurcation in the bilateral internal carotids. The aortic baroreceptors transmit efferent information via the vagus nerve to the tractus solitarius in the medulla, while the carotid sinus baroreceptors transmit information first via small Hering’s nerves and then the glossopharyngeal nerve to the tractus solitarius in the medulla. After arriving in the tractus solitarius, signals inhibit the vasoconstriction center in the medulla and stimulate the vagal parasympathetic center resulting in decreased peripheral resistance and decreased cardiac output, respectively. Normal reflex pathway function is a primary mechanism for maintaining stability in blood pressure during postural changes. For example, when transitioning from supine to standing there is a temporary decrease in perfusion to the carotid sinus baroreceptors, eliciting a rapid, reflexive compensation via sympathetic stimulation and parasympathetic inhibition that minimizes this decreased blood pressure to the carotids and brain. Animal models have demonstrated significant lability in blood pressure with routine daily activities in animals without baroreceptor function relative to those with preserved function. By nature, the baroreceptor reflex causes an oscillatory blood pressure cycle with high pressure causing reflexive decreases, and the reflexive decrease triggering a reflexive increase, and so on and so forth. The following are additional circulatory receptors and reflexes throughout the body. Abdominal compression reflex: Activation of baroreceptors causes increased sympathetic output, constricting abdominal muscle vascular pools, and increasing venous return to the heart. Atrial and pulmonary artery low-pressure receptors: Receptors that regulate reflexive blood pressure changes in response to blood volume changes. Atrial volume reflex: Increased atrial stretch causes dilation of afferent arterioles to the kidney, reduces antidiuretic hormone secretion from the hypothalamus, and releases an atrial natriuretic hormone, resulting in greater loss of fluid via the kidneys. Bainbridge reflex (atrial heart control reflex): Atrial stretch causes increased heart rate and contractility via sympathetic nervous system stimulation. Bezold-Jarisch reflex: Stimulation of chemoreceptors and mechanoreceptors in the left ventricle causes a parasympathetic response resulting in hypotension, bradycardia, and coronary artery dilation. Chemoreceptor reflex: Low blood pressure and other factors cause decreased partial oxygen pressure, increased hydrogen ion concentration, and increased carbon dioxide stimulating the carotid body and aortic body receptors. These receptors transmit signals to vasomotor centers via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves, which increase respiratory drive, increase parasympathetic activity, and increase sympathetic activity if hypoxia is prolonged. Central nervous system (CNS) ischemic response: Thought to be due to brain ischemia manifesting as increased carbon dioxide levels, which increases sympathetic output resulting in increased vasoconstrictor and cardiac accelerator function. Ischemia may occur secondary to increased intracranial pressure, with the subsequent sympathetic ischemic response activating arterial baroreceptors and causing a reflexive decrease in heart rate. This increased blood pressure with decreased heart rate in the setting of increased intracranial pressure is commonly referred to as Cushing's reflex. Oculocardiac reflex: Stretch receptors activated by ocular pressure or stretch to surround structures send afferent signals via the ciliary nerve, ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve, and then trigeminal nerve to the trigeminal ganglion. Increased parasympathetic tone results with efferent signals sent via the vagus nerve causing decreased heart rate. Decreased vasoconstriction and increased heart rate do not occur following baroreceptor stretch.
Answer C: Increased vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate can occur due to increased intracranial pressure, a response known as the Cushing reflex.
Answer D: Increased vasoconstriction and increased heart rate occur reflexively as a CNS ischemic response. This also may occur following low blood pressure that decreases baroreceptor firing. Increased blood pressure causes stretching of baroreceptors primarily located in the aortic arch and carotid sinus. This leads to reflexive inhibition of vasoconstrictor centers in the medulla and vagal parasympathetic stimulation, resulting in decreased sympathetic vasoconstriction and decreased heart rate, respectively. The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Cyanide primarily causes toxicity by impairing cellular aerobic respiration. The cyanide ion (CN-) binds to the ferric ion (Fe3+) in mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, inhibiting the final stage of the electron transport chain. Depletion of cellular ATP and the lactic acid produced by anaerobic metabolism can lead to profound acidosis. Symptoms of cyanide toxicity include altered mental status, weakness, headaches, loss of consciousness, seizures, respiratory failure, and cardiac arrest. Blood cyanide levels will be elevated, although therapy should not be delayed for the laboratory result. The patients blood sample may appear "cherry red" due to normal circulating levels of oxygen with impaired utilization. Circulating oxygen is not impaired and cyanosis is a late finding.
Answer B: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. Therefore, PaO2 will increase.
Answer C: Oxygen is present, but it is unable to be utilized. SvO2 will be increased. The most common and reliable sign of cyanide toxicity is an anion gap metabolic acidosis. Anion gap is calculated by subtracting serum chloride and bicarbonate (anions) from serum sodium and potassium (cations). Anion gap = ([Na+] +[K+]) – ([Cl−] + [HCO3−]). In clinical practice, potassium is usually excluded. Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 910, 1077. Miller Anesthesia, 8th edition, p. 2501. American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Cyanide Toxicity: Dx"

Myotonic dystrophy is characterized by gastric atony, not spasticity. Clinical manifestations of myotonic dystrophy are a result of delayed skeletal muscle relaxation after voluntary contraction. Two subtypes exist. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 is more common and can be congenital, child-onset, or most typically, autosomal dominant with adult-onset. Type 2 is rarer than type 1 and is typically associated with milder symptoms. Symptoms and associated findings of myotonic dystrophy include: - Muscle degeneration - Cataracts - Premature balding - Diabetes mellitus - Thyroid dysfunction - Adrenal insufficiency - Gonadal atrophy - Cardiac abnormalities (e.g., conduction dysfunction, cardiomyopathy, and mitral valve prolapse). Answers A & B & C: Respiratory muscle weakness can lead to a restrictive respiratory pattern and cause mild arterial hypoxemia, reduced ventilatory response to hypoxemia and hypercapnia, and an ineffective cough mechanism. Gastrointestinal muscle weakness can lead to gastric atony and delayed emptying, intestinal hypomotility (C), and pharyngeal muscle weakness. Each of these can contribute to an increased risk of pulmonary aspiration.  Patients with myotonic dystrophy have an increased risk of pulmonary aspiration due to gastric atony and delayed emptying, intestinal hypomotility, and pharyngeal muscle weakness.  Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, p. 624. Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 1605-1606.

Timely identification and treatment of symptomatic bradycardia can truly be life-saving. This patient is experiencing bradycardia with resultant systemic hypotension, altered mental status, and angina. According to the American Heart Association advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) guidelines, the first-line treatment for symptomatic bradyarrhythmia is atropine, 1 mg IV, repeated every 3-5 minutes to a maximum of 3 mg. If atropine is ineffective, the next step is to attempt transcutaneous pacing or administer dopamine or epinephrine by infusion. Illustration © TrueLearn, LLC Epinephrine is a second-line choice for bradycardia in adults. It is the first-line choice for children, however.
Answer C: Phenylephrine does not appear in the ACLS algorithms. If administered in this situation, it may result in reflex bradycardia, potentially further worsening perfusion.
Answer D: Transcutaneous pacing, while potentially helpful, is not the first-line treatment for bradycardia. It should be attempted only after failure of atropine to correct the bradyarrhythmia. Symptomatic bradyarrhythmias are life-threatening and require immediate treatment. The first-line therapy for symptomatic bradycardia is atropine. Atropine is indicated for symptomatic bradycardia regardless of the conduction cause. However, it may be ineffective for second-degree Type II and third-degree blocks. Early rapid filling contributes the largest volume of blood during diastole. Diastole is the period of cardiac cycle between the aortic valve and mitral valve closure. During this time, the left ventricle is filling with blood from the left atrium. At the end of diastole, the volume in the left ventricle is referred to as the end-diastolic volume (or preload). There are four phases during diastole: isovolumetric relaxation, early rapid filling, diastasis (slow filling), and late rapid filling (atrial contraction). Isovolumetric relaxation: this phase begins with the closure of the aortic valve and continues till the opening of the mitral valve. During this time, the left ventricle is relaxing, however there is no change in the ventricular volume (isovolumetric). Early rapid filling: this phase begins with the opening of the mitral valve. The left ventricle begins to fill with blood from the left atrium. The flow of blood is driven by the transmitral pressure gradient. This phase contributes the largest volume of blood to the left ventricle during diastole. Diastasis (slow filling): as the left ventricle fills, the pressure difference between the left ventricle and atrium decrease. This slows down the filling considerably, and contributes approximately 5% of the preload. This phase occurs mid-diastole. Late rapid filling (atrial contraction): the left atrium contracts, ejecting additional blood into the left ventricle. This phase can contribute 15-20% of the preload. Atrial contraction is the last phase of diastole. The mitral valve closes after the atrial contraction. Late rapid filling (atrial contraction) contributes about 15% of the end-diastolic volume. Early rapid filling is the largest contributor of preload.
Answer C: Left ventricular relaxation is a period during diastole where there is no change in the left ventricular volume (isovolumetric).
Answer D: Slow filling (diastasis) occurs as the left ventricle fills and the pressures between atrium and ventricle become equal. This contributes about 5% of the preload. Early rapid filling contributes the largest volume of blood during diastole. The phases of diastole are: isovolumetric relaxation, early rapid filling, diastasis, and atrial contraction. Atrial contraction normally contributes approximately 15% of the preload. In patients with poor left ventricular filling, as in diastolic dysfunction, the atrial contraction becomes very important. Oxygen diffusion is increased during exercise because of the recruitment of non-perfused capillary beds. Diffusion of a gas is a process by which the gas molecules move from an area of high partial pressure to an area of lower partial pressure. The movement of oxygen from the alveoli to the pulmonary capillary blood (and from the blood to the tissues) is passive. As oxygen moves from alveoli to the hemoglobin molecule, it must pass through: 1) the alveolar membrane (containing surfactant), 2) the capillary endothelium, 3) the plasma, 4) the red blood cell (RBC) membrane, and 5) the RBC intracellular fluid. Diffusion capacity of oxygen can be affected by changes to any of the factors mentioned above. The thickness of the alveolarcapillary membrane may affect the ability of oxygen to diffuse properly. During exercise, the total lung volume is increased, resulting in thinner, more distended alveoli. This increases the surface area of the lung allowing for greater oxygen diffusion. The tidal volume increases (up to 60%) with activity by encroaching into the inspiratory reserve volume. Therefore, during exercise, the inspiratory reserve is decreased. During exercise, increased pulmonary blood flow increases oxygen diffusion. The recruitment of capillary beds that were nonperfused at rest increases not only blood flow, but also the capillary cross-sectional area. Capillaries are recruited as groups, not individually. Areas with low capillary density are recruited first. This also improves the ventilation/perfusion ratio. RBC capillary transit time is the amount of time a single red blood cell spends in the capillary, where it is exposed to the alveolar gases. In other words, it is the amount of time a RBC has to pick up oxygen. At rest, the capillary transit time is approximately 0.8 seconds. Cardiac output is one of the factors that can change the capillary transit time. During exercise, the cardiac output increases causing a decrease in capillary transit time. There is no consensus on the impact of decreased transit time on oxygen diffusion during exercise. However, the minimum needed time for oxygen to diffuse into a RBC is 0.25 seconds. Capillary transit time decreases due to an increased cardiac output during exercise.
Answer B: Inspiratory reserve is decreased during exercise. Exercise increases oxygen diffusion by increasing lung surface area (thinner, more distended alveoli) and by increasing blood flow (capillary recruitment).  Lumb, Andrew. Gap junctions allow for quick propagation of the electrical signal in the cardiac myocyte. Underlying a functional and efficient cardiac cycle is the concept of impulse propagation. Impulse propagation describes the flow of the electrical current generated by shifting ion concentrations leading to coordinated depolarization and repolarization of the cardiac myocyte. Dysfunction within the system can lead to a myriad of arrhythmias from benign to fatal. Basic propagation of the initial depolarization begins from the sinoatrial (SA) SA node, travels to the right atrium via the Bachmann bundle to excite the left atrium. The impulse travels through pathways to the atrioventricular (AV) node, down the bundle of His, and finally terminates in the Purkinje fibers. The ion channel has two main properties, chemical and electrical, driving the various gradients to propagate the signal. In addition, the channels are selective for a single type of ion, are voltagegated, and are time-dependent. At the cellular level, the majority of propagation of the initial signal occurs from cell-to-cell interaction via gap junctions. The gap junction allows for quick depolarization of the next cell in an organized fashion without delay seen in other types of cells within the body. The rest of the propagation occurs through the aforementioned specialized conduction fibers (e.g., bundle of His, Purkinje fibers). Damage to the myocardium can damage these communication pathways, thus disrupting the propagation of a normal signal leading to potential risks of arrhythmias. Anchoring junctions function in the adhesion to each other as well as other components of the extracellular matrix. This provides tissues with structural cohesion. Examples of these junctions include desmosomes, hemidesmosomes, and adherens junctions.
Answer C: Tight junctions function in the formation of barriers that regulate the movement of water and solutes.
Answer D: Tricellular junctions (TCJ) seal epithelia at three corners of corresponding cells around it. They bond together cells in a lattice-like formation leading to increased structural stability. Gap junctions allow for quick propagation of the electrical signal in the cardiac myocyte. The major cation found in the ECF is sodium and the major cation found in the ICF is K+. Cell membrane proteins maintain this gradient by active transport. Action potentials and other intracellular processes function in relation to how this gradient is maintained. Electroneutrality must be maintained thus in the ECF compartment chloride ions balance the robust sodium concentration, and phosphate in addition to other organic ions balance the potassium inside the cell. Adult requirements for both sodium and potassium on a daily basis are approximately 75 mEq/kg and 40 mEq/kg, respectively. Fluids that most closely resemble that of plasma (Lactated Ringer, Normosol, Plasma-Lyte) tend to be the recommended resuscitation fluids for maintenance of appropriate electrolyte balances. Answers A & B: The major ECF cation is Na+, not K+. the major ECF anion is Cl-, not phosphate and organic ions. Sodium is the major extracellular cation while potassium is the major intracellular cation. Recall osmolality = ([Na+] * 2) + (Glucose/18) + (BUN/2.3) thus changes in either of these variable can lead to cellular shifts of water. This becomes particularly important with large sodium shifts or hyperglycemic states that can precipitate medical emergencies, such as seizures. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. The shunt fraction (Qs/Qt) can be calculated by using the venous admixture equation Qs/Qt = (CcO2 − CaO2) / (CcO2 − CvO2), where CcO2 is the oxygen content in pulmonary capillary blood, CaO2 is the oxygen content in arterial blood, and CvO2 is the oxygen content in mixed venous blood. The shunt fraction is the percentage of total cardiac output (Qt) that bypasses oxygenation from the lungs due to a right-to-left shunt. Even healthy patients have some component of right-to-left shunt due to the bronchial and thebesian circulation and atelectasis (intrapulmonary shunting). A normal shunt fraction is 2% to 3% but can be increased up to 10% in a healthy adult undergoing anesthesia primarily due to increased atelectasis and changes in ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) ratios. The term in the numerator (CcO2 − CaO2) represents the gap in oxygen content between pulmonary capillary blood and arterial blood, while the term in the denominator (CcO2 − CvO2) represents the maximal gap that could potentially occur if all of the mixed venous blood was shunted. The equation assumes that only 2 sources of blood mix together to result in the observed arterial blood, 1 source being mixed venous blood that has not been oxygenated at all (pure shunt) and fully oxygenated blood from the lungs. In reality, most of the difference between pulmonary capillary oxygenation and arterial oxygenation often comes from another source, namely alveoli with a low V/Q ratio. For example, a venous admixture of 5% could be explained by 10% to 15% of cardiac output perfusing poorly ventilated regions of the lungs. Venous admixture due to low V/Q will reverse by supplemental oxygen, but venous admixture due to pure shunt will not reverse by supplemental oxygen. Therefore, venous admixture, calculated by the Qs/Qt equation, represents all of the pure shunt plus some contribution from low V/Q alveoli. When venous admixture is due to perfusion of low V/Q alveoli, it will improve with supplemental oxygen, which is why many patients require some amount of supplemental oxygen to maintain high SpO2 after extubation. (21-20) / (21-15) = 1/6 ≈ 17%, not 5%. Five percent could be erroneously derived as the correct answer for this question by calculating (CaO2 − CvO2).
Answer C: (21-20) / (21-15) = 1/6 ≈ 17%, not 25%. Twenty-five percent could be erroneously calculated by taking (CaO2 − CvO2) / CaO2.
Answer D: (21-20) / (21-15) = 1/6 ≈ 17%, not 29%. Surgical stress leads to the increased secretion of glucose from counter-regulatory hormones and peripheral tissue resistance to insulin, resulting in hyperglycemia. Surgical stress and accidental injury lead to the increased secretion of the counter-regulatory hormones, including cortisol, catecholamines, and glucagon, resulting in an increased glucose production due to hepatic gluconeogenesis. The increase in glucose production, in conjunction with peripheral tissue resistance to insulin, leads to reduced glucose use and, subsequently, hyperglycemia. Serum insulin concentrations are inadequate to prevent hyperglycemia but do prevent ketosis from occurring. Hyperglycemia due to surgical stress ensures an adequate supply of glucose to glucose-consuming cells, including wound inflammatory and immune cells. Insulin resistance can persist for up to three weeks after elective cholecystectomy and for up to three years after major burn injuries. For patients in the intensive care unit, the severity of insulin resistance is associated with illness severity, body mass index, and degree of hypermetabolism. There is an increased secretion of catecholamines in response to surgical stress.
Answer B: Increased beta-2 adrenergic (not beta-1) stimulation leads to the acceleration of lipolysis through increased cyclic adenosine monophosphate concentrations, which stimulate the activity of hormone-sensitive lipase through protein kinase A. This accelerated lipolysis increases the supply of circulating free fatty acids.
Answer C: The increased secretion of counter-regulatory hormones, including glucagon, results in increased glucose production secondary to hepatic gluconeogenesis, not glycogenesis. Surgical stress leads to increased production of counter-regulatory hormones, including catecholamines, glucagon, and cortisol. This results in an increased production of glucose from hepatic gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance. A diastolic preponderance of coronary blood flow is normal in the left ventricle, not the right ventricle. This pattern suggests chronic pulmonary hypertension. Because of the different intraventricular pressures developing during systole, perfusion of the left ventricle - particularly the left ventricular subendocardium, takes place almost entirely during diastole. Whereas the right ventricle is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle. However, in cases of chronic pulmonary hypertension a "left ventricularization" of the right ventricle occurs, such that the right ventricle becomes hypertrophied, suffers a decrease in blood flow and blood flow reserve, and its perfusion becomes predominantly diastolic (which also means it will depend on aortic diastolic pressure to maintain coronary blood flow). Also similarly to the left ventricle, when the right ventricle becomes dilated oxygen demand increases. Recall that wall tension, one of the main determinants of oxygen demand, is proportional to the radius by the law of Laplace. The figure here shows a diagrammatic representation of normal blood flow in the left and right coronary arteries. For the purpose of simplicity, it is assumed that the patient has a left dominance, so that the right coronary artery represents purely right ventricular coronary blood flow pattern. Answers B & C & D: Under these conditions, the right ventricle is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle.  The normal right ventricle is perfused throughout the cardiac cycle. Flow to the left ventricle (and the right ventricle in cases of chronic pulmonary hypertension) is largely confined to diastole. For atrial flutter, 100 Joules of monophasic shock should be delivered. Time from cardiac arrest until the first shock administration affects survival significantly and defibrillation or cardioversion has an integral role in cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). For ventricular fibrillation (VF) and ventricular tachycardia (VT), directcurrent (DC) cardioversion is the therapy of choice. Most modern defibrillators are biphasic, with older models being monophasic and requiring a larger energy level. The energy level for defibrillation in adults is 200 Joules for biphasic shocks or 360 joules for monophasic shocks. After the first shock, if VF or VT does not terminate, the subsequent energy level should be kept the same or may be increased. Each shock should be inter-spaced with CPR for at least 2 minutes and successive shocks without CPR have not been shown to improve survival. In cases of atrial fibrillation, 100 to 200 Joules with monophasic shocks or 100 to 120 Joules of biphasic shocks should be administered for cardioversion. In cases of atrial flutter, 50 to 100 Joules of monophasic shocks should be administered. When possible, biphasic defibrillators should be used over monophasic defibrillators due to their better success rates at arrhythmia termination. Compared to manual defibrillators, automated external defibrillators analyze the rhythm transmitted by the pads placed on the chest and determine if defibrillation is indicated. Per the 2015 ACLS guidelines, it is acceptable to use the manufacturer's recommended dose for the first shock for ventricular fibrillation with a biphasic defibrillator. Note that for unwitnessed cardiac arrests, for arrests outside of the hospital or greater than 5 minutes since arrest, CPR should be initiated for up to 3 minutes prior to the first shock. Lastly, note that pulseless electrical activity (PEA) and asystole are nonshockable rhythms. Instead, epinephrine and uninterrupted CPR should be continued. For atrial fibrillation, 100 to 200 Joules with a monophasic waveform or 100 to 120 Joules with a biphasic waveform should be used. Answers C & D: Ventricular fibrillation and ventricular tachycardia should be treated with 200 Joules of biphasic waveform or 360 Joules of monophasic waveform. Monophasic defibrillators require more energy level than biphasic defibrillators. For biphasic shocks: • VF/VT: 200 J • Atrial fibrillation: 120 J For monophasic shocks: • VF/VT: 360 J • Atrial fibrillation: 200 J  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline 2014. Myocardial oxygen supply has several determinants. It is associated with oxygen content and blood flow. It is unaffected by left ventricular systolic pressure. First, the oxygen content is determined to evaluate oxygen availability or supply: CaO2 = (Hgb * 1.34 * SaO2) + (0.003 * PaO2) Where: CaO2 = arterial oxygen content (mL/dL), Hgb = hemoglobin (g/dL), SaO2 = oxygen saturation, PaO2 = arterial partial pressure of oxygen (mm Hg). Oxygen dissolved in arterial blood (0.003 x PaO2) raises the total value by only a small amount. If PaO2 is increased, there is little change in CaO2 and it is therefore considered of little significance by most when determining oxygen content. Optimizing Hgb amount is one way to ensure maximal oxygen content. Secondly, myocardial blood supply is determined by coronary blood flow (CBF), which has its own set of modifying components: 1) Heart rate: Left ventricular blood supply from the coronary arteries occurs primarily during diastole. A slower heart rate means more time is spent in diastole which allows more time for CBF to the left ventricle. 2) Coronary perfusion pressure: Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is represented as the difference between the aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) and the left ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP). CPP = AoDP - LVEDP 3) Coronary vascular resistance (CVR): Increased CVR such as from vasospasm or atherosclerosis worsens myocardial oxygen supply. Providing vasodilation with medications such as nitroglycerin improves CBF. Coronary blood flow is therefore represented by the following equation: CBF = CPP / CVR, or, CBF = (AoDP – LVEDP) / CVR. Myocardial oxygen extraction also plays a role in supply, but this value is usually at its maximum value and changes very little under times of stress. Left ventricular systolic pressure (LVSP) is more often associated with changing the myocardial oxygen demand (not supply) by changing afterload. An elevated LVSP will increase wall stress and require more myocardial oxygen. Coronary perfusion pressure (CPP) is represented as the difference between the aortic diastolic pressure (AoDP) and the left ventricular end diastolic pressure (LVEDP).
Answer B: Increased coronary vascular resistance such as from vasospasm or atherosclerosis worsens myocardial oxygen supply. Providing vasodilation with medications such as nitroglycerin improves CBF.
Answer C: Left ventricular blood supply from the coronary arteries occurs primarily during diastole. A slower heart rate means more time is spent in diastole which allows more time for CBF to the left ventricle.
Answer D: Optimizing Hgb amount is one way to ensure maximal oxygen content. Myocardial oxygen supply is affected by AoDP, LVEDP, heart rate, Hgb, and CVR. Left ventricular systolic pressure affects myocardial oxygen demand.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Myocardial Oxygen Supply and Demand" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 1074-1075.

Patients with acromegaly may present with peripheral neuropathy. The anterior pituitary is responsible for the production and release of six hormones, including growth hormone, thryoid stimulating hormone, adrenocorticotropic hormone, prolactin, and gonadotropins (follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormones). Overactivity of each of these hormones can cause systemic changes. Growth hormone is a peptide trophic hormone that promotes cellular hypertrophy, proliferation, and regeneration. Its excess causes acromegaly, which causes connective tissue, bone, and internal organ enlargement. Acromegaly results in enlargement of connective tissue, bone, and visceral organs. This can result in an increased risk of central or obstructive sleep apnea, difficult airways due to macroglossia and swollen epiglottides, hyperglycemia, hypertension, congestive heart failure, valvular disease, coronary artery disease, diabetes, hypothyroidism, and peripheral neuropathy. Hypertension is a more likely presentation due to extrinsic compression of vasculature from cellular hypertrophy.
Answer B: Skeletal, soft tissue, and connective tissue overgrowth results in macroglossia, prognathism, enlarged epiglottis, swollen vocal cords, and recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis.
Answer C: Hyperglycemia is a more likely presentation due to reduced hepatic uptake of glucose from excess growth hormone. Growth hormone is a peptide hormone made in the anterior pituitary that promotes anabolic functions for musculoskeletal and visceral organ development. Growth hormone excess results in acromegaly, which can cause significant airway and cardiovascular changes.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. “Endocrine Physiology: Pituitary” Miller Anesthesia, 8th edition. Pg 1130-1131.

The liver is one of the few organs in the body that receives a dual blood supply. It is supplied by both the hepatic artery and the portal vein. Typically, the hepatic artery supplies 25% of the hepatic blood flow while the portal vein supplies 75%. Blood flow in the liver is autonomically regulated and based on pre-portal organ venous return. This system is termed the hepatic arterial buffer response (HABR) which is responsible for maintaining constant hepatic blood flow. The system functions in a manner such that when portal venous blood flow decreases, the hepatic artery vasodilates to maintain perfusion. The main determinant controlling this hepatic blood flow is adenosine. It is produced in the space of Mall which surrounds the hepatic vasculature and diffuses into the portal vein. When the portal venous blood flow decreases, the adenosine accumulates resulting in vasodilation of the hepatic artery increasing blood flow to the liver by the hepatic artery. A reduction in blood flow in the portal vein will lead to an increase in liver adenosine.
Answer B: A reduction of blood flow in the portal vein will lead to an increase in blood flow in the hepatic artery.
Answer D: A reduction of blood flow in the portal vein will lead to local liver arteriole dilation. Decreased blood flow through the portal vein results in an increase of liver adenosine, local arteriole dilation, and increased hepatic artery blood flow. Pages 345-358.

Many respiratory changes occur in the obstetric patient due to both anatomic and hormonal alterations. As the pregnancy progresses, the diaphragm moves more cephalad which causes a decrease in the functional residual capacity. In order to compensate for this change, the thoracic rib cage increases in anteroposterior and transverse diameter which aids to cause only a slight decrease in the total lung capacity overall. The functional residual capacity decreases by about 20-30% as does the expiratory reserve volume and residual volume. In addition, there is an increase in the inspiratory reserve volume. Airway resistance remains unchanged as progesterone relaxes the bronchiolar smooth muscle which combats the increased airway resistance due to upper airway edema. These changes contribute to a rapid desaturation during apnea and necessitate prompt airway intervention to avoid complications. An increased inspiratory reserve volume is usually seen in the obstetric patient.
Answer B: Obstetric patients have an increased anteroposterior and transverse diameter of the thoracic rib cage to offset the decrease in the functional residual capacity seen from the cephalad movement of the diaphragm.
Answer C: Progesterone causes relaxation of the bronchiolar smooth muscle and mitigates the increase in airway resistance from upper airway edema. Respiratory changes in the parturient include a cephalad movement of the diaphragm with a concomitant increase in the anteroposterior and transverse diameter of the thoracic rib cage. There is a decrease in the functional residual capacity and its components as well as an increase in the inspiratory reserve volume. Airway resistance remains relatively unchanged.  Barash Anesthesia. Obstetrical Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Page1146. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Respiratory Anatomy"

Decreasing the tidal volume to 6 mL/kg (lung-protective strategy) could decrease the risk of renal injury related to positive pressure in the patient in this question by decreasing cytokine release. Multiple reports of studies have linked renal and lung injury together through multiple mechanisms. The ARDSnet trial provided evidence that lung-protective ventilation decreases the incidence of hemodynamic, coagulopathic, and renal complications with a lung-protective strategy. Unfortunately, renal effects secondary to mechanical ventilation are not as simplistic as alterations in cytokine release. Strategies employed to target specific renal consequences from positive pressure ventilation have not been proven effective. Renal effects from mechanical ventilation involve 3 broad categories: hemodynamic, neurohormonal, and biochemical. Induction of positive pressure ventilation affects hemodynamics by decreasing preload and increasing right ventricular afterload (both of which decrease cardiac output and renal blood flow) while promoting increased venous pressure, all of which have deleterious effects on the kidneys. Positive pressure ventilation also results in an increase in sympathetic nervous system output, which secondarily results in an increase in renin release through beta-1 receptor stimulation with resultant release of angiotensin-2 and aldosterone. This results in vasoconstriction with salt and water retention, which can decrease urine output. There is also an increase in the release of antidiuretic hormone (also seen with surgical stress), which increases free water reabsorption and decreases urine output; however, this is a minor component. Finally, there is a decrease in atrial natriuretic peptide, which decreases natriuresis and vasodilation. Biochemically, positive pressure ventilation induces cytokine release, which can cause endothelial activation, increase vascular permeability, and result in apoptosis of renal epithelial cells. The pattern of ventilation can have alterations in the amount of cytokine release and resultant renal injury as previously discussed regarding the ARDSnet trial. There is also evidence that positive pressure ventilation increases the release of nitric oxide and enhances nitric oxide synthase activity. The breakdown products of nitric oxide cause oxidative damage and increased vascular permeability and can result in cellular apoptosis. Sympathetic output is increased with positive pressure ventilation; however, this leads to decreased urine output.
Answer B: Antidiuretic hormone secretion would be decreased compared to a patient on positive pressure ventilation. Positive pressure ventilation exerts deleterious effects on renal function via alterations in hemodynamics, neurohormonal secretion, and biochemical mediator release.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Mechanical Ventilation: Renal Effects" Koyner JL, et al. Mechanical Ventilation and Lung-Kidney Interaction. Clin J Am Soc Nephrol. 2008 Mar;3(2):562-570.

Changes in plasma protein binding during pregnancy will require the dosing of phenytoin and other highly protein-bound medications to be modified. Because plasma albumin concentrations can decrease to around 70% of normal, the free concentration of drug that is available to bind will increase, resulting in less drug overall needed to achieve a desired therapeutic goal. The distribution of medications during pregnancy will change due to a variety of factors, including an increased cardiac output, and increased total body water, and a decrease in plasma protein binding. The increased cardiac output will result in more rapid delivery of medications to the peripheral circulation. Thus medications such as neuromuscular blocking drugs, that have a peripheral site of action, may have a more rapid onset in a pregnant patient though this effect is of uncertain clinical significance. The expansion of total body water by around 8 liters over the course of pregnancy, corresponding to around a 40% increase in circulating plasma volume. This volume expansion will cause an increase in the volume of distribution of certain hydrophilic medications. The decrease in plasma protein binding will tend to have the greatest effect on the pharmacokinetics of a pregnant woman when compared to these other changes in medication distribution. As mentioned above, plasma albumin levels will tend to decrease to around 70% of normal levels. This is combined with the fact that pregnant women have an increased concentration of free fatty acids and other endogenous substances that will tend to compete with protein-bound medications in binding to albumin, further decreasing their effective volume of distribution. The net effect of this is to lead to an increased concentration of circulating free drug and a decreased concentration of drug bound to protein following an equivalent dose of a protein-bound medication in a pregnant woman when compared to a similar non-pregnant patient. Chronic administration of a drug will tend to be partially compensated by increased compensatory clearance mechanisms, though the total dose that is necessary to achieve a therapeutic serum level will tend to decrease. Of note, it is because of this effect that it is important to recognize what is actually being measured when monitoring serum concentrations of protein-bound medications in pregnancy. If the free drug concentration is being measured, dose titrations are relatively easy. If, however, the total serum concentration is being measured, the dose calculation becomes slightly more complex and will likely need to account for serum albumin levels as well. The concentration of phenytoin that is bound to serum proteins will tend to decrease in pregnancy.
Answer B: In chronically administered drugs that are highly protein-bound, there will be a modest increase in plasma clearance to compensate for the increased free drug concentrations.
Answer D: Given the decreased effective volume of distribution due to decreased plasma protein-binding, the total drug needed to achieve a clinical effect will decrease. Plasma albumin concentrations will tend to decrease to around 70% of normal ranges during pregnancy. This will result in an increased concentration of free drug in the serum, as well as a decreased concentration of the drug that is bound to serum proteins. This results in less total drug that is needed to achieve a certain clinical effect.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Maternal Physiology: Protein Binding Of Drugs" Chestnut's Obstetric Anesthesia. Changes in Drug Disposition and Effect in 5th Edition. Pages 304 - 305.

Cytochrome p450 is a heme protein that utilizes molecular oxygen to oxidize organic compounds. Cytochrome p450 is not a single enzyme, but rather consists of a group of closely related proteins that are embedded in the endoplasmic reticulum. The structure of cytochrome p450 consists of iron (Fe), which serves as a binding site for oxygen molecules. Metabolism by cytochrome p450 has been extensively studied, and is involved in the oxidation of thousands of diverse drugs and chemicals. One atom of molecular oxygen is used to oxidize the drug, while the other atom is combined with hydrogen atoms from NADPH to form water. The liver is the principal site for drug metabolism. For many drugs, metabolism occurs in two phases. Phase I involves modifying the drug through oxidation, reduction, or hydrolysis. These reactions typically inactivate the drug. Phase II involves conjugation, where a molecule (glucuronic acid, sulfate) is added to the drug to make it more easily excreted from the kidneys and liver. Cytochrome p450 is the most important enzyme system in phase I and catalyzes the oxidation of many drugs. Conjugation is part of phase II metabolism, where molecules are added to the drug to make it more readily excreted. Cytochrome p450 is involved with phase I oxidation.
Answer B: Hydrolysis is part of phase I, but is not mediated by p450 group.
Answer D: Reduction is part of phase I metabolism. However, cytochrome p450 catalyzes oxidation in phase I. Cytochrome p450 is involved in phase I metabolism by oxidizing many drugs. Chronic barbiturate use increases cytochrome p450 activity. As a result, the metabolism of drugs by p450 is increased (as seen with benzodiazepines). Gibson G and Skett P. Myocardial oxygen consumption is determined by coronary blood flow and the difference between the arterial and venous concentrations of oxygen. Plainly stated, it is the flow of blood through the coronaries multiplied by the amount of oxygen extracted. Thus, to determine the myocardial oxygen consumption one needs to determine the CBF, arterial oxygen content, and venous oxygen content of coronary blood. The equation for determining myocardial oxygen consumption is as follows: MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), where MVO2 equals myocardial oxygen consumption, CBF equals coronary blood flow, AO2 equals arterial oxygen contents and VO2 equals venous oxygen contents. In this question, the term (AO2 – VO2) is solved for, yielding a gradient of 0.2 mL O2/mL blood. Using the equation for myocardial oxygen consumption, which is MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), yields a gradient of 0.2 mL O2/mL of blood when MVO2 = 2 mL O2/minute per 100 g and CBF = 10 mL/min per 100 g. Answers B & C: Using the equation for myocardial oxygen consumption, which is MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), yields a gradient of 0.2 mL O2/mL of blood when MVO2 = 2 mL O2/minute per 100 g and CBF = 10 mL/min per 100 g The equation for determining myocardial oxygen consumption is MVO2 = CBF * (AO2 – VO2), where MVO2 equals myocardial oxygen consumption, CBF equals coronary blood flow, AO2 equals arterial oxygen content and VO2 equals venous oxygen content. Acetylcholine (ACh) is synthesized in the presynaptic terminal by acetylation of choline with acetyl-CoA via choline acetyltransferase in the cytoplasm. Large amounts of ACh molecules are then stored together within vesicles near the cell membrane. After propagation of an action potential (via sodium channels), there is activation of voltage-gated calcium channels at the nerve terminal and calcium influx leading to "docking" of the ACh vesicles to SNARE proteins. The two fuse and ACh is released via exocytosis. A portion of the ACh molecules activate the nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, although a large amount of ACh is rapidly metabolized by acetylcholinesterase to form acetate and choline. Choline is recycled back into the nerve terminal. Acetylcholine is rapidly broken down by acetylcholinesterase in the synapse into acetate and choline. Choline is recycled back into the presynaptic neuron. Unlike norepinephrine, there is no reuptake of acetylcholine and it must be synthesized constantly.
Answer C: Butyrylcholinesterase, also known as pseudocholinesterase or plasma cholinesterase, is not found significant amounts in neurons or in the neuromuscular junction. As the name implies, this enzyme is primarily found in the plasma. It is responsible for the metabolism of a variety of compounds, including succinylcholine, mivacurium, and ester local anesthetics.
Answer D: Calcium influx is required for acetylcholine release via SNARE protein-mediated exocytosis into the synaptic cleft. Acetylcholine is synthesized in a variety of neuron terminals via choline acetyltransferase. The acetylcholine molecules are stored in vesicles which are released after propagation of an action potential leads to calcium influx. Specialized docking proteins (SNARE) are required for exocytosis.  ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. "Neuromuscular Physiology: Acetylcholine Synthesis and Release" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 368-370, 526-527.

Succinylcholine dosage will likely need to be increased (1.5-2 mg/kg) for proper intubating conditions secondary to a decreased number of functional acetylcholine receptors. Myasthenia gravis patients have autoantibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors and will likely require increased succinylcholine dosage for intubating conditions. Lambert-Eaton (myasthenic syndrome) patients have IgG antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels and typically require decreased succinylcholine dosage. Both patients would require decreased dosages of nondepolarizing neuromuscular blockers. This disease is not to be confused with Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, which is characterized by IgG antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. In Lambert-Eaton syndrome, succinylcholine dosage would likely need to be decreased, as these patients are very sensitive to depolarizing and non-depolarizing muscle relaxants.
Answer B: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder in which autoantibodies exist against the alpha-subunit of the muscletype nicotinic postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors, that causes neuromuscular transmission failure with associated muscle weakness and fatigue.
Answer C: Non-depolarizing muscle relaxant doses should be decreased. Succinylcholine dosage for intubation will likely need to be increased in myasthenia gravis patients.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "Myasthenia Gravis" Miller, Miller’s Anesthesia, 7th edition, pp. 1180-81, 2916.

Neonates have a high percentage of fetal hemoglobin. Normal hemoglobin levels range from 15-18 g/dL at birth. Fetal hemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen which in turn causes a left shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve. A left shift decreases the release of oxygen to the tissues. Neonates have hemoglobin levels of 15-18 g/dL, higher levels compared to children.
Answer C: The hemoglobin is primarily fetal hemoglobin in the newborn.
Answer D: Fetal hemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen with less oxygen released to the tissues. Neonates have a high percentage of fetal hemoglobin which has a higher affinity for oxygen and causes a left shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve. This shift decreases oxygen delivery to tissues. The normal hemoglobin range is 15-18 g/dL at birth.  Barash Anesthesia. Neonatal Anesthesia in Seventh Edition. Page 1192. ABA Anesthesiology Content Outline, 2014. Acetazolamide, not spironolactone, is effective for prophylaxis against symptoms of acute mountain sickness (AMS). Upon ascent to a high altitude, PaO2 and PaCO2 will significantly drop due to decreased atmospheric pressure and the resultant changes in respiratory drive. For example, at approximately 4500 meters, a PaO2 of 35-40 mm Hg and PaCO2 of 30-32 mm Hg could be expected. The initial hypoxia will trigger peripheral chemoreceptors to promote ventilation (and much more slowly, hematocrit will increase to improve oxygen delivery). However, this leads to a respiratory alkalosis due to increased minute ventilation. An adaptive mechanism to offset this alkalosis is the gradual reduction in plasma bicarbonate (primarily from increased secretion) which is preceded by a decrease in CSF bicarbonate. After 2-3 days of disequilibrium, the stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors by hypoxia goes unopposed once enough bicarbonate ions have passed into the blood stream from CSF and the pH of the CSF is restored to sea level values. Acute mountain sickness or high altitude sickness is a result of continuous exposure to hypoxia. The most common symptoms include headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, ataxia, peripheral edema, and dyspnea. Prophylaxis is recommended prior to any ascent to greater than 3000 meters above sea level. Prophylaxis may include a “staged ascent” in which several days are spent at increasing heights until the goal is reached. Also, the avoidance of any respiratory depressants is recommended so hypoxic pulmonary drive is not blunted. Acetazolamide (a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor) is a recommended pharmacologic AMS prophylactic measure as it augments the hypoxic ventilatory response promoting urinary bicarbonate loss. Treatment of AMS and its symptoms is primarily by altitude descent but can also include supplemental oxygen administration, dexamethasone administration (though symptoms often return once discontinued), and acetazolamide (especially for AMS-related insomnia). Decreased CSF bicarbonate is an adaptive mechanism that helps restore CSF pH to normal values in the setting of a respiratory alkalosis caused by high altitude.
Answer B: High altitude cerebral edema (HACE) may be caused by a significant increase in cerebral blood flow leading to hyperemia in the setting of hypoxia. It usually presents in the setting of preexisting AMS or HAPE and is usually recognized due to altered consciousness and/or ataxia. Treatment should be immediate descent and high FiO2. A hyperbaric bag can be placed around the entire body. This pressurized system increases barometric pressure and is useful in the treatment of all forms of AMS if descent is not immediately possible.
Answer C: High altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) is thought to be caused by increased pressure in the pulmonary vasculature. The increased pulmonary capillary permeability in patients with preexisting pulmonary hypertension may worsen their predisposition to developing HAPE. This is due to the further increase in pulmonary vascular resistance from hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV). Nifedipine and inhaled β2-agonists are used as prophylaxis and treatment to reduce HPV (most vasodilators impair HPV). Treatment strategy includes supplemental oxygen with gradual descent to lower altitudes.
Answer D: Acetazolamide, not spironolactone, is the diuretic recommended for AMS prophylaxis. Ascent to high altitudes leads to hypoxia and a resultant respiratory alkalosis. However, the body is able to acutely adapt over 2-3 days and reequilibrates PaO2, PaCO2, arterial pH, and CSF pH primarily by changes in ventilatory drive and increased bicarbonate excretion. However, a person may experience AMS, HAPE, and/or HACE prior to achieving an equilibrium driven by hypoxic ventilatory drive. AMS presents with non-specific symptoms including headache, nausea, vomiting, insomnia, and malaise. Prophylaxis can be accomplished with staged ascent and acetazolamide. Treatment includes descent, supplemental oxygen, and dexamethasone. More severe manifestations include HAPE and HACE, both of which should be treated with descent and supplemental oxygen. Forced-air warming is the most effective method to reduce heat loss during anesthesia. Hypothermia increases the risk of postoperative infection, myocardial infarction, arrhythmia, bleeding, and poor wound healing. The duration of stay in the postanesthesia care unit (PACU) is increased on average by 40 to 90 minutes for hypothermic patients. Prevention of hypothermia is vital to minimize these risks. Identifying hypothermia is the first step to preventing and treating hypothermia. The American Society of Anesthesiologists guidelines require temperature monitoring of patients whenever “significant changes in body temperature are intended, anticipated, or suspected.” This includes most cases. The core temperature may be measured in four locations: pulmonary artery, nasopharynx, distal esophagus, and tympanic membrane. Bladder and rectal temperatures are not technically core temperature measurements but are appropriate in most cases. In the first hour of anesthesia, redistribution of cool blood from the skin to the core is responsible for the initial drop in core temperature. Prewarming the skin with warmed blankets or, more effectively, a forced-air warmer can prevent this initial drop in temperature. Warming the ambient temperature is the most important factor in reducing heat loss after the initial redistributive heat loss in the operating room. Heat loss from the skin is proportional to exposed skin, so covering as much exposed skin as possible helps to prevent heat loss. A heat and moisture exchanger can be used to minimize evaporative losses from ventilation. The most effective way of rewarming a patient, whether inside or outside the operating room, is a forced-air warmer. The warming of hypothermic patients should continue in the PACU. While forced-air warmers are the most effective method, warm blankets may be used for patients with mild hypothermia. Before discharge from the PACU, patient temperatures should be warmer than 36°C, and they should feel comfortably warm. Although they are commonly used in pediatric anesthesia, heat-moisture exchangers have little effect on the temperature of adult patients, whereas a forced-air warmer can significantly improve a patient's intraoperative temperature.
Answer C: Warm blankets are useful to cover areas of the patient, thus preventing exposed skin, but they lose warmth as the operation continues and can not actively warm the patient.
Answer D: Using cooled or room-temperature fluids for resuscitation may cause temperature loss, but using warmed fluids can only prevent a drop in temperature. This method is not as effective as forced-air warming for warming a patient. Forced-air warmers are the most effective way to raise a patient's temperature in the preoperative, intraoperative, or postoperative setting.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Anesthesiology. 2000 Feb;92(2):578-96.

The minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of inhaled anesthetics is increased by use of monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOI). Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia. Other factors include increasing age (especially > 40), hypoxia, hypothermia, induced hypotension, anemia, and certain drugs including α-2 agonists, lithium, large doses of cholinesterase inhibitors, lidocaine, opioids, barbiturates, and calcium channel blockers. By contrast, there are fewer factors that increase MAC. These include hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g., as caused by MAOIs, acute amphetamine use, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa). In general, those factors that decrease central nervous system (CNS) metabolic activity, neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and down-regulate CNS responses to chronically elevated neurotransmitter levels decrease MAC. Those factors that increase CNS metabolic activity and neurotransmission, CNS neurotransmitter levels, and up-regulate CNS responses to chronically depressed neurotransmitter levels increase MAC. Answers A & B & D & E: Many factors decrease the MAC of anesthetic agents including acute ethanol ingestion, pregnancy, metabolic acidosis, and hyponatremia.  Hyperthermia, hypernatremia, chronic ethanol abuse, and increased central neurotransmitter levels (e.g. MAOIs, amphetamine, cocaine, ephedrine, and levodopa use) increase MAC requirements for anesthetic agents.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. "MAC / Factors That Increase, Decrease" Barash, Clinical Anesthesia, 6th edition, pp. 424-425.

The density spectral array will reveal high power in the slow-delta (0-4 Hz) and alpha (8-12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range with a propofol infusion at surgical levels of general anesthesia. The unprocessed electroencephalogram (EEG) result is the graphical representation of oscillatory local field potentials, measured at the scalp. The geometric organization of pyramidal neurons in the cortex facilitates the generation of large extracellular currents and local field potentials, easily recorded through the skull and scalp. Subcortical regions generate smaller field potentials, at varying geometric orientation and at a greater distance from the scalp, that make it difficult to record and characterize their activity on EEG. However, cortical and subcortical structures are richly interconnected, and subcortical structures influence the activity of cortical regions so that the EEG pattern recorded at the scalp reflects the states of both cortical and subcortical structures. Different anesthetic agents act at specific molecular targets and through distinct neural circuits producing characteristic changes in cortical and subcortical activity. These anesthetic-induced changes in brain electrophysiology, observed in the form of unprocessed EEG recordings, are reflective of the depth of anesthesia achieved by particular agents. The density spectral array is the two-dimensional representation of the decomposition of the raw EEG signal into the power content for each given frequency component. Propofol acts through postsynaptic γ-aminobutyric acid A (GABAA) receptors, increasing the chloride conductance and hyperpolarizing the postsynaptic membrane. Propofol enhances GABAergic inhibition of cortical pyramidal neurons by cortical inhibitory interneurons; it also enhances GABAergic inhibition from hypothalamic preoptic area projections to brainstem arousal centers and reduces thalamocortical excitatory input through augmentation of GABAergic inhibition at the thalamic reticular nucleus. Hyperpolarization of cortical pyramidal neurons and reduction of the subcortical excitatory input explain the slow and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) seen on EEG. At low infusion rates of propofol and mild to moderate levels of sedation, the EEG tracing is dominated by organized, regular beta-gamma oscillations (25-35 Hz) with a larger amplitude than gamma oscillations in the awake EEG and greater frontal coherence. Bolus administration of propofol for induction of general anesthesia results in predictable changes in the EEG tracing, with a transition from the awake pattern of low amplitude beta-gamma oscillations to high amplitude slow-delta and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) that correlates with loss of consciousness, apnea, and atonia. Repeated propofol boluses can convert the pattern of slow oscillations into burst suppression. Elderly (> 65 years) patients can enter burst suppression with standard induction doses of propofol. After the induction dose of propofol, the EEG transitions into a combination of slow-delta and alpha oscillations (0-4 Hz and 8-12 Hz, respectively) that correlates with a surgical plane of general anesthesia. The density spectral array makes this signature signal easy to recognize as a high power in the slow-delta (0-4 Hz) and alpha (8-12 Hz) range and lower power in beta and gamma range. Propofol infusions at an adequate rate for maintenance of general anesthesia preserve the characteristic EEG tracing with combined slow-delta and alpha oscillations. Isoflurane and the other volatile anesthetics achieve their physiological and clinical effects through mechanisms that are not fully understood. Multiple potential target sites have been identified through the brain and spinal cord. Volatile agents enhance GABAergic inhibition at cortical and subcortical levels, block two-pore potassium channels and hyperpolarization-activated cyclic nucleotide-gated channels, and act as antagonists at N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors. Isoflurane at sub–minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) produces EEG tracings that resemble those of propofol, with slow-delta and alpha oscillations, providing evidence that enhanced GABAergic inhibition may be its dominant mechanism of action. At MAC of isoflurane and above, a large amplitude theta oscillation appears (5-8 Hz), which may reflect its non-GABAergic mechanisms. The density spectral array pattern of evenly distributed power, from the slow through the theta and into the alpha range, is unique to volatile agents at or above MAC. Higher concentrations of isoflurane starting at 1.5 MAC achieve burst suppression on EEG. Burst suppression is an EEG pattern characterized by periods of isoelectric quiescence interspersed with periods of high-voltage activity with preserved spectral content within burst periods. Burst suppression correlates with a state of maximal reduction in neural activity and cerebral metabolic rate of oxygen. Isoflurane at sub-MAC produces EEG tracings that resemble those of propofol, with slow-delta and alpha oscillations. At MAC of isoflurane and above, a large amplitude theta oscillation appears (5-8 Hz). The density spectral array pattern of evenly distributed power from the slow, through the theta and into the alpha range, is unique to volatile agents at or above MAC.
Answer B: Higher concentrations of isoflurane, starting at 1.5 MAC, achieve burst suppression on EEG.
Answer C: Bolus administration of propofol for induction of general anesthesia results in predictable changes in the EEG tracing, with a transition from the awake pattern of low amplitude beta-gamma oscillations to high amplitude slow-delta and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) that correlates with loss of consciousness, apnea, and atonia. Different anesthetic agents act at specific molecular targets and through distinct neural circuits producing characteristic changes in cortical and subcortical activity. These anesthetic-induced changes in brain electrophysiology, observed in the form of unprocessed electroencephalogram (EEG) recordings, provide evidence of the depth of anesthesia achieved by particular agents. Bolus administration of propofol for induction of general anesthesia results in predictable changes in the EEG tracing, with a transition from the awake pattern of low-amplitude beta-gamma oscillations to high-amplitude slowdelta and delta oscillations (0-4 Hz) that correlates with loss of consciousness, apnea, and atonia. After the induction dose of propofol, the EEG reading transitions into a combination of slow-delta and alpha oscillations (0-4 Hz and 8-12 Hz, respectively) that correlates with a surgical plane of general anesthesia. Propofol infusions at an adequate rate for maintenance of general anesthesia preserve the characteristic EEG tracing with combined slow-delta and alpha oscillations. The main feature of insulin deficiency is the disruption in protein balance, which can lead to emaciation and wasting. Muscle protein degradation (proteolysis) is increased as amino acids are delivered to the liver and kidney to be used as substrates for gluconeogenesis. During the first 24 to 48 hours after cessation of nutrient intake, glycogenolysis occurs to provide glucose to the tissues. Glycogenolysis is stimulated by insulin deficiency and an increase in glucagon. This increased glucagon to insulin ratio also promotes gluconeogenesis (endogenous glucose production). Hypoglycemia is further prevented by increased catecholamine release secondary to beta-adrenergic stimulation, which accelerates lipolysis. Lipolysis leads to the breakdown of stored triglycerides in adipose tissue into glycerol and free fatty acids (FFA). In the setting of insulin deficiency and the lack of glycogenolysis, FFAs undergo hepatic conversion to ketone bodies (eg, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate), which are used as energy stores. The glycerol released during lipolysis and lactate produced by glycolysis are two substrates used for gluconeogenesis. As starvation continues, skeletal and smooth muscles undergo proteolysis into amino acids. Alanine and glutamine are among the amino acids transported to the liver, but some amino acids are transported to the kidney as substrates for gluconeogenesis. The brain adapts to low glucose availability by using ketone bodies for energy. Simultaneously, adenosine triphosphate is produced via the oxidation of FFAs released by lipolysis. In prolonged fasting and insulin deficiency, lipolysis is stimulated by catecholamine release via beta-adrenergic stimulation. Lipolysis leads to the breakdown of stored triglycerides into glycerol and free fatty acids.
Answer B: Glycogenolysis, not glycogenesis, occurs in the setting of insulin deficiency. As glycogenolysis decreases due to depleted glycogen stores, free fatty acids undergo hepatic conversion to ketone bodies used by the brain for energy.
Answer D: The brain does not use amino acids for energy. Rather, ketone bodies are formed by the conversion of free fatty acids by the liver, which are then used by the brain for energy in the setting of fasting and prolonged starvation. In the setting of insulin deficiency, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis are stimulated by an increase in the glucagon to insulin ratio. Hypoglycemia is further prevented in the setting of fasting by an increase in lipolysis via beta-adrenergic stimulation. The acceleration in lipolysis leads to the release of glycerol and free fatty acids from the breakdown of stored triglycerides in adipose tissue. Proteolysis is increased in prolonged starvation as amino acids are transported to the liver and kidney to be used as substrates for gluconeogenesis. Blood pressure *For Hypertensive Emergency, there also needs to be evidence of new or worsening target organ damage. Blood ejected from the left ventricle into the aorta leads to a peak pressure, termed the systolic pressure. When pressure falls within the aorta, this nadir is the diastolic pressure. The difference in these two pressures is what is known as the pulse pressure. As the pulse pressure moves distal to the heart, the systolic pressure rises while the diastolic pressure falls, thus creating a larger pulse pressure. Physiologically speaking, mean arterial pressure is determined by the cardiac output (CO), systemic vascular resistance (SVR), and central venous pressure (CVP). The mathematical relationship between these factors is as follows: MAP = (CO * SVR) + CVP. The AHA also defines severe hypotension as SBP < 70 mmHg and suggests using medications such as norepinephrine, particularly for low total peripheral resistance. The AHA does not provide MAP criteria for hypertension.
Answer B: Hypertension is defined as BP > 130/80 mmHg, or 140/90 mmHg by some sources (e.g. JNC).
Answer C: The AHA defines hypotension as MAP < 65 mmHg, which is also the cutoff value used by the Surviving Sepsis Campaign. Hypotension is commonly defined at SBP < 90 mmHg or MAP < 65 mmHg. Hypertension is defined as BP > 130/ 80 mmHg, with severe hypertension (hypertensive emergency) defined as BP > 180/110 mmHg. Laryngospasm in otherwise healthy, young individuals is the most common cause of negative pressure pulmonary edema (NPPE). On a chest radiograph, NPPE would present as bilateral fluffy infiltrates. Negative pressure pulmonary edema occurs as a result of exaggerated negative intrathoracic pressure. Negative intrathoracic pressure increases right ventricular return, increasing the hydrostatic pressure gradient in the pulmonary vasculature while simultaneously increasing left ventricular afterload, further worsening pulmonary pressures. As a result, fluid moves from the pulmonary capillaries across the vascular bed and into the pulmonary interstitium and alveoli. Negative pressure pulmonary edema can be caused by any cause of upper airway obstruction (eg, biting on an endotracheal tube, laryngospasm, etc) but is most common in patients who are young and/or muscular because these patients can generate a stronger negative inspiratory force. Negative pressure pulmonary edema typically presents as dyspnea with pink-frothy sputum and bilateral fluffy infiltrates on chest images. Treatment consists of breaking the obstruction (ie, treatment of laryngospasm) and applying positive pressure ventilation (PPV) with supportive therapy. For some patients, NPPE will resolve within hours, but other patients require 12 to 48 hours of treatment and may require administration of furosemide. Chest radiograph of bilateral pulmonary infiltrates illustrating typical radiographic findings from NPPE. Pneumothorax is not associated with laryngospasm or NPPE.
Answer C: Pleural effusions are not a typical finding of NPPE.
Answer D: Right lower lobar infiltrates would be more consistent with lobar pneumonia, which is not part of NPPE. Laryngospasm is the most common cause of negative pressure pulmonary edema, which is most common in patients who are young, healthy, and strong because these patients can generate the greatest negative inspiratory force. Negative pressure pulmonary edema occurs due to negative inspiratory pressure generated by inspiratory effort against an upper airway obstruction, which increases right ventricular return and left ventricular afterload, causing hydrostatic pressure in the pulmonary vasculature to increase and drive fluid from the pulmonary capillaries into the alveoli and interstitium. Negative pressure pulmonary edema presents with dyspnea, pink and frothy sputum, and bilateral fluffy infiltrates on a chest radiograph. Treatment is supportive with positive pressure ventilation, after which many patients recover quickly. Other patients may require furosemide administration.  American Board of Anesthesiology Keyword. Inhalational induction is delayed in the setting of a right-to-left intracardiac shunt. The rate of inhalational anesthetic induction is determined by minute ventilation, functional residual capacity, blood/gas solubility, cardiac output, cerebral blood flow, and the presence of intracardiac shunts. A right-to-left intracardiac shunt delays inhalational induction since the volatile anesthetic-rich blood returning to the left heart is diluted by volatile anesthetic-poor systemic venous blood from the right heart. In addition, the uptake of inhaled anesthetics is prolonged with a right-to-left shunt due to a decrease in pulmonary blood flow. The chart below shows a summary of the various shunts and how anesthetic agents are affected. The rate of inhalational induction is virtually unchanged in the setting of left-to-right intracardiac shunting.
Answer C: The rate of intravenous induction in the setting of left-to-right shunt is decreased minimally, or not changed at all, due to increased recirculation of drugs into the pulmonary circulation.
Answer D: Intravenous induction is accelerated in the setting of right-to-left intracardiac shunting due to a partial bypass of the pulmonary circulation.
